title: What Happens If You Don't Keep Your Disclosure Current
bodyText: You must give the tenant the manager and owner information in writing at or before the start of the tenancy (§76-1417(1)). The lease clause does that only if the lease is signed before the tenancy begins; if the tenant moves in first, give it in a separate writing beforehand. If you don't, whoever failed to disclose becomes the agent of each landlord for service of legal process and for receiving notices and demands (§76-1417(3)(a)). That person also becomes the agent for performing the landlord's obligations under the Act and the Lease, and for spending all rent collected from the property on them (§76-1417(3)(b)) — not a result most landlords want. You must also keep the information current (§76-1417(2)). Update the Landlord and Manager Disclosure clause promptly whenever this information changes.

title: Lease Provisions That Are Void Under Nebraska Law
bodyText: Nebraska law voids four categories of lease provision outright (§76-1415): a clause where the tenant waives rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; a confession-of-judgment clause; any provision requiring either party to pay the other's attorney's fees; and a clause exculpating or limiting the landlord's liability for the landlord's own active, actionable negligence (narrower than Kansas's broader exculpation ban — Nebraska's trigger is negligence-specific, not any liability limitation). A prohibited provision is simply unenforceable; the tenant can recover actual damages and attorney fees only if you deliberately used a provision you knew was prohibited. Other Nebraska statutes add to the list. A lease may not require the tenant to accept delivery of notices by electronic means (§76-1413(9)). The domestic-violence lock-change rules apply 'notwithstanding any provision in the rental agreement to the contrary' (§76-1431.04(2)(b)). Any waiver of the data-breach act is 'void and unenforceable' (§87-805), and so is any term that 'waives or limits in any way' a consumer right under the Data Privacy Act, where that act applies to you (§87-1110). And a lease the tenant was induced to sign by a deceptive trade practice is unenforceable by you (§87-303.07). Every future Nebraska clause needs to be checked against this list, the same way every Kansas clause is checked against "Lease Provisions That Are Void Under Kansas Law". Two practical points. The attorney-fee ban runs BOTH WAYS - §76-1415(1)(c) voids a provision that the tenant 'Agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees', so a mutual or reciprocal fee clause is prohibited here too, not just a one-way one. And a savings sentence does not rescue a banned term: adding 'nothing in this Lease limits any right you have under applicable law' leaves the prohibited provision in the agreement, which is what §76-1415(2) measures. Take the term out instead.

title: Statutory Attorney-Fee Awards Are Different From a Lease Clause
bodyText: Nebraska bans any lease clause that promises attorney fees to either party (§76-1415(1)(c)) - don't draft one. Separately, several sections of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act award attorney fees directly by statute when a party proves specific violations. Two run in the tenant's favour: a landlord's noncompliance with the security-deposit return requirements at §76-1416, where Nebraska courts have held a prevailing tenant's fee award is mandatory rather than discretionary once noncompliance is proven; and a tenant's willful noncompliance with the lease runs the other way. TWO RUN IN YOURS, and landlords routinely miss both. In an action for possession for nonpayment, or an action for rent where the tenant is still in possession, if the tenant's defense or counterclaim is without merit AND is not raised in good faith, you may recover reasonable attorney's fees (§76-1428(1)). And on a holdover, §76-1437(3) awards you reasonable attorney's fees on top of its damages figure. One more fee route sits outside the Act and is easy to miss. On a lawsuit of four thousand dollars or less, a plaintiff who wins a judgment and has an attorney may recover costs, interest at six percent a year starting thirty days after each claim accrued, and an attorney's fee of at least ten dollars on a judgment of fifty dollars or less, or ten dollars plus ten percent of the amount over fifty dollars on a larger one (§25-1801). It is available only if the claim was still unpaid ninety days after it accrued, it does not apply to a personal-injury claim, and it works for a tenant suing you as well as for you. All of these are statutory remedies the court applies regardless of what the lease says, not something the lease creates, so none of them conflicts with the attorney-fee-clause ban.

title: Security Deposit Amount Limits
bodyText:
Nebraska caps security, however it is labeled, at one month's periodic rent, plus an optional pet deposit of up to one-quarter of one month's periodic rent when appropriate (§76-1416(1)) — simpler than Kansas's stacked structure and lower than Colorado's 2-month cap. Money you hold as security counts toward the cap whatever you call it, so a 'cleaning deposit' or 'key deposit' held as security is still security.

The statute names prepaid rent separately from security: at the end of the tenancy both may be applied to unpaid rent and damages, and the balance and a written itemization go to the tenant within fourteen days (§76-1416(2)). Whether money collected as 'last month's rent' is prepaid rent or security by another name is not settled by the text, so the cautious course is to keep the deposit plus any prepaid last month's rent within one month's rent.

This cap doesn't apply to properties operated by a housing agency under the Nebraska Housing Agency Act. This is a ceiling, not something the lease needs to recite; enter your actual amount in the Security Deposit clause.

title: Penalty for Mishandling a Security Deposit
bodyText: If you don't comply with Nebraska's 14-day return and itemization requirement (§76-1416(2)), the tenant can recover the property and money due, court costs, and reasonable attorney fees (§76-1416(3)) — and Nebraska courts treat this fee award as mandatory once noncompliance is shown, not left to the court's discretion. If your noncompliance is willful and not in good faith, the tenant can also recover liquidated damages equal to one month's rent or twice the deposit amount, whichever is less.

title: What Nebraska's Entry Notice Must Include
bodyText:
Nebraska's 24-hour written entry notice requirement (§76-1423(3)) — which this library's Nebraska entry clause states in full — must include the intended purpose for entry and a reasonable window during which you anticipate entering, and must be provided to each individual unit. You don't have to give that notice in an emergency or where giving it is impracticable (§76-1423(3)), and in an emergency you may enter without the tenant's consent (§76-1423(2)).

Repeated lawful-but-harassing entry demands, and entry in an unreasonable manner, are both independently prohibited even when notice is technically given. Beyond consent, emergencies and noticed entry, you have no other right to enter: §76-1423(4) allows it only by court order, during a tenant's absence of more than seven days as §76-1432(2) allows, or after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the property.

title: Notice Periods for Tenant Noncompliance
bodyText:
For a material lease violation or a health/safety-related violation (§76-1421), give written notice describing the breach and stating the lease will terminate at least 30 days after receipt if not remedied within 14 days. If the tenant cures in good faith within that window, the lease continues — but if the same or a similar breach recurs within 6 months, you can terminate on 14 days' notice without offering another chance to cure (§76-1431(1)).

For nonpayment of rent, give written notice of the unpaid rent and your intent to terminate; the tenant then has 7 calendar days from that notice to pay before you can terminate (§76-1431(2)) — a longer window than Kansas's 3-day pay-or-quit period.

title: Fast-Track Eviction for Violent Crime or Drug Sales — No Cure Right
bodyText:
Nebraska gives you a faster eviction path — 5 days' written notice, with no right for the tenant to cure — if the tenant, a household member, a guest, or anyone under the tenant's control engages in violent criminal activity, illegal drug sales, or other conduct that threatens the health or safety of other tenants, you, or your employees, on the premises (§76-1431(4)). This is a statutory power, not something your lease needs to create.

Important carve-out (§76-1431(5)): you can't use this path when the conduct was by someone on the premises other than the tenant or a household member, and the tenant or a household member has taken at least one protective step. The steps are seeking a protective, restraining or similar order against that person, or reporting the conduct to law enforcement to start a criminal case against them. For domestic violence, certification from a qualified third party under the federal Violence Against Women Act also counts. The carve-out isn't limited to domestic violence. It doesn't protect a tenant who committed domestic violence, and if both the victim who took a step and the perpetrator are on the lease, you may use this path only against the perpetrator.

title: No Tenure-Based For-Cause Eviction Protection
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, where a tenant who has lived in a property for 12 months or more generally can't be removed without a specific legal cause or defined no-fault reason, Nebraska has no tenure-based just-cause requirement. A month-to-month tenancy can be ended with plain 30 days' written notice regardless of how long the tenant has lived there, no reason required (§76-1437(2)) — subject only to the retaliation prohibition (§76-1439) and fair housing law. One situation is different. If your building is being converted to condominiums, a residential tenant or subtenant in possession CANNOT be required to vacate on less than 60 days' notice, and during that period may be removed early only for nonpayment of rent, waste, or conduct that disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment - a genuine for-cause list, for that situation only. The terms of the tenancy also may not be altered during those 60 days, and failing to give the notice is a defense to your action for possession (§76-886). See the separate guidance on conversion buildings.

title: No Landlord Lien on Tenant Property
bodyText: Nebraska abolished a landlord's ability to claim a lien or security interest in a tenant's household goods, and abolished distraint for rent entirely (§76-1434). Don't include a clause purporting to give you a lien on tenant property for unpaid rent or damages — it wouldn't be enforceable.

title: Retaliation Against a Tenant Is Prohibited
bodyText: Nebraska law bars you from raising rent, cutting services, or bringing (or threatening) an eviction action because a tenant complained to a government agency about a health/safety code violation, or organized or joined a tenants' union (§76-1439(1)). This doesn't stop a genuine rent increase or service change unrelated to the complaint, and it doesn't stop you from pursuing possession if the code violation was actually caused by the tenant's own lack of care, the tenant is behind on rent, or fixing the violation would require work that effectively deprives the tenant of use of the unit (§76-1439(3)).

title: Nebraska's Holdover Damages Ceiling Is Higher Than the Standard Clause
bodyText:
Nebraska allows a landlord to recover up to three months' periodic rent or threefold the actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees, from a tenant whose holdover is WILLFUL AND NOT IN GOOD FAITH (§76-1437(3)) - a higher ceiling than Kansas's 1.5x cap, and the fee award is a genuine statutory remedy tied to this specific claim rather than a lease promise, so it does not run into the attorney-fee-clause ban.

Two things follow that are easy to miss. FIRST, the willfulness condition is real: for an ordinary holdover that is not willful and not in bad faith, Nebraska sets NO damages measure at all, and your remedy is the action for possession plus whatever actual damages you can prove.

SECOND, the statutory figure is a LUMP measure, not a daily rate, so it does not translate into a per-day charge. The standard holdover clause asks for holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law and otherwise defers to law, which keeps it lawful here but means it recovers nothing specific on a non-willful holdover. If you want a stated daily figure for that case, it has to be a lease term, and it has to be a reasonable estimate of your actual loss rather than a penalty.

If instead you consent to the tenant staying on after the term ends, §76-1437(3) sends you to §76-1414(4): unless you agree on a definite new term, the tenancy becomes week to week for a roomer who pays weekly rent and month to month in every other case.

title: Domestic Violence Protection Documentation and Landlord Costs
bodyText: Qualifying documentation for any of the three DV protections above is either a protective order/restraining order, or certification from a qualified third party (a nonprofit or tribal DV/sexual-assault services organization with a state affiliation agreement) under the federal Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act. You can charge the tenant for the actual, reasonable cost of a lock change. If the perpetrator fails to vacate within the notice period, you may recover court costs and attorney fees from the perpetrator specifically (not from the innocent tenant) once you win the resulting possession suit — this is a statutory fee award tied to the DV removal process, not a general lease attorney-fee clause, so it doesn't conflict with the attorney-fee-shifting ban.

title: You Can Delegate Some Maintenance Duties to the Tenant, Under Conditions
bodyText: Nebraska splits tenant maintenance duties by property type, and the split decides whether your lease can do the job at all. SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE (a structure maintained and used as a single dwelling unit; a unit sharing a wall still counts if it has direct access to a street and shares no heating, hot-water or other essential facility or service with another unit, §76-1410(16)): you and the tenant may agree that the tenant performs your waste-removal and water/heat duties, and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling, if the agreement is in writing, for good consideration and entered into in good faith (§76-1419(2)). The lease itself is that writing, so a lease clause works. ANYTHING ELSE - a duplex, an apartment, any dwelling unit that is not a single-family residence: an agreement that the tenant performs specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling binds the tenant only if it is set out in a SEPARATE WRITING signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration, and only if it does not diminish or affect your obligations to other tenants (§76-1419(3)). A paragraph in the lease is not a separate writing, so in a multi-unit property a lease clause assigning the tenant lawn care, snow clearing or repairs does not bind them - the duty stays with you. Waste removal and water and heat are different again. §76-1419(3) does not name them, so treat them as yours in a multi-unit property, even with a separate writing. Two traps. Keeping all COMMON AREAS clean and safe is your own duty under §76-1419(1)(c), so snow on a shared walk or entrance is yours regardless of what the lease says; and §76-1419(3)'s other-tenants proviso means a common-area task generally cannot be shifted even by a separate writing. Neither path tolerates a workaround: both require genuine good faith and not a device to evade your duties. A third path is separate from both: whatever the property type, you may employ a tenant to do your maintenance work (§76-1419(4)). The tenant then does the work as your employee, and the duty itself stays yours. Note that the standard Landscaping & Irrigation and Snow Removal clauses DO assign tasks to the tenant, so treat both as single-family-only in Nebraska.

title: What Accepting a Late Payment Actually Costs You in Nebraska
bodyText: If you accept rent knowing the tenant is in default, Nebraska law treats that as waiving one specific thing: your right to TERMINATE the lease for that particular breach (§76-1433). That is narrower than it sounds, and worth being precise about. You do NOT lose the late fee. You do not lose the rent, any damages claim, your right to insist on full and timely payment going forward, your right to charge a late fee next time, or your right to terminate for any different or continuing breach. What you lose is the ability to evict over that one late payment after you have taken the money for it. The statute also gives you a way to keep even that: it applies 'unless otherwise agreed after the breach has occurred.' Note the timing — the agreement has to come AFTER the breach, so no sentence written into the lease at signing can do this work, because the lease predates every breach under it. If you want to accept a late payment and still preserve the right to terminate for it, get the tenant's written agreement to that at the time you accept the payment. A short signed acknowledgment accompanying the receipt or late-fee charge is the practical form. This is a landlord practice question, not something lease drafting can solve — which is why your Nebraska late-fee clause is deliberately drafted to preserve only what survives automatically, and does not claim to preserve termination.

title: No Tenant-Facing Radon Disclosure Requirement, But Read the Nuance
bodyText: Nebraska doesn't require landlords to disclose radon information to tenants - only four states (Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Maine) currently require that. But do not read that as Nebraska having no radon law: it regulates radon in NEW CONSTRUCTION instead, and buildings built after September 1, 2019 must use radon resistant new construction under §§76-3501 to 76-3507 - see the separate guidance on that, because it reaches you if you built or bought new. Two adjacent Nebraska rules are easy to confuse with a tenant-disclosure duty and aren't the same thing: a real-estate seller disclosure statute (§76-2,120) that applies to sales and to any lease WITH AN OPTION TO PURCHASE, not to a straight rental; and a radon measurement/mitigation professional certification law that imposes civil and criminal penalties on radon PROFESSIONALS who misrepresent readings, not on landlords generally.

title: No Statewide Bed Bug Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Nebraska has no statewide bed bug disclosure statute. A dedicated Bed Bug Detection and Treatment Act has been introduced in the Legislature multiple times (2020, 2021, 2024) and failed to pass each time (indefinitely postponed). Landlords remain responsible for pest issues generally under the ordinary habitability duty (§76-1419), including bed bugs the tenant didn't cause — just no separate disclosure mandate.

title: No Statewide Mold Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Nebraska has no specific mold disclosure statute. Mold issues are handled through the ordinary habitability duty (§76-1419) and general misrepresentation/disclosure principles rather than a dedicated mold statute — the practical standard is whether you respond within a reasonable time after written notice and fix the moisture source.

title: No Move-In Inventory Requirement
bodyText: Unlike Kansas's 5-day written move-in inventory requirement (K.S.A. 58-2548), Nebraska landlords aren't required to document the property's condition at move-in to collect a security deposit. Still strongly recommended as a practical matter — it's your best evidence at move-out — just not a legal prerequisite in Nebraska the way it is in Kansas.

title: Nebraska's Protected Classes: the Federal List Plus Military or Veteran Status
bodyText:
The Nebraska Fair Housing Act protects race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, and sex — and, since 2025, MILITARY OR VETERAN STATUS, which has no federal analog. That class was added by Laws 2025, LB150 and now appears throughout the operative prohibition at §20-318(1)-(5) and (8), in the disability provisions' companion sections, and in §20-322(1). A related safe harbor at §20-322(6) lets you offer housing, favorable loan or lease terms, or other benefits LIMITED to veterans, servicemembers, or their family members without that being discrimination.

Nebraska still has no statewide protection for marital status, source of income, sexual orientation, or gender identity.

One more statewide rule sits outside the Fair Housing Act: a seller or lessor may not refuse to sell or lease a dwelling to a person because the person, a member of the person's family or someone who will live with the person has, or is suspected of having, HIV infection or AIDS (§20-168(2)). The Fair Housing Act's exemptions in §20-322 do not apply to that rule, and the person refused may sue you in the district court of the county where it happened (§20-168(5)).

Lincoln and Omaha each add sexual orientation and gender identity locally, and Lincoln adds source of income via a 2025 voter-approved measure — municipal complexity not resolved here.

title: No Statewide Housing-Voucher Acceptance Mandate
bodyText: Nebraska has no statewide law requiring landlords to accept housing vouchers (Section 8 or otherwise) — a state-level bill to add source-of-income as a protected class (LB223) has been proposed but not enacted as of this session. Lincoln has a local voter-approved ordinance (May 2025) requiring source-of-income acceptance within city limits specifically, currently facing a legal challenge — a municipal-only requirement, not a statewide one.

title: No Deposit Installment-Payment Right
bodyText: Nebraska law doesn't give tenants a right to pay the security deposit in installments — the deposit can be required up front, same as the general rule in CO/WY/KS.

title: General Unconscionability Doctrine Is Built Into the Base Act
bodyText: Nebraska's unconscionability doctrine (§76-1412) is written directly into the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act itself, not a separate consumer-protection statute the way Kansas's KCPA backstop is. A court that finds a rental agreement or any provision unconscionable when made can refuse to enforce it, sever the unconscionable provision, or limit its application — a real backstop against unfair lease terms even where a specific statute doesn't address the exact provision.

title: No Immigration-Status Inquiry Prohibition
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute prohibiting landlords from inquiring about immigration status. Only California, Illinois, and Colorado have been found to have a dedicated statute of this kind.

title: No State-Level Right-to-Call-Police Statute
bodyText: Nebraska has no state-level statute establishing a non-waivable tenant right to call police or emergency services. Any protection here would exist, if at all, at the municipal nuisance-ordinance level — the same category of city-by-city complexity keeping Ohio deliberately deferred in this project. Not audited here.

title: No Broad Service-Animal-Misrepresentation Penalty — Don't Trust the Confident Secondary Sources
bodyText: Unlike Kansas (K.S.A. 39-1112) and Wyoming, Nebraska does NOT have a broad statute criminalizing misrepresenting a pet as a service or emotional-support animal to a landlord. The only related Nebraska criminal provision, §28-1313, is much narrower: it makes it a Class III misdemeanor for a sighted person to carry or display a white cane or use a guide dog to falsely appear blind — aimed at impersonating a blind person, not at a tenant exaggerating a pet's status. A 2021 bill (LB309) that would have created the broader prohibition Kansas and Wyoming actually have was considered and not enacted. Multiple confident-sounding secondary sources misstate this as a general $1,000-fine, six-month-jail service-animal-fraud law — it isn't; that figure appears to come from conflating several states' laws.

title: No EV Charging Access Right
bodyText: Nebraska has no tenant right-to-charge statute for electric vehicles. No EV-charging-access requirement identified in any Nebraska statute or regulation.

title: No Tenant-Death Lease-Termination Statute
bodyText: Nebraska has no 'Letty's Act'-style statute automatically terminating a lease or excusing the estate from further rent liability upon a tenant's death. §76-1414(5) addresses a narrower, different question — the process for retrieving a deceased tenant's personal property — not lease termination or estate rent liability. The estate remains liable under ordinary contract principles.

title: Nebraska Gives the Tenant a Self-Help Remedy, Not a Landlord Relocation Mandate
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, where a serious habitability failure can require you to affirmatively provide alternate housing within 24 hours at your own cost (C.R.S. §38-12-503), Nebraska takes a different approach: if you deliberately or negligently fail to supply heat, water, or essential services, the tenant may procure reasonable substitute housing themselves and is excused from paying rent during that period, and — if your failure was deliberate — may also recover the actual and reasonable cost or fair and reasonable value of that substitute housing, up to an amount equal to the periodic rent. In any case under this section, deliberate or not, the tenant may also recover reasonable attorney's fees (§76-1427(1)). A tenant who uses any of these remedies may not also proceed under §76-1425, including its termination route, for the same breach (§76-1427(2)). This is a tenant self-help option triggered by the tenant's own choice, not an affirmative relocation duty that falls on you the moment a serious condition arises.

title: No Dedicated Tenant-Screening Fairness Act Identified
bodyText: Nebraska has no rental-application or tenant-screening fairness statute. Application fees are uncapped and non-refundable, with no requirement that the fee track the actual cost of a background/credit check. A bill (LB17) that would cap application fees at the actual consumer-report cost, bar charging a fee when no unit is available, and limit late/returned-check fees has been introduced but not enacted as of this session — worth monitoring, since it would meaningfully change this area if passed. Federal Fair Credit Reporting Act obligations still apply regardless of state law.

title: Carbon Monoxide Alarms - Nearly Every Nebraska Rental Turnover Triggers This
bodyText:
If your rental has a fuel-fired heater or appliance, a fireplace, or an attached garage, Nebraska's Carbon Monoxide Safety Act almost certainly applies to you. There is a section written specifically for rental property (§76-606), and it has two independent triggers. The first is any interior alteration, repair, fuel-fired appliance replacement, or addition requiring a permit on or after January 1, 2017.

The second is the one that catches nearly everyone: for an EXISTING rental, a CHANGE IN TENANT OCCUPANCY on or after January 1, 2017 (§76-606(2)). Every turnover since that date is a trigger. Unlike the first trigger, the second as printed carries no fuel-fired, fireplace or garage condition. The cautious course is an alarm in every rental. The age of the building is irrelevant, and no sale or renovation is needed.

Once triggered, an operational alarm must be installed on each habitable floor, or wherever an applicable building code specifies. Before each new tenancy you must replace any alarm that was stolen, removed, missing, or non-operational after the last occupancy, and provide the tenant with any batteries needed to make it operational at move-in.

During the tenancy the tenant must keep, test and maintain the alarms and notify you of any that go missing or stop working, or of a deficiency they cannot fix - and you must then replace or repair. Helpfully, outside those specific duties the statute says you are NOT responsible for ongoing maintenance, repair, replacement, or battery care (§76-606(3)(b)). Nobody may remove batteries or disable an alarm except to inspect, maintain, repair or replace it.

title: A Criminal Bad-Check Remedy Exists Separately From Your Lease's NSF Fee
bodyText:
Nebraska's bad-check statute (§28-611) is a CRIMINAL statute, and it gives the payee of a dishonored check — including a landlord — two routes to a small fixed recovery. Under §28-611(5), a person in violation who makes voluntary restitution must also pay ten dollars to the injured party plus any reasonable handling fee the injured party's financial institution charged. Under §28-611(7), a person convicted may be ordered to make restitution and pay the same ten dollars plus that handling fee.

Note what the ten dollars is not: it is not a cap on what your lease may charge as a returned-payment fee. Several secondary sources describe it as 'the maximum NSF fee a Nebraska landlord can charge,' which conflates a criminal restitution amount with your civil contractual fee. Nebraska has no general statutory cap on a lease NSF or returned-payment fee; the outer limit is the ordinary rule that such a fee must be a reasonable estimate of your actual harm rather than a penalty.

Also note this track requires the criminal elements — knowingly writing a check without sufficient funds — so it is not available for every bounced rent check.

title: A Real NE Lease Narrows Its Liability Disclaimer to 'Ordinary' Negligence — Worth Considering
bodyText: A real, attorney-reviewed Nebraska commercial lease product deliberately limits its liability disclaimer to the landlord's *ordinary* negligence, explicitly preserving liability for gross negligence or willful misconduct. That tracks Nebraska's actual exculpation ban precisely (§76-1415(1)(d) voids a liability-limitation clause only for the landlord's own active, actionable negligence — not all negligence). The current "Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance" clause's blanket 'Landlord is not liable for any such loss or damage' sentence doesn't carve out gross negligence or willful misconduct the way this real NE product does — a real commercial precedent that this gap matters enough for a working Nebraska lease to address it explicitly.

title: Nebraska's Service-Animal Statute Requires No Property Modification — But Nebraska's Fair Housing Act Still Requires You to Allow Tenant-Paid Ones
bodyText: Nebraska's service-animal housing statute expressly does not require you to modify your property: 'Nothing in sections 20-131.01 to 20-131.04 shall require any person who rents, leases, or provides housing accommodations for compensation to modify such person's property in any way to accommodate the special needs of any lessee' (§20-131.03). Read that narrowly — it limits the STATE SERVICE-ANIMAL scheme only. The Nebraska Fair Housing Act, a different statute, separately makes it discrimination to refuse 'to permit, at the expense of the person with a disability, reasonable modifications of existing premises' where necessary for full enjoyment (§20-319(2)(a)) — though in a rental you may, where reasonable, condition permission on the tenant restoring the interior afterward, reasonable wear and tear excepted. So: you need not modify at your own cost under the service-animal statute, but you generally must PERMIT tenant-funded modification under the Fair Housing Act. Treating §20-131.03 as a general 'no modifications' rule would be a serious misread.

title: Two Different Owner-Occupied Carve-Outs That Do Not Line Up
bodyText:
Nebraska has two separate owner-occupied carve-outs with DIFFERENT scopes, and they do not align. (1) The service-animal housing scheme excludes, by definition, 'any single-family residence in which the owner lives and in which any room is rented, leased, or provided for compensation to persons other than the owner or primary tenant' (§20-131.02(1)) — with NO cap on the number of rooms. (2) The Nebraska Fair Housing Act separately lets a person refuse to rent 'a room or rooms in his or her own home for any reason or for no reason,' but that exception stops applying to anyone renting 'more than four sleeping rooms' (§20-322(3)).

Consequence: if you live in your own single-family home and rent out five rooms, the Fair Housing Act applies to you — including its reasonable-accommodation duty — while the service-animal statute's no-additional-deposit rule does not, because your property was never a 'housing accommodation' under that scheme at all. Do not assume one carve-out implies the other.

title: Denying a Service Animal Is a Crime in Nebraska — and the Exposure Runs at You
bodyText: Nebraska attaches criminal liability to the LANDLORD, not the tenant. Under §20-129(1), a person who 'denies or interferes with' the rights of a person with a disability 'under section 20-127 or sections 20-131.01 to 20-131.04' is guilty of a Class III misdemeanor — and that section list expressly names the housing sections, so it reaches rental housing directly. A Class III misdemeanor carries up to three months' imprisonment and a $500 fine. There is NO Nebraska statute penalizing a tenant for misrepresenting a pet as a service or assistance animal. If you are weighing whether to challenge an animal, the asymmetry matters: wrongly refusing carries criminal exposure; being deceived does not give you a criminal remedy. One narrow limit worth knowing: §20-129(2)'s protection for a bona fide service-animal TRAINER is scoped only to §20-127 (public facilities) and does not extend to the housing sections.

title: Emotional Support Animals Get No Nebraska State-Law Housing Right
bodyText:
Nebraska's service-animal housing right (§§20-131.01 to 20-131.04) turns on the term 'service animal,' which Nebraska defines statewide by reference to 28 C.F.R. 36.104 'as such regulation existed on January 1, 2008' (§49-801(20)) — a frozen definition that did NOT follow later federal changes. The 2008 text covers 'any guide dog, signal dog, or other animal individually trained to do work or perform tasks' for a person with a disability.

Two consequences, and neither matches what you'd get from reading today's federal rule:

(1) SPECIES IS OPEN. Nebraska's definition is not limited to dogs. A trained cat, miniature horse, or other animal can qualify. The federal dogs-only limit arrived in 2010, two years after Nebraska's freeze date, and never entered Nebraska law. This is broader than Kansas, whose assistance-animal act is dogs-only.

(2) EMOTIONAL SUPPORT ANIMALS ARE STILL OUTSIDE THE STATE RIGHT, but only by implication — the animal must be 'individually trained to do work or perform tasks,' and an untrained comfort animal is not. The 2008 text contains no express emotional-support exclusion; that sentence was also added in 2010. So the exclusion is weaker and less explicit than Kansas's, which names comfort animals directly.

None of this lets you refuse an ESA. The federal Fair Housing Act's reasonable-accommodation duty and the Nebraska Fair Housing Act's own duty (§20-319(2)(b)), enforced by the Nebraska Equal Opportunity Commission, both still reach assistance animals including ESAs.

What changed federally is HUD's ENFORCEMENT posture, not the law: HUD withdrew its assistance-animal guidance on 2025-09-17 and on 2026-05-22 narrowed FHEO enforcement to individually-trained animals. Private suits and NEOC enforcement are not bound by HUD's enforcement priorities. Accommodating documented ESAs remains the safe course.

title: Nebraska Bars You From Even ASKING About Protected Characteristics
bodyText: Nebraska goes further than a bare non-discrimination rule. Under §20-318(5) it is unlawful to 'cause to be made any written or oral inquiry or record concerning the race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, sex, or military or veteran status of a person seeking to purchase, rent, or lease any housing.' This bans the INQUIRY and the RECORD, not just the decision — so a rental application form, a screening questionnaire, or a note-to-file capturing any of these characteristics is itself unlawful, regardless of whether it ever influenced an outcome. Review your application forms and any CRM or note-taking fields against this list. Separately, §20-318(6) bans including, honoring, or attempting to honor any restrictive covenant pertaining to housing — worth checking against HOA documents you pass through to tenants.

title: Which Nebraska Buildings the Smoke Detector Mandate Reaches - and Why Rentals Are Always Covered
bodyText:
Four Nebraska sections work together, and for a RENTAL the answer does not depend on when the building went up. §81-5,144 is the one that settles it: the owner of every apartment house, dwelling, hotel, lodging house, dormitory or mobile home, or the owner's agent, is responsible for supplying, installing, maintaining and testing the smoke detectors, and that section applies SOLELY to rental property, with no construction-date qualifier at all. So assume the duty applies to your Nebraska rental however old it is.

§81-5,142 is a different rule - it creates the general requirement to HAVE detectors and it IS date-keyed: subsection (1) covers dwelling units, lodging-house guest rooms and dormitories constructed or remodeled on or after January 1, 1982; subsection (2) gave pre-1982 guest rooms and dormitories until January 1, 1984; and subsection (3) covers pre-1982 dwelling units, mobile homes and modular housing units at the time of their REMODELING OR SALE, which is a trigger, not a deadline. On a sale, supplying detectors is the SELLER'S sole responsibility and cannot be assigned or imputed to anyone else.

§81-5,143 requires the detector to be mounted per the State Fire Marshal's rules and to sound an alarm inside the dwelling unit, guest room, dormitory or mobile home.

§81-5,145 handles local rules: a city or county may not set standards LESS stringent than the state's, must require detectors wired to a centralized electrical power source (a battery may be the backup) in buildings constructed on or after January 1, 1982, and may NOT require hardwiring in a building constructed before that date. Violating any of §§81-5,132 to 81-5,146 is a Class V misdemeanor (§81-5,146).

title: Nebraska's 2025 Electronic Notice Rules — Including One More Thing Your Lease Cannot Do
bodyText: Nebraska added a detailed electronic-notice regime in 2025 (§76-1413, Laws 2025, LB185). Notices and documents under a rental agreement may be delivered electronically, but only on strict conditions. Start with the one that constrains your lease: you may not require a tenant to accept electronic delivery as part of the rental agreement or as a condition of entering into or renewing it (§76-1413(9)). That is a prohibition on lease terms sitting OUTSIDE the main prohibited-provisions section, so it is easy to miss. To use electronic delivery you need the tenant's affirmative, un-withdrawn consent, given after you provide a clear statement of: their right to withdraw consent at any time with no conditions or consequences; which notices it covers; their right to a paper copy by mail and how to get one; and how to withdraw consent or update their address. The tenant must also receive your hardware and software requirements beforehand and must consent in a way demonstrating they can actually access that format. If those requirements later change materially, you must re-disclose and re-obtain consent. Where a law requires verification or acknowledgment of receipt, electronic delivery is permitted only if your method provides it — and if you don't get it, you must send by mail. If two electronic communications bounce within a thirty-day period, all future notices must go by first-class or other mail until the tenant re-consents in a way showing they can receive them. You must also fall back to another method if you have reason to believe a notice wasn't received or learn the address is no longer valid. Withdrawal of consent does not retroactively invalidate notices already delivered. Two more limits come from Nebraska's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, which §76-1413(5) incorporates, and neither can be contracted around. If you post a notice somewhere the tenant cannot print or save it, the notice is NOT ENFORCEABLE against them (§86-635(3)), and that rule may not be varied by agreement (§86-635(4)) - so a portal that blocks downloads defeats your own notice. And a tenant who agrees to receive one thing electronically may still refuse electronic delivery for other transactions, a right the lease cannot waive (§86-632(3)). The good news: Nebraska's UETA excludes only wills and most of the Uniform Commercial Code (§86-630(2)), so unlike some states it does NOT carve out default, cure or eviction notices - those may go electronically once you have proper consent.

title: What Self-Help and Bad Entry Practice Actually Cost in Nebraska
bodyText:
Two Nebraska remedies carry hard numbers worth knowing before you act.

UNLAWFUL OUSTER OR CUTTING OFF ESSENTIAL SERVICES (§76-1430): if you unlawfully remove or exclude a tenant, or willfully and wrongfully interrupt electricity, gas, water, or another essential service, the tenant may recover possession or terminate — and in either case recover an amount equal to three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages, plus a reasonable attorney's fee. Liquidated means they need not prove actual loss. Separately, §76-1436 bars recovering possession by any means other than a court action, abandonment, or surrender, and names service interruption as a prohibited means. There is no lawful self-help lockout in Nebraska.

ABUSE OF ENTRY (§76-1438(2)): if you enter unlawfully, enter lawfully but in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated lawful-but-harassing demands for entry, the tenant may obtain an injunction or terminate the lease, and may recover actual damages of not less than one month's rent, plus reasonable attorney's fees. Note the floor — a minimum recovery whether or not any real loss is proven.

The mirror provision at §76-1438(1) protects you: if a tenant refuses lawful access, you may compel it or terminate and recover actual damages and fees.

title: Termination Notice for Periodic Tenancies - Two Different Periods
bodyText: Nebraska sets two different notice periods depending on the tenancy. A week-to-week tenancy ends on at least SEVEN days' written notice; a month-to-month tenancy ends on at least THIRTY days' written notice (§76-1437(1)-(2)). Either party may give it. There is a drafting difference between the two that is easy to miss: the seven-day clock runs to 'the termination date specified in the notice,' but the thirty-day clock runs to 'the periodic rental date specified in the notice.' So a month-to-month termination notice must be keyed to a rent-due date, not an arbitrary calendar date - getting that wrong can invalidate the notice.

title: Servicemember Early Termination - Nebraska's Statute Is Narrower Than the Federal One
bodyText: Nebraska has its own servicemember termination statute at §55-702, separate from the URLTA and expressly in addition to the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. Where it applies: the servicemember gives written or electronic notice plus a copy of the orders. For a monthly-rent lease, termination takes effect thirty days after the first date the next rent payment is due after notice is delivered; for any other rental agreement, it takes effect on the last day of the month following the month notice was delivered. You may not impose an early-termination charge. Within sixty days of the termination date you must refund all rent paid for any period past that date, and the deposit is returned subject to §76-1416. The servicemember still owes anything already due and unpaid at termination. One provision to watch: if the servicemember re-rents from you within ninety days of returning from service, you may not charge any penalty, fee, loss of deposit, or additional cost because of the earlier termination — only the usual and customary charges any other tenant would pay. The statute does not impair contracts in existence before July 19, 2018. SCOPE: for residential leases this section is understood to reach only the case where the servicemember is required to move into government-owned or leased housing. For the far more common deployment or PCS situation out of a civilian rental, the operative right is the FEDERAL SCRA, not this statute.

title: Raising Rent, and Nebraska's 2025 Rent-Control Preemption
bodyText: Nebraska has no dedicated rent-increase notice statute for ordinary rentals. During a fixed term you cannot raise rent unless the lease allows it. On a periodic tenancy you change rent through the same mechanism you would use to end it - thirty days' written notice for month-to-month, seven for week-to-week (§76-1437) - and Nebraska draws no distinction between an oral and a written month-to-month tenancy for this purpose. Watch a common trap: many sources state a flat sixty-day rent-increase requirement for Nebraska. That sixty-day rule is §76-1490 and applies to MOBILE HOME space tenancies only, not to ordinary rentals. Separately, since 2025 Nebraska preempts local rent control. §13-331 bars any city, village, or county from enacting or enforcing an ordinance imposing rent controls on private property, applies notwithstanding any home rule charter, and makes a violating ordinance null and void. It carves out ordinances that increase affordable-housing supply through land-use or inclusionary-housing requirements, and voluntary programs where an owner agrees to rent restrictions.

title: No Eviction Record Sealing in Nebraska
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute allowing sealing, expungement, or restricted access to eviction (forcible entry and detainer) records. Two attempts failed: LB175 in 2024, defeated by filibuster, and LB92, the Residential Tenant Clean Slate Act, introduced January 2025, carried over, and indefinitely postponed on April 17, 2026. Because no statute exists, there is also no landlord right to object to a sealing petition - the question does not arise. Eviction filings remain publicly accessible court records.

title: Colorado-Style Habitability Protections Nebraska Does Not Have
bodyText: Four habitability-adjacent protections that exist in Colorado have no Nebraska equivalent. (1) NO BLANKET NON-WAIVER: Nebraska has no habitability-specific non-waivability section. Habitability rights are non-waivable only through the general bar at §76-1415(1)(a), and §76-1419 lets you shift some duties to the tenant only within narrow limits. For a single-family residence, the tenant may take on your waste-removal and water, hot-water and heat duties and specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling, by a writing made in good faith and for good consideration (§76-1419(2)). For any other dwelling unit, the tenant may take on only specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, by a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration, and only if it does not diminish or affect your obligations to other tenants (§76-1419(3)). Neither may be a device to evade your obligations. (2) NO VERBAL-NOTICE RULE: Nebraska does not address whether a lease may designate oral notice as sufficient. The URLTA requires a writing wherever it matters: the tenant's breach and essential-services notices (§§76-1425, 76-1427), your termination notices (§§76-1431, 76-1437), the 24-hour entry notice (§76-1423(3)(a)), the manager and owner disclosure (§76-1417(1)), the notice that ends your liability after a sale or a change of manager (§76-1420), the deposit itemization (§76-1416(2)) and any agreement shifting maintenance to the tenant (§76-1419(2), (3)(a)). Oral notice will not satisfy those provisions regardless (a writing may be electronic only as §76-1413 allows). Two of your duties run on notice that need not be written: you must comply with housing codes and make repairs 'after written or actual notice' (§76-1419(1)(a), (b)). (3) NO RENTER'S-INSURANCE BAN: Nebraska does not prohibit requiring renter's insurance, and does not specifically bar pushing landlord-responsible repairs onto it - though §76-1415(1)(d) independently voids clauses exculpating or indemnifying you for your own active and actionable negligence. (4) NO OPERATIONAL DUTIES: Nebraska imposes no duty to respond within a set time, communicate, document, or give notice of remediation. Its structure is tenant-remedy-triggered - the tenant gives written notice and statutory clocks then govern the tenant's remedies.

title: Other Provisions Nebraska Does Not Have
bodyText: Four more confirmed absences, each of which exists in a neighboring state. (1) NO PAYMENT-METHOD FEE BAN IDENTIFIED: no Nebraska statute was found prohibiting or capping a convenience fee for a particular rent payment method. The only Nebraska convenience-fee statutes, §13-609 and §81-118.01, govern GOVERNMENT payees and do not reach private landlords. Any such fee remains subject to the unconscionability doctrine at §76-1412. (2) NO FRAUDULENT-MISREPRESENTATION TERMINATION: unlike North Dakota, Nebraska has no statutory right to terminate for a false rental application. Your route is to incorporate the application into the lease as a representation, making a material falsehood a breach under §76-1431(1), backed by common-law fraud and rescission preserved by §76-1403. (3) NO DOUBLE-LETTING STATUTE: no Nebraska analog to North Dakota's ban on letting the same room twice with a rent-abatement remedy; the nearest provision is the general failure-to-deliver-possession remedy at §76-1426. (4) NO SMOKE-DETECTOR EVIDENTIARY OR INSURANCE SHIELD: unlike Kansas, whose statute makes non-compliance inadmissible on civil liability and bars insurers from reducing payment, Nebraska's series contains no such protection. Its only liability-adjacent language is the narrow no-violation-without-notice defense in §81-5,144.

title: No All-In Pricing or Fee-Transparency Law in Nebraska
bodyText: Nebraska has no analog to Colorado's Honest Pricing Act or any other statute requiring that advertised rent disclose mandatory fees, or that fees be bundled into a single all-in price. You may advertise base rent and disclose mandatory fees separately in the lease. Four real limits still apply. Nebraska's unconscionability doctrine sits inside the URLTA itself at §76-1412, letting a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable agreement or provision. Separately, §76-1415(2) makes a prohibited provision unenforceable and exposes you to actual damages and attorney's fees if you deliberately use one you know is prohibited. And federal unfair-and-deceptive-practices rules on fee disclosure apply regardless of state law. Nebraska's Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act also makes it deceptive to advertise a price 'in any manner calculated or tending to mislead' (§87-302(a)(10), in the version operative January 1, 2027). If a tenant is induced into a lease by such a practice, you cannot enforce the lease (§87-303.07). Whether a rental is 'goods or services' under that Act is unsettled, so advertise as if it is. The consumer-protection guidance explains both acts. Disclosing mandatory recurring fees clearly and up front is the safer practice even though Nebraska does not compel it.

title: Fire or Casualty - What You Owe Back, and When the Clock Starts
bodyText:
If fire or casualty damages the property enough to substantially impair the tenant's enjoyment of it, the tenant may move out immediately and notify you in writing within 14 days that they are ending the lease, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate only the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the loss in fair rental value (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1429).

Three details of Nebraska's fire-and-casualty rule catch landlords out. FIRST, the termination date is the date the tenant VACATED, not the date you received their notice: the tenant vacates first and then has fourteen days to notify you in writing, so a notice that arrives two weeks later still ends the tenancy as of the earlier move-out date, and rent is accounted for as of the date of the casualty itself (§76-1429).

SECOND, you owe back all prepaid rent plus the security deposit the tenant can recover under §76-1416 - the casualty does not convert the deposit into damages, and the §76-1416 return deadline and penalty still apply.

THIRD, a tenant who stays but loses part of the unit owes proportionally less rent, measured by the drop in FAIR RENTAL VALUE, not by floor area.

The one thing that stays with the tenant is damage caused by their own negligence. You cannot contract around any of this: §76-1415(1)(a) voids a lease term waiving the tenant's rights under the Act. And if the tenancy ends, §76-1405 puts a duty to mitigate damages on the aggrieved party, so re-letting effort is expected rather than optional.

title: Meth Labs: You Must Report, You Must Not Re-Rent, and You Can Terminate in Three Days
bodyText: Nebraska has a four-section scheme for methamphetamine-contaminated rentals that sits outside the landlord-tenant act entirely, and it imposes real duties on you. YOU MUST REPORT: a property owner with knowledge of a clandestine drug lab on their property must report it as soon as practicable to local law enforcement or the Nebraska State Patrol (§71-2433). YOU MUST NOT RE-RENT: you may not permit human habitation or use of contaminated property until rehabilitation is complete and the local public health department has released the property, and knowingly violating that carries a civil penalty of up to $1,000 enforced by the Department of Health and Human Services (§71-2434(3)). YOU PAY FOR THE OVERSIGHT: the local public health department may charge you for the costs of monitoring the rehabilitation (§71-2434(2)). YOU CAN GET THE TENANT OUT FAST: notwithstanding any other provision of law, if leased property contains a clandestine drug lab you may terminate the lease on THREE DAYS' written notice for the purpose of rehabilitating it (§71-2435) - no cure period, and it overrides the usual 14-day and 7-day notice mechanics. 'Contaminated property' reaches any enclosed area intended for human habitation that has been contaminated by methamphetamine, its residue, or other substances from such a lab (§71-2432(2)).

title: Selling the Property, or Changing Managers - How You Actually Get Off the Hook
bodyText:
Nebraska releases a selling landlord from future liability, but only if you do two specific things.

FIRST, give the tenant WRITTEN NOTICE of the conveyance: a landlord who conveys the premises in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the lease and the Act only as to events occurring AFTER that written notice (§76-1420(1)). Events before it stay yours.

SECOND, deal with the deposit separately: the release does NOT cover money and property the tenant is entitled to under §76-1416, so you remain personally liable for the security deposit and prepaid rent unless you ASSIGN them to the purchaser and give the tenant written notice of the assignment - which then does release you. Selling without assigning the deposit leaves you exposed for it after you no longer hold it.

The same structure covers a manager: a manager is relieved of liability as to events after written notice to the tenant that their management has ended (§76-1420(2)).

Two cautions. The section opens 'Unless otherwise agreed', so a lease or purchase agreement can change this allocation - check what yours says. And a change of owner or manager also restarts your §76-1417 disclosure duty, since the tenant is entitled to the current owner's and manager's name and address.

title: Your House Rules Are Enforceable Only If They Clear Six Tests
bodyText: Nebraska lets you adopt rules about the tenant's use and occupancy of the premises, but a rule is enforceable against the tenant only if ALL SIX of these hold (§76-1422): its purpose is to promote the appearance, convenience, safety or welfare of the tenants, to preserve your property from abusive use, or to distribute services and facilities fairly; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner; it is explicit enough to fairly inform the tenant what they must or must not do; it is not a device for evading your own obligations; and the tenant had notice of it when they entered into the lease. ADDING A RULE MID-TENANCY is allowed on different terms: a rule adopted after the lease is signed binds the tenant if you give reasonable notice of its adoption AND it 'does not work a substantial modification of his bargain'. So a new quiet-hours rule will usually stick; a new rule that effectively re-prices the tenancy or strips away something they bargained for will not. Enforcement runs through the ordinary noncompliance route at §76-1431, which means a rule violation is handled as a lease breach with the notice and cure mechanics that go with it - not as an independent ground for immediate termination.

title: Towing From Your Lot - No Signs, No Lawful Tow, and No Kickbacks
bodyText:
Nebraska conditions a private tow on posted signs, and the rule splits by city size. OUTSIDE Omaha and Lincoln, parking in a PROPERLY POSTED restricted lot without the consent of the owner or tenant authorized to give permission is an infraction, and the vehicle may be towed at the lot owner's or tenant's request (§60-2401.01).

IN Omaha (metropolitan class) and Lincoln (primary class), unless the city has adopted a conforming ordinance, vehicles parked without consent are subject to towing 'if the lot is properly posted' (§60-2401).

Either way the signs carry the whole thing, and §60-2402 sets what they must say: they must be readily visible and must state the purpose or purposes for parking on the lot, the hours of restricted parking, and WHO TO CONTACT for information about a towed vehicle. A lot with no signs, or signs missing any of those three items, gives you no lawful tow.

A space designated for disabled parking has two more conditions. Before removing a vehicle from it, you must notify the police or sheriff's department. And a sign at the space must clearly state that it is a tow-in zone (§18-1737(2)). The parking-rules guidance covers the designation sign as well (§18-1737(1)).

DO NOT TAKE A KICKBACK: an owner or tenant causing a vehicle to be towed 'shall not solicit or accept therefor a commission, gift, gratuity, or any form of compensation or wealth' from the towing business (§60-2411). Free towing arrangements and per-tow payments from the operator are exactly what this prohibits.

The rest is on the tower, not you, but it affects your tenants: the tower must verify that whoever ordered the tow is really the lot's owner or tenant (§60-2409), notify law enforcement of the plate within 24 hours (§60-2403), and send the vehicle's owner and any lienholder a certified-mail notice within 15 business days (§60-2410(2)). Towing and storage become a lien on the vehicle but never on its contents, and the vehicle can be disposed of after 90 days (§60-2410(1)).

title: Nebraska Does Regulate Radon - In New Construction, Not in Disclosure
bodyText: Nebraska requires no radon disclosure to tenants, but it does regulate radon in new buildings, and that reaches you if you build or bought new. New construction built after September 1, 2019 that is intended to be regularly occupied by people must be built using radon resistant new construction (§76-3504). The required minimum standards are specific: sealed or gasketed sump lids; a passive subslab depressurization system with a vent pipe of at least three inches running up through the building and terminating at least twelve inches above the roof and at least ten feet from any window or opening; separate vent pipes where interior footings divide the subslab material; visible interior vent pipes labelled 'Radon Reduction System' on each floor and in accessible attics; and an electrical circuit terminated in an approved box near the anticipated fan location so an active system can be added later. THERE ARE ONLY TWO EXEMPTIONS THAT APPLY TO A DWELLING (§76-3505): the project used the design of a licensed architect or professional engineer, or the county's average radon concentration is below 2.7 picocuries per liter as determined by the state. The third exemption - a local building official deciding it is unnecessary - is expressly unavailable 'other than for any residential dwelling unit', so it does not help a rental. Converting the passive system to an active one later is expressly permitted (§76-3506). Nebraska is among the highest-radon states in the country, so a passive system that was never activated is a live habitability and marketing question even though no statute makes you test or disclose.

title: Medical Cannabis Is Now Legal in Nebraska - Your Smoking Ban Still Works, Your Crime Clause Does Not
bodyText:
Nebraska voters legalized medical cannabis in 2024, and the practical effect on a lease is narrower than most landlords expect.

What changed: it is no longer an offense under state OR local law for a qualified patient to use, possess and acquire an allowable amount of cannabis for a medical condition, or for a caregiver to obtain and deliver it for them, and that conduct is removed from the Uniform Controlled Substances Act (§71-24,105).

What did NOT change: nothing in the act requires you to permit cannabis on your property, so a contractual no-smoking clause remains enforceable against a qualified patient as an ordinary lease term.

What you should stop relying on: any lease or statutory hook keyed to ILLEGAL or CRIMINAL drug activity. A registered patient's medical use is no longer illegal under state law, so it cannot support Nebraska's fast-track eviction for drug-related criminal activity under §76-1431, and treating it as criminal conduct is a real risk. Enforce it as a breach of your smoking or house-rules term instead, on the ordinary notice-and-cure track.

Two further cautions: cannabis remains illegal under federal law, which still matters for federally assisted housing; and a request to use a non-smoked form as a disability accommodation is a fair-housing question under §20-319(2)(b), not a cannabis question.

title: No Duty to Pay Interest on a Security Deposit
bodyText: Nebraska imposes no duty to hold a security deposit in an interest-bearing account, to pay the tenant interest on it, or to keep it in a separate or escrow account. You may hold it with your own funds and keep any interest it earns. What Nebraska does regulate is the amount (one month's rent, plus up to one quarter of a month's rent as a pet deposit) and the return: delivery or mailing of the balance and a written itemization within fourteen days after the tenancy ends, with a penalty for wrongful retention (§76-1416). If you operate in other states, do not carry this one across - deposit-interest duties are one of the most common state divergences in this area, and several states in this library do impose them.

title: How a Nebraska Eviction Runs - and the Second Statute Nobody Reads
bodyText: Nebraska has TWO possession procedures, and which one you are in matters. The landlord-tenant act's own route is an action for possession: you file a complaint for restitution of the premises (§§76-1440, 76-1441), the case is tried on a short statutory timetable, and on a judgment for you the court issues a writ of restitution (§76-1446), with appeal governed by §76-1447. For premises under the act, that is the route you must use: an action for possession 'shall be commenced in the manner described by sections 76-1440 to 76-1447' (§76-1440). Nebraska's older forcible entry and detainer statutes, §§25-21,219 to 25-21,235, have their own notice-to-leave, trial, restitution and appeal-bond mechanics. But their jurisdiction section 'shall not apply to actions for possession of any premises subject to' the act (§25-21,219). Use them only for premises the act does not cover, such as an occupier with no lease. Four things to keep straight. First, you cannot take possession yourself: self-help lockouts, removals and service shutoffs give the tenant remedies under §76-1430, and §76-1436 limits recovery of possession to the statutory process. Second, the tenant can turn the nonpayment case into a money fight - in an action for possession based on nonpayment, or an action for rent where the tenant is still in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the Act, and the court may order rent paid into court and net the two sides off (§76-1428). If no rent remains due after that netting, judgment on possession goes to the TENANT. Third, that cuts your way too: if the tenant's defense or counterclaim is without merit and not raised in good faith, you may recover reasonable attorney's fees (§76-1428(1)). And how you serve the summons matters: if ordinary service fails and you post and mail it under §76-1442.01, the court can give you possession but not a money judgment (§76-1446), so you'll need a separate action for the rent. Fourth, delay has a price for the tenant: the court may grant a continuance for good cause, but a further continuance needs agreement or extraordinary cause, and if a further continuance pushes the trial past the next rental period, the court may require the tenant to deposit the rent that comes due during the case with the clerk of the court (§76-1443).

title: Things Nebraska Has No Statute For
bodyText: Seven things landlords ask about that Nebraska has no statute on anywhere in its code, not merely nothing in the landlord-tenant act. (1) NO TENANT PROTECTION ON FORECLOSURE: Nebraska has no statute requiring notice to tenants of a pending foreclosure and none giving a tenant the right to stay after a foreclosure sale. The federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act is what governs, and it is federal law that does not depend on Nebraska adopting anything. (2) NO CASH-RENT RECEIPT DUTY: nothing requires you to give a written receipt for rent paid in cash. Give one anyway - it is your proof of payment as much as theirs. (3) NO HOLDING-DEPOSIT RULES: nothing regulates a pre-lease holding or reservation deposit, what it may be used for, or whether it is refundable if the applicant backs out. Your written agreement is the only thing governing it, so put the terms in writing. (4) NO STATE RENTAL REGISTRATION OR LICENCE: there is no statewide rental registry or landlord licence for an ordinary rental. One exception: unless exempt, units in a retirement community (more than ten units, marketed to retirees or with a minimum age limit tending to attract people nearing retirement) can't be leased before the community is registered with the State Real Estate Commission (§§76-1302(2), 76-1305(1)); Nebraska's landlord-registration row explains it. Omaha and Lincoln run their own programmes and are not resolved here. Separately, an out-of-state LLC that owns income-producing property in Nebraska is transacting business and may not maintain an action, including an eviction, until it has a certificate of authority, and an out-of-state corporation transacting business here faces the same bar (§§21-157(b), 21-162(a), 21-2,204(a)); see "No Nonresident-Landlord Agent Rule in Nebraska - but Two Other Sections Do the Same Work, and One of Them Bites". (5) NO SQUATTER-SPECIFIC REMEDY: Nebraska has no separate unauthorized-occupant or squatter-removal statute; an occupant with no right to be there is removed through the ordinary possession and forcible-entry routes, and the forcible entry and detainer statute names this case in terms: proceedings may be had 'when the defendant is a settler or occupier of lands or tenements, without color of title, and to which the complainant has the right of possession' (§25-21,220(5)), after a written notice to leave served at least three days before the action is filed (§25-21,221). (6) NO MOLD RULES: no mold disclosure duty, no remediation standard, no mold-specific habitability provision. (7) NO TYPOGRAPHY REQUIREMENTS FOR AN ORDINARY LEASE: no Nebraska statute makes an ordinary residential lease term depend on being bold, underlined, capitalised or in a minimum type size. There are three exceptions. First, for a dwelling unit that is not a single-family residence, an agreement that the tenant will do repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling binds only if it is 'set forth in a separate writing signed by the parties' (§76-1419(3)(a)). Second, if in the course of your business you buy a home in foreclosure from the owner who lives there and rent it back to them, the Nebraska Foreclosure Protection Act governs the paperwork: the equity purchase contract must be in at least twelve-point boldface type (§76-2719) and must contain the terms of the lease and a prescribed notice in at least fourteen-point boldface type (§76-2720(1)(g), (j)); §76-2724 voids certain of its terms; and the lease and every other document the homeowner signs must be in English with a certified translation into any other language the homeowner principally speaks (§76-2727). Third, if your lease makes binding arbitration the sole remedy for disputes, a set statement must appear in capitalized, underlined type next to the signature block (§25-2602.02). Without it, the arbitration clause can be unenforceable. Where federal law governs the contract, its absence does not void the clause; this library's arbitration row explains both.

title: Deposit Return Deadline, Itemization and Unclaimed Deposits
bodyText: If you keep any part of the deposit, deliver or mail the balance and a written itemization of what you kept within 14 days after the lease ends (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1416(2)). If the tenant gave no forwarding address or delivery instructions, mail it by first-class mail to the tenant's last known address. If that mailing comes back undeliverable, or the balance stays unclaimed for a year, report and send it to the State Treasurer as unclaimed property under the Uniform Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act (76-1416(2)). The note on unclaimed deposits explains the report date and the penalties. See the penalty note for what happens if you miss the deadline.

title: Domestic Violence: Lease Release, Removing the Abuser, and Lock Changes
bodyText:
Nebraska gives a tenant who, or whose household member, is a victim of domestic violence three rights, each triggered by a qualifying protective order or third-party domestic-violence certification plus written notice (see the documentation note).

Lease release (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1431.01): the tenant names a release date at least 14 and no more than 30 days after the notice and any household members also released; they owe rent for the month the lease ends but nothing after the release date, and no fee solely because of the release. The release doesn't extend to another tenant on the lease who isn't a household member.

Removing the abuser (76-1431.02): if the abuser is a co-tenant or other occupant of the unit, the victim can have them removed from the lease and excluded, and you then proceed against the abuser only under Nebraska's expedited removal procedure; you aren't liable for actions taken in good faith.

Lock change (76-1431.03, 76-1431.04): if the abuser isn't a co-tenant or occupant, change the locks within 24 hours of a written request; if you don't, the tenant may change them in a workmanlike manner with locks of similar or better quality, must tell you promptly, and must give you a new key or code.

On the lock change, one point runs your way: you may require the tenant to pay the actual and reasonable cost you incur in changing the locks (§76-1431.04(4)).

title: Your Basic Habitability Duties
bodyText: Nebraska requires you to: substantially comply, after written or actual notice, with minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety; make all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to keep the property fit and habitable; keep common areas clean and safe; maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, that you supply or are required to supply; provide waste receptacles and arrange removal; and supply running water and reasonable hot water and heat, unless the building isn't required by law to have them or the unit's heat or hot water comes from a tenant-controlled installation on a direct utility connection (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1419(1)). Where a minimum housing code applies to the property, your maximum duty under this section is set by the first item, substantial compliance with that code, and the section is not meant to change existing Nebraska tort law. There is no general excuse for conditions beyond your control. If your failure is caused by conditions beyond your control, the tenant cannot recover consequential damages but keeps the heat, water and essential-services remedies (§76-1425(2)), and those remedies are not intended to cover circumstances beyond your control and do not arise for a condition the tenant, the tenant's family or a guest caused deliberately or negligently (§76-1427(3)). See the note on delegating some duties to the tenant.

title: If You Can't Deliver Possession on Time
bodyText: If you fail to deliver possession as the lease requires, rent abates until you do, and the tenant may either end the lease on at least 5 days' written notice, in which case you return all prepaid rent and the full deposit, or demand that you perform, sue for possession against you or anyone wrongfully in possession, and recover damages. If your failure is willful and not in good faith, the tenant can recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1426).

title: When the Tenant Causes the Damage - You Can Charge Them, But You Cannot Stop Them Leaving
bodyText: If a tenant, occupant or guest causes damage that makes the home uninhabitable, Nebraska splits the answer in a way that catches landlords out. WHAT YOU CAN RECOVER: the tenant is liable for the damage. §76-1429(2) says that notwithstanding the rest of the casualty rule 'the tenant is responsible for damage caused by his negligence', and the Nebraska Supreme Court has gone further - because a specific statute holds a tenant responsible for negligent fire damage, a lease provision doing the same cannot be struck down as void against public policy or unconscionable (SFI Ltd. Partnership 8 v. Carroll). Your Tenant Maintenance clause already carries that liability. If the tenancy ends you may also pursue possession, a claim for rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach (§76-1435), which can include rent lost while the property is repaired - subject to §76-1405's duty to mitigate, so re-letting effort is expected. WHAT YOU CANNOT DO: stop the tenant leaving, or switch off the rent reduction. Nebraska's landlord-noncompliance and essential-services remedies each carry an express tenant-fault exception - the tenant may not terminate or claim for a condition caused by their own or their household's deliberate or negligent act (§§76-1425, 76-1427). The casualty section has NO such exception. §76-1429 makes the tenant pay for the damage but still lets them vacate and end the lease on 14 days' written notice, or stay and pay proportionally reduced rent, even where they caused the fire. A lease term saying rent will not abate or that a tenant at fault cannot terminate would take away a right the Act gives them, which §76-1415(1)(a) voids - and if you used it knowing it was prohibited, §76-1415(2) adds the tenant's actual damages and attorney's fees. Charge for the damage; do not try to trap the tenant in the lease.

title: Converting to Condominiums: 60 Days, a For-Cause-Only Window, and a Right of First Refusal
bodyText: If you are converting a building to condominiums, Nebraska gives the sitting residential tenants and subtenants a set of rights that override your ordinary notice position (§76-886). NOTICE: you must give each residential tenant and any subtenant in possession notice of the conversion, with the public-offering statement if there is one, no later than 60 days before they are required to vacate, hand delivered to the unit or sent by prepaid US mail, and the notice must set out generally the rights this section gives them. FOR THOSE 60 DAYS YOU ARE IN A FOR-CAUSE-ONLY WINDOW: no tenant or subtenant may be required to vacate on less than 60 days' notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste, or conduct that disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment - and you may not alter the terms of the tenancy during that period. If you skip the notice, that failure is a defense to your action for possession. RIGHT OF FIRST REFUSAL: for 60 days after the notice you may offer to sell each unit occupied for residential use to the tenant who leases it; if you make the offer and they do not buy within those 60 days, you may not offer that unit to anyone else on better price or terms for the next 30 days. If you sell in breach of that rule to a buyer who does not know of the breach, recording a deed that states you complied ends the tenant's right to buy that unit. It does not end the tenant's right to recover damages from you (§76-886(c)). That does not apply to a unit that will be restricted to non-residential use, or where the converted unit's boundaries do not substantially match the residential unit. TWO MORE POINTS: a conversion notice that specifies a date by which the unit must be vacated counts as a notice to vacate, and nothing in the section lets you terminate a lease in breach of its own terms. A tenant can waive these protections, but only by a written instrument signed AFTER the date of the notice - so your lease cannot do it in advance.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting Software
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute regulating algorithmic or software-assisted rent pricing. There is no ban on using revenue-management software, no disclosure duty if you do, and no state antitrust provision aimed at shared pricing data in rental housing. Federal antitrust law and any private litigation are a separate question this does not address.

title: In Nebraska Every Payment Under the Lease Is "Rent" - Which Cuts Both Ways
bodyText: Nebraska defines rent broadly by statute: 'Rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement' (§76-1410(13)). You do not need a lease sentence designating fees as additional rent - the definition already does it. The consequence runs both ways. In your favour, an unpaid fee that the lease requires the tenant to pay to you is on its face 'rent', which matters because §76-1431(2) lets you terminate when rent is unpaid and the tenant does not pay within seven calendar days of your written notice. Against you, anything the lease makes payable to you is swept into every other rule that turns on 'rent' - including the deposit cap, which is measured in rent, and the holdover and damages measures.
