Those measures, though, are written in 'periodic rent': the deposit cap and the pet deposit are measured in 'one month's periodic rent' (§76-1416(1)), and the holdover and ouster figures in 'three months' periodic rent' (§§76-1437(3), 76-1430). The Act does not define 'periodic rent', so whether a fee counts toward it is not settled by the text. The cautious course is to measure the deposit cap on the regular monthly rent alone, so adding a fee to the lease never lets you take a larger deposit. Note that the standard Tenant Default clause says that failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying rent, will not by itself support termination or eviction. That is a choice to ask for less than Nebraska law allows, not a legal requirement.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix the Tenant's Breach and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Nebraska did not adopt the URLTA provision that lets a landlord remedy a tenant's breach and charge the cost as rent. If the tenant fails to do something the lease or §76-1421 requires, your statutory routes are the notice-and-cure termination at §76-1431(1), damages and injunctive relief under §76-1431(3) - with attorney's fees if the noncompliance was willful - and, for a tenant who breaches the duty to maintain, the ordinary measures. There is no statutory self-help-and-bill mechanism, so doing the work yourself and adding it to the next rent demand is a contract claim, not a statutory one, and treating it as rent risks a defective nonpayment notice.

title: No Rule Against Blank Spaces, and No Duty to Give the Tenant a Copy
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute requiring a written lease to have every blank space completed, and no statute making an incomplete lease a material noncompliance. It also imposes no duty to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and no consequence for failing to - unlike states where that failure is a defense to enforcement. That is the rule for ordinary rentals. For a mobile home space, the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act requires each side to deliver a signed copy of a written rental agreement, and failing to is a material noncompliance (§76-1481). Fill in the blanks and hand over a copy anyway: both are ordinary evidence of what was agreed, and Nebraska's broad deceptive-practices standard is a live backstop even without a specific rule.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession in a Lease
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute writing a covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession into a residential lease. The one statutory provision on quiet enjoyment, §76-207, is about covenants in CONVEYANCES of real property - deed warranties broken by actual or constructive eviction by someone with paramount title - and does not reach a landlord and tenant. What Nebraska does give the tenant instead is specific and narrower: the habitability duties at §76-1419, the remedies for an unlawful ouster or a cut-off of services at §76-1430, and the bar on recovering possession except through the Act at §76-1436. A common-law implied covenant may still exist; that is case law, not statute.

title: Nebraska Prescribes No Lease or Notice Forms
bodyText: Nebraska prescribes no form for a residential lease and no wording you must copy into one. Your lease-side notices generally need only contain what the relevant section requires - for example a termination notice specifying the acts constituting the breach and the termination date under §76-1431(1), or 30 days to the periodic rental date under §76-1437(2). ONE IMPORTANT EXCEPTION, outside the landlord-tenant act: if a tenant leaves property behind, the notice you must send under Nebraska's Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act has to contain one of two statements set out WORD FOR WORD in the statute, and which one you use depends on whether you believe the property is worth less than two thousand dollars (§69-2304). That is prescribed statutory text in the strict sense, and a notice missing it is not a compliant notice - see the Handling of Property Left Behind guidance. The other places Nebraska prescribes contents are court filings in a possession case, and you draft two of them. The complaint for restitution you file must contain set items (§76-1441). The summons has set contents too (§76-1442). If the summons is served by posting on the door and first-class mail, you must file an affidavit describing your diligent efforts at ordinary service, why they failed, and the posting and mailing (§76-1442.01). That route also means no money judgment for you in the case (§76-1446). In a forcible entry and detainer case, the writ of execution follows the form §25-21,230 sets out, 'as nearly as practicable'. One more prescribed text sits outside ordinary renting: if in the course of your business you buy a home in foreclosure from the owner who lives there and lease it back to them, the equity purchase contract must contain the lease terms and a notice whose words §76-2720(1)(j) sets out, in at least fourteen-point boldface type.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute giving a tenant the right to install a security camera or video doorbell, and none restricting one. So it is governed by your lease: the No Alterations clause already requires your written consent before the tenant attaches anything to the property, and the Use of Property & Common Areas clause covers fixing things to exterior surfaces. Two cautions that are not lease questions. A camera that records audio can raise wiretapping issues, and one that overlooks another tenant's unit can raise privacy ones; neither is answered by the landlord-tenant act. Treat a request from a tenant with a disability as a reasonable-accommodation question instead.

title: Nebraska's Constitution Protects Gun Ownership - But It Does Not Bind You
bodyText: Nebraska's constitution contains a right to keep and bear arms, and landlords regularly assume it stops them restricting guns in a rental. It does not. Article I-1 lists among the inalienable rights 'the right to keep and bear arms for security or defense of self, family, home, and others, and for lawful common defense, hunting, recreational use, and all other lawful purposes', and then says those rights 'shall not be denied or infringed BY THE STATE OR ANY SUBDIVISION THEREOF'. That last clause is the whole point: it binds government, not a private landlord writing a lease. So a privately owned rental may restrict firearms by lease term, and Nebraska has no statute - unlike several other states in this library - making such a term unenforceable against a permit holder or protecting a tenant's firearms in rental housing. Two places the constitutional limit does bite. A city, village or county is a subdivision, so a local ordinance could not compel landlords to ban firearms, or ban them in rentals outright. And housing owned or operated by a public body is the state or a subdivision acting, so a public housing authority is bound where a private owner is not. Nothing in the standard lease restricts firearms, so this is a decision you can make either way rather than a problem to fix.

title: The Nebraska Fair Housing Act's Exemptions
bodyText: The Nebraska Fair Housing Act's bans apply 'Except as exempted by section 20-322', so check the exemptions separately. Three matter most to a landlord. (1) ROOMS IN YOUR OWN HOME: you may refuse to rent a room or rooms in your own home for any reason or no reason, and change tenants there as often as you like, but not if you make more than four sleeping rooms available to a person or family within your home (§20-322(3)). (2) OCCUPANCY LIMITS AND OLDER PERSONS: the Act does not limit reasonable local restrictions on the maximum number of occupants of a dwelling, and its familial-status rules do not apply to qualifying housing for older persons: housing under a state elderly program, housing solely occupied by people 62 or older, or housing for at least one person 55 or older per unit that meets the 80 percent occupancy and published-policy tests (§20-322(4)). (3) DRUG CONVICTIONS: the Act does not prohibit conduct against a person because the person has been convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance (§20-322(5)). These are state exemptions only: federal fair housing law has its own exemptions, and the HIV and AIDS housing rule in §20-168 has none.

title: Nebraska's Fire-and-Casualty and Mitigation Rules Cannot Be Varied by the Lease
bodyText: The plain answer: no. A Nebraska residential lease cannot shorten, condition or contract out of either the tenant's fire-and-casualty rights or the duty to mitigate damages. Section 76-1429(1) gives the tenant two choices when fire or casualty damages the dwelling unit or premises 'to an extent that enjoyment of the dwelling unit is substantially impaired': the tenant may '[i]mmediately vacate the premises and notify the landlord in writing within fourteen days thereafter of his intention to terminate the rental agreement, in which case the rental agreement terminates as of the date of vacating', or, 'if continued occupancy is lawful', vacate only the unusable part, 'in which case the tenant's liability for rent is reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value of the dwelling unit.' Section 76-1429(2) then requires the landlord to 'return all prepaid rent and security recoverable under section 76-1416' and fixes the accounting date as the date of the casualty. Section 76-1405(1) adds that 'the aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages' — which binds whichever party is suing, so it binds you when the tenant walks out and you sue for the rest of the term. Both are rights and obligations declared by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and section 76-1415(1)(a) says no rental agreement may provide that the tenant 'agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.' So a clause saying the tenant must give notice before vacating, or must give it within seven days instead of fourteen, or forfeits the exit right if the tenant caused the fire, or that rent continues in full while the unit is uninhabitable, or that the landlord has no duty to re-let, is unenforceable under section 76-1415(2) — and if you use a term you know is prohibited, the tenant 'may recover actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees' (§ 76-1415(2)). Three practical points. FIRST, the drafting contrast inside the Act is deliberate: eleven chapter 76 sections open 'unless otherwise agreed', including §§ 76-1414, 76-1420, 76-1424 and 76-1433, and neither § 76-1429 nor § 76-1405 is among them, so this is a legislative choice rather than a silence you can read your way into. SECOND, there is exactly one thing the lease may do here, and it is the thing the statute already does: § 76-1429(2) ends 'Notwithstanding the provisions of this section, the tenant is responsible for damage caused by his negligence', and the Nebraska Supreme Court has held that 'where a specific statute holds a tenant responsible for fire damages caused by his or her negligence, a court cannot hold a lease provision doing so as void against public policy or unconscionable' (SFI Ltd. Partnership 8 v. Carroll, 288 Neb. 698, 851 N.W.2d 82 (2014)). A tenant-negligence clause is safe; note that it makes the tenant pay for the damage and does not take away the tenant's exit. THIRD, the lease may add a landlord-side casualty termination, because § 76-1429 gives rights to the tenant only and the Act gives the landlord none — that is what "Landlord Termination After Fire or Casualty" clause is for, and its closing sentence preserving both of the tenant's limbs is what keeps it out of § 76-1415(1)(a). Waiver is possible only after the fact and only on the landlord's side: § 76-1433 lets the landlord accept rent with knowledge of a default, and § 76-1430's three months' rent for unlawful ouster shows what the Act charges for self-help, neither of which gives the lease any advance variation of § 76-1429.

title: In Nebraska You Must Re-Let - and Re-Letting Ends the Lease You Were Suing On
bodyText:
Many states let a landlord leave an abandoned unit empty, keep the lease alive and sue for the rent as it falls due. Nebraska does not. Section 76-1432(3) is written in the imperative: 'If the tenant abandons the dwelling unit, the landlord shall take immediate possession and shall make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental.' Two duties, both mandatory, and they start the moment the unit is abandoned - not when you get around to it. The sentence that follows is the one landlords miss: 'If the landlord rents the dwelling unit for a term beginning prior to the expiration of the rental agreement, it is deemed to be terminated as of the date the new tenancy begins.' So the moment you re-let, the old lease is over by operation of law. You cannot collect the departed tenant's rent and the new tenant's rent for the same month, and you cannot carry the old lease forward to the end of its stated term.

WHEN IS IT ABANDONMENT? Section 76-1432(3)'s own test is 'Total absence from the premises without notice to landlord for one full rental period or thirty days, whichever is less' - for a month-to-month tenancy that is the rental period, which can be shorter than thirty days. But the Nebraska Supreme Court has held that this 'does not abrogate or displace common law concerning abandonment of real estate leased for residential purposes', that abandonment occurs when a tenant 'with the intention to terminate contractual rights to exclusive possession or control of leased premises, voluntarily relinquishes or vacates' them, and that in the absence of explicit abandonment a landlord's self-help recovery inside the first thirty days 'may depend on unequivocal but circumstantial proof of the tenant's abandonment' (Mason v. Schumacher, 231 Neb. 929, 439 N.W.2d 61 (1989)).

That matters because section 76-1436 bars you from recovering possession 'by action or otherwise' except 'in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted' by the Act, and section 76-1430 charges three months' periodic rent for getting it wrong. Abandonment is the one safe self-help route, and you are betting on your proof.

WHAT YOU CAN STILL RECOVER. Section 76-1435 gives you possession plus 'a claim for rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement and reasonable attorney's fees as provided in subsection (3) of section 76-1431' - and section 76-1431(3) gives attorney's fees only where 'the tenant's noncompliance is willful.' Section 76-1416(2) lets you apply the deposit to 'the payment of rent and the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance.' Actual damages are the measure: lost rent until a reasonable re-letting, advertising and turnover costs, the shortfall if the fair market rent has dropped. Keep the receipts and the listing records.

And section 76-1405(1) puts the duty on top of all of it: 'The aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages.'

WHAT THE LEASE CANNOT DO. There is no 'unless otherwise agreed' in section 76-1432 or section 76-1405 - eleven chapter 76 sections open with that phrase and these two are not among them - and section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any provision by which the tenant 'agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under' the Act, with section 76-1415(2) adding the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees if you used a term you knew was prohibited.

So a clause saying the landlord need not re-let, that the tenant owes all rent for the balance of the term whatever happens, that rent keeps running after a new tenancy starts, or that acceleration applies instead of actual damages, is unenforceable. Your default clause should promise mitigation and claim actual damages, which is what Tenant Default already does.

title: No Nebraska Alarm-Tampering Fee - Charge the Actual Cost Instead
bodyText: Some states fix a dollar figure a landlord may charge a tenant who removes or disables a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm - Oregon allows up to a stated amount per occurrence. Nebraska has nothing of the kind. The Carbon Monoxide Safety Act (sections 76-601 to 76-607) prohibits the conduct without attaching any charge, penalty or remedy to it: section 76-606(5) says 'No person shall remove batteries from, or in any way render inoperable, a carbon monoxide alarm except as part of a process to inspect, maintain, repair, or replace the alarm or replace the batteries in the alarm' - and that is where the Act stops. There is no fine, no fee, no liquidated sum and no private action anywhere in the seven sections, and section 76-607 says only that cities, villages and counties remain free to adopt 'more stringent' alarm requirements, so a local ordinance is the one place a penalty could come from. The smoke-detector mandate sits in the State Fire Marshal statutes (sections 81-5,142 and 81-5,144) and allocates duties between owner and occupant; it likewise sets no charge. WHAT YOU CAN ACTUALLY RECOVER, AND HOW. Nebraska gives you an actual-cost route, not a fee. Section 76-1421(6) makes it a tenant duty to 'Not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or knowingly permit any person to do so', and section 76-1421(5) requires the tenant to 'Use in a reasonable manner all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances' - a disabled alarm is squarely inside both. Section 76-1416(2) then lets you apply the deposit to 'the payment of rent and the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or section 76-1421', itemized in the written statement you must deliver or mail within fourteen days of termination. Section 76-1431(3) lets you 'recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for any noncompliance by the tenant with the rental agreement or section 76-1421', with reasonable attorney's fees only 'if the tenant's noncompliance is willful.' And section 76-1414(1) confirms you may write the charge into the lease, because the parties 'may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by' the Act. So bill the cost of the alarm and the labour, keep the invoice, and itemize it. WHY NOT A FLAT FEE. Three reasons. First, no statute authorizes one, so it stands or falls as liquidated damages, and a sum untethered to your actual loss reads as a penalty. Second, the Act measures your recovery in actual terms throughout - 'actual damages' in sections 76-1432(1) and 76-1435, 'damages which the landlord has suffered' in section 76-1416(2) - and section 76-1412 lets a court strike an unconscionable provision. Third, in Nebraska every payment due under the lease is rent, which drags a standing per-occurrence fee into your rent accounting and your deposit ceiling. If you want a number in the lease anyway, make it a stated estimate of the replacement cost of the specific device, say it is an estimate and that you will charge the actual cost if it is lower, and keep it out of the deposit cap. SEPARATELY, DO NOT FORGET YOUR OWN SIDE OF SECTION 76-606(5): the prohibition runs against 'No person', which includes you and your maintenance staff. Nebraska's Carbon Monoxide Alarms clause already states it for both parties with the inspect-maintain-repair-replace exception intact; the Smoke Detectors clause already bars the tenant from disabling, obstructing or tampering with a smoke detector. The library also carries a shared detector-care clause used in seven other jurisdictions that adds a cost-recovery sentence; Nebraska does not use it, for the reason recorded in this row's notes, and you may of course add your own actual-cost sentence to the two Nebraska clauses instead.

title: Nebraska Allows a Lease Arbitration Clause - Under a Constitutional Test and a Formatting Rule That Void It If You Get Them Wrong
bodyText: Nebraska is one of the few states where a predispute arbitration clause has to clear a test written into the state constitution. Article I, section 13 opens 'All courts shall be open, and every person, for any injury done him or her in his or her lands, goods, person, or reputation, shall have a remedy by due course of law and justice administered without denial or delay' - and then carves out, by a 1996 amendment, that 'the Legislature may provide for the enforcement of mediation, binding arbitration agreements, and other forms of dispute resolution WHICH ARE ENTERED INTO VOLUNTARILY and which are not revocable other than upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any contract.' Before that amendment the Nebraska Supreme Court had held the predecessor statute unconstitutional to the extent it provided for arbitration of future disputes (State v. Nebraska Assn. of Pub. Employees, 239 Neb. 653, 477 N.W.2d 577 (1991)), and any predispute clause signed before June 11, 1997 is void as against public policy (Millennium Solutions, Inc. v. Davis, 258 Neb. 293, 603 N.W.2d 406 (1999)). The statute the Legislature then wrote tracks the constitution word for word: section 25-2602.01(b) makes a provision 'in a written contract to submit to arbitration any controversy thereafter arising between the parties' valid and enforceable 'if the provision is entered into voluntarily and willingly.' That is an extra element Nebraska requires and most states do not, and it is the element a boilerplate clause in a standard-form residential lease is least likely to satisfy. FOUR THINGS THAT WILL DEFEAT A LEASE ARBITRATION CLAUSE HERE. FIRST, THE FORMATTING RULE, and it is strict. Section 25-2602.02: 'The following statement shall appear in capitalized, underlined type adjoining the signature block of any standardized agreement in which binding arbitration is the sole remedy for dispute resolution: THIS CONTRACT CONTAINS AN ARBITRATION PROVISION WHICH MAY BE ENFORCED BY THE PARTIES.' A residential lease on a standard form is a standardized agreement. 'When a contract which attempts to establish binding arbitration as the sole remedy fails to strictly comply with this section, the arbitration clause is voidable and unenforceable' (Kramer v. Eagle Eye Home Inspections, 14 Neb. App. 691, 716 N.W.2d 749 (2006)) - strict compliance, so capitalized AND underlined AND adjoining the signature block AND in those exact words. One limit: where federal law governs the contract, leaving the statement out does not make the clause unenforceable (Aramark Uniform & Career Apparel v. Hunan, Inc., 276 Neb. 700, 757 N.W.2d 205 (2008)). Whether federal law governs a given residential lease is a question only case law settles, so include the statement anyway. SECOND, IT CANNOT REACH A PERSONAL-INJURY CLAIM. Section 25-2602.01(f)(1) says subsection (b) does not apply to 'a claim arising out of personal injury based on tort.' So the tenant who is hurt by a defective stair or a falling fixture goes to court whatever the lease says, and section 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence - 'The obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state' - means that is exactly the claim you were hoping to divert. THIRD, FEES. Section 76-1415(1)(c) forbids any rental agreement providing that the tenant 'agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees', and section 25-2611 allocates the arbitrators' and other expenses 'as provided in the award' 'unless otherwise provided in the agreement to arbitrate', 'not including counsel fees'. An arbitration clause that makes the loser pay fees, or splits the arbitrator's fee in a way that prices the tenant out, runs at section 76-1415(1)(c) and at section 76-1415(1)(a)'s bar on the tenant waiving 'rights or remedies under' the Act - and the Act's own fee awards under sections 76-1416(3), 76-1430 and 76-1438(2) are such remedies. FOURTH, THE FORUM. Section 25-2618(a) defines 'court' for the Uniform Arbitration Act as 'any district court of this state'; the county court has no jurisdiction to confirm an award (MBNA America Bank v. Hansen, 16 Neb. App. 536, 745 N.W.2d 609 (2008)). Your eviction, by contrast, is a county-court possession action under sections 76-1440 to 76-1446, and a writ of restitution issues from that court. Do not try to arbitrate possession. WHY THIS LIBRARY GIVES YOU NO ARBITRATION CLAUSE FOR NEBRASKA. The option is lawful - section 76-1406 confirms that 'a claim or right arising under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or on a rental agreement may be settled by agreement', and section 76-1414(1) lets the parties include any term the Act does not prohibit - but a clause printed in the standard form is the worst possible vehicle for a requirement that the agreement be 'entered into voluntarily and willingly', and it buys you nothing on the two disputes you actually have (possession and unpaid rent, both quick and cheap in county court) while surrendering nothing on the one you fear (personal injury, which section 25-2602.01(f)(1) keeps in court anyway). If you still want one, take it out of the lease: put it in a separately signed, separately dated addendum the tenant can decline without losing the unit, keep possession actions and the Act's remedies and fee awards expressly out of it, and reproduce section 25-2602.02's statement in capitalized underlined type adjoining the signature block. Then have a Nebraska lawyer look at it.

title: No Animal-Care Entry Right in Nebraska - But Section 76-1432(2) Gives You One After Seven Days
bodyText: A tenant is hospitalized, arrested or simply gone, and there is a dog inside. Nebraska gives you no entry right for the animal as such - but it gives you two real routes, and the trap is that neither of them is a clause in your lease. START WITH WHY A CLAUSE WILL NOT DO IT. Section 76-1423 lists what you may enter for: the tenant 'shall not unreasonably withhold consent to the landlord to enter into the dwelling unit in order to inspect the premises, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workmen, or contractors.' Caring for an animal is not on that list. Then subsection (4) closes the door: 'The landlord has no other right of access except by court order, as permitted by subsection (2) of section 76-1432, or if the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises.' That is an exhaustive sentence, and an advance consent printed in the lease sits badly against it, because section 76-1415(1)(a) makes a rental agreement term void where the tenant 'agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under' the Act, and freedom from entry outside section 76-1423 is such a right. The price of getting it wrong is set in section 76-1438(2): on an unlawful entry, or a lawful entry made in an unreasonable manner, the tenant may get an injunction or terminate the lease and 'may recover actual damages not less than an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees.' Note the floor - a minimum recovery whether or not the tenant proves any loss. ROUTE ONE: EMERGENCY. Section 76-1423(2): 'The landlord may enter the dwelling unit without consent of the tenant in case of emergency.' An animal in acute distress, or one that has become a danger or a health hazard to the building, is the natural case for it. Document what you saw and why you treated it as an emergency before you open the door, because you will be proving it later. ROUTE TWO, AND THE ONE WORTH KNOWING: SEVEN DAYS. Section 76-1432(2): 'During any absence of the tenant in excess of seven days, the landlord may enter the dwelling unit at times reasonably necessary.' There is no purpose limit on that sentence, so once the tenant has been absent more than seven days you may enter to feed, water or remove an animal, and section 76-1423(4) expressly names this as one of the three exceptions to its closed list. Make the seven days work for you: section 76-1424 says 'The rental agreement may require that the tenant notify the landlord of any anticipated extended absence from the premises in excess of seven days no later than the first day of the extended absence', and section 76-1432(1) lets you 'recover actual damages from the tenant' if the tenant willfully fails to give that notice. Nebraska's Notice of Extended Absence clause already carries this. WHAT YOU CANNOT PROMISE YOURSELF IN THE LEASE. Do not write a clause saying animal control will come and take the animal. Section 28-1012(1) says a law enforcement officer or animal control officer who has reason to believe an animal has been abandoned or is being cruelly neglected or mistreated 'may seek a warrant authorizing entry' upon private property 'to inspect, care for, or impound the animal.' They need the warrant; you cannot waive it for them, and their decision is theirs. What you can do is report: section 28-1017 sets up the reporting channel for animal abandonment, cruel neglect and cruel mistreatment, and anyone who reports 'is immune from liability except for false statements of fact made with malicious intent.' So call it in, and say what you saw. THE PRACTICAL SEQUENCE. Try to reach the tenant, and keep the record. If it is an emergency, enter under section 76-1423(2) and document why. If it is not, report to animal control or law enforcement and let section 28-1012 run. If the tenant has been gone more than seven days, enter under section 76-1432(2). If none of that fits, ask the county court for an order - section 76-1423(4) names a court order first among its exceptions for a reason. One last thing: do not treat the animal as abandoned property. Section 76-1432(3) sets abandonment of the unit at 'one full rental period or thirty days, whichever is less', and the Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act route in section 76-1414(5) is for goods, not for a living animal.

title: You Cannot Leave an Appliance Behind and Disclaim It - What Nebraska Actually Lets You Exclude
bodyText: The common move is a lease paragraph saying the washer and dryer in the basement are 'not included' and the landlord will not maintain them. In Nebraska that paragraph mostly does not work, and the reason is a single phrase. Section 76-1419(1)(d) makes you 'maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her.' Two things follow. First, the duty tracks supply - so if you leave the appliance there for the tenant's use, you supplied it. Section 76-1410(12) puts it beyond argument: 'Premises means a dwelling unit and the structure of which it is a part and FACILITIES AND APPURTENANCES THEREIN and grounds, areas, and facilities held out for the use of tenants generally or whose use is promised to the tenant.' Second, 'or required to be supplied' means a promise creates the duty even where no statute would - so the moment the appliance goes into your Appliances & Equipment Included list, you have signed up to maintain it, and a later paragraph taking it back out is working against your own lease. THE ONLY LAWFUL WAY TO SHIFT IT, AND IT IS NOT A DISCLAIMER. Nebraska does not have an 'items not included' mechanism. What it has is section 76-1419(2) and (3), and those are agreements to PERFORM duties, not clauses abolishing them. The split turns on property type and the formalities are different for each; Nebraska's own education row on delegating maintenance duties sets this out and should be read before you draft anything. The headline is that for a dwelling unit which is NOT a single-family residence as section 76-1410(16) defines it, you need a separate writing signed by both parties and supported by adequate consideration, and it cannot diminish your obligations to other tenants - a paragraph inside the lease will not do. Section 76-1419(4) adds a different route that is often the practical one: 'Notwithstanding any provision of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a landlord may employ a tenant to perform the obligations of the landlord.' THREE THINGS YOU CAN NEVER EXCLUDE. Section 76-1419(1)(f) - running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat - cannot be shifted at all except in a single-family residence under section 76-1419(2), so a water heater or a furnace is never an excludable appliance. Section 76-1419(1)(b)'s duty to 'make all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition' reaches anything whose failure makes the home unfit, whatever the lease calls it. And section 76-1419(1)(c) keeps all common areas on you, which is where the shared laundry usually is. DO NOT WRITE THE EXCULPATORY HALF AT ALL. Clauses of this kind usually end by disclaiming liability for the excluded item. Section 76-1415(1)(d) voids any rental agreement term by which the tenant 'agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord or to indemnify the landlord for that liability arising due to active and actionable negligence or the costs connected therewith', and section 76-1415(2) makes the term unenforceable and adds the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees if you used it knowing it was prohibited. Nebraska's bar is wider than the common 'gross fault or intentional act' carve-out other states use: it catches ordinary active negligence, including negligence that damages property rather than injuring anyone. WHAT TO DO INSTEAD, IN ORDER OF SAFETY. Remove the item before the tenancy starts - that is the only exclusion Nebraska really recognises. If you leave it, leave it off the Appliances & Equipment Included list, record in the move-in condition sheet that it is present, as-is, not part of the let and that the tenant may ask you to remove it, and do not promise to maintain it anywhere. If you want the tenant to maintain it, use section 76-1419(2) or (3) with the right formalities for the property type, or employ them under section 76-1419(4). Keep the health-and-safety core out of all of it. ONE DEFINITION TRAP WORTH NAMING. Section 76-1410(15) says a 'Roomer' is a person 'occupying a dwelling unit that lacks a major bathroom or kitchen facility', and that 'Major facility ... in the case of a kitchen means refrigerator, stove, or sink.' That is a classification sentence - it tells you whether an occupant is a roomer, and whether your tenancy is week-to-week under section 76-1414(4). It is not a requirement that you supply a refrigerator, a stove or a sink, and it should not be read as one in either direction.

title: Nebraska Defines Notice Three Ways - and Giving It Does Not Require the Tenant to Receive It
bodyText: Some states let the lease add an extra way of giving actual notice - Oregon expressly permits an agreed additional method such as a text message. Nebraska has no provision of that kind. What it has instead is a definition broad enough that you usually do not need one, and a short list of places the lease may designate. START WITH WHAT COUNTS AS NOTICE. Section 76-1413(1): 'A person has notice of a fact if: (a) Such person has actual knowledge of it; (b) Such person has received a notice or notification of it; or (c) From all facts and circumstances known to such person at the time in question, such person has reason to know that it exists. A person knows or has knowledge of a fact if such person has actual knowledge of it.' Three independent routes, and the third is constructive - what the party had reason to know from the circumstances. THEN THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST TO YOU. Section 76-1413(2): 'A person notifies or gives a notice or notification to another by taking steps reasonably calculated to inform the other in ordinary course WHETHER OR NOT THE OTHER ACTUALLY COMES TO KNOW OF IT.' You give notice by doing the reasonable thing; the tenant's claim never to have read it does not undo it. The one exception is built into the same section: where a law 'expressly requires verification or acknowledgment of receipt', section 76-1413(11)(a) lets you deliver electronically only by a method that supplies it. WHERE IT HAS TO GO, AND WHAT THE LEASE MAY SET. Section 76-1413(2) tells you when a notice is received. To the tenant: 'Delivered in hand to the tenant'; 'Mailed to the tenant at the place held out by the tenant as the place for receipt of the communication, or in the absence of such designation, to the tenant's last-known place of residence'; or 'Delivered by electronic means.' To the landlord: 'Delivered at the place of business of the landlord through which the rental agreement was made or at any place held out by the landlord as the place for receipt of the communication'; or 'Delivered by electronic means.' So what the lease usefully fixes is the PLACE each party holds out, not an extra method - and the fallback for a tenant who designates nothing is the last-known place of residence, which is why you should keep a forwarding address in the file. YOUR REPAIR DUTY ACCEPTS ORAL NOTICE. This is the practical trap. Section 76-1419(1)(a) and (1)(b) both read 'after WRITTEN OR ACTUAL notice' - so a tenant who tells your maintenance man in the hallway that the furnace is out has started your clock, and a lease clause demanding that all repair requests be in writing does not change the statute. Log every oral report with a date. WHERE NEBRASKA DOES INSIST ON A WRITING, actual notice will not substitute: your notices terminating for noncompliance or nonpayment under section 76-1431(1) and (2), your twenty-four-hour entry notice under section 76-1423(3)(a), your deposit itemization under section 76-1416(2), the periodic-tenancy terminations under section 76-1437(1) and (2), the section 76-1417 disclosure, the tenant's fourteen-day casualty notice under section 76-1429(1)(a), and the agreements shifting maintenance duties under section 76-1419(2) and (3). Section 76-1410(18) is the saving grace: 'Writing or written, when used in reference to a notice or document to be provided by or to a landlord or tenant, includes a notice or document provided by electronic means in accordance with section 76-1413.' SO CAN YOUR LEASE MAKE A TEXT MESSAGE GOOD NOTICE? Not as a substitute for a statutory writing. Section 76-1413(4) defines 'delivered by electronic means' as delivery to a consented electronic MAIL address, or a posting on an electronic network or site plus separate notice of the posting sent by electronic mail or another consented method. A bare SMS is not on that list, and section 76-1413(10) says the section 'does not affect any requirement related to the content or timing of any notice or document required under applicable law' - so you cannot agree your way around either. What a text does do is prove actual knowledge under section 76-1413(1)(a) and help show you took steps reasonably calculated to inform under section 76-1413(2), so use it as a belt alongside the statutory method, never instead of it. And remember section 76-1413(9): you may not require a tenant to accept electronic delivery as part of the lease or as a condition of entering into or renewing it. Nebraska's full electronic-consent machinery, which is detailed and unforgiving, is set out in the Nebraska education row on the 2025 electronic notice rules; read it before you switch any notice to email.

title: No Duty to Warn Your Tenant About a Foreclosure - But in a Condemnation the Tenant Is a Party by Statute
bodyText: Nebraska splits this question in two, and the two halves come out opposite ways. FORECLOSURE, RECEIVERSHIP AND TAX SALE: NO DUTY. Nothing in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and nothing elsewhere in Nebraska's landlord-tenant law, requires you to tell a tenant that the property is being foreclosed, that a receiver has been appointed, that a construction lien has been filed or that the taxes are being enforced. The only provisions in the Act that use the words 'notify the tenant' are your own notices under section 76-1431, the restitution complaint under section 76-1441, and section 76-1420 - which is not a duty at all but an escape hatch, and it is worth using for your own sake. Section 76-1420(1) relieves a landlord who conveys the premises 'in a good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser' of liability 'as to events occurring subsequent to WRITTEN NOTICE TO THE TENANT of the conveyance', and separately requires assignment of deposits and prepaid rents with written notice to the tenant before you are off the hook for those. Nebraska's education row on selling the property sets that out. Note the legislature's own choice here: the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act DOES impose the duty the residential act omits - section 76-1487 says that upon termination of a landlord's interest in a mobile home park the landlord 'shall, within a reasonable time, (1) transfer the rental deposit ... to the landlord's successor in interest and NOTIFY THE TENANT IN WRITING of the transfer and of the transferee's name and address or (2) return the deposit', the notice stating the amount and given by mail or personal service. Same legislature, same chapter, mandatory language for mobile home parks and none for apartments. That silence is a decision, not an oversight. TWO THINGS THAT FOLLOW ANYWAY. Your buyer or the foreclosure purchaser inherits the deposit problem: section 76-1416(5) says 'the holder of the landlord's interest in the premises at the time of the termination of the tenancy is bound by this section', so the deposit duty runs with the property whatever the sale documents say. And a new owner or manager restarts your section 76-1417 duty to disclose in writing the name and address of the manager and of an owner or authorised agent for service of process - section 76-1417(2) says the information 'shall be kept current and this section extends to and is enforceable against any successor landlord, owner, or manager', and section 76-1417(3) makes a person who fails to comply the agent of each landlord for service and for performing the landlord's obligations. CONDEMNATION IS DIFFERENT: YOUR TENANT IS ALREADY A PARTY. Read section 76-701(2): 'Condemnee means any person, partnership, limited liability company, corporation, or association owning or having an encumbrance on any interest in property that is sought to be acquired by a condemner OR IN POSSESSION OF OR OCCUPYING ANY SUCH PROPERTY.' A tenant in possession is a condemnee in their own right. So section 76-706 entitles them to notice directly from the condemner: 'Notice of intention to acquire the property and of the time and place of meeting of the board of appraisers to have the damages assessed shall be served upon the condemnee at least ten days prior to the meeting of the board of appraisers', served in the manner of a summons in a civil action. ONE GAP IN THAT PROTECTION, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT WILL LAND ON YOU. Section 76-710 requires the appraisers' report to be transmitted to the condemnee within ten days, but adds: 'When title or interest in a single parcel of land is held by several condemnees the transmission of such copy to any one of such owners of interest shall be considered compliance with such requirement.' So the court may satisfy that step by sending the report to you alone, and your tenant may never see the number or learn that their appeal clock is running. Tell them. It costs nothing and it is the one step the statute lets fall between you. FINALLY, A RECORDING POINT WORTH KNOWING BEFORE A FORECLOSURE, NOT AFTER. A lease for more than one year is outside section 76-211's exception for 'leases for one year or for a less time', so it is an instrument that can be recorded - and section 76-238(1) makes an unrecorded instrument void as against a creditor or later purchaser in good faith without notice who records first, 'However, such instruments are valid between the parties to the instrument.' A long unrecorded lease is good against you and weak against the bank. If the tenancy matters to the deal, record it or get a subordination and non-disturbance agreement; do not assume possession alone will carry it. Federal law may give a tenant further post-foreclosure rights, and that is outside this library's Nebraska research - take advice before you treat a foreclosure sale as ending a tenancy.

title: Nebraska Has No Children Clause - and Writing One Would Break the Law
bodyText: Nevada requires a residential lease to address occupancy by children as part of a required-content list. Nebraska requires the opposite, and if you have carried a 'children' paragraph in from another state's form, take it out. FAMILIAL STATUS IS A PROTECTED CLASS AND THE DEFINITION IS WIDE. Section 20-311: 'Familial status shall mean one or more minors being domiciled with: (1) A parent or another person having legal custody of such individual; or (2) The designee of a parent or other person having legal custody, with the written permission of the parent or other person', and 'The protections afforded against discrimination on the basis of familial status shall apply to any person who is pregnant or is in the process of securing legal custody of any minor.' So it reaches a grandparent with custody, a designee holding written permission, an expectant tenant and a tenant mid-adoption - not only the conventional parent-and-child household. Section 20-318 then makes it unlawful, among other things, to refuse to rent, to 'discriminate against any person in the TERMS, CONDITIONS, OR PRIVILEGES of sale or rental of a dwelling or in the provision of services or facilities in connection therewith' because of familial status, or to publish any 'notice, statement, or advertisement' indicating a preference or limitation based on it. A lease term is a term and condition of the rental, and a listing is an advertisement. AND NEBRASKA BANS THE QUESTION, NOT JUST THE DECISION. Section 20-318(5) makes it unlawful to 'cause to be made any written or oral inquiry or record concerning the race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, sex, or military or veteran status of a person seeking to purchase, rent, or lease any housing.' Asking how many children an applicant has, or writing it on the file, is itself the violation - the outcome is irrelevant. Nebraska's education row on the protected-class inquiry ban goes through what that means for your application form, your screening questionnaire and your notes; read it before you redesign either. The practical consequence for this topic is blunt: a required 'occupancy by children' paragraph would make you collect exactly the record section 20-318(5) forbids. WHAT YOU MAY DO INSTEAD: COUNT PEOPLE, NOT CHILDREN. Section 20-322(4)(a) preserves one thing and only one: 'Nothing in the act shall limit the applicability of any REASONABLE LOCAL RESTRICTIONS regarding the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling, and nothing in the act regarding familial status shall apply with respect to housing for older persons.' Read that carefully, because it is narrower than landlords assume. It protects a LOCAL restriction - a city or county occupancy ordinance - and it protects it only if reasonable. It does not protect an occupancy limit you invented. So if you want a cap, find the actual ordinance for the municipality the property sits in, write the cap to match it, and state the occupants by name rather than by category. The library's Permitted Occupants clause does it the right way: it names who may live there and requires notice of an additional occupant, with no reference to children or to age. HOUSING FOR OLDER PERSONS IS A REAL EXEMPTION WITH REAL CONDITIONS. If you are running age-restricted housing, section 20-322(4)(b) defines it three ways: provided under a state programme the commission determines is designed to assist elderly persons; 'intended for and solely occupied by persons sixty-two years of age or older'; or 'intended and operated for occupancy by at least one person fifty-five years of age or older per unit.' The fifty-five route is the one with teeth - subdivision (b)(iii) requires commission regulations covering significant facilities and services designed for older persons' physical or social needs (or that the housing is necessary to provide important housing opportunities for older persons), that 'at least eighty percent of the units are occupied by at least one person fifty-five years of age or older per unit', and 'the publication of and adherence to policies and procedures which demonstrate an intent by the owner or manager to provide housing for persons fifty-five years of age or older.' Subdivision (4)(c) protects you from losing the status because of residents in place as of September 6, 1991 who do not meet the age test, or because of vacant units reserved for qualifying occupants. If you are not running all of that, you are not exempt, and a 'no children' or 'adults only' rule is simply unlawful. ONE MORE PLACE THIS BITES: HOUSE RULES. A rule restricting children's use of a pool, playground, laundry or common area by age is a condition of the rental and a 'provision of services or facilities in connection therewith' under section 20-318(2). Safety rules that apply to everyone - no glass in the pool area, no unsupervised use of equipment by anyone who cannot swim - are the defensible form. 'Children must be accompanied by an adult at all times' is not.

title: No Duty to Hand the Tenant the HOA Documents - But Section 76-1422(6) Means You Should Anyway
bodyText: Maryland requires it in one county, Puerto Rico requires a statement in the lease with a copy to the board, and Connecticut has a common-interest-community notice. Nebraska requires nothing: no statute obliges a landlord letting a unit in a condominium or a homeowners' development to disclose the association's obligations, give the tenant the declaration, bylaws, rules or budget, or notify the association that the unit has been let. The Nebraska Condominium Act's disclosure machinery is purchaser-side only - section 76-884 makes the seller furnish a purchaser 'before conveyance a copy of the declaration other than the plats and plans, the bylaws, the rules or regulations of the association' and the assessment figures, and the public-offering statement sections work the same way. A tenant is not a purchaser. THE REASON YOU GIVE THEM THE DOCUMENTS ANYWAY IS THAT YOU CANNOT ENFORCE WHAT YOU DID NOT DISCLOSE. Section 76-1421(8) makes it a tenant duty to 'abide by all bylaws, covenants, rules or regulations of any applicable condominium regime, cooperative housing agreement, or neighborhood association not inconsistent with landlord's rights or duties.' Note how wide that is - bylaws AND covenants, not just the rule book - and note its qualifier. But a rule reaches your tenant through section 76-1422, and subdivision (6) is unambiguous: a rule or regulation is enforceable against the tenant only if 'the tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement.' And for anything the association adopts later: 'A rule or regulation adopted after the tenant enters into the rental agreement is enforceable against the tenant if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the tenant and it does not work a substantial modification of his bargain.' So the documents you never handed over are documents you cannot enforce, and an association amendment that genuinely changes the deal may not bind your tenant even with notice. Attach the current declaration, bylaws and rules to the lease, get a receipt, and forward amendments as they come. THE SURPRISE: THE DECLARATION MAY TAKE YOUR VOTE AWAY AND GIVE YOUR TENANT RECORDS ACCESS. Section 76-868(c): 'If the declaration requires that votes on specified matters affecting the condominium be cast by LESSEES rather than unit owners of leased units: (i) the provisions of subsections (a) and (b) of this section apply to lessees as if they were unit owners; (ii) unit owners who have leased their units to other persons MAY NOT CAST VOTES on those specified matters; and (iii) lessees are entitled to NOTICE OF MEETINGS, ACCESS TO RECORDS, and other rights respecting those matters as if they were unit owners.' Unit owners still get notice of those meetings under section 76-866. Most declarations do not do this, but some do, and if yours does then letting the unit costs you your vote on those matters and gives your tenant a statutory right to the association's records under section 76-876. Read the declaration before you let, not after. WHAT ABOUT THE FINES? The library's Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance clause puts association fines caused by the tenant's violation on the tenant, and that is lawful here - section 76-1414(1) permits terms the Act does not prohibit, and section 76-1416(2) lets you apply the deposit to 'the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or section 76-1421.' Two cautions. The association will bill you, not the tenant, because you are the unit owner; the clause gives you a claim against the tenant, not a redirection of the bill. And the fine has to arise from a rule that actually binds the tenant under section 76-1422(6), which brings you back to disclosure. ONE THING YOU MUST NOT PASS THROUGH. Section 20-318(6) makes it unlawful to 'include in any transfer, sale, rental, or lease of housing any restrictive covenants or honor or exercise or attempt to honor or exercise any restrictive covenant pertaining to housing', and section 20-317 defines a restrictive covenant as 'any specification limiting the transfer, rental, or lease of any housing because of race, creed, religion, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status, ancestry, or military or veteran status.' Old declarations sometimes still carry such language. Do not forward it, do not enforce it, and do not let your lease incorporate it by a blanket reference you have not read.

title: No Certificate-of-Occupancy Disclosure, No Rental Registry - and the Condemnation Notice Gets Recorded Against Your Title
bodyText: New York makes a landlord tell the tenant whether the building has a valid certificate of occupancy and what it permits. Nebraska has no such requirement, and it has no statewide rental registration or licensing scheme either. The phrase 'certificate of occupancy' appears exactly once in the whole of Nebraska's property, civil-procedure, civil-rights and consumer statutes, and it is not about renting: section 76-894 says that where a condominium public-offering statement is required, 'no interest in that unit may be conveyed, until the declaration is recorded and the unit is substantially completed, as evidenced by a recorded certificate of substantial completion executed by an architect, a surveyor, or a professional engineer, or by issuance of a certificate of occupancy authorized by law.' That is a purchaser-side rule about conveying a new condominium unit. It says nothing to a tenant. OCCUPANCY CERTIFICATES ARE A MUNICIPAL MATTER, AND YOU HAVE TO GO AND LOOK. Section 18-2146: 'Each city and village shall adopt a minimum standards housing ordinance if such city or village has completed an approved workable program or is in the process of the preparation of such a program.' The certificate, the inspection, the rental licence if there is one, and the penalty for letting without one, all live in that ordinance and in the local building code. This library's Nebraska research does not reach city ordinances, so before you let a unit - and especially a converted basement, a garage apartment or a divided house - check the municipal code for the city or village the property sits in, and keep the certificate in the file. WHAT HAPPENS IF THE UNIT IS DECLARED UNFIT, AND WHY IT WILL NOT STAY QUIET. Section 18-1722.01: 'Whenever the governing body of a municipality has decided by resolution or other determination that a property is unsafe or unfit for human occupancy because of one or more violations of its minimum standard housing ordinance or has decided by resolution or other determination that a building is unsafe because of one or more violations of its local building or construction code, IT SHALL BE THE DUTY OF SUCH MUNICIPALITY TO POST THE PROPERTY accordingly AND TO FILE a copy of such resolution or other determination IN THE OFFICE OF THE REGISTER OF DEEDS of the county to be recorded. No fee shall be charged for such recording or for the release of such recording.' Three things follow. The duty is the municipality's, not yours - which is why there is no disclosure obligation on you. The determination is posted on the building, so your tenant and their visitors will see it. And it is RECORDED, so it shows up in the title and the lender's and insurer's searches, and it stays there until somebody obtains a release, which the statute makes free. THE COST FALLS ON YOU, NOT ON THE TENANT. Section 76-1416(4) second sentence: 'a tenant shall not be liable for damages directly related to the tenant's removal from the premises by order of any governmental entity as a result of the premises not being fit for habitation due to the negligence or neglect of the landlord.' So if the city orders your tenant out because of a condition you neglected, you cannot charge them for the lost term, and you cannot keep the deposit against it. Add section 76-1419(1)(a) - substantially comply, after written or actual notice, 'with the requirements of the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety' - and section 76-1418's duty to 'deliver possession of the premises to the tenant in compliance with the rental agreement and section 76-1419' at the commencement of the term, and the shape is clear: no disclosure duty, full exposure. ONE DEFINITION YOU SHOULD NOT MISREAD. Section 76-1410(3) carries two terms, not one: 'Building and housing codes include any law, ordinance, or governmental regulation concerning fitness for habitation, or the construction, maintenance, operation, occupancy, use, or appearance of any premises, or dwelling unit. MINIMUM HOUSING CODE shall be limited to those laws, resolutions, or ordinances or regulations, or portions thereof, dealing specifically with health and minimum standards of fitness for habitation.' The broad term is what section 76-1421(1) makes the tenant comply with; the narrow one is what section 76-1419(1)(a) measures your duty by, and section 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence makes subdivision (1)(a) your MAXIMUM duty where such a code applies. Do not swap them. SHOULD YOU DISCLOSE ANYWAY? There is nothing to stop you, and a short lease recital that the property has a current certificate of occupancy for use as a dwelling, if true, costs nothing and is worth having if a dispute ever turns on whether the let was lawful. Do not recite it if you have not seen the certificate - section 87-303.07 makes a lease induced by a deceptive trade practice unenforceable by the lessor, which is a steep price for a sentence you did not check.

title: Nebraska Does Not Regulate Application Fees at All - Which Is Why the Deposit Cap Is the Only Thing Watching You
bodyText: Forty-eight states have something to say here. Nebraska has nothing: no cap on a rental application or screening fee, no annual adjustment, no refund right if the fee goes unused or the unit goes to an earlier applicant, no duty to hold the money until earlier applicants are screened, no pre-application disclosure of estimated rent, fees, availability date or screening criteria, no exemption for a minor household member, no unit-count threshold, and no rental application fairness act of any kind. The words 'screening fee' and 'tenant screening' do not appear anywhere in Nebraska's property, civil-procedure, civil-rights or consumer statutes, and every statutory 'application fee' is a professional-licensing fee - an appraiser's credential, an abstracter's registration, a board's charge. THE ONE PROVISION THAT CAN REACH YOUR FEE IS THE DEPOSIT CAP, AND IT IS WORDED TO CATCH RELABELLING. Section 76-1416(1): 'A landlord may not demand or receive SECURITY, HOWEVER DENOMINATED, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent, except that a pet deposit not in excess of one-fourth of one month's periodic rent may be demanded or received when appropriate.' 'However denominated' is the operative phrase - calling money an administrative fee, a move-in fee, a processing fee or a holding fee does not take it outside the ceiling if what it actually does is secure the tenancy. The honest distinction is function, not label: money paid as the price of running a screening, earned when the screening is run, and never credited against rent or deposit, is a fee for a service; money collected to take the unit off the market, or that rolls into the first month's rent or the deposit if the applicant signs, is security 'however denominated' and counts against your one month. Keep them in different buckets and say in writing which is which. NOTE WHAT 'RENT' DOES AND DOES NOT CATCH. Section 76-1410(13) defines rent as 'all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement' - which is why every charge in a Nebraska lease is rent. An application fee taken before there is any rental agreement is not paid 'under' one, so it starts outside that definition. The moment you fold it into the lease as a charge, it becomes rent, with everything that follows. Whether charges that are rent also enlarge or consume the section 76-1416(1) ceiling, which is measured in 'one month's PERIODIC rent' - a term the Act never defines - is genuinely unsettled in Nebraska. The cautious course is to assume a nonrefundable up-front charge counts against the cap. THE LEGISLATURE'S SILENCE HERE IS A CHOICE, NOT AN OVERSIGHT. It capped exactly this kind of charge in a neighbouring act. For a consumer rental-purchase agreement, section 69-2110(1) says the lessor 'may contract for and receive' a closed list: '(a) An initial nonrefundable administrative fee of NOT MORE THAN TEN DOLLARS', a disclosed security deposit, a delivery charge of not more than ten dollars (twenty-five for more than five items) in lieu of the administrative fee, late fees of five dollars monthly or three dollars for shorter periods with business-day grace periods, and a reinstatement fee of not more than five dollars. Ten dollars, closed list, for renting a washing machine. For renting a house, nothing. WHAT STILL CONSTRAINS YOUR APPLICATION, AND IT IS NOT ABOUT MONEY. Section 20-318(5) makes it unlawful to 'cause to be made any written or oral inquiry or record concerning the race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, sex, or military or veteran status of a person seeking to purchase, rent, or lease any housing.' That is a ban on the question and on the note-to-file, not merely on the decision, and it governs the form you hand every applicant. Nebraska's education row on the inquiry ban is the one to read before you redesign the form. Charging every applicant the same fee on the same terms, and applying the same criteria, is also the cheapest defence you have against a section 20-318(1) or (2) claim, because a fee waived for some applicants and not others is itself a term and condition of the rental. PRACTICAL COURSE. Set the fee at what screening actually costs you, document that, and charge it uniformly. State in writing, before you take it, that it is nonrefundable, what it pays for, and that it is not a deposit and will not be credited to rent. Do not take a holding payment unless you are ready to treat it as security inside the section 76-1416(1) cap. And note that federal law governs what you must tell an applicant you turn down on the strength of a consumer report - the Fair Credit Reporting Act is federal, and Nebraska's own section 20-149 puts its duty on the consumer reporting agency, not on you.

title: No Auto-Renewal Statute in Nebraska - and Holding Over Converts the Tenancy to Month-to-Month, Not to Another Full Term
bodyText: North Dakota, California, New York and Wisconsin each regulate automatic renewal of a lease - formatting, pre-renewal notice, or an affirmative opt-in. Vermont reaches leases through a general consumer auto-renewal statute written around the word 'lessor'. Nebraska has neither kind. There is no lease auto-renewal statute, no pre-renewal notice requirement, no formatting or conspicuousness rule for a renewal clause, and no general consumer-contract auto-renewal act that could be read across: the phrase 'automatically renew' appears in Nebraska's held statutes only in a certificate-of-deposit limitation provision, an unclaimed-property presumption and the Rental-Purchase Agreement Act's definitions, and it appears nowhere in the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act or the Consumer Protection Act. Inside the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act itself - sections 76-1401 to 76-1449 - the word 'renew' appears only in section 76-1413's electronic-consent machinery and in the Act's own applicability sections. SO AN AUTO-RENEWAL CLAUSE IS LAWFUL CONTRACT TERRITORY. Section 76-1414(1): 'The landlord and tenant may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law including rent, term of the agreement, and other provisions governing the rights and obligations of the parties.' Nothing in section 76-1415 prohibits a renewal clause, so you may write one. WHAT HAPPENS IF YOU DON'T, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT CATCHES LANDLORDS OUT. Section 76-1437(3): 'If the tenant remains in possession WITHOUT THE LANDLORD'S CONSENT after expiration of the term of the rental agreement or its termination, the landlord may bring an action for possession and if the tenant's holdover is willful and not in good faith the landlord, in addition, may recover an amount not more than three months' periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees. IF THE LANDLORD CONSENTS to the tenant's continued occupancy, subsection (4) of section 76-1414 applies.' And section 76-1414(4): 'Unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy shall be week to week in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent, and in all other cases MONTH TO MONTH.' So accepting rent after the term ends does not renew the lease for another year - it converts the tenancy to month-to-month, terminable by either side on thirty days' written notice under section 76-1437(2). If you wanted another fixed year, you had to write it or sign it. TWO THINGS TO GET RIGHT IF YOU DO WRITE A RENEWAL CLAUSE. First, state the renewed term and the rent, or the mechanism for setting the rent, with enough precision to stand on its own - Nebraska courts construe ambiguities in a lease against the party who prepared it (D & R Realty v. Bender, 230 Neb. 301, 431 N.W.2d 920 (1988), noted with section 76-1414), and a lease for more than one year is void under section 36-105 unless it is 'in writing and signed by the party by whom the lease or sale is to be made', with rent an essential term of that writing. A renewal that extends the total commitment past a year lives or dies by the writing. Second, the opt-out has to be real and workable: say how many days' notice a tenant must give to stop the renewal, make the window at least as long as the thirty days section 76-1437(2) would give them anyway, and remember that a notice requirement you impose on the tenant is a term you will have to prove they had notice of. THE DRAFTING SILENCE IS DELIBERATE, AND THE PROOF IS NEXT DOOR. Nebraska's Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act, in the same chapter, requires sixty days' written notice of a rent increase - section 76-1490: 'Each tenant shall be notified in writing of any rent increase by actual notice or by United States mail at least sixty days prior to the effective date of the increase.' There is no equivalent anywhere in the residential act, and a renewal at a higher rent is the commonest way a rent increase actually arrives. So for an apartment or house there is no statutory notice period for the increase and none for the renewal; the only notice periods in play are section 76-1437(1)'s seven days for a week-to-week tenancy and (2)'s thirty days for a month-to-month one, both running to a termination date and both available to either party. One last practical point: whatever your clause says, give the tenant written notice well before the renewal date telling them the new term and the new rent, and keep proof you sent it. Nebraska will not require it, and it is still the difference between a renewal you can rely on and a month-to-month tenancy you did not choose.

title: No Balcony Inspection Mandate in Nebraska - Your Duty Comes From Habitability and the Adopted Fire Code Instead
bodyText: California and Maryland make owners of multifamily buildings have balconies, decks and other exterior elevated elements inspected on a cycle by a licensed professional, with records kept and repairs made to a deadline. Nebraska has nothing of the kind. There is no inspection interval, no qualified-inspector requirement, no record-keeping duty, no reporting duty and no certification. The word 'balcony' appears twice in the whole of Nebraska's held property, civil-procedure, civil-rights and consumer statutes, and both times it is doing a different job: section 76-839(4) of the Condominium Act classifies 'any shutters, awnings, window boxes, doorsteps, stoops, porches, balconies, patios, and all exterior doors and windows or other fixtures designed to serve a single unit, but located outside the unit's boundaries' as 'limited common elements allocated exclusively to that unit', and section 76-846(b)(8) requires a condominium plat to show 'the location and dimensions of limited common elements, including porches, balconies, and patios'. Those are allocation and mapping rules, not safety rules. THAT CLASSIFICATION STILL MATTERS TO YOU IF YOU OWN A CONDOMINIUM UNIT. A balcony serving your unit is a LIMITED common element, not part of the unit - so who repairs it, and who pays, is set by the declaration and the bylaws rather than by your lease, and you cannot promise your tenant a repair you have no right to carry out. Read the declaration before you let, and tell the tenant who to call. WHERE YOUR ACTUAL DUTY COMES FROM. Section 76-1419(1)(b) - 'make all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition' - and section 76-1419(1)(c) - 'keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition.' A shared balcony, walkway or external stair is a common area, so subdivision (1)(c) is unqualified and continuous: it is not triggered by notice and it cannot be shifted to a tenant, because section 76-1419(3)'s other-tenants proviso blocks that for any multi-unit building. A private balcony serving one dwelling falls under (1)(b), where the duty attaches after written or actual notice - which is why a tenant's offhand report of a soft deck board starts your clock and should be logged. Section 76-1419(1)(a) adds substantial compliance with 'the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety', and section 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence makes that subdivision your MAXIMUM duty where such a code applies, with the same subsection reserving existing tort law in terms: 'The obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state.' That reservation is the point. No inspection statute means no statutory schedule to comply with; it does not mean no liability when a balcony fails. AND THERE IS A CODE, IT IS JUST NOT IN THE LANDLORD-TENANT LAW. Nebraska's State Fire Code adopts the National Fire Protection Association's Fire Code and Life Safety Code by pamphlet number and edition year, and those documents do address guards, railings and exit components. The State Fire Marshal statutes sit in chapter 81 and the municipal building code sits in the city or village ordinance, and neither is within this library's Nebraska statutory research - so the two documents that actually tell you what a balcony must be able to carry are documents you have to go and get. Ask the fire marshal's office or the local building department which code edition applies to your building, and whether anything in it requires periodic inspection of exterior elevated elements. WHAT TO DO IN THE ABSENCE OF A MANDATE. Inspect anyway, on a schedule you write down, and keep the records - photographs, dates, who looked, what was found, what was done. Pay attention to the connection between the balcony and the wall, to any wood that stays wet, and to guard height and spacing. Section 76-1423(1) gives you the access: the tenant 'shall not unreasonably withhold consent to the landlord to enter into the dwelling unit in order to inspect the premises', and section 76-1423(3)(a) tells you how to ask - at least twenty-four hours' written notice stating the intended purpose and a reasonable period for the entry. Put a reasonable occupancy or load limit in your house rules rather than in the lease if you need one, and make it satisfy section 76-1422: a rule binds the tenant only if its purpose is to promote 'the appearance, convenience, safety, or welfare of the tenants', it is reasonably related to that purpose, it applies to all tenants fairly, it is explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do, it is not a device to evade your own duties, and the tenant had notice of it when the lease was made.

title: No Cold-Weather Notice Rule in Nebraska - Use the Seven-Day Absence Notice You Already Have
bodyText: Minnesota makes a tenant give the landlord notice before vacating in cold weather, so that the heat is not switched off and the pipes do not burst behind them. Nebraska has no such rule, in a state where that happens every January. The phrases 'cold weather', 'freezing weather' and 'heating season' appear nowhere in Nebraska's held statutes, and the only hits for 'freeze' and 'winter' are an exemption schedule, two unfair-competition provisions and an asset-freezing power - nothing to do with a dwelling. The Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act has no counterpart either, so this is not a case of the Legislature protecting one kind of tenancy and not another; it simply never addressed it. WHAT YOU DO HAVE IS BETTER THAN NOTHING AND IS ALREADY IN YOUR LEASE. Section 76-1424: 'The rental agreement MAY REQUIRE that the tenant notify the landlord of any anticipated extended absence from the premises in excess of seven days no later than the first day of the extended absence.' And section 76-1432(1) gives it teeth: 'If the rental agreement requires the tenant to give notice to the landlord of an anticipated extended absence in excess of seven days as required in section 76-1424 and the tenant WILLFULLY fails to do so, the landlord may recover ACTUAL DAMAGES from the tenant.' Then section 76-1432(2): 'During any absence of the tenant in excess of seven days, the landlord may enter the dwelling unit at times reasonably necessary.' That is the Nebraska answer to the Minnesota problem - not a cold-weather notice, but a seven-day absence notice plus an entry right, and it works all year. Two things make it effective rather than decorative. The notice duty exists only if your lease requires it, so check that it does; Nebraska's Notice of Extended Absence clause carries it. And section 76-1432(1)'s damages require WILLFUL failure, so a tenant who simply forgot is a bad case - which is a reason to remind tenants of the duty in writing each autumn rather than to rely on the clause alone. YOU MAY ALSO REQUIRE THE TENANT TO KEEP THE HEAT ON, AND YOU SHOULD. Section 76-1414(1) lets the parties include any term the Act does not prohibit, and nothing prohibits a clause requiring the tenant to maintain a stated minimum temperature where the tenant controls the heat, not to shut off a utility account before the end of the term, and to drain or protect outside taps. Section 76-1421(5) already obliges the tenant to 'use in a reasonable manner all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances', and section 76-1421(6) not to 'deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises' - letting a pipe freeze by turning off the furnace in December is squarely inside both, and the cost is recoverable through section 76-1416(2) and section 76-1431(3). State a number in the clause; 'keep the property adequately heated' is an argument waiting to happen. BUT DO NOT WRITE IT AS A WAIVER OF THE HEAT DUTY, BECAUSE THAT PART IS NOT YOURS TO GIVE AWAY. Section 76-1419(1)(f) makes you 'supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat except where the building that includes the dwelling unit is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant and supplied by a direct public utility connection.' For a dwelling unit that is NOT a single-family residence as section 76-1410(16) defines it, section 76-1419(3) cannot shift that duty at all - it reaches only 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling' - so in a duplex or an apartment building a clause making the tenant responsible for heat is void however it is drafted. Only section 76-1419(2), for a single-family residence, in writing for good consideration and in good faith, can move it. And if you get it wrong the remedy is immediate: section 76-1427(1) lets a tenant who gives written notice procure heat and 'deduct their actual and reasonable cost from the rent', claim the diminution in fair rental value, or take substitute housing rent-free for the period, with attorney's fees in any case and an extra recovery if your failure was deliberate. That is the only procure-and-deduct right in Nebraska's landlord-tenant law, and heat is what it is for. Note its limits, which protect you: section 76-1427(3) says the rights 'do not arise until the tenant has given written notice to the landlord or if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of his family, or other person on the premises with his consent', and that the section 'is not intended to cover circumstances beyond the landlord's control.' A frozen pipe the tenant caused by turning off the heat is their condition, not your breach.

title: No Asbestos Disclosure to a Tenant - Except on a Lease With an Option to Purchase
bodyText: Unlike lead-based paint, where a federal rule puts a disclosure in every pre-1978 lease, asbestos has no tenant-facing disclosure requirement in Nebraska's landlord-tenant law. Nothing in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act mentions asbestos, no statute requires you to tell a tenant that a building contains asbestos, and there is no survey, management-plan or record-keeping duty for a residential rental in the statutes this library researched.
