Every statutory use of the word 'asbestos' in Nebraska's property, civil-procedure, civil-rights and consumer chapters belongs to one thing, and it is not disclosure: the Cumulative Successor Asbestos-Related Liabilities Act, sections 25-21,283 to 25-21,289, which caps the asbestos liabilities a successor corporation inherits from a merger, together with section 25-224 on product-liability limitation periods. Those are corporate and tort provisions. They say nothing to a landlord about a building. THE ONE PLACE A DISCLOSURE DUTY DOES BITE: A LEASE WITH AN OPTION TO PURCHASE. Section 76-2,120 reaches further than its 'seller' label suggests. Subsection (1)(d): 'Seller shall mean an owner of real property who sells or attempts to sell, INCLUDING LEASE WITH OPTION TO PURCHASE, residential real property'. Subsection (2) repeats it: 'The requirements of this section shall also apply ... to any lease with the option to purchase residential real property.' 'Residential real property' means property 'being used primarily for residential purposes on which no fewer than one or more than four dwelling units are located' (subsection (1)(c)). And the contents list in subsection (4) has a catch-all that plainly reaches known asbestos: '(g) Any hazardous conditions, including substances, materials, and products on the real property which may be an environmental hazard.' So if you offer a rent-to-own, a lease-purchase or a lease with an option on a one-to-four-unit residential property, you must complete and sign the statutory disclosure statement, and a known asbestos condition goes in it. The standard is knowledge, not inspection - subsection (5) says the statement is completed 'to the best of the seller's belief and knowledge', you may mark an item unknown and still comply, but you must update it 'whenever the seller has knowledge that information on the disclosure statement is no longer accurate', on or before the effective date of the contract binding the purchaser. WHAT STILL APPLIES TO AN ORDINARY LEASE, DISCLOSURE OR NO DISCLOSURE. Section 76-1419(1)(b) makes you 'make all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition', and section 76-1419(1)(a) requires substantial compliance with 'the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety'. Damaged, friable or disturbed asbestos is a health-and-safety condition, and the same subsection ends by reserving the law that will actually be used against you: 'The obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state.' Section 76-1415(1)(d) then closes the escape route - a lease term by which the tenant 'agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord or to indemnify the landlord for that liability' is unenforceable under section 76-1415(2), with the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees if you used it knowing it was prohibited. An asbestos waiver in a Nebraska lease is worth nothing and costs you something. THE RULES THAT MATTER MOST ARE NOT IN THIS LIBRARY, AND YOU SHOULD GO AND FIND THEM. Nebraska has an Asbestos Control Act in chapter 71, sections 71-6301 to 71-6317, administered by the Department of Health and Human Services, and it has now been read: it is a LICENSING regime and it imposes no disclosure duty on an owner and nothing at all owed to an occupant. Its duties fall on business entities, licensees, individual workers, project designers and project monitors. One part of it reaches you directly, though, and it is not about telling anyone anything. Section 71-6302 bars a business entity from engaging in an 'asbestos project' without a licence, then excepts an entity which '(2) uses its own employees for an asbestos project for the purpose of renovating, maintaining, or repairing its own facilities', and separately excepts small projects - under two hundred sixty linear feet, or under one hundred sixty square feet and linear feet in combination. So if your own maintenance staff do the work in your own buildings you need no licence. But the same section continues: 'Business entities not required to hold a license shall provide a training course to inform the employees of the health and safety aspects of the asbestos project, including the applicable state standards', the course must meet the section 71-6310.01 standard, and it 'shall be available for review and approval upon inspection by the department.' Being exempt from the licence is not being exempt from the Act. What remains outside this library's research is the Administrative Code that implements it, so is the State Fire Marshal material in chapter 81, and so is federal law, which regulates asbestos work through renovation, demolition and worker-protection rules. The practical point for a landlord is that the exposure comes from DISTURBING asbestos, not from owning it: the moment you remodel, demolish, re-roof, re-side, remove flooring or have a contractor cut into anything in an older building, licensing, notification and work-practice rules can attach, and they attach to the work rather than to the tenancy. Before any work on a pre-1990 building, ask the contractor for their asbestos licensing and ask DHHS what notification the job needs. PRACTICAL COURSE FOR THE LEASE. Do not put an asbestos waiver in it. Do not volunteer a bare 'the property may contain asbestos' recital, which tells the tenant nothing and may be read as knowledge you then failed to act on. If you know of asbestos-containing material in the unit, say where it is, say that it is intact and is to be left undisturbed, and tell the tenant in the lease to report any damage to it immediately - that converts your knowledge into a section 76-1419(1)(b) notice loop you can actually manage, and a tenant who drills into it anyway is inside section 76-1421(6)'s duty not to 'deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises'.

title: Nebraska Has No Accessory Dwelling Unit Statute - and the Granny Flat You Rent Out May Not Be a 'Single-Family Residence'
bodyText: Massachusetts allows one accessory dwelling unit and its rental by right and bars owner-occupancy conditions; West Virginia stops cities restricting them. Nebraska has no statute of that kind in its landlord-tenant, property, civil-rights or consumer law. The phrase 'accessory dwelling unit' does not appear in any of those chapters, nor in any act of the 2025 or 2026 sessions, and neither does 'missing middle'. Whether a basement apartment, a garage conversion or a backyard cottage may exist at all, and whether it may be rented, is decided by the zoning ordinance and building code of the city or village the property sits in - and by nothing in the statutes this library researched. THE LEGISLATURE KNOWS HOW TO DO THIS WHEN IT WANTS TO, WHICH IS WHY THE SILENCE MATTERS. Section 18-1758 is a full state preemption for a different kind of rental. Subsection (2): 'A municipality shall not adopt or enforce an ordinance or other regulation that expressly or effectively prohibits the use of a property as a short-term rental.' Subsection (3) lets a municipality regulate one specifically 'only if the municipality demonstrates that the primary purpose of the ordinance or other regulation is to protect the public's health and safety', with a listed set of permitted subjects. Subsection (6) requires that a municipality 'apply an ordinance or other regulation regulating land use to a short-term rental in the same manner as another similar property', including 'residential use and other zoning matters'. And subsection (7) leaves private restrictions alone: the section 'shall not be construed to affect regulations of a private entity, including a homeowners association organized under the Condominium Property Act or the Nebraska Condominium Act.' Nebraska wrote all that for a thirty-day rental in 2019 and has written nothing like it for an accessory dwelling unit. The gap is a choice, not an accident - and the one thing to take from section 18-1758 is subsection (7): even a permissive ordinance will not help you if the covenants forbid the unit, and section 76-1421(8) separately makes your tenant abide by 'all bylaws, covenants, rules or regulations of any applicable condominium regime, cooperative housing agreement, or neighborhood association not inconsistent with landlord's rights or duties.' THE LANDLORD-TENANT CONSEQUENCE THAT CATCHES PEOPLE OUT, AND THIS IS THE PART WORTH READING TWICE. Once you let the unit, the Act applies to it like any other dwelling unit - section 76-1410(4): 'Dwelling unit means a structure or the part of a structure that is used as a home, residence, or sleeping place by one person who maintains a household or by two or more persons who maintain a common household.' A converted garage is 'the part of a structure'. What changes is whether it counts as a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE, and that decides how much of your maintenance duty you can shift. Section 76-1410(16): 'Single-family residence means a structure maintained and used as a single dwelling unit. Notwithstanding that a dwelling unit shares one or more walls with another dwelling unit, IT IS a single-family residence IF it has direct access to a street or thoroughfare AND shares neither heating facilities, hot water equipment, nor any other essential facility or service with any other dwelling unit.' Run your unit through that test honestly. A detached backyard cottage with its own door onto the street, its own furnace and its own water heater passes, and section 76-1419(2) then lets you agree in the lease itself, for good consideration and in good faith, that the tenant performs your waste-removal and water-and-heat duties and specified repairs. A basement apartment reached through the main house, or one on the house's furnace or water heater, FAILS the test - and then section 76-1419(3) applies, which reaches only 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling', requires a separate writing signed by both parties and supported by adequate consideration, cannot diminish your obligations to other tenants, and CANNOT SHIFT the section 76-1419(1)(e) waste duty or the section 76-1419(1)(f) running-water, hot-water and reasonable-heat duty at all. Most accessory units fail on the shared-furnace limb, and most landlords assume they pass. Nebraska's education row on delegating maintenance duties sets out the two paths in full. THE OTHER RISK IS THE PERMIT, NOT THE LEASE. Section 18-2146 requires each city and village to adopt a minimum standards housing ordinance on the stated condition, and section 18-1722.01 says that once the governing body determines a property 'unsafe or unfit for human occupancy because of one or more violations of its minimum standard housing ordinance', or a building unsafe under its building or construction code, 'it shall be the duty of such municipality to post the property accordingly and to file a copy of such resolution or other determination in the office of the register of deeds of the county to be recorded.' An unpermitted conversion is exactly the thing that attracts such a determination, and the determination goes on your title. Get the permit and the certificate of occupancy before you advertise, not after. And if you are selling the property on a lease with an option to purchase, section 76-2,120(4)(h) makes you disclose 'any title conditions which affect the real property, including encroachments, easements, and ZONING RESTRICTIONS', with section 76-2,120(1)(d) and (2) extending that statute to 'any lease with the option to purchase residential real property' - so an unpermitted accessory unit becomes a disclosable item in that transaction. ONE OPEN POINT, STATED RATHER THAN GLOSSED. Nebraska does have a Municipal Density and Missing Middle Housing Act in chapter 19 - section 19-5505 requires an affordable housing action plan in some circumstances, and a 2026 act cross-references it. Chapter 19 has now been read, and the answer is no on all three counts - but the reason is worth knowing, because it is the kind of thing a keyword search gets wrong. The Act DOES define an accessory dwelling unit, at section 19-5503(1): 'an interior, attached, or detached residential structure that is used in connection with, or that is an accessory to, a single-family dwelling and is located on the same lot or parcel as such single-family dwelling.' So the term is in Nebraska law. What it is not in is the Act's only mandate on a city's zoning. Section 19-5505(4) says that a city which fails to adopt an affordable housing action plan 'shall be required to allow the development of: (a) Middle housing in all areas in the city zoned for residential use that allow for the development of detached single-family dwellings; and (b) A duplex on each lot or parcel' so zoned - and section 19-5503(6) makes 'middle housing' a closed five-item list: '(a) Duplexes; (b) Triplexes; (c) Quadplexes; (d) Cottage clusters; or (e) Townhouses.' An accessory dwelling unit is not on that list and is not a duplex. Across the whole of Nebraska's statutes the phrase appears three times - the definition above, section 19-5504 (a reporting provision) and section 81-15,279 (a mobile-home-park definitions section) - and not once in a provision that requires a city to allow one, addresses renting one, or bars an owner-occupancy condition. Two further limits: section 19-5503(3) confines 'City' to metropolitan, primary and first-class cities of at least twenty thousand inhabitants, so the Act does not reach smaller municipalities at all; and section 19-5505's trigger is failure to adopt a plan, so a city that adopted one owes nothing under (4) even as to middle housing. The practical advice is unchanged and now rests on a read statute rather than an unread one: your accessory unit lives or dies by the local ordinance. Before you build or convert, ask the city planning department about both that Act and the local ordinance, and get the answer in writing.

title: You Cannot Put a Collection-Cost or Attorney-Fee Clause in a Nebraska Lease
bodyText:
Nebraska has no statute authorizing a landlord to add a collection fee to past-due rent, and it closes off the usual way leases try to do it. Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1415(1)(c) says no rental agreement may provide that the tenant "[a]grees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees." Read the words: Nebraska's version of the 1972 URLTA model bans the clause in BOTH directions, so a term shifting legal or collection-counsel costs to the tenant is barred even if you drafted it to look mutual. Under § 76-1415(2) such a term is simply unenforceable — and if you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know to be prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages AND the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees. A fee clause that never pays off can therefore cost you money.

What you do get comes from statute, not from your lease, and you get it only by suing. Under § 76-1431(3) you may recover damages and injunctive relief for any tenant noncompliance, and reasonable attorney's fees if the noncompliance is WILLFUL. Separately, on any lawsuit of four thousand dollars or less, § 25-1801 gives a plaintiff costs, six percent interest running from thirty days after the claim accrued, and a statutory attorney's fee of ten dollars (or ten dollars plus ten percent of the judgment above fifty dollars) — but only if the claim went unpaid for ninety days after it accrued before you filed, and the Nebraska courts treat each condition in § 25-1801 as something you must plead and prove. Nothing in either section lets you bill the tenant a percentage "collection charge" before judgment.

Practical course: leave collection fees, collection-agency commissions and attorney-fee shifting out of the lease entirely. Bill the rent, the late fee and any charge your lease genuinely supports as rent, then pursue the balance in court and ask for the statutory fee. Nebraska has no statute capping or authorizing a private collection charge on a rent debt — contrast the Rental-Purchase Agreement Act, where the Legislature wrote an itemised fee schedule for a different consumer contract (§ 69-2110(1)(d)). Charges for serving notices or for the cost of an eviction are a separate question: see the notice-service-fee and eviction-penalty-clause-ban material.

title: A Confession-of-Judgment Clause Is Void in a Nebraska Lease
bodyText:
Do not put a confession-of-judgment or cognovit clause in a Nebraska residential lease. Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1415(1)(b) says no rental agreement may provide that the tenant "[a]uthorizes any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement." Under § 76-1415(2) the provision is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a lease containing a term you know to be prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages and the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees. That makes the clause worse than useless: it is a liability, not a shortcut.

The prohibition is on the LEASE TERM, not on the procedure. Nebraska still has confession of judgment on the books. Under § 25-1309 a person against whom a cause of action exists may personally appear in a court of competent jurisdiction and, with the creditor's assent, confess judgment; § 25-1310 requires the debt or cause of action to be briefly stated; § 25-1311 makes the judgment enforceable like any other and treats the confession as a release of errors; and § 25-1312 requires an attorney who confesses judgment to produce the warrant of attorney at the time and to file the original or a copy. Sections 25-906 and 25-907 cover the different device of an offer to confess judgment, before or after suit, which shifts costs if the plaintiff refuses it and then recovers no more. So a tenant can still agree to a judgment after a dispute has arisen, in court, with you assenting — what you cannot do is take that agreement in advance, in the lease.

Note what § 25-1312 tells you about why the lease clause is barred: a cognovit term is exactly an attempt to manufacture a standing "warrant of attorney" at signing. Nebraska treats that as a prohibited lease provision, and it writes the same ban into other consumer contracts — a consumer rental-purchase agreement may not contain a provision "[r]equiring a confession of judgment" (§ 69-2107(1)). If a form lease you bought from another state carries a cognovit or "confessed judgment" paragraph, strike it before you use it here.

title: No Statute Bars Collecting Rent After a Vacate Order — But Three Other Things Bite
bodyText:
Nebraska has no statute that bars a landlord from collecting rent, or makes rent irrecoverable, because a dwelling has been condemned or ordered vacated. There is no "no rent for an illegal unit" rule and no certificate-of-occupancy precondition to suing for rent. Do not read that as a safe harbour, because three Nebraska provisions reach the same facts from different directions.

First, the damages bar. Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1416(4) closes with a sentence that is easy to miss because it sits in the security-deposit section: "a tenant shall not be liable for damages directly related to the tenant's removal from the premises by order of any governmental entity as a result of the premises not being fit for habitation due to the negligence or neglect of the landlord." Note the two conditions — a governmental order to leave, AND unfitness caused by your negligence or neglect. Where both are met you lose the damages claim arising from that removal, including anything you would otherwise have withheld from the deposit for it.

Second, the tenant's own exits. If the condition is a noncompliance with § 76-1419 materially affecting health and safety, § 76-1425(1) lets the tenant terminate on written notice (termination not less than thirty days out, defeated if you cure within fourteen days), and § 76-1425(4) then requires you to return all prepaid rent and security recoverable under § 76-1416. If the premises are damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty so that enjoyment is substantially impaired, § 76-1429(1) gives the tenant either immediate vacating with written notice inside fourteen days, or a rent liability "reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value" for the unusable part. And in any action for possession for nonpayment, or for rent while the tenant is in possession, § 76-1428(1) lets the tenant counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the Act, with the court able to order rent paid into court and to net the two sides out; if no rent remains due after that, judgment on possession goes to the tenant.

Third, the record. Nebraska's statutory words for this are not "condemned." Under § 18-1722.01, once a municipality's governing body determines by resolution or other determination that a property is unsafe or unfit for human occupancy under its minimum standard housing ordinance, or that a building is unsafe under its building or construction code, the MUNICIPALITY must post the property and file a copy of the determination with the register of deeds to be recorded, at no fee. The duty is the city's, not yours, and it creates no landlord disclosure obligation — but it does mean the determination becomes both a posted placard and a recorded instrument against the property. Separately, § 18-1722 lets a city that does the repair or demolition itself levy the cost as a special assessment lien or sue the owner for it. What "minimum housing code" means for your § 76-1419(1)(a) duty is narrow: § 76-1410(3) limits it to laws, resolutions, ordinances or regulations "dealing specifically with health and minimum standards of fitness for habitation."

title: Two Consumer Acts Reach Your Lease, and One Can Make It Unenforceable
bodyText:
Nebraska has two separate consumer statutes, and the one landlords usually ignore is the one with teeth against a lease.

The Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act (§§ 87-301 to 87-306) contains § 87-303.07: "If a buyer or LESSEE is induced by a violation of section 87-302 or 87-303.01 to enter into a sale or LEASE, the agreement is unenforceable by the seller or LESSOR and the buyer or lessee, at his or her option, may rescind the agreement or retain the merchandise delivered and the benefit of any services performed without any obligation to pay for them." That is not a damages remedy you can insure around — it is a bar on YOUR enforcement of the lease. The triggers are § 87-302 (the enumerated deceptive trade practices) and § 87-303.01(1) ("An unconscionable act or practice by a supplier in connection with a consumer transaction"), and § 87-303.01(2) makes unconscionability a question of law for the court after both sides get to present evidence of setting, purpose and effect. The Act's definitions section (§ 87-301) defines neither 'supplier' nor 'consumer transaction', so whether the unconscionability route reaches a residential lease is a question only the courts can settle; plan around § 87-302, which needs only a person acting 'in the course of his or her business, vocation, or occupation'. Note one specific route in: § 87-302(a)(20) makes a violation of ANY provision of the Nebraska Foreclosure Protection Act a deceptive trade practice — so if you buy a house out of foreclosure and rent it back to the former owner, a slip in that Act can run through § 87-302(a)(20) into § 87-303.07 and leave you unable to enforce the lease.

Important caution about reading § 87-302: the version of that section now published is the one OPERATIVE JANUARY 1, 2027 (Laws 2026, LB838, § 27). Its list runs to twenty-six items, mostly about goods, marks, advertising, pyramid schemes, privacy policies, file-sharing and social-media advertising. Before 1 January 2027 the enumerated list is the pre-LB838 text, so check which version applies to the conduct you are asking about. What the list does NOT contain, in either shape, is any item about blank spaces in a signed document or about failing to give the tenant a copy at signing. Nebraska wrote that warning elsewhere, which tells you the silence is a choice: the Rental-Purchase Agreement Act's prescribed disclosure includes the line "DO NOT SIGN THIS IF IT CONTAINS ANY BLANK SPACES" (§ 69-2105), and the Seller-Assisted Marketing Plan Act requires a copy of the fully completed contract and all other documents the seller requires to be signed to be given to the purchaser at the time of signing (§ 59-1741). Neither reaches a residential lease.

The Consumer Protection Act (§§ 59-1601 to 59-1623) is the other statute. Section 59-1602 makes "[u]nfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce" unlawful, and § 59-1601(2) defines trade and commerce as "the sale of assets or services and any commerce directly or indirectly affecting the people of the State of Nebraska," with "assets" reaching real property. Section 59-1609 gives a person injured in business or property a district-court action for an injunction, actual damages, costs and a reasonable attorney's fee, with discretionary enhanced damages capped at one thousand dollars for a § 59-1602 violation. Read § 59-1617(1) before you rely on either side of this: the Act does not apply to actions or transactions "otherwise permitted, prohibited, or regulated under laws administered by" a long list of regulators "or any other regulatory body or officer acting under statutory authority of this state or the United States," and § 59-1617(2) closes with "No penalty or remedy shall result from a violation of the Consumer Protection Act except as expressly provided in such act." Whether a residential tenancy regulated by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act falls inside that exemption is not settled by the statute's text — treat it as live, not resolved.

Practical course: assume both acts can reach your leasing conduct, keep your advertising, condition representations and fee descriptions accurate, and never sign a tenant onto a document with blanks in it even though no Nebraska statute forbids it for a lease.

title: Nebraska Prescribes No Drug-Free Housing Addendum — But § 28-417(1)(e) Is Why You Want the Term
bodyText:
No Nebraska statute requires, authorizes, prescribes the wording of, or regulates a drug-free or crime-free housing addendum. There is no state addendum form, no statute saying an owner may use one notwithstanding an association's rules, and no statute letting a city require participation in a crime-free housing program. If you use such an addendum here it is an ordinary contract term, governed by § 76-1414(1) ("terms and conditions not prohibited by" the Act), limited by § 76-1415's four prohibited provisions and by § 76-1412's unconscionability test, and — if you adopt it as a RULE rather than as part of the signed lease — by all six conditions in § 76-1422, including that the tenant have notice of it when entering into the rental agreement.

There is a strong reason to carry the substance anyway, and it is not the eviction route. Under § 28-417(1)(e) it is unlawful for ANY person "[t]o keep or maintain any store, shop, warehouse, dwelling house, building, vehicle, boat, aircraft, or place whatever which such person knows or should know is resorted to by persons using controlled substances in violation of the Uniform Controlled Substances Act for the purpose of using such substances or which is used for the keeping or selling of the same in violation of the act." That is a Class III misdemeanor under § 28-417(2). Read the standard: "knows or SHOULD KNOW." Nebraska wrote no landlord exemption and no good-faith safe harbour into it, so a landlord who ignores reports about a unit is exposed in his or her own right, not merely as a party to a lease. A written drug prohibition, consistently enforced and documented, is the practical answer to a constructive-knowledge charge.

Where to put it: the library carries the substance in the Criminal Activity clause rather than in a separate addendum, so that one Nebraska-accurate statement of the prohibition and of the § 76-1431(5) limit lives in one place. You may of course attach your own drug-free addendum instead or in addition; if you do, the Addendum Precedence clause governs any conflict with the lease, and anything the addendum says about terminating for the conduct must leave the § 76-1431(5) limit intact or it will give away a remedy the statute preserves for you. Do not import an addendum written for a federally assisted property and assume it works unchanged on a private Nebraska tenancy.

title: No Pre-Set Charge Schedule — Nebraska Deducts Only Damages You Actually Suffered
bodyText:
Nebraska has no statute letting a lease pre-set what a deposit deduction will cost. There is no carpet-cleaning schedule, no flat turnover or repainting charge, no prescribed tenant notice that unlocks one, and no "non-refundable portion" device. Do not attach a price list to your lease and expect it to control.

The measure is in Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1416(2): on termination, prepaid rent and security "may be applied to the payment of rent and the amount of damages which the landlord HAS SUFFERED by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or section 76-1421." "Has suffered" is a backward-looking, actual-loss measure. A number fixed at signing is not a loss you have suffered, and a lease term that purports to make it conclusive runs into § 76-1415(1)(a), which voids any provision by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under" the Act — the tenant's § 76-1416(2) and (3) rights among them. Section 76-1412 then gives a court power to refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision, to enforce the rest without it, or to limit its application.

Notice which way Nebraska aims its liquidated-damages devices. Inside the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act the phrase appears in exactly two places and both run against the LANDLORD: § 76-1416(3) (willful, bad-faith failure to comply with the return duty — one month's periodic rent or twice the deposit, WHICHEVER IS LESS) and § 76-1430 (unlawful ouster or willful diminution of essential services — a flat three months' periodic rent, with no proof of loss required). The Legislature plainly knew how to write a fixed-sum remedy; it wrote none for the landlord's side of a deposit deduction. It did write one for a different tenancy — § 76-14,104(2) of the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act gives a landlord up to one and one-half months' periodic rent as liquidated damages for a willful bad-faith holdover — which makes the silence in the deposit section a choice rather than an oversight.

What to do instead: describe in the lease the CATEGORIES you may charge for (unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning if the unit is left substantially less clean than it was), keep the invoices and photographs, and put the real figures in the § 76-1416(2) written itemization you must deliver or mail within fourteen days of the termination of the tenancy. One exception worth knowing: § 76-1429(2) ends "Notwithstanding the provisions of this section, the tenant is responsible for damage caused by his negligence" — so a lease term holding the tenant liable for negligent damage is on firm statutory ground, provided the amount you charge is still your actual loss.

title: An Unclaimed Deposit Makes You a Statutory Holder — One Year, Not Three or Five
bodyText:
Nebraska turns an unreturned deposit into state property faster than most states, and it puts real penalties on the landlord who sits on it.

The trigger is short. Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1416(2) says that if the mailing of the deposit balance "is returned as undeliverable, or if the returned balance of the security deposit remains outstanding for ONE YEAR, it shall be considered abandoned property to be reported and paid to the State Treasurer in accordance with the Uniform Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act." One year, measured from the point the balance is outstanding — not the three- or five-year dormancy other states use. The Unclaimed Property Act's own catch-all for intangible property, § 69-1308(a), is FIVE years; § 76-1416(2) overrides it for a residential security deposit. Note also that the Act does not name security deposits anywhere: the phrase "security deposit" appears in only three sections of the twelve chapters searched, and none of them is in the Unclaimed Property Act. You get in through § 76-1416(2)'s express direction and through § 69-1301(e), which defines a "holder" as "any person in possession of property subject to the act belonging to another ... or is indebted to another on an obligation subject to the act." That is you.

Once you are a holder, four duties attach. (1) Due diligence BEFORE you report: under § 69-1310(e), if you know where the tenant is and the claim is not time-barred, you must communicate with the tenant and take necessary steps to prevent abandonment from being presumed, and you "shall exercise due diligence to ascertain the whereabouts of the owner." (2) The annual report: § 69-1310(d) requires it to be filed BEFORE NOVEMBER 1 each year as of the preceding JUNE 30, verified under § 69-1310(b) and (f), with the property accompanying the report unless the State Treasurer excuses it for good cause. If your total reportable intangible property for a year is fifty dollars or less you may skip that year and report it in a year when the total exceeds fifty dollars. (3) Records: § 69-1322(d)(1) makes you keep the owner's name and last-known address for SEVEN YEARS after the property becomes reportable. (4) Delivery, which is also your protection: § 69-1313 says once you pay or deliver, the state takes custody and you are "relieved of all liability to the extent of the value of the property so paid or delivered" for any claim then existing or later made — and if you later pay a tenant who appears entitled, the State Treasurer reimburses you on proof.

The penalties are in § 69-1324 and they are not nominal. Late payment or delivery: interest under § 45-103 as that section stood on the date the property should have been paid, running from that date. Willful failure to render a report or perform another duty: a civil penalty of ONE HUNDRED DOLLARS FOR EACH DAY, capped at five thousand dollars. Willful failure to pay or deliver: twenty-five percent of the value of the property. Willful refusal to pay or deliver: a Class II misdemeanor. The Treasurer may waive or remit any of the interest or penalty for good cause (§ 69-1324(d)), may demand a verified report within thirty days (§ 69-1322(a)), may examine your records (§ 69-1322(b)), and may assess the cost of that examination against you up to the value of the property found reportable (§ 69-1322(c)).

Two drafting points. First, do not write a clause forfeiting an unclaimed deposit to yourself. The money is directed to the State Treasurer by statute, and a term by which the tenant gives up that right is a provision by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under" the Act, void under § 76-1415(1)(a). Second, do not write a dormancy or administration charge against the balance. Section 69-1308(a) does speak of income or increment "after deducting any lawful charges," but for a residential deposit the only lawful application is the § 76-1416(2) one — rent and damages you have actually suffered — so a holding charge has no source and would also push you over the § 76-1416(1) one-month ceiling if you took it as security.

title: Last Month's Rent in Advance — the One-Month Cap Question Nebraska Has Not Answered
bodyText:
Two different questions hide under "last month's rent," and Nebraska answers one of them cleanly and the other not at all.

The clean one: the tenant has no right to make you apply the deposit to the last month's rent. Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1416(2) says that "UPON TERMINATION of the tenancy, property or money held by the landlord as prepaid rent and security MAY BE APPLIED to the payment of rent and the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered." The timing is termination, and the power is the landlord's. Nebraska wrote no provision like the states that expressly forbid a tenant to apply a deposit to the final month's rent, and it wrote none permitting it either; the question is left to the lease, and your Use of Security Deposit clause already closes it by saying the deposit will not relieve the tenant of rent due before termination.

The unanswered one is about the CAP, and it is worth money. Section 76-1416(1) reads: "A landlord may not demand or receive SECURITY, HOWEVER DENOMINATED, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent, except that a pet deposit not in excess of one-fourth of one month's periodic rent may be demanded or received when appropriate." So a one-month ceiling, measured on "security, however denominated." Does money you collect at signing and label "last month's rent" count against that ceiling? Nebraska's text cuts both ways and no provision resolves it. Pointing one way: "however denominated" is an anti-relabelling phrase, and when the Legislature wrote the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act ten years later it expressly carved advance rent out of the capped deposit — § 76-1469 defines "rental deposit" as money to secure performance "OTHER THAN a deposit which is exclusively an advance payment of rent," and § 76-1483 then caps the rental deposit at one month — a carve-out it never added to § 76-1416(1). Pointing the other way: § 76-1416's own catchline is "Security deposits; PREPAID RENT," subsection (2) names "prepaid rent AND security" as two things, and §§ 76-1425(4), 76-1426(1), 76-1429(2) and 76-1430 all say the landlord shall return "all prepaid rent and security" — treating prepaid rent as its own category. Section 76-1414(1) and (3) also let the parties agree when rent is payable, so rent made payable at the start of the term is arguably rent on the agreed schedule rather than security.

Until a Nebraska court or the Legislature settles it, take the cautious course: keep the total money you demand at or before signing — security deposit plus any pet deposit plus anything called last month's rent, advance rent, move-in fee or holding deposit — inside one month's periodic rent, plus the separate pet deposit of up to one-quarter of one month's periodic rent where appropriate. The downside of being wrong is not small: § 76-1416(3) gives the tenant the property and money due, court costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and if the failure is willful and not in good faith, liquidated damages of one month's periodic rent or twice the deposit, whichever is less. If you do collect a final month's rent up front, make the lease identify the specific month it pays and the date it is payable, rather than describing it as a deposit or as security for performance.

title: You Cannot Make the Deposit Refund Depend on a Surrender Notice or a Forwarding Address
bodyText:
Nebraska has no statute conditioning a tenant's right to a deposit refund on the tenant giving notice of surrender, delivering keys by a certain hour, requesting the refund in writing, or supplying a forwarding address. Several states have one; Nebraska wrote the opposite.

Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1416(2) makes the duty unconditional and then tells you exactly what to do when the tenant gives you nothing: "The balance, if any, and a written itemization shall be delivered or mailed to the tenant within fourteen days after the date of termination of the tenancy. IF NO MAILING ADDRESS OR INSTRUCTIONS ARE PROVIDED BY THE TENANT TO THE LANDLORD, the landlord shall mail, by first-class mail, the balance of the security deposit to be returned, if any, and a written itemization of the amount of the security deposit not returned to the tenant's LAST-KNOWN MAILING ADDRESS." So the tenant's silence does not suspend the clock; it changes where you send the money. A lease term making the refund turn on a surrender notice or a forwarding address would be a provision by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under" the Act, unenforceable under § 76-1415(1)(a) and (2) — and deliberate use of a term you know to be prohibited gives the tenant actual damages and the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees.

There is one wrinkle you should know about and should not rely on. The annotations printed with § 76-1416 pull in two directions: Hilliard v. Robertson, 253 Neb. 232 (1997), is summarised as holding that the fourteen-day language "refers to the time allowed the landlord to return the deposit, not the time in which a demand must be made by the vacating tenant," while Mason v. Schumacher, 231 Neb. 929 (1989), is summarised as holding that under subsection (3) a tenant must establish that the landlord did not comply with a demand for return in order to recover the deposit plus an attorney fee. Those are case summaries, not statutory text. Treat them as a possible limit on the tenant's FEE RECOVERY, never as a condition on your DUTY: your duty runs from the date of termination of the tenancy, with or without a demand.

What you may lawfully do: ask. A lease paragraph requesting a forwarding address and move-out instructions is not prohibited — § 76-1414(1) permits terms the Act does not bar — and it is useful, because supplying one takes you out of the last-known-address fallback. Phrase it as a request and a cooperation obligation, not as a precondition to the refund, and keep your own record of the last-known address either way. The surrender obligations themselves (returning keys, leaving the unit clean and empty) belong in the Surrender at End of Term clause, which carries no deposit condition.

title: No Rule on Who Pays for Common-Area Lights — But You Keep the Safety Duty Either Way
bodyText:
Nebraska has no statute about common-area lighting. Nothing requires you to supply it, nothing sets a light level, nothing bars you from wiring hall, stair, porch or basement lights to a tenant's electric meter, and nothing gives a tenant a remedy specific to being billed for them. There is also no Nebraska analogue to the small-building rules some states have, which allow a tenant to be charged for common-area lights only under a written lease and only from the start of a new tenancy.

What does apply is the maintenance scheme, and it has a trap in it. Common areas are inside the premises you are responsible for: § 76-1410(12) defines "premises" to include "grounds, areas, and facilities held out for the use of tenants generally or whose use is promised to the tenant." Section 76-1419(1)(c) then requires you to "[k]eep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition," and § 76-1419(1)(d) requires you to "[m]aintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her." Note that phrase: if your lease promises common-area lighting, it becomes a facility "required to be supplied" and the maintenance duty attaches to it.

Now the trap. The delegation provisions do not reach the common-area duty at all. Section 76-1419(2) lets you shift the waste-removal and water-and-heat duties — subdivisions (1)(e) and (1)(f) — plus specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling, but ONLY for a single-family residence, in writing, for good consideration, in good faith and not to evade your obligations. For any other dwelling unit, § 76-1419(3) reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling," and only in a separate signed writing with adequate consideration that "does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises." Neither subsection can transfer the § 76-1419(1)(c) duty to keep common areas safe. So if you put the stairwell light on a tenant's meter and that tenant stops paying the electric bill, the bill is the tenant's problem and the dark stairwell is still yours. Under § 76-1425(2) a tenant can recover damages and get injunctive relief for that, with reasonable attorney's fees if your noncompliance is willful.

Practical course: if a shared light is on a tenant's meter, say so plainly in the utilities paragraph, say which fixtures it covers, and keep the fixtures and wiring in working order yourself. Consider metering shared lighting to the house account instead — it is cheap insurance against a § 76-1419(1)(c) claim. One Nebraska contrast shows the Legislature could have legislated here and chose not to: for mobile-home parks it wrote an express utility-explanation duty — § 76-1482 requires a written explanation of utility rates, charges and services to the prospective tenant before the rental agreement is signed, unless the tenant pays the utility company directly and required outlets for provided utilities (§ 76-1492(1)(e)), and for condominiums it provided that where the declaration requires it, "the costs of utilities not separately metered must be assessed in proportion to usage" (§ 76-873(c)(3)). No comparable provision exists for an ordinary Nebraska rental.

title: No Government Pre-Approval of a Lease — Nebraska Has No Communal or Tribal Land Regime
bodyText:
Nebraska has no communal, tribal or native-land tenure in its statutes, and no statute makes any residential lease depend on a government officer's approval before it is valid. There is no approving official, no rule about who holds rent collected before approval, and no provision about possession taken in advance of approval. If you are leasing privately held Nebraska land, nothing in state law stands between your signature and a binding lease.

Two Nebraska formality rules do decide whether you have a lease at all, and they are the ones to check instead. First, § 36-105: "Every contract for the leasing for a longer period than ONE YEAR, or for the sale of any lands, shall be VOID unless the contract or some note or memorandum thereof be in writing and signed by the party by whom the lease or sale is to be made." That is the lessor's signature, and the consequence is voidness, not unenforceability. Second, where the let property is the owner's homestead, Nebraska's homestead statute requires both spouses to execute and acknowledge an instrument encumbering it — whether a lease counts as an "encumbrance" is unsettled, and the cautious course is to have both spouses sign and acknowledge.

On the specific question of land held in trust for a tribe or allotted to a tribal member within Nebraska's borders: that is a matter of federal and tribal law, and no Nebraska statute purports to govern it. The territorial reach of the state's landlord-tenant act is stated in § 76-1407 — it "applies to, regulates, and determines rights, obligations, and remedies under a rental agreement, wherever made, for a dwelling unit located within this state" — with no carve-out for tribal land and no approval mechanism. Nebraska's statutes mention a tribe in only one place that matters to a landlord, and it is not about land: § 76-1410(11) lets a "federally recognized Indian tribe whose governmental body is within the borders of Nebraska" be a "qualified third party" certifying domestic violence. If you are letting a dwelling on trust or allotted land, get advice on the federal leasing rules and the relevant tribe's own code before you rely on a Nebraska form lease; nothing in this library speaks to those regimes.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure in Nebraska — and the Word Does Not Appear in the Statutes
bodyText:
Nebraska has no defective-drywall disclosure. The word "drywall" does not appear anywhere in the twelve statute chapters searched, nor does "gypsum," "sheetrock" or "plasterboard" outside a condominium boundary definition. There is no corrosive-drywall statute, no imported-building-material statute, no registry and no required lease rider. A landlord renting a Nebraska house built during the 2001-2009 period that produced the problem elsewhere has no statutory tenant-disclosure duty about it.

That leaves the ordinary duties, and they are enough to matter. Section 76-1419(1)(b) requires you to "[m]ake all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition" — note "after written or ACTUAL notice," so a tenant complaint starts your clock whether or not it is in writing — and § 76-1419(1)(d) requires you to maintain in good and safe working order all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facilities and appliances "supplied or required to be supplied" by you, which is where corroded copper lines and failing coils would be litigated. Section 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence reserves existing tort law, so a nondisclosure claim about a known defect is not channelled into the Act. If a condition makes the unit unfit, § 76-1425(1) gives the tenant a termination route and § 76-1425(2) gives damages, injunctive relief and attorney's fees where your noncompliance is willful.

Two Nebraska disclosure duties sit nearby and neither reaches drywall. The owner-and-manager disclosure under § 76-1417(1) covers names and addresses only. And § 76-2,120, the Seller Property Condition Disclosure statute, reaches "any lease with the option to purchase residential real property" (§ 76-2,120(2)), so a lease-option landlord becomes a statutory seller and must deliver the prescribed statement — but the contents are set by § 76-2,120(3) and (4) and are not drywall-specific. There is also no Nebraska statewide bed-bug or tenant-facing radon disclosure, which the library already covers; drywall is the same pattern.

Practical course: if you actually know a unit has defective drywall, disclose it in writing and fix it. The reason is not a disclosure statute — it is § 76-1419(1)(b), the reserved tort law, and the fact that a known uninhabitable condition you concealed is the worst possible posture in a § 76-1425 action.

title: No Designated-Repairer Rule — You May Require Your Contractor, With Two Limits
bodyText:
Nebraska has no designated-repairer statute. Nothing requires a lease to name an approved contractor or service company, nothing authorizes a landlord to compel the tenant to use one, and nothing regulates what such a term may charge. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act simply does not address it.

So the term is governed by § 76-1414(1) — the parties "may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by" the Act or other rule of law. A clause saying the tenant must get your written approval before engaging anyone to work on the property, and must use a licensed and insured contractor, is lawful here and sensible. The library carries that substance in the No Alterations clause, which already requires your prior written consent before the tenant changes anything, so no separate designated-repairer clause is offered. Add your own naming a specific vendor if you want one.

Two limits to respect. First, delegation. If what you are really doing is handing the tenant a maintenance duty, you are in § 76-1419(2) or (3), and the difference between them is the sharpest trap in the Act. For a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE as § 76-1410(16) defines it, § 76-1419(2) lets you agree that the tenant performs the (1)(e) waste-removal and (1)(f) water-and-heat duties and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling — in writing, for good consideration, in good faith, and not to evade your obligations. For ANY OTHER dwelling unit, § 76-1419(3) reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling," in a SEPARATE writing signed by the parties with adequate consideration, and it "does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises." It cannot shift the (1)(e) or (1)(f) duties at all. Section 76-1419(4) is the cleaner route where it fits: "Notwithstanding any provision of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a landlord may employ a tenant to perform the obligations of the landlord."

Second, pricing. If your designated vendor is yourself or an affiliate and the charge exceeds your actual cost, you are exposed on two fronts: § 76-1412 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision, enforce the remainder without it, or limit its application, and § 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant waives or foregoes rights or remedies under the Act. Nebraska wrote the express version of this rule for a different tenancy, which is why the silence here is a choice rather than a gap: under § 76-1492(2) a mobile-home-park landlord "shall not impose any condition connected with the rental or occupancy of a mobile home space which requires the tenant's exclusive use of a seller of fuel, furnishings, goods, services, or mobile homes unless such condition is necessary to protect the health, safety, aesthetic value, or welfare of mobile home tenants in the park," may impose reasonable standardization requirements, and if conditions are imposed that result in charges, "the charges shall not exceed the actual cost incurred in providing the tenant with the goods or services." Treat that actual-cost standard as the benchmark a Nebraska court is most likely to reach for, even though it does not bind an ordinary rental.

title: Nebraska's Reasonable-Accommodation Duty, the Direct-Threat Limit, and the Four-Room Exemption
bodyText:
The Nebraska Fair Housing Act carries a reasonable-accommodation duty of its own, and it is separate from the service-animal statute the library covers elsewhere. Under § 20-319(2)(b), discrimination includes "[a] refusal to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices, or services when such accommodations may be necessary to afford the person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling." That is the duty that reaches a reserved accessible parking space, an exception to a no-pets rule, a different rent due date tied to benefit payments, a change in how you communicate notices, or permission for a live-in aide. Section 20-319(1)(a) and (b) also make the protection travel: it covers a disability of the renter, of "[a]ny person associated with" the renter, and of "[a] person residing in or intending to reside in the dwelling" after it is rented.

The companion duty is about physical changes, and it is the tenant's money. Section 20-319(2)(a) makes it discrimination to refuse to permit, AT THE EXPENSE OF THE PERSON WITH A DISABILITY, reasonable modifications of existing premises where necessary to afford full enjoyment, "except that in the case of a rental, the landlord may, when it is reasonable to do so, condition permission for a modification on the renter agreeing to restore the interior of the premises to the condition that existed before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted." Read the limits in that sentence: the restoration condition reaches the INTERIOR only, it must be reasonable to impose, and wear and tear is excluded. Nebraska wrote nothing more. There is no provision requiring that condition to be stated in the lease, no authority for a restoration escrow or deposit, and no interest-bearing-account rule for one. That matters, because the deposit cap bites: § 76-1416(1) bars demanding or receiving "security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent," so a restoration deposit on top of a full one-month deposit is money you may not lawfully hold. Take the restoration promise as a written agreement, not as cash.

Three limits run in your favour. First, § 20-319(8): nothing in the section requires a dwelling to be made available to an individual "whose tenancy would constitute a direct threat to the health or safety of other individuals or whose tenancy would result in substantial physical damage to the property of others." Second, § 20-308.01 defines disability by reference to 42 U.S.C. 12102 "as such section existed on January 1, 2021" — a frozen reference, so later federal amendments do not move the state definition — and adds that disability "shall not include current, illegal use of or addiction to a controlled substance as defined in section 28-401." Section 20-322(5) separately says nothing in the Act prohibits conduct against a person convicted of the illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance. Third, and the one most Nebraska small landlords never learn: § 20-319(1) opens "Except as exempted by section 20-322," and § 20-322(3) says nothing in the Act limits the right of a person to refuse to rent a room or rooms in HIS OR HER OWN HOME "for any reason or for no reason" — but that exception "shall not apply to any person who makes available for rental or occupancy MORE THAN FOUR SLEEPING ROOMS to a person or family within his or her own home." Four or fewer rooms in your own home and the Act's disability provisions do not reach you at all; the fifth room turns them on.

New construction is a separate duty with a bright line. Section 20-319(2)(c) imposes accessible design and construction on "covered multifamily dwellings" first occupied after September 1, 1991, and § 20-319(6) defines those as buildings of four or more units WITH one or more elevators, and ground-floor units in other buildings of four or more units. The required features are accessible public and common use portions, doors wide enough for wheelchair passage, an accessible route into and through the dwelling, accessible light switches, outlets, thermostats and environmental controls, bathroom-wall reinforcements for later grab bars, and maneuverable kitchens and bathrooms. Section 20-319(3) gives a compliance safe harbour: meeting ANSI A117.1 satisfies the adaptive-design requirements. Section 20-319(4)(a) deems compliance with a political subdivision's own adopted version to satisfy them, but § 20-319(5)(b) says a subdivision's determination "shall not be conclusive in enforcement proceedings" before the Equal Opportunity Commission.

What it costs to get wrong: after a Commission hearing, § 20-337(3)(a) allows an order for actual damages and injunctive or equitable relief, and § 20-337(3)(b) allows a civil penalty to vindicate the public interest of up to ten thousand dollars for a first adjudicated practice, twenty-five thousand for a second within five years and fifty thousand for a third within seven years. An aggrieved person may instead sue in district court within two years under § 20-342(1)(a)(i), recovering actual damages, injunctive relief and — at the court's discretion — reasonable attorney's fees and costs under § 20-342(3)(b). The state text provides no punitive damages.

title: No Right for a Tenant to House Disaster-Displaced Guests — It Is a Lease Question Here
bodyText:
Nebraska has no statute allowing a tenant to take in people displaced by a fire, flood, tornado or declared emergency notwithstanding the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none barring it either. There is no suspension of occupancy caps during an emergency, no notice-and-permission procedure, and no immunity for a tenant who shelters a displaced relative. Whatever your lease says is what governs.

Start from what the Act gives you. Section 76-1410(17) defines a tenant as "a person entitled under a rental agreement to occupy a dwelling unit TO THE EXCLUSION OF OTHERS" — so occupancy rights flow from the agreement, not from the emergency. Section 76-1424 provides that "[u]nless otherwise agreed, the tenant shall occupy his dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit," and lets the rental agreement require notice of an anticipated absence over seven days. Section 76-1414(1) lets you include any term the Act does not prohibit, so a guest-duration limit and a named-occupants list are lawful. If you prefer to handle it by rule rather than by lease paragraph, § 76-1422 requires the rule to clear all six of its conditions, including that its purpose be to promote the appearance, convenience, safety or welfare of tenants, preserve your property from abusive use, or make a fair distribution of services and facilities; that it apply to all tenants fairly; that it be explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do; and that the tenant have notice of it when entering into the rental agreement. A rule adopted mid-tenancy binds only on reasonable notice and only if it does not work "a substantial modification of his bargain" — which a sudden guest ban during an emergency might well be.

Two things to keep in view before you enforce a limit. First, occupancy limits are a fair housing pressure point. Section 20-322(4)(a) preserves "any reasonable local restrictions regarding the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling" and says nothing in the Act regarding familial status applies to housing for older persons — but a limit you invent yourself, applied in a way that falls on families with children, is not protected by that subsection. Second, your guest rules carry real weight the other way: under § 76-1431(4) the five-day no-cure termination route reaches activity by a "guest, or other person who is under the tenant's control or who is present upon the premises with the tenant's consent," so a tenant's visitors are already within your reach for serious misconduct without any special disaster provision.

Practical course: decide in advance, in writing, how long a guest may stay before becoming an occupant who must be screened and added to the lease, and write a short, humane exception for a genuine emergency — a stated number of additional days on written notice to you. Nebraska gives you complete freedom here and no safety net if your lease is silent, which is the usual reason this becomes a dispute.

title: No Declared-Disaster Tenancy Rule — Casualty Is the Only Route Nebraska Wrote
bodyText:
Nebraska has no declared-disaster provision in its landlord-tenant law. A gubernatorial or presidential disaster declaration does not end a tenancy, does not suspend rent, does not start a relocation-benefit obligation, does not toll a notice period and does not create a tenant right of first refusal to return. There is no rent-freeze or price-gouging statute to constrain what you charge afterwards either.

The only route the Legislature wrote is the general fire-and-casualty provision, and it is tenant-triggered. Under § 76-1429(1), where the dwelling unit or premises are damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty to an extent that enjoyment of the unit is substantially impaired, the TENANT may either immediately vacate and notify you in writing within fourteen days of an intention to terminate — in which case the agreement terminates as of the date of vacating — or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part, with "the tenant's liability for rent ... reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value of the dwelling unit." Section 76-1429(2) then requires you to return all prepaid rent and security recoverable under § 76-1416, times the accounting as of the date of the casualty, and ends: "Notwithstanding the provisions of this section, the tenant is responsible for damage caused by his negligence." Nothing in § 76-1429 gives YOU a termination right, and nothing abates rent automatically — the tenant must act.

Three other provisions matter when a storm takes out utilities rather than the building. Section 76-1427(1)(a) is the only procure-and-deduct right anywhere in the Act: on a failure to supply heat, running water, hot water or essential services, the tenant may, after written notice, procure reasonable amounts of the service during the failure and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from the rent. Section 76-1425(2) adds that where your noncompliance "is caused by conditions or circumstances beyond his or her control, the tenant may not recover consequential damages, but retains remedies provided in section 76-1427" — the nearest thing Nebraska has to a force-majeure rule, and note how narrow it is: it removes consequential damages only, and only from the § 76-1425 claim. There is no general act-of-God excuse in the Act. And § 76-1403 keeps the background law alive: "Unless displaced by the provisions of" the Act, "the principles of law and equity, including the law relating to capacity to contract, mutuality of obligations, principal and agent, real property, public health, safety and fire prevention, estoppel, fraud, misrepresentation, duress, coercion, mistake, bankruptcy, or other validating or invalidating cause, supplement the act's provisions" — which is the door through which impossibility and frustration arguments come in.

Nebraska did write a displacement regime, just not for landlords: §§ 76-1220 and 76-1238 put relocation-assistance advisory duties on a "displacing agency," meaning a government body acquiring property, and § 76-1238(2)(c) even carves out a major disaster, a presidentially declared national emergency and any other emergency requiring immediate removal for health or safety. That the Legislature legislated disaster displacement for condemning agencies and not for landlords makes the silence a choice.

Practical course: your lease should say what happens on casualty — whether you may terminate, how rent is apportioned, and how insurance proceeds and relocation are handled — because § 76-1429 answers only the tenant's side and § 76-1414(1) lets you add terms the Act does not prohibit. Keep your own insurance, and do not rely on a force-majeure clause to excuse a habitability failure, because § 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant waives or foregoes rights or remedies under the Act.

title: Double-Letting Is Not Named in the Statutes — But § 76-1426 Is Expensive
bodyText:
Nebraska has no statute captioned "double letting" and no provision forbidding a landlord in terms from renting the same unit or room to two tenants. It does not need one. Letting a unit twice means failing to deliver possession to one of them, and that is one of the few places in the Act where the Legislature wrote a multiplied remedy against the landlord.

Start with the definition: § 76-1410(17) says a tenant is "a person entitled under a rental agreement to occupy a dwelling unit TO THE EXCLUSION OF OTHERS." A second letting of the same space is inconsistent with the first tenant's status, not merely with the first tenant's expectations. Section 76-1418 then makes the duty explicit: "At the commencement of the term the landlord shall deliver possession of the premises to the tenant in compliance with the rental agreement and section 76-1419." The same section gives you the tools to fix the problem — you may bring an action for possession against any person wrongfully in possession and recover the § 76-1437(3) damages — and a defence: "If the landlord makes reasonable efforts to obtain possession of the premises, he shall not be liable for an action under this section." That defence is the whole game, and it is available only if you actually move.

The cost of not moving is in § 76-1426. If you fail to deliver possession as § 76-1418 requires, "rent ABATES until possession is delivered," and the tenant may either (1) terminate on at least five days' written notice, in which case "the landlord shall return all prepaid rent and security," or (2) demand performance and, at the tenant's election, maintain an action for possession against any person wrongfully in possession or wrongfully withholding possession and recover the damages sustained. Then the sting in the tail: "If a person's failure to deliver possession is WILLFUL AND NOT IN GOOD FAITH, an aggrieved person may recover from that person an amount NOT MORE THAN three months' periodic rent OR THREEFOLD THE ACTUAL DAMAGES sustained by him, WHICHEVER IS GREATER, and reasonable attorney's fees." Note the shape: it is a ceiling with a greater-of alternative, not a flat multiplier — the court may award less — but the ceiling is set by whichever of the two measures is larger, so a tenant with real relocation and storage losses is not capped at three months' rent. And note "an aggrieved person ... from that person": the liability is not limited to the landlord, so a holdover occupant or an agent who double-booked can be the defendant.

A deliberate double-letting is the paradigm of "willful and not in good faith." Practical course: keep one calendar and one ledger of commitments per unit; never take a second deposit on a unit you have already committed, since § 76-1416(1) caps security at one month's periodic rent and holding two deposits on one unit is hard to explain; and if a prior tenant holds over, start the § 76-1418 possession action at once and document it, because the reasonable-efforts defence turns on what you did, not on whose fault it was. For a room let in a shared house, the same analysis applies: § 76-1410(4) defines a dwelling unit as a structure or part of a structure used as a home, residence or sleeping place, and § 76-1410(15) treats a roomer in a unit lacking a major bathroom or kitchen facility as having a dwelling unit too.

title: No Confidentiality Duty for the Domestic-Violence Paperwork You Receive
bodyText: Nebraska hands you a tenant's most sensitive document and then says nothing about keeping it. Sections 76-1431.01, 76-1431.02 and 76-1431.03 each require the tenant to "[p]rovide to the landlord a copy of the documentation" - a protective order, restraining order or similar relief, or a qualified third party's certification - before the lease release, the perpetrator removal or the 24-hour lock change is triggered. None of those sections, and no other Nebraska statute, imposes a confidentiality duty on the landlord, limits what you may do with the copy, requires you to destroy it, or creates a penalty for disclosing it. There is no Nebraska address-confidentiality program provision in the landlord-tenant act either. Three things that look like they might fill the gap do not. The real-estate agency statutes do impose a confidentiality duty on a licensee, but Section 76-2406 defines "confidential information" as information made confidential by law or "by written instructions from the client" - and in a Section 76-2417 landlord's-agency the client is you, not the tenant, so that duty protects your information, not the victim's. Nebraska's data-breach statute reaches only "personal information" as Section 87-802(5) defines it - a name plus a Social Security, driver's license, financial-account, electronic-identification or biometric element, or an email/username plus a password - and a protective order or a DV certification carries none of those on its own. And the Data Privacy Act's own emergency-contact carve-out at Section 87-1104(16) is about emergency-contact data, not DV documentation. SO THE CAUTIOUS COURSE IS YOUR OWN POLICY, NOT THE STATUTE'S. Treat the documentation as need-to-know: keep it out of the tenant file that maintenance and leasing staff open, do not recite it in a notice served on anyone else, and do not name the perpetrator's victim in the Section 76-1431.02 five-day notice beyond what the statute requires. The exposure if you leak it is not statutory - it is the ordinary tort and the practical one, because a disclosure that puts a victim back in front of a perpetrator is the fact pattern that produces a negligence claim and a very bad record in the possession suit you are probably already in.

title: A Domestic-Violence Release Does Not Start the Deposit Clock
bodyText: Nebraska has no domestic-violence deposit rule, and the consequence runs in your favour - but only if you read the two statutes together. Section 76-1416(2) starts the deposit clock at one event and one event only: the balance and a written itemization must go out "within fourteen days after the date of termination of the TENANCY." Section 76-1431.01 releases a victim tenant and any household members the tenant names from the RENTAL AGREEMENT. Those are not the same thing. Where the released tenant was the only tenant, the tenancy ends on the release date the tenant set (at least 14 and no more than 30 days after the notice), and your fourteen days run from there. Where there are other tenants on the lease who are not household members of the released tenant, Section 76-1431.01(5) says in terms that they "are not released," so the tenancy continues, there is no termination, and no deposit obligation is triggered at all - you are not required to split the deposit, account for a departing co-tenant's share, or hold anything separately. The same is true of a Section 76-1431.02 perpetrator removal: the remaining tenant stays, so there is nothing to return yet. TWO LIMITS ON THAT. First, Section 76-1431.01(4) says a released tenant and household member "[a]re not subject to any fee solely because of termination of the rental agreement," so you cannot charge an early-termination fee, a re-letting fee or an administrative fee against the deposit for the release itself - and you cannot charge for processing the paperwork. Second, Section 76-1431.01(3) keeps them liable for "rent for the month in which the tenant terminated the rental agreement" and (4)(a) cuts off liability for rent and damage "incurred after the release date," so what you may lawfully deduct is rent through that month and damage up to the release date, and nothing after. Nebraska does not make the clock wait for all occupants to deliver possession the way Massachusetts does; it does something simpler and better for you - it never starts until the tenancy itself ends.

title: Section 76-1431(5) Read Exactly: It Blocks One Route, and It Is Not Only About Domestic Violence
bodyText: Nebraska's only eviction protection for a crime victim sits in Section 76-1431(5), and it is almost always described wrongly in two directions at once. READ WHAT IT BLOCKS. Subsection (5)(a) opens "A landlord shall not take action UNDER SUBSECTION (4) OF THIS SECTION" - that is the five-day, no-cure fast track for violent criminal activity, illegal controlled-substance sales and other health-or-safety-threatening conduct. It blocks that one route. It does not suspend Section 76-1431 as a whole: your ordinary Section 76-1431(1) thirty-day notice with a fourteen-day cure, your Section 76-1431(2) seven-day nonpayment notice, your Section 76-1431(3) damages, injunction and willful-noncompliance attorney's fees, and your Section 76-1437 end-of-term and periodic terminations are all untouched. A tenant who is a DV victim and who does not pay rent is still a tenant who does not pay rent. READ WHO IT COVERS - IT IS WIDER THAN DOMESTIC VIOLENCE. The bar applies where the qualifying activity "is conducted by a person on the premises OTHER THAN THE TENANT OR A HOUSEHOLD MEMBER" and the tenant or household member takes at least one of three measures. Only the third is DV-specific. Measure (i) is seeking "a protective order, restraining order, or other similar relief which would apply to the person conducting such activity." Measure (ii) is reporting "such activity to a law enforcement agency in an effort to initiate a criminal action against the person conducting the activity." Neither says domestic violence. A tenant who reports a neighbour's or a stranger's gunfire, assault or drug dealing on the premises, in an effort to get that person charged, has taken measure (ii) and you may not use the five-day route against that tenant - DV or no DV. Measure (iii) is the DV one: if the activity is an act of domestic violence, certification from a qualified third party under the federal Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act of 2013 (Section 76-1410(11) defines the qualified third party). READ THE GATE, BECAUSE IT IS WHAT MOST SUMMARIES DROP. If the activity was conducted BY the tenant or BY a household member, subsection (5) never engages, however many protective orders or police reports exist. And subsection (5)(b) is two sentences, both of which help you: "This subsection shall not apply to a tenant who is a perpetrator of an act of domestic violence," and where both the victim who took the measures and the perpetrator are parties to the rental agreement, "a landlord shall only take action under subsection (4) of this section against the perpetrator." That second sentence is a mandate, not a permission - and Section 76-1431.02(3) sharpens it: once the victim delivers qualifying documentation and written notice, "the landlord SHALL proceed under subsection (4) of section 76-1431 against only the cotenant or occupant who is the perpetrator," serving the five-day notice on the date the victim named. Two practical notes. There is no tenure-based or good-cause eviction protection in Nebraska to layer on top of this (see "No Tenure-Based For-Cause Eviction Protection"), and nothing in Section 76-1431(5) requires the tenant to prove the measure worked - seeking relief and reporting are enough.

title: Nebraska's DV Housing Citations Have Not Moved - They Were Added, in Two Waves
bodyText: Some states renumbered their domestic-violence statutes into a new chapter, which strands every lease and handbook that cited the old numbers. Nebraska did not. Its landlord-tenant DV provisions were CREATED where they now sit, in two waves, and no section has been relocated or repealed. Wave one, 2021: LB320 added the definitions at Section 76-1410(1) (act of domestic violence), (6) (household member) and (11) (qualified third party), the carve-outs from the five-day fast track at Section 76-1431(5), and the lease-release right at Section 76-1431.01. Wave two, 2025: LB80 added Section 76-1431.02 (removing a perpetrator who is a co-tenant or occupant), Section 76-1431.03 (the tenant may require a lock change within 24 hours) and Section 76-1431.04 (how the lock is changed, who keeps a key, and who pays), and extended the Act's own citation range at Section 76-1401. LB80 did NOT amend Section 76-1431, whose history still ends with LB320 - so a lease citing Section 76-1431(5) to LB80 has the wrong act. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR PAPERWORK. There is no stale-citation problem to fix, but there is an INCOMPLETE-citation problem: a lease or handbook written before 2025 cites at most Sections 76-1431(5) and 76-1431.01, and is missing the entire perpetrator-removal and lock-change regime. If your documents predate 2025, that is the gap to close. SECOND, AND LESS OBVIOUS: Nebraska's DV sections do not define domestic violence themselves. Section 76-1410(1) borrows six definitions from two other chapters - abuse as defined in Section 42-903, sexual assault under Sections 28-319 to 28-320.01, domestic assault under Section 28-323, stalking under Section 28-311.03, labor or sex trafficking under Section 28-831, and knowing and intentional abuse, neglect or exploitation of a vulnerable or senior adult under Section 28-386. Each of those borrowed sections can be amended without anyone touching chapter 76, and one just was: Section 28-323 was amended by Laws 2026, LB965, Section 14, operative July 18, 2026. So the right practice is not to recite the definition in your lease at all - cite Section 76-1410(1) and let it point where it points. A lease that spells out what counts as domestic violence will go out of date silently, in a chapter you are not watching.

title: No Submetering Disclosure Rule - and Two Reasons to Be Careful Before You Install a Meter
