bodyText: Nebraska's landlord-tenant act says nothing about metering. There is no submetering disclosure requirement, no rule about how a master-metered building allocates electricity or gas among tenants, no accuracy or calibration standard for a landlord's own meter, no price-posting duty, and no cap on what you may charge a tenant for resold energy. The whole of chapter 76 contains two references to a meter and neither is a landlord duty. Your allocation method is therefore a matter of contract, which puts three Nebraska-specific points in front of you. FIRST, WHATEVER YOU CHARGE IS RENT. Section 76-1410(13) defines rent as "all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement," so a submeter charge, a flat utility add-on or a ratio-allocation charge is rent. That helps you - an unpaid utility charge is reachable by the Section 76-1431(2) seven-day nonpayment notice - and it cuts the other way, because everything measured in rent is measured including it (see "In Nebraska Every Payment Under the Lease Is "Rent" - Which Cuts Both Ways"). SECOND, SAY IT IN THE LEASE OR YOU CANNOT COLLECT IT. Because nothing requires a disclosure, nothing supplies a default: if the lease does not state the method, there is no statutory fallback to argue from, and Section 76-1419(3) cannot shift the Section 76-1419(1)(f) running-water-and-heat duty at all for any unit that is not a single-family residence. State the method, the billing period, and when payment is due. THIRD, THE METER ITSELF IS THE RISK, NOT THE DISCLOSURE. Sections 25-21,275 to 25-21,278 give a utility a civil action for "unauthorized metering," which Section 25-21,275(5) defines as "removing, moving, installing, connecting, reconnecting, or disconnecting any meter or metering device for utility service by a person other than an authorized employee or agent of such utility." The action requires that the act result in damages to the utility (Section 25-21,276(1)) and, for the $750-or-actual-damages measure, proof that it was willful or intentional (Section 25-21,276(2)) - so a submeter installed downstream of the utility's own meter, which does not change what the utility measures or bills, should not expose you. But "should not" is the honest word: have the work done by the utility or a licensed electrician, keep the utility's revenue meter untouched, and do not move or rewire it. Touching that meter can also be a crime. Interfering with a utility meter without the supplier's consent is a Class III misdemeanor, and proof of it is prima facie evidence against the person in possession of the premises (§28-515.02(1)(d), (2), (3)). Section 25-21,277(2) also puts a rebuttable presumption of knowledge on the customer of record who controlled access to that part of the system - in a master-metered building, that is you. CONTRAST WORTH SEEING: Nebraska DOES require a utility disclosure, just not here. Section 76-1482, in the Mobile Home Act, requires the landlord to give "a written explanation of utility rates, charges, and services to the prospective tenant before the rental agreement is signed unless the utility charges are to be paid by the tenant directly to the utility company." The legislature wrote exactly the disclosure this topic asks about, for mobile-home parks, and did not write it for ordinary rentals. Lifting Section 76-1482's practice into your own lease is free and it is the cautious course.

title: No Background-Screening Requirement for Rental-Property Employees
bodyText: Nebraska imposes no screening duty on the people who work on your rental property. There is no statute requiring a criminal background check, a fingerprint submission, a reference check or a registry search before you hire a maintenance technician, a leasing agent, an on-site manager or a cleaning contractor who will hold keys to occupied units. Florida's apartment-employee screening statute has no Nebraska counterpart, and no Nebraska statute bars you from screening either. THE CONTRAST IS SHARP AND IT IS IN THE SAME CHAPTER. Nebraska does require fingerprint-based national criminal history record checks before issuing a credential - for real property APPRAISERS at every level (Sections 76-2228.01, 76-2230, 76-2231.01, 76-2232 and 76-2233) and for the owners and controlling persons of an appraisal management company (Section 76-3207). The legislature wrote the fingerprint-and-record-check machinery for a property-adjacent occupation, in chapter 76, and did not write it for anyone who actually enters a tenant's home. So the silence is a choice, not an oversight in your search. WHAT THAT LEAVES YOU WITH IS ORDINARY NEGLIGENT-HIRING EXPOSURE, AND YOU HAVE MORE OF IT HERE THAN IN A STATE WITH A STATUTE, because a statute both tells you what to do and caps the argument about what was reasonable. Two Nebraska-specific points sharpen it. First, Section 76-1423(4) makes the landlord's access rights exhaustive - the statute's words are that the landlord "has no other right of access except" the ones listed - so an employee who lets himself into a unit outside those grounds is doing something the statute does not authorize, and you chose him. Second, Section 28-417(1)(e) makes it unlawful for any person to keep or maintain a dwelling house or building which that person "knows or should know is resorted to" by persons using controlled substances, a Class III misdemeanor under Section 28-417(2) with no landlord safe harbour - and what your on-site staff knows is the most likely route by which you "should know." Who you hire is therefore part of your criminal exposure, not only your civil one. PRACTICAL COURSE: screen anyone who will hold a key or enter an occupied unit, document that you did, and comply with the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's disclosure, authorization and adverse-action steps if you use a consumer reporting agency - that federal regime, not a Nebraska statute, is what actually governs the mechanics of the check.

title: No Energy-Data Release Statute - Which Means Consent Is Your Only Route
bodyText: Vermont's statute lets a lease clause stand as the tenant's authorization for the utility to hand the owner the tenant's energy usage data for benchmarking. Nebraska has no such statute, and nothing close to one: no whole-building aggregation rule, no benchmarking mandate, no obligation on a utility to release tenant usage to a building owner, and no statutory form of consent. Nebraska's landlord-tenant act does not mention energy data at all. WHAT FOLLOWS IS PRACTICAL, NOT LEGAL-TECHNICAL. Because there is no statutory authorization, a lease clause purporting to authorize release does not bind the utility - the utility's release is governed by its own tariff and by its board or commission, not by your lease. So a benchmarking clause buys you the tenant's consent and nothing else, and whether the data arrives still depends on the utility's own rules. Nebraska is an all-public-power state, so in practice the decision sits with a public power district, a municipal utility or a public power and irrigation district - bodies whose rate schedules and customer-data policies are not in the statutes at all. ASK THEM FIRST, AND THEN GET CONSENT IN THE FORM THEY WANT. A clause that recites a consent the utility will not accept is worse than no clause, because it looks like compliance. TWO NEBRASKA POINTS WORTH KNOWING. First, a tenant's utility usage is not "personal information" under Section 87-802(5) - that definition reaches a name plus a Social Security, driver's licence, financial-account, electronic-identification or biometric element, or an email or username plus a password - so the data-breach statute does not turn usage data into a notification problem for you. Second, Nebraska's Data Privacy Act is gated by a small-business test (Section 87-1103(1)(c)) and so reaches only some landlords; where it applies, consent mechanics there are the ones to follow, and Section 87-1110 voids any waiver of its provisions. Neither statute supplies the authorization the Vermont-style clause assumes.

title: Your LLC Cannot Send a Property Manager to County Court - But It Must Send an Employee to Small Claims
bodyText: In Nebraska this is settled by STATUTE, not by a court rule, and the rule flips depending on which courtroom you are in. COUNTY COURT - WHERE YOUR EVICTION GOES. Section 25-2702: "No person shall appear in the county court to represent another, or act as attorney therein for any person other than himself or herself, unless he or she is regularly admitted as an attorney in this state." An action for possession is commenced by filing a complaint for restitution "with the clerk of the district or county court" (Section 76-1441(1)), and in practice that is the county court. An LLC, corporation or partnership is a separate person from the human being who manages it, so sending a property manager, a leasing agent, a non-lawyer member or an out-of-state paralegal to appear for the entity is appearing "to represent another." Only you, appearing for yourself as an individual owner, are outside the prohibition. If title is in an entity - and for most landlords it is - the entity needs a Nebraska-admitted lawyer for the possession hearing, and the trial is held "not less than ten nor more than fourteen days after the issuance of the summons" (Section 76-1446), so there is no time to discover this late. SMALL CLAIMS COURT - WHERE YOUR DEPOSIT OR RENT CLAIM MAY GO, AND WHERE THE RULE REVERSES. Section 25-2803(3) does not merely permit a non-lawyer to appear for an entity; it requires it. The subsection reads, in full and in its own order: "An individual shall represent himself or herself in the Small Claims Court. A partnership shall be represented by a partner or one of its employees. A limited liability company shall be represented by a member, a manager, or one of its employees. A union shall be represented by a union member or union employee. A corporation shall be represented by one of its employees. An association shall be represented by one of its members or by an employee of the association. Any other kind of organization or entity shall be represented by one of its members or employees." And Section 25-2803(2): "No party shall be represented by an attorney in the Small Claims Court except as provided in sections 25-2804 and 25-2805" - in practice, on a motion for new trial or to set aside a default (Section 25-2804(7)) or after a transfer. FIVE LIMITS ON USING IT. First, Small Claims has no possession jurisdiction - Section 25-2802(1) reaches civil actions for "money or damages or the value of the personal property claimed," so you cannot get a writ of restitution there; it is for unpaid rent and damage claims only. Second, the ceiling is seven thousand five hundred dollars beginning July 1, 2025 (Section 25-2802(4)), exclusive of interest and costs. Third, Section 25-2803(6) caps you at two claims in any calendar week and TEN CLAIMS IN ANY CALENDAR YEAR - a real constraint on a portfolio landlord, and Section 25-2803(5) bars filing an assigned claim, so you cannot route claims through a collection assignee. Fourth, and easy to miss, Section 25-2803(4): "Only a party, natural or otherwise, who has been a party to the transaction with the defendant for which the claim is brought may file and prosecute a claim in the Small Claims Court." If you bought the building and inherited the tenancy, you were not a party to the transaction with the tenant for the rent that accrued before you took title, so Small Claims is not available to you for it even though Section 76-1416(5) makes you the one bound on the deposit - and (5) closes the obvious workaround by barring an assigned claim. Fifth, the tenant can take it away from you: under Section 25-2805, "Except as provided in section 25-2618.01, any defendant in an action or such defendant's attorney may transfer the case to the regular docket of the county court by giving notice to the court at least two days prior to the time set for the hearing," and under Section 25-2804(4) a counterclaim above the jurisdictional limit transfers the whole matter automatically - at which point Section 25-2702 applies again and your employee can no longer appear. The one exception is worth knowing: Section 25-2618.01(a) lets a party submit a controversy otherwise covered by a valid arbitration agreement to Small Claims, and 25-2618.01(b) then provides that it "shall not be transferred to the regular docket of the county court under section 25-2805" - so where your lease has an arbitration clause and you submit under that section, the defendant cannot move the case, and appellate review narrows to the six grounds in 25-2618.01(c). PRACTICAL COURSE: budget for Nebraska counsel on any possession action by an entity, and treat Small Claims as a money-only tool whose principal risk is that the tenant moves it to a courtroom where your non-lawyer cannot follow.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Right - and the One Casualty Rule You Cannot Draft Around
bodyText: Colorado gives a landlord an opt-in right to end a tenancy after an environmental event. Nebraska gives you nothing of the kind. There is no wildfire, smoke, flood, air-quality, mold, contamination or declared-disaster termination statute in the landlord-tenant act, no force-majeure provision, and no act-of-God excuse anywhere in chapter 76. NEBRASKA HAS EXACTLY ONE EVENT-DRIVEN TERMINATION RULE, AND IT BELONGS TO THE TENANT. Section 76-1429 applies where "the dwelling unit or premises are damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty to an extent that enjoyment of the dwelling unit is substantially impaired." The tenant may "[i]mmediately vacate the premises and notify the landlord in writing within fourteen days thereafter of his intention to terminate" - and then "the rental agreement terminates as of the date of vacating," not the date you got the notice - or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate only the unusable part, in which case "the tenant's liability for rent is reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value." On termination you return all prepaid rent and the security recoverable under Section 76-1416, accounting "as of the date of the casualty," and the tenant stays liable for damage caused by their own negligence. THAT RULE IS NOT WAIVABLE. Section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any rental-agreement term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under" the Act, and Section 76-1415(2) makes a prohibited provision unenforceable and exposes you to the tenant's actual damages and attorney's fees if you deliberately used a term you knew was prohibited. So an environmental-event clause that purported to give YOU the sole right to decide whether the tenancy continues after a casualty, or that required the tenant to stay, or that cut off the proportional rent reduction, would be void in the part that bites and would put you inside Section 76-1415(2). YOU MAY STILL ADD A CLAUSE, AND THIS IS HOW. Section 76-1414(1) lets the parties include "terms and conditions not prohibited by" the Act, so a landlord-side environmental-event termination right is permissible as long as it sits ALONGSIDE Section 76-1429 rather than in place of it: make it an additional, optional right exercisable by Landlord on written notice for events Section 76-1429 does not reach - a government-ordered evacuation or closure, an uninhabitable air-quality or contamination condition that is not "fire or casualty" damage, a utility interruption from an external event - say expressly that it does not limit the tenant's Section 76-1429 rights or any other right under the Act, and provide for proration of rent and return of the deposit on the Section 76-1416 timetable. The library does not ship that clause for Nebraska; if you want it, have it drafted to those limits. ONE MORE THING WORTH KNOWING: Nebraska's common law already does part of the work. The annotation printed with Section 76-1414, D & R Realty v. Bender, 230 Neb. 301, 431 N.W.2d 920 (1988), states that where a substantial portion of leased premises is destroyed or rendered incapable of use the lessee is entitled to an apportionment of rent "in the absence of an expressed assumption of the risk of such destruction" - so an express risk-allocation term in your lease is doing real work, and its absence is doing real work against you.

title: No Hardship Stay in Nebraska - Only a Continuance and a Bonded Appeal, Both of Which Cost the Tenant Money
bodyText: Nebraska gives a court no power to stay an eviction because the tenant would suffer hardship - no weather stay, no illness stay, no school-term stay, no stay to let a rental-assistance application clear. What the tenant can get is a continuance or a bonded appeal, and both are priced. IN A LANDLORD-TENANT ACT POSSESSION CASE. The trial itself is fast: "not less than ten nor more than fourteen days after the issuance of the summons" (Section 76-1446), and on your judgment the court declares the forfeiture and, at your request, issues a writ of restitution directing the sheriff or constable to restore possession "on a specified date not more than ten days after issuance." Section 76-1443 is the only delay tool: "The court may grant a continuance for good cause shown by either party, but no subsequent continuance shall be granted except by agreement or unless extraordinary cause be shown" - and for a subsequent continuance that pushes the trial into the next rental period, "the court may require a tenant to deposit with the clerk of the court such rental payments as accrue during the pendency of the suit." Ask for that deposit; it is the statute's own answer to a stalling continuance. Appeal: Section 76-1447 lets either party appeal as in other civil actions, but "[a]n appeal by the defendant shall stay the execution of any writ of restitution" only "so long as the defendant deposits with the clerk of the district court the amount of judgment and costs, or gives an appeal bond with surety therefor, and thereafter pays into court, on a monthly basis, an amount equal to the monthly rent called for by the rental agreement at the time the complaint was filed." No deposit, no bond, no monthly payment - no stay. IN A FORCIBLE ENTRY AND DETAINER CASE (the parallel route; see "How a Nebraska Eviction Runs - and the Second Statute Nobody Reads"). Section 25-21,225 is tighter than Section 76-1443: "No continuance shall be granted for a longer period than seven days, unless upon cause shown to the court of the existence of extraordinary causes and then not unless the defendant applying therefor shall give an undertaking ... conditioned for the payment of any rents that have or may accrue, and any additional damages that may be sustained ... by reason of the continuance." The annotation printed with it, Federal Nat. Mortgage Assn. v. Marcuzzo, 289 Neb. 301, 854 N.W.2d 774 (2014), says a court "should not grant an indefinite continuance in a forcible entry and detainer action, because doing so defeats the speedy nature of the remedy" - that is the sentence to quote when a continuance request has no end date. On appeal, Section 25-21,234: "No appeal shall operate as a supersedeas unless the appellant, within thirty days after the entry of the judgment, deposits ... a cash bond or undertaking" conditioned, for a defendant, on satisfying the judgment and costs and paying "a reasonable rent for the premises during the time he or she shall have unlawfully withheld the same." AND THE PROVISION MOST LANDLORDS DO NOT KNOW EXISTS: Section 25-21,235 lets you get possession ANYWAY. Even where the tenant has filed a proper supersedeas bond, "the judgment for restitution of the premises may be enforced, in the discretion of the court," if you post a bond conditioned on paying the tenant's costs and damages should you ultimately lose. ONE TRAP CLOSED: Nebraska's general stay-of-execution statutes, Sections 25-1505 to 25-1514, do not reach you. Section 25-1507 opens "On all judgments for the recovery of MONEY ONLY," so the nine-month stay in Section 25-1505 cannot be used against a judgment for restitution of the premises - a point the annotation to Section 25-1505 makes as well. Do not let a tenant invoke it, and do not assume you are exposed to it.

title: The One Eviction-Cost Clause Nebraska Bans - and the Three Fee Awards It Gives You Instead
bodyText: Nebraska does not have a general ban on eviction-related penalty clauses. It has one targeted ban, and it is the one landlords reach for most. SECTION 76-1415(1)(c): "No rental agreement may provide that the tenant ... [a]grees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees." Read the words. It is not limited to one-way clauses - a mutual or reciprocal fee provision is prohibited here too, because the subsection names both parties' fees. It is not limited to eviction - it reaches a fee clause of any kind. And it does not require that the clause be invoked: Section 76-1415(2) says a prohibited provision "included in a rental agreement is unenforceable," and adds that "[i]f a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees." So the exposure attaches to HAVING the term, not to enforcing it, and a savings clause does not cure it - the prohibited provision is still in the agreement, which is what Section 76-1415(2) measures. Take it out. TWO NEIGHBOURING BANS IN THE SAME SUBSECTION, both of which bite on eviction drafting: Section 76-1415(1)(b) voids a clause authorizing "any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement" - so no agreed judgment for possession, no cognovit, no stipulated-judgment-on-default term. Section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant waives rights or remedies under the Act - so no waiver of the Section 76-1428 counterclaim, no waiver of notice, no agreed shortening of the Section 76-1431 cure periods, no agreed waiver of a continuance or appeal. WHAT NEBRASKA DOES NOT BAN. There is no statutory cap or prohibition on a lease term making the tenant responsible for filing fees, service costs, court costs, posting or lockout charges, or on a liquidated-damages term for a wrongful holdover - those are left to the ordinary law of penalties and unconscionability, and to Section 76-1415(1)(a) if the term dresses up a waiver. There is no statutory late-fee cap in the landlord-tenant act (the Nebraska dollar figures landlords sometimes quote are Section 69-2110(1)(d) in the Rental-Purchase Act and do not apply to a lease). AND HERE IS THE PART THAT PAYS: the fee shifting you lose by clause, you partly get by statute, and it applies regardless of what the lease says. Section 76-1431(3): "If the tenant's noncompliance is willful, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney's fees." Section 76-1428(1): "If the defense or counterclaim by the tenant is without merit and is not raised in good faith, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney's fees." Section 76-1437(3): on a willful, bad-faith holdover you may recover "an amount not more than three months' periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees." And in a Section 76-1431.02 domestic-violence removal, Section 76-1431.02(4)(c)(i) entitles you to "court costs and reasonable attorney's fees from the perpetrator." None of those is a lease term, so none of them conflicts with the Section 76-1415(1)(c) ban - and a lease clause reciting them adds nothing and risks being read as the prohibited promise. Plead the statute instead.

title: The Lease Can Fix Where Your Notices Go - It Cannot Name Who Takes the Summons
bodyText: Nebraska draws a line that most leases blur, and getting it wrong costs you the hearing. NOTICES UNDER THE ACT - THE LEASE HAS REAL POWER HERE. Section 76-1413(2) says a person receives a notice when it comes to their attention and, "[i]n the case of the tenant," when it is "[d]elivered in hand to the tenant," "[m]ailed to the tenant at the place held out by the tenant as the place for receipt of the communication, or in the absence of such designation, to the tenant's last-known place of residence," or "[d]elivered by electronic means." So the tenant can designate a place, and in the landlord's own case Section 76-1413(2)(b)(i) recognises "any place held out by the landlord as the place for receipt of the communication." Use the lease to fix the notice addresses on both sides, and keep them current. Electronic delivery is available but conditional: Section 76-1413(7) requires the tenant's affirmative, un-withdrawn consent after a clear and conspicuous statement of the right to withdraw it, the notices it covers, the right to a paper copy and the hardware and software needed - and Section 76-1413(9) bars making acceptance of electronic delivery a lease term or a condition of entering or renewing. COURT PAPERS - THE LEASE HAS NO POWER AT ALL. The summons in a possession action is governed by Section 76-1442, not by Section 76-1413: it "may be served and returned as in other cases or by any person, except that the summons shall be served within three days, excluding nonjudicial days, from the date of issuance and shall be returnable within five days." "As in other cases" routes you to Sections 25-505.01 to 25-516.01, and Section 25-508.01(1) is a closed list: "An individual party ... may be served by personal, residence, certified mail, or designated delivery service." Residence service means leaving the summons "at the usual place of residence of the individual to be served, with some person of suitable age and discretion residing therein" (Section 25-505.01(1)(b)) - a person who happens to live there, not a person the lease named. There is no Nebraska provision letting a lease appoint an agent to accept a summons for a residential tenant, and the annotation printed with Section 25-508.01, Anthony K. v. State, 289 Neb. 523, 855 N.W.2d 802 (2014), is the warning: certified mail signed for by someone not authorized to sign for the party was not good service. A clause saying "Tenant appoints [X] to accept service of process" is worth nothing and may lull you into bad service. WHAT TO DO WHEN YOU CANNOT FIND THE TENANT. Nebraska has a real answer, and it is Section 76-1442.01, not a lease clause: if "diligent efforts have been made to serve the summons in the manner provided in sections 25-505.01 to 25-516.01 but such efforts were unsuccessful," the summons may be served "by posting a copy on the front door of the dwelling unit and mailing a copy by first-class mail to the defendant's last-known address," and you file an affidavit describing the diligent efforts, why they failed, and the posting and mailing. ONE PRICE FOR USING IT, AND IT IS THE WHOLE POINT: Section 76-1446 provides that "[i]f the plaintiff serves the summons in the manner provided in section 76-1442.01, the action shall proceed as other actions for possession EXCEPT THAT A MONEY JUDGMENT SHALL NOT BE GRANTED FOR THE PLAINTIFF." Posted service gets you the unit back and nothing else - no rent judgment, no damages, no costs. If the money matters, serve properly or sue for it separately. Also file the address you do have: Section 76-1441(1) requires the complaint to state the statutory authority, the facts with particularity, a reasonably accurate description of the premises, and compliance with the Act's notice provisions, and it may notify the tenant that personal property remains.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure - Fourteen Days Is the Only Clock, and It Starts Whether You Hear From the Tenant or Not
bodyText: Virginia lets a tenant ask for an expedited deposit disposition. Nebraska has no such procedure - no accelerated route, no tenant request that shortens the clock, no agreed waiver of the waiting period, and no fee you may charge for handling a deposit faster. Section 76-1416 is the whole of it, and it is one clock with one trigger. THE TRIGGER IS TERMINATION, NOT A DEMAND. Section 76-1416(2): on termination of the tenancy, prepaid rent and security may be applied to rent and to "the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or section 76-1421," and "[t]he balance, if any, AND A WRITTEN ITEMIZATION shall be delivered or mailed to the tenant within fourteen days after the date of termination of the tenancy." The annotation printed with the section is explicit: "The 14-day limitation language in subsection (2) of this section refers to the time allowed the landlord to return the deposit, not the time in which a demand must be made by the vacating tenant" (Hilliard v. Robertson, 253 Neb. 232, 570 N.W.2d 180 (1997)). So do not wait to be asked. Your fourteen days are already running. IF THE TENANT LEFT NO ADDRESS, THE STATUTE TELLS YOU WHAT TO DO. "If no mailing address or instructions are provided by the tenant to the landlord, the landlord shall mail, by first-class mail, the balance ... and a written itemization ... to the tenant's last-known mailing address. If the mailing is returned as undeliverable, or if the returned balance of the security deposit remains outstanding for one year, it shall be considered abandoned property to be reported and paid to the State Treasurer in accordance with the Uniform Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act." An unreachable tenant is not a reason to keep the money; it is a one-year hold and then a report to the Treasurer. THE PRICE OF MISSING IT. Section 76-1416(3): the tenant "may recover the property and money due him or her, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees" - and Nebraska courts have held that fee award is mandatory, not discretionary, once noncompliance is proven (Black v. Brooks, 285 Neb. 440, 827 N.W.2d 256 (2013)). On top of that, if your failure "is willful and not in good faith," liquidated damages of "one month's periodic rent or two times the amount of the security deposit, WHICHEVER IS LESS." That "whichever is less" is the Act's only landlord-favourable formula - do not let a secondary source tell you Nebraska doubles the deposit. TWO MORE POINTS THE STATUTE SETTLES. Section 76-1416(4): the deposit statute does not preclude other damages, but "a tenant shall not be liable for damages directly related to the tenant's removal from the premises by order of any governmental entity as a result of the premises not being fit for habitation due to the negligence or neglect of the landlord." Section 76-1416(5): "The holder of the landlord's interest in the premises at the time of the termination of the tenancy is bound by this section" - so a buyer inherits the obligation and cannot point at the seller. WHAT YOU CAN ACTUALLY DO FASTER: nothing in Section 76-1416 stops you paying out early. Inspect at move-out, itemize, and pay within days rather than fourteen - there is no statutory interest to earn by holding it (see "No Duty to Pay Interest on a Security Deposit") and no fee you could charge for the service.

title: Nebraska's Foreign-Ownership Ban Reaches Leases Over Five Years - and Says You Need Not Ask
bodyText: Nebraska does have a foreign-ownership restriction, and it does reach leaseholds - but almost no residential landlord is caught by it, and the statute says in so many words that you do not have to screen for it. The Foreign-owned Real Estate National Security Act, sections 76-3701 to 76-3717, was enacted in 2024 and rewritten in 2025. Section 76-3703(1)(a) provides that a 'nonresident alien, foreign corporation, or foreign government, or an agent, trustee, or fiduciary thereof' 'shall not purchase, acquire title to, or take any real estate or any leasehold interest extending for a period for more than five years or any other greater interest less than fee in any real estate in this state by descent, devise, purchase or otherwise on or after January 1, 2025.' Three features of that sentence decide the practical question. FIRST, the carve-out is FIVE YEARS, not one year. A twelve-month residential lease, a two-year lease and a month-to-month tenancy all fall outside the ban, because none of them is a 'leasehold interest extending for a period for more than five years.' Landlords in states whose statutes exempt only leaseholds under one year - so that an ordinary annual lease is inside the prohibition - should not carry that assumption into Nebraska. SECOND, the Act exempts the ground most rentals sit on. Section 76-3710(1) provides that the Act 'shall not apply to any real estate lying within the corporate limits of cities and villages, or within three miles of such corporate limits,' nor to a manufacturing or industrial establishment described in section 76-3709. So an apartment building in Omaha, Lincoln, Grand Island or any incorporated village, and anything within three miles of the line, is outside the Act altogether. What remains inside it is rural property - the farmhouse, the acreage, the hunting cabin more than three miles out. THIRD, there is one class the exemption does not save. Section 76-3710(2) pulls a 'restricted entity, or an agent, trustee, or fiduciary thereof, who purchases, acquires, holds title to, or is the LESSOR OR LESSEE of any real estate lying within the corporate limits of cities and villages, or within three miles of such corporate limits' back under sections 76-3703 and 76-3709 and subjects it to divestment. 'Restricted entity' is defined in section 76-3702(6) as a person on the OFAC sanctions lists as they existed on January 1, 2025, or a person or foreign government the United States Secretary of Commerce has determined engaged in 'a long-term pattern or serious instances of conduct significantly adverse to the national security of the United States' under 15 C.F.R. 791.4 as it existed on February 7, 2025. That is a sanctions-list test, not a nationality test. Note the drafting gap honestly: section 76-3703(1)(a)'s five-year line is written for nonresident aliens, foreign corporations and foreign governments and does not name 'restricted entity,' while section 76-3710(2) says a restricted-entity lessor or lessee IS 'subject to sections 76-3703 and 76-3709' - so whether a restricted entity may take a short urban lease is not settled on the face of the text. Treat a sanctions-list match as a hard stop regardless of lease length. Now the part that matters most to you. Section 76-3715 says: 'Nothing in the Foreign-owned Real Estate National Security Act shall be construed to require any person to determine or inquire whether another person is subject to or in violation of the act, and such person shall bear no civil or criminal liability under the act for the failure to make such determination or inquiry. The Attorney General, retained outside counsel, and Director of Agriculture are responsible for determining whether a person is subject to or in violation of the act.' You therefore have NO duty to ask an applicant's citizenship, immigration status or days of physical presence in the United States, and no exposure for not asking - and you must not ask, because the Nebraska Fair Housing Act bars the question itself. Section 20-318(5) makes it unlawful to 'cause to be made any written or oral INQUIRY or record concerning the race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, sex, or military or veteran status of a person seeking to purchase, rent, or lease any housing.' That is an inquiry ban, not merely a ban on acting on the answer, so a citizenship, nationality or days-of-presence question on an application form is itself an unlawful act, quite apart from section 20-318(1) and (2), which make it unlawful to refuse to rent or to discriminate in 'the terms, conditions, or privileges of ... rental of a dwelling' because of national origin. The Foreign-owned Real Estate National Security Act gives you no reason to take that risk and section 76-3715 expressly relieves you of any need to. Do not add a lease representation that the tenant is not a nonresident alien; the Act gives you no reason to want one. The enforcement machinery is the state's, not yours: section 76-3712 routes complaints to the Department of Agriculture, puts investigation and subpoena power with the Attorney General or retained outside counsel, offers thirty days to elect voluntary divestment and a one-hundred-eighty-day grace period to carry it out, and then an action in district court where 'the burden is on the state to prove by clear and convincing evidence' that the real estate is subject to divestment. Two pieces of section 76-3712 bear directly on a tenancy. Section 76-3712(6)(b)(iv) requires service of the divestment petition on 'any person residing on the real estate subject to divestment at the time the petition is filed' - so a tenant in a divestment case gets served, and will come to you with the papers. And section 76-3712(8) provides that 'if the interest is a lease, easement, or interest other than fee title, the court shall have power to declare such interest terminated' - a court can end a lease outright in a divestment decree, which is a risk to a tenant's possession no notice provision in your lease can control. One trap on the sell side: section 76-3712(4)(e) provides that 'no person shall sell or otherwise transfer real estate to another person prohibited under the act,' with 'a civil penalty not to exceed fifty thousand dollars per parcel.' That sits uneasily beside section 76-3715's no-duty-to-inquire rule, and 'otherwise transfer' is not defined. If you are letting rural ground more than three miles outside a municipality on a term longer than five years, or selling it, that is the one transaction where a lawyer should look at the counterparty before you sign - not because the Act makes you screen, but because the penalty for a transfer is not covered by the inquiry immunity in terms. Finally, section 76-3714 protects the chain of title in the other direction: 'no title to an interest in real estate shall be invalid, voided, or subject to divestiture by reason of a violation of the Foreign-owned Real Estate National Security Act by any former owner or other person who held a former interest in such real estate.' A past owner's violation does not cloud what you hold now.

title: How Bad Does a Defect Have To Be? Nebraska's Materiality Line Gates Termination, Not Damages
bodyText: Nebraska has a materiality threshold for habitability complaints, but it is narrower than landlords assume, and the single most expensive misreading of it is thinking it applies to everything a tenant can sue for. It does not. Start with the text. Section 76-1425(1) opens: 'if there is a material noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement OR a noncompliance with section 76-1419 materially affecting health and safety, the tenant may deliver a written notice ... and that the rental agreement will terminate upon a date not less than thirty days after receipt of the notice if the breach is not remedied in fourteen days.' Those are two different tests for two different kinds of breach. A broken promise in your lease has to be MATERIAL. A breach of the statutory habitability duties in section 76-1419 has to MATERIALLY AFFECT HEALTH AND SAFETY. Either one, met, lets the tenant start the clock that ends the tenancy. Now the part that catches people. Section 76-1425(2) reads: 'the tenant may recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for ANY noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement or section 76-1419.' No materiality. No health-and-safety qualifier. The word 'material' that appears in subsection (1) is simply absent from subsection (2), and that is a deliberate drafting choice, not an oversight - because when the Legislature wrote the mobile-home-park counterpart ten years later it put the word in: section 76-1498(2) reads 'for any MATERIAL noncompliance by the landlord.' Same sentence, same Act family, one word different. So in an ordinary residential tenancy under the URLTA, a defect too small to support termination is still large enough to support a damages claim and an injunction. The Nebraska Supreme Court has confirmed the two routes are independent: 'so long as a tenant has given notice when required by section 76-1419, a tenant can seek damages or injunctive relief under subsection (2) of this section without sending notice under subsection (1)', and the conjunction 'and' in subsection (2) 'serves to vest a tenant with two distinct options for relief' (Vasquez v. CHI Properties, 302 Neb. 742, 925 N.W.2d 304 (2019)). Nebraska does not define 'material' or 'materially affecting health and safety' anywhere. Section 76-1410 carries eighteen definitions and neither phrase is among them, and there is no enumerated list of serious defects of the kind some states publish. Materiality is decided case by case on the facts. What the statute gives you instead of a list is a CEILING, and it is the most useful thing in this topic for a landlord. Section 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence says: 'If there exists a minimum housing code applicable to the premises, the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a) of this section.' Subdivision (1)(a) is 'substantially comply, after written or actual notice, with the requirements of the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety.' And section 76-1410(3) defines the term tightly: 'minimum housing code shall be limited to those laws, resolutions, or ordinances or regulations, or portions thereof, dealing specifically with health and minimum standards of fitness for habitation' - which is narrower than the same subsection's definition of 'building and housing codes.' So in a municipality that has a minimum housing code, your maximum exposure under section 76-1419 is substantial compliance with the health-and-habitability portions of that code after notice; the open-ended 'fit and habitable' language in (1)(b) does not stack on top of it. Outside such a municipality there is no ceiling and (1)(b) governs on its own terms. Four more things that decide real cases. FIRST, notice is an element, not a courtesy. Subdivisions (1)(a) and (1)(b) of section 76-1419 both read 'after written or actual notice,' and 'actual notice' means a maintenance request, a phone call or your own inspection will do - you do not get to insist on a form. SECOND, timing is not a defence. Vasquez holds the duties to 'put and keep' the premises fit 'are not limited under the plain language to conditions arising after commencement of the lease term,' so a defect that existed before the tenant moved in is squarely inside section 76-1419. THIRD, essential services skip materiality entirely. Section 76-1427(1) attaches whenever, contrary to the lease or section 76-1419, 'the landlord deliberately or negligently fails to supply running water, hot water, or heat, or essential services,' and gives the tenant, on written notice, the right to procure the service and 'deduct their actual and reasonable cost from the rent,' or recover diminution in fair rental value, or procure substitute housing and stop paying rent for the period - plus, if the failure was deliberate, the cost or value of substitute housing up to one period's rent, and reasonable attorney's fees in any case. There is no materiality screen and no thirty-day runway; the only gate is written notice under section 76-1427(3). Section 76-1427(2) does make it an election: a tenant who proceeds under section 76-1427 'may not proceed under section 76-1425 as to that breach.' FOURTH, the tenant's own doing is a complete answer. Section 76-1425(1)'s last sentence: 'the tenant may not terminate for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of his or her family, or other person on the premises with his or her consent.' Section 76-1427(3) carries the same carve-out, and section 76-1439(3) preserves your possession action where the code violation 'was caused primarily by the tenant's lack of reasonable care.' Note the vocabulary does not transfer between sections: fire and casualty under section 76-1429 use 'substantially impaired,' not 'material,' and a willfulness finding under section 76-1425(2) adds the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees. Practical upshot: do not build a lease clause around a materiality threshold. A clause saying the tenant may complain or sue only about 'material' defects, or only about conditions affecting health and safety, would try to raise the bar section 76-1425(2) deliberately left low, and section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant 'agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.' What protects you is not a clause - it is documented notice handling and a prompt, recorded repair response, because a fixed defect is not a damages claim.

title: No Deposit-Alternative Fee Statute in Nebraska - and 'However Denominated' Catches the Fee Anyway
bodyText: Nebraska has no fee-in-lieu-of-deposit statute. There is no provision authorising an insurance-backed or surety-backed deposit alternative, no right for the tenant to switch from the fee to a conventional deposit, no offer-to-all requirement, no credit-reporting protection tied to a no-deposit lease, and no state agency charged with writing regulations for such a programme - so there is no 'the fee is barred until the regulations issue' problem of the kind some states have. If you want to run a deposit-alternative programme in Nebraska you are not forbidden; you are unregulated, which is a different and in some ways worse position, because the one statute that does apply was written to catch exactly this. Section 76-1416(1) reads: 'A landlord may not demand or receive security, HOWEVER DENOMINATED, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent, except that a pet deposit not in excess of one-fourth of one month's periodic rent may be demanded or received when appropriate.' Two words in that sentence decide the topic. 'However denominated' means the label on the money is irrelevant - call it a deposit, a move-in fee, a risk fee, a deposit waiver fee, a damage fee, an administrative fee or a deposit alternative, and if its function is security for the tenant's performance it counts against the one-month ceiling. 'Demand or receive' is the test for whether it is yours: money the landlord demands or receives is caught; a premium the tenant pays directly to a third-party surety or insurer under a contract between the tenant and that company, which the landlord neither demands nor receives, is not security held by the landlord at all. That is the line to stay on the right side of, and it is a narrow one, because if you require the tenant to buy the product you are arguably demanding it. The consequence of being caught is not just the cap. Section 76-1416(2) then applies to the whole of it: on termination the money 'may be applied to the payment of rent and the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or section 76-1421,' and 'the balance, if any, and a written itemization shall be delivered or mailed to the tenant within fourteen days after the date of termination of the tenancy.' So a fee you collected and called nonrefundable becomes refundable to the extent it exceeds your proven damages, and you owe a written itemization within fourteen days. The fourteen days run from termination of the tenancy, not from the tenant's demand (Hilliard v. Robertson, 253 Neb. 232, 570 N.W.2d 180 (1997)). Miss it and section 76-1416(3) gives the tenant 'the property and money due him or her, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees' - attorney's fees as of right, not at the court's discretion, and the Nebraska Supreme Court has held those fees are recoverable even for pro bono work (Black v. Brooks, 285 Neb. 440, 827 N.W.2d 256 (2013)). If the failure was 'willful and not in good faith' add liquidated damages of 'one month's periodic rent or two times the amount of the security deposit, whichever is less.' Note that last formula carefully: 'whichever is less' is in the landlord's favour and is the only such formula in the Act - most of the Act's money provisions run the other way, and section 76-1430 charges a flat three months' rent for an unlawful ouster with no proof of loss required. Three further points. FIRST, if you do nothing special you still have a lawful pet deposit of up to one-fourth of one month's rent, and it sits on top of the one-month security figure under section 76-1416(1)'s own 'except that' clause. SECOND, there is one carve-out from the cap and it is institutional, not a drafting opportunity: subsection (1) 'shall not be applicable to housing agencies organized or existing under the Nebraska Housing Agency Act' (section 71-1572 et seq.). A private landlord is not a housing agency. THIRD, on credit reporting, Nebraska imposes no notice duty on a landlord before reporting a damage claim to a credit bureau or placing it with a collector. The only Nebraska credit-reporting statute in this area, section 20-149, binds 'any consumer reporting agency doing business in this state' to give a consumer a copy of its file on request at a reasonable charge, with a Class IV misdemeanour for violation - it is a duty of the AGENCY, not of the landlord who furnishes the information. Your furnisher obligations come from the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act and the federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, so treat the federal rules as live and get them checked before you report anything. What this means for drafting. Do not write a lease clause calling a sum 'a nonrefundable fee in lieu of security deposit' - 'however denominated' makes the words do no work, and section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant 'agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act,' which is what a clause purporting to make security non-returnable would be. If you want a genuine alternative, structure it as a product the tenant buys from a third party, keep the money out of your hands, give the tenant a real choice between that product and a conventional deposit so you are not 'demanding' it, and keep your own deposit figure inside one month's periodic rent. That is a contract design question, not a statutory permission, and Nebraska has given you no safe harbour for it.

title: No Statute Bans a Fee for a Service You Don't Provide - the Deceptive Trade Practices Act Makes the Whole Lease Unenforceable Instead
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute of the Colorado kind banning a landlord from charging a fee for a service that is not actually provided. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act regulates no rental fee at all - not application fees, not amenity fees, not administrative, technology, trash, valet or parking fees - and the only dollar ceiling in the Act is the one-month security cap in section 76-1416(1). Every time the word 'fee' appears near the word 'landlord' in chapter 76 it is an attorney's-fee provision, not a charging authority. So the short answer is: no bespoke prohibition, and no statutory list of permitted fees either. That is not the end of it, and the consequence that does exist is worse than a fee ban. THREE ROUTES REACH YOU. FIRST, and most severe, the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Section 87-302(a) applies to any 'person' who, 'in the course of his or her business, vocation, or occupation,' among other things: '(5) Represents that goods or services have sponsorship, approval, characteristics, ingredients, uses, benefits, or quantities that they do not have'; '(8) Represents that goods or services are of a particular standard, quality, or grade ... if they are of another'; '(10) Advertises goods or services with intent not to sell them as advertised or advertises the price in any manner calculated or tending to mislead or in any way deceive a person'; '(16) Uses any scheme or device to defraud by means of ... obtaining money or property by knowingly false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises'; and '(18) Mails or causes to be sent an unsolicited billing statement, invoice, or other document that appears to obligate the consumer to make a payment for services or merchandise he or she did not order.' Section 87-303.01 adds that 'an unconscionable act or practice by a supplier in connection with a consumer transaction shall be a violation' of the Act, with unconscionability 'a question of law for the court.' Then comes the sentence that matters. Section 87-303.07: 'If a buyer or lessee is induced by a violation of section 87-302 or 87-303.01 to enter into a sale or lease, the agreement is unenforceable by the seller or lessor and the buyer or lessee, at his or her option, may rescind the agreement or retain the merchandise delivered and the benefit of any services performed without any obligation to pay for them.' Read that against a lease. If the tenant signed because you advertised a pool, a fitness room, a gated entrance, covered parking, in-unit laundry, trash valet or a concierge that does not exist or is not in service, and you billed a fee for it, the tenant's remedy is not a refund of the fee - it is that the LEASE IS UNENFORCEABLE BY YOU, and the tenant may stay and keep the benefit of what you did perform without any obligation to pay for it. It says 'lessee' and 'lessor' in terms, and the Nebraska Supreme Court has read the section as limited to the buyers and lessees it names (Lindsay Internat. Sales & Serv. v. Wegener, 301 Neb. 1, 917 N.W.2d 133 (2018)). CURRENCY WARNING ON THIS ONE, because it is unusual. The version of section 87-302 printed in the statutes today carries the notation 'Operative Date: January 1, 2027' and a Source line ending 'Laws 2026, LB838, section 27'. The subdivisions quoted above - (5), (8), (10), (16) and (18) - are long-standing and are in both the current and the incoming text, but if you are relying on any other subdivision, check which version you are reading, because section 87-303.07's trigger is section 87-302. SECOND, the Consumer Protection Act. Section 59-1602: 'Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce shall be unlawful.' Section 59-1609 lets 'any person who is injured in his or her business or property' sue to enjoin and recover actual damages, costs 'including a reasonable attorney's fee,' and a discretionary increase - capped for a section 59-1602 violation at one thousand dollars. One real limit: 'to be actionable under the Nebraska Consumer Protection Act, the unfair or deceptive act or practice must have an impact upon the public interest' (Nelson v. Lusterstone Surfacing Co., 258 Neb. 678, 605 N.W.2d 136 (2000)) - a one-off dispute with a single tenant may not qualify, but a fee charged across a portfolio is precisely a public-interest pattern. THIRD, inside the Act itself, the duty you create by promising. Section 76-1419(1)(d) requires the landlord to 'maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her.' The phrase 'or required to be supplied' is the mechanism: a lease promise or an advertised amenity makes the thing something you are required to supply, and from then on failing to keep it working is a section 76-1419 noncompliance. Section 76-1425(2) then gives the tenant 'damages and ... injunctive relief for ANY noncompliance' - no materiality threshold in that subsection - plus reasonable attorney's fees if the noncompliance is willful. And section 76-1412(1) lets a court 'refuse to enforce the agreement, enforce the remainder of the agreement without the unconscionable provision, or limit the application of any unconscionable provision' where a rental agreement or any provision 'was unconscionable when made.' WHAT TO DO. You may charge whatever fees the market bears, because nothing caps them - but write each one so the service it names is one you actually deliver, describe it in words you can prove, and stop billing it the moment the service stops. If an amenity goes out of service for a period, suspend the fee for that period and say so in writing. Do not describe a fee as covering a service in the lease if the service is optional, intermittent or seasonal without saying which. Remember too that section 76-1416(1) catches security 'however denominated,' so a fee that functions as security counts against the one-month cap no matter what service it is named after, and section 76-1415(1)(c) forbids any term by which the tenant 'agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees,' so you cannot put a fee-recovery clause behind any of this.

title: Nebraska Freezes the Standards It Borrows - Two Different Formulas, and Your Contractor Is Probably Working to the Wrong Edition
bodyText: When a Nebraska statute borrows a standard written by somebody else - a trade association's code, a federal regulation, a federal statute - it almost always freezes it as of a stated date rather than adopting whatever that body publishes next. That matters to a landlord for one blunt reason: the edition your contractor, inspector or alarm vendor is working to is probably NOT the edition Nebraska adopted, and the gap is years wide. Nebraska uses TWO different freezing formulas, and they look nothing alike. FORMULA ONE, the one you will meet most often, is 'as such ... existed on [date].' The clearest landlord-facing example is the Carbon Monoxide Safety Act. Section 76-606(2) requires that 'the owner of an existing single-family dwelling or existing dwelling unit in a multifamily dwelling that is used for rental purposes and that has a change in tenant occupancy on or after January 1, 2017, shall ensure that an operational carbon monoxide alarm is INSTALLED on each habitable floor of the dwelling or dwelling unit' (there is a parallel trigger in section 76-606(1) for permitted interior alterations, repairs, fuel-fired appliance replacements or additions). The whole duty turns on the word 'installed,' and section 76-602(4) defines it: 'installed means that a carbon monoxide alarm is installed in a dwelling unit in accordance with the NATIONAL FIRE PROTECTION ASSOCIATION STANDARD 720 AS SUCH STANDARD EXISTED ON JANUARY 1, 2015, and in accordance with the instructions for installation from the manufacturer.' January 1, 2015. The Act has not been amended since it was passed - its Source line is 'Laws 2015, LB34' throughout - so the reference has not moved in more than a decade, whatever NFPA has done with Standard 720 in the meantime. If that standard has since been revised, renumbered, merged into another document or withdrawn, Nebraska's statute still points at the 2015 text, and compliance means the 2015 text. Get the 2015 edition of NFPA 720 in front of whoever installs your alarms rather than asking them for 'current code.' You will find the same formula wherever a Nebraska statute reaches outside the state: section 76-1413(16) (the electronic-notice section) says it 'shall not be construed to modify, limit, or supersede the federal Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act, 15 U.S.C. 7001 et seq., AS SUCH ACT EXISTED ON JANUARY 1, 2025'; section 76-3702(6) fixes the sanctions lists used by the Foreign-owned Real Estate National Security Act 'as such sanctions lists existed on January 1, 2025' and a federal regulation 'as such regulation existed on February 7, 2025'; section 20-149 fixes the federal credit-reporting sections 'as such sections existed on January 1, 2016'; section 87-302(a)(23)(iii)(A) fixes a federal definition 'as such section existed on January 1, 2024.' FORMULA TWO is a pamphlet number plus an edition year, and it is the one that will bite you because it is invisible to anyone searching for Formula One. The State Fire Code, section 81-503.01(2), does not say 'as such code existed on' anything. It names documents: NFPA Pamphlet Number 1, the Fire Code, 2012 EDITION, and NFPA Pamphlet Number 101, the Life Safety Code, 2012 EDITION. Nebraska's adopted fire and life-safety standards are therefore pinned to 2012 editions. Section 81-503.01 was amended by Laws 2025, LB434, section 4, so the fire code side of this is live law that moved recently; treat everything in this paragraph as the shape of the rule rather than its current letter, and have the current section 81-503.01 pulled before you rely on an edition year. NOW THE PART THAT IS EASIEST TO GET BACKWARDS. Not everything Nebraska incorporates is frozen. In the very same Carbon Monoxide Safety Act, each duty offers an alternative placement rule: the alarm goes on each habitable floor 'or in a location specified in ANY BUILDING CODE ADOPTED BY THE STATE OR BY THE POLITICAL SUBDIVISION in which the dwelling or dwelling unit is located' (sections 76-603, 76-604(1) and (2), 76-606(1) and (2)). That reference has no freeze date at all - it floats with whatever the state or your city adopts. And section 76-607 adds that 'nothing in the Carbon Monoxide Safety Act shall be construed to limit a city, village, or county from adopting or enforcing any requirements for the installation and maintenance of carbon monoxide alarms that are more stringent than the requirements set forth in the act.' So one sentence of one definition is frozen to 2015 while the local building code beside it is live and may be stricter. The same is true of the habitability duty: section 76-1410(3) defines 'building and housing codes' as 'any law, ordinance, or governmental regulation concerning fitness for habitation, or the construction, maintenance, operation, occupancy, use, or appearance of any premises, or dwelling unit,' with no date, and section 76-1419(1)(a) requires substantial compliance 'with the requirements of the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety' - also undated. Your code-compliance duty under the landlord-tenant act moves when your city moves; your carbon-monoxide installation standard does not. WHAT TO DO ABOUT IT. Keep the division straight in your own records: for a borrowed trade standard, write down the edition or date the Nebraska section names and buy that edition; for a local code, check the current ordinance and assume it can change under you. Do not put an edition year into a lease - a clause promising compliance with 'the 2012 Fire Code' or 'NFPA 720 (2015)' freezes your own obligation at a date the law may move off, and a clause promising compliance with 'all applicable codes' promises more than the statute asks and hands the tenant a contract claim under section 76-1425(2), which allows damages for 'any noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement.' Say nothing about codes in the lease and your duty stays what the statute makes it. One last allocation point specific to carbon monoxide: section 76-606(3) puts replacement, battery supply at move-in and repair-on-notice on the owner, section 76-606(3)(b) says that apart from those items the owner 'is not responsible for the maintenance, repair, or replacement of a carbon monoxide alarm or the care and replacement of batteries,' section 76-606(4) puts keeping, testing and maintaining the alarms and notifying the owner of problems on the tenant, and section 76-606(5) makes it unlawful for 'any person' to remove batteries from or render inoperable a carbon monoxide alarm except as part of inspecting, maintaining, repairing or replacing it. That split is worth restating in the lease in the statute's own words, because the tenant's testing-and-notice duty is the half you will need if an alarm is found dead.

title: Nebraska's Fire Code: Pinned to 2012 NFPA Editions, Enforced Locally, and Not the Same Thing as Your Habitability Duty
bodyText: Nebraska has a State Fire Code, it reaches residential occupancies, and almost nothing about it works the way landlords expect. WHERE IT COMES FROM. Section 81-503.01(1) directs that 'the State Fire Marshal shall adopt and promulgate rules and regulations constituting a State Fire Code,' and lists what the Code must cover 'at a minimum' - fire prevention; the storage, sale and use of flammable liquids, combustibles and fireworks; 'electrical wiring and heating, protection equipment devices, materials, furnishings, and other safeguards within structures necessary to promote safety and reduce loss by fire'; 'the means and adequacy of exits, in case of fire, in assembly, educational, institutional, RESIDENTIAL, mercantile, office, storage, and industrial-type occupancies as such structures are defined in the State Fire Code'; 'all other buildings, structures, and enclosures in which numbers of persons congregate from time to time for any purpose, whether privately or publicly owned'; liquefied petroleum gas equipment; hazardous materials; regulated-substance storage tanks; and accessibility standards adopted under section 81-5,147. 'Residential' is on the list in terms, so the exits provisions reach your building. WHAT IT IS PINNED TO. Section 81-503.01(2) provides that the rules 'shall conform GENERALLY to the standards recommended by the National Fire Protection Association, Pamphlet Number 1, known as the Fire Code, 2012 EDITION, the National Fire Protection Association, Pamphlet Number 101, known as the Life Safety Code, 2012 EDITION, and associated pamphlets, BUT NOT WHEN DOING SO WOULD IMPOSE AN UNDULY SEVERE OR COSTLY BURDEN WITHOUT SUBSTANTIALLY CONTRIBUTING TO THE SAFETY OF PERSONS OR PROPERTY.' Three things follow, and the third is the one people get wrong. FIRST, the edition years are 2012 - more than a decade behind current NFPA publications. SECOND, the words are 'conform generally,' not 'adopt' - and the closing qualifier lets the Fire Marshal depart from NFPA where conformity would be unduly severe or costly without substantially improving safety. THIRD, and therefore: NFPA 1 and NFPA 101 are NOT Nebraska law. What binds you is the Fire Marshal's adopted rules and regulations. Quoting an NFPA edition at an inspector, or having a consultant certify compliance with NFPA 101, does not answer the question of whether you comply with the Nebraska State Fire Code, and the rules are in the Nebraska Administrative Code rather than the statutes - they were not available to this research and you need them pulled. WHO ENFORCES IT, AND WHO INSPECTS YOU. Section 81-503.01(3): 'the State Fire Marshal shall enforce the State Fire Code through inspections, code compliance, and orders. Plans for compliance with the State Fire Code shall be reviewed by the State Fire Marshal. Plans submitted after remodeling or construction has begun shall be accompanied by a late submittal fee penalty' - a penalty that the 2025 amendment raised from a flat fifty dollars to one hundred dollars plus fifty percent of the plan review fee set under section 81-505.01(4)(a), in addition to that review fee. If you are remodeling, get plans in BEFORE work starts. But note what section 81-502(1)(c) does and does not say. It makes it the Fire Marshal's duty to 'make an investigation for fire safety of the premises and facilities of' liquor establishments on the Liquor Control Commission's request, licensed foster care facilities, certain Department of Health and Human Services programmes and residential child-caring agencies, licensed hospitals and other health care facilities, and 'mobile home parks for which a license or renewal of a license is sought, upon request of a local government.' An apartment building, a duplex and a rented single-family house are NOT on that list. There is no routine, mandatory state fire-safety inspection of ordinary rental housing in Nebraska. What there is instead is local: section 81-502(3) lets the State Fire Marshal 'delegate the authority set forth in this section and section 81-503.01 to qualified local fire prevention personnel,' with power to overrule a local decision and to revoke the delegation for cause on thirty days' notice after a hearing. In practice your fire-code counterparty is your city or county fire prevention office exercising delegated state authority, plus whatever local ordinance your municipality has adopted on its own. THE DISTINCTION THAT COSTS LANDLORDS MONEY. A fire-code violation is not automatically a breach of your landlord-tenant duties. Section 76-1419(1)(a) requires you to 'substantially comply, after written or actual notice, with the requirements of the applicable MINIMUM HOUSING CODES materially affecting health and safety,' and section 76-1410(3) defines that term narrowly: 'minimum housing code shall be limited to those laws, resolutions, or ordinances or regulations, or portions thereof, dealing specifically with health and minimum standards of fitness for habitation.' A fire code is not obviously a minimum housing code. It is, however, within the same subsection's broader definition of 'building and housing codes' - 'any law, ordinance, or governmental regulation concerning fitness for habitation, or the construction, maintenance, operation, occupancy, use, or appearance of any premises, or dwelling unit' - which is the term section 76-1421(1) uses for the TENANT's duty to 'comply with all obligations primarily imposed upon tenants by applicable minimum standards of building and housing codes materially affecting health or safety.' So a fire-code defect reaches you through section 76-1419(1)(b)'s open-ended duty to 'make all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition' rather than through (1)(a) - which matters, because where a minimum housing code applies section 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence caps your duty at (1)(a), and that cap does not obviously cover a fire-code item. Do not assume the ceiling protects you here. ONE CRIMINAL TRAP, AND IT IS EASY TO WALK INTO. Section 28-1251(1): 'it shall be unlawful for any person, association, partnership, limited liability company, or corporation to conduct fire alarm tests and fire alarm inspections without prior written certification by the State Fire Marshal as to the qualifications of such persons conducting such tests and inspections,' and section 28-1251(4) makes 'unlawful testing or inspection of fire alarms' a Class III misdemeanour. The offence is committed by the person doing the testing, so the handyman or the vendor's technician bears the charge - but the test you paid for was not a lawful test, and you have no compliance record. Ask for the State Fire Marshal certification before anyone touches an alarm panel, and keep a copy. Section 28-1251 was amended in 2025 by the same act that amended section 81-503.01. TWO MORE THINGS WORTH KNOWING. If a municipality determines your property is unsafe or unfit, section 18-1722.01 makes it 'the duty of such municipality to post the property accordingly and to file a copy of such resolution or other determination in the office of the register of deeds of the county to be recorded,' with 'no fee ... charged for such recording or for the release of such recording.' That determination therefore becomes both a placard on your building and a recorded instrument against the title, and the release is free - so chase the release once you have cured. And the Mobile Home Act, which does not apply to ordinary rentals, shows what the Legislature wrote when it wanted a regulatory order to run through to the tenant: section 76-14,102 lets a mobile-home-park landlord enter, do the work and bill it 'as additional rent' where the tenant fails to remedy 'any condition which is ordered to be changed by the State Fire Marshal' within fourteen days of written notice, and provides that 'if the landlord is assessed any fine, cost, or charge as a result of the tenant's failure to comply with an order issued by the State Fire Marshal ... the landlord may require the tenant to pay such fine, cost, or charge.' The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no such section. Outside a mobile home park your route for a tenant-caused fire-code violation is the ordinary one: notice under section 76-1431(1) and damages under section 76-1431(3), or a lease clause you wrote yourself.

title: No Statutory Sprinkler Duty and No Retrofit Mandate - the Requirement, If There Is One, Is in Rules and Local Code
bodyText: No Nebraska statute requires a fire sprinkler system in a rental dwelling, and no Nebraska statute imposes a retrofit duty on an existing building. The word 'sprinkler' does not appear anywhere in the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy, nor in any of the three hundred sixty-three slip laws of the 2025 and 2026 sessions. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act says nothing about suppression systems; section 76-1419 lists the landlord's maintenance duties and sprinklers are not among them. That is a real absence at the statutory level, and it is also the least useful part of the answer, because a sprinkler requirement in Nebraska does not come from a statute. HERE IS WHERE IT ACTUALLY COMES FROM, AND WHY YOU CANNOT IGNORE IT. Section 81-503.01(1) directs the State Fire Marshal to 'adopt and promulgate rules and regulations constituting a State Fire Code,' and requires that Code to cover, at a minimum, 'electrical wiring and heating, protection equipment devices, materials, furnishings, and other safeguards within structures necessary to promote safety and reduce loss by fire' and 'the means and adequacy of exits, in case of fire, in assembly, educational, institutional, RESIDENTIAL, mercantile, office, storage, and industrial-type occupancies.' Section 81-503.01(2) requires those rules to 'conform generally to the standards recommended by the National Fire Protection Association, Pamphlet Number 1, known as the Fire Code, 2012 edition, the National Fire Protection Association, Pamphlet Number 101, known as the Life Safety Code, 2012 edition, and associated pamphlets, but not when doing so would impose an unduly severe or costly burden without substantially contributing to the safety of persons or property.' Sprinkler requirements for residential occupancies are a classic subject of NFPA 101 and of the building codes a municipality adopts. So the statute delegates the subject rather than deciding it, and the operative requirement sits in the Fire Marshal's rules (Nebraska Administrative Code) and in whatever building code your city or village has adopted. Two consequences. FIRST, the phrase 'Nebraska has no sprinkler law' is true and misleading at the same time. Before you build, convert, add units to or substantially remodel a building, get the current State Fire Code rules and your municipality's adopted building code checked by someone who reads them for a living. Section 81-503.01(3) makes plan review mandatory - 'plans for compliance with the State Fire Code shall be reviewed by the State Fire Marshal' - and penalises late submission: plans filed after remodeling or construction has begun carry a late submittal fee penalty on top of the review fee, which the 2025 amendment raised from a flat fifty dollars to one hundred dollars plus fifty percent of the review fee. Submit before you start. SECOND, nobody is coming to check on you routinely, which is a trap rather than a comfort. Section 81-502(1)(c) makes it the State Fire Marshal's duty to investigate for fire safety the premises of liquor establishments, licensed foster care facilities, certain Department of Health and Human Services programmes and residential child-caring agencies, licensed health care facilities, and 'mobile home parks for which a license or renewal of a license is sought.' An apartment building, duplex or rented house is not on that list. Section 81-502(3) lets the Fire Marshal 'delegate the authority set forth in this section and section 81-503.01 to qualified local fire prevention personnel,' so in practice fire-code enforcement on rental housing is your city or county fire prevention office. The absence of a scheduled state inspection means a deficiency can sit for years and then surface in the worst possible setting - after a fire, in a tort case, where section 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence ('the obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state') leaves your negligence exposure exactly where the common law puts it. WHAT NEBRASKA DOES REQUIRE IN A RENTAL, STATUTORILY. Two detection duties, not suppression. Section 76-606 of the Carbon Monoxide Safety Act requires the owner of a rental dwelling with a fuel-fired heater or appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage to ensure an operational carbon monoxide alarm is installed on each habitable floor on a change in tenant occupancy on or after January 1, 2017, or on any permitted interior alteration, repair, fuel-fired appliance replacement or addition, with replacement of missing or non-operational alarms before a new occupancy, batteries supplied to the tenant at move-in, and repair or replacement on the tenant's notice (section 76-606(3)); the tenant must keep, test and maintain the alarms and notify the owner of problems (section 76-606(4)); and no person may remove batteries from or render an alarm inoperable except as part of inspecting, maintaining, repairing or replacing it (section 76-606(5)). Smoke detectors are governed by the Smoke Detector Act in chapter 81 - treat it as a live duty and have it checked. And whatever system you do have, section 28-1251(1) makes it 'unlawful for any person, association, partnership, limited liability company, or corporation to conduct fire alarm tests and fire alarm inspections without prior written certification by the State Fire Marshal as to the qualifications of such persons conducting such tests and inspections,' a Class III misdemeanour under section 28-1251(4). Use a certified inspector and keep the certification on file. DRAFTING. Do not promise sprinklers, a monitored fire alarm, or 'compliance with all fire codes' in the lease. Section 76-1419(1)(d) makes you maintain in good and safe working order all facilities and appliances 'SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED' by you, and 'or required to be supplied' is the phrase that converts a lease promise into a statutory maintenance duty; section 76-1425(2) then allows the tenant 'damages and ... injunctive relief for ANY noncompliance.' If your building has a suppression or alarm system, the lease should say the tenant must not obstruct, tamper with, disable, hang anything from or paint over any sprinkler head, detector, alarm device or extinguisher, and must report any damage immediately - that is a tenant duty you can enforce under section 76-1431(1) and (3), and it tracks section 76-1421(6)'s duty not to 'deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises.' Say nothing about what the system is or what standard it meets.

title: Foreclosure in Nebraska Ends the Lease at the Fall of the Hammer - No State Tenant Protection, but Federal Law Gives a Bona Fide Tenant 90 Days or the Lease Term
bodyText: Nebraska has no tenant-protection-at-foreclosure statute. There is no sixty-day or ninety-day notice for a bona fide tenant, no provision making the lease bind the purchaser, no requirement that the foreclosing party or the buyer tell the tenant anything, no eviction-record protection, and no equity-skimming statute of the Kansas kind.
