What Nebraska has instead is two statutes that do the opposite, and every landlord with a mortgage or a trust deed on a rented property should know exactly what they say. THE NONJUDICIAL ROUTE, WHICH IS THE NORMAL ONE. Nebraska deeds of trust are foreclosed by trustee's sale under the Nebraska Trust Deeds Act, sections 76-1001 to 76-1018. Section 76-1010(2) provides that 'the trustee's deed shall operate to convey to the purchaser, WITHOUT RIGHT OF REDEMPTION, the trustee's title and all right, title, interest, and claim of the trustor and his or her successors in interest AND OF ALL PERSONS CLAIMING BY, THROUGH, OR UNDER THEM, in and to the property sold, including all such right, title, interest, and claim in and to such property ACQUIRED BY THE TRUSTOR OR HIS OR HER SUCCESSORS IN INTEREST SUBSEQUENT TO THE EXECUTION OF THE TRUST DEED,' and that all such rights 'shall be deemed to be terminated AS OF THE TIME THE TRUSTEE OR THE ATTORNEY FOR THE TRUSTEE ACCEPTS THE HIGHEST BID AT THE TIME OF THE SALE.' A tenant holding under a lease you granted after the trust deed was recorded is a person claiming by, through or under the trustor, holding an interest acquired after the trust deed was executed. The lease is therefore terminated the moment the auctioneer accepts the high bid - not on confirmation, not on delivery of the deed, not after notice. THE JUDICIAL ROUTE SAYS THE SAME THING. Section 25-1530(2): 'all right, title, interest, and claim of the mortgagor and his or her successors in interest, and of all persons claiming by, through, and under the mortgagor and his or her successors in interest, in and to the property sold, including all such right, title, interest, and claim in and to such property acquired by the mortgagor or his or her successors in interest subsequent to the execution of the mortgage, shall be deemed terminated as of the time the sheriff or master commissioner accepts the highest bid at the sale' - subject only to the redemption right in section 25-1530(1) and confirmation of the sale under section 25-1531. And read who may redeem: section 25-1530(1) gives the right to 'the OWNERS of any real estate against which a decree of foreclosure has been rendered,' who may redeem 'at any time before the sale of the same shall be confirmed by a court of competent jurisdiction by paying into court the amount of such decree or judgment together with all interests and costs,' plus twelve percent interest to a third-party purchaser. A tenant is not an owner. So there is no Nebraska answer to the question some states give of treating a tenant as a lienholder with redemption rights - the tenant has nothing to redeem with. On an EXECUTION sale, section 25-1533 provides that the sheriff's deed 'shall vest in the purchaser as good and as perfect an estate in the premises therein mentioned as was vested in the party at or after the time when such lands and tenements became liable to the satisfaction of the judgment' - so the purchaser's estate is measured as of the judgment lien, and a lease granted later does not bind the purchaser. No Nebraska statute makes a tenant a tenant at will or redirects rent to the purchaser; the result is reached by extinguishment rather than by conversion. THE NOTICE POINT, WHICH IS THE CRUELLEST PART. A tenant gets no notice of the default or of the sale. Section 76-1008 requires the trustee to mail the notice of default within ten days of its recording, and the notice of sale at least twenty days before the sale, only to 'each person whose name and address is set forth in a REQUEST therefor WHICH HAS BEEN RECORDED prior to the filing for record of the notice of default,' plus each party to the trust deed under section 76-1008(3). The Nebraska Supreme Court has read the section exactly that way: 'unless the person or institution is a party to the trust deed at issue, that person or institution is not entitled to notice unless it is requested under subsection (1) of this section' (First Neb. Ed. Credit Union v. U.S. Bancorp, 293 Neb. 308, 877 N.W.2d 578 (2016)). A tenant may file and record a request under section 76-1008(1) at any time after the trust deed is recorded and before a notice of default is recorded - but no tenant knows that, and the window closes at the recording of the default. If the trustor's address is not in the trust deed and no request is recorded, the only notice is publication 'at least three times, once a week for three consecutive weeks, in a newspaper of general circulation' under section 76-1008(4). WHERE A LEASE DOES SURVIVE, AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING. Section 76-1010(2) and section 25-1530(2) both terminate only interests 'acquired ... SUBSEQUENT TO THE EXECUTION' of the trust deed or mortgage. A lease that predates the encumbrance, and that is good against the lender under the recording act, is not caught. Section 76-238(1) provides that recordable instruments 'shall take effect and be in force from and after the time of delivering such instruments to the register of deeds for recording, and not before, as to all creditors and subsequent purchasers in good faith without notice,' and are 'void as to all creditors and subsequent purchasers without notice whose deeds, mortgages, or other instruments are recorded prior.' Section 76-211 requires deeds of real estate 'or any interest therein ... except leases for one year or for a less time' to be signed, acknowledged and recorded. Note the trap in section 76-238(2): for agricultural or residential real estate (defined in (3)(d) as 'not more than four units designed for use for residential purposes'), POSSESSION BY A RELATIVE within the third degree does not give notice where the relative claims under a lease entered into on or after July 16, 2004, purporting to extend beyond one year, that has not satisfied section 76-211 - unless the creditor got a written copy of the lease first. If you let to family on a long lease, record it or hand the lender a copy. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU AS A LANDLORD. You cannot promise a tenant that the lease survives a foreclosure, because Nebraska law says it does not and federal law protects only a bona fide tenant (see below). Any lease clause purporting to bind a future purchaser is worthless - and worse, if it induced the tenant to sign, you have a representation problem (see section 87-302 and the remedy in section 87-303.07, which makes a lease induced by a deceptive practice 'unenforceable by the seller or lessor'). What you can and should do is the opposite: include a short, honest subordination-and-attornment paragraph saying that the lease is subject to any existing or future mortgage or deed of trust, that the tenant will recognise and attorn to a purchaser or successor who elects to continue the tenancy, and that rent is payable to whoever lawfully holds the landlord's interest. That costs the tenant nothing Nebraska law gives them and saves an argument later. Keep your deposits and prepaid rent straight too: section 76-1416(5) provides that 'the holder of the landlord's interest in the premises at the time of the termination of the tenancy is bound by this section,' and section 76-1420(1) keeps YOU liable for the deposits after a conveyance unless there was a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser, an actual assignment of deposits and prepaid rents, AND written notice to the tenant - a foreclosure sale will not satisfy all three, so expect the deposit exposure to stay with you. FEDERAL LAW CHANGES THE RESULT FOR A BONA FIDE TENANT. The federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act of 2009 (Pub. L. 111-22, section 702, 12 U.S.C. 5220 note) is in force. It expired at the end of 2014 and was restored, without a sunset, from June 23, 2018 by Pub. L. 115-174, section 304. It applies to 'any foreclosure on a federally-related mortgage loan or on any dwelling or residential real property', so it reaches a Nebraska trustee's sale and a judicial sale alike. The 'immediate successor in interest' takes the property subject to two things. First, it must give 'a notice to vacate to any bona fide tenant at least 90 days before the effective date of such notice.' Second, a tenant with a bona fide lease entered into before the notice of foreclosure may stay 'until the end of the remaining term of the lease'. There is one exception: the successor may end the lease on the date it sells the unit to 'a purchaser who will occupy the unit as a primary residence', still subject to the 90-day notice. A month-to-month or at-will tenant gets the 90-day notice. The 'notice of foreclosure' date is 'the date on which complete title to a property is transferred to a successor' (added by Pub. L. 111-203, section 1484). A tenancy is bona fide only if (1) the tenant is not the mortgagor or the mortgagor's child, spouse or parent, (2) it was an arm's-length transaction, and (3) the rent is not substantially less than fair market rent, unless it is reduced by a government subsidy. So a family lease on a related-party rent is not protected. A Section 8 voucher tenancy has its own rule: the successor takes subject to the lease and the housing assistance payments contract (Pub. L. 111-22, section 703). In practice the federal Act overrides section 76-1010(2)'s immediate termination for a protected tenant. How a court enforces it in Nebraska, and whether the tenant can sue on it directly, are questions only case law could settle. The cautious course for a buyer or lender: give every occupant the 90-day notice and honour a bona fide lease to its end.

title: No Duty To Tell a New Tenant the Property Is in Foreclosure - and Why You Should Anyway
bodyText: Nebraska imposes no duty on an owner who has received a notice of default, or been served with a foreclosure complaint, to tell a prospective tenant before the lease is signed. Nothing in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act requires it. Section 76-1417, the Act's only disclosure section, requires disclosure of the manager and the owner, not the owner's financial position. There is no notice-of-default rider, no required form, no statutory penalty for silence, and no termination right for a tenant who finds out later. If you are looking for Nebraska's equivalent of the Vermont, Nevada, Minnesota or Arizona disclosure statutes, it does not exist. SO WHAT DOES NEBRASKA HAVE, AND WHY IS IT NOT THIS. Nebraska does have a Foreclosure Protection Act, sections 76-2701 and following, and it does mention leases. But read who it binds. It regulates 'foreclosure consultants' and 'equity purchasers' - the people who approach a homeowner whose house is in foreclosure. 'Residence in foreclosure' means 'a residence or dwelling that is occupied as the HOMEOWNER'S PRINCIPAL PLACE OF RESIDENCE and against which any type of foreclosure action, including, but not limited to, the filing of a notice of default of a deed of trust or the filing of a lawsuit to foreclose a mortgage or other lien, has been commenced' (section 76-2712). So the Act protects an owner-occupier, not a tenant, and it is aimed at the counterparty, not the owner. The place it touches a lease is section 76-2720(1)(g), which requires every equity purchase contract to include 'the terms of any rental agreement or lease' - alongside the possession date (1)(f), disclosure of any obligations the purchaser assumes (1)(c), the specifics of any repurchase option (1)(h), a notice of cancellation (1)(i), and in (1)(j) a prescribed notice 'in at least fourteen-point, boldface type.' That is a disclosure made BY the buyer TO the distressed homeowner about the sale-leaseback they are proposing. It is not a landlord's disclosure to a tenant. If you are buying a house out of foreclosure and letting the former owner stay on as your tenant, you are an equity purchaser and the whole Act applies to you - including the certified-translation duty in section 76-2727, which names 'any equity purchase contract, rental agreement, lease' in terms, the three-business-day cancellation right in section 76-2721, and section 76-2724 voiding waiver. That is a different transaction from an ordinary letting and it is not what this topic is about. WHY SILENCE IS STILL A BAD IDEA, EVEN WITHOUT A DUTY. The absence of a disclosure statute is not the absence of exposure, for three reasons. FIRST, foreclosure in Nebraska destroys the tenancy outright. Section 76-1010(2) provides that a trustee's deed conveys 'without right of redemption' all right, title, interest and claim 'of all persons claiming by, through, or under' the trustor acquired 'subsequent to the execution of the trust deed,' terminated 'as of the time the trustee or the attorney for the trustee accepts the highest bid'; section 25-1530(2) does the same on a judicial foreclosure. A tenant who signs a twelve-month lease on a property already in default may lose possession in weeks, having paid a deposit and moved. SECOND, that is precisely the fact pattern a deceptive-practices claim is built from. Section 87-302(a) reaches a person who, in the course of business, 'represents that goods or services have ... characteristics ... uses, benefits, or quantities that they do not have,' or 'uses any scheme or device to defraud by means of ... obtaining money or property by knowingly false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises'; and section 87-303.07 then provides that 'if a buyer or LESSEE is induced by a violation of section 87-302 or 87-303.01 to enter into a sale or LEASE, the agreement is UNENFORCEABLE BY THE SELLER OR LESSOR and the buyer or lessee, at his or her option, may rescind the agreement or retain the merchandise delivered and the benefit of any services performed without any obligation to pay for them.' Letting a twelve-month lease on a property you know is being sold out from under the tenant, while representing the term as twelve months, is the kind of representation that feeds that section. (Note on currency: the version of section 87-302 now printed in the statutes carries 'Operative Date: January 1, 2027'; the subdivisions quoted are long-standing text, but check which version you are reading, because section 87-303.07's trigger is section 87-302.) Section 59-1602 of the Consumer Protection Act adds that 'unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce shall be unlawful,' with damages, costs and a reasonable attorney's fee under section 59-1609, subject to a public-interest requirement. THIRD, your deposit exposure does not go away with the property. Section 76-1416(5) binds 'the holder of the landlord's interest in the premises at the time of the termination of the tenancy,' and section 76-1420(1) keeps you liable unless there was a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser, an actual assignment of deposits and prepaid rents, AND written notice to the tenant - three things a foreclosure sale will not deliver. Expect the deposit claim, with the section 76-1416(3) attorney's fees, to land on you. PRACTICAL COURSE. If a notice of default has been recorded or a foreclosure action commenced against a property you are letting, do three things. Tell the tenant in writing before they sign, and keep the acknowledgment - it costs you nothing Nebraska law gives you and takes the inducement argument away. Offer a month-to-month tenancy rather than a fixed term, so you are not representing a term you cannot deliver. And tell the tenant, in the same writing, that under section 76-1008(1) any person may record a request in the register of deeds' office for copies of the notice of default and the notice of sale, that the request must be recorded BEFORE a notice of default is filed, and that without it the tenant gets no notice of the sale at all. That last item is in the tenant's interest rather than yours, which is exactly why including it is the best evidence you were not concealing anything.

title: No Relief from Forfeiture and No Tenant Redemption - the Court Must Declare the Lease Forfeited
bodyText: Nebraska gives a residential tenant no statutory relief from forfeiture and no right to redeem a terminated tenancy. There is no pay-and-stay provision, no post-judgment cure window, no deposit-with-the-clerk route to reinstatement, and no provision letting a court suspend or excuse a forfeiture on equitable grounds. The statute runs the other way, and it is worth reading the words. Section 76-1446 provides that 'if judgment is rendered against the defendant for the restitution of the premises, the court SHALL DECLARE THE FORFEITURE OF THE RENTAL AGREEMENT, and shall, at the request of the plaintiff or his or her attorney, issue a writ of restitution, directing the constable or sheriff to restore possession of the premises to the plaintiff on a specified date not more than ten days after issuance of the writ of restitution.' 'Shall declare' - the forfeiture is a mandatory consequence of the restitution judgment, not a discretionary remedy the court weighs. The same section sets the trial 'not less than ten nor more than fourteen days after the issuance of the summons,' to be 'tried by the court without a jury,' and provides that where the plaintiff served by the alternative method in section 76-1442.01 'a money judgment shall not be granted for the plaintiff' - so an alternative-service case gets you possession and the forfeiture but not the money. WHERE THE TENANT'S ONLY CURE WINDOWS ARE, AND THEY ARE BOTH BEFORE TERMINATION. Section 76-1431(1) requires you, for a material noncompliance with the lease or a section 76-1421 noncompliance materially affecting health and safety, to give written notice specifying the acts and omissions and stating that the agreement terminates on a date 'not less than thirty days after receipt of the notice if the breach is not remedied in fourteen days,' and 'if the breach is remediable by repairs or the payment of damages or otherwise and the tenant adequately remedies the breach prior to the date specified in the notice, the rental agreement will not terminate.' Section 76-1431(2) gives a rent default its own window: 'if rent is unpaid when due and the tenant fails to pay rent within SEVEN CALENDAR DAYS after written notice by the landlord of nonpayment and his or her intention to terminate the rental agreement if the rent is not paid within that period of time, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement.' Those are the cure rights, and they close when the notice period runs. Once the agreement has terminated, nothing in the Act lets the tenant undo it. HOW CERTAIN IS THAT ABSENCE? It is proved by the presence of the same rule next door, twice, for a borrower rather than a tenant. Section 76-1012(1) gives a defaulting TRUSTOR under a deed of trust a statutory right to cure: within one month of the recording of the notice of default (two months in the case covered by section 76-1006(1)(b)(i)), the trustor, a successor in interest, a subordinate lienholder or a junior beneficiary may pay the entire amount then due plus costs and trustee's fees, 'and thereby cure the default theretofore existing and thereupon all proceedings theretofore had or instituted shall be dismissed or discontinued, and the obligation and trust deed SHALL BE REINSTATED and shall be and remain in force and effect THE SAME AS IF NO ACCELERATION HAD OCCURRED.' Section 76-1903 separately gives a mortgagor a notice of right to cure. And section 25-1530(1) gives 'the OWNERS of any real estate against which a decree of foreclosure has been rendered' a right to redeem at any time before confirmation by paying the decree with interest and costs. So the Nebraska Legislature wrote a cure-and-reinstate right and a redemption right, and gave both to people with an ownership or security interest, and neither to a tenant. That is a demonstrated choice, not a silence. THE ONE ROUTE BACK, AND IT IS YOURS TO CONTROL. Section 76-1433: 'acceptance of rent with knowledge of a default by tenant or acceptance of performance by the tenant that varies from the terms of the rental agreement or rules or regulations subsequently adopted by the landlord constitutes a WAIVER of his right to terminate the rental agreement for that breach, UNLESS OTHERWISE AGREED AFTER THE BREACH HAS OCCURRED.' Read that twice, because it cuts both ways. It means the tenant's effective reinstatement right in Nebraska is your decision to take the money - and it means that if you take rent after you have served a termination notice, knowing of the default, you have waived the termination for that breach and your possession case is gone. If you intend to accept a payment without reviving the tenancy, get a written agreement to that effect, and note the timing requirement: the agreement must be made AFTER the breach has occurred, so a clause in the lease saying 'acceptance of rent is never a waiver' does not satisfy section 76-1433 and, because it would strip the tenant of a protection the Act gives, runs into section 76-1415(1)(a)'s bar on any term by which the tenant 'agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.' Use a separate post-breach writing, not boilerplate. TWO MORE PRACTICAL POINTS. First, do not write a forfeiture clause that tries to add consequences to a termination - accelerated rent for the whole remaining term, automatic forfeiture of the deposit, liquidated damages. Section 76-1416(2) lets the deposit be applied only to 'the payment of rent and the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or section 76-1421,' with a written itemization within fourteen days of termination; section 76-1405(1) imposes a duty to mitigate on 'the aggrieved party,' which binds you when you sue for the balance of the term; and section 76-1415(1)(c) bars any attorney's-fee term in either direction. A forfeiture-of-deposit clause is unenforceable and advertises that the rest of your lease was not checked. Second, the forcible entry and detainer route is not an alternative: section 25-21,219 ends 'this section shall not apply to actions for possession of any premises subject to the provisions of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act.' Residential possession goes through sections 76-1440 to 76-1447, and section 76-1446 is where the forfeiture is declared.

title: Your Termination Notice Need Not State a Reason - But Your Court Complaint Must State Facts With Particularity
bodyText: Nebraska has no good-cause requirement for ending a residential tenancy, and no statute requiring a termination notice to state a reason. You may end a periodic tenancy for no reason at all, and the notice need not explain itself. Section 76-1437(1): 'the landlord or the tenant may terminate a week-to-week tenancy by a written notice given to the other at least seven days prior to the termination date specified in the notice.' Section 76-1437(2): 'the landlord or the tenant may terminate a month-to-month tenancy by a written notice given to the other at least thirty days prior to the periodic rental date specified in the notice.' Note what those sentences require and what they do not. They require a WRITING, they require a termination DATE 'specified in the notice,' and in the month-to-month case the date must be a 'periodic rental date' - so you cannot end a month-to-month tenancy mid-month by counting thirty days from today; count to the next rental date that is at least thirty days out. They require no statement of cause, no form of words, no recitation of the statute, and no reason the tenant could contest. The same is true of a fixed-term lease: it ends when its term ends and no notice of non-renewal is required by statute at all. NOW THE PART THAT CATCHES LANDLORDS WHO READ ONLY THE FIRST HALF. 'No cause required' is a rule about the NOTICE. It is not a rule about the COMPLAINT. Section 76-1441(1) provides that the complaint for restitution 'shall contain (a) the specific statutory authority under which possession is sought; (b) the facts, with particularity, on which he or she seeks to recover; (c) a reasonably accurate description of the premises; and (d) the requisite compliance with the notice provisions of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.' So when you go to court you must name the subsection you are proceeding under, plead the facts WITH PARTICULARITY, and plead that you complied with the notice rules. A no-cause month-to-month termination is pleaded as a section 76-1437(2) case with the facts being the service and content of the notice and the expiry of the period - which is why the notice, the proof of delivery and the date arithmetic are the whole case. Section 76-1441(2) adds that a case brought under section 76-1431(4) - the five-day, no-right-to-cure route for violent criminal activity, illegal controlled-substance sales or activity threatening health or safety - 'shall include in the complaint the incident or incidents giving rise to the suit for recovery of possession.' Section 76-1441(1) also lets the complaint notify the tenant that personal property remains on the premises and may be disposed of under section 69-2308 or section 76-1414(5), and allows other causes of action relating to the tenancy to be joined, 'but such causes of action shall be answered and tried separately, if requested by either party in writing.' WHERE A REASON IS REQUIRED, IT IS BECAUSE YOU CHOSE A CURE-BASED ROUTE. Section 76-1431(1) requires a notice 'specifying the acts and omissions constituting the breach' and stating that the agreement terminates on a date not less than thirty days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in fourteen days. That is a cause-stating notice, and its specificity is an element: a vague notice fails. If you do not want to litigate the cause, use section 76-1437(2) instead and give no reason. FOUR LIMITS ON THE NO-CAUSE POWER, AND THEY ARE THE WHOLE OF THE LAW HERE. FIRST, retaliation. Section 76-1439(1) provides that 'a landlord may not retaliate by increasing rent or decreasing services or by bringing or threatening to bring an action for possession after (a) the tenant has complained to a government agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a minimum building or housing code of a violation applicable to the premises materially affecting health and safety; or (b) the tenant has organized or become a member of a tenants' union or similar organization.' The remedy is section 76-1430 (which is a fixed sum, not a ceiling - three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages) plus a defence to your possession action, under section 76-1439(2). But read section 76-1439(3), which preserves the action where 'the violation of the applicable minimum building or housing code was caused primarily by lack of reasonable care by the tenant or other person in his household or upon the premises with his consent,' where 'the tenant is in default in rent,' or where compliance 'requires alteration, remodeling, or demolition which would effectively deprive the tenant of use of the dwelling unit' - and note the closing sentence: 'the maintenance of the action does not release the landlord from liability under subsection (2) of section 76-1425.' Also note how narrow subsection (1) is: it lists two triggers only. A complaint made to YOU rather than to a government agency is not on the list. SECOND, discrimination. Section 20-318 makes it unlawful to 'refuse to sell or rent ... or otherwise make unavailable or deny' a dwelling, or to 'discriminate against any person in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling,' because of 'race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, sex, or military or veteran status' - and section 20-318(5) goes further and makes it unlawful to 'cause to be made any written or oral INQUIRY or record concerning' any of those characteristics of a person seeking to rent. A no-cause notice is still unlawful if the reason you did not state was one of those. THIRD, domestic violence. Sections 76-1431.01 to 76-1431.04 give a tenant who is a victim of an act of domestic violence a release from the rental agreement and a perpetrator-removal and lock-change regime, and section 76-1431(5) bars the five-day route where the activity was conducted by someone other than the tenant or a household member and the tenant or household member sought a protective order, reported the activity to law enforcement, or obtained qualified-third-party certification under the federal Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act of 2013. FOURTH, self-help is barred whatever your reason. Section 76-1436: 'a landlord may not recover or take possession of the dwelling unit by action or otherwise, including willful diminution of services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water, or other essential service to the tenant, except in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.' The price of getting that wrong is section 76-1430's three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages with no proof of loss required. PRACTICAL COURSE. Keep no-cause and for-cause terminations in separate lanes and never mix them in one notice. If you are ending a month-to-month tenancy because you are tired of the tenant, send a section 76-1437(2) notice that says only that the tenancy terminates on the stated periodic rental date, give it in writing, and prove delivery. Do not add a paragraph explaining why - every sentence of explanation is a fact the tenant can test and a retaliation or discrimination theory you have handed over. Do not promise in the lease that you will only terminate for cause or will give reasons; the law does not require it and the promise becomes a term you can be sued on under section 76-1425(2), which allows damages for 'any noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement.'

title: No Guest-Rights Statute - But the Tenant, Not You, Licenses Who Comes Into the Unit
bodyText:
Nebraska has no guest-rights statute. There is no provision guaranteeing a tenant's guests or suppliers access to a building, no ban on charging a guest fee, no statutory definition of 'guest' in the landlord-tenant act, and no non-waivable visitor right of the kind a few states give in buildings of three or more households.

The word 'guest' appears in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act in exactly one place - section 76-1431(4), where a guest's conduct is a GROUND FOR EVICTING THE TENANT. Everywhere else the Act speaks of a 'person on the premises with his consent' (section 76-1421(6) and (7)). So the statutory picture is almost entirely landlord-side. That makes it all the more important to understand the one thing that is not, because it is in the criminal code rather than chapter 76 and it defeats the clause most landlords want to write.

THE TENANT LICENSES ENTRY TO THE DWELLING UNIT. YOU DO NOT. Nebraska's trespass offences both turn on the absence of a licence. Section 28-520(1)(a): a person commits first degree criminal trespass if 'he or she enters or secretly remains in any building or occupied structure, or any separately secured or occupied portion thereof, KNOWING THAT HE OR SHE IS NOT LICENSED OR PRIVILEGED TO DO SO' - a Class I misdemeanour.

Section 28-521(1): second degree criminal trespass is committed if, 'KNOWING THAT HE OR SHE IS NOT LICENSED OR PRIVILEGED TO DO SO,' a person 'enters or remains in any place as to which notice against trespass is given by (a) actual communication to the actor; or (b) posting in a manner prescribed by law or reasonably likely to come to the attention of intruders; or (c) fencing or other enclosure manifestly designed to exclude intruders' - a Class III misdemeanour, rising to Class II 'if the offender defies an order to leave personally communicated to him or her by the owner of the premises or other authorized person.'

Then section 28-522(3) makes it an affirmative defence that 'the actor reasonably believed that the owner of the premises OR OTHER PERSON EMPOWERED TO LICENSE ACCESS THERETO would have licensed him to enter or remain,' and the Nebraska Supreme Court has held that 'a valid license from ANY owner or other person empowered to license access to a property is sufficient to show that a defendant reasonably believed that he or she was licensed to be on the premises. A defendant need not show that every owner licensed his or her presence' (State v. McCave, 282 Neb. 500, 805 N.W.2d 290 (2011)).

A tenant with the exclusive right of occupancy - section 76-1410(17) defines 'tenant' as 'a person entitled under a rental agreement to occupy a dwelling unit TO THE EXCLUSION OF OTHERS' - is a person empowered to license access to that unit.

CONSEQUENCE: you cannot ban a named person from your tenant's dwelling unit and make them a trespasser there while the tenant has invited them in. A lease clause saying 'Landlord may prohibit any guest from the Premises' promises something Nebraska law does not deliver, and a no-trespass letter served on a tenant's guest will not support a prosecution as to the unit itself. If you have written that clause, it is a representation problem, not just a dead letter.

(Note also section 28-521(2): intentionally causing 'an electronic device, such as an unmanned aircraft, to enter into, upon, or above the property of another, INCLUDING SUCH PROPERTY OWNED BY SUCH PERSON AND LEASED OR RENTED TO ANOTHER, with the intent to observe another person without his or her consent in a place of solitude or seclusion' is second degree criminal trespass. The statute names the landlord's own rented property expressly. Do not fly a drone over an occupied rental.)

WHERE YOUR POWER IS REAL. COMMON AREAS. 'Premises' under section 76-1410(12) means 'a dwelling unit and the structure of which it is a part and facilities and appurtenances therein and grounds, areas, and facilities held out for the use of tenants generally or whose use is promised to the tenant,' and section 76-1419(1)(c) makes you keep 'all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition.' You are the person empowered to license access to the lobby, laundry, hallways, parking and grounds, so a notice against trespass under section 28-521(1)(a) directed at a specific person as to those areas does work - and a person who defies a personally communicated order to leave commits the Class II version. Keep the ban to the common areas and route the person to and from the tenant's door.

RULES AND REGULATIONS. Section 76-1422 lets you 'adopt rules or regulations, however described, concerning the tenant's use and occupancy of the premises,' enforceable under section 76-1431 against the tenant ONLY IF all six conditions are met: '(1) its purpose is to promote the appearance, convenience, safety, or welfare of the tenants in the premises, preserve the landlord's property from abusive use, or make a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for the tenants generally; (2) it is reasonably related to the purpose for which it is adopted; (3) it applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner; (4) it is sufficiently explicit in its prohibition, direction, or limitation of the tenant's conduct to fairly inform him of what he must or must not do to comply; (5) it is not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord; and (6) THE TENANT HAS NOTICE OF IT AT THE TIME HE ENTERS INTO THE RENTAL AGREEMENT.'

A rule adopted later 'is enforceable against the tenant if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the tenant and it does not work a substantial modification of his bargain.'

Condition (6) is the one that hollows out most guest policies: if the guest rules were not delivered to the tenant before signing, they are not enforceable, and a later guest-limit rule may well be a substantial modification of the bargain. Deliver the rules with the lease and get a receipt.

OCCUPANCY RATHER THAN VISITING. Section 76-1424: 'unless otherwise agreed, the tenant shall occupy his dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit. The rental agreement may require that the tenant notify the landlord of any anticipated extended absence from the premises in excess of seven days no later than the first day of the extended absence.'

A guest-duration limit is best framed not as a ban on visitors but as a definition of when a visitor has become an occupant who must be added to the lease and screened - that is a use-and-occupancy rule, which is what section 76-1422 authorises.

ENFORCEMENT RUNS THROUGH THE TENANT, ALWAYS. Section 76-1421(6) makes the tenant 'not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or KNOWINGLY PERMIT ANY PERSON TO DO SO'; section 76-1421(7) makes the tenant 'conduct himself and REQUIRE OTHER PERSONS ON THE PREMISES WITH HIS CONSENT to conduct themselves in a manner that will not disturb his neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises.' Breach is a section 76-1431(1) noncompliance, with the thirty-day/fourteen-day cure notice, and section 76-1431(3) gives you damages for 'any noncompliance by the tenant with the rental agreement or section 76-1421,' plus reasonable attorney's fees if the noncompliance is willful.

And for the serious cases, section 76-1431(4) is the five-day, no-right-to-cure route against 'any tenant or occupant' where 'the tenant, occupant, member of the tenant's household, GUEST, or other person who is under the tenant's control or who is present upon the premises with the tenant's consent, engages in any violent criminal activity on the premises, the illegal sale of any controlled substance on the premises, or any other activity that threatens the health or safety of other tenants, the landlord, or the landlord's employees or agents' - with the listed examples in (4)(a) to (d) and the important exception in section 76-1431(5), which bars the route where the activity was by someone other than the tenant or a household member and the tenant or household member sought a protective order, reported it to law enforcement, or obtained qualified-third-party certification under the federal Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act of 2013.

GUEST FEES. Nothing in Nebraska bans or regulates a guest fee; nothing authorises one either. Two cautions if you charge one. It is 'rent' - section 76-1410(13) defines rent as 'all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement' - so non-payment runs through section 76-1431(2)'s seven-calendar-day notice. And if it functions as security rather than a charge, section 76-1416(1)'s cap on 'security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent' catches it.

A fee that bears no relation to any service and operates to deter visitors is also the kind of term a court can address under section 76-1412(1), which lets it 'refuse to enforce the agreement, enforce the remainder of the agreement without the unconscionable provision, or limit the application of any unconscionable provision' where a rental agreement or any provision 'was unconscionable when made.'

title: No Nebraska Statute Allocates Hunting Rights in a Farm Lease - Reserve Them in Writing or Litigate the Silence
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute of the Arkansas kind - nothing saying that a tenant of rented farmland has no hunting or fishing rights unless the owner grants them in writing, and nothing saying the tenant does have them. There is no default rule to rely on either way, which means the whole question is decided by what your lease says, and if your lease says nothing you are into a contract-construction argument about whether the grant of possession for farming carried the right to hunt. THREE THINGS A NEBRASKA FARM LANDLORD SHOULD KNOW BEFORE WRITING THE LEASE. FIRST, THE RESIDENTIAL ACT DOES NOT APPLY, AND THAT CUTS BOTH WAYS. Section 76-1408 provides that, 'unless created to avoid the application of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act,' the listed arrangements 'are not governed by the act,' and item (7) is 'occupancy under a rental agreement covering premises used by the occupant primarily for AGRICULTURAL PURPOSES.' So none of chapter 76's landlord-tenant machinery reaches a farm tenancy: not section 76-1414's default terms, not section 76-1415's prohibited provisions, not section 76-1416's deposit cap or fourteen-day return, not section 76-1419's habitability duties, not section 76-1437's thirty-day periodic-tenancy notice, and not sections 76-1440 to 76-1447's possession procedure. A farm lease is governed by its own words and by general contract and property law. Note the exclusion's opening qualifier, which applies to all eight items: an arrangement 'created to avoid the application of' the Act is NOT excluded, so you cannot label a house lease agricultural to escape the Act. Note too item (8), 'a lease of improved or unimproved residential land for a term of five years or more,' which is a separate exclusion and catches long land leases whether or not they are agricultural. And note what the exclusion means for the house on the farm: if you let the farmhouse to someone whose occupancy is not primarily agricultural, that tenancy is inside the Act even though the ground around it is not. Write the farmhouse and the ground as separate leases rather than one document, or you will be arguing about which regime governs. SECOND, WASTE IS YOUR REMEDY, AND ITS TEETH DEPEND ON YOUR COVENANT. Section 76-120 provides that 'when conduct claimed to constitute waste is made the basis of a claim for damages, the claimant is limited to a recovery of compensatory damages and is not entitled to multiple damages or to declare a forfeiture of the place wasted or of the interest of the defendant in the place wasted, EXCEPT IN ACCORDANCE WITH COVENANTS, AGREEMENTS OR CONDITIONS BINDING SUCH DEFENDANTS.' So without a covenant you get compensatory damages only and cannot forfeit the lease; with an express covenant or condition you can. If you care about timber, tree belts, fences, waterways, terraces, soil, game cover or a shelterbelt, say so in a covenant and attach the forfeiture to it, because section 76-120 will not give you one by default. THIRD, THE LEASE MUST BE IN WRITING IF IT RUNS OVER A YEAR, AND YOU ARE THE ONE WHO HAS TO SIGN. Section 36-105: 'every contract for the leasing for a longer period than one year, or for the sale of any lands, shall be VOID unless the contract or some note or memorandum thereof be in writing and SIGNED BY THE PARTY BY WHOM THE LEASE OR SALE IS TO BE MADE.' A multi-year farm lease signed only by the tenant is void. Section 36-202(1) independently voids 'every agreement that, by its terms, is not to be performed within one year from the making thereof' unless written and subscribed by the party to be charged. And on recording: section 76-211 requires 'deeds of real estate, or any interest therein ... EXCEPT LEASES FOR ONE YEAR OR FOR A LESS TIME' to be signed, acknowledged and recorded, while section 76-238(1) provides that recordable instruments 'take effect and be in force from and after the time of delivering such instruments to the register of deeds for recording, and not before, as to all creditors and subsequent purchasers in good faith without notice,' and are 'void as to all creditors and subsequent purchasers without notice whose deeds, mortgages, or other instruments are recorded prior.' Section 76-238(2) adds a trap aimed squarely at farm country: for AGRICULTURAL real estate (defined in (3)(b) as land 'primarily used for the production of agricultural products,' with (3)(a) listing 'grain and feed crops; forages and sod crops; and animal production, including breeding, feeding, or grazing of cattle, horses, swine, sheep, goats, bees, or poultry'), POSSESSION BY A RELATIVE within the third degree of consanguinity or affinity does NOT serve as notice to a creditor or subsequent purchaser where the relative claims under a lease entered into on or after July 16, 2004, purporting to extend beyond one year, that has not satisfied section 76-211 - unless the creditor or purchaser received a written copy of the lease before recording. Family farm leases are the normal case in Nebraska and this is the provision that defeats them. Record the lease or deliver a copy to the lender. WHAT THE GAME LAWS IN CHAPTER 37 DO SAY. They do not allocate hunting rights between you and your tenant either, but three provisions matter. FIRST, WHO GIVES PERMISSION. Section 37-722 makes it 'unlawful for anyone to take any wildlife upon any private lands without permission of the owner', and says 'owner means the actual owner of the land and ANY TENANT or agent IN POSSESSION or charge thereof for him or her.' So a farm tenant in possession can give a hunter lawful permission unless your lease takes that power away. A lease reservation binds the tenant as a contract. Whether it also stops the tenant's permission counting under section 37-722 is a question only a court could settle. The cautious course: reserve the right in the lease, and also tell hunters directly or post the land. SECOND, PERMIT PRIVILEGES THE TENANT GETS FROM THE STATUTE. Section 37-403 lets a person who 'owns or operates farm or ranch land and who actually resides on a portion of' it, with immediate family living there, hunt upland game birds and most small game on that land without a permit or habitat stamp. Section 37-455(3)(a) and (5)(a) let a Nebraska resident who 'owns or leases eighty acres or more of farm or ranch land for agricultural purposes' get half-price limited deer, antelope and wild turkey permits for that land. Section 37-456.01 adds a free-earned elk permit for an owner or lessee of eighty acres. No statute says whether your lease can stop a qualifying tenant using those privileges on the leased land. If you reserve hunting, say expressly that the reservation covers hunting under any landowner, operator or leaseholder permit or exemption. THIRD, LIABILITY TO HUNTERS. For sections 37-729 to 37-736, 'Owner includes tenant, lessee, occupant, or person in control of the premises' (section 37-729(2)), and hunting is a recreational purpose. An owner who lets people use land for recreation without charge owes them no duty to keep it safe (sections 37-731 and 37-732). Section 37-734 keeps liability 'for willful or malicious failure to guard or warn' and 'where the owner of land charges the person or persons who enter'. So selling hunting access, by you or the tenant, gives up that protection. WHAT TO PUT IN THE LEASE. Because there is no default, write the allocation expressly and in these terms. State that the lease grants the tenant possession for agricultural purposes only and reserves to the landlord all hunting, fishing, trapping and other recreational rights, together with the right to enter for those purposes and to grant them to others. State that the tenant will not hunt, fish or trap, will not permit others to do so, and will not grant, sell or advertise hunting or fishing access, without the landlord's prior written consent. State who may consent to third-party entry and in what form. Add a covenant protecting cover, trees, fences, waterways and wildlife habitat, with an express condition allowing termination for breach so that section 76-120's bar on forfeiture does not apply. Deal with liability: say who carries insurance for recreational users, who is responsible for the conduct of a person they bring on, and whether either of you may charge for access (section 37-734). If instead you intend the tenant to have the hunting, say that too and say whether the tenant may sublease or sell access. The one thing not to do is leave it out on the assumption that the law supplies an answer, because in Nebraska it does not.

title: No Flood Disclosure Duty to a Tenant - and Flood Is Not Even on Nebraska's Seller Disclosure List
bodyText: Nebraska requires no flood disclosure to a residential tenant. There is no separate signed rider, no state model form, no point-size requirement, no obligation to say whether the property is in a special flood hazard area or has flooded before, and no tenant termination remedy for a flood or for a failure to disclose one. Section 76-1417, the only disclosure section in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, requires the landlord to disclose in writing 'at or before the commencement of the tenancy the name and address of (a) the person authorized to manage the premises; and (b) an owner of the premises or a person authorized to act for and on behalf of the owner for the purpose of service of process and for the purpose of receiving and receipting for notices and demands' - and nothing else. The word 'flood' does not appear in any landlord-tenant provision in Nebraska's statutes. WHAT MAKES THIS MORE THAN AN ORDINARY ABSENCE. Nebraska also leaves flood off the list where you would most expect to find it. Section 76-2,120 requires a seller of residential real property - and by section 76-2,120(1)(d) and (2) that includes a 'lease with option to purchase' and a sale of improvements 'coupled with a ground lease' - to give the purchaser a written disclosure statement of the property's condition, and section 76-2,120(4) PRESCRIBES WHAT IT MUST COVER: the condition of included appliances, the electrical system, the heating and cooling systems, the water system, the sewer system; 'the condition of all improvements on the real property and any defects that materially affect the value of the real property or improvements'; 'any hazardous conditions, including substances, materials, and products on the real property which may be an environmental hazard'; title conditions 'including encroachments, easements, and zoning restrictions'; whether utility connections are public, private or community; any private transfer fee obligation under section 76-3107; and 'information relating to compliance with the requirements for a carbon monoxide alarm as provided in sections 76-604 and 76-605.' Eleven enumerated items, and flooding, flood zone, flood history, drainage and water intrusion are not among them. The Legislature wrote out a specific list for the transaction where a buyer's whole investment is at stake, and did not put flood on it. So a flood disclosure is not something Nebraska forgot about for tenants while requiring it for buyers - it is simply not a statutory subject here. Two qualifications on section 76-2,120 all the same, because they could reach a flood-prone property in a sale: subsection (4)(f)'s 'any defects that materially affect the value' and (4)(g)'s environmental-hazard item are open-ended, and a known history of flooding or a known drainage defect is the kind of thing a court could put inside either. Section 76-2,120(5) requires the statement to be completed 'to the best of the seller's belief and knowledge,' lets the seller mark an item unknown, and requires an update 'on or before the effective date of any contract which binds the purchaser to purchase the real property' whenever the seller learns the statement is no longer accurate. If you are letting with an option to purchase, you are a 'seller' under subsection (1)(d) and that statement is due - and note that subsection (2) attaches the duty to 'any lease with the option to purchase' while subsection (5) times delivery to the contract that binds the purchaser to purchase, which an option does not do until exercised. The safe course is to deliver at lease signing. WHY YOU SHOULD DISCLOSE ANYWAY, IN ONE PARAGRAPH. Silence about a known flood risk is the fact pattern a deceptive-practices claim is built from, and in Nebraska the remedy is not a fine. Section 87-302(a) reaches a person who, in the course of business, '(5) represents that goods or services have ... characteristics ... uses, benefits, or quantities that they do not have,' or '(16) uses any scheme or device to defraud by means of ... obtaining money or property by knowingly false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises.' Section 87-303.07 then provides that 'if a buyer or LESSEE is induced by a violation of section 87-302 or 87-303.01 to enter into a sale or LEASE, the agreement is UNENFORCEABLE BY THE SELLER OR LESSOR and the buyer or lessee, at his or her option, may rescind the agreement or retain the merchandise delivered and the benefit of any services performed without any obligation to pay for them.' (Currency note: the version of section 87-302 now printed carries 'Operative Date: January 1, 2027'; the subdivisions quoted are long-standing, but section 87-303.07's trigger is section 87-302 so check which version you are reading.) Beyond that, letting a basement apartment you know takes water engages section 76-1419(1)(b)'s duty to 'make all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition,' enforceable for 'any noncompliance' under section 76-1425(2) with no materiality threshold, and the Nebraska Supreme Court has held those duties 'are not limited under the plain language to conditions arising after commencement of the lease term' (Vasquez v. CHI Properties, 302 Neb. 742, 925 N.W.2d 304 (2019)) - a pre-existing flooding problem is squarely inside section 76-1419. And if a flood does damage the unit, section 76-1429 gives the tenant the exit: on damage 'to an extent that enjoyment of the dwelling unit is substantially impaired' the tenant may vacate and terminate on written notice within fourteen days, or vacate the unusable part with rent reduced in proportion to the diminution in fair rental value, with section 76-1429(2) requiring return of all prepaid rent and security. You cannot contract out of that; section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant 'agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.' WHAT TO DO. Disclose in writing what you know - whether the property is in a mapped flood hazard area, whether it has flooded, which parts, when, and what was done about it - and have the tenant sign for it. Tell the tenant plainly that your insurance does not cover their belongings and that renter's flood coverage is theirs to buy if they want it; you may require liability insurance as a lease term but do not describe it to the tenant as protecting their property. Do not write a clause saying the tenant accepts the risk of flooding, waives claims for water damage, or has no remedy if the unit floods - section 76-1415(1)(a) makes it unenforceable and section 76-1415(1)(d) separately voids any term by which the tenant 'agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord or to indemnify the landlord for that liability,' with section 76-1415(2) adding the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees if you deliberately use a term you know is prohibited. Finally, two things: flood zone designations and the National Flood Insurance Program are federal, so treat any federal lender or insurance disclosure requirement as live and unverified; and a Nebraska city, village or natural resources district may impose a floodplain disclosure or occupancy rule by ordinance.

title: You May Refuse a Home Child Care Business - But If You Allow One, the Unit Becomes a Smoke-Free Workplace and You Are the Proprietor
bodyText: Nebraska has nothing like Oregon's ORS 90.358. No statute requires a Nebraska landlord to allow a tenant to operate a family child care home, none sets conditions on which the landlord must allow it, and none authorises the landlord to demand a liability waiver or insurance as the price of allowing it. The subject is simply not legislated at the landlord-tenant level, which means the decision is yours and the terms are whatever your lease says. YOUR POWER TO SAY NO, AND WHERE IT COMES FROM. Section 76-1424: 'unless otherwise agreed, the tenant shall occupy his dwelling unit ONLY AS A DWELLING UNIT.' A licensed child care business run out of the unit is not occupancy only as a dwelling unit, so the default already sits with you - but note the opening words 'unless otherwise agreed,' which means the lease can displace it and silence can be argued about. Say it expressly. Section 76-1422 lets you 'adopt rules or regulations, however described, concerning the tenant's use and occupancy of the premises,' enforceable under section 76-1431 against the tenant only if all six of its conditions are met: the purpose must be 'to promote the appearance, convenience, safety, or welfare of the tenants in the premises, preserve the landlord's property from abusive use, or make a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for the tenants generally'; it must be 'reasonably related to the purpose for which it is adopted'; it must apply 'to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner'; it must be 'sufficiently explicit in its prohibition, direction, or limitation of the tenant's conduct to fairly inform him of what he must or must not do to comply'; it must not be 'for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord'; and - the condition that kills most house rules - 'THE TENANT HAS NOTICE OF IT AT THE TIME HE ENTERS INTO THE RENTAL AGREEMENT.' A rule adopted later is enforceable only 'if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the tenant and it does not work a substantial modification of his bargain.' So a no-business or child-care-by-consent rule has to be delivered with the lease, and you want a receipt. THE LINE YOU MUST NOT CROSS WHILE DOING IT. Refusing a BUSINESS is not the same as refusing CHILDREN, and the difference is the difference between a lawful rule and a fair-housing claim. Section 20-318 makes it unlawful to 'refuse to sell or rent after the making of a bona fide offer, refuse to negotiate for the sale or rental of or otherwise make unavailable or deny, refuse to show, or refuse to receive and transmit an offer for a dwelling to any person because of race, color, religion, national origin, disability, FAMILIAL STATUS, sex, or military or veteran status,' and to 'discriminate against any person in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling or in the provision of services or facilities in connection therewith' on the same grounds; section 20-318(3) reaches any 'notice, statement, or advertisement' indicating such a preference or limitation; and section 20-318(5) makes it unlawful even to 'cause to be made any written or oral INQUIRY or record concerning' those characteristics of a person seeking to rent. Write your rule as a prohibition on operating a licensed or commercial business from the unit without written consent, applied to every tenant alike, and never as anything about children, family size or how many people are in the household. And when you grant consent, grant it in writing on stated terms, so you are not granting it to some tenants and refusing others without a record of why. IF YOU DO ALLOW IT, THERE IS A CONSEQUENCE THAT IS NOT OBVIOUS AND IT LANDS ON YOU. Nebraska's Clean Indoor Air Act has a provision whose effect most landlords and most tenants have never heard of. Section 71-5726 states the general rule that 'a private residence is not a public place' - which is why smoking in a rented home is normally not a Clean Indoor Air Act matter at all. But section 71-5724 makes a private residence BECOME a 'place of employment' while it is being used as a licensed child care program with one or more children present who are not occupants of the residence, and section 71-5724 defines 'place of employment' as an indoor area under the proprietor's control that an employee accesses 'without regard to whether the employee is present or work is occurring at any given time,' with the list expressly including a hallway. Section 71-5729 prohibits smoking in a place of employment. Section 71-5725 defines a 'proprietor' as 'any employer, owner, operator, supervisor, manager, or other person who controls, governs, or directs the activities in a place of employment or public place.' Section 71-5731 requires a proprietor to 'take necessary and appropriate steps to ensure compliance with the act at such place.' The text does not settle whether a landlord who does not run the program is a proprietor. Read one way, any owner is. Read the other way, only an owner who controls or directs the activities there is. The cautious course is to assume you may be one. Put together: when you consent to a tenant running a licensed child care program in the unit, that unit becomes a smoke-free workplace while non-occupant children are present, and you should act as if the duty to ensure compliance may be yours as well as the tenant's. Before you consent, also read the Child Care Licensing Act in chapter 71, which sets what 'licensed child care program' means and is not covered here. A SECOND NON-OBVIOUS CONSEQUENCE, IF YOU OWN MORE THAN ONE PROPERTY NEARBY. A licensed child care facility in one of your units can restrict who may live in the others. Section 29-4017(1) permits a political subdivision to enact a residency restriction for sex offenders 'only if the restrictions are limited to sexual predators, extend no more than five hundred feet from a school or CHILD CARE FACILITY,' and meet subsection (2); section 29-4017(3) makes any restriction not meeting those requirements void. Section 29-4017(2)(c) exempts a sexual predator who 'established a residence after July 1, 2006, and the school or child care facility triggering the restriction was established AFTER the initial date of the sexual predator's residence at that location' - so existing residents are not displaced, but in a city with such an ordinance a new child care home in your building creates a five-hundred-foot zone affecting whom you may let to in future. Check whether your municipality has enacted a restriction under section 29-4017 before you consent. WHAT TO PUT IN THE CONSENT, SINCE NO STATUTE SETS THE TERMS. Because Nebraska legislates none of this, everything is contract, and section 76-1414(1) authorises it: 'the landlord and tenant may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law.' Reasonable terms to require are: proof of current state licensure and of compliance with it, maintained throughout; a maximum number of children and permitted hours; commercial general liability insurance in a stated amount naming you as an additional insured, with proof on renewal (nothing in chapter 76 bars requiring a tenant to carry insurance - note that the only Nebraska insurance provision of this kind is section 76-1475(2) in the Mobile Home Act, which means the Legislature wrote one for mobile home parks and none for ordinary tenancies, so yours comes from the lease); a no-smoking undertaking covering the unit and any common area while children are present, with the Clean Indoor Air Act named as the reason; responsibility for the conduct of the children and of parents dropping off and collecting, which tracks section 76-1421(7)'s requirement that the tenant 'conduct himself and require other persons on the premises with his consent to conduct themselves in a manner that will not disturb his neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises'; parking and drop-off arrangements; and a right to revoke the consent on notice if any condition is broken, which keeps you inside section 76-1431(1)'s notice-and-cure route rather than leaving you arguing about whether a business breach is material. TWO THINGS YOU MAY NOT REQUIRE. Section 76-1415(1)(d) voids any term by which the tenant 'agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord or to indemnify the landlord for that liability arising due to active and actionable negligence or the costs connected therewith' - so a blanket hold-harmless or indemnity covering your own negligence is unenforceable, and an indemnity must be limited to liability arising from the child care operation itself. Section 76-1415(1)(c) voids any term by which the tenant 'agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees,' in both directions. Section 76-1415(2) adds that a prohibited provision 'is unenforceable' and that if you 'deliberately use a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited,' the tenant 'may recover actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees.' And remember that none of the consent terms displaces your own duties: section 76-1419(1)(c) still requires you to keep 'all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition,' and for a unit that is not a single-family residence section 76-1419(3) lets you shift only 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling,' and only by a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration that 'does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises.'

title: The Water, Hot-Water and Heat Duty Has Exactly Two Exceptions - and "There Is No Water Out Here" Is Not One of Them
bodyText: Some states let the lease switch off the water or hot-water duty when the property has no well and no utility service to draw on. Nebraska does not, and the reason is worth understanding before you write a clause that will not hold. Section 76-1419(1)(f) requires you to 'Supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat except where the building that includes the dwelling unit is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant and supplied by a direct public utility connection.' Read the two exceptions carefully, because they are the whole list. THE FIRST is regulatory, not factual: the building must be one that 'is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose.' That is a question about what a building code or ordinance demands of this structure, not a question about whether water happens to be available at the site. A rural acreage with a dry well is still a building that the law may require to be equipped for water; the absence of water is the breach, not the excuse. THE SECOND is architectural: heat or hot water is generated by an installation 'within the exclusive control of the tenant AND supplied by a direct public utility connection.' Both halves are required. A tenant-controlled water heater fed off the landlord's master gas account does not qualify, because the connection is not the tenant's direct one. Neither does a shared boiler the tenant can adjust. Nebraska has no third exception, and in particular no 'no well or utility water available' limb of the kind Alaska writes into its statute. Now the part landlords get wrong. You cannot add an exception by agreement except on one narrow path. Section 76-1419(2) lets the landlord and tenant of a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE agree that the tenant performs the duties in subdivisions (1)(e) and (1)(f) - waste removal and the water, hot-water and heat duty - plus specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling, 'but only if the transaction is in writing, for good consideration, entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord.' Section 76-1419(3), which governs every dwelling unit that is NOT a single-family residence, reaches only 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling' and never names (1)(e) or (1)(f) at all. The contrast between the two subsections is the point: the Legislature listed (1)(e) and (1)(f) where it meant them to be shiftable and left them out where it did not. In a duplex, a fourplex or an apartment building, the water, hot-water and heat duty cannot be moved onto the tenant by any agreement, separate writing or consideration. And check what 'single-family residence' actually means here before you rely on subsection (2). Section 76-1410(16) defines it as 'a structure maintained and used as a single dwelling unit,' and then adds that a unit sharing a wall still counts 'if it has direct access to a street or thoroughfare and shares neither heating facilities, hot water equipment, nor any other essential facility or service with any other dwelling unit.' Both limbs must be satisfied. A converted house with two units on one furnace fails the shared-heating limb no matter how it is described in the lease, and the same furnace that makes the delegation attractive is the fact that defeats it. One more thing that is easy to misread as an exception and is not. Section 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence says that where a minimum housing code applies to the premises, 'the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a) of this section' - substantial compliance with that code after notice. That is a CEILING on the open-ended habitability language, and section 76-1410(3) keeps 'minimum housing code' narrow: 'those laws, resolutions, or ordinances or regulations, or portions thereof, dealing specifically with health and minimum standards of fitness for habitation.' It does not create a water exception; it measures the duty by the code instead of by the statute's own words. Practical course: write the water, hot-water and heat obligation into your lease as yours, and if the unit genuinely runs on a tenant-controlled installation with the tenant's own direct utility account, say exactly that in the lease and keep the account documentation, because that is the fact the exception turns on. If the property is a true single-family residence and you want the tenant to carry those duties, use a signed written agreement with stated consideration rather than a boilerplate paragraph, and do not use it as a device to get out from under a problem you already know about - subsection (2) withholds its protection from an agreement entered into 'for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord.'

title: No Habitability Presumption in Nebraska - the Tenant Proves It, and Notice Comes First
bodyText: Several states tilt the evidence in a habitability fight before anyone testifies. California presumes a dwelling untenantable on proof of certain defects; Maryland's rent-escrow statute carries presumptions; Massachusetts and Maine attach consequences to a code violation as such. Nebraska does none of this. There is no presumption, no prima facie rule and no deemed-uninhabitable list anywhere in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and no definition of 'material' or of 'materially affecting health and safety' either - section 76-1410 carries eighteen definitions and neither phrase is among them. What that means in practice is that the tenant who wants to terminate, abate or recover damages has to prove the condition, prove the standard it breached and prove the degree, on ordinary civil burdens, with no statutory shortcut from 'the inspector wrote me up' to 'the landlord is in breach.' A municipal code citation is evidence; it is not a presumption. Three features of the Act do the work other states give to presumptions, and all three run your way. FIRST, NOTICE IS A CONDITION OF THE DUTY, NOT JUST OF THE REMEDY. Section 76-1419(1)(a) and (1)(b) - the minimum-housing-code duty and the fit-and-habitable duty - both begin 'after written or actual notice.' The obligation to repair does not attach until you have notice. Nebraska deliberately did not write a constructive-notice or should-have-known presumption into those subdivisions, and 'actual notice' is defined by section 76-1413(1) as actual knowledge, receipt of a notice, or reason to know from all facts and circumstances known to you at the time - a knowledge test applied to what you knew, not a presumption applied to what you should have inspected. SECOND, THERE IS A CEILING. Section 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence: 'If there exists a minimum housing code applicable to the premises, the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a) of this section' - substantial compliance with that code after notice. And section 76-1410(3) keeps the term narrow: 'Minimum housing code shall be limited to those laws, resolutions, or ordinances or regulations, or portions thereof, dealing specifically with health and minimum standards of fitness for habitation,' which is narrower than the same subsection's definition of 'building and housing codes.' So in a municipality with a minimum housing code, the measure of your duty is that code's health-and-fitness portions, not an open-ended habitability standard that a presumption could be hung on. THIRD, THE ACT RESERVES TORT LAW RATHER THAN DISPLACING IT. The last sentence of section 76-1419(1) says 'The obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state.' A tenant injured by a defect still has whatever negligence claim Nebraska common law gives, and that claim is governed by common-law proof rules, not by a statutory presumption. Do not over-read the absence, though. Nebraska DOES have one evidentiary rule that runs against a landlord, and it is not a habitability rule: section 76-1416(4) provides that 'a tenant shall not be liable for damages directly related to the tenant's removal from the premises by order of any governmental entity as a result of the premises not being fit for habitation due to the negligence or neglect of the landlord.' That is a liability bar triggered by a governmental removal order plus landlord negligence - closer to a condemnation rule than a presumption, and it is the one place in the Act where a government finding about habitability has an automatic consequence. And section 76-1439 prohibits retaliation after a code complaint or union membership without creating any presumption that an adverse act following a complaint was retaliatory, which many URLTA states do create - so the tenant carries that burden too. Practical course: keep a dated written record of every repair request and every response, because in a state with no presumption the contemporaneous file usually decides the case, and the notice date is the date your duty began.

title: Nebraska Does Not Make You Put a Habitability Promise in the Lease - and Putting One In Can Enlarge Your Duty
bodyText: Maryland requires a residential lease to state that the landlord will deliver the premises in a condition fit for human habitation, with that language in the document itself. Nebraska requires nothing of the kind. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has exactly one thing it insists appear in writing at or before the commencement of the tenancy, and it is not about condition: section 76-1417(1) requires the landlord to disclose in writing the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or a person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving notices and demands. Everything else about lease content is permissive. Section 76-1414(1) reads: 'The landlord and tenant may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law including rent, term of the agreement, and other provisions governing the rights and obligations of the parties.' There is no mandated habitability recital, no mandated condition statement, and no statutory form of lease at all. Your duties under section 76-1419 attach by operation of the statute whether or not the lease mentions them, so saying nothing costs you nothing. Here is the part that is worth real money, and it points the opposite way from what landlords expect. SAYING MORE THAN THE STATUTE SAYS CAN ENLARGE YOUR DUTY. Section 76-1419(1)(d) requires you to 'Maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her.' The phrase 'or required to be supplied' is the hook: a promise in your lease to supply something is what makes it a thing you are required to supply, and the statutory maintenance duty then attaches to it. Promise central air, a dishwasher, a garage door opener or a washer and dryer, and you have bound yourself to maintain each of them in good and safe working order for the life of the tenancy. The statute would not have reached an appliance you simply left in the unit without promising it. So the drafting rule in Nebraska is the reverse of the Maryland rule: describe what you are actually supplying, in specific terms, and do not add a general flourish about delivering the premises fit, habitable, in excellent condition or in good repair. A general condition warranty adds nothing the statute does not already give the tenant and hands them a contract claim measured by your words rather than by section 76-1419's words - and section 76-1425(1) treats 'material noncompliance by the landlord WITH THE RENTAL AGREEMENT' as its own termination trigger, separate from statutory habitability. Two further points. There is no required typeface, point size or placement for anything in a Nebraska residential lease, and no statutory acknowledgment-of-receipt requirement for a condition statement. And Nebraska does have a statutory move-in condition mechanism in neither direction - it imposes no move-in inventory or checklist duty on you, and gives you no statutory presumption from one, so if you want a documented starting condition you create it by agreement and photographs, not by statute. Nothing stops you from including a condition statement if a lender, insurer or management agreement asks for one; just scope it to facts you can verify on the day of delivery and avoid open-ended promises about the future.

title: You Can Move Who Does the Work. You Cannot Waive the Standard - and Here Is the Sentence That Draws the Line
bodyText: There is a real difference between an agreement that reassigns WHO performs a habitability duty and an agreement that removes the duty, and Nebraska permits the first in narrow circumstances while flatly refusing the second. Get the two confused and you will write a clause that is not merely unenforceable but exposes you to damages and fees. THE BAR. Section 76-1415(1)(a): 'No rental agreement may provide that the tenant ... Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.' Note the statute's own wording - 'waive OR TO forego' - and note that there is no exception, no qualifier and no good-consideration escape in that subdivision. The habitability duties in section 76-1419 and the tenant remedies in sections 76-1425 and 76-1427 are rights and remedies under the Act, so a clause by which the tenant accepts the unit 'as is,' disclaims the landlord's repair duty, waives any habitability claim, or agrees that the unit is fit regardless of condition, is caught. Section 76-1415(2) then does two things: the provision is simply unenforceable, and 'If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees.' A savings sentence does not rescue it; the prohibited term is still in the agreement, which is what subsection (2) measures. THE ONE PERMITTED MOVE, AND THE SENTENCES THAT CARRY THE QUALIFIER.
