Section 76-1419(2) lets the landlord and tenant of a single-family residence agree that the tenant performs the subdivision (1)(e) waste duty and the subdivision (1)(f) water, hot-water and heat duty, plus specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling - 'BUT ONLY IF the transaction is in writing, for good consideration, entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord.' Section 76-1419(3), for every dwelling unit that is not a single-family residence, reaches only 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling' and only if '(a) The agreement of the parties is entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord and is set forth in a SEPARATE WRITING SIGNED BY THE PARTIES and supported by adequate consideration; and (b) The agreement does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises.' Read what those permissions actually do. They allocate PERFORMANCE. Neither says the standard drops, neither says the premises may be less than fit, and neither relieves you if the tenant does not do what they agreed to do - the tenant's failure gives you a contract claim against the tenant, not a defence against a habitability claim by anyone else in the building, which is exactly what subsection (3)(b) is there to prevent. SO WHAT STAYS NON-WAIVABLE: all of it. The standard itself in every case; and in any unit that is not a single-family residence, even the question of who performs, as to the (1)(e) waste duty and the (1)(f) water, hot-water and heat duty, because subsection (3) never names them. NO RENT-REDUCTION-FOR-CONDITIONS DEAL. Maine lets a tenant accept specified substandard conditions in exchange for a stated rent reduction, with any heat-level agreement in a separate document. Nebraska has no counterpart. A clause reciting that the tenant accepts a known defect because the rent is below market is a section 76-1415(1)(a) waiver however it is priced, and the discount is not consideration that buys it, because subsection (1)(a) does not trade. WHAT YOU CAN DO INSTEAD, AND IT IS NOT NOTHING - THE ACT SAYS SO IN A SECTION ALMOST NOBODY READS. Section 76-1406 is one sentence long: 'A claim or right arising under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or on a rental agreement may be settled by agreement.' So the Act expressly authorises settlement. Put that next to section 76-1415(1)(a) and the line is clean: a RENTAL AGREEMENT may not provide that the tenant waives rights or remedies, but a claim that has arisen may be settled by agreement. The difference is the instrument and the timing, not the subject matter. Section 76-1410(14) defines 'rental agreement' as the agreements and valid rules 'embodying the terms and conditions concerning the use and occupancy of a dwelling unit and premises' - a release of an accrued repair claim is not a term concerning use and occupancy. And the Act plainly contemplates settlements as a separate thing: section 76-1412(2) directs the court, when unconscionability is raised, to allow evidence 'as to the setting, purpose, and effect of the rental agreement OR SETTLEMENT.' The Legislature authorises a post-event waiver expressly where it wants one, too: section 76-886(f), in the condominium-conversion statute, says 'Any tenant may waive any provision of this section by a written instrument executed after the date of notice.' Cautious course, and the one to follow: never put a habitability waiver in a lease, a lease addendum, a renewal or a house rule; if a dispute has already arisen, settle it under section 76-1406 in a stand-alone release signed after the fact, for real and separately stated consideration, describing the specific claim being released and nothing forward-looking. Keep it genuinely backward-looking, because a 'settlement' that releases claims the tenant has not yet got is the section 76-1415(1)(a) waiver wearing a different hat. And expect the court to test whatever you sign: section 76-1412 reaches a settlement by its own words, and section 76-1411 imposes 'an obligation of good faith' on every duty under the Act and on 'every act which must be performed as a condition precedent to the exercise of a right or remedy.'

title: No Contamination Disclosure Duty in a Nebraska Lease - But a Recorded Environmental Covenant Reaches Your Tenant Anyway
bodyText: Nebraska imposes no duty on a residential landlord to disclose contamination, a cleanup history, or a remediation order to a tenant or a prospective tenant. There is no brownfield-status recital required in an instrument conveying an interest in the property, of the kind Mississippi requires, and no cleanup regulation in the statutes that orders recorded use limitations to be copied into a residential lease. The word 'brownfield' does not appear at all in the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy. What Nebraska does have is the Uniform Environmental Covenants Act, sections 76-2601 to 76-2613, and it matters to a landlord in three ways that have nothing to do with a disclosure form. ONE: THE COVENANT BINDS THE TENANT'S USE WHETHER OR NOT THE LEASE MENTIONS IT. Section 76-2602(4) defines an environmental covenant as 'a servitude arising under an environmental response project that imposes activity and use limitations,' and section 76-2602(1) defines those limitations as 'restrictions or obligations created under the act with respect to real property.' Section 76-2605(a) says a covenant that complies with the Act 'runs with the land,' and section 76-2605(b) makes it valid and enforceable even though it is not appurtenant, imposes an affirmative obligation on a person having an interest in the real property, does not touch or concern the land, or involves no privity of estate or contract. Section 76-2608(a) requires it to be recorded in every county where any part of the property lies, and section 76-2608(b) subjects it to Nebraska's ordinary recording and priority law. So if the covenant was recorded before your lease, the tenancy takes subject to it, and section 76-2606 confirms the direction of travel: the Act 'does not authorize a use of real property that is otherwise prohibited by zoning' and a covenant 'may prohibit or restrict uses of real property which are authorized by zoning or by law other than the act.' A covenant can forbid what zoning allows - a vegetable garden over a capped area, a basement bedroom, irrigation from an on-site well - and the tenant will not know unless you tell them. TWO: THERE IS A DELIVERY REQUIREMENT, AND YOUR TENANT IS ON ITS LIST, BUT IT IS NOT YOUR LEASE DUTY. Section 76-2607(a) provides that 'A copy of an environmental covenant shall be provided by the persons and in the manner required by the agency to ... (3) Each person in possession of the real property subject to the covenant,' along with signatories, holders of recorded interests and the local government. A tenant in possession is such a person. But read the whole subsection: the duty runs to 'the persons and in the manner required by the agency' - the agency, which section 76-2602(2) identifies as the Department of Water, Energy, and Environment or the federal or state agency that approves the response project, decides who delivers it and how. It is not a landlord-to-tenant disclosure rule, it carries no timing tied to the lease, and section 76-2607(b) adds that 'The validity of a covenant is not affected by failure to provide a copy.' Do not treat the delivery requirement as your safe harbour or as your obligation; find out from the covenant and the agency which it is. THREE: A PRIOR LEASE IS NOT SWEPT IN. Section 76-2603(d)(1) is the rule landlords miss: 'A prior interest is not affected by an environmental covenant unless the person that owns the interest subordinates that interest to the covenant,' and (d)(2) says the Act 'does not require a person that owns a prior interest to subordinate that interest.' A leasehold existing when the covenant is created is a prior interest. So a sitting tenant is not bound by a covenant recorded during their tenancy unless they subordinate, and section 76-2603(d)(3) says a subordination agreement 'may be contained in an environmental covenant ... or in a separate record.' If the agency wants your sitting tenants bound, that is a signature you have to go and get, and section 76-2604(c) lets the agency condition its approval on exactly that. Who can sue you if the covenant is breached is a short list and you are on it twice over. Section 76-2611(a) allows a civil action for injunctive or other equitable relief by a party to the covenant, the agency, any person the covenant expressly empowers, 'A person whose interest in the real property or whose collateral or liability may be affected by the alleged violation,' and the local government. Section 76-2611(c) protects a person from remediation liability 'solely because it has the right to enforce an environmental covenant,' and section 76-2611(d) preserves every other damages right anyone has. PRACTICAL COURSE. Nebraska does not offer you a statutory disclosure clause here, and the library does not carry one for this state, but nothing stops you from writing your own, and on a covenanted property you should. Pull the recorded covenant from the register of deeds in every county the property touches - section 76-2608(d) also requires the department to publish a list of the documents provided to it - attach it to the lease as an exhibit, restate the specific activity and use limitations as tenant obligations in plain words, require the tenant to permit the access the covenant grants, because section 76-2604(b)(3) allows a covenant to carry 'Rights of access to the property granted in connection with implementation or enforcement,' and pass through any notice-on-transfer or periodic-reporting requirement the covenant contains under section 76-2604(b)(1) and (b)(2). None of that is mandated; all of it is cheaper than discovering mid-tenancy that the obligation is yours and the conduct is the tenant's. Separately, and do not confuse the two regimes: the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule applies to pre-1978 target housing regardless of any of this, and Nebraska's own Seller Property Condition Disclosure Statement under section 76-2,120 is purchaser-side - it reaches a lease with an option to purchase, not an ordinary tenancy.

title: No Duty to Hand the Tenant Health-District Rules - but Your Local Housing Code Still Sets Your Ceiling
bodyText: Nevada requires a landlord, on request, to give the tenant a copy of the health district's rental regulations and to refer the tenant to the district. Nebraska has nothing like it. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act contains one mandatory lease-time written disclosure and it is about people, not rules: section 76-1417(1) requires the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or a person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving notices and demands. There is no duty to furnish a health code, a housing code, an inspection report, a district's regulations, or a tenant-rights pamphlet, and no tenant-referral duty. Nebraska has no statewide landlord registration or rental licensing scheme either. What local public health rules do in Nebraska is set the MEASURE of your repair duty, not the content of your lease. Section 76-1419(1)(a) requires you to 'Substantially comply, after written or actual notice, with the requirements of the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety,' and the closing sentence of section 76-1419(1) then makes that the outer limit: 'If there exists a minimum housing code applicable to the premises, the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a) of this section.' Section 76-1410(3) keeps the term tight: 'Minimum housing code shall be limited to those laws, resolutions, or ordinances or regulations, or portions thereof, dealing specifically with health and minimum standards of fitness for habitation,' which is narrower than the same subsection's broader definition of 'building and housing codes.' Two practical consequences. FIRST, FIND OUT WHETHER YOUR CITY OR COUNTY HAS A MINIMUM HOUSING CODE, because the answer changes the shape of your exposure rather than merely adding to it. Where one applies, you are measured by substantial compliance with its health-and-fitness portions after notice, and the open-ended 'fit and habitable' language in section 76-1419(1)(b) does not stack on top of that ceiling. Where none applies, the open-ended standard is what you are measured by. Either way the duty runs from NOTICE - both (1)(a) and (1)(b) say 'after written or actual notice' - so your repair log is the document that decides most disputes. SECOND, DO NOT ADOPT THE CODE AS A HOUSE RULE WITHOUT THINKING. If you want tenants bound to specific health or sanitation requirements, section 76-1422 lets you adopt rules, but it will enforce them only if each of six conditions is met: the rule promotes the appearance, convenience, safety or welfare of tenants, preserves your property from abusive use, or fairly distributes services; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies to all tenants fairly; it is explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do; it is 'not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord'; and 'The tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement.' That fifth condition is the trap here: a rule that recites the health code in order to move a code obligation of yours onto the tenant is a rule adopted to evade your obligations and is unenforceable. A rule adopted later binds the tenant only on reasonable notice of its adoption and only if it 'does not work a substantial modification of his bargain.' Section 76-1421(1) already obliges the tenant to 'Comply with all obligations primarily imposed upon tenants by applicable minimum standards of building and housing codes materially affecting health or safety' - note 'primarily imposed upon tenants,' which is the statute itself drawing the line you cannot redraw by rule. Where you do want to give the tenant local rules, there is no harm in it and some benefit: delivering them at signing creates the section 76-1422(6) notice you need for any house rule built on them, and gives you a dated receipt. Just describe them as information, not as a transfer of your duty.

title: "Reasonable Heat at All Times" With No Thermostat Number - and the Only Place in the Act Where the Tenant Can Spend Your Rent
bodyText: Nebraska's heat duty is short, unqualified by any number, and backed by the single most dangerous tenant remedy in the Act. Section 76-1419(1)(f) requires the landlord to 'Supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat except where the building that includes the dwelling unit is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant and supplied by a direct public utility connection.' Three things follow. 'AT ALL TIMES,' NOT A HEATING SEASON. Nebraska sets no heating season, no start or end date and no outdoor-temperature trigger. States that run heat duties from October to May give you a defence in September; Nebraska does not. 'REASONABLE HEAT' IS NOT A NUMBER. There is no statutory temperature anywhere in the Act - no minimum degrees, no daytime and nighttime split, no measurement point in the room. Whether heat was reasonable is a fact question, and in a municipality with a minimum housing code the practical answer usually comes from that code, because section 76-1419(1)(a) requires substantial compliance with it after notice and the closing sentence of section 76-1419(1) makes that code 'the landlord's maximum duty under this section.' Section 76-1410(3) limits 'minimum housing code' to provisions 'dealing specifically with health and minimum standards of fitness for habitation,' so look for the health-and-habitability portions of the local code, not the building code generally. THE EXCEPTION IS NARROW AND BOTH HALVES OF THE SECOND LIMB MATTER. You are excused only where the building 'is not required by law to be equipped' for heat - a code question, not a question of what is convenient - or where the unit is 'so constructed' that heat or hot water comes from an installation within the tenant's EXCLUSIVE control AND supplied by a DIRECT PUBLIC UTILITY CONNECTION. A tenant-adjustable thermostat on your boiler is not exclusive control. A tenant-controlled furnace fed from your master gas account is not a direct public utility connection. Both halves, or you still owe the heat. NOW THE REMEDY, BECAUSE IT IS WHY THIS TOPIC IS WORTH MONEY. Section 76-1427(1) applies when, contrary to the rental agreement or section 76-1419, 'the landlord deliberately or negligently fails to supply running water, hot water, or heat, or essential services.' On written notice specifying the breach, the tenant may '(a) Procure reasonable amounts of hot water, running water, heat and essential services during the period of the landlord's noncompliance and DEDUCT THEIR ACTUAL AND REASONABLE COST FROM THE RENT; (b) Recover damages based upon the diminution in the fair rental value of the dwelling unit; or (c) Procure reasonable substitute housing during the period of the landlord's noncompliance, in which case THE TENANT IS EXCUSED FROM PAYING RENT for the period of the landlord's noncompliance.' And the closing paragraph: in addition to (a) and (c), 'if the failure to supply is deliberate, the tenant may recover the actual and reasonable cost or fair and reasonable value of the substitute housing not in excess of an amount equal to the periodic rent, and in any case under this subsection reasonable attorney's fees.' So a deliberate heat failure can cost you the rent for the period, the tenant's hotel bill up to one month's rent, and their lawyer. Nebraska has no general repair-and-deduct statute; section 76-1427(1)(a) is the ONLY provision in the Act that lets a tenant spend your rent on a repair, and heat is squarely inside it. Three limits that are yours to use. Section 76-1427(3): 'The rights under this section do not arise until the tenant has given written notice to the landlord or if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of his family, or other person on the premises with his consent. This section is not intended to cover circumstances beyond the landlord's control.' Written notice is a precondition, tenant-caused failures are excluded, and a utility-wide outage or a blizzard that stops a parts delivery is outside the section. Section 76-1427(2): 'If the tenant proceeds under this section, he may not proceed under section 76-1425 as to that breach' - an election of remedies, so the tenant cannot deduct for heat under section 76-1427 and also terminate and sue for the same breach under section 76-1425. And section 76-1425(2) independently bars consequential damages where your noncompliance 'is caused by conditions or circumstances beyond his or her control,' while preserving the section 76-1427 remedies. CAN YOU PUT THE HEAT DUTY ON THE TENANT? Only on one path, and most buildings are not on it. Section 76-1419(2) allows an agreement that the tenant performs the subdivision (1)(e) and (1)(f) duties - which is where heat lives - but only for a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE, only in writing, for good consideration, in good faith and not to evade your obligations. Section 76-1419(3), which covers everything else, reaches only 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling' and never mentions (1)(f), so in a duplex or an apartment building the heat duty cannot be moved at all. And section 76-1410(16) requires a single-family residence to have 'direct access to a street or thoroughfare' and to share 'neither heating facilities, hot water equipment, nor any other essential facility or service with any other dwelling unit' - the shared furnace that makes delegation attractive is the fact that disqualifies it. WHAT TO PUT IN THE LEASE. Say which heating equipment serves the unit, say who holds the utility account for it and in whose name, and if you are relying on the (1)(f) exception, say so specifically and keep the tenant's own account documentation, because the exception turns on that fact. Do not write a clause disclaiming the heat duty or capping your liability for heat failures - section 76-1415(1)(a) voids a term by which the tenant waives rights or remedies under the Act, and section 76-1415(2) adds actual damages and attorney's fees if you deliberately used a term you knew was prohibited. Contrast worth knowing if you also own a mobile home park: the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act imposes no heat duty at all. Section 76-1492(1) requires the park landlord to keep the park fit and habitable, keep common areas clean and safe, maintain facilities supplied or required to be supplied, provide for waste removal, and 'Furnish outlets for provided utilities' - outlets, not heat. Do not carry the section 76-1419(1)(f) duty across to park spaces, or the park remedies back to an apartment.

title: A Holding Deposit Is Outside the Deposit Statute Until the Lease Exists - Then "However Denominated" Swallows It
bodyText: Nebraska has no holding-deposit statute. The words 'holding deposit,' 'earnest money,' 'application deposit' and 'reservation fee' appear nowhere in the landlord-tenant act or anywhere else in the code's property, contract and consumer chapters. What governs instead is a two-stage analysis, and the stage the money is in when you take it decides everything. BEFORE A RENTAL AGREEMENT EXISTS, THE ACT DOES NOT REACH THE MONEY. Section 76-1416(1) is written as a restriction on a 'landlord' taking money from a 'tenant,' and both terms are defined by relationship, not by role: section 76-1410(17) defines 'tenant' as 'a person entitled under a rental agreement to occupy a dwelling unit to the exclusion of others,' and section 76-1410(14) defines 'rental agreement' as 'all agreements, written or oral, between a landlord and tenant ... embodying the terms and conditions concerning the use and occupancy of a dwelling unit and premises.' An applicant who has handed you $300 to take the unit off the market, with nothing agreed about use and occupancy, is not yet a tenant. So the Act does not tell you how much you may take, how you must hold it, when you must return it, or what itemisation you owe, and there is no statutory penalty. Section 76-1403 names what fills the gap: 'Unless displaced by the provisions of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the principles of law and equity, including the law relating to capacity to contract, mutuality of obligations, principal and agent, real property, public health, safety and fire prevention, estoppel, fraud, misrepresentation, duress, coercion, mistake, bankruptcy, or other validating or invalidating cause, supplement the act's provisions.' In plain terms: ordinary contract law, plus fraud and misrepresentation. Whether you may keep the money if the applicant walks away turns on what you wrote on the receipt, and on whether the retained amount is a genuine pre-estimate of your loss rather than a penalty. WATCH THE ORAL-AGREEMENT TRAP, BECAUSE IT CLOSES FAST. 'Rental agreement' expressly includes ORAL agreements. If you and the applicant have settled the unit, the rent and the start date, a rental agreement may already exist even though nobody has signed anything, and at that moment the money becomes security under section 76-1416 and you become a landlord subject to every duty in the Act. Taking a deposit at the end of a showing where you have agreed terms is close to the line. ONCE THE AGREEMENT EXISTS, 'HOWEVER DENOMINATED' DOES THE WORK. Section 76-1416(1): 'A landlord may not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent, except that a pet deposit not in excess of one-fourth of one month's periodic rent may be demanded or received when appropriate.' That phrase is deliberately indifferent to labels. Money you took as a holding deposit and then credit to the tenant's account, a move-in fee, a reservation fee, a key deposit, a cleaning deposit, a redecorating deposit - if it functions as security, it counts against the one-month ceiling, and the ceiling is on what you may 'demand or receive,' not on what you keep. Add a nonrefundable-sounding name to it and you have not changed the arithmetic. Once it is security, section 76-1416(2) runs a fourteen-day clock from 'the date of termination of the tenancy' for the balance plus a written itemisation - from termination, not from the tenant's demand - and section 76-1416(3) exposes you to court costs and reasonable attorney's fees, plus liquidated damages of one month's periodic rent or twice the deposit, whichever is less, where the failure is 'willful and not in good faith.' AN APPLICATION FEE IS A DIFFERENT ANIMAL, AND NEBRASKA DOES NOT CAP IT. A true fee charged to cover the cost of screening, which is earned when the screening is done and is never credited to rent or returned, is not 'security' and is not held for anything - it is payment for a service. Nebraska regulates no residential application fee: in the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy, the fourteen sections that use the phrase 'application fee' are all occupational-licensing or court-procedure fees, none of them a rental application. The distinction that matters is function, not wording: money held against future performance is security; money consumed in performing a service is a fee. Do not blur them in one receipt. WHAT TO DO. Decide in advance which of the two things you are taking, and write it on a signed receipt before the money changes hands. For a holding deposit, say in writing how long the unit is held, exactly what happens to the money if the applicant signs (credited to rent or to the security deposit, naming which), what happens if the applicant does not sign, what happens if you decline the application after screening - that money should come back, because you are the one who ended it - and whether any part is retained and on what basis. Keep the retained figure tied to a real cost you can show. For an application fee, state what it pays for, that it is earned on completion of the screening and that it is not credited to rent. Hold the two sums separately, and never let the combination of holding deposit plus first month's security exceed one month's periodic rent once the lease is signed, because the cap is measured on what you received. One more thing a Nebraska landlord should not get wrong in this sequence. If a rental agreement HAS been formed and you then fail to deliver possession - you rented it to someone else, or the previous tenant has not gone - section 76-1426 applies: rent abates until possession is delivered, the tenant may terminate on five days' written notice and recover all prepaid rent and security, or demand performance and sue for damages; and 'If a person's failure to deliver possession is willful and not in good faith, an aggrieved person may recover from that person an amount not more than three months' periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees.' That is the exposure behind double-booking a unit on which you have taken a deposit, and returning the money does not answer it.

title: No Home-Business Right in Nebraska - the Statutory Default Is Already Yours, and the Words That Keep It Are "Unless Otherwise Agreed"
bodyText: West Virginia protects a home-based business as a permitted use of a dwelling by statute. Nebraska has no such statute, and the phrases 'home-based business,' 'home occupation' and 'family child care home' appear nowhere in the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy. Nebraska also gives no renter a statutory right to run child care, a salon, a repair shop or any other trade out of a rented unit, and no statute protects such a use against either an association or a landlord. What Nebraska gives you instead is a default rule that already says no, and it is worth reading for its first two words. Section 76-1424: 'UNLESS OTHERWISE AGREED, the tenant shall occupy his dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit. The rental agreement may require that the tenant notify the landlord of any anticipated extended absence from the premises in excess of seven days no later than the first day of the extended absence.' Three consequences. ONE: residential-use-only is the statutory baseline whether or not you write it into the lease. You do not need a clause to get it, and your standard residential-use clause is a restatement of the default rather than the source of it. TWO: 'unless otherwise agreed' means the permission runs the other way - the lease can allow a business use, and if it does, the agreement displaces the statutory default to the extent of what you agreed. So the risk in this area is not that a statute overrides your restriction; it is that your own lease, an email, or a course of dealing in which you knowingly accepted a business operating in the unit amounts to an agreement otherwise. THREE: there is no middle category. The statute's standard is occupancy 'only as a dwelling unit,' with no statutory carve-out for an incidental, de minimis or wholly remote business. A tenant working from a laptop is occupying the unit as a dwelling; a tenant seeing six clients a day in the living room is not, and the line between them is a fact question you will be arguing without a statutory definition to point at. IF YOU WANT TO ALLOW IT, SAY WHAT YOU ARE ALLOWING. Nebraska does not supply the terms, so they are entirely yours: name the specific activity, and say that anything else remains prohibited; require any licence or permit the activity needs and proof of it, bearing in mind that Nebraska's child-care and other licensing statutes sit in chapter 71 and zoning sits with the municipality, so this is not a question the landlord-tenant act answers; cap client or customer visits and deliveries, and address parking, because section 76-1421(7) obliges the tenant to conduct themselves and require their guests to conduct themselves 'in a manner that will not disturb his neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises' and a business is the fastest way to a neighbour complaint; require the tenant's own liability insurance for the activity and a statement from your own insurer, since a commercial use in a residential unit is a classic coverage exclusion; and require compliance with any applicable condominium or association documents, which section 76-1421(8) already obliges the tenant to abide by - 'all bylaws, covenants, rules or regulations of any applicable condominium regime, cooperative housing agreement, or neighborhood association not inconsistent with landlord's rights or duties' - and which section 18-1758(7) confirms municipal law does not override: that subsection provides that the short-term-rental preemption 'shall not be construed to affect regulations of a private entity, including a homeowners association organized under the Condominium Property Act or the Nebraska Condominium Act.' TWO TRAPS IN THE OTHER DIRECTION. First, do not write the permission as a blanket consent to 'any lawful business,' because you will have agreed otherwise under section 76-1424 for uses you have never seen. Second, a business-use restriction imposed later as a house rule is not automatically enforceable: section 76-1422 enforces a rule only if, among six conditions, 'The tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement,' and a rule adopted afterwards binds only on reasonable notice of its adoption and only if it 'does not work a substantial modification of his bargain.' Restricting a use the tenant was already making may be exactly such a modification. Put the restriction in the lease at signing instead. Worth knowing for contrast, because it is the one place Nebraska took the opposite approach to a use of a dwelling: short-term rentals. Section 18-1758(2) provides that 'A municipality shall not adopt or enforce an ordinance or other regulation that expressly or effectively prohibits the use of a property as a short-term rental,' with section 18-1758(3) allowing health-and-safety regulation only. So the Legislature does protect one non-traditional use of a dwelling by statute - against cities, not against landlords, and only that one. Nothing in it touches your lease or creates any home-business right.

title: Nebraska Gives You No Exemption-Waiver Words - and the One Waiver It Does Authorise Is for Farm Mortgages, Not Leases
bodyText: Several states hand a creditor statutory language for waiving a debtor's homestead or personal-property exemption, and some let a lease carry it. Virginia, Alabama, Georgia and Kansas each have a version. Nebraska has none, and the shape of its silence tells you it is deliberate rather than accidental. WHAT THE EXEMPTIONS ARE. Section 40-101 exempts from judgment liens and from execution or forced sale 'a homestead not exceeding one hundred twenty thousand dollars in value consisting of the dwelling house in which the claimant resides, its appurtenances, and the land on which the same is situated,' up to 160 acres outside an incorporated city or village, or at the claimant's option two contiguous lots inside one. Section 25-1552(1) exempts $5,000 in personal property other than wages, and section 25-1556(1) adds specific items without regard to that sum: '(a) The immediate personal possessions of the debtor and his or her family; (b) all necessary wearing apparel,' the debtor's interest up to $3,000 'in household furnishings, household goods, household computers, household appliances, books, or musical instruments,' up to $5,000 in trade implements and tools other than a motor vehicle, up to $5,000 in a motor vehicle, and 'any professionally prescribed health aids.' Both dollar figures are indexed: section 25-1552(2) and section 25-1556(2) require the Department of Revenue to adjust them every fifth year from 2023 for the five-year change in the CPI-U, so check the current figures rather than quoting these. WHY A LEASE WAIVER IS NOT AVAILABLE. Nebraska enacted a waiver mechanism for exactly one situation, and it is not a lease. Section 76-1904, which applies to a mortgage or trust deed 'upon agricultural land,' lets the mortgagor designate a homestead in the instrument, or disclaim, or waive the right to designate - and it then imposes formalities that show how seriously the Legislature treats the waiver. The disclaimer under section 76-1904(3)(a) must state that no part of the homestead is or will be on the described land and that the mortgagor understands the consequence; the waiver under section 76-1904(3)(b) must contain 'a statement that the mortgagor or trustor understands that he or she has the right to make a designation of homestead' and that executing the acknowledgment waives it; each must be 'set forth as a preface to the mortgage or trust deed' and filed for record; and each subdivision ends with the same sanction - 'Failure by the mortgagee or trustee to file a written acknowledgment as provided in this subdivision shall nullify any purported waiver.' In the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy, that is the only exemption-waiver machinery; it is confined to agricultural mortgages, and nothing like it exists for a residential lease. The code has no waiver-of-exemption language on point at all. So a clause in your lease reciting that the tenant waives the homestead exemption or the personal-property exemptions has no statutory authority behind it, no prescribed words to copy, and no recording route - and you should not use one. WHERE THE EXEMPTION ACTUALLY BITES YOU, WHICH IS AFTER JUDGMENT. These are execution exemptions, not defences to the claim. You can sue for unpaid rent and damages and get a judgment. What the exemptions do is take property out of reach when you try to collect on it. And here the lists matter, because both are closed. Section 40-103 makes the homestead 'subject to execution or forced sale in satisfaction of judgments obtained (1) on debts secured by mechanics', laborers', or vendors' liens upon the premises and (2) on debts secured by mortgages or trust deeds upon the premises executed and acknowledged by a claimant.' A money judgment for rent is neither. Section 25-1557 is the parallel list for chapter 25: nothing in the chapter exempts property 'from execution or attachment for unpaid wages; for money due and owing by an attorney at law ...; or for enforcement of an award of or judgment for child support, alimony, or maintenance or a judgment for property division awarded to a former spouse.' Rent is not on that list either. So a former tenant's homestead and their exempt household goods are generally beyond your judgment, and no lease language changes it. TWO MORE THINGS A NEBRASKA LANDLORD SHOULD NOT GET WRONG. First, do not try to reach the same property by taking security instead. Section 76-1434 is two sentences: '(1) A lien or security interest on behalf of the landlord in the tenant's household goods is not enforceable. (2) Distraint for rent is abolished.' A lease clause granting you a lien on the tenant's furniture is unenforceable on its face, and distraint - seizing goods for rent without process - is simply gone. Second, if the property you are renting out is itself your homestead or your spouse's, section 40-104 is the provision to worry about, and it runs against you rather than the tenant: 'the homestead of a married person cannot be conveyed or encumbered unless the instrument by which it is conveyed or encumbered is executed and acknowledged by both spouses.' Whether a lease is an 'encumbrance' within that sentence is not settled by the text and should be treated as an open question; the cautious course for a landlord letting a room, a basement unit or a house that is or may be a homestead is to have both spouses sign and acknowledge the lease. One point of clean law worth knowing: Nebraska's homestead exemption from execution is purely STATUTORY. The word 'homestead' appears in the Nebraska Constitution only in article VIII, section 2's property-tax provisions, which permit the Legislature to exempt part of the value of a residence occupied as a homestead FROM TAXATION. There is no constitutional homestead-exemption clause to make these rights non-waivable as a matter of constitutional law, so the reason a lease waiver fails here is the absence of any authorising statute and the presence of section 76-1904's contrary example, not a constitutional bar.

title: No Infirmity or Senior Early-Out in Nebraska - the Lease Runs, and Your Mitigation Duty Is What Actually Limits the Bill
bodyText: Several states let an older or infirm tenant end a lease early - on a doctor's certificate, on admission to a care facility, or on reaching an age with a notice period. Minnesota, Michigan, Nevada, New York, Tennessee and Kentucky all have a version. Nebraska has none. There is no age-based termination right, no medical-certificate route, no care-facility-admission route, and no disability-based termination right in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or anywhere else in the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy. The word 'infirmity' appears once in all of chapter 76 and it is in section 76-835.01, the Condominium Act's unconscionability section, which lists physical or mental infirmity as a factor a court may weigh in deciding whether a CONTRACT was unconscionable - a condominium purchase contract, not a lease, and a ground for refusing enforcement rather than a right to terminate. 'Nursing home,' 'assisted living' and 'long-term care' appear nowhere in chapter 76 at all. That Nebraska's silence is deliberate is easy to show, because the Legislature has written early-release rights into this very Act for other situations and recently. Section 76-1431.01 gives a tenant who is a victim of an act of domestic violence, or whose household member is, a release from the rental agreement on producing a protective order or a qualified third-party certification and a written notice naming an effective date 'at least fourteen days after the date the tenant provides the documentation and written notice and no more than thirty days after such date,' with the tenant remaining 'liable for rent for the month in which the tenant terminated the rental agreement.' Nebraska also has a servicemember early-termination statute outside the URLTA, which the library carries separately. Two targeted rights, drafted with notice periods and documentation requirements, and no third one for illness or age. SO WHERE DOES THAT LEAVE YOU WHEN IT HAPPENS? It happens often - a tenant has a stroke, a family member moves them into care, the family calls you. Nebraska's answer is contract, modified by three things that all cut the bill down. FIRST, YOU HAVE A DUTY TO MITIGATE, AND IT IS STATUTORY. Section 76-1405(1): 'The remedies provided by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act shall be so administered that the aggrieved party may recover appropriate damages. THE AGGRIEVED PARTY HAS A DUTY TO MITIGATE DAMAGES.' That sentence is unqualified and it is not one of the eleven chapter 76 sections that open 'unless otherwise agreed,' so your lease cannot contract out of it. Practically: when the unit is given up, re-let it. Rent you could reasonably have earned comes off what you can claim, and a claim for the whole remaining term with the unit sitting empty is not a claim Nebraska will give you in full. SECOND, A TERMINATION FEE IS LAWFUL ONLY IF IT IS NOT CHARGED ON A STATUTORY TERMINATION. An early-termination charge in the lease is a term 'not prohibited' and so permitted by section 76-1414(1) - but section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any provision by which the tenant 'Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under' the Act, so the fee must not be charged where the tenant is exercising a right the Act gives them. Since Nebraska gives no infirmity right, a negotiated early exit on grounds of health is a purely contractual exit and your fee can apply to it. Do not let the clause reach the domestic-violence release under section 76-1431.01 or a statutory termination for your own breach. THIRD, DEATH IS A DIFFERENT TOPIC AND NEBRASKA ADDRESSES ONLY THE PROPERTY. Section 76-1414(5) does not terminate a lease on the tenant's death. What it does is give the tenant the option, on your request, to name a person 'authorized by the tenant to enter the tenant's dwelling unit to retrieve and store the tenant's personal property if the tenant dies,' and then set a timetable: you must make a reasonable attempt to contact that person within ten days of the death; the authorized person has twenty days after contact to say they will claim the property and twenty days after that notification to remove it; you must grant reasonable access on presentation of valid government-issued identification; and if you let the authorized person take the property, you have 'no further liability to the tenant, the tenant's estate, or the tenant's heirs for lost, damaged, or stolen personal property.' If nobody is named, cannot be reached, or does not respond within twenty days, you may dispose of the property under the Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act, section 69-2301 et seq. Asking every tenant to name an authorized person at signing is free, and the liability release in that subsection is the reason to do it. THE PRACTICAL COURSE. Treat an infirmity exit as a negotiation, not a claim. Get the surrender in writing, dated, signed by the tenant or by an agent under a power of attorney or by a conservator, so that you are not arguing later about capacity - section 76-1403 brings in 'the law relating to capacity to contract' for exactly this situation. Then re-let promptly and bill the shortfall, which is what the mitigation duty leaves you. If you want to offer more than that, you may: nothing stops you from writing your own medical-hardship release into the lease, and some landlords do because it converts an ugly dispute into a known number. Keep it conditional on written notice, documentation you specify, a stated notice period and payment of rent through the effective date, and keep it out of any clause that could be read as reaching a statutory right.

title: No Duty to Tell a Tenant About an Open Code or Condemnation Order - Because Nebraska Puts It on the Building and in the Deed Records Instead
bodyText: Minnesota, Wisconsin, Rhode Island and New Hampshire each make a landlord tell a prospective tenant about outstanding inspection orders, code violations or a condemnation. Nebraska imposes no such duty on anyone. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's one mandatory lease-time written disclosure is section 76-1417(1), and it is about manager and owner identity for service of process and receiving notices - nothing about the condition of the building or about any order affecting it. There is no outstanding-order disclosure, no inspection-report delivery duty, no duty to report a pending abatement proceeding, and no penalty attached to silence. What Nebraska did instead is make the order PUBLIC rather than make the landlord speak, and the mechanism is worth knowing because it is both your exposure and your own due-diligence tool. Section 18-1722.01: 'Whenever the governing body of a municipality has decided by resolution or other determination that a property is unsafe or unfit for human occupancy because of one or more violations of its minimum standard housing ordinance or has decided by resolution or other determination that a building is unsafe because of one or more violations of its local building or construction code, IT SHALL BE THE DUTY OF SUCH MUNICIPALITY TO POST THE PROPERTY ACCORDINGLY AND TO FILE A COPY OF SUCH RESOLUTION OR OTHER DETERMINATION IN THE OFFICE OF THE REGISTER OF DEEDS OF THE COUNTY TO BE RECORDED. No fee shall be charged for such recording or for the release of such recording.' Two things follow. First, if you are buying rental property, the determination is recordable and should show in a title search, and the building itself should be posted - so a prospective landlord who does not look has nobody to blame. Second, it is the municipality's duty, not yours, which is why nothing in the statute creates a landlord disclosure obligation and why there is no sanction on a landlord for failing to mention it. The abatement machinery around it is section 18-1722: if the owner 'fails, neglects, or refuses to comply with notice by or on behalf of any city or village to repair, rehabilitate, or demolish and remove a building or structure which is an unsafe building or structure and a public nuisance,' the city may do the work and then either '(1) Levy the cost as a special assessment against the lot or real estate upon which the building or structure is located,' which 'shall be a lien on the real estate,' or '(2) Collect the cost from the owner ... and enforce the collection by civil action.' Section 18-1720(1) is the enabling power: cities and villages 'may by ordinance define, regulate, suppress, and prevent nuisances, declare what constitutes a nuisance, and abate and remove such nuisances,' within their corporate limits and their extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction. So the consequence of an open order is a lien or a judgment against you, not a disclosure penalty. NOW THE PART THAT SHOULD CHANGE YOUR BEHAVIOUR ANYWAY, BECAUSE SILENCE IS NOT SAFETY. An outstanding order is nearly always evidence of the breach your tenant will sue on. Section 76-1419(1)(a) requires you to 'Substantially comply, after written or actual notice, with the requirements of the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety,' and a resolution under section 18-1722.01 is by definition a determination of violations of the minimum standard housing ordinance - delivered to you, so the notice element is satisfied the moment it arrives. Section 76-1425(1) then lets the tenant terminate on written notice if 'a noncompliance with section 76-1419 materially affecting health and safety' is not remedied in fourteen days, with termination on a date not less than thirty days after receipt; section 76-1425(2) lets the tenant 'recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for ANY noncompliance,' with reasonable attorney's fees if your noncompliance is willful; and section 76-1425(4) requires you to return all prepaid rent and security recoverable under section 76-1416 if the agreement is terminated. Section 76-1416(4) adds a specific sting for the condemnation case: 'a tenant shall not be liable for damages directly related to the tenant's removal from the premises by order of any governmental entity as a result of the premises not being fit for habitation due to the negligence or neglect of the landlord.' If the city turns your tenant out, you cannot charge them for the consequences of the move. And do not expect a retaliation defence to shield you from the complaint that started it: section 76-1439(1)(a) bars retaliating by raising rent, cutting services, or bringing or threatening a possession action after 'The tenant has complained to a government agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a minimum building or housing code of a violation applicable to the premises materially affecting health and safety,' with the tenant entitled to the section 76-1430 remedies and a defence to possession. Section 76-1439(3) preserves your possession action in three situations - the violation was 'caused primarily by lack of reasonable care by the tenant or other person in his household or upon the premises with his consent,' the tenant is in default in rent, or compliance 'requires alteration, remodeling, or demolition which would effectively deprive the tenant of use of the dwelling unit' - and that third one is the realistic route when a condemnation makes the unit unusable. Note the closing sentence, though: 'The maintenance of the action does not release the landlord from liability under subsection (2) of section 76-1425.' PRACTICAL COURSE. Disclose it anyway, in writing, before signing. Nebraska does not make you, and the library carries no Nebraska disclosure clause on this ground because no statute supports one - but you may write your own, and a short recital naming the order, its date, what you are doing about it and by when converts a hidden defect into a documented and dated condition the tenant accepted knowingly. It will not waive their habitability rights, because section 76-1415(1)(a) voids a provision by which the tenant waives rights or remedies under the Act, so do not draft it as a waiver or an 'as is'; draft it as disclosure plus your repair commitment, and keep the commitment, since a promise in the lease becomes a thing 'required to be supplied' and a material noncompliance with the rental agreement in its own right under section 76-1425(1).

title: What Makes an Inspection Lawful in Nebraska - the Per-Unit Notice, the Two Escape Hatches, and Why Your Inspection Clause Is Not Consent
bodyText:
Nebraska attaches a money penalty to a defective inspection entry, and the penalty is not the interesting part - the library already states it. What decides whether you pay it is whether the notice you gave satisfied section 76-1423(3), and that is where multi-unit landlords running annual, seasonal or pre-sale inspections get caught.

START WITH THE CLOSED LIST, BECAUSE IT IS THE MOST MISREAD SENTENCE IN THE SECTION. Section 76-1423(4): 'The landlord has NO OTHER RIGHT OF ACCESS except by court order, as permitted by subsection (2) of section 76-1432, or if the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises.'

The two routes into an occupied unit are therefore (i) the tenant not unreasonably withholding consent under section 76-1423(1), after notice under section 76-1423(3), and (ii) emergency under section 76-1423(2). There is no third route, and the statute says so.

A clause in your lease granting you a right to inspect on your own terms does not create one: it may record the tenant's agreement about purposes and scheduling, but it cannot be the right of access, because subsection (4) says you have no other right. And it cannot be advance consent that dispenses with notice, because section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any provision by which the tenant 'Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under' the Act, and section 76-1415(2) adds actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees if you deliberately used a term you knew was prohibited. Treat your inspection clause as a scheduling and cooperation provision, not as a key.

NOW THE NOTICE ITSELF, WHICH HAS FOUR ELEMENTS AND ONE OF THEM IS A TRAP FOR BUILDINGS. Section 76-1423(3): 'The landlord shall not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant. Except in case of emergency or if it is impracticable to do so, the landlord shall: (a) Give the tenant at least TWENTY-FOUR HOURS' WRITTEN NOTICE of the landlord's intent to enter. SUCH NOTICE SHALL BE PROVIDED TO EACH INDIVIDUAL UNIT and include THE INTENDED PURPOSE FOR ENTRY and A REASONABLE PERIOD during which the landlord anticipates making entry; and (b) Enter only at reasonable times.'

So: at least twenty-four hours; in writing; to EACH INDIVIDUAL UNIT; stating the purpose; and stating a reasonable entry window.

The per-unit requirement is the one that fails in practice. A notice taped to the lobby door, a notice in the laundry room, a line in the monthly newsletter, a post in a tenant portal with no separate delivery, or one notice handed to a building manager for a twelve-unit inspection does not satisfy 'provided to each individual unit.' Neither does a notice saying only 'annual inspection, sometime next week' - 'next week' is not a reasonable period, and a purpose must be stated.

Note also what the subsection does NOT say: it sets a floor of twenty-four hours, not a ceiling, and it does not say the tenant must be home or must consent again on the day. Section 76-1423(1) obliges the tenant not to unreasonably withhold consent to entry 'in order to inspect the premises, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workmen, or contractors' - inspection is first on that list, so a tenant who stonewalls a properly noticed inspection is the one in breach, and section 76-1438(1) then lets you obtain injunctive relief to compel access or terminate the rental agreement, and recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees in either case.

ON ELECTRONIC DELIVERY: 'written' includes a notice delivered by electronic means, but only in accordance with section 76-1413 - section 76-1410(18) says so expressly - and section 76-1413(9) provides that 'A landlord shall not, as part of a rental agreement or as a condition of entering into or renewing a rental agreement, require a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means.' So emailing inspection notices works only for tenants who have given the section 76-1413(7) consent, and you cannot make that consent a condition of the lease. For everyone else, paper to the unit.

THE TWO ESCAPE HATCHES, AND HOW FAR THEY GO. The notice duty and the reasonable-times duty are both prefaced 'Except in case of emergency or IF IT IS IMPRACTICABLE TO DO SO.' The emergency hatch is separately confirmed by section 76-1423(2): 'The landlord may enter the dwelling unit without consent of the tenant in case of emergency.'

The impracticability hatch is narrower than it looks and is not a convenience clause - it excuses notice when giving notice cannot practically be done, not when it is awkward or when the contractor can only come tomorrow. Nebraska does not define it, so document the reason contemporaneously: what you learned, when, why twenty-four hours' written notice to the unit was not practicable, and what you did instead.

There is a third situation that is not an exception but an independent right: section 76-1432(2) - 'During any absence of the tenant in excess of seven days, the landlord may enter the dwelling unit at times reasonably necessary.' That is the cross-reference in section 76-1423(4). It requires an actual absence exceeding seven days, and the entry must be at times reasonably necessary. Do not stretch it: section 76-1432(3) sets abandonment at 'Total absence from the premises without notice to landlord for one full rental period or thirty days, whichever is less,' and Nebraska's courts have treated a self-help recovery during the first thirty days of an absence as depending on unequivocal proof of abandonment.

WHAT A DEFECTIVE INSPECTION ENTRY COSTS. Section 76-1438(2) gives the tenant an injunction to prevent recurrence OR termination of the rental agreement, and in either case 'actual damages NOT LESS THAN an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees.' That is a FLOOR, not a cap - it does not read 'whichever is less,' the way the security-deposit penalty in section 76-1416(3) does - so a single unlawful entry with no provable loss still costs a month's rent plus the tenant's lawyer, and the tenant can walk out of the lease on top of it.

The trigger is drafted three ways: 'an unlawful entry OR a lawful entry in an unreasonable manner OR... repeated demands for entry otherwise lawful but which have the effect of unreasonably harassing the tenant.' Entering without the section 76-1423(3) notice, outside emergency and impracticability, is an unlawful entry, because subsection (4) leaves you no other right of access. And the third limb means a landlord who keeps giving proper notice can still be liable - serving inspection notices on the same tenant week after week is actionable on its own terms.

PRACTICAL COURSE. Build one inspection-notice template that names the purpose and a window of a few hours on a stated date, print one per unit, deliver per unit, log the date and method, and keep the log. Give more than twenty-four hours as a matter of routine so that a delivery dispute does not put you under the floor. Schedule inspections at reasonable times and do not re-notice a reluctant tenant repeatedly - use section 76-1438(1) instead, which is the remedy the statute gives you for refused access.

title: Your Nebraska Eviction Has No Jury Anyway - and a Jury-Waiver Clause in the Lease Is Not One of the Three Ways Nebraska Lets a Jury Be Waived
bodyText: Before asking whether a tenant can waive a jury, ask whether there is a jury to waive. In a Nebraska residential possession action there is not, and the statute says so in six words. SECTION 76-1446: 'Trial of the action for possession shall be held not less than ten nor more than fourteen days after the issuance of the summons. THE ACTION SHALL BE TRIED BY THE COURT WITHOUT A JURY.' That is the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's own possession procedure. No demand is needed, none is available, and a jury-waiver clause adds nothing to it. The same section also tells you the rest of the shape: if you served the summons by the alternative method in section 76-1442.01, 'the action shall proceed as other actions for possession except that A MONEY JUDGMENT SHALL NOT BE GRANTED FOR THE PLAINTIFF'; on judgment for restitution the court declares the forfeiture of the rental agreement and, at your request, issues a writ of restitution directing the constable or sheriff to restore possession 'on a specified date not more than ten days after issuance'; and you must then comply with the Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act and section 76-1414(5) in removing personal property left behind. SO WHERE COULD A JURY TURN UP? In the money case. A suit for unpaid rent, for damage to the unit, for holdover damages, or a tenant's counterclaim or separate action for damages under section 76-1425(2), section 76-1427, section 76-1430, section 76-1438(2) or section 76-1416(3), brought as an ordinary civil action rather than inside the summary possession proceeding, is triable to a jury like any other contract or tort claim. Article I, section 6 of the Nebraska Constitution provides that 'The right of trial by jury shall remain inviolate, but the Legislature may authorize trial by a jury of a less number than twelve in courts inferior to the District Court, and may by general law authorize a verdict in civil cases in any court by not less than five-sixths of the jury.' And section 25-1104 and the sections following it govern how issues are tried. AND HERE IS WHY A LEASE CLAUSE WILL NOT DO THE JOB. Section 25-1126 is the waiver statute, and it is a list of methods, not a licence: 'The trial by jury may be waived by the parties in actions arising on contract and with assent of the court in other actions (1) by the consent of the party appearing, when the other party fails to appear at the trial by himself or herself or by attorney, (2) by written consent, in person or by attorney, FILED WITH THE CLERK, and (3) by oral consent in open court entered upon the record.' All three are tied to a pending action. A clause signed at lease signing, years before any suit, is not consent of a party appearing at a trial, is not a written consent filed with the clerk in that action, and is not oral consent in open court on the record. Nebraska's courts have described the section as setting reasonable limits on a constitutional right and as providing an exclusive list of the manners in which a waiver occurs (Jacobson v. Shresta, 288 Neb. 615, 849 N.W.2d 515 (2014)) - and whether a Nebraska court would nevertheless enforce a pre-dispute contractual waiver is for the courts, so treat the clause as giving you nothing you can rely on. The cautious course is to leave it out. If you want the money case tried to a judge, do it the way the statute allows: get written consent filed with the clerk, or consent on the record, once the action exists. TWO MORE REASONS NOT TO PUT ONE IN. First, the Legislature voids jury waivers when it decides to, and the examples are in this very title: section 76-2724(1) makes a provision in an equity purchase contract void as against public policy if it attempts to 'Waive any of the rights specified in sections 76-2719 to 76-2727 OR THE RIGHT TO A JURY TRIAL,' and section 76-2715(1) does the same for a foreclosure consulting contract - each also voiding out-of-state jurisdiction or choice of law, venue outside the county where the residence in foreclosure sits, and costs or fees greater than actual. Nebraska has not written that sentence for a residential lease, so a lease jury waiver is not void BY STATUTE; but the pairing shows the Legislature's attitude to the term, and a court asked to enforce one in a consumer lease has section 76-1412's unconscionability power to hand. Second, a jury waiver in a residential lease sits close to the line section 76-1415(1)(a) draws: 'No rental agreement may provide that the tenant ... Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.' A jury is not itself an Act right, so the subdivision does not catch the clause squarely - but if the clause is drafted broadly enough to reach the tenant's Act remedies, or is bundled with a waiver of counterclaims or of the section 76-1410(2) definition of 'Action', which 'includes recoupment, counterclaim, setoff, suit in equity, and any other proceeding in which rights are determined, including an action for possession,' then it is caught, and section 76-1415(2) adds the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees where you deliberately used a term you knew was prohibited. WHAT NOT TO BUNDLE WITH IT. Do not add a class-action waiver, a venue or choice-of-law clause moving disputes out of Nebraska, or an attorney-fee clause. The fee clause is expressly void here: section 76-1415(1)(c) voids a provision by which the tenant 'Agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees,' and it runs both ways, so a reciprocal fee clause is prohibited too. And if you are considering binding arbitration instead of a jury, that is a different rule with a formatting requirement attached - section 25-2602.02 prescribes capitalized, underlined type adjoining the signature block for a standardized agreement in which binding arbitration is the sole remedy, and strict compliance is required - so do not treat an arbitration clause as a quiet substitute for the jury waiver you were told to leave out.

title: Nebraska Has No Key-Control Policy Mandate - But Duplicating Your Master Key Without Written Permission Is a Crime, and It Must Be Stamped
bodyText: Nevada makes a large apartment complex keep a written key-control policy and screen the employees who hold keys. Nebraska requires no key-control policy, no key log, no key-custody procedure and no employee background check - the phrase 'key control' appears nowhere in the code. But Nebraska is not silent about keys, and the provision it does have is criminal, applies to any landlord who keeps a master key, and is almost never found because its catchline says nothing about rentals. SECTION 28-1316(1)(c). 'A person commits the offense of unlawful use of locks and keys if he or she ... (c) Duplicates a master key for anyone unless written permission has been granted by the person who has legal control of the master key. ALL MASTER KEYS SHALL BE STAMPED WITH THE WORDS DO NOT DUPLICATE. ALL DUPLICATIONS OF MASTER KEYS SHALL ALSO BE STAMPED WITH THE WORDS DO NOT DUPLICATE.' Section 28-1316(3): 'Unlawful use of locks and keys is a Class III misdemeanor,' which under section 28-106(1) carries a maximum of three months' imprisonment or a five-hundred-dollar fine, or both, with no minimum. AND THE DEFINITION IS WIDER THAN YOU THINK. Section 28-1315(4), which applies to section 28-1316: 'Master key shall mean a key planned and cut to operate all locks in a series or group of locks, each lock having its own key other than the master key for that individual lock only, and each lock constructed as a part of the series or group for operation with the master key. For the purpose of section 28-1316, SUBMASTER KEYS, GRAND MASTER KEYS, GREAT GRAND MASTER KEYS, EMERGENCY KEYS, AND OVERRIDING KEYS ARE TO BE CONSIDERED AS MASTER KEYS.' So the building master, the floor or wing submaster, the maintenance override and the emergency key are all master keys for this purpose. Section 28-1315(5) separately defines 'keyed-alike locks' as a group designed to operate with the same change key - a common arrangement in small multi-unit buildings, and one that is NOT a master-key system under subsection (4), because a master-key system requires each lock to have its own change key as well. WHAT THIS MEANS OPERATIONALLY. First, the duplication offence is drafted around WRITTEN PERMISSION FROM THE PERSON WITH LEGAL CONTROL. If you are that person, nobody - not your handyman, not your on-site manager, not a hardware-store key cutter, not the locksmith - may cut a copy of your master without your written permission, and if they do, they commit the offence. The corollary runs at you too: if you hold a master for a property you manage but do not own, or for a condominium whose association controls the system, find out who has legal control and get the permission in writing before you cut a copy. Second, the stamping sentences are written as unqualified commands - 'All master keys SHALL be stamped' - and they apply to duplicates as well as originals. They sit inside the subsection that defines the offence, so whether an unstamped master key is by itself the crime, as opposed to being evidence in a duplication prosecution, is not resolved by the text. The cautious course is simple and cheap: stamp them. Have every master, submaster, override and emergency key stamped DO NOT DUPLICATE, and stamp every duplicate you authorise. Third, section 28-1316(2) lists exceptions, and they are motor-vehicle exceptions - an owner of two or more vehicles holding a change key that works on more than one, re-keying vehicles alike, a person making or duplicating original change keys for such an owner, and stamping any other type of key DO NOT DUPLICATE. There is no landlord exception, no property-management exception and no emergency-access exception anywhere in the section. WHAT A SENSIBLE POLICY LOOKS LIKE, SINCE NEBRASKA WILL NOT WRITE ONE FOR YOU. Nothing requires the following and the library offers no Nebraska key-control clause, because no statute supports one - but you may adopt your own, and a landlord with a master-key system should: keep every master, submaster, override and emergency key stamped; keep a signed log of who holds which key, with dates issued and returned; name in writing the person with legal control of the master system and require their written permission for any duplication; re-key or re-pin when a key holder leaves, when a master goes missing and at turnover; and keep contractors and vendors off the master entirely, issuing a change key for the unit they are working in instead. If you screen employees who hold keys, do it because your insurer or your own judgment says so, not because Nebraska requires it - it does not. TWO BOUNDARIES. A key-control policy is not a right of entry. Holding a master key gives you no access a tenant has not given or a statute has not granted: section 76-1423(4) says 'The landlord has no other right of access except by court order, as permitted by subsection (2) of section 76-1432, or if the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises,' and section 76-1423(3) requires at least twenty-four hours' written notice to each individual unit, stating the purpose and a reasonable entry window, except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable. And a key-control policy is not a house rule unless it meets section 76-1422's six conditions, including that 'The tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement'; a rule adopted later binds only on reasonable notice and only if it 'does not work a substantial modification of his bargain.' Charging the tenant for keys or re-keying is a separate question: you may recover the amount of damages suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance under section 76-1416(2), and anything you take up front as security is caught by section 76-1416(1)'s 'security, however denominated' ceiling of one month's periodic rent, so a 'key deposit' counts against the cap.

title: The Knowing-Use Penalty Reaches Only Four Kinds of Clause - and Nebraska's Newest Prohibited Term Is Not One of Them
bodyText: Nebraska has a knowing-use penalty, and the sentence that creates it also limits it. Section 76-1415(2): 'A PROVISION PROHIBITED BY SUBSECTION (1) OF THIS SECTION included in a rental agreement is unenforceable. If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees.' Read the first six words. The penalty attaches to a provision prohibited by SUBSECTION (1) - the four categories in section 76-1415(1): waiving or foregoing rights or remedies under the Act; authorising any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement; agreeing to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees, which runs both ways so a reciprocal fee clause is caught; and agreeing to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence, or to indemnify the landlord for that liability or the costs connected with it. Nothing else. THAT LIMIT MATTERS BECAUSE SECTION 76-1415(1) IS NOT THE ONLY SOURCE OF A FORBIDDEN LEASE TERM IN NEBRASKA, AND THE OTHERS CARRY NO SECTION 76-1415(2) PENALTY. The clearest example is the newest. Section 76-1413(9), added by Laws 2025, LB185, provides: 'A landlord shall not, as part of a rental agreement or as a condition of entering into or renewing a rental agreement, require a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means.' That is a prohibition on a lease term, in the same Act - but it is not a provision prohibited by section 76-1415(1), so section 76-1415(2) does not supply its penalty. Section 76-1413 gives no damages remedy of its own either; the closest it comes is subsection (12), under which a failure to comply with subsection (7)(d) - the notice you must give when hardware or software requirements change - 'may be treated, at the election of the tenant, as a withdrawal of consent.' What remains is the Act's general enforcement provision, section 76-1405(2): 'Any right or obligation declared by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is enforceable by action unless the provision declaring it specifies a different and limited effect,' with section 76-1405(1) directing that remedies be administered so the aggrieved party recovers appropriate damages and imposing a duty to mitigate. So the consequence of a section 76-1413(9) violation is an action for appropriate damages and whatever injunctive relief a court will give - not the automatic actual-damages-plus-fees package that follows a section 76-1415(1) term. Do not treat that as good news: it means the exposure is less predictable, not that the term is safe. The same reasoning applies to the other sources of ineffective lease language in Nebraska law, each of which has its own regime. Section 86-632(3), part of the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, says a party who agrees to conduct a transaction electronically 'may refuse to conduct other transactions by electronic means' and that 'The right granted by this subsection may not be waived by agreement.' Section 86-635(4) says the requirements of that section - including subsection (3), under which an electronic record is unenforceable against a recipient whose ability to store or print it the sender inhibited - 'may not be varied by agreement,' subject to two narrow exceptions in (4)(a) and (4)(b). Those are non-waivability rules routed into a Nebraska tenancy by section 76-1413(5), which subjects electronic delivery under that section to the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act. None of them is a section 76-1415(1) provision, and none of them triggers section 76-1415(2). NOW THE TRIGGER, BECAUSE IT IS NOT STRICT LIABILITY AND IT IS NOT A FREE PASS EITHER. The penalty requires two things in the same sentence: that the landlord 'DELIBERATELY uses a rental agreement containing' the provision, and that the provisions are 'KNOWN BY HIM OR HER to be prohibited.' A landlord who inherits a form from a predecessor or a national template and has genuinely never been told it is unlawful here is in a different position from one who has been told, by a tenant, a lawyer, a court or a letter, and keeps using the form. Three practical consequences. First, the first complaint is the expensive one, because it supplies the knowledge element for every lease you sign afterwards, and 'deliberately uses' is satisfied by continuing to hand out the same form. Second, a savings sentence does not help. Adding 'nothing in this Lease limits any right you have under applicable law' leaves the prohibited provision in the agreement, and what subsection (2) measures is a rental agreement CONTAINING the provision. Take the term out. Third, there is no statutory minimum. The measure is ACTUAL damages plus reasonable attorney's fees, so a void clause that caused no loss produces a fee award and little else - which is a real exposure rather than a trivial one, because Nebraska's fee awards under this Act are not nominal: the Supreme Court has held that the Act's mandatory attorney-fee provisions include fees for pro bono work (Black v. Brooks, 285 Neb. 440, 827 N.W.2d 256 (2013), noted with section 76-1416). Compare the Act's other penalty shapes so you do not misprice this one: section 76-1438(2) gives the tenant 'actual damages not less than an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees' for abuse of entry - a FLOOR; section 76-1416(3)'s security-deposit liquidated damages are 'one month's periodic rent or two times the amount of the security deposit, WHICHEVER IS LESS' - a ceiling, and the Act's only landlord-favourable formula; and the unlawful-ouster remedy is a fixed liquidated sum. Section 76-1415(2) is none of those: it is uncapped, unfloored actual damages, plus fees. A FOURTH CONSEQUENCE THAT IS EASY TO MISS. Section 76-1415(2) says the prohibited provision 'is unenforceable' - it does not say the lease is void. The rest of the agreement stands, and section 76-1412 gives the court the matching powers for an unconscionable term: 'refuse to enforce the agreement, enforce the remainder of the agreement without the unconscionable provision, or limit the application of any unconscionable provision to avoid an unconscionable result.' So the realistic outcome of a bad clause is that you lose the clause, pay the tenant's lawyer, and keep the lease. PRACTICAL COURSE. Audit your form against the four section 76-1415(1) categories, then separately against section 76-1413(9) and the electronic-delivery rules, because the two lists have different penalties and only one of them is in section 76-1415. Date the audit and keep it. If someone tells you a clause is unlawful here, fix the form before the next signing, not after the next complaint - the knowledge element does not go away once it has been supplied.

title: Six Remedies, One Election, Two Defences - How Nebraska's Tenant Remedies Interlock When You Are the One in Breach
bodyText: Nebraska gives a tenant six separate remedies for a landlord's breach, and the expensive mistakes are not about any one of them - they are about which one the tenant has chosen, because the choice changes what you owe, whether attorney's fees are automatic, and whether you have a defence at all. THE SIX, AND WHAT EACH ONE IS KEYED TO. (1) TERMINATION FOR NONCOMPLIANCE, section 76-1425(1). Available for 'a material noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement OR a noncompliance with section 76-1419 materially affecting health and safety.' The tenant serves a written notice specifying the acts and omissions and stating that the agreement will terminate on a date 'not less than thirty days after receipt of the notice if the breach is not remedied in FOURTEEN DAYS.' Note the two clocks: you get fourteen days to cure, and termination lands no sooner than thirty days after receipt. If you 'adequately remedies the breach prior to the date specified in the notice,' the agreement does not terminate. But if 'substantially the same act or omission which constituted a prior noncompliance of which notice was given recurs within six months,' the tenant may terminate on just fourteen days' written notice with no cure period at all - so the second failure of the same kind within six months is the one that ends the tenancy. The subsection closes with a defence for you: 'The tenant may not terminate for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of his or her family, or other person on the premises with his or her consent.'
