(2) DAMAGES AND INJUNCTION, section 76-1425(2), 'for ANY noncompliance' with the rental agreement or section 76-1419 - no materiality threshold, no health-and-safety qualifier. Fees only 'If the landlord's noncompliance is willful.' And section 76-1425(3) is explicit that this is cumulative: 'The remedy provided in subsection (2) of this section is IN ADDITION TO any right of the tenant arising under subsection (1).' (3) ESSENTIAL SERVICES, section 76-1427, for a deliberate or negligent failure to supply running water, hot water, heat or essential services: procure the service and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from the rent; or recover damages based on the diminution in fair rental value; or procure substitute housing and be excused from rent for the period - plus, for a deliberate failure, the cost or value of the substitute housing up to one month's rent, 'and in any case under this subsection reasonable attorney's fees.' (4) FAILURE TO DELIVER POSSESSION, section 76-1426: rent abates until possession is delivered, and the tenant may terminate on five days' written notice and recover all prepaid rent and security, or demand performance and sue; and a willful, bad-faith failure exposes 'not more than three months' periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees.' (5) UNLAWFUL OUSTER OR SERVICE CUT-OFF, section 76-1430: possession or termination, plus 'an amount equal to three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages, and a reasonable attorney's fee.' (6) ABUSE OF ACCESS, section 76-1438(2): injunction or termination, plus 'actual damages not less than an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees.' Alongside those sit the casualty route in section 76-1429 and the counterclaim-and-rent-into-court mechanism in section 76-1428, both of which the library covers elsewhere. NOW THE ELECTION, WHICH IS THE PART ALMOST NOBODY READS. Section 76-1427(2): 'If the tenant proceeds under this section, he may not proceed under section 76-1425 AS TO THAT BREACH.' That is a one-way gate, and it is your most useful sentence in a heat-or-water dispute. A tenant who has deducted the cost of a space heater from the rent, or moved to a motel and stopped paying, has proceeded under section 76-1427 - and cannot then run the section 76-1425(1) termination clock or claim section 76-1425(2) damages for the same failure. Watch the limiting words 'as to that breach': a separate, different breach is still open to them, and a recurring failure may be argued either way. Note also the asymmetry in fees. Under section 76-1425(2) fees require WILLFULNESS. Under section 76-1427 fees come 'in any case under this subsection' - no willfulness needed. So the tenant who picks section 76-1427 gets fees more easily and gives up section 76-1425; the tenant who picks section 76-1425 keeps the termination route and takes on a willfulness burden for fees. THE TWO DEFENCES THE ACT GIVES YOU, AND THEIR LIMITS. First, TENANT-CAUSED CONDITIONS. Section 76-1425(1)'s closing sentence bars termination for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, their family, or a person on the premises with their consent; section 76-1427(3) applies the same exclusion to the essential-services rights; and section 76-1429(2) preserves tenant liability for negligent casualty damage - 'Notwithstanding the provisions of this section, the tenant is responsible for damage caused by his negligence.' Second, CIRCUMSTANCES BEYOND YOUR CONTROL, and this one is narrower than it sounds. Section 76-1425(2): 'If the landlord's noncompliance is caused by conditions or circumstances beyond his or her control, the tenant may not recover CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES, BUT RETAINS REMEDIES PROVIDED IN SECTION 76-1427.' Read what survives. Beyond-control removes consequential damages under section 76-1425(2) - it does not remove direct damages, it does not remove the injunction, it does not remove the section 76-1425(1) termination right, and the statute says in so many words that the section 76-1427 remedies remain. Section 76-1427(3) adds its own version - 'This section is not intended to cover circumstances beyond the landlord's control' - so the two sections pull in opposite directions on the same facts and the safest assumption is that a utility-wide outage or a genuine act of God limits your damages exposure without ending the tenant's right to leave. THREE RULES THAT SIT OVER ALL SIX. Section 76-1405(1): remedies 'shall be so administered that the aggrieved party may recover appropriate damages,' and 'The aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages' - which runs against the tenant too, so a tenant who sat on a leak while damage accumulated has a mitigation problem of their own. Section 76-1405(2): every right or obligation declared by the Act 'is enforceable by action unless the provision declaring it specifies a different and limited effect.' And section 76-1411: 'Every duty under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and every act which must be performed as a condition precedent to the exercise of a right or remedy under the act imposes an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement' - which is the hook for arguing that a notice or a demand was not made in good faith. WHAT YOU CANNOT DO ABOUT ANY OF IT. You cannot contract out. Section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any provision by which the tenant 'Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under' the Act; section 76-1415(1)(c) voids an attorney-fee clause in either direction; and section 76-1415(2) adds the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees where you deliberately used a term you knew was prohibited. What you CAN do is settle: section 76-1406 provides that 'A claim or right arising under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or on a rental agreement may be settled by agreement' - after the claim exists, in a separate instrument, not as a lease term. PRACTICAL COURSE. When a notice arrives, do three things before you do anything else. Identify which section the tenant is invoking, because that fixes your clock and their fees. Diary the cure date from the date of RECEIPT, not from the date on the letter, and calendar the fourteen-day cure and the six-month recurrence window. And record whether the condition was tenant-caused or beyond your control, contemporaneously, because both are statutory defences and both are proved by what you wrote down at the time.

title: How Long You Have to Sue - Five Years on the Lease, One Year on Forcible Detainer, and a Part Payment Restarts the Clock
bodyText: Nebraska puts no limitation period inside the landlord-tenant act. The deadlines come from chapter 25, and which one applies turns on what you are suing for, not on who you are suing. FIVE YEARS - A WRITTEN LEASE. Section 25-205(1): 'an action upon a specialty, or any agreement, contract, or promise in writing, or foreign judgment, can only be brought within five years.' A signed written lease is an agreement in writing, so a claim for unpaid rent, for damage the tenant owes under the lease, or for any other breach of the lease document has five years from the date that claim accrued. FOUR YEARS - AN ORAL TENANCY, OR A CLAIM THE STATUTE RATHER THAN THE LEASE CREATES. Section 25-206: 'An action upon a contract, not in writing, expressed or implied, or an action upon a liability created by statute, other than a forfeiture or penalty, can only be brought within four years.' A month-to-month tenancy with nothing in writing is a contract not in writing. So is a claim for the fair rental value of the unit under section 76-1414(2) where there was no agreement at all. Note the carve-out at the end of that sentence - 'other than a forfeiture or penalty' - which is why the treble-damages and three-months'-rent measures in sections 76-1437(3) and 76-1430 should not be assumed to share the four-year period. Section 25-212 is the catch-all for anything chapter 25 does not name, also four years. TEN YEARS - GETTING THE PROPERTY BACK. Section 25-202(1): 'An action for the recovery of the title or possession of lands, tenements, or hereditaments ... can only be brought within ten years after the cause of action accrues.' The Nebraska Supreme Court applied exactly that to a holdover tenant: an action under section 76-1437(3) to recover possession from a tenant who stayed on after the lease ended 'is an action for the possession of real property and is therefore subject to the 10-year statute of limitations ... as provided in section 25-202', and it accrues 'at the point the lease expires or is terminated and the tenant remains in possession of the property without the consent of the landlord.' Blankenau v. Landess, 261 Neb. 906, 626 N.W.2d 588 (2001). ONE YEAR - FORCIBLE ENTRY AND DETAINER. Section 25-203: 'An action for the forcible entry and detainer, or forcible detainer only, of real property, can only be brought within one year after the cause of such action shall have accrued.' That is the short fuse, and it is on the summary route, not on the possession claim itself. If you let an unauthorized occupant sit for more than a year you may have lost the quick statutory remedy while still owning the ten-year possession claim. PART PAYMENT RESTARTS THE CLOCK, AND SO DOES A WRITTEN ACKNOWLEDGMENT. Section 25-216: 'In any cause founded on contract, when any part of the principal or interest shall have been voluntarily paid, or an acknowledgment of an existing liability, debt or claim, or any promise to pay the same shall have been made in writing, an action may be brought in such case within the period prescribed for the same, after such payment, acknowledgment or promise.' Two practical consequences. A departed tenant who sends you fifty dollars toward an old balance has just given you a fresh five years on a written lease - 'a new right of action accrues after each payment' (Pick v. Pick, 184 Neb. 716, 171 N.W.2d 766 (1969), annotated under section 25-205). And an email or letter in which the tenant admits owing the balance does the same thing, because the acknowledgment limb requires writing while the payment limb does not. Keep both. WHAT YOU CANNOT DO ABOUT ANY OF THIS IN THE LEASE. Do not write a clause shortening the time the tenant has to sue you. Section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any rental agreement provision by which the tenant 'Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act', and section 76-1415(2) makes a deliberately used prohibited provision cost you the tenant's actual damages and attorney's fees. Tolling: section 25-213 extends the period for a plaintiff who was under twenty, a person with a mental disorder, or imprisoned when the claim accrued, and section 25-201 gives a party at least one year after a stay lifts. Section 25-221 lets any party have the limitation issue tried separately and first, which is worth knowing if you are the one defending.

title: No Statewide Rental Registry - Except the One Nobody Cites, and It Carries a Class I Misdemeanor
bodyText: For the ordinary Nebraska rental - a house, a duplex, an apartment building - there is no statewide registration, no landlord licence and no state rental registry. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act creates none, and the phrases 'rental registration', 'rental registry', 'landlord registration' and 'rental licence' appear nowhere in Nebraska's property, municipal, civil-procedure, civil-rights, consumer or commercial chapters. Omaha and Lincoln run their own programmes by ordinance, so check the city you are letting in. THERE IS ONE STATE REGISTRATION REGIME THAT REACHES A RESIDENTIAL LANDLORD, AND IT IS EASY TO WALK INTO. The Retirement Subdivisions and Communities Act, sections 76-1301 to 76-1315, is administered by the State Real Estate Commission (section 76-1303(1)) and it is built around leasing, not only selling. Section 76-1302(6) defines a 'Developer' as 'any person who, directly or indirectly, sells or leases, or offers to sell or lease, or advertises for sale or lease any lots in a retirement subdivision or any units in a retirement community.' Section 76-1302(11) defines 'Disposition' to 'include sale, lease, assignment, award by lottery, or any other transaction by which a person acquires the use or occupancy of a lot or unit.' And section 76-1305(1) is the bar: 'No person may offer or dispose of any lot or unit in any retirement subdivision or community located in this state ... prior to the time such subdivision or community is registered in the manner prescribed by sections 76-1301 to 76-1315.' WHAT TRIPS IT. Section 76-1302(2): a 'Retirement community' is 'any complex or proposed complex of MORE THAN TEN UNITS, whether contained in one or more buildings or whether constructed on separate lots, offered for sale or lease as part of a common promotional plan when such community is advertised or represented as a retirement community or as a community primarily for retirees or elderly persons, OR WHEN THERE IS A MINIMUM AGE LIMIT TENDING TO ATTRACT PERSONS WHO ARE NEARING RETIREMENT AGE.' Section 76-1302(1) does the same for ten or more lots. Read the last limb again: a minimum age limit alone can bring you inside, with no retirement branding at all. Section 76-1302(3) counts a 'Unit' as any apartment or structure intended primarily as a residence, 'including a single residence dwelling', so scattered houses marketed together count. WHAT COMPLIANCE COSTS, AND WHAT NONCOMPLIANCE COSTS. Registration is a statement of record filed with the Commission under section 76-1306(1) - title opinion, audited or examined prospective financial statements, copies of every instrument the resident will sign, zoning and tax statement, public-offering statement - with a fee set by regulation and capped at two hundred dollars (section 76-1306(2)). Registration takes effect on 'the sixtieth day after the filing of the statement of record or such earlier date as the agency may determine' (section 76-1309(1)), so this is not a same-week errand. Section 76-1310 adds an annual report within thirty days of each anniversary. Section 76-1305(2) requires a current public-offering statement delivered with 'under no circumstances less than forty-eight hours' to examine it before disposition, and section 76-1305(3) gives a three-business-day cancellation right that 'may not be waived and any attempt to obtain such a waiver is unlawful'. Get it wrong and section 76-1315(3) makes offering or disposing without having complied 'a Class I misdemeanor'; section 76-1315(2) lets a court 'render any contract entered into in this state in violation of sections 76-1301 to 76-1315 void and unenforceable' with the money back plus judgment-rate interest and reasonable attorney's fees; section 76-1315(4) lets the Attorney General seek 'a civil penalty of not more than ten thousand dollars for each violation, with each day of continued violation to constitute a separate offense'; and section 76-1315(5) authorises a cease and desist order. Section 76-1313 adds, where the developer or association is a Nebraska nonprofit corporation governing one community, an annual resident election of at least one voting member of the governing body - a governance obligation, not just paperwork. THE LIMIT AND THE OPEN QUESTION. Section 76-1304 exempts an isolated resale by a purchaser for his or her own account, court-ordered leases, public housing under a local housing authority, and health care facilities licensed under the Health Care Facility Licensure Act - so a licensed assisted-living or nursing facility is out. The genuinely unsettled point is the entrance fee. Section 76-1302(13) defines 'Lease', for the Act's purposes, as 'a contract for the use and occupancy of real estate primarily as a residence when the contract term is for more than one year or is for life and when the lessee is required to pay an entrance fee', and section 76-1302(18) says an entrance fee is a transfer 'more than reasonably necessary to cover a damage deposit and an advance of the first and last month's rent'. If that definition controls the word 'lease' wherever it appears in sections 76-1302(1), (2), (6) and (11), an age-restricted apartment complex renting month to month with an ordinary deposit is outside the Act. If instead section 76-1302(11)'s catch-all - 'any other transaction by which a person acquires the use or occupancy of a lot or unit' - controls, it is inside. Section 76-1302's own chapeau ('unless the context otherwise requires') leaves that open. THE CAUTIOUS COURSE: if you market more than ten residential units, or ten or more lots, under one name with an age floor, assume you are inside until the Real Estate Commission tells you otherwise - the downside is a misdemeanor and voidable leases, and the upside of guessing wrong the other way is a two-hundred-dollar fee. SEPARATELY, WHETHER YOU NEED A REAL ESTATE LICENCE TO MANAGE RENTALS IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION. Section 81-885.02(1) makes it 'unlawful for any person, directly or indirectly, to engage in or conduct, or to advertise or hold himself or herself out as engaging in or conducting the business, or acting in the capacity, of a real estate broker, associate broker, or real estate salesperson within this state without first obtaining a license ... unless he or she is exempted from obtaining a license under section 81-885.04.' Section 81-885.01(2) makes a 'Broker' anyone who, for compensation, negotiates a rent or lease or 'collects rents or attempts to collect rents'. Section 81-885.04 lists who is exempt. Section 81-885.04(1) exempts an owner or lessor acting on property 'owned or leased by him, her, or it', and its regular employees, in the regular course of managing it. An equitable interest is not ownership for this purpose. Section 81-885.04(4) exempts 'the resident manager of an apartment building, duplex, apartment complex, or court' who 'resides on the premises', and 'any employee, parent, child, brother, or sister of the owner'. So you can manage your own rentals without a licence. If you manage for someone else for pay, and fit no exemption, you need a licence before you advertise or sign on the owner's behalf. Nebraska has no provision of the Georgia kind requiring an out-of-state owner of a single-family or duplex rental to engage an in-state broker, and no in-state-contact mandate beyond section 76-1417's disclosure of the manager's and owner's names and addresses - which is already a lease clause in this library. An out-of-state company is the exception. Section 21-157(b) provides that 'the ownership in this state of income-producing real property ... constitutes transacting business in this state', so an out-of-state LLC that owns a Nebraska rental needs a certificate of authority from the Secretary of State, and section 21-162(a) provides that it 'may not maintain an action or proceeding in this state unless it has a certificate of authority to transact business in this state.' An out-of-state corporation transacting business here may not maintain a proceeding until it obtains one and owes a civil penalty of five hundred dollars a day, up to ten thousand dollars a year (section 21-2,204(a), (d)).

title: No Nebraska Lead-Safe Certificate, No Registry, Nothing to Attach to the Lease - and the One Lead Fund the State Built Was for Owner-Occupied Homes and Was Repealed in 2026
bodyText: New Jersey makes a landlord attach a lead-safe certificate to the lease as an exhibit. Rhode Island, New Hampshire, Delaware and Vermont each run some version of a certificate, registry or compliance statement. Nebraska has none of that. There is no state lead-safe certificate, no lead-safe registry, no state inspection or clearance you can be certified against, and nothing lead-related that Nebraska law requires you to attach to or recite in a residential lease. WHAT NEBRASKA'S LEAD STATUTE ACTUALLY DOES, READ IN FULL. Section 71-2518(1) directs that 'The Division of Public Health of the Department of Health and Human Services shall establish a lead poisoning prevention program' with two components: (a) a coordinated plan to prevent childhood lead poisoning and minimise public exposure to lead-based paint hazards, which must state the elevated-blood-lead standard in micrograms per deciliter, require testing of a child enrolled in medical assistance in accordance with the medicaid state plan, and recommend testing for a child living in a high-prevalence zip code or meeting the department's screening questionnaire; and (b) an educational and community outreach plan. Subsection (2) requires all blood-lead test results in Nebraska to be reported to the department and, on notice of an elevated level, has the department contact the local public health department or the child's physician and offer technical assistance. Subsection (3) says the section does not require the department to pay for testing except in the medical-assistance cases. Read that list again and notice who is bound: the department, the laboratories reporting results, and nobody else. There is no landlord duty anywhere in it - no inspection, no abatement standard, no certification, no clearance testing, no recordkeeping, no tenant notice, and no trigger tied to a change of tenancy or a renovation. THE SIBLING CONTRAST, WHICH IS WHY THE SILENCE IS A CHOICE. Nebraska did once build a lead-paint programme with money in it, it deliberately pointed that money away from rentals, and it has now abolished it. Section 81-1211 created the Lead-Based Paint Hazard Control Cash Fund in the Department of Economic Development and directed that the department 'shall use the entirety of the fund to award a grant to a city of the metropolitan class to carry out lead-based paint hazard control on OWNER-OCCUPIED PROPERTIES', contingent on federal notification under the Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act of 1992, 42 U.S.C. 4852, as that section existed on January 1, 2015, with no more than fifteen percent of grant proceeds for administration. Owner-occupied, not tenant-occupied. Then in 2025 the Legislature swept the remaining balance of the fund into the General Fund (Laws 2025, LB264, section 41), and in 2026 it repealed section 81-1211 outright (Laws 2026, LB1072, section 241, in an act approved April 7, 2026 whose section 244 declares an emergency so that it took effect on approval). A legislature that writes a lead-hazard-control grant, confines it to owner-occupied homes, empties the fund and then deletes the section has not overlooked rental housing - it has decided about it twice. Compare the same Act elsewhere in Nebraska's own statutes: the Carbon Monoxide Safety Act at section 76-606 gives landlords a real trigger-based duty on a change of tenant occupancy, so the Legislature plainly knows how to attach a safety duty to a tenancy when it means to. SO WHERE DOES YOUR CERTIFICATION OBLIGATION COME FROM? Federal law, and it is not a certificate you give the tenant. The federal lead disclosure requirement at 42 U.S.C. 4852d applies to any residential dwelling built before 1978 and is already handled by this library's Lead-Based Paint Disclosure clause and the EPA/HUD pamphlet and record-keeping that go with it. Separately, the federal renovation, repair and painting rules certify the FIRM AND THE WORKER who disturbs paint in a pre-1978 unit - a contractor credential, not a property certificate, and Nebraska has enacted no statute of its own creating, mirroring or administering such a credential. PRACTICAL COURSE. Do the federal disclosure properly, because that is where every Nebraska lead exposure for a landlord sits. Hire only firms that hold the federal renovation certification for work on pre-1978 units and keep the certificate and the invoice in the file: Nebraska gives you no statutory safe harbour, and section 76-1419(1)(a) and (1)(b) still require you to comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and to keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition, which is the channel through which a lead hazard becomes a landlord problem here even with no lead statute to point at. If you want to document a clearance for your own protection, put it in the file as evidence - do not describe it to the tenant as a state certificate, because there is no such thing in Nebraska.

title: Nebraska Adds Nothing to the Federal Lead Disclosure - the State's Lead Pamphlet Is the Health Department's Job, Not Yours
bodyText:
Maryland hands the landlord a packet of state-specific lead notices to deliver. Massachusetts has its own certification form. Rhode Island, New Hampshire, Vermont and Delaware each bolt state notices on top of the federal disclosure. Nebraska bolts on nothing. For a Nebraska rental the federal pre-1978 disclosure, the EPA/HUD pamphlet and the records you keep under 42 U.S.C. 4852d are the whole of your lead paperwork. There is no Nebraska lead notice, no state lead pamphlet you must hand over, no state lead addendum, no state lead certificate, no state lead rider and no state lead warning that has to appear in or with the lease.

THE DETAIL THAT LOOKS LIKE A DUTY AND IS NOT, SO READ IT CAREFULLY. Nebraska's lead statute does require a pamphlet - and it requires the health department to write it, not you to deliver it. Section 71-2518(1) directs that 'The Division of Public Health of the Department of Health and Human Services shall establish a lead poisoning prevention program', and subdivision (1)(b) requires that program to include 'An educational and community outreach plan regarding lead poisoning prevention that shall, at a minimum, include the development of appropriate educational materials targeted to health care providers, child care providers, public school personnel, OWNERS AND TENANTS OF RESIDENTIAL DWELLINGS, and parents of young children. Such educational materials shall be made available to the general public via the department's website.'

Owners of residential dwellings appear in that sentence as an AUDIENCE for materials the department writes, not as an obligor. The verb is the department's and the delivery channel is the department's website. Nothing in the section says a landlord must obtain the materials, give them to a tenant, mention them in a lease, keep proof of delivery, or do anything else.

Compare how Nebraska writes a sentence when it does mean to bind a landlord: section 76-1417(1) says 'The landlord... SHALL DISCLOSE TO THE TENANT IN WRITING at or before the commencement of the tenancy' the manager's and owner's names and addresses, and section 76-606(2) says 'The owner of an existing single-family dwelling or existing dwelling unit in a multifamily dwelling that is used for rental purposes and that has a change in tenant occupancy on or after January 1, 2017, SHALL ENSURE that an operational carbon monoxide alarm is installed'. Both name the landlord or owner and both use 'shall'. Section 71-2518(1)(b) does neither.

THE REST OF SECTION 71-2518 CONFIRMS IT. Subdivision (1)(a) sets the elevated-blood-lead standard, requires testing for a child enrolled in medical assistance in accordance with the medicaid state plan, and recommends testing for a child in a high-prevalence zip code or one who meets the department's screening questionnaire. Subsection (2) makes laboratories report every blood-lead test result in Nebraska to the department and, on notice of an elevated result, has the department contact the local public health department or the child's physician and offer technical assistance. Subsection (3) says the section does not require the department to pay for testing outside the medical-assistance cases. Nobody in that chain is a landlord. There is no notice to the landlord when a child in his building tests high, and correspondingly no statutory trigger that converts such a result into a disclosure duty for the next tenant.

AND THE STATE'S ONLY OTHER LEAD PROVISION IS GONE. Section 81-1211 created the Lead-Based Paint Hazard Control Cash Fund and confined it to a grant for 'lead-based paint hazard control on owner-occupied properties'. The Legislature swept its balance into the General Fund in 2025 (Laws 2025, LB264, section 41) and repealed the section outright in 2026 (Laws 2026, LB1072, section 241, effective on approval April 7, 2026 under that act's emergency clause). So there is no state lead programme a notice could hang off and no state lead money a condition could attach to.

WHAT TO DO. Run the federal disclosure properly and keep the signed acknowledgment: that is the only lead document with legal force in a Nebraska tenancy, and this library's Lead-Based Paint Disclosure clause carries it. If you want to be useful beyond that, print the DHHS lead materials from the department's website and include them with the lease - voluntarily. Hand them over as information, never as a required state notice, and do not write a clause saying Nebraska law requires the tenant to receive them, because it does not.

And do not let the absence of a lead notice fool you into thinking lead is not your problem: section 76-1419(1)(a) and (1)(b) still require you to comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and to keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition, and an ordinary habitability or negligence claim about a lead hazard needs no lead statute behind it.

title: No Maximum Lease Term in Nebraska - But Cross One Year and Four Separate Statutes Change the Rules, and a Homestead Adds a Fifth
bodyText: Nebraska sets no ceiling on how long a residential lease may run. There is no maximum term, no renewal cap and no statute of the kind the District of Columbia has requiring a seal, the owner's personal signature or a power of attorney for a long lease. Ninety-nine-year leases have been litigated in Nebraska for a century and treated as ordinary property interests - 'Lease for ninety-nine years is a chattel real and therefore real estate' (Lindburg v. Bennett, 117 Neb. 66, 219 N.W. 851 (1928), annotated under section 76-201). What Nebraska does instead is draw one line, at ONE YEAR, four times over, and you need to know all four because they do different work. ONE - VALIDITY. Section 36-105: 'Every contract for the leasing for a longer period than one year, or for the sale of any lands, SHALL BE VOID unless the contract or some note or memorandum thereof be in writing and signed by the party by whom the lease or sale is to be made.' Void, not merely unenforceable. Three points from the annotations. Only the LESSOR need sign - 'Vendor only is required to sign contract or memorandum' (Iske v. Iske, 95 Neb. 603, 146 N.W. 918 (1914); Ballou v. Sherwood, 32 Neb. 666, 49 N.W. 790 (1891); Robinson v. Cheney, 17 Neb. 673, 24 N.W. 378 (1885)) - though the tenant must still be named or described well enough to be identified (Barkhurst v. Nevins, 106 Neb. 33, 182 N.W. 563 (1921)), and a typed or printed name counts if the signer recognises it as his signature (Department of Banking, Receiver v. Wilken, 217 Neb. 796, 352 N.W.2d 145 (1984)). A void long lease does NOT vanish - 'Lease for term exceeding one year is void; but if lessee enters, is valid for one year' (Friedhoff & Co. v. Smith, 13 Neb. 5, 12 N.W. 820 (1882); Osgood v. Shea, 86 Neb. 729, 126 N.W. 310 (1910); Dewey & Stone v. Payne & Co., 19 Neb. 540, 26 N.W. 248 (1886)) - so an oral three-year deal becomes a one-year tenancy you cannot extend, which is the worst of both worlds if you were counting on years two and three. And the trap: an ORAL LEASE FOR EXACTLY ONE YEAR IS VOID IF MADE BEFORE THE TERM STARTS (Prigge v. Olson, 154 Neb. 131, 47 N.W.2d 344 (1951)), because the year plus the gap exceeds one year, while a lease that MAY end inside a year is fine (McCormick v. Drummett, 9 Neb. 384, 2 N.W. 729 (1879)). TWO - CREATION, ASSIGNMENT AND SURRENDER. Section 36-103: 'No estate or interest in land, OTHER THAN LEASES FOR A TERM OF ONE YEAR from the making thereof ... shall hereafter be created, granted, ASSIGNED, SURRENDERED, or declared, unless by operation of law, or by deed of conveyance in writing, subscribed by the party creating, granting, assigning, surrendering or declaring the same.' Read the verbs. The writing requirement reaches not just the grant of a long lease but its assignment and its SURRENDER - so if you and a long-term tenant agree to tear up a three-year lease two years in, do it in a signed writing subscribed by the party surrendering, or you may still have a lease. THREE - EXECUTION FORMALITY AND RECORDABILITY. Section 76-211: 'Deeds of real estate, OR ANY INTEREST THEREIN, in this state, EXCEPT LEASES FOR ONE YEAR OR FOR A LESS TIME, if executed in this state, must be signed by the grantor or grantors, being of lawful age, and be acknowledged or proved and recorded as directed in sections 76-216 to 76-237.' The acknowledgment (a notary, under section 76-216) and recording directive therefore reaches any lease longer than a year. Whether failing to record costs you anything is a separate subject and is covered at lease-registration. FOUR - DEFINITIONAL. Section 76-201 defines 'real estate' for sections 76-201 to 76-281 and 76-2,126 as 'embracing all chattels real, EXCEPT LEASES FOR A TERM NOT EXCEEDING ONE YEAR', which is the mechanism that pulls a long lease into the deeds-and-conveyances article in the first place. THE FIFTH LINE, AND IT CAN VOID THE WHOLE INSTRUMENT: A HOMESTEAD. If the property you are letting is the homestead of a MARRIED owner, section 40-104 says: 'Except as otherwise provided in this section, the homestead of a married person cannot be conveyed or encumbered unless the instrument by which it is conveyed or encumbered IS EXECUTED AND ACKNOWLEDGED BY BOTH SPOUSES.' The Nebraska Supreme Court is emphatic about the consequence: 'A valid acknowledgment of both spouses must appear on the face of an instrument purporting to convey or encumber the homestead of a married person OR THE INSTRUMENT IS VOID' (Mutual of Omaha Bank v. Watson, 297 Neb. 479, 900 N.W.2d 545 (2017)). WHETHER A LEASE IS AN 'ENCUMBRANCE' WITHIN SECTION 40-104 IS UNSETTLED. Every annotation to the section concerns a deed, a mortgage, a contract for sale, an option or a will - not one is a lease - and the 2015 amendment carved purchase agreements out of the acknowledgment requirement while saying nothing whatever about leases. Note also that section 40-104 lets a conservator under the Nebraska Probate Code, or an attorney in fact under a power of attorney granting the power to sell and convey real property, convey or encumber either spouse's interest. THE CAUTIOUS COURSE IS CHEAP, SO TAKE IT: where a married owner is letting property that is or was the family home, have BOTH spouses sign AND acknowledge the lease before a notary, and do it for any lease you record and for any lease longer than a year. It costs a notary appointment. The downside of being wrong is a void instrument. A tenant-side homestead waiver is not the answer - Nebraska's homestead-waiver doctrine is about failing to assert the privilege before a sale, not about contracting it away in advance - and in any event section 76-1415(1)(a) voids a rental-agreement term by which the tenant waives rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act. TWO MORE THINGS ABOUT LENGTH. If the rental agreement fixes no definite term at all, section 76-1414(4) supplies one: week to week for a roomer paying weekly rent, 'and in all other cases month to month'. And at the far end, section 76-1408(8) takes 'A lease of improved or unimproved residential land for a term of five years or more' outside the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act entirely - a five-year line that has nothing to do with the one-year lines above, and which this library covers at the scope topic.

title: You Never Have to Record a Nebraska Lease - But an Unrecorded Long Lease Is Good Against Your Tenant and Worthless Against Your Lender's Buyer
bodyText: No Nebraska statute requires a residential lease to be recorded, and no Nebraska statute makes any right under a lease depend on recording it. There is no lease registry, no filing fee you must pay and no deadline you can miss. Recording is permissive - but it is not pointless, and the reason is worth five minutes before you sign a long lease. WHAT RECORDING BUYS, IN THE STATUTE'S OWN WORDS. Section 76-238(1): recordable instruments 'shall take effect and be in force FROM AND AFTER THE TIME OF DELIVERING such instruments to the register of deeds for recording, AND NOT BEFORE, as to all creditors and subsequent purchasers in good faith without notice. All such instruments are VOID as to all creditors and subsequent purchasers without notice whose deeds, mortgages, or other instruments are recorded prior to such instruments. HOWEVER, SUCH INSTRUMENTS ARE VALID BETWEEN THE PARTIES TO THE INSTRUMENT.' That last sentence is the whole answer to the question landlords actually ask. An unrecorded lease binds you and your tenant completely. What recording protects against is a third party - your lender's assignee, a judgment creditor, a buyer - who takes without notice. Section 76-237 fixes the moment: an instrument 'shall be considered recorded from the time of such delivery' to the register of deeds. Section 76-245 fixes the place: 'in the county in which such real estate, or any part thereof, is situated.' WHAT YOU MUST DO FIRST, AND IT IS A REAL GATE. You cannot record a lease you only signed. Section 76-241: 'All deeds, mortgages and other instruments of writing SHALL NOT BE DEEMED LAWFULLY RECORDED unless they have been previously acknowledged or proved in the manner prescribed by statute.' Section 76-216 says what that means: 'The grantor must acknowledge the instrument with an acknowledgment as defined in section 64-205' - in practice, signing before a notary. And section 76-211 pulls a long lease into this machinery: 'Deeds of real estate, or any interest therein, in this state, EXCEPT LEASES FOR ONE YEAR OR FOR A LESS TIME, if executed in this state, must be signed by the grantor or grantors, being of lawful age, and be acknowledged or proved and recorded as directed in sections 76-216 to 76-237.' So a lease of a year or less is outside the recording article; a longer one is inside it. THE RELATIVES RULE, WHICH IS THE ONE NEBRASKA-SPECIFIC TRAP HERE. Ordinarily a tenant's visible possession puts a buyer or creditor on inquiry notice even without a recording. Section 76-238(2) switches that off for family tenancies: possession of agricultural or residential real estate 'by a party RELATED TO THE OWNER OF RECORD of the real estate WITHIN THE THIRD DEGREE OF CONSANGUINITY OR AFFINITY shall not serve as notice to a creditor or subsequent purchaser' where that party claims under a lease (a) entered into on or after July 16, 2004, (b) 'purporting to extend beyond a term of one year', and (c) which has not satisfied section 76-211 - unless the creditor or purchaser got a written copy of the lease before recording. Section 76-238(3)(c) spells out the third degree: parents, grandparents, great-grandparents, children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, brothers, sisters, uncles, aunts, nephews, nieces, their spouses, and partnerships, limited liability companies and corporations in which every partner, member or shareholder is so related. Section 76-238(3)(d) defines 'residential real estate' for THIS SECTION as real estate 'containing not more than four units designed for use for residential purposes' - a section-local definition that must not be carried into the landlord-tenant act, which has its own. So: if you are letting to your son, your niece or an LLC owned entirely by in-laws on a lease longer than a year, their occupancy gives a lender or buyer nothing. Acknowledge and record it, or hand the lender a written copy before it records. WHAT RECORDING DOES NOT BUY, AND THIS IS THE DISAPPOINTING PART. It does not save the lease from a foreclosure of a mortgage or trust deed that was recorded first. Section 76-1010(2) says the trustee's deed on a trust-deed sale 'shall operate to convey to the purchaser, WITHOUT RIGHT OF REDEMPTION, the trustee's title and all right, title, interest, and claim of the trustor and his or her successors in interest AND OF ALL PERSONS CLAIMING BY, THROUGH, OR UNDER THEM', including interests acquired after the trust deed was executed, and that all such interests 'shall be deemed to be terminated as of the time the trustee or the attorney for the trustee accepts the highest bid at the time of the sale.' A tenant holding under a lease you granted after the trust deed claims through you, so recording the lease changes its priority against nothing senior. THE ONE RECORDING THAT GENUINELY HELPS A TENANT is a different document: section 76-1008(1) lets 'Any person desiring a copy of any notice of default and of any notice of sale under any trust deed' file for record, at any time after the trust deed is recorded and before a notice of default is recorded, 'a duly acknowledged request for a copy of any such notice', in substantially the form the section prints; section 76-1008(2) then requires the trustee to mail the notice of default within ten days of its recording and the notice of sale at least twenty days before the sale. Without such a request the tenant gets nothing. Section 76-1008(5) is careful that filing the request 'shall not affect the title to trust property or be deemed notice to any person' that the requester claims any interest - so it is a notice subscription, not a claim. THE PRACTICAL CALL. For a month-to-month or one-year residential tenancy, do not record: there is nothing to protect and section 76-211 does not reach it. For a lease longer than a year - and above all for a lease to a relative, a lease with an option to purchase, or a lease a tenant is spending money on improvements under - acknowledge it before a notary and record it in the county where the property sits, or record a short memorandum of lease instead if you would rather not put the rent on the public record. Keep in mind that a recording is public: everything in the instrument you record is readable by anyone.

title: Nebraska Prescribes Almost Nothing a Residential Lease Must Contain - One Disclosure, and It Doesn't Even Have to Be in the Lease
bodyText: Nevada and Oregon hand a landlord a list of items every written lease must contain. Maryland requires a written lease at all above a certain term. Nebraska does neither. There is no statutory list of required lease contents, no mandatory lease form, no required recitals and - with one exception - nothing the law says the document itself must say. THE ONE AFFIRMATIVE REQUIREMENT is the owner-and-manager disclosure (§76-1417). It must be in writing at or before the start of the tenancy and kept current, and it need not be in the lease. This library's required-disclosures guidance sets out its terms, timing and the agency consequence of missing it. THERE IS ALSO NO REQUIREMENT THAT THE LEASE BE WRITTEN AT ALL, up to a year. Section 76-1414(1) says the parties 'may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law including rent, term of the agreement, and other provisions governing the rights and obligations of the parties' - may, not shall. Above one year a writing becomes a validity question rather than a content question, and this library covers it at lease-term-limitation. WHAT FILLS THE GAPS WHEN YOUR LEASE IS SILENT, which is the practical reason the absence of a content list is survivable. Section 76-1414(2): 'In absence of agreement, the tenant shall pay as rent the fair rental value for the use and occupancy of the dwelling unit.' Section 76-1414(3): rent 'shall be payable without demand or notice at the time and place agreed upon by the parties', and 'Unless otherwise agreed, rent is payable at the dwelling unit and periodic rent is payable at the beginning of any term of one month or less and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the beginning of each month', uniformly apportionable day to day. Section 76-1414(4): 'Unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy shall be week to week in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent, and in all other cases month to month.' Section 76-1410(13) defines rent as all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement, so you do not need a sentence designating fees as additional rent. Those defaults mean a thin lease is enforceable - it is just enforceable on the statute's terms rather than yours, which is a reason to write terms you care about rather than a reason to copy a statutory list. WHY THE SILENCE IS A CHOICE AND NOT AN OVERSIGHT: NEBRASKA WROTE CONTENT LISTS FOR EVERY OTHER KIND OF LETTING. Mobile home space: section 76-1482 requires 'a written explanation of utility rates, charges, and services to the prospective tenant BEFORE THE RENTAL AGREEMENT IS SIGNED unless the utility charges are to be paid by the tenant directly to the utility company' - a pre-signing content duty with no residential counterpart. Self-service storage: section 76-1605(3) requires that 'The rental agreement shall contain a statement, IN BOLD TYPE, advising the occupant: (a) Of the existence of the lien; and (b) That personal property stored in the leased space may be sold to satisfy the lien if the occupant is in default.' Rental-purchase of goods: section 69-2108 prescribes the agreement's contents and section 69-2110 caps its fees item by item. Equity-purchase of a home in foreclosure: section 76-2720 prescribes the contract's contents including, at (1)(g), 'The terms of any rental agreement or lease'. The Legislature has written mandatory contents for storage lockers, mobile home spaces, rent-to-own televisions and foreclosure-rescue contracts. It has written one sentence for a residential lease, and that sentence is about who you are and where to serve you. THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE. Because nothing is required, nothing in your lease is unenforceable for being missing - and correspondingly nothing you leave out will be supplied in your favour. Write the manager-and-owner disclosure, the rent amount, the due date and place, the term, and the rules you intend to enforce (section 76-1422 makes a rule enforceable only if the tenant had notice of it when the agreement was entered into). Then check the opposite direction, because that is where Nebraska does legislate: section 76-1415(1) voids four classes of provision - waiver of the tenant's rights or remedies under the Act, confession of judgment, an agreement to pay either party's attorney's fees, and exculpation or indemnification for the landlord's active and actionable negligence - and section 76-1415(2) lets a tenant recover actual damages and attorney's fees where the landlord 'deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited.'

title: No Clause in a Nebraska Lease Has to Be Initialed - But Two Things Do Need a Separate Signature, and One Needs Capitals and an Underline
bodyText: North Dakota makes a landlord obtain the tenant's initials next to a particular lease provision. Nebraska has no requirement of that kind for any residential lease term. No statute makes any clause depend on being initialed, separately acknowledged, or signed anywhere other than at the end of the document, and no statute makes a clause unenforceable for want of initials. If your lease has initial lines for the pet clause, the late-fee clause or the lead-based-paint addendum, they are there because you or your form supplier wanted the evidence - not because Nebraska requires them. Keep them; they are good evidence. Just do not tell a tenant the law requires them, and do not assume a missing set of initials voids anything. WHY THE SILENCE IS A DELIBERATE CHOICE: NEBRASKA KNOWS EXACTLY HOW TO WRITE AN INITIALING REQUIREMENT. Section 76-2713(4), for a foreclosure consulting contract: the contract 'shall be dated and personally signed, with EACH PAGE BEING INITIALED by each homeowner of the residence in foreclosure and the foreclosure consultant, and shall be acknowledged by a notary public in the presence of the homeowner at the time the contract is signed by the homeowner.' Per-page initials, a personal signature and a notary, all in one sentence. And section 69-2110(2)(b), for a rental-purchase of goods, lets the parties contract for a liability-damage-waiver fee only if 'The consumer has SIGNED OR INITIALED an affirmative written request to purchase the product or service after receiving a written disclosure of the cost of such product or service.' The Legislature has required initials on each page of one contract and a signature or initials on one optional charge in another. For a residential lease it has required neither, anywhere. THREE THINGS THAT DO IMPOSE A SIGNING FORMALITY, AND TWO OF THEM CAN REACH YOUR LEASE. FIRST, A SEPARATE SIGNED WRITING FOR A MAINTENANCE SHIFT IN A MULTI-UNIT PROPERTY. Section 76-1419(3)(a): a landlord and tenant of a dwelling unit other than a single-family residence may agree that the tenant perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling only if the agreement 'is entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord and IS SET FORTH IN A SEPARATE WRITING SIGNED BY THE PARTIES AND SUPPORTED BY ADEQUATE CONSIDERATION'. That is not an initialing rule, but it is stricter: a paragraph inside the lease is not a separate writing at all, however many initials sit beside it. SECOND, AN ARBITRATION STATEMENT IN CAPITALS AND UNDERLINE NEXT TO THE SIGNATURE BLOCK. Section 25-2602.02: 'The following statement shall appear in capitalized, underlined type adjoining the signature block of any STANDARDIZED AGREEMENT in which binding arbitration is the sole remedy for dispute resolution: THIS CONTRACT CONTAINS AN ARBITRATION PROVISION WHICH MAY BE ENFORCED BY THE PARTIES.' A standard-form residential lease is a standardized agreement, so if your lease makes arbitration the sole remedy, this statute reaches it - and the annotated consequence is real: 'When a contract which attempts to establish binding arbitration as the sole remedy fails to strictly comply with this section, the arbitration clause is voidable and unenforceable' (Kramer v. Eagle Eye Home Inspections, 14 Neb. App. 691, 716 N.W.2d 749 (2006)). READ THE OTHER ANNOTATION BEFORE YOU RELY ON EITHER DIRECTION, THOUGH: 'When a contract containing an arbitration clause is governed by federal law, the failure to include the statutory language of this section does not make the arbitration clause unenforceable' (Aramark Uniform & Career Apparel v. Hunan, Inc., 276 Neb. 700, 757 N.W.2d 205 (2008)). So the section bites only where the Federal Arbitration Act does not displace it, and whether it does in a given residential tenancy is not something this row resolves. The cheap course is to include the statement exactly as the section prints it, in capitals and underlined, immediately next to the signature block - it costs one line and removes the question. THIRD, AND FOR COMPLETENESS: section 76-1433 lets a landlord preserve the right to terminate after accepting rent 'unless otherwise agreed AFTER THE BREACH HAS OCCURRED', so that agreement must be a separate document signed later - no clause or set of initials in the original lease can do it, as this library's waiver-by-acceptance note explains. WHAT TO DO. There is nothing to comply with on initials. Use them where you want proof that the tenant read something that will be contested later - the pet clause, the rules list that section 76-1422(6) makes enforceable only if the tenant had notice of it when the agreement was entered into, a utility-allocation method - and keep the fully initialed copy. If arbitration is your sole remedy, add the section 25-2602.02 statement. If you are shifting maintenance in anything other than a single-family house, use a separate signed document, not initials in the lease.

title: No Minimum Type Size for a Nebraska Lease - Twenty Other Nebraska Contracts Have One, and a Lease With an Arbitration Clause Still Needs Capitals and an Underline
bodyText: New York makes small print inadmissible: a contract in type smaller than a set size cannot be received in evidence. Nebraska has nothing of that kind for a residential lease. No statute sets a minimum point size for a lease or for any clause in one, no statute makes a lease or clause inadmissible, unenforceable or void for being set too small, and no statute requires any lease term to be in bold, in capitals, in a box or on the first page. Print your lease in whatever size you like - and then read the rest of this, because the absence is narrower than it sounds in one direction and broader in another. THE ABSENCE IS REAL AND IT IS A CHOICE, NOT AN OVERSIGHT. Nebraska legislates type size constantly; it has simply never done it for a lease. Across twelve Nebraska statute chapters there are twenty sections that fix a point size or a typeface for a document, and not one of them is a residential lease. A sample, so you can see the pattern: section 76-2713(2) requires a foreclosure consulting contract to be 'printed in at least twelve-point type' and section 76-2713(5) requires a notice in that contract 'printed in at least fourteen-point, boldface type ... located in immediate proximity to the space reserved for the homeowner's signature'; sections 76-2719, 76-2720 and 76-2722 do the same for an equity purchase contract and its cancellation notice; section 76-2110 requires a ten-point boldface double-spaced statement in a condominium and time-share disclosure statement; section 76-2111(6) requires, 'In immediate proximity to the space reserved for the purchaser's signature, a conspicuous statement printed in double-spaced, boldface type of a minimum size of ten points' in a membership camping contract; sections 59-1732, 59-1742 and 59-1744 do it for seller-assisted marketing plans; section 69-2105 does it for a rental-purchase disclosure; sections 87-604 and 87-606 do it for invention development contracts; section 25-3303 does it for nonrecourse civil litigation funding; section 76-3112 does it for a private transfer fee record document. There is even a RELATIVE font rule: section 59-1730 requires a disclosure 'in type size equal to or larger than that used to depict the commercial symbol' - so the Legislature has used absolute point sizes, boldface, capitals, double-spacing, placement next to the signature line and relative sizing, in twenty places, and in none of them is the document a lease. TWO FORMATTING RULES THAT CAN STILL REACH YOUR LEASE, AND THEY ARE NOT POINT-SIZE RULES. FIRST, ARBITRATION. Section 25-2602.02: 'The following statement shall appear in CAPITALIZED, UNDERLINED type adjoining the signature block of any STANDARDIZED AGREEMENT in which binding arbitration is the sole remedy for dispute resolution: THIS CONTRACT CONTAINS AN ARBITRATION PROVISION WHICH MAY BE ENFORCED BY THE PARTIES.' No point size is specified, so this is not a type-size rule - but it is a formatting rule, it reaches 'any standardized agreement', and a standard-form residential lease is one. The annotated consequence: 'When a contract which attempts to establish binding arbitration as the sole remedy fails to strictly comply with this section, the arbitration clause is voidable and unenforceable' (Kramer v. Eagle Eye Home Inspections, 14 Neb. App. 691, 716 N.W.2d 749 (2006)). The limit, which matters just as much: 'When a contract containing an arbitration clause is governed by federal law, the failure to include the statutory language of this section does not make the arbitration clause unenforceable' (Aramark Uniform & Career Apparel v. Hunan, Inc., 276 Neb. 700, 757 N.W.2d 205 (2008)). So if arbitration is your sole remedy, put the statutory sentence in capitals and underlined right next to the signature block. It is one line and it closes the question. SECOND, IF YOU ALSO RENT STORAGE. Section 76-1605(3) requires that a self-service storage rental agreement 'shall contain a statement, IN BOLD TYPE', advising the occupant of the operator's lien and that stored property may be sold on default. Again no point size, but a mandatory bold-type recital in a letting document - which is a reminder that the right question is not 'does Nebraska set a point size' but 'does any statute condition this document on how it is formatted'. WHAT TO DO ANYWAY. Nothing is required, so this is drafting judgment rather than compliance. Print the whole lease in a size an ordinary tenant can read, and set the terms you most expect to be disputed - the rent amount and due date, the late fee, the rules you want enforced under section 76-1422(6), the lead-based-paint disclosure required by federal law - in a way that is plainly legible. The reason is not a formatting statute. It is that Nebraska construes a lease against its drafter: 'Ambiguities in a lease should be construed against the person preparing the lease' (D & R Realty v. Bender, 230 Neb. 301, 431 N.W.2d 920 (1988), annotated under section 76-1414), and a term a tenant can show was buried is a term you will be arguing about on the worst available footing.

title: Nebraska Lets You Price and Write a Month-to-Month Differently From a Twelve-Month - But Three Other Rules Do Limit How Differently You Treat Tenants
bodyText: Washington bars a landlord from imposing terms on a month-to-month tenant that are more burdensome than the terms offered for a fixed term, and caps the rent difference between the two. Oregon has its own version. Nebraska has nothing of the kind. There is no statute requiring parity between tenancy types, no cap on the premium you may charge for month-to-month, no rule that a shorter term must carry the same deposit, fees, pet policy or rules, and no requirement that you even offer both. Section 76-1414(1) is the whole of the authority you need: the landlord and tenant 'may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions NOT PROHIBITED by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law including rent, term of the agreement, and other provisions governing the rights and obligations of the parties.' A month-to-month premium is a term not prohibited. WHAT THE ACT DOES SAY ABOUT TENANCY TYPE IS ONLY ABOUT NOTICE, AND IT IS SYMMETRICAL. Section 76-1414(4): absent a definite term, the tenancy is 'week to week in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent, and in all other cases month to month.' Section 76-1437(1): either party may end a week-to-week tenancy by written notice given 'at least seven days prior to the termination date specified in the notice.' Section 76-1437(2): either party may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice given 'at least thirty days prior to the periodic rental date specified in the notice.' Note two things. The Act distinguishes the two tenancy types for notice only, and in both cases it gives the LANDLORD and the TENANT exactly the same period - so a lease clause giving the tenant a longer notice obligation than the statute gives, or giving yourself a shorter one, is a term by which the tenant forgoes a right under the Act and is unenforceable under section 76-1415(1)(a), with actual damages and attorney's fees under section 76-1415(2) if you used it deliberately. That is the one genuine parity rule in Nebraska's landlord-tenant act, and it runs between landlord and tenant, not between lease types. THREE LIMITS THAT DO CONSTRAIN DIFFERENTIAL TREATMENT, AND THEY ARE THE ONES TO WATCH. FIRST, HOUSE RULES MUST BE EVEN-HANDED. Section 76-1422 makes a rule or regulation enforceable against the tenant only if, among other conditions, '(3) It applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner', and '(2) It is reasonably related to the purpose for which it is adopted', and '(6) The tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement.' So you may charge a month-to-month tenant more rent, but a RULE - quiet hours, parking, laundry, common-area use - that bites only on the month-to-month tenants in the building is not enforceable against them. Price and terms are free; rules are not. SECOND, YOU CANNOT SHIFT MAINTENANCE TO ONE TENANT IN A WAY THAT TOUCHES ANOTHER. Section 76-1419(3)(b): an agreement that a tenant of a non-single-family unit perform specified repairs or maintenance binds the tenant only if it 'does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises.' THIRD, AND THE REAL RISK: THE DIFFERENCE MUST NOT TRACK A PROTECTED CLASS. Section 20-318(2) makes it unlawful to 'Discriminate against any person in the TERMS, CONDITIONS, OR PRIVILEGES of sale or rental of a dwelling or in the provision of services or facilities in connection therewith because of race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, sex, or military or veteran status.' A month-to-month premium is lawful; a month-to-month premium that in practice lands on one protected group is where the exposure is. And remember section 20-168 sits OUTSIDE the Fair Housing Act and its exemptions: a seller or lessor 'shall not refuse to sell or lease a dwelling ... on the basis that the individual, a member of the individual's family, or a person who will be residing with the individual is suffering or is suspected of suffering from' HIV infection or AIDS. ONE EXPRESS PERMISSION TO BE UNEQUAL, ADDED IN 2025. Section 20-322(6): 'Nothing in the act shall prohibit otherwise nondiscriminatory conduct intended to benefit veterans or servicemembers or their family members, such as providing housing limited to veterans or servicemembers or their family members, providing FAVORABLE CONDITIONS OF LOANS, LEASES, MORTGAGES, OR CONTRACTS, or otherwise offering benefits that are limited to veterans or servicemembers or their family members.' So a veteran discount, a waived fee or a shorter-notice option offered only to servicemembers is expressly safe. AND ONE DIFFERENCE YOU MUST NOT MAKE AT ALL. Section 76-1439(1) bars a landlord from retaliating 'by increasing rent or decreasing services or by bringing or threatening to bring an action for possession' after the tenant has complained to a code-enforcement agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, or 'has organized or become a member of a tenants' union or similar organization.' Section 76-1439(2) routes the tenant to the section 76-1430 remedies - three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages plus a reasonable attorney's fee - and gives a defence to your possession action, while preserving 'reasonable rent increases or changes in services notwithstanding the occurrence of' those acts. If you are moving a complaining tenant from a fixed term to a month-to-month at a higher rate, be able to show the change was the reasonable one you would have made anyway. PRACTICAL COURSE. Decide your month-to-month premium on business grounds and apply it by a written, consistent policy to every tenancy of that type in the building. Keep the rules identical across tenancy types. Put any veteran or servicemember benefit in writing and say it is offered under section 20-322(6).

title: Nebraska Caps No Residential Late Fee and Requires No Grace Period - Which Means the Only Limit Is One You Cannot Look Up
bodyText:
Minnesota caps a residential late fee at a percentage of rent. Maine, Delaware and Hawaii each set a ceiling and a mandatory grace period. Nebraska sets none of it. There is no percentage cap, no dollar cap, no mandatory grace period, no limit on how often a late fee may be charged, no disclosure formula and no requirement that the fee bear any stated relationship to your loss. The words 'late fee' and 'late charge' appear nowhere in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Your late fee is whatever the lease says, under section 76-1414(1): the parties 'may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law'.

THE SILENCE IS A CHOICE, AND THE PROOF IS TWO STATUTES AWAY. Nebraska does cap late fees - in minute detail - for a different kind of letting. Section 69-2110(1)(d), in the Consumer Rental Purchase Agreement Act: '(i) For consumer rental purchase agreements with monthly renewal dates, a late fee of NOT MORE THAN FIVE DOLLARS may be assessed on any payment not made within FIVE BUSINESS DAYS after the payment is due; (ii) For consumer rental purchase agreements with more frequent than monthly renewal dates, a late fee of NOT MORE THAN THREE DOLLARS may be assessed on any payment not made within THREE BUSINESS DAYS after payment is due; and (iii) A late fee... may be collected ONLY ONCE on any accrued payment no matter how long such payment remains unpaid, may be collected at the time it accrues or at any time thereafter, and SHALL NOT BE ASSESSED AGAINST A PAYMENT THAT IS TIMELY MADE even though an earlier late fee has not been paid in full.'

The same section caps the administrative fee at ten dollars, the delivery charge at ten or twenty-five dollars, the reinstatement fee at five dollars, and a liability-damage waiver at eight percent of the payment. That is a legislature that knows exactly how to cap a late fee on a lease of goods, and has written nothing for a lease of a home. The Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act has no late-fee cap either; neither does the Self-Service Storage Facility Act.

WHAT ACTUALLY LIMITS YOUR LATE FEE, AND YOU WILL NOT FIND IT IN A STATUTE. Nebraska's limit on an agreed sum payable on breach is the common-law rule distinguishing liquidated damages from a penalty, and that rule is judge-made: it is not codified anywhere in Nebraska's property, civil-procedure, civil-rights or consumer chapters, and no annotation in those chapters states it. This row therefore does not tell you what the Nebraska test is, because it cannot be read off the statutes - it tells you that it exists and that it is the only thing standing between your late fee and a court.

The practical consequence is the same either way: set the fee at a figure you could defend as a reasonable estimate of what a late payment actually costs you to administer, not at a figure designed to punish or to deter. A fee that grows daily without limit, or one large enough that its purpose is obviously coercive, is the one that gets tested.

THREE NEBRASKA-SPECIFIC CONSEQUENCES THAT MATTER MORE THAN THE MISSING CAP.

FIRST, YOUR LATE FEE IS RENT. Section 76-1410(13) defines rent as all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement. That helps you - an unpaid late fee is on its face rent, so it is reachable through section 76-1431(2)'s seven-calendar-day nonpayment notice - and it cuts against you, because every rule measured in rent is measured including it, starting with section 76-1416(1)'s security cap of 'one month's periodic rent'. This library covers that two-way effect at fees-as-rent.

SECOND, YOU CANNOT MAKE THE TENANT PAY YOUR LAWYER. Section 76-1415(1)(c) voids a rental-agreement provision by which the tenant 'Agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees', and section 76-1415(2) lets a tenant who was given a deliberately prohibited provision recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. So a late-fee clause must not bolt collection costs or legal fees onto the fee. Note the contrast: section 76-1431(3) gives you statutory attorney's fees where the tenant's noncompliance is willful - a statutory remedy, not a lease promise, and therefore unaffected by the ban.

THIRD, TAKING THE LATE RENT COSTS YOU THE RIGHT TO EVICT FOR THAT LATENESS, NOT THE FEE. Section 76-1433 makes acceptance of rent with knowledge of a default a waiver of the right to terminate for that breach, 'unless otherwise agreed after the breach has occurred'. The fee, the rent, the damages claim and the right to insist on timeliness in future all survive; this library's waiver-by-acceptance note sets out the mechanics and why no sentence written at signing can preserve the termination right.

PRACTICAL COURSE. Pick a flat fee you can justify as administrative cost, state a grace period even though none is required, charge the fee once per late payment rather than daily, do not compound it, and do not add collection or legal costs. Write it into the lease, because without a lease term there is no fee at all - Nebraska supplies none by default.

title: Every Liquidated-Damages Sum in Nebraska's Landlord-Tenant Law Runs Against the Landlord - and the Deposit Can Only Be Applied to Damages You Actually Suffered
bodyText: Massachusetts has a consumer-protection regulation expressly letting a landlord retain an agreed damages amount on a tenant's breach. Nebraska has no statute and no provision of its consumer or landlord-tenant law that gives you that permission. Nothing says an agreed sum is enforceable, nothing says it is not, and nothing sets a safe figure. What Nebraska does have is worth knowing precisely, because the statutory picture runs entirely the other way. THE ACT USES THE PHRASE 'LIQUIDATED DAMAGES' THREE TIMES IN A RESIDENTIAL TENANCY, AND ALL THREE ARE THE TENANT'S REMEDY AGAINST YOU. Section 76-1416(3): if you fail to return the deposit balance with a written itemization within fourteen days of the termination of the tenancy, the tenant recovers the money, court costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and if your failure 'is willful and not in good faith, the tenant may recover an amount equal to one month's periodic rent or two times the amount of the security deposit, WHICHEVER IS LESS, as liquidated damages.' Section 76-1430: if you unlawfully remove or exclude the tenant, or willfully and wrongfully cut off an essential service, the tenant 'may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, in either case, recover an amount equal to THREE MONTHS' PERIODIC RENT AS LIQUIDATED DAMAGES, and a reasonable attorney's fee' - a FIXED SUM, not a ceiling, and it requires no proof of loss. And in the Mobile Home Act, section 76-1489 mirrors the deposit penalty with the same whichever-is-less formula. There is no counterpart running in the landlord's favour anywhere in either act. THE ONE PLACE THE ACT FIXES A SUM FOR YOU IS NOT LIQUIDATED DAMAGES AND HAS TWO CONDITIONS. Section 76-1437(3): if the tenant stays on without your consent after the term ends you may bring an action for possession, and 'if the tenant's holdover is WILLFUL AND NOT IN GOOD FAITH' you may recover in addition 'an amount NOT MORE THAN three months' periodic rent OR THREEFOLD THE ACTUAL DAMAGES sustained by him, WHICHEVER IS GREATER, and reasonable attorney's fees.' Read the three qualifiers: it is a ceiling and not a fixed sum, it is unavailable unless the holdover is both willful and in bad faith, and for an ordinary holdover the Act gives you no damages measure at all. This library covers the holdover figure itself at the holdover topic. THE REAL CONSTRAINT ON AN AGREED SUM IS THE DEPOSIT STATUTE, AND IT IS EXPLICIT. Section 76-1416(2): on termination, 'property or money held by the landlord as prepaid rent and security MAY BE APPLIED TO THE PAYMENT OF RENT AND THE AMOUNT OF DAMAGES WHICH THE LANDLORD HAS SUFFERED by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or section 76-1421.' Damages the landlord HAS SUFFERED - actual, proven loss, not a figure the lease fixed in advance. A clause converting the deposit, or a stated part of it, into a non-refundable agreed sum for early termination, for cleaning, for repainting or for 'administrative costs' does not sit inside that sentence, and section 76-1416(1)'s cap applies to 'security, HOWEVER DENOMINATED', so renaming it does not take it outside the deposit rules either. Section 76-1416(3)'s penalty is what you face for getting the return wrong, and the fourteen days run from the date of termination of the tenancy, not from the tenant's demand. AND YOU CANNOT REACH AN AGREED SUM THROUGH A WAIVER. Section 76-1415(1)(a) makes unenforceable any rental agreement provision by which the tenant 'Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act', and section 76-1415(1)(c) kills any provision by which the tenant 'Agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees'. Section 76-1415(2) adds that where you 'deliberately use a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited', the tenant recovers actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. So a clause that fixes a sum and simultaneously purports to foreclose the tenant's itemization and return rights is exposed twice over. WHAT NEBRASKA'S LIMIT ON AN AGREED SUM ACTUALLY IS, STATED HONESTLY. It is the common-law rule distinguishing enforceable liquidated damages from an unenforceable penalty, and it is judge-made: it is not codified anywhere in Nebraska's property, civil-procedure, civil-rights or consumer chapters. For comparison, when Nebraska does legislate a liquidated sum it hedges it heavily - section 25-21,276(2) gives a utility 'Liquidated damages of seven hundred fifty dollars' for diversion of service, but only 'upon proof of willful or intentional' conduct, only where the act 'results in damages to the utility' under subsection (1), and only '(b) ... if the amount of actual damage or loss is NOT SUSCEPTIBLE OF REASONABLE CALCULATION' as the alternative to (a) actual damages. Even the Legislature treats an agreed sum as a fallback for unquantifiable loss, which is exactly the shape the common-law doctrine takes. PRACTICAL COURSE. Do not write a liquidated-damages clause into a Nebraska residential lease for ordinary breaches, and do not label any part of the deposit non-refundable. Where you genuinely cannot quantify a loss in advance - an early-termination fee is the usual case - state a figure that is a reasonable estimate of what the re-letting actually costs you, say in the clause that it is an estimate of actual loss and not a penalty, and keep the records that would prove it. Then collect it as a debt rather than out of the deposit, because section 76-1416(2) measures the deposit against damages you have suffered and section 76-1416(3) prices the mistake at one month's rent or twice the deposit, whichever is less, plus fees.

title: Only Two of Your Six Habitability Duties Can Ever Be Shifted to a Tenant - and Only in a Single-Family House
bodyText: New Hampshire lets a lease shift one named condition - common-area garbage removal - to the tenant, and only if the landlord first provides the containers. Nebraska's structure is different and more restrictive than most landlords assume, and the whole answer is in which subdivisions section 76-1419 names and which it does not. YOUR SIX DUTIES, AND THE TWO THAT ARE NAMED AS SHIFTABLE. Section 76-1419(1) imposes six: (a) substantially comply, after written or actual notice, with applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety; (b) make all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition; (c) keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition; (d) maintain in good and safe working order all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, 'SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED' by the landlord; (e) provide and maintain appropriate receptacles for ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste and arrange for their removal; and (f) supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat, subject to two narrow exceptions. Now the shifting provisions. Section 76-1419(2): 'The landlord and tenant of A SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE may agree that the tenant perform the landlord's duties SPECIFIED IN SUBDIVISIONS (1)(e) AND (1)(f) of this section and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, and remodeling, but only if the transaction is in writing, for good consideration, entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord.' Section 76-1419(3): 'The landlord and tenant of a dwelling unit OTHER THAN A SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE may agree that the tenant is to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling only if: (a) The agreement of the parties is entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord and is set forth in a SEPARATE WRITING SIGNED BY THE PARTIES and supported by ADEQUATE consideration; and (b) The agreement does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises.' FOUR CONSEQUENCES FALL OUT OF THAT DRAFTING, AND EACH ONE COSTS LANDLORDS MONEY. ONE: SUBDIVISIONS (1)(a), (1)(b), (1)(c) AND (1)(d) ARE NEVER SHIFTABLE, in any building, by any agreement. Subsection (2) names only (1)(e) and (1)(f). Subsection (3) names no subdivision at all. Code compliance, the fit-and-habitable duty, common areas, and the systems and appliances you supply stay yours. TWO: IN ANYTHING THAT IS NOT A SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE, (1)(e) AND (1)(f) CANNOT BE SHIFTED EITHER. Subsection (3) is the only route for a duplex, an apartment or any other non-single-family unit, and it reaches only 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling'. The Legislature wrote '(1)(e) and (1)(f)' into subsection (2) and left the words out of subsection (3). So a lease in a four-plex making the tenant responsible for taking the bins out, or for the hot water, does not shift the duty - even in a separate signed writing. THREE: WHAT SUBSECTION (3) ACTUALLY TRANSFERS IS WORK, NOT DUTY. Both subsections use the same trailing phrase - 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, and remodeling' - and only subsection (2) couples it with the words 'perform the landlord's duties specified in subdivisions (1)(e) and (1)(f)'. Read together, subsection (3) lets you assign discrete tasks to a tenant; it does not make the tenant's failure to do them your excuse. If the tenant you paid to clear the gutters does not clear them and water gets in, the section 76-1419(1)(b) duty was yours the whole time, and section 76-1419(3)(b) makes that explicit for anyone else in the building. FOUR: A PARAGRAPH IN THE LEASE IS NOT A SEPARATE WRITING. Subsection (3)(a) requires the agreement to be 'set forth in a separate writing signed by the parties'. For a single-family residence subsection (2) requires only that 'the transaction is in writing', so the lease itself will do; in a multi-unit property it will not. Note the consideration difference too: subsection (2) says 'good consideration', subsection (3)(a) says 'ADEQUATE consideration' - a different word, and the stricter one, for the multi-unit case. A rent credit stated in dollars is the safe way to satisfy it. THE OPTION MOST LANDLORDS SHOULD USE INSTEAD, WHICH THE ACT PUTS IN ONE SENTENCE. Section 76-1419(4): 'Notwithstanding any provision of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a landlord may EMPLOY A TENANT to perform the obligations of the landlord.' That is a clean, unconditional permission with none of subsection (2) or (3)'s preconditions - no single-family limit, no separate writing, no adequate-consideration test, no good-faith gate on its face. Employing the tenant to mow, shovel or clean, for pay, is the route the statute leaves open in a multi-unit building where a duty shift is impossible.
