It does not transfer the duty either, but it gets the work done lawfully and it is far harder to attack than a shift that does not qualify. TWO FURTHER LIMITS WORTH KEEPING IN VIEW. Section 76-1419(1)'s closing sentences: where a minimum housing code applies to the premises, 'the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a)' - a ceiling, not an addition - and 'The obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state.' And the duties are not limited to conditions arising after the term begins: the duties 'to comply with minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety and to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition are not limited under the plain language to conditions arising after commencement of the lease term' (Vasquez v. CHI Properties, 302 Neb. 742, 925 N.W.2d 304 (2019), annotated under section 76-1419). NEBRASKA IMPOSES NO LANDLORD PRECONDITION OF THE NEW HAMPSHIRE KIND - nothing requires you to supply the containers, the equipment or the training before a shift or an employment arrangement is valid. The conditions Nebraska imposes are all about the FORM AND FAIRNESS OF THE AGREEMENT, not about what you provide first.

title: Possession AND Rent AND Damages - But Serve the Summons the Easy Way and You Forfeit the Money Judgment
bodyText: Nebraska answers the possession-or-rent question in one sentence. Section 76-1435: 'If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord is ENTITLED TO POSSESSION AND MAY HAVE A CLAIM FOR RENT AND A SEPARATE CLAIM FOR ACTUAL DAMAGES for breach of the rental agreement and reasonable attorney's fees as provided in subsection (3) of section 76-1431.' Three things to take from it. You do not have to choose: possession, rent and damages are cumulative, not alternative. The damages claim is for ACTUAL damages for breach - not an agreed sum, not a multiple. And the attorney's fees are not a lease promise but the statutory award at section 76-1431(3), available 'If the tenant's noncompliance is WILLFUL' - which matters because section 76-1415(1)(c) voids any lease provision by which the tenant agrees to pay your attorney's fees, so the statute is the only route to them. YOU CAN SUE FOR THE MONEY WITHOUT TERMINATING, AND YOU CAN COMBINE IT - WITH A CATCH. Section 76-1431(3): 'Except as provided in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the landlord may recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for any noncompliance by the tenant with the rental agreement or section 76-1421.' That is a free-standing damages right; it does not depend on termination or on a possession action. And section 76-1441(1) lets you put the money claim in the possession complaint - the complaint 'may also contain other causes of action relating to the tenancy, BUT SUCH CAUSES OF ACTION SHALL BE ANSWERED AND TRIED SEPARATELY, IF REQUESTED BY EITHER PARTY IN WRITING.' So joining the rent claim is allowed, and either side can split it off, which means joining it does not slow the possession case but does not guarantee you a single hearing either. THE TRAP THAT COSTS LANDLORDS THE MONEY JUDGMENT. Section 76-1442.01 lets you serve the summons by posting a copy on the front door and mailing a copy by first-class mail to the tenant's last-known address, on filing an affidavit describing 'the diligent efforts made to serve the summons in the manner provided in sections 25-505.01 to 25-516.01, the reasons why such service was unsuccessful', and that posting and mailing were done. It is the practical answer to a tenant who cannot be found. But read section 76-1446: 'If the plaintiff serves the summons in the manner provided in section 76-1442.01, the action shall proceed as other actions for possession EXCEPT THAT A MONEY JUDGMENT SHALL NOT BE GRANTED FOR THE PLAINTIFF.' Posting-and-mailing buys you possession and nothing else. If the unpaid rent is worth chasing, get personal service; if it is not, post and mail and get the unit back. That is the single most consequential choice in a Nebraska eviction and it is made at the service stage, before anyone has looked at the merits. WHAT THE POSSESSION ACTION LOOKS LIKE. Section 76-1440: an action for possession of premises subject to the Act 'shall be commenced in the manner described by sections 76-1440 to 76-1447' - the Act's own procedure, not the general forcible-entry route. Section 76-1441(1): file a complaint for restitution with the clerk of the DISTRICT OR COUNTY court stating '(a) the specific statutory authority under which possession is sought; (b) the facts, with particularity, on which he or she seeks to recover; (c) a reasonably accurate description of the premises; and (d) the requisite compliance with the notice provisions' of the Act. Section 76-1446: trial 'not less than ten nor more than fourteen days after the issuance of the summons', 'by the court without a jury'; on judgment for restitution the court 'shall declare the forfeiture of the rental agreement' and, at your request, issue a writ of restitution directing the constable or sheriff to restore possession 'on a specified date not more than ten days after issuance of the writ'. And then comply with the Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act and section 76-1414(5) for anything the tenant left behind. For a termination based on violent criminal activity, illegal controlled-substance sale or other activity threatening health or safety, section 76-1441(2) requires the complaint to 'include the incident or incidents giving rise to the suit'. THE MONEY-ONLY ROUTE, AND YES THERE IS A SMALL-CLAIMS OPTION. For rent alone, with no possession sought, the Small Claims Court has 'subject matter jurisdiction in all civil actions of any type when the amount of money or damages or the value of the personal property claimed does not exceed the jurisdictional amount' (section 25-2802(1)), and section 25-2802(4) sets that amount at 'seven thousand five hundred dollars beginning July 1, 2025' - so $7,500 as things stand, exclusive of interest and costs. Jurisdiction lies where the defendant resides or does business or where the cause of action arose (section 25-2802(3)). The filing fee is six dollars and twenty-five cents (section 25-2804(2)) and notice must be served at least five days before the hearing (section 25-2804(3)). FOUR SMALL-CLAIMS RULES THAT CATCH LANDLORDS. No party may be represented by an attorney (section 25-2803(2)), so you appear yourself: 'A limited liability company shall be represented by a member, a manager, or one of its employees. A corporation shall be represented by one of its employees.' Only a party 'who has been a party to the transaction with the defendant for which the claim is brought' may file (section 25-2803(4)) - so a management company that was not a party to the lease cannot bring it. No assigned claims (section 25-2803(5)), which rules out selling the debt and having the buyer sue there. And if the tenant files a setoff or counterclaim exceeding the limit, 'the court shall cause the ENTIRE MATTER to be transferred to the regular county court docket' (section 25-2804(4)). Small claims also cannot give you a prejudgment attachment or garnishment (section 25-2804(5)). Above $7,500, or where you want a lawyer, the claim goes to county or district court. TWO LIMITS ON SELF-HELP YOU CANNOT DRAFT AROUND. Section 76-1436: 'A landlord may not recover or take possession of the dwelling unit by action or otherwise, INCLUDING WILLFUL DIMINUTION OF SERVICES to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water, or other essential service to the tenant, EXCEPT in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.' And section 76-1434 prohibits landlord liens and distraint of the tenant's property. On abandonment specifically, section 76-1432(3) requires you to 'take immediate possession' and 'make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental', and treats 'Total absence from the premises without notice to landlord for one full rental period or thirty days, WHICHEVER IS LESS' as abandonment - so the mitigation duty is real and it starts early.

title: A Nebraska Lockout for Unpaid Rent Costs You Three Months' Rent Plus the Tenant's Lawyer - and There Is No Opt-In Version
bodyText: Texas lets a landlord lock out a delinquent tenant if the lease says so, on written notice and with twenty-four-hour key access. Nebraska has no such option, no opt-in version of it, and no lease term that can create one. If the rent is unpaid your only route to the unit is the court. THE PROHIBITION, IN TWO SENTENCES. Section 76-1436: 'A landlord MAY NOT RECOVER OR TAKE POSSESSION of the dwelling unit BY ACTION OR OTHERWISE, INCLUDING WILLFUL DIMINUTION OF SERVICES to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water, or other essential service to the tenant, EXCEPT in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.' Note what the exceptions are and are not: abandonment, surrender, or the Act's own procedure. Unpaid rent is not an exception - it is a ground for the section 76-1431(2) seven-day notice and then the action for possession under sections 76-1440 to 76-1447. And section 76-1434 closes the other self-help door: '(1) A lien or security interest on behalf of the landlord in the tenant's household goods is not enforceable. (2) Distraint for rent is abolished.' So you cannot hold the goods either. WHAT IT COSTS, AND THE FIGURE IS NOT A CEILING. Section 76-1430: 'If the landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises or willfully and wrongfully diminishes services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water or other essential service to the tenant, the tenant may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, IN EITHER CASE, RECOVER AN AMOUNT EQUAL TO THREE MONTHS' PERIODIC RENT AS LIQUIDATED DAMAGES, AND A REASONABLE ATTORNEY'S FEE. If the rental agreement is terminated the landlord shall return all prepaid rent and security recoverable under section 76-1416.' Read that carefully, because it is harsher than the usual landlord assumption. It is a FIXED SUM, not a cap and not a maximum - the tenant does not have to prove any loss at all, and three months' periodic rent is what the section awards. The tenant chooses between getting back in and ending the lease, and gets the money either way. The attorney's fee is mandatory in form ('and a reasonable attorney's fee'), and if the tenancy ends you also hand back all prepaid rent and the deposit. On a $1,200 unit that is $3,600 plus fees plus the deposit, for a lockout that saved you a few weeks of court. TWO THINGS A LEASE CANNOT DO ABOUT IT. Section 76-1415(1)(a) makes unenforceable any rental agreement provision by which the tenant 'Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act' - so a clause consenting to a lockout, or waiving the section 76-1430 remedy, is void, and section 76-1415(2) adds the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees if you 'deliberately use a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited'. And section 76-1415(1)(c) voids any clause making the tenant pay your attorney's fees, so you cannot even balance the fee exposure. CUTTING OFF A UTILITY IS THE SAME OFFENCE, AND THE WORDING IS BROADER THAN PEOPLE EXPECT. Both section 76-1436 and section 76-1430 reach 'causing the interruption' as well as interrupting - so letting the account lapse, or telling the utility to disconnect, counts. The sections name 'electric, gas, water or other essential service'. Where the tenant pays a utility directly on their own account this does not reach you; where the service runs through you, it does. THE ONLY LOCK-CHANGING POWER NEBRASKA GAVE A LANDLORD IS A DUTY, NOT A REMEDY - AND IT WAS ENACTED IN 2025. Sections 76-1431.03 and 76-1431.04 require a landlord to change a tenant's locks WITHIN TWENTY-FOUR HOURS of a written request where the tenant or a household member has suffered domestic violence at the hands of someone who is not a cotenant and has obtained a protective or restraining order or a qualifying certification. Section 76-1431.04(1) prescribes how - replace the whole mechanism with one of equal or better quality, or rekey, or reset the entry code on a keyless lock. Section 76-1431.04(2) lets the tenant change the locks themselves if you do not, on notice to you and on giving you a new key or code. Section 76-1431.04(3) lets you keep a copy of the key or code, and section 76-1431.04(4) lets you 'require the tenant to pay for the ACTUAL AND REASONABLE COST incurred by the landlord in changing the locks' - actual and reasonable, so a flat lock-change fee in the lease is the wrong instrument. That is the whole of Nebraska's statute law about locks in a tenancy: a landlord obligation with a twenty-four-hour clock, and no landlord power anywhere. WHAT TO DO WHEN THE RENT IS UNPAID. Serve the section 76-1431(2) notice - written, stating the nonpayment and your intention to terminate if the rent is not paid within seven calendar days - and if it is not paid, file the complaint for restitution under section 76-1441. Section 76-1446 puts trial not less than ten nor more than fourteen days after the summons issues, and the writ of restitution then directs the constable or sheriff to restore possession within ten days. That is the fast route, and it is the only one. And if the tenant has genuinely gone, do not guess: section 76-1432(3) treats 'Total absence from the premises without notice to landlord for one full rental period or thirty days, whichever is less' as abandonment, on which you 'shall take immediate possession' and 'make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental' - and the annotation to that section warns that 'In the absence of a tenant's explicit abandonment of residential premises, legitimation of a landlord's self-help recovery of the leased premises during the first thirty days of the tenant's absence may depend on unequivocal but circumstantial proof of the tenant's abandonment' (Mason v. Schumacher, 231 Neb. 929, 439 N.W.2d 61 (1989)). Getting abandonment wrong puts you straight back into section 76-1430.

title: No Crime-Free Lease Law in Nebraska - But Two Statutes Name the Landlord by Title and Order Him to Help the Police, and a Drug House Is a Misdemeanor With No Safe Harbour
bodyText: Tennessee makes a landlord cooperate with a child-abuse investigation. Several states run statutory crime-free lease programmes. Nebraska has none of that: no crime-free lease statute, no required crime-free addendum, no general duty to report tenant activity to the police (but see the child-abuse duty below), no duty to attend a landlord-training programme, and no statutory nuisance-abatement cooperation regime. The words 'crime-free' appear nowhere in Nebraska's property, municipal, civil-procedure, criminal-procedure, civil-rights or consumer chapters. But two statutes do name the landlord expressly and require assistance, and a third creates a criminal exposure most landlords have never heard of. ONE - WIRETAP ASSISTANCE. Section 86-293(5): an order authorising interception of a wire, electronic or oral communication 'shall, upon request of the applicant, DIRECT THAT A PROVIDER, LANDLORD, CUSTODIAN, OR OTHER PERSON FURNISH TO THE APPLICANT ALL INFORMATION, FACILITIES, AND TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE necessary to accomplish the interception inconspicuously and with a minimum of interference with the services that such provider, landlord, custodian, or person is giving to the person whose communications are to be intercepted.' You are compensated 'for expenses incurred in providing such facilities or assistance at the PREVAILING RATES'. Read the next sentence carefully, because it is asymmetric: 'A PROVIDER that has received an order as provided in this subsection may, under seal, move the court to modify or quash the order on the ground that its assistance with respect to the interception cannot be performed in a timely or reasonable fashion.' The motion-to-quash right is given to a provider. The landlord is named in the duty and not in the escape. TWO - PEN REGISTER AND TRAP-AND-TRACE. Section 86-2,101(1): on request of an authorised officer, 'a provider, LANDLORD, custodian, or other person SHALL FURNISH ... FORTHWITH all information, facilities, and technical assistance necessary to accomplish the installation of the pen register' where a court has so directed under section 86-2,100. Section 86-2,101(2) does the same for a trap-and-trace device and adds that the landlord 'shall install such device forthwith on the appropriate line'. The protections here are better than in the wiretap section: section 86-2,101(3) gives reasonable compensation for reasonable expenses; section 86-2,101(4) says 'No cause of action shall lie in any court against any provider, its officers, employees, or agents, or other specified persons for providing information, facilities, or assistance in accordance with the terms of a court order'; and section 86-2,101(5) makes 'A good faith reliance on a court order, a legislative authorization, or a statutory authorization ... a complete defense against any civil or criminal action'. Both duties are gated on a COURT ORDER. An officer asking at the door, without one, is asking - not ordering - and nothing in either section authorises you to open a tenant's unit, hand over a key or disclose tenant information on request. Your entry rights come from section 76-1423 and nowhere else. THREE - THE ONE THAT SHOULD WORRY YOU: KEEPING A PLACE RESORTED TO FOR DRUGS IS A CRIME. Section 28-417(1)(e) makes it unlawful for ANY PERSON 'To keep or maintain any store, shop, warehouse, DWELLING HOUSE, BUILDING, vehicle, boat, aircraft, or place whatever WHICH SUCH PERSON KNOWS OR SHOULD KNOW IS RESORTED TO by persons using controlled substances in violation of the Uniform Controlled Substances Act for the purpose of using such substances or which is used for the keeping or selling of the same in violation of the act.' Section 28-417(2): 'Any person who violates this section shall be guilty of a Class III misdemeanor.' Three features make this the sharpest landlord-side criminal exposure in Nebraska law. The standard is 'knows OR SHOULD KNOW' - constructive knowledge, so deliberate ignorance is not a defence. The section names a dwelling house and a building in terms. And it contains no landlord safe harbour at all: nothing says a landlord who has begun eviction proceedings, or who has reported the activity, is excused. The practical answer is that acting on credible information is the protection the statute does not give you - document what you were told, and move under section 76-1431(4). FOUR - AND THE TRAP IN THE OTHER DIRECTION. Section 76-1431(4) is the fast route against criminal activity: after FIVE DAYS' written notice of termination and WITHOUT THE RIGHT OF THE TENANT TO CURE, you may sue for possession where the tenant, an occupant, a household member, a guest or another person under the tenant's control or present with the tenant's consent engages in violent criminal activity, the illegal sale of a controlled substance, or other activity threatening the health or safety of other tenants, you or your staff. But section 76-1431(5)(a) takes that route away where the activity was 'conducted by a person on the premises OTHER THAN THE TENANT OR A HOUSEHOLD MEMBER' and the tenant or household member does any one of three things: '(i) ... seeks a protective order, restraining order, or other similar relief which would apply to the person conducting such activity; (ii) ... REPORTS SUCH ACTIVITY TO A LAW ENFORCEMENT AGENCY in an effort to initiate a criminal action against the person conducting the activity; or (iii) If the activity is an act of domestic violence, ... receives certification of the activity from a qualified third party' under the federal Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act of 2013. Section 76-1431(5)(b) adds that the protection does not apply to a tenant who is a perpetrator of domestic violence, and that where both the victim and the perpetrator are parties to the rental agreement you may proceed under subsection (4) against the perpetrator only. SO A TENANT WHO CALLS THE POLICE ON A THIRD PARTY BECOMES PROTECTED FROM THE FIVE-DAY ROUTE, and a crime-free clause that treats a police call to the unit as itself a breach is pointed at exactly the conduct the statute shields. BE PRECISE ABOUT WHAT SECTION 76-1431(5) TAKES AWAY: it says 'A landlord shall not take action UNDER SUBSECTION (4) OF THIS SECTION'. It does not touch subsection (1) - the ordinary thirty-day-with-fourteen-day-cure route for a material noncompliance - or subsection (2), the seven-day nonpayment route. A clause or a letter saying the whole section does not apply, or that no termination is possible, overstates the statute. FIVE - THE ONE REPORTING DUTY THAT BINDS EVERYONE. Section 28-711(1) requires 'any physician, any medical institution, any nurse, any school employee, any social worker, the Inspector General appointed under section 50-1805, or any other person' who 'has reasonable cause to believe that a child has been subjected to child abuse or neglect' to report it to the proper law enforcement agency or to the department's toll-free number, and section 28-717 makes a willful failure to report a Class III misdemeanor. That includes you and anyone who enters units for you. The vulnerable-adult duty in section 28-372(1) is narrower: it binds listed professionals and caregivers, and anyone else 'may report'. SIX - WHAT THERE IS NO DUTY TO DO. There is no Nebraska duty to run a criminal background check, no duty to consult the sex-offender registry, and no immunity if you do or do not. Section 29-4009(1) makes registry information not confidential except for ten listed categories available only to law enforcement, including '(h) The name of any employer of a sex offender' - so you may lawfully consult the public registry, you cannot obtain those categories, and Nebraska wrote no protective-purpose limitation and no reliance immunity in either direction.

title: Nebraska Does Not Make You Carry Liability Insurance - and Because It Voids the Clause That Would Protect You Instead, You Should Carry It Anyway
bodyText: New Jersey requires a residential landlord to carry liability insurance and to register the policy with the municipality. Rhode Island requires a disclosure about it. Nebraska requires neither. No Nebraska statute obliges a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, in any amount, for any number of units; there is no minimum limit, no filing or registration of a policy, no certificate to produce, and no disclosure to the tenant about whether you have one or what it covers. Nothing in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act mentions insurance at all. THE LEGISLATURE DOES MANDATE LIABILITY INSURANCE FOR RESIDENTIAL PROPERTY - JUST NOT FOR YOU. Section 76-871(a), in the Nebraska Condominium Act: 'Commencing not later than the time of the first conveyance of a unit to a person other than a declarant, THE ASSOCIATION SHALL MAINTAIN, to the extent reasonably available: (1) Property insurance on the property including the common elements insuring against all risks of direct physical loss ... not less than eighty percent of the actual cash value ...; and (2) LIABILITY INSURANCE, INCLUDING MEDICAL PAYMENTS INSURANCE, in an amount determined by the executive board but not less than any amount specified in the declaration, covering all occurrences commonly insured against for death, bodily injury, and property damage arising out of or in connection with the use, ownership, or maintenance of the common elements.' Section 76-871(c) even requires notice to unit owners if the insurance is not reasonably available. So Nebraska knows how to write a liability-insurance mandate for residential buildings, chose to write it for condominium associations, and wrote nothing for landlords. THE ONLY INSURANCE PROVISION IN NEBRASKA'S TENANCY LAW POINTS AT THE TENANT, AND ONLY FOR MOBILE HOME SPACE. Section 76-1475(2), in the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act: 'A rental agreement MAY REQUIRE A TENANT TO MAINTAIN LIABILITY INSURANCE WHICH NAMES THE LANDLORD AS AN INSURED with respect to the mobile home space rented by the tenant. For purposes of this subsection, liability insurance shall mean insurance that protects the landlord from negligence on the part of the tenant and any invitees or guests of the tenant.' That is the only tenant-liability-insurance provision in Nebraska law, it is an express permission rather than a requirement, and it sits in the mobile-home act. The residential act has no counterpart - which does not mean you cannot ask a residential tenant for renter's liability coverage, because section 76-1414(1) lets the parties include 'terms and conditions not prohibited', but it does mean you have no statute to point at when the tenant asks why. NOW THE REASON THIS ABSENCE MATTERS MORE IN NEBRASKA THAN IN MOST STATES. The alternative to insurance is a clause disclaiming liability, and Nebraska voids it. Section 76-1415(1)(d): no rental agreement may provide that the tenant 'Agrees to the EXCULPATION OR LIMITATION of any liability of the landlord arising due to ACTIVE AND ACTIONABLE NEGLIGENCE of the landlord or to INDEMNIFY the landlord for that liability arising due to active and actionable negligence or the costs connected therewith.' Section 76-1415(2) makes such a provision unenforceable and, if you deliberately used a rental agreement containing provisions you knew to be prohibited, lets the tenant recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. And section 76-1415(1)(c) voids any clause making the tenant pay your attorney's fees, so you cannot shift the cost of defending the claim either. Note the limit of the ban - the annotation records that the Act 'applies only to residential leases and does not prohibit exculpatory clauses or limitations on the landlord's liability in commercial leases' (Bedrosky v. Hiner, 230 Neb. 200, 430 N.W.2d 535 (1988)). For a home, the clause is void. YOUR TORT EXPOSURE IS REAL AND THE ACT SAYS SO EXPRESSLY. Section 76-1419(1) ends: 'The obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state.' So the statutory habitability duties sit on top of ordinary negligence law rather than replacing it. And the duties reach further back than landlords expect - the duties 'to comply with minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety and to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition are NOT LIMITED under the plain language to conditions arising AFTER COMMENCEMENT of the lease term' (Vasquez v. CHI Properties, 302 Neb. 742, 925 N.W.2d 304 (2019), annotated under section 76-1419), so a defect that predated the tenancy is within the duty. PRACTICAL COURSE. Carry liability insurance in an amount that reflects what a serious injury claim costs, because Nebraska gives you no statutory cap, no exculpatory clause and no fee-shifting clause to fall back on. Where you do want tenant-side coverage, ask for it as a lease term under section 76-1414(1) and keep it separate from anything resembling an exculpation or indemnity for your own negligence - a clause requiring the tenant to insure AND to indemnify you for your own active and actionable negligence is void in its indemnity limb under section 76-1415(1)(d), and this library already narrows its Nebraska liability language to ordinary negligence for exactly that reason. If you own in a condominium, do not assume the association's section 76-871 policy covers you as a landlord: it covers the association, and section 76-871(d)(1) makes each unit owner an insured 'with respect to liability arising out of his or her interest in the COMMON ELEMENTS or membership in the association' - not for what happens inside the unit you let.

title: No Conservation-Charge Notice, No Submetered-Water Rules, No Monthly Dual-Reading Statement - Nebraska Regulates None of It, and the Figure Everyone Quotes Is Wrong
bodyText: South Carolina makes a landlord notify each new tenant about an energy-efficiency meter conservation charge appearing on the utility bill, or else allow a rent deduction. Alaska limits when one may be assessed on a rental at all. New Hampshire and Maine have their own versions. Kansas regulates submetered water in detail: the landlord escapes utility regulation only if it charges no more than the city or district rate, no surcharge for the meter itself is allowed, and the tenant must get a monthly statement showing both meter readings. NEBRASKA HAS NONE OF IT. There is no conservation charge in Nebraska statute, no notice duty about one, no rent-deduction remedy if notice is not given, no cap on what you may charge a tenant for submetered water, no requirement that you charge the municipal rate, no bar on a meter surcharge, and no required monthly statement or dual-reading disclosure. The phrases are simply not there: 'conservation charge' appears in no section of Nebraska's property, municipal, civil-procedure, criminal, civil-rights, commercial or consumer chapters, and neither does 'submetered water', 'water meter', 'weatherization' or 'city rate'. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS A NEBRASKA WATER CHARGE: YOUR LEASE, AND THAT IS ALL. Section 76-1414(1) lets the parties include 'terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law including rent, term of the agreement, and other provisions governing the rights and obligations of the parties.' So your allocation method - a submeter, a per-occupant split, a square-footage ratio, a flat monthly amount - is a contract term, and there is no statutory default to fall back on if you leave it out. Three Nebraska-specific consequences follow. FIRST, WHATEVER YOU CHARGE IS RENT, because section 76-1410(13) defines rent as all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement - which helps you, since an unpaid water charge is reachable by the section 76-1431(2) seven-day nonpayment notice, and hurts you, since everything measured in rent is measured including it. SECOND, YOU CANNOT SHIFT THE WATER DUTY ITSELF IN A MULTI-UNIT BUILDING. Section 76-1419(1)(f) requires you to supply running water and reasonable hot water at all times, and section 76-1419(2) permits that duty to be moved to the tenant only for a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE; section 76-1419(3), the only route for a duplex or apartment, does not name subdivision (1)(f) at all. Billing the tenant for water is not the same thing as making the water the tenant's problem, and only the first is available in a multi-unit property. THIRD, IF THE WATER STOPS, THE REMEDY IS THE TENANT'S, NOT A BILLING QUESTION: section 76-1436 and section 76-1430 together make a willful interruption of water an unlawful ouster worth three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages plus a reasonable attorney's fee. WHY THE SILENCE IS A CHOICE: NEBRASKA WROTE A UTILITY DISCLOSURE FOR ONE KIND OF TENANCY AND A PROPORTIONAL-USAGE RULE FOR ANOTHER. Section 76-1482, in the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act: 'The landlord or any person authorized to enter into a rental agreement on the landlord's behalf SHALL PROVIDE A WRITTEN EXPLANATION OF UTILITY RATES, CHARGES, AND SERVICES to the prospective tenant BEFORE THE RENTAL AGREEMENT IS SIGNED unless the utility charges are to be paid by the tenant directly to the utility company.' That is the disclosure the residential act does not have. And section 76-873(c), in the Nebraska Condominium Act, provides that 'TO THE EXTENT REQUIRED BY THE DECLARATION' certain common expenses are assessed differently, including at (c)(3) utilities not separately metered assessed in proportion to usage 'IF REASONABLY DETERMINED' - a proportional-usage rule, but a doubly conditional one, so it is not a free-standing mandate and must never be quoted as though it were. Between them the Legislature wrote a pre-signing utility disclosure for mobile home space and a conditional proportional-usage rule for condominiums, and wrote nothing for an ordinary rental. TWO THINGS THAT GET MISREAD, AND BOTH ARE WORTH GETTING RIGHT. ONE - THE UTILITY-DIVERSION STATUTES ARE NOT A BAN ON SUBMETERING. Sections 25-21,275 to 25-21,278 give a UTILITY a private action. Section 25-21,276(1) allows it only 'when such act results in damages to the utility'. Section 25-21,276(2) makes the measures available only 'upon proof of willful or intentional' conduct, and then gives '(a) The amount of actual damage or loss if the amount of the damage or loss is susceptible of reasonable calculation; OR (b) Liquidated damages of seven hundred fifty dollars IF the amount of actual damage or loss is NOT susceptible of reasonable calculation.' Three gates, and the $750 is the fallback for unquantifiable loss rather than a standing exposure. A submeter installed downstream of the utility's own revenue meter does not reduce what the utility measures or is paid, so on its face none of the three gates is met. Do not let anyone tell you Nebraska prices your submeter at $750 - but do have the work done by the utility or a licensed contractor, and keep the paperwork. Leave the utility's own meter alone: interfering with it without the supplier's consent is a Class III misdemeanor, with no damages or willfulness gate (§28-515.02(1)(d), (3)). TWO - THE 'ELECTRIC SUPPLIER' DEFINITION IS NOT ABOUT YOU. Section 70-1001.01 opens 'For purposes of sections 70-1001 to 70-1028.02' - the Nebraska Power Review Act, which allocates service territory among public power entities and certifies generation and transmission facilities - and defines at subdivision (7) 'Electric supplier or supplier of electricity' as 'any legal entity supplying, producing, storing, or distributing electricity within the state for sale at wholesale or retail.' Read in isolation that sweeps broadly enough to describe a landlord reselling power through a submeter. It is a definition serving a facility-certification and territory statute, and it makes no claim about a landlord's obligations in either direction. So: whether a Nebraska landlord who submeters electricity or water becomes a regulated supplier for any purpose is not answered by that definition. The cautious course is the obvious one - charge no more than you are billed, keep the method and the arithmetic in writing in the lease, give the tenant the readings even though no statute requires it, and ask the municipal utility or the Public Service Commission before you resell at a markup.

title: Six Separate Sources Make a Nebraska Lease Term Ineffective - and Only One of Them Carries a Penalty
bodyText:
Nebraska has no single "non-waivable rights" section. Six separate statutes, drawn from four different acts, make a lease term ineffective - and the thing landlords and drafters get wrong is assuming they all carry the same consequence. They do not. Only the first group carries a damages penalty.

THE FOUR URLTA CATEGORIES (section 76-1415(1)). No rental agreement may provide that the tenant: "(a) Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; (b) Authorizes any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement; (c) Agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees; or (d) Agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord or to indemnify the landlord for that liability arising due to active and actionable negligence or the costs connected therewith."

Read (c) again. It is BIDIRECTIONAL - "the landlord's OR TENANT'S attorney's fees" - which is a Nebraska change from the 1972 uniform text. A "mutual" or "prevailing party" fee clause is not cured by being reciprocal. It is prohibited. Take it out rather than balancing it.

AND THE PENALTY REACHES ONLY THOSE FOUR. Section 76-1415(2): "A provision prohibited by subsection (1) of this section included in a rental agreement is unenforceable. If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees." Note the opening words - "A provision prohibited by subsection (1) of this section". The actual-damages-plus-fees exposure is keyed to subsection (1) and goes no further. It has two triggers that must both be met: deliberate use, and provisions known to be prohibited. Mere inclusion makes the term unenforceable; it does not by itself cost you money.

FIFTH SOURCE: ELECTRONIC DELIVERY - AND NO PENALTY ATTACHES. Section 76-1413(9): "A landlord shall not, as part of a rental agreement or as a condition of entering into or renewing a rental agreement, require a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means." This is a prohibition on lease terms sitting outside section 76-1415, added by Laws 2025, LB185. Section 76-1415(2) does not reach it, and section 76-1413 gives itself no damages remedy - its subsection (12) attaches only to a failure under subdivision (7)(d).

SIXTH AND SEVENTH: TWO UETA RULES THAT CANNOT BE VARIED. Section 76-1413(5) routes the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act into every rental agreement notice. Inside that act, section 86-632(3) says a party who agrees to transact electronically "may refuse to conduct other transactions by electronic means. The right granted by this subsection may not be waived by agreement." And section 86-635(4) says "The requirements of this section may not be varied by agreement" - the requirements being that an electronic record satisfies a writing requirement only if it is "capable of retention by the recipient at the time of receipt", and that "If a sender inhibits the ability of a recipient to store or print an electronic record, the electronic record is not enforceable against the recipient" (section 86-635(1) and (3)). Practical consequence: a view-only tenant portal that blocks printing or saving does not deliver a writing, and no lease sentence can fix that. Neither of these two carries the section 76-1415(2) penalty either.

THE TWO DATA STATUTES, WHICH ARE NOT THE SAME AS EACH OTHER. Section 87-1110 (Data Privacy Act): "Any provision of a contract or agreement that waives or limits in any way a consumer right described in sections 87-1107 to 87-1109 is contrary to public policy and is void and unenforceable." That one is GATED - section 87-1103(1) applies the act only to a person who conducts business in Nebraska or produces a product or service consumed by Nebraska residents, AND processes or sells personal data, AND "(c) Is not a small business as determined under the federal Small Business Act, as such act existed on January 1, 2024, except to the extent that section 87-1118 applies". So most individual landlords fall outside it - but section 87-1118 reaches a small business anyway: it may not sell personal data that is sensitive data without prior consumer consent. Section 87-1110 carries no damages remedy of its own.

Section 87-805 (the 2006 data-breach act) is the opposite shape: "Any waiver of the provisions of the Financial Data Protection and Consumer Notification of Data Security Breach Act of 2006 is contrary to public policy and is void and unenforceable." ANY waiver, and there is NO small-business exemption. Section 87-803(1) reaches "An individual or a commercial entity that conducts business in Nebraska and that owns or licenses computerized data that includes personal information about a resident of Nebraska". A landlord holding tenant applications, bank details or ID scans on a computer is inside it. Do not flatten these two into one rule.

SO WHAT DOES ENFORCE THE OTHER FIVE? Section 76-1405(2): "Any right or obligation declared by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is enforceable by action unless the provision declaring it specifies a different and limited effect." That is the general enforcement hook, and it is what a tenant uses for a section 76-1413(9) term - not section 76-1415(2).

THREE THINGS YOU MAY LAWFULLY DO, AND THE LINE IS INSTRUMENT AND TIMING. (1) Settle. Section 76-1406, one sentence: "A claim or right arising under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or on a rental agreement may be settled by agreement." Section 76-1415(1)(a) bars a waiver term IN A RENTAL AGREEMENT; section 76-1406 permits settling an ACCRUED CLAIM. Same subject, different instrument and different moment. (2) Preserve a termination right after a late payment. Section 76-1433 makes acceptance of rent with knowledge of a default a waiver of the right to terminate for that breach "unless otherwise agreed after the breach has occurred" - again, after, so nothing in the lease can do it. (3) On a condominium conversion, section 76-886(f): "Any tenant may waive any provision of this section by a written instrument executed after the date of notice." That is the mirror image of the whole pattern - a statutory PERMISSION to waive, lawful only by a separate instrument executed after the date of notice.

Finally, unconscionability sits over all of it as a separate overlay: section 76-1412(1) lets a court refuse to enforce a rental agreement or any provision of it that "was unconscionable when made", and subsection (2) requires the parties be given a reasonable opportunity to present evidence on "the setting, purpose, and effect" once the issue is raised by a party or by the court itself.

title: A Tenant's Unpaid City Sewer Bill Becomes a Lien on Your Property - and No Lease Clause Stops It
bodyText:
Nebraska gives cities and villages a sewer charge that attaches to the real estate, not to the person who used the service. Section 18-509(1) lets the mayor and city council of any city, or the board of trustees of any village, set up by ordinance "a rental or use charge, to be collected from users of any system of sewerage", and then says what matters to you: "The charges shall be charged to each property served by the sewerage system, SHALL BE A LIEN UPON THE PROPERTY SERVED, and may be collected either from the owner OR the person, firm, or corporation requesting the service."

Read that disjunctive carefully. The city may go after the person who asked for service - your tenant - or it may go after you, and either way the charge is already a lien on the property. There is no statutory exemption for a non-occupying owner, no affidavit you can file to be taken out of the chain, and nothing in the section that turns on who the lease says must pay. Nebraska wrote no owner-protection proviso into this section at all.

THE SAME RULE, EXPANDED, FOR A COMMUNITY IMPROVEMENT DISTRICT. If the property sits in a community improvement district whose sanitary sewer system is connected to a city or village system, section 18-3522(5) lets the city or village collect its charge "without enacting an ordinance or adopting any resolution for such purpose" from the users and from the owners of the property served; again the charge "shall be a lien upon the property served" and "may be collected from the owner or the person, firm, or corporation using the service." It adds a second collection route: if the charge is not paid when due, the city or village may sue, "or it may be assessed against the premises served as a special assessment", with the city clerk delivering a certified copy of the ordinance to the county treasurer, who "shall collect the assessment as provided by law". That puts the tenant's unpaid sewer charge onto the property's tax collection, which is where it stops being a billing dispute and starts being a title problem.

WHAT YOUR LEASE CAN AND CANNOT DO ABOUT IT. It cannot defeat the lien - the lien arises under the ordinance and the statute, and the city is not a party to your lease. What the lease can do is give you a contractual claim against the tenant and an early warning system: make the tenant's municipal utility accounts an express obligation, require evidence of payment on request, and require notice of any shutoff or delinquency notice the tenant receives. Remember that under section 76-1410(13) "Rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement", so if you make the tenant reimburse you for a sewer charge you had to pay, that reimbursement is rent - which means non-payment runs through the seven-day nonpayment route at section 76-1431(2), and also that the amount counts against the one-month security-deposit ceiling in section 76-1416(1), which is measured in periodic rent.

ONE MORE WAY A MUNICIPAL CHARGE LANDS ON YOUR PROPERTY. It is not a utility bill, but it works the same way and catches landlords by surprise: section 18-1748 lets a city or village require the OWNER to repair or replace a sewer connection line serving the property that is "broken, clogged, or otherwise in need of repair or replacement", and the owner's duty expressly "include[s] those portions upon the owner's property and those portions upon public property or easements up to and including the point of junction with the public main." The city gives notice by registered letter or certified mail to the owner's or the owner's agent's last-known address, and "If within thirty days of mailing such notice the property owner fails or neglects to cause such repairs or replacements to be made, the city or village may cause such work to be done and assess the cost upon the property served". Subsection (2) does the same for a deteriorated driveway approach. Thirty days from mailing, to the last-known address - which is a reason to keep your address current with the city as well as with your tenant.

Practical upshot: treat a municipal sewer account on a rented Nebraska property as your own credit risk whoever is named on it. Checking the account balance before you return a security deposit is cheaper than discovering the lien later, and under section 76-1416(2) a charge the tenant was contractually obliged to pay is "the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement", which is what the deposit may be applied to - provided you deliver the written itemization within fourteen days of the date of termination of the tenancy.

CAN THE CITY REFUSE TO TURN THE WATER ON FOR YOUR NEW TENANT BECAUSE OF THE LAST ONE'S BILL? Nebraska answers that only in part, and narrowly. Section 70-1601: "No applicant for the services of a public or private utility company furnishing water, natural gas, or electricity at retail in this state shall be denied service because of unpaid bills for similar service WHICH ARE NOT COLLECTIBLE AT LAW BECAUSE OF STATUTES OF LIMITATIONS OR DISCHARGE IN BANKRUPTCY PROCEEDINGS." Read the qualifier: the protection bites only where the old bill is already uncollectible - time-barred or discharged in bankruptcy. A current, collectible arrear left by a previous occupant is outside the section, and nothing in Nebraska law stops the charge sitting on the property as a lien under section 18-509(1) in the meantime. So the practical sequence is: check the municipal account balance before you re-let, not after.

title: No Military Air Installation Disclosure in Nebraska - Even Though It Has Offutt
bodyText:
Nebraska imposes no lease disclosure for property near a military air installation, and no termination right tied to one. There is no noise-zone disclosure, no accident-potential-zone disclosure, no military-impact-district disclosure, and no distance-based trigger of any kind. That is a deliberate silence rather than an oversight, and it is worth seeing why.

NEBRASKA WROTE A STATUTORY PROPERTY DISCLOSURE AND LEFT MILITARY ZONES OUT OF IT. Section 76-2,120 requires "Each seller of residential real property located in Nebraska" to give the purchaser a written disclosure statement of the property's condition, and subsection (4) sets out what must be disclosed as a closed list: the condition of included appliances, the electrical system, the heating and cooling systems, the water system, the sewer system, all improvements and any defects materially affecting value, "Any hazardous conditions, including substances, materials, and products on the real property which may be an environmental hazard", "Any title conditions which affect the real property, including encroachments, easements, and zoning restrictions", utility connections and whether they are public, private or community, any private transfer fee obligation under section 76-3107, and carbon monoxide alarm compliance under sections 76-604 and 76-605. Military proximity, aircraft noise and accident potential zones appear nowhere on that list. The legislature built a disclosure form for Nebraska residential property, kept amending it through 2015, and never put a military air installation on it.

AND THAT STATUTE IS NOT A LEASE STATUTE ANYWAY. Section 76-2,120 is purchaser-facing. It reaches a lease only in one direction: subsection (1)(d) defines "Seller" to include an owner who sells "including lease with option to purchase", and subsection (2) says "The requirements of this section shall also apply ... to any lease with the option to purchase residential real property." So if you grant a purchase option, you are a statutory seller and owe the statement. An ordinary residential lease is outside it entirely.

THE SAME CHOICE SHOWS UP IN NEBRASKA'S OTHER DISCLOSURE STATUTES. Nebraska does write location-based disclosures - it just writes them for buyers. Section 18-3513, enacted in 2026, requires the broker or salesperson "or, if none, the owner of the real estate" to distribute a community improvement district's annual statement to "any prospective purchaser" and to obtain the PURCHASER's acknowledgment, timed to "the date on which the purchaser becomes obligated to purchase". Section 31-727.03 does the equivalent for sanitary and improvement districts. Both are purchaser-side only. Twice, fifty years apart, the legislature wrote a location disclosure, picked its audience, and left tenants out.

WHAT THIS MEANS IF YOU RENT NEAR AN INSTALLATION. First, nothing is required - no disclosure, no acknowledgment, no termination right. Second, the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act termination right your lease already references is a servicemember protection, not a noise disclosure, and it is triggered by orders rather than by location. Third, a voluntary disclosure is still worth considering as a practical matter: aircraft noise and overflight are exactly the kind of condition a tenant will complain about in month two, and section 76-1412 lets a court examine "the setting, purpose, and effect" of a rental agreement for unconscionability when the issue is raised. A short, factual, non-promissory sentence identifying known overflight or noise - with no representation about its level or frequency - costs nothing and removes the surprise. Do not dress it up as a statutory disclosure, because there is no statute behind it, and do not pair it with a waiver: section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant "Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies" under the landlord-tenant act, so a noise-complaint waiver would be both unenforceable and, if used deliberately and knowingly, exposure under section 76-1415(2).

Finally, be careful with municipal rules, which this guidance does not cover. Cities and villages may zone, and section 18-1720 lets them "define, regulate, suppress, and prevent nuisances" within their corporate limits and extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction. Airport and installation compatibility zoning in Nebraska is a local and aeronautics-chapter subject, so if your property sits under an approach corridor, check the city or county zoning overlay - not the landlord-tenant act.

title: Suing a Minor Tenant in Nebraska - A Guardian Must Be Appointed First, and the Judgment Stays Open Until Age Twenty-One
bodyText:
Nebraska does not bar you from naming a minor as a defendant in a possession action. It does something more awkward: it makes the case unworkable until a guardian is appointed, and it leaves the judgment open to attack for years afterwards.

A MINOR MUST BE DEFENDED BY A GUARDIAN FOR THE SUIT. Section 25-309: "Except as provided by the Nebraska Probate Code and section 43-104.05, the defense of an infant must be by a guardian for the suit, who may be appointed by the court in which the action is prosecuted, or by a judge thereof, or by a county judge. THE APPOINTMENT CANNOT BE MADE UNTIL AFTER SERVICE OF THE SUMMONS in the action as directed by this code." Note the sequencing - you serve first, and only then can anyone ask for a guardian. In a summary possession action that is running on a short statutory clock, that is a real scheduling problem, and it is yours to solve.

WHO ASKS, AND WHEN. Section 25-310: "The appointment may be made upon the application of the infant, if he be of the age of fourteen years, and apply within twenty days after the return of the summons. If he be under the age of fourteen or neglect so to apply, the appointment may be made upon the application of any friend of the infant, OR ON THAT OF PLAINTIFF IN THE ACTION." So the fourteen-year-old defendant gets twenty days from the return of the summons to apply, and if the minor does not, the plaintiff - you - may apply. Plan on doing it rather than waiting.

AND THE JUDGMENT IS NOT FINAL THE WAY YOU THINK. Section 25-1317: "It shall not be necessary to reserve, in a judgment or order, the right of an infant to show cause against it after his attaining twenty years of age; but in any case in which, but for this section, such reservation would have been proper, the infant, WITHIN ONE YEAR AFTER ARRIVING AT THE AGE OF TWENTY YEARS, may show cause against such order or judgment." So a money judgment against a minor tenant is exposed until a year after the minor turns twenty, and the judgment does not have to say so for that to be true. A limitation period runs the same way: section 25-213 gives a person who was "within the age of twenty years" when the cause of action accrued the full statutory period measured "after such disability is removed".

THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE, WHICH IS A LEASING DECISION RATHER THAN A LITIGATION ONE. Everything above is why a minor should not be your only contracting tenant. If you want to rent to a young adult whose majority you have not confirmed, put an adult of full age on the lease as a co-tenant or guarantor who is jointly and severally liable. That gives you a defendant whose defense needs no guardian, whose judgment is final when entered, and against whom collection does not wait for a birthday. Nebraska lets you do this: section 76-1414(1) says "The landlord and tenant may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law including rent, term of the agreement, and other provisions governing the rights and obligations of the parties."

TWO TRAPS ABOUT AGE NUMBERS. First, do not borrow an age threshold from a statute written for another purpose. The numbers in Nebraska's code are section-local: section 25-310 turns on fourteen, sections 25-213 and 25-1317 turn on twenty, and section 28-807(1) defines "Adult" as eighteen or older for the obscenity chapter alone. None of those is the age of majority. Second, the age of majority itself is nineteen. Section 43-2101(1): "All persons under nineteen years of age are declared to be minors, but in case any person marries under the age of nineteen years, his or her minority ends."

THE EIGHTEEN-YEAR-OLD EXCEPTION, WHICH MATTERS FOR LEASING. Section 43-2101(2)(a)(i) lets a person "Eighteen years of age or older and who is not a ward of the state" "Enter into a binding contract or lease of whatever kind or nature and shall be legally responsible for such contract or lease." So an eighteen-year-old who is not a state ward can sign a binding lease. A married person under nineteen is no longer a minor at all.

No statute says whether that eighteen-year-old is still an "infant" who must be defended by a guardian for the suit under section 25-309. Only a court could settle it. Take the cautious course: if a tenant is eighteen and not yet nineteen, plan to apply for a guardian for the suit after service. Better still, add a co-tenant or guarantor who is nineteen or older. If the tenant is under eighteen and unmarried, or is a ward of the state, use the adult co-signer instead of relying on capacity.

One thing Nebraska does NOT have: any statute barring a minor from being named as an eviction defendant, and no capacity rule written for residential leases alone. Section 43-2101(2)(a)(i)'s eighteen-year rule covers any "contract or lease of whatever kind or nature". Beyond it, the capacity question is handled by general law, which section 76-1403 preserves - "Unless displaced by the provisions of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the principles of law and equity, INCLUDING THE LAW RELATING TO CAPACITY TO CONTRACT, ... supplement the act's provisions."

title: Nebraska's Seven-Day Nonpayment Notice - What It Must Say, How You May Deliver It, and Why You Cannot Tape It to the Door
bodyText:
Nebraska's nonpayment notice is short, has no prescribed form, and has one delivery trap that invalidates more notices than anything else.

WHAT THE STATUTE ACTUALLY REQUIRES. Section 76-1431(2) is one sentence: "If rent is unpaid when due and the tenant fails to pay rent within seven calendar days after written notice by the landlord of nonpayment and his or her intention to terminate the rental agreement if the rent is not paid within that period of time, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." So the notice must be (1) written, (2) of the nonpayment, and (3) of your intention to terminate if the rent is not paid within that period. Seven CALENDAR days, not business days. Nothing else is required: no statutory wording, no bold or conspicuous type, no point size, no agency form, no itemization requirement, no statement of tenant rights, no recital of where to get legal help, and no proof-of-delivery filing before you may sue.

STATE THE INTENTION, NOT JUST THE ARREARS. The commonest defective notice in a no-prescribed-form state is a demand for money that never says what happens next. Section 76-1431(2) requires notice of nonpayment AND of your intention to terminate if it is not paid within the period. A notice that only states the balance has not given the statutory notice. Say the amount, say that it must be paid within seven calendar days after the notice, and say that you intend to terminate the rental agreement if it is not.

HOW YOU MAY DELIVER IT. Section 76-1413(2)(c) sets out the only three ways a tenant RECEIVES a notice: "(i) Delivered in hand to the tenant; (ii) Mailed to the tenant at the place held out by the tenant as the place for receipt of the communication, or in the absence of such designation, to the tenant's last-known place of residence; or (iii) Delivered by electronic means." POSTING ON THE DOOR IS NOT ON THAT LIST. Nebraska knows how to authorize door-posting, and did - for the court summons only. Section 76-1442.01 permits service of the summons "by posting a copy on the front door of the dwelling unit and mailing a copy by first-class mail to the defendant's last-known address", and only when authorized by section 76-1442, and only on an affidavit "describing the diligent efforts made to serve the summons" the ordinary way and why that failed - and if you use it, section 76-1446 says "a money judgment shall not be granted for the plaintiff." None of that reaches your pre-suit nonpayment notice. Deliver that in hand or by mail.

ELECTRONIC DELIVERY IS AVAILABLE BUT CONDITIONAL. Section 76-1410(18), added in 2025, says "Writing or written, when used in reference to a notice or document to be provided by or to a landlord or tenant, includes a notice or document provided by electronic means in accordance with section 76-1413." So an emailed nonpayment notice can be a written notice - but only if the tenant has affirmatively consented under section 76-1413(7) after receiving the prescribed disclosures, and only if the consent has not been withdrawn. And you cannot engineer that consent: section 76-1413(9) says "A landlord shall not, as part of a rental agreement or as a condition of entering into or renewing a rental agreement, require a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means." If the tenant has not separately consented, email is not delivery.

FOUR THINGS NEBRASKA DOES NOT GIVE YOU, EACH OF WHICH EXISTS SOMEWHERE ELSE. (1) THE LEASE CANNOT BE THE NOTICE. Several states let a conspicuously worded lease paragraph serve as the statutory nonpayment notice. Nebraska has no such provision, and section 76-1431(2)'s notice is triggered by the nonpayment - a document signed at move-in cannot give notice of a default that has not happened. (2) THE LEASE CANNOT SHORTEN OR WAIVE THE SEVEN DAYS. Section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant "Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act", and section 76-1415(2) adds actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees where a landlord deliberately uses a provision known to be prohibited. There is no portfolio-size or property-type exception of the Colorado kind. (3) THERE IS NO ONCE-PER-TWELVE-MONTHS LIMIT ON THE TENANT'S TENDER DEFENCE, and no move-in eviction acknowledgment that unlocks a faster track. (4) THERE IS NO NOTICE-SERVICE FEE, in either direction - Nebraska neither authorizes you to charge one nor bans one, which is covered separately.

TWO POINTS THAT WORK IN YOUR FAVOUR. First, "rent" is broad: section 76-1410(13) says "Rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement", so a fee the lease obliges the tenant to pay you is itself rent that can be the subject of a section 76-1431(2) notice. Second, if the tenant counterclaims in the possession action and the counterclaim "is without merit and is not raised in good faith", section 76-1428(1) lets you recover reasonable attorney's fees - a statutory award, not a lease term, so it does not collide with the attorney-fee-clause ban.

Finally, keep the nonpayment route separate from the lease-breach route. A material breach of the lease or of section 76-1421 runs on section 76-1431(1)'s different clock - fourteen days to cure, termination no sooner than thirty days after receipt - and nonpayment is not a breach you process that way.

title: A Nebraska Lease Cannot Shorten or Waive the Notice to Quit - and the Three-Day Notice You May Have Heard About Does Not Apply to You
bodyText:
Some states let a lease shorten the statutory notice to quit, or let the tenant waive it outright in prescribed type. Nebraska is not one of them, and the reasoning is worth having because the landlord-tenant act and the old forcible-entry statutes sit next to each other and are easy to mix up.

THE NOTICE PERIODS ARE STATUTORY RIGHTS, SO A WAIVER IS VOID. Section 76-1415(1)(a): no rental agreement may provide that the tenant "Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act." The notice periods are rights under the act - seven days to cure nothing on a week-to-week termination and thirty days on a month-to-month termination under section 76-1437(1) and (2); fourteen days to cure with termination no sooner than thirty days after receipt under section 76-1431(1); seven calendar days to pay under section 76-1431(2); five days with no cure right on the violent-criminal-activity route under section 76-1431(4). A lease sentence cutting any of those, or having the tenant give them up, is unenforceable under section 76-1415(2) - and if you deliberately use a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant "may recover actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees." Nebraska wrote no portfolio-size exception, no single-family exception, and no bold-type waiver route.

NOW THE THREE-DAY NOTICE, WHICH IS WHERE PEOPLE GO WRONG. Section 25-21,221 says "It shall be the duty of the party, desiring to commence an action under sections 25-21,219 to 25-21,235, to notify the adverse party to leave the premises ... This notice shall be served at least three days before commencing the action by leaving a written copy with such adverse party, or at his usual place of abode, if he cannot be found. Where the defendant or his usual place of abode cannot be found in the county where the premises are located, such notice may be served by leaving such notice at or posting it on the detained premises." That is a real Nebraska notice to quit - and it is not yours. It is keyed to "an action under sections 25-21,219 to 25-21,235", and section 25-21,219 closes with "This section shall not apply to actions for possession of any premises subject to the provisions of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act."

Read that non-application clause precisely: it says "THIS SECTION shall not apply", not that the whole range does not apply. The reason the three-day duty still does not attach to your residential case is different - section 25-21,221's own trigger is an action under sections 25-21,219 to 25-21,235, and a residential possession action is brought under sections 76-1441 and following instead. Do not reason from the non-application clause to the whole chapter; reason from each section's own trigger.

AND ONE PLACE WHERE THE ACT OVERRIDES CHAPTER 25 EXPRESSLY. Section 76-1431(4) opens "Notwithstanding subsections (1) and (2) of this section or section 25-21,221, and except as provided in subsection (5) of this section, a landlord may, after five days' written notice of termination of the rental agreement and without the right of the tenant to cure the default, file suit ...". That is an override, not an importation - it is there to make clear that the five-day violent-criminal-activity route is not slowed down by the three-day duty, and it is not evidence that section 25-21,221 otherwise applies to residential cases.

THINGS NOT TO PUT IN THE LEASE, BECAUSE THEY ARE DEAD WEIGHT OR WORSE. A clause purporting to shorten any statutory notice period: void. A clause in which the tenant waives notice to quit, however conspicuously typed: void. A clause reciting that the tenant waives a jury in a possession action: pointless, because section 76-1446 says "The action shall be tried by the court without a jury" - there is no jury to waive, and promising the tenant a jury-related procedure in a possession action promises something that does not exist. (Note the contrast: section 25-21,219 does mention "The court or the jury, as the situation warrants", which is exactly why the two regimes must not be blended.) A clause authorizing anyone to confess judgment: separately prohibited by section 76-1415(1)(b).

WHAT YOU CAN DO INSTEAD, AND IT IS NOT NOTHING. Section 76-1406: "A claim or right arising under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or on a rental agreement may be settled by agreement." Once a default has occurred you may settle it, including by agreeing a move-out date with the tenant - and section 76-1433 recognises the same timing logic, making acceptance of rent with knowledge of a default a waiver of your right to terminate for that breach "unless otherwise agreed after the breach has occurred." The line throughout is instrument and timing: a term in the rental agreement is prohibited; a separate agreement about an accrued claim is permitted.

title: No Nebraska Rule on Charging the Tenant for Serving a Notice - Which Does Not Mean You Should Draft One
bodyText:
Some states cap what a landlord may charge for serving a notice to quit, and some ban the charge outright. Nebraska does neither. There is no statute authorizing a notice-service, posting, delivery or default-letter fee, and none prohibiting one. That silence is worth understanding before you write a fee into a lease, because three other Nebraska rules reach the charge anyway.

FIRST, IF AN ATTORNEY IS INVOLVED, THE CLAUSE IS VOID. Section 76-1415(1)(c) prohibits any rental agreement providing that the tenant "Agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees." It is bidirectional on its face - a mutual or prevailing-party version is not cured by being reciprocal - and section 76-1415(2) makes the provision unenforceable, with the tenant able to recover "actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees" if you deliberately use a provision known to be prohibited. So a lease clause charging the tenant for a demand letter or notice prepared or served by your lawyer is exactly the prohibited term, however it is labelled. A "notice preparation fee" that is in substance the attorney's bill does not escape by being renamed.

SECOND, WHATEVER YOU DO CHARGE IS RENT - WITH CONSEQUENCES ON BOTH SIDES. Section 76-1410(13): "Rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement." In your favour, an unpaid notice fee is on its face rent, so it can be the subject of the seven-calendar-day nonpayment notice under section 76-1431(2). Against you, it is swept into every rule measured in rent - including the security deposit ceiling, which section 76-1416(1) measures as "one month's periodic rent", and the holdover and ouster measures.

THIRD, THE FEE IS TESTABLE FOR UNCONSCIONABILITY. Section 76-1412(1) lets the court, as a matter of law, refuse to enforce a rental agreement or any provision of it "was unconscionable when made", enforce the remainder without it, or limit its application; subsection (2) requires that once the issue is raised by a party or by the court on its own motion, the parties get "a reasonable opportunity to present evidence as to the setting, purpose, and effect of the rental agreement or settlement". A notice fee that plainly exceeds any real cost of a stamp and an envelope is the kind of charge that invites the inquiry, and a Nebraska landlord has no statutory safe harbour to point at because the legislature set no figure.

WHAT NEBRASKA DOES GIVE YOU, AND IT IS BETTER THAN A LEASE FEE. Statutory fee awards, which the court applies regardless of what the lease says and which therefore do not collide with the section 76-1415(1)(c) ban. Section 76-1428(1): in an action for possession based on nonpayment, or an action for rent where the tenant is in possession, "If the defense or counterclaim by the tenant is without merit and is not raised in good faith, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney's fees." Section 76-1431(3): "If the tenant's noncompliance is willful, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney's fees." Section 76-1437(3): on a willful, bad-faith holdover, not more than three months' periodic rent or threefold actual damages, whichever is greater, "and reasonable attorney's fees." Court costs follow the judgment under ordinary practice.

THE CAUTIOUS COURSE. Do not draft a notice-service fee. Nothing authorizes it, it converts into rent, it is exposed to the unconscionability inquiry, and if the notice came from a lawyer the clause is prohibited outright. If you want the cost of serving notices covered, price it into rent, where it is lawful, visible and inside the figures every other rule is measured against. If you want something from the lease, ask for the thing Nebraska actually permits: an obligation on the tenant to keep a current address "held out by the tenant as the place for receipt of the communication" in the words of section 76-1413(2)(c)(ii), which is what makes a mailed notice effective and is worth more to you than a fee.

title: Nebraska Has No Way to Make Money Nonrefundable by Saying So - "However Denominated" Is the Whole Problem
bodyText:
In several states a fee is outside the security-deposit rules if the lease says in writing that it is nonrefundable. Nebraska gives you no such switch. There is no statute permitting a nonrefundable designation for residential up-front money, no notice or acknowledgment requirement for one, and - the point that matters - a label does not change the character of the money.

THE OPERATIVE WORDS. Section 76-1416(1): "A landlord may not demand or receive SECURITY, HOWEVER DENOMINATED, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent, except that a pet deposit not in excess of one-fourth of one month's periodic rent may be demanded or received when appropriate, but this subsection shall not be applicable to housing agencies organized or existing under the Nebraska Housing Agency Act." "However denominated" is an anti-labelling instruction aimed squarely at this practice. Nebraska uses that phrase in only a handful of places in the whole code, and section 76-1416 is the landlord-tenant one. A lease sentence declaring money nonrefundable is a denomination. It is the thing the statute says it will look past.

AND THE LEGISLATURE KNEW HOW TO WRITE THE OPPOSITE RULE, BECAUSE IT DID - SOMEWHERE ELSE. The word "nonrefundable" appears in exactly three sections of the twelve chapters searched, and all three are in the Rental-Purchase Agreement Act, which governs rent-to-own goods rather than housing. Section 69-2110(1)(a) permits "An initial nonrefundable administrative fee of not more than ten dollars"; section 69-2104(1)(i) requires the lessor to itemize "any initial nonrefundable administrative fee or delivery charge" in its disclosures; and section 69-2103(11) folds that fee into the total of payments to acquire ownership. So Nebraska has a nonrefundable-fee permission, a dollar cap on it, and a disclosure duty for it - written for consumer goods leasing, and deliberately not written into the residential landlord-tenant act. A silence next to a legislature that wrote the same rule next door is a choice, not a gap.

WHAT FOLLOWS FOR YOUR LEASE. Treat every dollar you take before or at move-in that secures the tenant's performance or secures you against damage as security inside the section 76-1416(1) ceiling of one month's periodic rent, whatever you call it. Cleaning fee, redecorating fee, administrative fee, move-in fee, key deposit, nonrefundable pet fee: if its function is security, the ceiling counts it. And remember the ceiling is measured in "one month's PERIODIC rent" while section 76-1410(13) defines rent as "all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement" - so you cannot inflate the ceiling by adding fees to the rent line either, at least not safely; the Act does not define "periodic rent", and the library's fees-as-rent guidance flags that the point is unresolved in both directions.

THE RETURN MACHINERY APPLIES TO ALL OF IT. Section 76-1416(2) requires that on termination "The balance, if any, and a written itemization shall be delivered or mailed to the tenant within fourteen days after THE DATE OF TERMINATION OF THE TENANCY" - not from the tenant's demand. If you treated part of the money as nonrefundable and therefore itemized nothing for it, you have a section 76-1416(2) failure on your hands, and section 76-1416(3) gives the tenant "the property and money due him or her, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees", plus liquidated damages of one month's periodic rent or twice the deposit, whichever is less, if the failure was willful and not in good faith.

THE LAWFUL WAY TO GET RECURRING NON-RETURNABLE MONEY. Charge it as rent rather than as an up-front fee. Section 76-1414(1) lets the parties agree "terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law including rent", and rent, once earned, is not refundable because it was never security. Monthly pet rent, monthly parking rent and a higher base rent all sit outside section 76-1416(1) entirely. An up-front "nonrefundable fee" does not.

ONE GENUINELY OPEN POINT, WHICH THIS GUIDANCE DOES NOT PRETEND TO SETTLE. Section 76-1416(1)'s pet-deposit exception is qualified by the words "when appropriate", and the Act says nothing about what makes a pet deposit appropriate. Whether an up-front nonrefundable pet FEE is "security, however denominated" that must sit inside the caps, and what "when appropriate" requires, are construction questions Nebraska's statute does not answer on its face. The cautious course is the one above: treat all up-front pet money as security inside both caps, and use recurring pet rent for anything you do not intend to return.

title: No Separate-Document Requirement for Up-Front Fees in Nebraska - and the One Place the Act Does Demand a Separate Writing
bodyText:
Some states say a nonrefundable fee counts only if it is disclosed in a separate written notice, or in a document the tenant signs apart from the lease. Nebraska has nothing of the kind - no separate notice, no separate signature line, no acknowledgment, no prescribed heading and no type size. There is also nothing to disclose in a separate document, because Nebraska does not recognise a nonrefundable designation for residential up-front money at all: section 76-1416(1) limits "security, however denominated" to one month's periodic rent, with a pet deposit of up to one-fourth of one month's periodic rent "when appropriate". A separate-notice rule presupposes a designation that works, and Nebraska does not have one.

THE ABSENCE IS DEMONSTRATED BY THE ONE PLACE THE ACT USES THE DEVICE. Nebraska's landlord-tenant act does demand a separate writing - exactly once, and for something else entirely. Section 76-1419(3)(a): a landlord and tenant of a dwelling unit other than a single-family residence may agree that the tenant perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling only if "The agreement of the parties is entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord and IS SET FORTH IN A SEPARATE WRITING SIGNED BY THE PARTIES and supported by adequate consideration". Searching all twelve chapters held, the phrase "separate writing" occurs in only two sections, and section 76-1419 is the landlord-tenant one. So the legislature had the separate-writing device in hand, used it for maintenance delegation where it wanted a document the tenant could not miss, and used it nowhere in the deposit section. Section 76-886(f) shows the same instinct in the Condominium Act - a conversion tenant may waive the section's protections only "by a written instrument executed after the date of notice".

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD, AND WHY A SEPARATE PAGE IS STILL A GOOD IDEA. Nothing requires it, so treat it as drafting hygiene rather than compliance. Put every dollar the tenant pays before or at move-in on one itemized schedule in or attached to the lease: the security deposit, the pet deposit, prepaid rent, and any first-month proration. Then check the arithmetic against both section 76-1416(1) ceilings. That schedule is what you will need fourteen days after the tenancy ends, when section 76-1416(2) requires the balance and "a written itemization" to be delivered or mailed to the tenant "within fourteen days after the date of termination of the tenancy" - and the itemization is far easier to write if the intake was itemized in the first place.
