TWO THINGS NOT TO DO. Do not use a separate document to try to put money outside the deposit rules; a separate page is still a denomination, and section 76-1416(1) looks past denominations. And do not pair the schedule with a waiver or acknowledgment that the tenant gives up any deposit right - section 76-1415(1)(a) voids a term by which the tenant "Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies" under the act, and section 76-1415(2) adds the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees where a landlord deliberately uses a provision known to be prohibited. A signature on a separate sheet does not change that analysis; if anything it makes deliberate use easier to prove.

title: No Nonresident-Landlord Agent Rule in Nebraska - but Two Other Sections Do the Same Work, and One of Them Bites
bodyText:
Nebraska has no statute that singles out an out-of-state owner. There is no requirement to name an in-state agent in every lease, no bar on an individual owner suing until a designation is filed, no registration for nonresident individual landlords, and nothing of that kind tucked into a receivership or code-enforcement chapter. An out-of-state company is different (see the last paragraph). What Nebraska has instead is a disclosure duty that applies to every landlord and happens to answer the same question - plus a long-arm statute that makes the whole worry about reaching an absent owner largely academic.

THE DUTY EVERY LANDLORD HAS, WHICH IS WHERE AN OUT-OF-STATE OWNER COMPLIES. Section 76-1417(1): "The landlord or any person authorized to enter into a rental agreement on his or her behalf shall disclose to the tenant IN WRITING AT OR BEFORE THE COMMENCEMENT OF THE TENANCY the name and address of: (a) The person authorized to manage the premises; and (b) An owner of the premises or a person authorized to act for and on behalf of the owner FOR THE PURPOSE OF SERVICE OF PROCESS and for the purpose of receiving and receipting for notices and demands." Read (b) again. It is the in-state agent requirement, written as a disclosure rather than as a filing, and it reaches you whether you live in Omaha or Phoenix. You may name yourself, if you are willing to be served; the statute does not require the person named to be a Nebraska resident. Subsection (2) adds that "The information required to be furnished by this section shall be kept current and this section extends to and is enforceable against any successor landlord, owner, or manager."

THE CONSEQUENCE OF NOT DOING IT IS THE PART THAT SHOULD WORRY AN ABSENTEE OWNER. Section 76-1417(3): "A person who fails to comply with subsection (1) of this section BECOMES AN AGENT OF EACH PERSON WHO IS A LANDLORD for the purpose of: (a) Service of process and receiving and receipting for notices and demands; and (b) PERFORMING THE OBLIGATIONS OF THE LANDLORD under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and under the rental agreement AND EXPENDING OR MAKING AVAILABLE FOR THE PURPOSE ALL RENT COLLECTED FROM THE PREMISES." If you own from out of state through an on-site manager and the disclosure is not made, your manager becomes your statutory agent not just for service but for performing your obligations and for spending your rent on them. Section 76-1410(7) reinforces the point from the other side: "Landlord means the owner, lessor, or sublessor of the dwelling unit or the building of which it is a part, and it also means A MANAGER OF THE PREMISES WHO FAILS TO DISCLOSE as required by section 76-1417." Keep the disclosure current and in writing, and keep it current on every renewal and every change of manager.

YOU ARE REACHABLE IN NEBRASKA ANYWAY. Section 25-536 lets a Nebraska court exercise personal jurisdiction over a person who acts directly or by an agent, as to a cause of action arising from the person "(e) HAVING AN INTEREST IN, USING, OR POSSESSING REAL PROPERTY IN THIS STATE". Owning a rental house in Nebraska is that, so a nonresident owner is suable here without any designation, and section 25-540 sets out how service outside the state may be made. That is why Nebraska never needed a nonresident-agent statute: the long-arm reaches the owner directly.

THERE IS AN OPTIONAL DESIGNATION, AND IT EXISTS FOR YOUR BENEFIT, NOT THE TENANT'S. Section 25-528 lets "any person, association or corporation, owning or claiming any interest in or lien upon any real estate lying within this state" file with the register of deeds of the county where the land lies a written appointment of "some person, who shall be a resident of the county in which said lands lie, upon whom process may be served in any suit, action or proceeding, concerning or affecting such real estate". The appointment is acknowledged like a deed and must "specifically describe the lands affected", and once filed, "No service made by publication shall be valid in respect to any such owner or claimant". So the real effect is that an absentee owner who files one cannot be proceeded against by publication - a protection against losing a case you never heard about. It may be revoked, in writing, acknowledged and recorded the same way. This is permissive. Nothing requires it and no lease has to mention it.

INCOME-TAX WITHHOLDING. Nothing in the landlord-tenant act or the civil procedure chapter imposes a duty on a tenant or a property manager to withhold Nebraska income tax on rent paid to a nonresident owner; check the revenue chapter separately. ONE THING THAT DOES BITE AN OUT-OF-STATE COMPANY. Section 21-157(b): "the ownership in this state of income-producing real property ... constitutes transacting business in this state." So an out-of-state LLC that owns a Nebraska rental must qualify with the Secretary of State and obtain a certificate of authority (section 21-155(b)), and until it does it "may not maintain an action or proceeding in this state" - including an eviction - although its leases stay valid and it may defend a suit (section 21-162(a), (b)). An out-of-state corporation transacting business here "may not maintain a proceeding in any court in this state until it obtains a certificate of authority", a court may stay its case, and it owes a civil penalty of five hundred dollars a day, up to ten thousand dollars a year (section 21-2,204(a), (c), (d)); for a corporation, owning property "without more" is not transacting business (section 21-2,203(b)(9)), so whether renting it out is more is a case-law question. Get the certificate before you need to file.

title: Nothing Extra Goes in a Nebraska Notice to Vacate - and No Rule Freezes the Unit While One Is Pending, With One Exception
bodyText:
Nebraska adds nothing to a notice to vacate beyond what the section creating the notice asks for. There is no required statement of tenant rights, no legal-aid or agency contact, no reason requirement, no prescribed heading or type size, no state-agency form to attach, no proof-of-delivery filing before you may sue, and no required recital of where the tenant may get the deposit back. Each notice contains what its own section says and nothing more. The phrase "notice to quit" does not even appear in Nebraska's residential act - searching all twelve chapters examined, it occurs once, in the old forcible-entry chapter at section 25-21,221, which does not apply to a residential possession action.

WHAT EACH NOTICE DOES HAVE TO CONTAIN. Section 76-1437(1): a week-to-week tenancy ends on "a written notice given to the other at least seven days prior to THE TERMINATION DATE SPECIFIED IN THE NOTICE." Section 76-1437(2): a month-to-month tenancy ends on "a written notice given to the other at least thirty days prior to THE PERIODIC RENTAL DATE SPECIFIED IN THE NOTICE." Those two phrases are different and the difference is the whole content requirement: the week-to-week notice must specify a termination date, the month-to-month notice must specify a periodic rental date. Section 76-1431(1) requires a breach notice "specifying the acts and omissions constituting the breach and that the rental agreement will terminate upon a date not less than thirty days after receipt of the notice if the breach is not remedied in fourteen days". Section 76-1431(2) requires the nonpayment notice to state the nonpayment and your intention to terminate if the rent is not paid within the seven-calendar-day period. Section 76-1431(4) requires five days' written notice of termination on the violent-criminal-activity route. That is the complete list of content requirements.

NOW THE QUESTION THAT CATCHES PEOPLE OUT: MAY YOU START WORK ON THE UNIT WHILE THE NOTICE RUNS? Nebraska has no statute of the kind some jurisdictions have forbidding alterations that render a unit uninhabitable while a notice to vacate is pending. But do not read that as permission, because three sections make the same conduct expensive by a different route.

First, your habitability duties do not pause. Section 76-1419(1) says "The landlord SHALL" do each of six things, including "(b) Make all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition" and "(f) Supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat". Nothing in that section is suspended by the service of a termination notice, and nothing in the section opens with "unless otherwise agreed" for those two duties.

Second, and this is the real exposure, section 76-1430: "If the landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises or willfully and wrongfully diminishes services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water or other essential service to the tenant, the tenant may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, in either case, recover AN AMOUNT EQUAL TO THREE MONTHS' PERIODIC RENT AS LIQUIDATED DAMAGES, and a reasonable attorney's fee." That is a FIXED SUM, not a ceiling and not a cap - no proof of loss is required. Shutting the water off, pulling a furnace, or gutting a bathroom while the tenant is still in possession is how a landlord turns a lawful thirty-day notice into a three-months'-rent judgment.

Third, timing matters for a different reason. Section 76-1439(1) bars retaliation "by increasing rent or decreasing services or by bringing or threatening to bring an action for possession" after the tenant has complained to a code-enforcement agency or joined a tenants' union, with the tenant getting the section 76-1430 remedies and a defence to possession. Subsection (3) preserves your possession action where the code violation "was caused primarily by lack of reasonable care by the tenant", where the tenant is in default in rent, or where "(c) Compliance with the applicable minimum building or housing code requires alteration, remodeling, or demolition which would effectively deprive the tenant of use of the dwelling unit". That last one is the lawful route to a vacant unit for major work - bring the possession action on that ground rather than starting demolition around a sitting tenant.

THE ONE PLACE NEBRASKA DOES FREEZE THE TENANCY WHILE A NOTICE RUNS. Condominium conversion. Section 76-886(a) requires sixty days' notice to residential tenants and subtenants in possession, and provides that during that period "the terms of the tenancy may not be altered", with failure to give the notice being "a defense to an action for possession"; subsection (d) provides that a conversion notice specifying a vacate date "shall constitute a notice to vacate". So the drafting device exists in Nebraska law - the legislature simply confined it to conversions. The conversion regime is covered in full by the library's conversion-notice guidance and is not restated here.

PRACTICAL RULE. Write the notice to the words of its own section, date it, say what it has to say and nothing speculative, deliver it one of the three ways section 76-1413(2)(c) recognises - in hand, by mail to the address the tenant holds out, or electronically where the tenant has separately consented - and leave the unit alone until possession has actually ended.

title: Nuisance in Nebraska - What the City Can Assess Against Your Building, What You Can Be Charged With, and the One Statute That Appears to Let You Self-Help (Do Not)
bodyText:
Nebraska has no single nuisance act aimed at rental housing. It has four separate exposures that land on the owner of a building, and they come from three different chapters. None of them is in the landlord-tenant act, which is why they are easy to miss.

1. THE CITY DEFINES THE NUISANCE, AND THEN ASSESSES THE COST TO YOUR LOT. Section 18-1720(1): "All cities and villages in this state may by ordinance define, regulate, suppress, and prevent nuisances, declare what constitutes a nuisance, and abate and remove such nuisances", exercisable "within its corporate limits and extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction." So the operative definition is usually municipal, not statutory. The money consequence is section 18-1722: if the owner of a building "fails, neglects, or refuses to comply with notice by or on behalf of any city or village to repair, rehabilitate, or demolish and remove a building or structure which is an unsafe building or structure and a public nuisance, the city or village may proceed with the work specified in the notice", after which the governing body may "(1) Levy the cost as a special assessment against the lot or real estate upon which the building or structure is located. Such special assessment shall be a lien on the real estate and shall be collected in the manner provided for special assessments; or (2) Collect the cost from the owner ... and enforce the collection by civil action". That is a lien ahead of nothing in particular but collected like a tax, and the trigger is simply failing to comply with the city's notice. Related and separately recorded: where a municipality determines a property is unsafe or unfit for human occupancy under its minimum standard housing ordinance, section 18-1722.01 makes it the municipality's duty to post the property and to file a copy of the determination with the register of deeds - so the determination becomes both a posted notice and a recorded instrument on your title.

2. MAINTAINING A NUISANCE IS A CRIME, AND SO IS KEEPING A DWELLING RESORTED TO FOR DRUGS. Section 28-1321(1): "A person commits the offense of maintaining a nuisance if he erects, keeps up or continues and maintains any nuisance to the injury of any part of the citizens of this state"; subsection (4) makes it a Class III misdemeanor and subsection (5) says "The court, in case of conviction of such offense, shall order every such nuisance to be abated or removed." Subsection (2) lists the classic instances - noxious exhalations and offensive smells from a trade or business, obstructing water, corrupting a watercourse, obstructing a public way.

The one that reaches a landlord hardest has a catchline that mentions neither dwellings nor landlords. Section 28-417(1)(e) makes it unlawful for ANY PERSON "To keep or maintain any store, shop, warehouse, DWELLING HOUSE, BUILDING, vehicle, boat, aircraft, or place whatever which such person KNOWS OR SHOULD KNOW is resorted to by persons using controlled substances in violation of the Uniform Controlled Substances Act for the purpose of using such substances or which is used for the keeping or selling of the same in violation of the act", and section 28-417(2) makes it a Class III misdemeanor. Note two things. The standard is CONSTRUCTIVE knowledge - "knows or should know" - and there is NO landlord safe harbour anywhere in the section. If you have been told about drug activity in a unit and done nothing, the section is written to reach you.

3. THE OBSCENITY NUISANCE REGIME CAN CLOSE YOUR BUILDING, AND YOU POST THE BOND TO GET IT BACK. Sections 28-807 to 28-829 carry a full abatement apparatus. Section 28-821 deems a person convicted more than twice who continues the business to be maintaining a nuisance. Section 28-822 lets any city, village or county, through its chief law enforcement officer, "bring an action in equity to abate such a nuisance and to perpetually enjoin the person maintaining the same". Section 28-823 lets the court restrain removal of the personal property and contents, and then says what matters to an owner who is not the wrongdoer: "The owner of any real or personal property closed or restrained or to be closed or restrained may appear ... and upon payment of all costs incurred and upon THE FILING OF A BOND BY THE OWNER OF THE REAL PROPERTY with sureties ... IN THE FULL VALUE OF THE PROPERTY ..., conditioned that such owner will immediately abate the nuisance and prevent the same from being established or kept", the court may release the property if satisfied of the owner's good faith. Section 28-825 provides that on judgment the abatement order "shall include an order directing the effectual closing of the place against its use for any illegal purpose unless otherwise released", continuing for one year, and requires the renewal for one year of any bond furnished by the owner. So the owner's route out is costs plus a bond in the full value of the property - which is why a landlord in this position needs counsel immediately, not a lease clause.

4. REAL PROPERTY CAN BE FORFEITED, AND THE INNOCENT-OWNER STANDARD IS DIFFERENT FROM THE DRUG-PREMISES STANDARD. Section 25-21,302(1)(b)(viii) subjects to forfeiture "Any real property, including any right, title, and interest in the whole of or any part of any lot or tract of land, used in furtherance of a violation of" the Child Sexual Abuse Material Prevention Act or section 28-813, 28-831, 28-1102, 28-1103, 28-1104, 28-1105, 28-1105.01 or 28-1107. The protection is at subsection (2): "No property shall be forfeited under this section, to the extent of the interest of an owner, by reason of any act or omission established by the owner to have been committed or omitted WITHOUT HIS OR HER ACTUAL KNOWLEDGE OR CONSENT." And there is a provision written for exactly your situation: section 25-21,302(1)(c)(ii) says "If the confiscating authority has reason to believe that the property is LEASED OR RENTED PROPERTY, then the confiscating authority shall notify the owner of the property WITHIN FIVE DAYS after the confiscation or within five days after forming reason to believe that the property is leased or rented property." Compare the two standards side by side: forfeiture is defeated by proving no ACTUAL knowledge or consent, while the drug-premises crime at section 28-417(1)(e) reaches you if you SHOULD HAVE KNOWN. Being ignorant protects your title and does not necessarily protect you from the misdemeanor.

THE TRAP: SECTION 28-826 LOOKS LIKE A SELF-HELP POWER AND YOU MUST NOT USE IT AS ONE. Section 28-826 reads: "If a tenant or occupant of a building or tenement under lawful title used such place for the purposes of committing a violation of sections 28-807 to 28-829, and if such tenant or occupant is convicted of such violation, such conviction shall make the lease or other title which he holds VOID AT THE OPTION OF THE OWNER, and without any act of the owner, cause the right of possession to revert and vest in such owner, who may WITHOUT FURTHER PROCESS OF LAW MAKE IMMEDIATE ENTRY upon the premises and retake possession." For a dwelling unit inside the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, taking that sentence at face value is how a landlord buys a judgment. Section 76-1403 says the general law supplements the Act only "Unless displaced by the provisions of" the Act - and section 76-1430 displaces self-help in terms: "If the landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises ... the tenant may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, in either case, recover an amount equal to THREE MONTHS' PERIODIC RENT AS LIQUIDATED DAMAGES, and a reasonable attorney's fee." That is a fixed sum requiring no proof of loss. Section 76-1423(4) says the same thing about access: "The landlord has no other right of access except by court order, as permitted by subsection (2) of section 76-1432, or if the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises." THE CAUTIOUS COURSE, AND IT IS NOT A CLOSE CALL: use the termination half of section 28-826 if you wish - a conviction makes the lease void at your option - and then take possession the way the Act requires, through the possession action, or on the five-day no-cure route in section 76-1431(4) if the conduct fits. No Nebraska decision harmonising section 28-826 with section 76-1430 was located, and case law is outside what was examined here, so do not treat the "without further process of law" words as reliable for a residential tenancy.

WHAT NEBRASKA DOES NOT HAVE. No nuisance receivership. A title sweep for "receiver" across all twelve chapters examined returns nineteen sections and not one is a nuisance receivership; section 25-1081's nine grounds for appointing a receiver are the equity and foreclosure grounds plus "(8) in all cases provided for by special statutes", and no special statute provides one for a nuisance property, so no court is taking your rents on that basis. There is also no statute making the landlord a necessary defendant in a third party's abatement action, no drug-nuisance suit by tenants or neighbours, no ten-voters petition route, no rent escrow or subsidy-suspension mechanism, and no requirement that your lease summarise a criminal statute. Your lease-side tools are the ordinary ones: the tenant's duty under section 76-1421(7) to "Conduct himself and require other persons on the premises with his consent to conduct themselves in a manner that will not disturb his neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises", the house-rules route in section 76-1422, the thirty-day-with-fourteen-day-cure route in section 76-1431(1), and the five-day no-cure route in section 76-1431(4). Finally, note that section 28-1303 makes it a Class III misdemeanor to raise an artificial pond or produce stagnant waters "manifestly injurious to the public health and safety" by a dam or obstruction in a river or stream, with court-ordered abatement - relevant only if your property includes a watercourse, but it is the one standing-water nuisance crime in the code.

title: Nebraska Lets You Agree Almost Anything - and Names the Four Gates Every Optional Term Has to Pass
bodyText:
Nebraska states the freedom-of-contract rule expressly, which is useful because it means an optional clause does not need a statute behind it. Section 76-1414(1): "The landlord and tenant may include in a rental agreement TERMS AND CONDITIONS NOT PROHIBITED by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law including rent, term of the agreement, and other provisions governing the rights and obligations of the parties." So the question for any optional term is never "does a statute authorise this?" It is "is this prohibited?" - and Nebraska gives you four places to check.

GATE 1 - THE FOUR PROHIBITED CATEGORIES. Section 76-1415(1) voids a term by which the tenant (a) waives or foregoes rights or remedies under the act, (b) authorizes anyone to confess judgment, (c) "Agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees" - bidirectional, so a mutual version is prohibited too - or (d) agrees to exculpation, limitation of liability or indemnity for the landlord's active and actionable negligence. Section 76-1415(2) makes such a provision unenforceable and adds the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees where the landlord deliberately uses a provision known to be prohibited.

GATE 2 - UNCONSCIONABILITY. Section 76-1412(1) lets the court, as a matter of law, refuse to enforce the agreement or any provision of it "was unconscionable when made", enforce the remainder without the offending provision, or limit its application "to avoid an unconscionable result". Subsection (2) gives the parties a reasonable opportunity to present evidence on "the setting, purpose, and effect" once the issue is raised by a party or by the court on its own motion. This is the gate an unusual fee or an aggressive remedy actually runs into, and it is tested at the time of making, not at enforcement.

GATE 3 - "OR OTHER RULE OF LAW". Section 76-1414(1)'s own words reach beyond the act. Section 76-1403 explains how: "Unless displaced by the provisions of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the principles of law and equity, including the law relating to capacity to contract, mutuality of obligations, principal and agent, real property, public health, safety and fire prevention, estoppel, fraud, misrepresentation, duress, coercion, mistake, bankruptcy, or other validating or invalidating cause, supplement the act's provisions." So a term can be lawful under the act and still fail on ordinary contract or real-property grounds - and some prohibitions on lease terms sit entirely outside section 76-1415, the clearest being section 76-1413(9): "A landlord shall not, as part of a rental agreement or as a condition of entering into or renewing a rental agreement, require a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means."

GATE 4 - THE FORM THE TERM TAKES. If what you want is a house rule rather than a lease paragraph, section 76-1422 imposes six conditions and the sixth is a delivery problem: a rule is enforceable against the tenant only if, among other things, "(6) The tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement." A rule adopted later binds the tenant only "if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the tenant and it does not work a substantial modification of his bargain." A clause that leans on house rules without a delivery-and-receipt sentence is hollow.

WHAT SECTION 76-1414 ITSELF SUPPLIES AS DEFAULTS, WHICH YOU MAY VARY. Subsection (2): "In absence of agreement, the tenant shall pay as rent the fair rental value for the use and occupancy of the dwelling unit." Subsection (3): "Rent shall be payable without demand or notice at the time and place agreed upon by the parties. UNLESS OTHERWISE AGREED, rent is payable at the dwelling unit and periodic rent is payable at the beginning of any term of one month or less and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the beginning of each month. Unless otherwise agreed, rent shall be uniformly apportionable from day to day." Subsection (4): "Unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy shall be week to week in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent, and in all other cases month to month." Each of those is a default you can and usually should displace expressly.

AND A DRAFTING TEST THAT TELLS YOU WHICH DEFAULTS YOU MAY NOT TOUCH. Across chapter 76, exactly eleven sections open or contain the phrase "unless otherwise agreed": sections 76-1414, 76-1420, 76-1424, 76-1433, 76-1475, 76-1476, 76-1477, 76-1495, 76-14,106, 76-2331 and 76-3303 - the last four being Mobile Home Act and unrelated provisions. The landlord-tenant sections that do NOT carry the phrase are telling you they are not defaults. Sections 76-1431 and 76-1437, the termination and notice sections, are not on the list; neither is section 76-1405, the remedies and mitigation section, nor section 76-1429 on casualty. When you cannot find "unless otherwise agreed" in the section you want to vary, assume you cannot vary it.

TWO MORE THINGS WORTH KNOWING WHEN YOU DRAFT AN OPTIONAL TERM. Ambiguity is construed against you: the annotation to section 76-1414 records that "Ambiguities in a lease should be construed against the person preparing the lease" (D & R Realty v. Bender, 230 Neb. 301, 431 N.W.2d 920 (1988)) - a lead rather than a holding examined here, but it points the right way for a form lease. And every payment you create is rent: section 76-1410(13) says "Rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement", which means each optional fee you invent is swept into the nonpayment route in your favour and into the deposit ceiling and damages measures against you.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure in Nebraska - but the Shared Meter Is Still Your Problem
bodyText:
This is a three-part California-style disclosure package, and Nebraska has none of the three. Taking them in turn, because the practical answer is different for each.

FORMER ORDNANCE LOCATION: NOTHING. No Nebraska statute requires a landlord to disclose that the property is within any distance of a former federal or state ordnance location, and the word "ordnance" appears in only two sections of the twelve chapters searched, both of them explosives-control definitions in the criminal code rather than disclosures. Nebraska also left the subject out of the one disclosure form it did write: section 76-2,120(4)'s contents list for the residential property condition disclosure statement runs to eleven items and the closest is "(g) Any hazardous conditions, including substances, materials, and products on the real property which may be an environmental hazard" - a seller duty, not a landlord one, and it reaches a lease only through section 76-2,120(2)'s extension to "any lease with the option to purchase residential real property."

PENDING DEMOLITION: NOTHING AIMED AT TENANTS, AND ONE THING AIMED AT YOU. There is no duty to tell a prospective or sitting tenant that you have applied for a demolition permit, and no corresponding termination right. What Nebraska has instead is an exposure running the other way. Section 18-1722 provides that if the owner of a building "fails, neglects, or refuses to comply with notice by or on behalf of any city or village to repair, rehabilitate, or demolish and remove a building or structure which is an unsafe building or structure and a public nuisance", the city may do the work and then either "(1) Levy the cost as a special assessment against the lot or real estate", which "shall be a lien on the real estate", or "(2) Collect the cost from the owner ... and enforce the collection by civil action". And demolition does appear once inside the landlord-tenant act, as a shield for you rather than a duty: section 76-1439(3)(c) preserves your possession action, notwithstanding the retaliation bar, where "Compliance with the applicable minimum building or housing code requires alteration, remodeling, or demolition which would effectively deprive the tenant of use of the dwelling unit." That is the lawful route to a vacant unit for major work.

SHARED OR SINGLE METER SERVING MORE THAN ONE UNIT: NO DISCLOSURE, BUT A HARD LIMIT ON WHAT YOU MAY CHARGE FOR. Nebraska has no shared-meter disclosure, no shared-meter consent requirement and no rule allocating a master-metered bill between units. The words "shared meter", "master meter", "single meter", "submeter" and "submetering" return nothing at all in the twelve chapters searched. What constrains you is the habitability section. Section 76-1419(1)(f) makes the landlord "Supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat except where the building that includes the dwelling unit is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, OR THE DWELLING UNIT IS SO CONSTRUCTED THAT HEAT OR HOT WATER IS GENERATED BY AN INSTALLATION WITHIN THE EXCLUSIVE CONTROL OF THE TENANT AND SUPPLIED BY A DIRECT PUBLIC UTILITY CONNECTION." Read the second exception carefully: it needs exclusive tenant control AND a direct public utility connection. A unit on a shared or master meter has neither, so the duty stays with you.

And you cannot contract out of it in a multi-unit building. Section 76-1419(2) lets the landlord and tenant "OF A SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE" agree that the tenant perform the duties in subdivisions (1)(e) and (1)(f), in writing, for good consideration, in good faith and not to evade the landlord's obligations. Section 76-1419(3), which governs "a dwelling unit other than a single-family residence", reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" - it does not name (1)(e) or (1)(f) at all. So for anything that is not a single-family residence under section 76-1410(16), the water-and-heat duty cannot be shifted by agreement, however the lease is worded. If the tenant's unit shares a meter and you have made the tenant responsible for the bill, you have an unenforceable term and a live section 76-1427 exposure: that section lets a tenant who gives written notice procure water, hot water, heat or essential services and "deduct their actual and reasonable cost from the rent", or recover diminution in fair rental value, or procure substitute housing rent-free - plus reasonable attorney's fees, and a deliberate failure adds the cost or value of the substitute housing up to one month's periodic rent.

THE ABSENCE IS A DRAFTING CHOICE, BECAUSE NEBRASKA WROTE BOTH RULES NEXT DOOR. A utility disclosure exists in Nebraska - in the Mobile Home Act. Section 76-1482: "The landlord or any person authorized to enter into a rental agreement on the landlord's behalf shall provide A WRITTEN EXPLANATION OF UTILITY RATES, CHARGES, AND SERVICES to the prospective tenant BEFORE THE RENTAL AGREEMENT IS SIGNED unless the utility charges are to be paid by the tenant directly to the utility company." That is the only mandatory utility disclosure in Nebraska landlord-tenant law and it does not apply to an apartment or a rented house. A proportional-allocation rule for unmetered utilities also exists - in the Condominium Act, and doubly conditioned. Section 76-873(c) opens "To the extent required by the declaration", and (c)(3) then says "the costs of insurance may at the discretion of the association be assessed in proportion to risk and, IF REASONABLY DETERMINED, the costs of utilities not separately metered must be assessed in proportion to usage." So the legislature had both tools and put neither in the residential act.

THE CAUTIOUS COURSE. Nothing requires a disclosure, so treat all three as voluntary. On the meter, do the thing that actually protects you: if the unit is not a single-family residence, keep water, hot water and heat as your obligation and price them into rent rather than billing them through - a bill-through term for those services is unenforceable and invites section 76-1427. If the unit IS a single-family residence and you want the shift, do it the way section 76-1419(2) requires: in writing, for good consideration, and not as a device to evade your obligations. And if you do voluntarily disclose a shared meter, state the fact only; a disclosure paired with the tenant's waiver of the water-and-heat duty runs straight into section 76-1415(1)(a).

title: Amenities You Hold Out Become Part of the "Premises" You Must Maintain - Nebraska's Quiet Trap for Pools, Laundries and Gyms
bodyText:
Nebraska has no catch-all facilities statute of the California or Massachusetts kind - no list of locks, mailboxes, screens, window coverings, garbage receptacles or lighting that a rental must have. What it has is a definition, and the definition quietly does more work than any list would.

THE DEFINITION IS THE RULE. Section 76-1410(12): "PREMISES means a dwelling unit and the structure of which it is a part and facilities and appurtenances therein and grounds, areas, and FACILITIES HELD OUT FOR THE USE OF TENANTS GENERALLY OR WHOSE USE IS PROMISED TO THE TENANT." Two separate triggers, and neither of them is ownership or necessity: a facility is part of the premises if it is held out for tenants generally, or if its use is promised to this tenant. Advertising a pool, a fitness room, a laundry, a clubhouse, a dog run, a rooftop, a storage locker or assigned covered parking is holding it out. Writing it into one tenant's lease is promising it. Either way it joins the premises.

AND YOUR DUTIES ATTACH TO THE PREMISES, NOT THE UNIT. Section 76-1419(1) says "The landlord shall: ... (b) Make all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep THE PREMISES in a fit and habitable condition; (c) Keep ALL COMMON AREAS OF THE PREMISES in a clean and safe condition; (d) Maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her; (e) Provide and maintain appropriate receptacles and conveniences for the removal of ashes, garbage, rubbish, and other waste incidental to the occupancy of the dwelling unit and arrange for their removal from the appropriate receptacle".

The five words that matter are in (1)(d): "SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED". That phrase is the mechanism by which your own promise creates a statutory maintenance duty. Nothing in Nebraska law required you to install a pool pump, a laundry room or a gym. Once you have, or once the lease or your marketing says you will, those are facilities required to be supplied - and section 76-1419(1)(d) obliges you to maintain them in good and safe working order, with the duty enforceable by action under section 76-1405(2). Subsection (1)(c)'s "clean and safe" duty for common areas is not qualified by a notice requirement the way (1)(a) and (1)(b) are.

WHAT YOU MAY NOT DO ABOUT IT. You may not contract the duty onto the tenant in a multi-unit building beyond narrow limits. Section 76-1419(2) allows a wider shift only "of a single-family residence", in writing, for good consideration, in good faith and not to evade your obligations. Section 76-1419(3), for "a dwelling unit other than a single-family residence", allows an agreement only as to "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" and only if it is "entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord and is set forth in a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration". A general lease sentence putting amenity upkeep on tenants does not satisfy that. You may, however, employ the tenant to do the work: section 76-1419(4) is the express option for that.

AND YOU MAY NOT WAIVE IT, EXCULPATE IT OR INDEMNIFY AGAINST IT. Section 76-1415(1)(a) voids a term by which the tenant waives or foregoes rights or remedies under the act, and (1)(d) voids a term agreeing "to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord or to indemnify the landlord for that liability". So the familiar "use the pool and gym at your own risk; Landlord is not liable" sentence is the prohibited term if what it limits is your own active negligence. Keep an assumption-of-risk recital narrow and factual, and do not let it reach your negligence. Note also that section 76-1419(1)'s closing words reserve the question: "The obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state."

THE REMEDY SIDE, SO YOU CAN SIZE THE RISK. If what fails is a service rather than an amenity, section 76-1427(1) applies: on written notice specifying the breach, a tenant may procure water, hot water, heat or essential services and "deduct their actual and reasonable cost from the rent", recover damages based on diminution in fair rental value, or procure substitute housing and stop paying rent for the period - with reasonable attorney's fees in any case, and a deliberate failure adding the cost or value of the substitute housing up to one month's periodic rent. That is the ONLY procure-and-deduct right in Nebraska's landlord-tenant act; there is no general repair-and-deduct, so an amenity failure that is not an essential service runs through section 76-1425 or an action for damages instead. And if you shut an amenity down in a way that amounts to willfully and wrongfully diminishing services by interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service, section 76-1430's fixed three months' periodic rent plus attorney's fee is the figure.

HOW TO DRAFT AROUND IT, WHICH IS THE WHOLE PRACTICAL POINT. Decide deliberately what you hold out. Say in the lease exactly which facilities are provided and on what terms, and say which are not provided at all - the library's services-and-utilities clause is the place for that. Reserve the right to close, suspend or remove a non-essential amenity for repair, for safety, for seasonal reasons or permanently, and reserve it before the tenant signs rather than discovering later that the pool is part of the premises. Keep amenity rules in a form that satisfies section 76-1422: its purpose must promote "the appearance, convenience, safety, or welfare of the tenants in the premises" or "make a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for the tenants generally", it must be reasonably related to that purpose, apply fairly to all tenants, be explicit enough to inform the tenant what to do, not be a device for evading your obligations, and - the one that kills most amenity rules - "The tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement." A rule adopted later binds only on reasonable notice and only if it "does not work a substantial modification of his bargain", so removing a promised amenity mid-term by house rule will not work.

Two last Nebraska specifics. Tenant-side duties cover the facilities too: section 76-1421(5) requires the tenant to "Use in a reasonable manner all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances including elevators in the premises", and section 76-1421(8) requires the tenant to "Abide by all bylaws, covenants, rules or regulations of any applicable condominium regime, cooperative housing agreement, or neighborhood association not inconsistent with landlord's rights or duties" - which is how HOA amenity rules reach your tenant. And section 76-1424 lets you require notice of an extended absence: "The rental agreement may require that the tenant notify the landlord of any anticipated extended absence from the premises in excess of seven days no later than the first day of the extended absence."

title: No Parking-Rules Notice Regime in Nebraska - the General House-Rules Test Governs, and One Posting Rule Does Reach Your Lot
bodyText:
Texas and a few other states run a dedicated parking and towing rules regime: the rules have to be delivered before the lease is signed, under a prescribed heading, with limits on changing them mid-term, limits on the vehicle information you may demand, and a permit that expires with the lease. Nebraska has none of that. There is no parking-specific notice statute, no prescribed heading, no restriction on the vehicle data you may collect, no permit-duration rule, and no parking-specific limit on mid-term changes.

WHAT GOVERNS INSTEAD, AND IT IS STRICTER THAN PEOPLE EXPECT ON ONE POINT. Parking rules are house rules, so section 76-1422 governs them, and its sixth condition is a delivery rule in substance even though it is not framed as a notice requirement: a rule is enforceable against the tenant only if, among the other five tests, "(6) The tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement." So your parking rules must be in the tenant's hands when the lease is signed, not handed over at move-in - which is functionally the pre-execution delivery requirement the Texas statute spells out, arrived at from the other direction. The remaining tests matter for parking in particular: the rule's purpose must promote "the appearance, convenience, safety, or welfare of the tenants in the premises", preserve the landlord's property from abusive use, or "make a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for the tenants generally"; it must be reasonably related to that purpose; it must apply "to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner"; it must be "sufficiently explicit in its prohibition, direction, or limitation of the tenant's conduct to fairly inform him of what he must or must not do to comply"; and it must not be "for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord". A parking rule enforced against some tenants and not others fails test (3), and a vague "no inappropriate vehicles" rule fails test (4).

MID-TERM CHANGES. Section 76-1422's closing sentence: "A rule or regulation adopted after the tenant enters into the rental agreement is enforceable against the tenant if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the tenant and it does not work a substantial modification of his bargain." There is no fixed notice period and no cap on changes - but the second half is the real limit. Introducing paid parking where parking was included, or taking away an assigned space the lease promised, is the kind of change that modifies the bargain substantially. Compare what Nebraska did write for mobile home parks: section 76-1494 requires park rules to be written, requires that "(6) The prospective tenant is given a copy of any existing rules and regulations before entering into the rental agreement", and then says "Notice of all additions, changes, deletions, or amendments to the rules and regulations shall be given to all mobile home tenants SIXTY DAYS before they become effective", with a shorter route only on the written consent of "at least one adult resident from a minimum of sixty percent of the households". A sixty-day rule-change notice exists in Nebraska; the legislature put it in the Mobile Home Act and not in the residential act. That is a drafting choice, and it tells you the residential standard really is just "reasonable notice" plus no substantial modification.

ONE POSTING REQUIREMENT THAT DOES REACH A PRIVATE RENTAL LOT. If you designate accessible parking, section 18-1737(1) applies to "any person in lawful possession of any offstreet parking facility" - which is you - and it is permissive as to designating but mandatory as to how: the designation "shall be made by posting aboveground and immediately adjacent to and visible from each stall or space, including access aisles, a sign which is in conformance with the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices adopted pursuant to section 60-6,118 and the federal Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 and the federal regulations adopted in response to the act, as the act and the regulations existed on January 1, 2026." And if you want to remove a car from one of those spaces, section 18-1737(2) lets "The owner or person in lawful possession of an offstreet parking facility, AFTER NOTIFYING THE POLICE OR SHERIFF'S DEPARTMENT", cause the removal of a vehicle not displaying the proper permit or plates - but only "if there is posted aboveground and immediately adjacent to and visible from such stall or space, including access aisles, a sign which CLEARLY AND CONSPICUOUSLY STATES THE AREA SO DESIGNATED AS A TOW-IN ZONE." Two signs, in other words: the accessible-space sign and the tow-in-zone sign. One helpful detail for you: section 18-1737(3) ends by providing that "In the case of a privately owned offstreet parking facility, a city or village shall not require the owner or person in lawful possession of such facility to inform the city or village of a violation of this section prior to the city or village issuing the violator a handicapped parking infraction citation" - so you are not a gatekeeper for the citation. Note that this section was amended in each of the last three sessions (most recently Laws 2026, LB781, section 1, effective April 15, 2026), so check it before you order signs, and note that the ordinary private-lot towing and sign rules live in a different chapter and are covered by the library's towing guidance rather than here.

THE CAUTIOUS COURSE, ALL OF IT DRAFTING RATHER THAN COMPLIANCE. Attach the parking rules to the lease as an exhibit the tenant signs or initials, so section 76-1422(6) notice is documented rather than asserted. State the number of spaces, which spaces, the hours of any restriction, who to contact about a towed vehicle, and whether parking is included in rent or charged separately - and if charged separately, remember section 76-1410(13) makes it rent, which pulls it into the nonpayment route in your favour and into the deposit ceiling and damages measures against you. Reserve the right to reassign a space of comparable convenience on reasonable notice rather than an unqualified right to change the rules, which is what keeps you on the right side of the substantial-modification limit. And do not pair the rules with a waiver of liability for vehicle damage caused by your own negligence: section 76-1415(1)(d) voids a term agreeing to "the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord or to indemnify the landlord for that liability".

title: No Pesticide-Application Notice Duty in Nebraska - but Entry, Habitability and Your Own Promise All Still Apply
bodyText:
Nebraska imposes no tenant-facing pesticide notice. There is no duty to tell a tenant before a pesticide is applied in or around the unit, no duty to post a treated area, no re-entry interval you must pass on, no written statement of the product used, no tenant notification registry to check, and no annual notice for a building on a routine treatment programme. There is also no pest-control disclosure to make at signing.

WHAT DOES APPLY, AND THERE ARE FOUR THINGS. First, ENTRY. A pest treatment is an entry, so section 76-1423 governs it. "Except in case of emergency or if it is impracticable to do so, the landlord shall: (a) Give the tenant at least twenty-four hours' written notice of the landlord's intent to enter. Such notice shall be provided to each individual unit and include THE INTENDED PURPOSE FOR ENTRY and a reasonable period during which the landlord anticipates making entry; and (b) Enter only at reasonable times" (section 76-1423(3)). The purpose requirement is doing the work a pesticide-notice statute would do in another state: a compliant Nebraska entry notice for a treatment has to say that the entry is for pest treatment. That is not a pesticide disclosure, and it is not nothing. Section 76-1423(2) allows entry without consent in an emergency, and section 76-1423(4) makes clear there is no other right of access - so a standing no-notice right to treat does not exist and cannot be written into the lease.

Second, HABITABILITY. An infestation is a condition question, not a notice question. Section 76-1419(1)(b) requires the landlord to "Make all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition", and (1)(c) to "Keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition". Note that (1)(b) is triggered by written OR ACTUAL notice - a tenant's phone call starts the clock. If a minimum housing code applies to the premises, section 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence makes subdivision (1)(a) the ceiling on your duty, and section 76-1410(3) defines "minimum housing code" narrowly as laws or ordinances "dealing specifically with health and minimum standards of fitness for habitation".

Third, THE TENANT'S SIDE. Section 76-1421 requires the tenant to "(2) Keep that part of the premises that he occupies and uses as clean and safe as the condition of the premises permit", "(3) Dispose from his dwelling unit all ashes, rubbish, garbage, and other waste in a clean and safe manner", and "(4) Keep all plumbing fixtures in the dwelling unit or used by the tenant as clean as their condition permits". Those are the duties a cooperation requirement in your lease hangs on, and a tenant-caused infestation is a breach you process through section 76-1431(1) - written notice specifying the acts and omissions, termination no sooner than thirty days after receipt if not remedied in fourteen days.

Fourth, AND THIS IS THE ONE DRAFTERS WALK INTO. If your lease or your advertising promises periodic pest treatment, you have created a duty. Section 76-1419(1)(d) requires the landlord to maintain in good and safe working order "all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her" - the words "or required to be supplied" are how a promise becomes a statutory obligation. And you cannot push treatment duties onto the tenant in a multi-unit building by a general lease sentence: section 76-1419(3) permits an agreement that the tenant perform "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" for a unit other than a single-family residence only if it is "entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord and is set forth in A SEPARATE WRITING SIGNED BY THE PARTIES and supported by adequate consideration". Section 76-1419(2) allows a wider shift only for a single-family residence, in writing and for good consideration. Section 76-1419(4) expressly allows you to employ the tenant to do the work instead.

THE CAUTIOUS COURSE, WHICH IS CHEAP. Nothing requires a pesticide notice, so treat it as practice rather than compliance: when you schedule a treatment, give the section 76-1423(3)(a) notice stating pest treatment as the purpose and the anticipated window, and add the applicator's product information and any re-entry interval the applicator gives you. There is no downside - you already have to give the notice and state the purpose - and it answers the tenant who is pregnant, immunocompromised or keeping fish or birds before the fact rather than afterwards. Do not promise "regular" treatment in the lease unless you intend to deliver it, and if you do promise it, put the schedule in the lease where both sides can see it rather than leaving it as marketing.

TWO SCOPE WARNINGS THIS GUIDANCE MAKES EXPRESSLY. Nebraska's Pesticide Act regulates applicators and product registration, and it sits in a chapter of the statutes outside what was examined here; its duties run to licensed applicators and the Department rather than to landlords, but if you apply restricted-use products yourself rather than hiring a licensed applicator, check that Act before you do. And city codes are not covered: a municipality may impose extermination duties through its own minimum housing ordinance, which section 18-1720(1) and section 76-1410(3) both contemplate.

title: No Pet-and-Eviction Fact Sheet Has to Go Out With a Nebraska Lease
bodyText: Maryland makes a landlord who knows the tenant keeps a dog or cat hand over a state-written fact sheet about pets and eviction with the lease. Nebraska has nothing of the kind. In the Nebraska statute chapters that govern a tenancy, the word "pet" appears in exactly one section — Sec. 76-1416, the security-deposit cap, which allows "a pet deposit not in excess of one-fourth of one month's periodic rent" and says nothing about disclosure. There is no state-issued pet brochure, no required pet-and-eviction notice, and no statutory list of what a pet addendum has to contain. So: your pet addendum is yours to write, and nothing has to accompany it. Two practical consequences. First, because Nebraska gives the tenant no pet-specific fact sheet, the only notice the tenant gets about what happens if the pet becomes a problem is what your own lease says — write the pet rules into the lease or into rules and regulations delivered before signing, because Sec. 76-1422(6) makes a rule enforceable against the tenant "only if ... the tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement." Second, an assistance animal is not a pet; a reasonable-accommodation request is governed by federal law and by Sec. 20-131.04, not by your pet addendum, and no pet deposit or pet rent may be charged for one. Also worth checking locally: Nebraska city ordinances (Lincoln and Omaha both license and limit animals) and the Nebraska Administrative Code, because a municipal pet-licensing or dangerous-dog ordinance can impose duties the state statutes do not.

title: Pet Money in Nebraska: the Deposit Is Security, the Rent Is Rent, and "Nonrefundable" Is the Trap
bodyText:
Nebraska does not exclude pet money from its deposit statute the way Idaho, Missouri, Indiana, Oklahoma and Michigan do. Sec. 76-1416(1) bars a landlord from demanding or receiving "security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent, except that a pet deposit not in excess of one-fourth of one month's periodic rent may be demanded or received when appropriate."

Read that sentence in order. The pet deposit is not carved out of "security" — it is an extra slice of security the statute permits on top of the one-month ceiling. Three things follow.
- (1) The quarter-month pet allowance is conditional: "when appropriate." It is money for a pet, so it is available when there is a pet, and it does not become a general extra deposit for a tenant with no animal.
- (2) Because the pet deposit is security, Sec. 76-1416(2) governs it on the way out: within fourteen days after termination you must deliver or mail the balance with a written itemization, and Sec. 76-1416(3) exposes you to the tenant's costs and attorney's fees — plus liquidated damages of one month's rent or twice the deposit, whichever is less, for a willful bad-faith failure. Itemize pet damage line by line against the pet deposit, in the same accounting as the rest of the deposit.
- (3) Nebraska sets no cap at all on PET RENT, and pet rent is a cleaner instrument than a fee: Sec. 76-1410(13) says "Rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement," so a monthly pet charge is rent, you keep it, and nothing has to be returned. The cost of that choice is that pet rent raises "one month's periodic rent" — the very figure your deposit cap is measured against — so build the pet rent into the figure before you set the deposit.

What to avoid: a one-time "nonrefundable pet fee." No statute says whether it is "security, however denominated," which must be itemized and returned, or a payment under the rental agreement and so rent. Only a court could settle that. The safe courses are a refundable pet deposit inside the quarter-month limit, or pet rent, or both.

An assistance animal is not a pet: no pet deposit and no pet rent may be charged for one.

title: No Plain-Language or Readability Rule for a Nebraska Lease — but One Formatting Rule Does Reach It
bodyText: New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, Hawaii and the Virgin Islands put a readability standard on consumer contracts, and in several of them a residential lease is inside it: short sentences, everyday words, captioned and divided sections, sometimes a dollar ceiling that decides whether the statute applies. Nebraska enacted no such statute. There is no Nebraska plain-language act, no readability or reading-level test, no requirement that a lease be divided into captioned sections, no dollar threshold, and no Attorney General review of lease forms. A lease is not unenforceable in Nebraska for being long, dense or written in legal English. Two scope limits on that, both of which matter when you are drafting. FIRST, Nebraska does have one formatting rule that reaches an ordinary standard-form lease, and it is easy to trip: Sec. 25-2602.02 requires that "THIS CONTRACT CONTAINS AN ARBITRATION PROVISION WHICH MAY BE ENFORCED BY THE PARTIES" appear "in capitalized, underlined type adjoining the signature block of any standardized agreement in which binding arbitration is the sole remedy for dispute resolution." A pre-printed lease is a standardized agreement. So if your lease makes arbitration the sole remedy, that sentence has to be capitalized, underlined and next to the signatures. Two Nebraska appellate decisions are reported as holding, one that a strict-compliance failure makes the arbitration clause voidable and unenforceable, the other that the section is displaced where federal law governs the contract; read them before relying on them. SECOND, the absence of a readability rule is not the absence of a standard. Nebraska's deceptive-trade-practices and consumer-protection statutes still reach a lease term that misleads, and a term buried or obscured is the classic fact pattern for them. The drafting advice is therefore unchanged by the absence: write it so a tenant can follow it, caption your sections, and keep the arbitration notice where the statute puts it.

title: No "Statement of Consumer Restrictions" Page on a Nebraska Lease — Because Nebraska Voids the Waivers Instead
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Plain Language Consumer Contract Act makes a landlord put a separate statement at the front of the lease listing every term that restricts the tenant's rights — every waiver, every confession of judgment, every limitation of remedy — with optional Attorney General preapproval of the form and a $50,000 transaction ceiling. Nebraska has no counterpart. There is no front-page consumer statement, no required list of restrictive terms, no form-filing or preapproval route with the Nebraska Attorney General, and no dollar threshold anywhere in this area. The reason is worth knowing, because it changes what you do rather than merely what you skip. Nebraska regulates the same risk at the opposite end: instead of making you DISCLOSE the waivers, Sec. 76-1415(1) makes four of them UNENFORCEABLE outright. No rental agreement may provide that the tenant waives or foregoes rights or remedies under the Act, authorizes anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement, agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees, or agrees to exculpate or limit the landlord's liability for its own active and actionable negligence (or to indemnify the landlord for it). And Sec. 76-1415(2) adds a penalty: a landlord who deliberately uses a lease containing a provision known to be prohibited owes the tenant actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. So there is nothing to list on a front page, because the terms a Pennsylvania statement would have to disclose are void here anyway. The practical course: do not draft a "consumer restrictions" page for a Nebraska lease, and do not import one from a multistate form — a page that lists waivers you cannot enforce is an admission under Sec. 76-1415(2), not a protection. Spend the effort instead on screening the lease against the four Sec. 76-1415(1) categories.

title: No Candidate or Canvasser Right of Access to a Nebraska Apartment Building — and the One Limit on Keeping Them Out
bodyText: Minnesota makes a multiple-unit building let candidates in; Maryland makes a landlord maintain a voter information area. Nothing of the kind was found in Nebraska: no statutory right of access for a candidate, a campaign worker, a petition circulator or a canvasser, no voter-information posting duty, and no protection for political literature or yard signs in a rental. So the common areas are yours to control, through house rules under Sec. 76-1422 and, if someone will not leave, through criminal trespass. Second-degree criminal trespass under Sec. 28-521(1) reaches a person who "enters or remains in any place as to which notice against trespass is given by: (a) Actual communication to the actor; or (b) Posting in a manner prescribed by law or reasonably likely to come to the attention of intruders; or (c) Fencing or other enclosure manifestly designed to exclude intruders" — so a no-solicitation sign at the entrance, or telling the canvasser to leave, is the mechanism, and under Sec. 28-521(5) defying an order to leave personally communicated by the owner raises the offense to a Class II misdemeanor. HERE IS THE LIMIT, and it is the part that gets landlords into trouble. Trespass turns on being "not licensed or privileged" to be there. Your tenant can license a visitor into the tenant's own unit, and a candidate the tenant invited is not trespassing in the leased premises however firm your no-solicitation rule is. Your rule can govern the lobby, the halls and the grounds; it cannot bar a person the tenant has invited into the dwelling unit. A second limit: Sec. 76-1439(1)(b) makes it retaliation to raise the rent, cut services, or bring or threaten a possession action because "the tenant has organized or become a member of a tenants' union or similar organization," and Sec. 76-1439(2) gives the tenant the Sec. 76-1430 remedies and a defense to possession. Tenant organizing is therefore protected even though canvassing is not. Finally, do not write this as a flat "no political activity" lease clause: a clause purporting to control what the tenant does inside the unit, or who the tenant may invite in, reaches past what Nebraska lets you enforce. Keep the rule to the common areas and to solicitation by non-residents.

title: Nebraska Does Regulate Swimming Pools — and in 2026 It Handed Enforcement to Your City or County
bodyText: If your property has a pool, Nebraska is not a silent state. The Environmental Safety Act (Secs. 81-15,261 to 81-15,291) runs a statewide pool programme, and Laws 2026, LB759 rewrote who enforces it, operative July 18, 2026. What the statute itself says, after LB759: (1) Sec. 81-15,265(1) — the Department of Water, Energy, and Environment "shall adopt and have available minimum sanitary and safety requirements in the form of regulations for the design, construction, equipment, and operation of swimming pools and bather preparation facilities," including waiver and variance provisions, and "No swimming pool shall be constructed until plans and specifications have been approved by the department." So a new pool at an apartment complex is a plan-review item before a shovel goes in the ground. (2) Sec. 81-15,265(2) — your city, county or local public health department "shall by resolution, ordinance, or regulation adopt and enforce minimum sanitary and safety requirements for the equipment and operation of swimming pools ... which meet or exceed" the department's. (3) Sec. 81-15,268(1) — the local government with jurisdiction inspects the pool, and (2) may charge an inspection fee up to actual cost. (4) Sec. 81-15,268(3) — "The owner and operator of any swimming pool shall operate such swimming pool in compliance with minimum sanitary and safety requirements established by the local government," shall retain operation and analytical records for three years, and shall make them available to the local government on request. (5) Sec. 81-15,268(5) — "The operator of any swimming pool shall maintain a certificate of competency for swimming pools," from a course on the department's acceptable list. (6) Sec. 81-15,270 — an owner or operator who fails to keep the certificate or to comply with the local minimum requirements "shall be subject to enforcement, penalties, or other remedies as established by such local government." WHICH POOLS ARE COVERED. Sec. 81-15,264(2) says a swimming pool "includes, but is not limited to, a pool serving a community, a subdivision, an apartment complex, a condominium". Sec. 81-15,264(4) leaves out "a pool at a private residence intended only for the use of the owner and guests." So an apartment-complex pool is covered, and so is a hot tub or spa under (3). For a pool at a single rented house or duplex, the statute does not say. It covers a basin built "solely for the purpose of public swimming", and a pool for your tenants is neither public nor only for the owner. Only a court could settle that. The cautious course: ask the local government whether it treats your pool as covered before you open it to tenants. The department's rule (196 NAC 1-001.21) separately defines a "short-term rental pool" at a single-family home let for under 30 days, and says its operating standards are not intended for those pools; a local government may still regulate them. WHAT THE DEPARTMENT'S RULES REQUIRE. The statute sets no fence height, but the department's rules do (Title 196, Nebraska Administrative Code, effective September 23, 2026). An apartment or condominium pool is a "Class B" pool (196 NAC 1-001.05). For a new or modified pool, 196 NAC 1-005.08 requires an enclosure "not less than 6 feet high", a "self-closing and latching gate or door" with its latch controls at least 48 inches up, openings too small for a 4-inch sphere, and "no direct access to the pool from ... apartments". Under 196 NAC 2, a Class B pool must have a certified pool operator on site or able to be there within 60 minutes, keep proof of the certificate in the office, and keep the enclosure free of 4-inch openings. It must also have a rescue tube or ring buoy and a 12-foot shepherd's crook. Where no lifeguard is on duty, it must post "WARNING – NO LIFEGUARD ON DUTY". Chapter 2 is the minimum. Your city, county or local public health department adopts it or something stricter, so check its version and get the plan review before you build. No rule requires a pool-safety notice at lease signing. On top of all that, Sec. 76-1419(1)(c) makes you "keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition," which reaches a pool, pool deck and gate independently of the pool programme — and where a minimum housing code applies to the premises, Sec. 76-1419's closing sentence caps your duty under that section at substantial compliance with the code. One drafting trap. Pool rules belong in your rules and regulations, and the tenant must have notice of them when the lease is signed (Sec. 76-1422(6)). But do NOT write a "swim at your own risk, Landlord not liable" clause: Sec. 76-1415(1)(d) makes a lease provision exculpating or limiting the landlord's liability for its own active and actionable negligence — or indemnifying the landlord for it — unenforceable, and Sec. 76-1415(2) gives the tenant damages and attorney's fees if you use such a provision deliberately. Rules about conduct, hours, guests and children are enforceable; a liability waiver is not.

title: No Tenant Right to a Window or Portable Air Conditioner in Nebraska — Heat Is a Duty, Cooling Is Not
bodyText: Washington (RCW 59.18.740) and Oregon give a tenant an affirmative right to install a portable or window cooling device, and Washington makes a lease that restricts window units say so. Nebraska gives the tenant no such right, imposes no maximum indoor temperature, and requires no lease disclosure about window units. You may prohibit or condition window and portable units, and the ordinary No Alterations clause is where that belongs. The textual basis is a contrast inside one subsection, which is worth knowing because it answers the habitability version of the question too. Sec. 76-1419(1)(f) requires the landlord to "supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat" — heat is named, cooling is not, anywhere in the Act. Sec. 76-1419(1)(d) then requires the landlord to "maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by him or her." So air conditioning enters Nebraska law only through (1)(d), and only once you supply it. That cuts two ways. If the unit comes with central air or a window unit you provided, or if your listing or lease promises it, you must keep it in good and safe working order — "or required to be supplied" catches what you contracted to supply as well as what the law requires. If you supply no cooling at all, a hot apartment is not by itself a Nebraska habitability breach, and the tenant has no statutory route to install a unit over your objection. Two practical cautions. First, Sec. 76-1419(2) and (3) let you shift some duties to the tenant by agreement, but (2) is confined to a single-family residence and (3) reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" — so you cannot write away the (1)(d) duty on an air conditioner you supplied in a duplex or apartment. Second, if you do permit window units, say in the lease who installs, who maintains, who removes it and who repairs the window and sill, because a unit the tenant installs is the tenant's alteration and a unit you supplied is your Sec. 76-1419(1)(d) appliance — and the line between them is the lease.

title: No Tenant Right to Plug-In Solar in Nebraska — and One Thing You Cannot Sign Away
bodyText: Virginia gives tenants of landlords with more than four units a right to a plug-in solar device from 2027, Vermont (30 V.S.A. Sec. 256(g)) gives a notice-then-install right with the landlord confined to reasonable restrictions delivered inside a set window, and Maine (35-A Sec. 3475) lets a tenant install a plug-in solar or battery device without utility approval subject to restoring the building. Nebraska has none of this. No statute gives a Nebraska tenant a right to install a solar panel, a plug-in solar device or a battery on the unit's exterior, a balcony or a window; there is no notice-and-reasonable-restrictions procedure, no unit-count threshold, no restoration standard, and no rule voiding a lease term that forbids it. A "no exterior installations" or No Alterations clause is fully enforceable here, and so is a condition requiring your written consent, specifying who removes the device and who repairs the surface it was mounted to. Two things to keep in view. FIRST, the absence is not universal across energy fixtures: Nebraska's carbon monoxide and smoke alarm duties are real, and if you do permit a tenant device that ties into the electrical system, Sec. 76-1419(1)(d) makes you maintain in good and safe working order all electrical facilities "supplied or required to be supplied" by you — so consenting to a hard-wired installation can pull it into your maintenance column in a way a plug-in device does not. Keep consent limited to plug-in devices if you give it at all. SECOND, there is one Nebraska rule in this area that no lease can get around, and it runs the other way: Sec. 76-3004 provides that "No interest in any wind or solar resource located on a tract of land and associated with the production or potential production of wind or solar energy on the tract of land may be severed from the surface estate." So you cannot grant anyone — a tenant, a solar developer or a third party — a standalone, severed interest in the property's solar resource. Solar on a Nebraska rental is arranged by lease, licence or easement over the surface estate, not by carving out the resource. Nebraska does have a voluntary solar and wind easement regime, in chapter 66 rather than in the landlord-tenant act, and that is the instrument to use if a tenant or a provider wants protected access to sunlight; it was not readable here (see the notes).

title: Nebraska Has No Small-Landlord Exemption — Its Thresholds Count Units in a Building, Not Doors in Your Portfolio
bodyText: Ohio, Virginia, Illinois, Kentucky, West Virginia, Maryland, Massachusetts and Connecticut all tier landlord duties by how many units the landlord has. Nebraska does not. Owning one rental house and owning four hundred doors puts you under the same Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Sec. 76-1408 lists the only exclusions from the Act and every one of them is about the KIND of arrangement, not its size: residence at an institution incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counseling or religious service; occupancy under a contract of sale; occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization; transient occupancy in a hotel or motel; occupancy by an employee whose right to occupy is conditional on employment about the premises; occupancy by a condominium owner or a cooperative proprietary lessee; premises used primarily for agricultural purposes; and "a lease of improved or unimproved residential land for a term of five years or more." There is no unit count anywhere in it, and the whole list is prefaced "Unless created to avoid the application of" the Act — so a structure built to dodge the Act fails even if it fits a category. Nebraska does use counted thresholds, but they count something else, and getting the unit of measurement wrong is the error to avoid. (1) PER UNIT, not per portfolio: "single-family residence" under Sec. 76-1410(16) is a two-limb test — a structure maintained and used as a single dwelling unit; a unit sharing a wall still qualifies "if it has direct access to a street or thoroughfare and shares neither heating facilities, hot water equipment, nor any other essential facility or service with any other dwelling unit." Both limbs must be met. It matters because only for a single-family residence may Sec. 76-1419(2) shift the waste-removal and water-and-heat duties to the tenant; in a duplex or apartment Sec. 76-1419(3) reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling," so those two duties cannot be moved at all. (2) PER BUILDING: Sec. 20-319(6) defines "covered multifamily dwellings" for the Nebraska Fair Housing Act's accessible-design rules as "buildings consisting of four or more units if such buildings have one or more elevators" and "ground floor units in other buildings consisting of four or more units," for first occupancy after September 1, 1991. A fifth building does not pull your four three-plexes in. (3) PER COMPLEX, and this is the one landlords miss: Sec. 76-1302(2) defines a "retirement community" as any complex "of more than ten units ... offered for sale or lease as part of a common promotional plan" when it is advertised as such "or when there is a minimum age limit tending to attract persons who are nearing retirement age" — an age limit alone is a trigger, and registration under Secs. 76-1301 to 76-1315 follows. See the separate guidance on that Act; the reach of the word "lease" in it is genuinely unsettled. (4) INSIDE YOUR OWN HOME, read conjunctively: Sec. 20-322(3) lets a person refuse to rent a room in his or her own home "for any reason or for no reason," but "this exception shall not apply to any person who makes available for rental or occupancy more than four sleeping rooms to a person or family within his or her own home." Both limbs — your own home AND not more than four sleeping rooms — have to hold; lose either and ordinary fair-housing law applies. (5) SECTION-LOCAL, so do not borrow it: Sec. 76-238(3)(d)'s "not more than four units" definition of residential real estate exists only for the recording-and-possession-as-notice rule in that section and says nothing about any landlord duty. Practical upshot: do not look for a small-landlord carve-out in Nebraska, because there is none; and when you meet a four-unit or ten-unit line here, read what it is counting before you apply it.

title: No Possession Bond in Nebraska — and the Confessed Judgment Behind Tennessee's Version Is Void Here
bodyText: Tennessee gives a landlord a statutory end-of-term possession bond carrying a confessed judgment, usable only outside the counties where its act applies. Texas has a different animal of the same name — a bond the landlord posts to take possession before the case is decided. Nebraska has neither, and the mechanism at the heart of the Tennessee version is specifically prohibited: Sec. 76-1415(1)(b) says no rental agreement may provide that the tenant "[a]uthorizes any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement," and Sec. 76-1415(2) makes such a provision unenforceable and gives the tenant actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees if a landlord deliberately uses a lease containing a provision known to be prohibited.
