So do not carry a confession-of-judgment or cognovit clause, a power of attorney to confess, or an end-of-term bond provision into a Nebraska lease from a multistate form. Nebraska does have one bond in a possession case, and it runs the other way — it protects you. Sec. 76-1447 provides that "An appeal by the defendant shall stay the execution of any writ of restitution, so long as the defendant deposits with the clerk of the district court the amount of judgment and costs, or gives an appeal bond with surety therefor, and thereafter pays into court, on a monthly basis, an amount equal to the monthly rent called for by the rental agreement at the time the complaint was filed." Three things follow. A tenant's appeal does NOT automatically stay your writ; the stay is conditional on the deposit or bond. The condition is continuing, not one-off — the monthly payments into court must keep coming, and the figure is the rent in the agreement at the time the complaint was filed, not a court's later estimate. And if the tenant neither deposits nor bonds, the writ can go forward while the appeal runs. If a tenant appeals, check the file for the deposit or bond and for each month's payment; a missed month is your opening to move on the writ. Nothing about Sec. 76-1447 belongs in the lease — it operates by statute whatever the lease says, and a clause purporting to waive the tenant's appeal or stay rights would run straight into Sec. 76-1415(1)(a).

title: After the Writ: What Nebraska Makes You Do With the Property Still in the Unit
bodyText: Winning possession does not let you clear the unit. Sec. 76-1446 ties the two together expressly: after the court issues the writ of restitution directing the sheriff or constable to restore possession "on a specified date not more than ten days after issuance," the same section says "The plaintiff shall comply with the Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act and subsection (5) of section 76-1414 in the removal of personal property remaining on the premises at the time possession of the premises is restored." So the abandoned-property statute is not just for a tenant who walked away; it governs a set-out. The sequence. STORAGE IS YOUR CHOICE, CARE IS NOT: Sec. 69-2306 lets you "leave personal property on the vacated premises or ... remove and store the property in a place of safekeeping," but "The landlord shall exercise reasonable care in storing the property" and you are liable for loss "caused by the landlord's intentional or negligent act." There is no statutory inventory requirement and no bonded-warehouse option. NOTICE: under Sec. 69-2303 you give written notice to the former tenant and to anyone you reasonably believe owns the property, describing it well enough for the owner to identify it — you need not describe the contents of a locked or tied trunk, valise, box or container, or of a locked mobile home, but the Sec. 69-2309 liability shield does not cover property you left out of the notice. The notice states that reasonable storage costs may be charged, where the property may be claimed, and the claim deadline, which must be at least seven days after personal delivery or at least fourteen days after mailing; it goes by personal delivery or first-class mail to the last known address, and also to any other address where you have reason to believe it will actually reach the person. It must be given within six months of lease expiration or of discovery of the abandonment, whichever is later. RELEASE: Sec. 69-2307 requires you to release the property to the former tenant, or to anyone you reasonably believe is the owner, on payment of the reasonable costs of storage and advertising if they claim it by the notice date — and, if the notice announced a public sale, right up until the sale on payment of costs incurred to that point. Sec. 69-2310 caps the arithmetic: the tenant may be charged storage for all the property, another owner only for the property they claim, and "the landlord may not charge more than one person for the same costs." Sec. 69-2302(9) caps storage itself at the fair rental value of the space reasonably required, plus the actual removal, disassembly and transport costs. DISPOSAL: Sec. 69-2308(1) requires a public sale by competitive bidding unless "the landlord reasonably believes that the total resale value of the property not released is less than two thousand dollars," in which case you may keep or dispose of it as you choose — and at the point you decide, any locked container or mobile home "shall be opened, if practicable, with as little damage as possible, and its contents evaluated." A sale needs newspaper advertisement once a week for two consecutive weeks (or, with no local paper, posting in at least six conspicuous places at least ten days ahead), no sooner than ten days after the first publication and with the last publication at least five days before the sale. Unclaimed proceeds net of storage, advertising and sale costs go to the State Treasurer within thirty days under the Uniform Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act. THE SEPARATE FOURTEEN-DAY ROUTE PEOPLE MISS: Sec. 69-2311 is a second, parallel duty. If a residential tenant asks in writing within fourteen days of vacating, describing the property and giving a mailing address, you must surrender it — and if you want your removal and storage costs first, your demand has to be in writing, itemised by nature and amount, and mailed or personally presented within five days after you actually receive the request. The tenant then has a mutually agreed reasonable time, not later than seventy-two hours after tendering payment, to collect. WHAT IT COSTS TO GET THIS WRONG: Sec. 69-2312 makes a landlord who retains property in violation of the Act liable for actual damages up to the value of the property plus reasonable attorney's fees and costs, with three days presumed a reasonable time to surrender. TWO LIMITS ON YOUR PROTECTION. Sec. 69-2309's immunity is three-tiered and not absolute: releasing to the former tenant immunises you completely; releasing to a believed owner, or disposing of property under Sec. 69-2308, immunises you against everyone you notified and against anyone you did not notify UNLESS that person proves you believed or should have believed they had an interest and that you knew or should on reasonable investigation have known their address. And Sec. 69-2314 says the Act's remedy "shall not be exclusive," so compliance does not foreclose other claims. FINALLY, the former tenant who comes back after the writ: once possession is restored, the tenant is no longer licensed or privileged to be there, which is what Sec. 28-520(1)(a) (first-degree criminal trespass, Class I misdemeanor) and Sec. 28-521 turn on — but do not self-help. Let the sheriff or constable execute the writ, and call law enforcement rather than removing a returning occupant yourself; Sec. 76-1430 and Sec. 76-1423(4) are still there.

title: No Duty to Test a Small Private Well or Give a Nebraska Tenant the Results — but a Well Serving 25 People Is a Public Water System
bodyText: New Jersey, Oregon, Maryland and Connecticut make a landlord on a private well test the water and hand the tenant the results, sometimes on a fixed cycle and sometimes at lease signing. Nothing of the kind was found in Nebraska. For an ordinary rental on its own well, no statute requires a landlord to test the well, to give a tenant test results, to disclose a nitrate or coliform exceedance, or to post a water-quality notice — and Nebraska is a state where that silence is conspicuous, because its rural rentals run on domestic wells and nitrate is its signature groundwater problem. Two things confirm the direction rather than merely the silence. FIRST, the one well notice Nebraska does require runs to a BUYER, not a tenant. Sec. 76-2,124(1) makes "[a]ny person transferring OWNERSHIP of real property not inside the corporate limits of a municipality" complete and give the transferee, at or before closing, a water resources update notice stating whether surface water rights are attached and "whether there are any water wells, except water wells used solely for domestic purposes and constructed prior to September 9, 1993, on the real property." It is a registration-updating form, it says nothing about water quality, and it is triggered by a transfer of ownership — a lease is not one. So the legislature addressed rural wells in a conveyance and left the lease alone. SECOND, Nebraska moved in the opposite direction in 2026: Laws 2026, LB759 is titled, among other things, "to eliminate provisions relating to a private water supply and private sewage disposal facilities," and it outright repealed a block of Environmental Safety Act sections. Whatever state oversight of a private water supply existed before, less exists now. THE BIG-WELL EXCEPTION, WHICH IS A REAL TEST-AND-NOTIFY REGIME. If your well serves enough people, you are not a private well owner at all. Section 71-5301(9)(a) makes a "public water system" any system "for providing the public with water for human consumption through pipes" that "has at least fifteen service connections or regularly serves an average of at least twenty-five individuals daily at least sixty days per year." A rural apartment complex or mobile home park on its own well can cross that line. Then section 71-5303(1) applies: "No person shall operate or maintain a public water system without first obtaining a permit". Section 71-5302 applies the state drinking water standards and monitoring rules to it, section 71-5307 requires a licensed operator, and section 71-5304.02 lets the Department of Water, Energy, and Environment require notice "to the persons served" of a violation or missed test. Count your units and occupants before you assume you are outside it. Below that size, the Department's private-well rule (178 NAC 9, 1985) reaches only listed facilities, including "mobile home parks". There it requires a bacteria and nitrate test of a new or repaired well. Ordinary rentals are not on the list. WHAT TO DO ANYWAY. Sec. 76-1419(1)(f) requires you to "supply running water" — quantity, with no quality standard attached — and Sec. 76-1419(1)(b) requires you to keep the premises "in a fit and habitable condition," which is where contaminated drinking water would be argued, not in any well statute. So the risk is a habitability and negligence risk, not a disclosure-penalty risk. Test the well, keep the lab reports, and give the tenant a copy: a test you took and shared is the cheapest evidence that the premises were fit, and a result you had and concealed is the opposite. If a result exceeds a drinking-water standard, treat it as a repair obligation under Sec. 76-1419(1)(b) and fix or filter it. Put in the lease who pays for testing and who maintains the well, pump and any treatment system — nothing in Nebraska law allocates that, so the lease is the only allocation there is, subject to Sec. 76-1419(3)'s limits on shifting maintenance in anything other than a single-family residence. And check locally: your county or local public health department may have well rules, and those are not state statutes.

title: Nebraska Needs No Writing for a Repair Promise — Which Is Exactly Why You Should Put One in Writing
bodyText: Wisconsin (ATCP 134.07) makes a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve the unit worthless unless it is in writing, carries a completion date, and is given before the lease is signed. Nebraska imposes no such formality — and the consequence runs the opposite way from what landlords expect. Here, the promise binds you whether or not it was written. Sec. 76-1410(14): "Rental agreement means ALL AGREEMENTS, WRITTEN OR ORAL, between a landlord and tenant, and valid rules and regulations adopted under section 76-1422 embodying the terms and conditions concerning the use and occupancy of a dwelling unit and premises." So the walkthrough sentence — "we'll get that dishwasher fixed before you move in," "the fence goes up in the spring" — is part of the rental agreement by definition. Two statutes then give it teeth. Sec. 76-1419(1)(d) makes you maintain in good and safe working order all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances "SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her" — "required to be supplied" reaches what you agreed to supply, not just what the law makes you supply. And Sec. 76-1425 is the remedy: on a material noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement, the tenant may serve written notice specifying the acts and omissions and that the agreement terminates on a date not less than thirty days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in fourteen days; if substantially the same act or omission recurs within six months, the tenant may terminate on fourteen days' notice with no cure period at all. Sec. 76-1425(2) adds damages and injunctive relief for ANY noncompliance with the rental agreement or Sec. 76-1419, with reasonable attorney's fees if the noncompliance is willful. Sec. 76-1425(4) then makes you return all prepaid rent and security recoverable under Sec. 76-1416. WHAT TO DO. Write your repair promises down, with a completion date for each, and attach the list to the lease. Not because Nebraska requires it — it does not — but because the alternative is litigating what was said at a showing, against a statute that counts oral agreements. A dated written list converts a disputed promise into a defined obligation you can discharge and prove you discharged. AND BE CAREFUL WITH THE OPPOSITE CLAUSE. The tempting term is a disclaimer: "Landlord has made no promises to repair other than those listed." We do not offer one for Nebraska, and the reason is Sec. 76-1415(1)(a): no rental agreement may provide that the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under" the Act, and Sec. 76-1415(2) makes such a provision unenforceable and exposes a landlord who deliberately uses it to the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. A clause whose work is to strip an oral agreement of the status Sec. 76-1410(14) gives it is at least arguably that — and a clause that is arguably void is worse than no clause, because it invites the argument without delivering the protection. You may add your own if your counsel is comfortable; the safer route is the affirmative one, which is to list what you promised and do it. Finally, note what you cannot fix by agreement: Sec. 76-1419(2) lets you shift the waste-removal and water-and-heat duties only in a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE, and Sec. 76-1419(3) reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" in anything else — so a repair list is a promise you are making, not a duty you are moving.

title: No Proposition 65-Style Chemical Warning for a Nebraska Rental
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 makes a landlord warn tenants about listed chemicals present at the property — in the lease, on a sign, or both — and the sanction is a private right of action with per-day penalties. Nebraska has nothing comparable. There is no Nebraska list of chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, no exposure-warning duty, no warning sign requirement for a residential building, no "clear and reasonable warning" standard, and no bounty-hunter enforcement provision. Do not carry a Prop 65 warning block into a Nebraska lease from a multistate form: it has no legal effect here, it invites questions about conditions at the property that you then have to answer, and a warning about a hazard you have not actually identified is a statement you may be held to. What you do owe, and it is a different thing entirely: the FEDERAL lead-based paint disclosure under 42 U.S.C. 4852d and 24 C.F.R. part 35 for target housing built before 1978, which is already in the library as the Lead-Based Paint Disclosure clause, and a carbon monoxide alarm under Sec. 76-606 on the triggers that section sets. Beyond those two, Nebraska's chemical-hazard exposure for a landlord sits in habitability and negligence, not in disclosure: Sec. 76-1419(1)(b) requires you to "[m]ake all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition," and where a minimum housing code applies to the premises, Sec. 76-1419's closing sentence caps your duty under that section at substantial compliance with the code — while adding that "[t]he obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state." So if you know of a chemical hazard, the answer in Nebraska is to fix it, not to paper it; and if a tenant asks, answer accurately, because Nebraska's deceptive-trade-practices law reaches a misleading statement in a consumer transaction even without a specific disclosure duty.

title: No Property-Tax-Portion-of-Rent Statement in Nebraska — Its Tax Relief Goes to the Owner, Not the Renter
bodyText: Nevada makes a landlord give every tenant an annual statement each July, and again on every rent change unless the lease already provides for it, showing what portion of the rent represents property taxes. West Virginia has a senior-tenant version. Nebraska requires nothing of the kind: no annual statement, no statement on a rent change, no certification of rent paid, and no form for a tenant to use in claiming anything. The structural reason is worth knowing, because it tells you the duty is not going to appear from some other direction. Those statements exist to feed a RENTER-side property tax rebate — the tenant needs a number from the landlord to claim it. Nebraska does not relieve property tax that way. Its Property Tax Credit Act works at the other end: Sec. 77-4212 sets a minimum statewide amount of relief each tax year, the Property Tax Administrator allocates it among the counties by credit allocation valuation, and the county treasurer allocates it among the taxing units so that it lands as a credit against the real property tax itself. The person who benefits is whoever owes the property tax — the owner. There is no renter claim, so there is nothing for a landlord to certify. TWO PRACTICAL POINTS THAT DO FOLLOW. First, if you want to pass a property tax increase through to the tenant, that is a matter of your lease and nothing else: Sec. 76-1410(13) makes "all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement" rent, so a tax escalator is enforceable as rent if the lease provides for it and silent means no. Build it into the rent figure or write an explicit escalator; do not assume a right to bill it later. Second, if a tenant asks what share of their rent is property tax — for a federal filing, a benefits application or their own budgeting — you may answer, and it is good practice to do so accurately if you do, but you are not obliged to and you take on nothing by declining. If you choose to give a figure, give a real one from the tax statement rather than an estimate, because Nebraska's deceptive-practices law reaches an inaccurate statement in a consumer transaction even where no statute required the statement at all.

title: Nebraska Does Void a Lease for a Prohibited Use — and the Statute That Says So Can Get You Sued If You Act On It
bodyText: Rhode Island annuls a lease by statute when the premises are used for a prohibited purpose. Nebraska has a provision of the same family, and a landlord who reads only that provision can walk into a three-month penalty. THE STATUTE. Sec. 28-826: "If a tenant or occupant of a building or tenement under lawful title used such place for the purposes of committing a violation of sections 28-807 to 28-829, and if such tenant or occupant is convicted of such violation, such conviction shall make the lease or other title which he holds void at the option of the owner, and without any act of the owner, cause the right of possession to revert and vest in such owner, who may without further process of law make immediate entry upon the premises and retake possession." Read the conditions. It needs a CONVICTION, not an arrest or a suspicion. The range Secs. 28-807 to 28-829 is Nebraska's OBSCENITY article — it is not the drug article and not the prostitution sections — so the trigger is narrow. And the lease is void "at the option of the owner," so nothing happens automatically; you elect. THE TRAP. Sec. 28-826's last words invite you to "without further process of law make immediate entry upon the premises and retake possession." In a residential tenancy that collides with three other provisions: Sec. 76-1403 lets other law supplement the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act only "[u]nless displaced by the provisions of" the Act; Sec. 76-1423(4) says "[t]he landlord has no other right of access except by court order, as permitted by subsection (2) of section 76-1432, or if the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises"; and Sec. 76-1430 gives a tenant unlawfully removed or excluded a FIXED sum — three months' periodic rent plus reasonable attorney's fees, with no proof of loss required. THE CAUTIOUS COURSE: elect to treat the lease as void under Sec. 28-826 if you like, serve the notice, and then take possession THROUGH THE COURT under Secs. 76-1440 to 76-1446. Do not take the self-help invitation. THE NUISANCE MACHINERY, WHICH RUNS AGAINST YOUR BUILDING AND NOT ONLY AGAINST YOUR TENANT. Under Sec. 28-822 a city, village or county, through its chief law enforcement officer, may sue in equity to abate an obscenity nuisance and to perpetually enjoin the person maintaining it, and a person who keeps using the place for that purpose "shall be punished as for contempt." Sec. 28-825 then makes an order of abatement part of the judgment: removal and sale of the personal property used in conducting the nuisance, and — this is the part that costs the owner — either renewal for one year of any bond the owner of the real property furnished, or continuation for one year of any closing order, or "an order directing the effectual closing of the place against its use for any illegal purpose unless otherwise released." A one-year closing order on a rental unit is a total loss of that unit's income. YOUR ESCAPE ROUTE AND ITS PRICE. Sec. 28-823 lets the owner of the real property appear between the filing of the complaint and the hearing on the permanent injunction and, on payment of all costs incurred and on filing a bond "with sureties to be approved by the clerk of the district court in the full value of the property" conditioned on immediately abating the nuisance and preventing it from being re-established, obtain release of the property — but only if the court is "satisfied with the good faith of the owner of the real property." Note also Sec. 28-825's sting for anyone claiming innocent ownership of seized contents: "Every defendant in the action is presumed to have had knowledge of the general reputation of the place." So move fast; the window is before the permanent-injunction hearing. TWO MORE REASONS NOT TO WAIT, BOTH BINDING YOU DIRECTLY. Sec. 28-804(1): a person "who has or exercises control over the use of any place which offers seclusion or shelter for the practice of prostitution and who knowingly grants or permits the use of such place for the purpose of prostitution commits the offense of keeping a place of prostitution" — a Class IV FELONY under Sec. 28-804(2), or a Class III felony if any person using the place is under eighteen. And Sec. 28-417(1)(e) makes it unlawful for any person "[t]o keep or maintain any store, shop, warehouse, dwelling house, building, vehicle, boat, aircraft, or place whatever which such person KNOWS OR SHOULD KNOW is resorted to by persons using controlled substances ... for the purpose of using such substances or which is used for the keeping or selling of the same," a Class III misdemeanor under Sec. 28-417(2) — with a constructive-knowledge standard and no landlord safe harbour anywhere in the section. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR LEASE. The purpose limitation itself has statutory backing: Sec. 76-1424 provides that "[u]nless otherwise agreed, the tenant shall occupy his dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit" — and because Sec. 76-1424 is one of the chapter 76 sections that open "[u]nless otherwise agreed," your Residential Use Only clause can widen or narrow it. What your clause cannot do is manufacture a self-help right or waive the Secs. 76-1440 to 76-1446 process, and a clause saying the lease is "automatically void" on any criminal use overstates Sec. 28-826 in three ways at once: it drops the conviction requirement, it drops the limitation to the obscenity article, and it converts an option into an automatic forfeiture.

title: No Recycling Notice in Nebraska — but You Cannot Hand Apartment Tenants the Trash Duty Either
bodyText: Oregon (ORS 90.318) makes a landlord tell tenants where and how to recycle on the premises, and Maryland and Massachusetts impose apartment recycling duties. Nebraska requires no recycling notice, provides no recycling service duty, and sets no diversion target for a rental property. The word "recycling" appears in Nebraska statute only in the scrap-metal dealer provisions and the degradable-packaging and container rules, none of which reaches a landlord. What Nebraska does impose is the waste duty underneath it, and it is stricter than most landlords assume. Sec. 76-1419(1)(e) requires the landlord to "[p]rovide and maintain appropriate receptacles and conveniences for the removal of ashes, garbage, rubbish, and other waste incidental to the occupancy of the dwelling unit and arrange for their removal from the appropriate receptacle." Both halves are yours: the receptacles AND the arrangement for removal. HERE IS THE PART THAT CATCHES PEOPLE. You can move that duty to the tenant only in a single-family residence. Sec. 76-1419(2) permits the landlord and tenant "of a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE" to agree that the tenant perform the duties specified in subdivisions (1)(e) and (1)(f), in writing, for good consideration, in good faith and not to evade the landlord's obligations. For anything else, Sec. 76-1419(3) reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" — it does not name (1)(e) at all. So a clause in a duplex or apartment lease making the tenant responsible for arranging refuse collection does not work, however it is drafted and however much consideration it recites. And "single-family residence" is a defined two-limb test: Sec. 76-1410(16) requires a structure maintained and used as a single dwelling unit, and a unit sharing a wall still qualifies only "if it has direct access to a street or thoroughfare and shares neither heating facilities, hot water equipment, nor any other essential facility or service with any other dwelling unit." WHAT TO DO ABOUT RECYCLING. Because no state rule applies, the only rules are your city's or county's and whatever your hauler's contract says. If you provide recycling containers, that is a convenience you supplied and you should say in the lease or in house rules who may use them, what may go in them, and who pays a contamination or overage charge from the hauler — none of that is prescribed, so silence means arguments. Put it in rules and regulations rather than leaving it oral, and remember Sec. 76-1422(6): a rule is enforceable against the tenant "only if ... the tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement." If you want to charge the tenant for a hauler's contamination fee, say so expressly; Sec. 76-1410(13) makes every payment under the rental agreement "rent," which is what makes an express charge collectible and an unexpressed one uncollectible. Finally, check your municipality: Lincoln and Omaha run their own solid-waste programmes and those ordinances are not state law and are not resolved here.

title: Nebraska Gives a Tenant No Right to Buy Back the Eviction — No Deadline, No Protected Third-Party Check, No Required Reservation Wording
bodyText: Several states build a payment-based off-ramp into the eviction. Virginia lets a tenant redeem up to forty-eight hours before the eviction and makes a landlord who accepts partial rent use mandated reservation wording. Massachusetts (ch. 239, Sec. 3) bars levy where a nonpayment judgment has been fully paid with use and occupancy, even though the landlord need not accept the payment. Delaware (25 Del. C. Sec. 5716A(b)(4), (7)) makes a charity's or government agency's check count as the tenant's payment and forbids the landlord from restricting the payment method. Nebraska has none of the three. There is no redemption deadline measured back from the eviction. There is no statute barring the sheriff from executing a writ of restitution because the judgment has been paid — Sec. 76-1446 issues the writ "at the request of the plaintiff or his or her attorney" and directs the officer to restore possession on a date not more than ten days after issuance, and nothing in the Act conditions that on whether money has since changed hands. There is no provision requiring you to accept a payment from a church, a county general-assistance office, a nonprofit or a rental-assistance programme, no provision making such a payment count as the tenant's, and nothing stopping you from requiring that rent be paid by a particular method — Sec. 76-1414(3) makes rent "payable without demand or notice at the time and place agreed upon by the parties," so the lease sets the place and the lease can set the method. And no Nebraska statute prescribes reservation wording for a partial payment. THE ONE WAY MONEY STOPS A NEBRASKA WRIT, and it runs through an appeal rather than a redemption. Sec. 76-1447: "An appeal by the defendant shall stay the execution of any writ of restitution, so long as the defendant deposits with the clerk of the district court the amount of judgment and costs, or gives an appeal bond with surety therefor, and thereafter pays into court, on a monthly basis, an amount equal to the monthly rent called for by the rental agreement at the time the complaint was filed." That is a stay conditioned on an appeal plus a deposit or bond plus continuing monthly payments — not a cure, and not reinstatement of the tenancy. WHAT THIS MEANS IN PRACTICE, AND WHERE THE REAL RISK IS. The absence of a redemption statute does not mean money is safe to take. Nebraska's rule is the opposite of a redemption rule: it puts the decision in your hands and penalises an unconsidered yes. Under Sec. 76-1433 acceptance of rent with knowledge of the default waives your right to terminate for that breach unless otherwise agreed AFTER the breach occurred — so taking a partial payment, or a third party's payment, after you have served your notice can end your possession case even though no statute gave the tenant a right to make it. The Nebraska Prescribes No Lease or Notice Forms guidance and the No Relief from Forfeiture guidance cover that mechanism and the drafting trap in the lease; what this row adds is the point that a THIRD PARTY's cheque carries the same risk as the tenant's, because Sec. 76-1433 turns on your acceptance of rent and your knowledge of the default, not on who tendered it. SO: decide before the envelope is opened. If you want the money and not the tenancy, get a signed post-breach agreement reserving the termination at the moment you take it. If you want the tenancy over, return the payment promptly and document that you did. If a charity or agency offers to pay, you may accept or decline — and if you accept, treat it exactly as you would the tenant's own payment, with the same post-breach writing. Finally, two housekeeping points for the lease: you may specify acceptable payment methods, but Sec. 76-1413(9) separately prohibits requiring the TENANT to receive notices by electronic means, so do not let a payment-portal clause slide into a notice-delivery requirement; and because Sec. 76-1410(13) makes every payment under the rental agreement "rent," a payment labelled as something else (a fee, a charge, a deposit toward arrears) may still be "rent" for Sec. 76-1433 purposes.

title: No Religious or Cultural Display Right - But Your Decoration Rule Still Has to Be Neutral
bodyText: Nebraska has no mezuzah or religious-display statute. Nothing in Nebraska law gives a tenant an affirmative right to affix a religious or cultural object to a door, doorpost, entry or common-area surface, and nothing requires you to carve an exception into a decoration rule. Do not read the First Freedom Act (§§ 20-701 to 20-704) as doing that work: § 20-703 restricts only "state action", and § 20-702(5) defines state action as the implementation or application of a law, ordinance, rule, regulation or policy by the state, a political subdivision, a local government, a municipality or a public official. A private landlord is none of those, so the Act imposes no duty on you - notwithstanding that § 20-702(2) defines "Person" broadly enough to include a corporation. What does constrain you is fair housing, and it bites on the rule rather than on the object. Under § 20-318(2) it is unlawful to "[d]iscriminate against any person in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling or in the provision of services or facilities in connection therewith because of race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, sex, or military or veteran status", and under § 20-318(3) it is unlawful to publish any notice, statement or advertisement about a rental that indicates a religious preference or limitation - a house rule handed to every tenant is a statement about the rental. So a rule that names religious items, or that bans religious displays while tolerating seasonal, patriotic or sports decorations, is a Nebraska Fair Housing Act exposure even though no display statute exists. Two practical consequences. Write the rule about the physical act and not the message - no adhesive, no fasteners, no holes or penetration of door frames, no painting, nothing attached to exterior or common-area surfaces - and apply it to every object equally. And get it into the tenant's hands at signing: a rule or regulation is enforceable against the tenant only if it satisfies all six tests in § 76-1422, including (3) that "[i]t applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner" and (6) that "[t]he tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement." A rule you adopt later binds the tenant only on reasonable notice of its adoption and only if it does not work a substantial modification of the bargain. If a tenant asks for an exception for a religious item, grant whatever you would grant for a comparable secular one; a lease term purporting to make the tenant waive fair-housing or Act rights is unenforceable under § 76-1415(1)(a).

title: Nebraska Never Stops You From Asking for Rent - It Lets the Tenant Subtract From It
bodyText: No Nebraska statute bars you from demanding, collecting or suing for rent because the unit is substandard, because a code inspector has written it up, because the property is unregistered or unlicensed, or because you have not fixed something. Nebraska has no analogue to California's bar on collecting rent while a cited condition goes unrepaired, and no code-order rent suspension. What Nebraska does instead is let the tenant reduce what is owed, and every route is triggered by the tenant and requires the tenant's written notice first. There are five, and they are not cumulative. (1) ESSENTIAL SERVICES, the only deduct-from-rent right in the Act: if you deliberately or negligently fail to supply running water, hot water, heat or essential services contrary to the lease or § 76-1419, the tenant may "[p]rocure reasonable amounts of hot water, running water, heat and essential services during the period of the landlord's noncompliance and deduct their actual and reasonable cost from the rent" (§ 76-1427(1)(a)). (2) The tenant may instead "[r]ecover damages based upon the diminution in the fair rental value of the dwelling unit" (§ 76-1427(1)(b)). (3) The closest thing Nebraska has to a rent bar: the tenant may "[p]rocure reasonable substitute housing during the period of the landlord's noncompliance, in which case the tenant is excused from paying rent for the period of the landlord's noncompliance" (§ 76-1427(1)(c)) - and if the failure was deliberate the tenant also recovers the cost or value of the substitute housing up to one periodic rent, plus reasonable attorney's fees in any § 76-1427 case. (4) In your possession action for nonpayment, or in a rent action while the tenant is in possession, the tenant "may counterclaim for any amount which he or she may recover under the rental agreement or the" Act; the court "may order the tenant to pay into court all or part of the rent accrued and thereafter accruing", and "[i]f no rent remains due after application of this section, judgment shall be entered for the tenant in the action for possession" (§ 76-1428(1)). (5) Fire or casualty: a tenant who vacates the unusable part of the unit has rent "reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value" (§ 76-1429(1)(b)). Three limits worth knowing. There is no general repair-and-deduct in Nebraska - § 76-1427(1)(a) is it, and it reaches only water, hot water, heat and essential services. The tenant must elect: "[i]f the tenant proceeds under this section, he may not proceed under section 76-1425 as to that breach" (§ 76-1427(2)). And none of it arises "until the tenant has given written notice to the landlord", nor at all where the condition was caused by the tenant, a family member or a person on the premises with the tenant's consent, nor for circumstances beyond your control (§ 76-1427(3)). One more exposure that is not a rent bar but behaves like one: if a governmental entity orders the tenant out because the premises are not fit for habitation through your negligence or neglect, "a tenant shall not be liable for damages directly related to the tenant's removal" (§ 76-1416(4)). And where a municipality determines a property unsafe or unfit under its minimum standard housing ordinance, § 18-1722.01 obliges the municipality to post the property and to file the determination with the county register of deeds to be recorded - a recorded cloud on your title, at no fee to remove.

title: There Is No Nebraska Rent-Increase Notice - So Use the Right Instrument Instead
bodyText: Nebraska has no rent-increase notice statute for an ordinary residential tenancy, written or oral, and no price-gouging or emergency rent-freeze statute was found anywhere in the code searched. That is not permission to send whatever you like: because there is no statutory notice of increase, the increase has to ride on an instrument that does exist. FIXED TERM: rent is "payable without demand or notice at the time and place agreed upon by the parties" (§ 76-1414(3)), so during the term the rent is whatever the lease says. You cannot raise it by notice. Your only routes are a rent-change schedule or formula written into the lease before signing, or a signed amendment the tenant agrees to - § 76-1414(1) authorises either. There is also no statutory nonrenewal notice for a fixed term; if you simply let it expire and the tenant stays without your consent, you are in § 76-1437(3) holdover territory, and if you consent, § 76-1414(4) makes the new tenancy month to month. PERIODIC TENANCY: the only statutory notice is the notice that ends the tenancy - seven days for week to week, thirty days for month to month (§ 76-1437(1) and (2)) - so a rent increase is effected either by the tenant agreeing to a new rental agreement at the new figure, or by a compliant termination notice accompanied by an offer of a new tenancy at the new rent. Watch the two clocks: the seven-day notice runs to "the termination date specified in the notice" but the thirty-day notice runs to "the periodic rental date specified in the notice", so a month-to-month notice keyed to an arbitrary calendar date can fail. DELIVERY: a notice is received by the tenant when it is delivered in hand, mailed to the place the tenant holds out or the tenant's last-known residence, or delivered by electronic means (§ 76-1413(2)(c)) - posting it on the door is not on that list - and you may not require the tenant to accept electronic delivery as part of the lease or as a condition of entering or renewing it (§ 76-1413(9)). TWO TRAPS. The sixty-day rent-increase notice attributed to Nebraska all over the internet is § 76-1490, and it is mobile-home space only: "Each tenant shall be notified in writing of any rent increase by actual notice or by United States mail at least sixty days prior to the effective date of the increase." And an increase is unlawful if it retaliates for a code complaint to a government enforcement agency or for tenants'-union activity (§ 76-1439(1)), though § 76-1439(2) preserves "reasonable rent increases" even then and § 76-1439(3) preserves a possession action where the tenant is in default in rent.

title: The Tenant's Counterclaim Is Free - Paying Rent Into Court Is the Judge's Choice, and You Have to Ask Twice
bodyText: Nebraska has a rent-into-court rule, but it is nothing like the registry statutes some states use, and the difference decides how you run the case. THE COUNTERCLAIM IS PERMISSIVE AND UNCONDITIONAL. § 76-1445 lets the tenant "appear and answer and assert any legal or equitable defense, setoff, or counterclaim", and § 76-1428(1) lets the tenant "counterclaim for any amount which he or she may recover under the rental agreement or the" Act - "Action" is defined to include "recoupment, counterclaim, setoff, suit in equity, and any other proceeding in which rights are determined, including an action for possession" (§ 76-1410(2)). Nothing conditions the tenant's right to defend on depositing money first. THE DEPOSIT IS DISCRETIONARY. Where the tenant counterclaims, "the court from time to time may order the tenant to pay into court all or part of the rent accrued and thereafter accruing and shall determine the amount due to each party" (§ 76-1428(1)). Ask for the order; it is not automatic, and a judge who does not order it has not erred. Then the netting runs: "[t]he party to whom a net amount is owed shall be paid first from the money paid into court, and the balance by the other party. If no rent remains due after application of this section, judgment shall be entered for the tenant in the action for possession." So a counterclaim that wipes out the arrears does not merely reduce your judgment - you lose possession. SCOPE LIMIT WORTH KNOWING. § 76-1428(1) applies by its own words only "[i]n an action for possession based upon nonpayment of the rent or in an action for rent where the tenant is in possession". In a possession action grounded on a § 76-1431(1) breach or on § 76-1431(4) violent criminal activity, the rent-into-court machinery is not engaged at all, although § 76-1445 still lets the tenant counterclaim. And § 76-1428(2): if the tenant is no longer in possession, the tenant may still counterclaim "but the tenant is not required to pay any rent into court." THE SECOND DEPOSIT POWER, which almost nobody asks for: § 76-1443 allows one continuance for good cause and then only by agreement or for extraordinary cause, and adds that "[f]or any subsequent continuance extending the initial trial date into the next periodic rental period, the court may require a tenant to deposit with the clerk of the court such rental payments as accrue during the pendency of the suit." If the tenant asks for a second continuance, ask for that deposit in the same breath. YOUR FEE HOOK. "If the defense or counterclaim by the tenant is without merit and is not raised in good faith, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney's fees" (§ 76-1428(1)) - which matters because § 76-1415(1)(c) voids a lease term making the tenant agree to pay your fees, so the statute is the only route. FINALLY, THERE IS NO JURY: "[t]he action shall be tried by the court without a jury" and trial is set "not less than ten nor more than fourteen days after the issuance of the summons" (§ 76-1446). A jury-demand rent-escrow route, which is how some states get rent paid in, does not exist here, and a jury-waiver clause scoped to a possession action is dead weight.

title: Nebraska Wrote the "No Rent Without the Duty" Rule for Mobile Home Parks and Not for You - Which Cuts Both Ways
bodyText: Some states say in terms that no instrument may let anyone take the rent while shedding the habitability duty. Nebraska says that - but only for mobile home parks. § 76-1478, inside the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act, is one sentence: "A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed, or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with section 76-1492" (§ 76-1492 being the mobile-home landlord's repair and common-area duties). There is no counterpart anywhere in §§ 76-1401 to 76-1449. The legislature wrote the rule in 1984 for one act and has never written it for ordinary rentals, so the silence is a choice rather than a gap. What answers the question for an ordinary Nebraska tenancy is the Act's definitions and its successor provisions, which fix the duty on a role and not on whoever banks the money. "Landlord" means "the owner, lessor, or sublessor of the dwelling unit or the building of which it is a part, and it also means a manager of the premises who fails to disclose as required by section 76-1417" (§ 76-1410(7)), and "Owner" expressly "includes a mortgagee in possession" (§ 76-1410(9)). The disclosure duty "extends to and is enforceable against any successor landlord, owner, or manager" (§ 76-1417(2)), and on deposits "[t]he holder of the landlord's interest in the premises at the time of the termination of the tenancy is bound" (§ 76-1416(5)). THE LEASE ROUTE IS CLOSED: a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under" the Act, and such a provision is unenforceable (§ 76-1415(1)(a), (2)). THE SALE ROUTE IS NARROW AND CONDITIONAL: on a good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser you are relieved of liability only as to events after written notice to the tenant of the conveyance, and you stay liable for the tenant's § 76-1416 money unless the deposits and prepaid rent are assigned to the purchaser with written notice to the tenant (§ 76-1420(1)) - and that whole subsection opens "Unless otherwise agreed", so the lease can change it. THE ROUTE THAT IS NOT CLOSED, and you should assume the worst about it: § 76-276 preserves "the creation, provision, assignment, granting, or enforcement of a security interest in rents arising from real estate pursuant to sections 52-1701 to 52-1708", so a lender can be collecting your rents without ever becoming the "landlord" under § 76-1410(7). Nothing in the Act says that shifts the § 76-1419 duty to the lender, and nothing says it relieves you. Practical consequence: if you assign rents, plan on remaining the § 76-1419 obligor, keep the § 76-1417 disclosure current in your own name, and do not let the assignment be the reason a repair does not happen.

title: No Rent Receipt Duty - and the One Nebraska Receipt Statute Was Written to Exclude You
bodyText: No Nebraska statute requires a landlord to give a receipt for rent, in cash or otherwise, and failing to give one is not a defence to anything. The legislature's silence here is demonstrable rather than assumed, because it wrote the rule next door and then excluded real property from it. Under the Consumer Rental Purchase Agreement Act, "[t]he lessor shall furnish the consumer upon request with an itemized written receipt for payment in cash or any other method of payment which itself does not provide evidence of payment" (§ 69-2106) - a request-triggered, itemised, cash-and-cash-equivalent receipt duty, which is exactly the duty states with a rent-receipt statute impose. But § 69-2103(10) defines the property that Act covers as "any property that is not real property under the laws of this state", so a dwelling lease is outside it by design. Nothing equivalent exists in §§ 76-1401 to 76-1449. There is also no Nebraska statute creating a presumption that earlier rent was paid because the tenant holds a receipt for later rent - the kind of evidence rule Puerto Rico and Guam have. GIVE A RECEIPT ANYWAY, and here is the Nebraska-specific reason rather than the general one. Your fastest remedy turns on a date: if rent is unpaid when due and the tenant does not pay "within seven calendar days after written notice by the landlord of nonpayment and his or her intention to terminate the rental agreement", you may terminate (§ 76-1431(2)). A disputed cash payment is a dispute about whether that notice was good when you sent it. Worse, § 76-1433 makes "[a]cceptance of rent with knowledge of a default by tenant" a waiver of your right to terminate for that breach "unless otherwise agreed after the breach has occurred" - and a pre-breach reservation in the lease does not save you - so what you accepted, when, and against which month is the whole case. A dated, itemised receipt stating the period the payment is applied to, and which also records any amount still outstanding, is the cheapest record you can make of all three facts. Note that applying payments is itself a term you can set: § 76-1414(1) authorises it and the standard Application of Payments clause does it, and § 76-1410(13) makes every payment under the lease "rent", so a receipt that does not say which charge was paid leaves the allocation open.

title: No Rent-Reporting Law in Nebraska - You May Report, With One Duty Attached
bodyText: Nebraska has no rent-reporting statute of any kind. There is no duty to offer positive rent reporting to tenants, no lease signature block for the tenant's election, no size threshold that switches such a duty on, no duty to notify a tenant in writing before you report late rent to a credit bureau, and no prohibition on requiring a tenant to participate in a reporting programme. Nebraska's only credit-reporting statute in the chapters searched, § 20-149, binds "[a]ny consumer reporting agency doing business in this state" and requires it to give a consumer a copy of its file on request - it imposes nothing on a landlord and reaches you only if you are the agency. So reporting rent, positive or negative, is a business decision rather than a regulated one. Two things do constrain it. FIRST, federal law, which is where the real rules live: once you furnish information about a tenant to a consumer reporting agency you are a furnisher under the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, with its accuracy, dispute-investigation and correction obligations (15 U.S.C. 1681s-2), and the lease cannot change that. SECOND, and this is Nebraska-specific and routinely missed: a rent-reporting service is a nonaffiliated, third-party service provider, and § 87-808(2)(a) requires that "[a]n individual or commercial entity that discloses computerized data that includes personal information about a Nebraska resident to a nonaffiliated, third-party service provider shall require BY CONTRACT that the service provider implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices" appropriate to the information and reasonably designed to protect it. Rent-reporting files normally carry a name plus a Social Security number, which is "personal information" under § 87-802(5)(a)(i), so the contract requirement is engaged - and § 87-805 makes any waiver of the Act "contrary to public policy and ... void and unenforceable". Practical course: if you report, sign a written data-security undertaking with the service before you send the first file, keep the reporting voluntary and in writing with the tenant, and tell the tenant when you begin reporting even though no Nebraska statute makes you. Note the lease-side consequence of § 76-1410(13): every payment under the lease is "rent", so if you report, late fees and other charges you have swept into rent are part of what gets reported.

title: Nebraska Does Not Sales-Tax Residential Rent - But Short Lettings and Separately Charged Extras Are a Different Question
bodyText: Nebraska's sales tax is imposed by a closed list, and renting a dwelling for thirty days or more is not on it. § 77-2703(1) imposes the tax "upon the gross receipts from all sales of tangible personal property sold at retail in this state", on the gross receipts of public utilities, community antenna television and satellite operators and those connecting or installing those services, on retailers of the intellectual and entertainment properties in § 77-2701.16(3), on admissions, on warranties and service and maintenance agreements covering taxable items, on bundled transactions, on "the gross receipts from the provision of services defined in subsection (4) of section 77-2701.16", and on products delivered electronically under § 77-2701.16(9). The lease of real property appears nowhere in it. And § 77-2701.16(4)'s enumerated taxable services - building cleaning and maintenance, pest control and security; motor vehicle washing, waxing, towing and painting; computer software training; installing and applying tangible personal property; "services of recreational vehicle parks"; repair labour on taxable tangible personal property; animal specialty services; detective services - likewise do not include letting a dwelling, although note that an RV park IS on that list. So an ordinary residential tenancy produces no Nebraska sales tax, and there is nothing to collect, display separately or remit. THREE PLACES TO BE CAREFUL. (1) SHORT LETTINGS. Nebraska has a statewide short-term-rental statute, and its tax subsection is permissive and explicit: a municipality "may adopt or enforce an ordinance or other regulation that imposes a sales tax or an occupation tax on short-term rentals if the tax is otherwise permitted by applicable law" (§ 18-1758(4)), with "[s]hort-term rental" defined as a residential property "that is rented wholly or partly for a fee for a period not longer than thirty consecutive days" (§ 18-1758(1)(b)). Below thirty days, three state-law taxes apply. First, state sales tax: § 77-2701.33(2) makes a "sale" of "[t]he renting or furnishing for periods of less than thirty days of any room or rooms, lodgings, or accommodations in any hotel, motel, inn, tourist camp, tourist cabin, or any other place ... in which rooms, lodgings, or accommodations are regularly furnished for a consideration". The Department of Revenue's rule exempts accommodations "supplied to the same tenant for a period of thirty (30) continuous days or more" (Reg-1-046.02). Second, a state lodging tax: § 81-3715 adds "an additional sales tax of one percent" on occupancy of space "furnished by any hotel". "Hotel" includes "tourist homes ... lodging houses" and any facility where the public may obtain sleeping accommodations (§ 81-3707), and "occupancy" is a stay of "less than a period of thirty days" (§ 81-3708). Third, a county may add up to two percent for each of two visitor funds (§ 81-3716). A city may add its own tax under § 18-1758(4). Whether an occasional short letting of one home is a place where accommodations are "regularly furnished" is a question only a court or the Department could settle. The cautious course: get a sales tax permit and collect before you take short bookings. Note the lines differ: § 18-1758 counts thirty days or fewer, and the tax statutes count fewer than thirty. (2) SEPARATELY CHARGED EXTRAS. The tax reaches the "lease or rental price" of tangible personal property (§ 77-2701.16(1)), so a charge broken out of rent for something that is personal property rather than part of the dwelling - furniture rental, an appliance rental, an equipment or amenity rental - is the one place a residential landlord can create a taxable receipt out of what looks like rent. The Department's rule treats property "incidental to the lease or rental of real estate, such as furniture for a furnished apartment" as bought for your own use. You pay sales tax when you buy it and cannot buy it tax-free for resale (Reg-1-018.05C). No rule says whether a separately stated furniture or appliance charge is still "incidental". If you want to avoid the question, do not break those charges out. (3) WHAT YOU MAY NOT SAY. If you ever are a retailer of a taxable item, § 77-2703(1)(b) makes it unlawful to "advertise, hold out, or state to the public or to any customer, directly or indirectly, that the tax or part thereof will be assumed or absorbed by the retailer, that it will not be added to the selling, renting, or leasing price" or that it will be refunded; and § 77-2703(1)(c) requires the tax to be "displayed separately from the list price". Finally, Nebraska has no statute barring you from passing a tax through to a tenant and no statute barring a pass-through of a repealed local tax. The pass-through rests on the lease, and § 76-1410(13) then makes it "rent" - which means it counts toward the § 76-1416(1) one-month deposit cap and the other measures the Act takes in periodic rent.

title: No State Rental Inspection - But the City Code Sets Your Ceiling, and You Cannot Promise an Inspector Access
bodyText: Nebraska runs no statewide rental inspection programme and no statewide rental registry or landlord licence. There is no mandatory state fire-safety inspection of an apartment building or a rental house either: § 81-502(1)(c)'s inspection list is closed, and rental housing is not on it. Inspection of rentals in Nebraska is a municipal matter, and the statutes that set it up matter to you in three ways. FIRST, THE CITY CODE SETS THE CEILING ON YOUR OWN DUTY, which is the most important and least known consequence. § 18-2146 requires that "[e]ach city and village shall adopt a minimum standards housing ordinance if such city or village has completed an approved workable program or is in the process of the preparation of such a program." Where such an ordinance applies, § 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence says "the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a) of this section" - that is, by substantial compliance, after written or actual notice, with "the requirements of the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety." So the local code both raises and caps your habitability duty, and the Act tells you which code it means: "Minimum housing code shall be limited to those laws, resolutions, or ordinances or regulations, or portions thereof, dealing specifically with health and minimum standards of fitness for habitation" (§ 76-1410(3)) - narrower than the same subdivision's broad definition of "[b]uilding and housing codes". Read your city's ordinance; it is the operative standard and it is not in the statutes - and § 18-132 tells you where to find it. A city council or village board "may adopt by ordinance the conditions, provisions, limitations, and terms of a plumbing code, an electrical code, a fire prevention code, a building or construction code, and any other standard code ... by reference to such code, or portions thereof, alone, without setting forth in the ordinance" its terms, and once incorporated it "shall have the same force and effect as though it had been written in its entirety in such ordinance"; § 18-132(2) then requires that "[n]ot less than one copy of such standard code, or portion thereof, shall be kept for use and examination by the public in the office of the city clerk or village clerk ... as long as such standard code is in effect". So the standard that caps and defines your habitability duty may not be printed in the ordinance book at all - ask the city clerk for the incorporated code, and note that § 18-132(3) routes any building or construction code through § 71-6406. SECOND, WHAT A FAILED INSPECTION ACTUALLY COSTS. If the governing body determines a property "unsafe or unfit for human occupancy because of one or more violations of its minimum standard housing ordinance", or a building unsafe under its building or construction code, § 18-1722.01 makes it "the duty of such municipality to post the property accordingly and to file a copy of such resolution or other determination in the office of the register of deeds of the county to be recorded" - a recorded cloud on your title, with no fee for the recording or its release. And under § 18-1722, if you fail or refuse to comply with a notice to repair, rehabilitate or demolish an unsafe building that is a public nuisance, the city may do the work and then either levy the cost "as a special assessment against the lot or real estate", which "shall be a lien on the real estate", or sue you for it. THIRD, AND THE TRAP: YOUR LEASE CANNOT GIVE AN INSPECTOR ACCESS. § 76-1423(1) lets you in, on the tenant's not-unreasonably-withheld consent, "in order to inspect the premises, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workmen, or contractors." A government housing inspector is not on that list, and § 76-1423(4) is exhaustive: "The landlord has no other right of access except by court order, as permitted by subsection (2) of section 76-1432, or if the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises." A lease clause purporting to make the tenant consent in advance to an inspector's entry is also an agreement to "waive or to forego rights or remedies" under the Act and so unenforceable under § 76-1415(1)(a). THE CAUTIOUS COURSE: treat a code inspection as your own § 76-1423(1) inspection, give the § 76-1423(3)(a) notice - at least twenty-four hours in writing, to each individual unit, stating the purpose and a reasonable anticipated window - and attend. If the tenant refuses lawful access you have § 76-1438(1): injunctive relief to compel access or termination, plus actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. If the tenant refuses the inspector, that is between the tenant and the city; the inspector's own authority to compel entry comes from the ordinance and from administrative-warrant law, neither of which is in the statutes.

title: No Renter's-Insurance Rules in Nebraska - and the Mobile Home Act Shows You How to Draft the One Sentence That Can Go Wrong
bodyText:
Nebraska regulates a renter's-insurance requirement in an ordinary residential lease not at all. There is no statutory advisory you must give, no requirement that the tenant choose the carrier, no proof-of-coverage deadline, no force-placement scheme, no cap on an administrative or placement fee, and no flood or coverage notice to deliver before signing. The requirement is lawful because § 76-1414(1) lets the parties include "terms and conditions not prohibited by" the Act, and that is the whole of your authority.

The legislature's silence is demonstrable rather than assumed, because it wrote the rule next door - and the way it wrote it is the drafting lesson. § 76-1475(2), in the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act, provides that "[a] rental agreement may require a tenant to maintain liability insurance which names the landlord as an insured with respect to the mobile home space rented by the tenant", and then defines the term it has just used: "For purposes of this subsection, liability insurance shall mean insurance that protects the landlord from negligence ON THE PART OF THE TENANT and any invitees or guests of the tenant." Note what that definition does - it ties the landlord's status as an insured to the TENANT'S negligence and no further.

There is no counterpart in §§ 76-1401 to 76-1449, so in an ordinary lease you have the power without the guardrail, and the guardrail matters because of § 76-1415(1)(d): no rental agreement may provide that the tenant "[a]grees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord or to indemnify the landlord for that liability arising due to active and actionable negligence or the costs connected therewith", and such a provision "is unenforceable" with actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees if you use it knowingly (§ 76-1415(2)).

An unqualified requirement that the tenant's policy name you as an additional insured for all liability arising at the premises is, in substance, an agreement to indemnify you for your own active and actionable negligence, and is void pro tanto in exactly that band. So if you want to be named, say what the Mobile Home Act says: an additional insured only as to liability arising from the tenant's own acts or omissions and those of the tenant's household and persons on the premises with the tenant's consent.

THREE MORE NEBRASKA CONSEQUENCES.
- (1) Any premium, fee or placement charge the tenant pays YOU is "rent", because "[r]ent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement" (§ 76-1410(13)) - so an unpaid insurance charge is rent you can serve a seven-day § 76-1431(2) notice on, and it is also swept into every rule measured in rent.
- (2) Do not hold the money as a reserve against damage: § 76-1416(1) caps "security, however denominated" at one month's periodic rent plus a pet deposit of up to one quarter of a month, and a charge you retain to cover damage is security whatever you call it.
- (3) The Act gives you no insurance-based route around your own duties: § 76-1419(1) is yours regardless of what the tenant insures, and § 76-1419(2) and (3) are the only delegation routes.

A proof-of-coverage deadline, a lapse-notice duty and a remedy for lapse are therefore pure contract - write them in, with a cure period, or you have a requirement with no consequence.

title: Nebraska Gives You No Way Out of an Expensive Repair - Cost Is Not an Excuse, and the Casualty Section Is the Tenant's Only
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute letting a landlord terminate a tenancy because a repair would cost too much. There is no cost threshold, no percentage-of-value test and no uneconomic-to-repair route anywhere in the Act, and the one section that looks like it should help you is not yours. § 76-1429 gives the TENANT the choices: on fire or casualty damage "to an extent that enjoyment of the dwelling unit is substantially impaired" the tenant may vacate immediately and terminate by written notice within fourteen days, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part with rent "reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value". The landlord gets one thing out of it - on termination you return prepaid rent and recoverable security, accounting as of the date of the casualty, and the tenant remains "responsible for damage caused by his negligence" (§ 76-1429(2)). You get no termination right at all. Nor can the lease rewrite that section: eleven chapter 76 sections open with "[u]nless otherwise agreed" and § 76-1429 is not one of them, while § 76-1415(1)(a) voids a term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies" under the Act. AND COST IS NOT AN EXCUSE FOR NOT REPAIRING. § 76-1419(1) has no expense ceiling - its only ceiling is the local minimum housing code where one applies - and the escape hatches are narrower than they look: § 76-1425(2)'s "conditions or circumstances beyond his or her control" removes the tenant's CONSEQUENTIAL damages while leaving the duty and the § 76-1427 remedies intact, and § 76-1427(3)'s closing sentence ("not intended to cover circumstances beyond the landlord's control") is likewise about causes, not budgets. An expensive repair is not beyond your control. SO WHAT ARE YOUR ROUTES? Four, in order of reliability. (1) END A PERIODIC TENANCY: § 76-1437(2) lets you terminate month to month on at least thirty days' written notice to the periodic rental date, for any reason or none, and this is the real answer most of the time. (2) SETTLE: § 76-1406 says "[a] claim or right arising under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or on a rental agreement may be settled by agreement" - so a negotiated surrender after the damage occurs is lawful even though a lease term waiving the tenant's § 76-1429 rights in advance is not. The line is instrument and timing, not subject matter. (3) USE A LEASE CASUALTY CLAUSE, which is what the library's Landlord Termination After Fire or Casualty clause is for - it is pure contract and it has to live alongside § 76-1429 rather than displace it. (4) Where the building is genuinely finished, the municipality's own repair-or-demolish machinery under § 18-1722 may overtake the question, but that comes with a special assessment that "shall be a lien on the real estate" if the city does the work. FOR CONTRAST, so you can see that the silence is deliberate: Nebraska DID write a no-restore route, in the Condominium Act. § 76-871(h) requires damaged property to "be repaired or replaced promptly by the association unless (i) the condominium is terminated, (ii) repair or replacement would be illegal under any state or local health or safety statute or ordinance, or (iii) eighty percent of the unit owners ... vote not to rebuild." Note what the legislature chose as the trigger - termination, illegality, or a supermajority vote - and not cost. Even where Nebraska lets an owner walk away from a rebuild, it does not do it with a price tag.

title: No Rent Escrow in Nebraska, So No Small-Landlord Exemption and No Notice to Give
bodyText: There is nothing for you to disclose here, and the reason is structural. Nebraska has no rent-escrow remedy at all: a tenant cannot deposit rent with a court or an escrow agent pending repairs, and no Nebraska statute creates such a fund. With no escrow remedy there is no exemption from it, so there is no small-landlord exemption and no exemption notice of the Ohio kind. Two related points are worth having straight. FIRST, NEBRASKA HAS NO SIZE-BASED EXEMPTION FROM ANYTHING IN THE ACT. There is no unit-count threshold, no owner-occupancy carve-out and no small-landlord provision anywhere in §§ 76-1401 to 76-1449. The Act's exclusions at § 76-1408 are about the KIND of arrangement, not the size of the landlord - institutional residence incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counselling or religious service; occupancy under a contract of sale; fraternal or social organization quarters; transient hotel or motel occupancy; a landlord's employee whose occupancy is conditional on the employment; a condominium owner or cooperative proprietary lessee; premises used primarily for agricultural purposes; and a lease of residential land for five years or more - and the whole list is gated by its own preamble, "[u]nless created to avoid the application of" the Act, so a structure built to fall inside an exclusion does not. The only entity-based carve-out in the Act is in the deposit cap: § 76-1416(1)'s ceiling "shall not be applicable to housing agencies organized or existing under the Nebraska Housing Agency Act", and that is about who the landlord is, not how many units it has. SECOND, WHAT THE TENANT ACTUALLY HAS, so you know what you are managing instead of an escrow. The only right to take money off the rent is § 76-1427(1)(a), and it reaches only running water, hot water, heat and essential services, only on the tenant's prior written notice, and only where your failure was deliberate or negligent; there is no general repair-and-deduct in Nebraska. Beyond that the tenant has § 76-1425's thirty-day termination with a fourteen-day cure, § 76-1425(2) damages and injunctive relief, and § 76-1428(1)'s counterclaim in your possession action - where the court MAY order rent paid into court, which is the nearest Nebraska thing to escrow and is the judge's discretion, not the tenant's right. THE TRAP TO AVOID: do not try to supply the missing regime by putting a no-withholding, no-escrow or no-setoff sentence in the lease. A term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under" the Act is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a rental agreement containing a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant "may recover actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees" (§ 76-1415(1)(a), (2)). An unqualified "Tenant shall pay rent without deduction or setoff" is that term. The standard Rent Payment clause survives only because it ends "except as permitted by applicable law" - keep those words.

title: Everything Nebraska Actually Makes You Disclose - It Is a Short List, and the Timing Matters More Than the Wording
bodyText: Nebraska's disclosure list for a residential tenancy is unusually short, and the one item that always applies is about timing rather than text. ALWAYS: OWNER AND MANAGER IDENTITY. § 76-1417(1) requires the landlord or anyone authorised to make a rental agreement on the landlord's behalf to "disclose to the tenant in writing AT OR BEFORE THE COMMENCEMENT OF THE TENANCY the name and address of: (a) The person authorized to manage the premises; and (b) An owner of the premises or a person authorized to act for and on behalf of the owner for the purpose of service of process and for the purpose of receiving and receipting for notices and demands." Two things follow that catch people out. It does NOT have to be in the lease - a separate signed sheet handed over at or before commencement complies - but equally, putting it in the lease does not help if the lease is signed after the tenant has already moved in. And § 76-1417(2) makes it a continuing duty: the information "shall be kept current and this section extends to and is enforceable against any successor landlord, owner, or manager." Miss it and § 76-1417(3) makes you the agent of every landlord for service of process, for receiving notices and demands, and for "[p]erforming the obligations of the landlord" under the Act and the rental agreement "and expending or making available for the purpose all rent collected from the premises." ALWAYS, IF THE BUILDING PREDATES 1978: the federal lead-based paint disclosure and the EPA pamphlet, under 42 U.S.C. 4852d and its regulations - federal law that does not depend on Nebraska. Nebraska itself has no lead disclosure duty; § 71-2518 is a Department of Health and Human Services prevention programme and imposes nothing on a landlord. ONLY IF YOU WANT ELECTRONIC NOTICES: before the tenant consents, you must give "a clear and conspicuous statement" of the tenant's right to withdraw consent at any time without conditions or consequences, of the transactions and types of documents the consent covers, of the right to paper by mail and how to get a paper copy, and of how to withdraw consent or update an email address, plus a statement of the hardware and software requirements (§ 76-1413(7)(b), (7)(c)(i)) - and you may not require the tenant to accept electronic delivery as part of or as a condition of the lease (§ 76-1413(9)). ONLY IN SPECIAL SITUATIONS: a sale-leaseback of a home in foreclosure where you are the equity purchaser brings in § 76-2727, which requires that "[a]ny equity purchase contract, rental agreement, lease, or option or right to repurchase" and any related notice or instrument signed by the homeowner "shall be written in English and shall be accompanied by a written translation from English into any other language principally spoken by the homeowner, certified by the person making the translation as a true and correct translation"; a conversion to condominiums brings its own tenant notice; an age-restricted complex of more than ten units may bring the Retirement Subdivisions and Communities Act's public-offering statement and non-waivable cancellation right, which is a genuinely unsettled question and is dealt with separately; and if a licensed real estate broker or property manager handles the letting, § 76-2421(1)(a) requires THAT LICENSEE - not you - to give a "seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant" a written copy of the commission-approved brokerage disclosure pamphlet at the earliest practicable opportunity. NOW THE LONG LIST OF WHAT NEBRASKA DOES NOT REQUIRE, because that is most of it: no mould, bed bug, radon, methamphetamine, flood, utility or submetering, deposit-location, energy-cost, smoking-policy, rent-control-coverage or just-cause-coverage disclosure; no state-prescribed lease form and no wording you must copy; no requirement that any form be the first page or in any particular type size; and no duty to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease at all. FOR SCALE, so you can see the silence is deliberate: when Nebraska wanted a real disclosure regime it wrote one. § 69-2104 gives consumer rental-purchase agreements a twelve-item pre-contract schedule - description, number and timing of payments, total to ownership, who bears repair cost, new-or-used, cash price, itemised initial payment, the purchase-option summary, who maintains the property, the date and the parties' names - and § 69-2110 caps the fees to go with it. Dwellings got none of that.

title: No Nebraska Tenant Rights Guide to Hand Over - and No Statutory Summary Either
bodyText: Nebraska requires no rights-and-responsibilities guide, handbook, pamphlet or summary of the law to be given to a residential tenant - not before signing, not at renewal, and not with a signed acknowledgment. No state agency is directed to publish one for tenancies, there is no statutory summary of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act to attach, and nothing turns on whether you hand anything over. The Act's own statement of purpose is the closest it comes, and it is addressed to courts rather than to you: the Act "shall be liberally construed and applied to promote its underlying purposes and policies", which include "[t]o simplify, clarify, modernize, and revise the law governing the rental of dwelling units and the rights and obligations of landlord and tenant" (§ 76-1402(1), (2)(a)). THE SILENCE IS A CHOICE, NOT AN OVERSIGHT, and three Nebraska statutes show it. The legislature DID mandate a state-approved pamphlet in a transaction that expressly names tenants - but it put the duty on the real estate licensee, not the owner: § 76-2421(1)(a) requires a licensee offering brokerage services, at the earliest practicable opportunity during or following first substantial contact with "a seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant", to "[p]rovide that person with a written copy of the current brokerage disclosure pamphlet which has been prepared and approved by the commission". It DID write a long itemised pre-contract disclosure schedule - for consumer rentals of personal property, at § 69-2104, and § 69-2103(10) defines that Act's subject as "any property that is not real property", so dwellings were deliberately left out. And it DID assign publication duties to an agency in the housing field - § 20-325(2) requires the Equal Opportunity Commission to "[p]ublish and disseminate reports, recommendations, and information" about discriminatory housing practices - without creating any landlord delivery duty to go with it. The one Nebraska regime that comes close is conditional and contested: an age-restricted complex of more than ten units may fall inside the Retirement Subdivisions and Communities Act, whose § 76-1305 bars offering or disposing of a unit before registration and requires a public offering statement with an examination period and a cancellation right that "may not be waived".
