Whether that Act reaches a month-to-month age-restricted apartment complex is genuinely open and is dealt with in its own guidance - do not assume it does or does not. PRACTICAL COURSE. There is no official Nebraska tenant handbook with statutory force, so do not describe anything you hand out as the state's. If you want to give new tenants a plain-language summary - and it is a good idea, because most Nebraska disputes are about the deposit and the notice periods - write your own or use a legal-aid publication, say plainly who wrote it, and keep it consistent with the lease. Then put the four things that actually have legal consequences where the statute wants them: the § 76-1417(1) owner-and-manager disclosure in writing at or before commencement; the federal lead disclosure and EPA pamphlet for pre-1978 housing; the house rules in the tenant's hands at signing, because § 76-1422(6) makes a rule enforceable only if "[t]he tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement"; and a copy of the signed lease, which Nebraska does not require you to give but which is your own best evidence.

title: No Duty to Give Tenants a Code Variance — But a Variance Moves the Ceiling on Your Repair Duty
bodyText:
Nebraska has NO statute requiring a landlord to hand a tenant a health-code or housing-code variance, to attach one to the rental agreement, or to post one. Massachusetts does exactly that (105 Mass. Code Regs. 410.700(D)); Nebraska has no counterpart, and no state sanitary code for dwellings for a variance to be granted from. Nebraska's housing code is MUNICIPAL. Section 18-2146 requires a city or village to adopt a minimum standards housing ordinance only "if such city or village has completed an approved workable program or is in the process of the preparation of such a program" — so whether a code even exists where your property sits depends on the municipality, and so does any variance procedure.

THE ONE STATUTORY VARIANCE MECHANISM THAT REACHES A DWELLING is section 18-1906, and it is narrow. In cities of the METROPOLITAN CLASS only (Omaha), the municipal plumbing board may "grant a variance from the ordinances, rules, and regulations in the kind and size of materials to be used or in the manner in which the work is to be performed" where there are "practical difficulties or unnecessary hardships". Three things to note: the variance "shall apply only to a single building"; it "shall not be considered as a part of the ordinances, rules, and regulations of the plumbing board"; and a request carries "a reasonable fee, payable to the general fund, as set by the city council". The section says NOTHING about telling an occupant. Appeals go to the Building Board of Review.

WHY YOU SHOULD STILL KEEP THE PAPER, AND THIS IS THE LANDLORD-SIDE POINT. Section 76-1419(1)(a) makes you "substantially comply, after written or actual notice, with the requirements of the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety", and the unnumbered sentence that closes subsection (1) reads: "If there exists a minimum housing code applicable to the premises, the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a) of this section." A lawfully granted variance changes what the applicable code REQUIRES, so it bears directly on the ceiling that sentence sets. Keep the written grant, with its date and the building it names, in the property file: it is your evidence of what the code required of that building, and section 76-1419's own text ties your maximum duty to the code rather than to a tenant's expectations. The same sentence cuts the other way if you lose or never obtained the grant.

Two limits on the paragraph above, both stated so you do not over-read it. A variance from a PLUMBING-materials or workmanship rule under section 18-1906 is not a variance from "health and minimum standards of fitness for habitation", which is what section 76-1410(3) confines "minimum housing code" to; and section 76-1419(1)(b)'s duty to "put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition" is drafted separately from (1)(a). Nebraska law does not say whether a code variance can lower (1)(b) as well, and nothing here should be read as a licence to leave a unit unfit because a city signed a paper.

PRACTICAL COURSE: there is nothing to disclose because nothing requires it, but volunteering the variance in writing when a tenant asks about a condition it covers costs nothing and removes the argument that you concealed it. Do not write a lease clause saying the tenant "accepts" a variance or waives code compliance: section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any rental agreement term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act", and section 76-1415(2) lets a tenant who shows you deliberately used a term known to be prohibited recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Nebraska Has No Seasonal Tenancy — A Summer Let Is a Full URLTA Tenancy, and the Thirty-Day Short-Term Rental Shield Does Not Reach It
bodyText:
Nebraska has NO seasonal-tenancy statute. There is no seasonal exemption from the landlord-tenant act, no nonrenewable seasonal lease form, no shortened notice for a seasonal let, and no seasonal disclosure. The phrase does not exist in Nebraska law. What matters is what fills the gap, because the default is the one most likely to surprise a landlord: a three-month summer rental of a house or cabin is a FULL tenancy under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, with every duty that attaches to a year-round lease.

THE EXCLUSION LIST IS CLOSED AND SEASONALITY IS NOT ON IT. Section 76-1408 lists the eight arrangements "not governed by the act": institutional residence incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counseling or religious service; occupancy under a contract of sale; occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization; "[t]ransient occupancy in a hotel or motel"; occupancy by an employee whose right to occupy is conditional on employment about the premises; occupancy by a condominium owner or cooperative proprietary lessee; premises used primarily for agricultural purposes; and "[a] lease of improved or unimproved residential land for a term of five years or more". A short season is nowhere in that list. The only short-stay exclusion is (4), and it requires a HOTEL OR MOTEL — renting out a lake cabin or a spare house for the summer is not transient hotel occupancy, however short the stay.

AND THE LIST HAS AN ANTI-AVOIDANCE CHAPEAU. Section 76-1408 opens "Unless created to avoid the application of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act". So dressing a tenancy up as something on the list in order to escape the Act defeats the exclusion itself. Do not label a lease "seasonal license", "vacation agreement" or "transient occupancy" in the hope of moving it outside the Act. The label does no work; the arrangement does.

WHAT THAT COSTS YOU IN PRACTICE, on a summer let as much as on an annual lease: security of no more than one month's periodic rent plus a pet deposit of no more than one-fourth of a month (section 76-1416(1)); the fourteen-day return with written itemization and its willful-failure penalty (section 76-1416(2) and (3)); the maintain-fit-premises duties of section 76-1419; the entry rules of section 76-1423; and the statutory notice and cure periods before any termination. There is no self-help lockout at the end of the season.

THE THIRTY-DAY LINE, WHICH IS THE ONE PLACE NEBRASKA DOES DRAW A SHORT-STAY DISTINCTION. Section 18-1758 bars a municipality from adopting or enforcing an ordinance that "expressly or effectively prohibits the use of a property as a short-term rental", permits regulation only on a demonstrated public-health-and-safety purpose, and permits occupation and sales taxes. But section 18-1758(1)(b) defines a short-term rental as a residential property "rented wholly or partly for a fee for a period not longer than THIRTY CONSECUTIVE DAYS." A three-month summer tenancy is longer than thirty days, so it is NOT a short-term rental and section 18-1758's protection against a municipal ban does not reach it. A nightly or weekly operation is protected; a seasonal lease is exposed to ordinary zoning.

HOW TO END A SEASON CLEANLY. Fix a DEFINITE TERM in writing, with dates. Section 76-1414(4) says that "[u]nless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy shall be week to week in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent, and in all other cases month to month" — and a month-to-month tenancy takes thirty days' written notice before the periodic rental date under section 76-1437(2). A season with no stated end date therefore becomes a month-to-month tenancy you must give notice to terminate. With a definite term, the term simply expires. Writing is not a validity requirement for a term of one year or less (section 36-105 voids only a lease "for a longer period than one year" without a writing signed by the lessor), but write it anyway: the writing is what proves the definite term that keeps you out of section 76-1414(4).

IF THE TENANT WILL NOT LEAVE, section 76-1437(3) is your remedy, not a lockout: the landlord "may bring an action for possession and if the tenant's holdover is willful and not in good faith the landlord, in addition, may recover an amount not more than three months' periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees." Note the sting in the same subsection: "If the landlord consents to the tenant's continued occupancy, subsection (4) of section 76-1414 applies" — accept rent for September and the expired summer lease becomes a month-to-month tenancy needing thirty days' notice.

title: Where the Deposit Sits: No Escrow Rule If You Hold It Yourself, a Separate Trust Account the Moment a Licensed Manager Does
bodyText:
Nebraska regulates the EXIT of a security deposit, not its CUSTODY — unless somebody other than the owner is holding it. That split is the whole answer, and it is the opposite of what most multi-state deposit-holding rules look like.

IF YOU HOLD YOUR OWN TENANT'S DEPOSIT, NOTHING IN NEBRASKA LAW TELLS YOU WHERE TO PUT IT. There is no escrow mandate, no requirement that the account be separate from your operating money, no requirement that the bank be federally insured or located in Nebraska, no duty to name the depository to the tenant or in the lease, no surety-bond alternative, no bond for self-managing owners, and no unit-count threshold that switches any of it on. Section 76-1416 — the only security-deposit section in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act — says only what happens at the end: on termination, "property or money held by the landlord as prepaid rent and security may be applied to the payment of rent and the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered", and "[t]he balance, if any, and a written itemization shall be delivered or mailed to the tenant within fourteen days after the date of termination of the tenancy." It never says where the money lives in the meantime. There is likewise no deposit interest to account for; interest and the return deadline are covered by the library's own Nebraska rows on those subjects.

THE LEGISLATURE KNOWS HOW TO WRITE A HOLDING RULE AND WROTE ONE NEXT DOOR. Section 76-1484, in the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act, is one sentence long and does exactly what the URLTA does not: "All rental deposits shall be held by the landlord for the tenant. Rental deposits may be held in a trust account, which may be a common trust account and which may be an interest-bearing account. Any interest earned on a rental deposit shall be the property of the landlord." Two more siblings make the point harder. Section 76-1715, in the Time-Share Act, requires a developer's deposit to be "placed in escrow, in an account designated solely for that purpose, in an institution whose accounts are insured by a governmental agency or instrumentality", registered with the commission and open to its examination — and at (3) allows "a surety bond ... in an amount equal to fifty thousand dollars" in lieu of escrow, which is the escrow-or-bond architecture other states use for residential deposits. Section 76-1305 does something comparable for retirement subdivisions. So Nebraska's residential silence is a demonstrated choice, not an oversight.

NOW THE PART MOST NEBRASKA LANDLORDS DO NOT KNOW. The moment an off-site licensed property manager or broker collects your tenants' deposits, a real holding rule attaches — to THEM, under the Nebraska Real Estate License Act, not under the landlord-tenant act. Section 81-885.24 lets the State Real Estate Commission censure, fine, suspend or revoke a licensee for, among other "unfair trade practices": "(3) Failing to account for and remit any money coming into his or her possession belonging to others"; "(4) Commingling the money or other property of his or her principals with his or her own"; and "(5) Failing to maintain and deposit in a SEPARATE TRUST ACCOUNT all money received by a broker acting in such capacity, or as escrow agent or the temporary custodian of the funds of others, in a real estate transaction UNLESS ALL PARTIES HAVING AN INTEREST IN THE FUNDS HAVE AGREED OTHERWISE IN WRITING." This bites on landlords for two practical reasons. First, collecting rent for someone else for compensation is itself brokerage under section 81-885.01(2), and an independent off-site manager who is not a resident manager living on the premises, your employee, your parent, child, brother or sister, or a licensed broker's employee is acting as a broker and must be licensed (section 81-885.04(1) and (4)). Second, the words "unless all parties ... have agreed otherwise in writing" mean your MANAGEMENT AGREEMENT can vary the trust-account arrangement — so read that clause before you sign, because a management agreement that moves your tenants' deposits into the manager's general funds is the document that makes it lawful as between you and the manager.

TWO THINGS THIS DOES NOT DECIDE. Section 81-885.24(5) says "in a real estate transaction", and the License Act's text does not say whether taking a residential security deposit on a lease is a "real estate transaction" for that subdivision; the better reading is that it is, because section 81-885.01(2) puts "rent, lease" and "collects rents" inside the definition of brokerage, but the point is not settled by the words of (5) itself. And nothing in section 81-885.24 gives the TENANT a remedy — it is a licensing and discipline provision enforced by the Commission, so a tenant whose deposit the manager lost still sues under section 76-1416, where section 76-1416(5) makes "[t]he holder of the landlord's interest in the premises at the time of the termination of the tenancy" bound by the section.

PRACTICAL COURSE for an owner holding deposits directly: keep them in a separate account anyway, even though no statute requires it. Not because of a holding rule, but because section 76-1416(2) and (3) require you to deliver a balance and a written itemization within fourteen days and expose you to court costs, reasonable attorney's fees and — where the failure is "willful and not in good faith" — liquidated damages of "an amount equal to one month's periodic rent or two times the amount of the security deposit, whichever is less". A separate account is the cheapest evidence you have that the money was always there to return.

title: You Cannot Draft Around the Deposit Statute — But You Can Settle an Accrued Deposit Claim
bodyText:
Every security-deposit right Nebraska gives a tenant is non-waivable BY THE LEASE, and the bar is explicit rather than implied. Section 76-1415(1) opens "No rental agreement may provide that the tenant: (a) Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act". Section 76-1416 — the cap, the fourteen-day return, the written itemization, the penalty, the successor-holder rule — is inside that Act. So a lease term that waives, shortens, caps or conditions any of it is dead on arrival.

WHAT IT COSTS TO TRY. Section 76-1415(2): "A provision prohibited by subsection (1) of this section included in a rental agreement is unenforceable. If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees." Note what the trigger is: DELIBERATE use of a term the landlord KNOWS is prohibited. Recycling a form from another state is the ordinary way landlords walk into it, and the fee award is the part that hurts, because section 76-1416(3) already gives the tenant fees for a deposit failure as a matter of right rather than at the court's discretion.

THE THREE CLAUSES THAT FAIL MOST OFTEN, each with the subdivision that kills it.

1. "The deposit is non-refundable" or "the first $300 of the deposit is a non-refundable cleaning fee." Section 76-1416(1) reaches "security, HOWEVER DENOMINATED". Nebraska's definition has no express-agreement carve-out, so renaming the money does not take it outside the statute — it stays security, it counts against the one-month cap, and the fourteen-day return and itemization duties still attach to it. Worse than inert: a "non-refundable fee" charged ON TOP of a full one-month deposit puts you over the cap.

2. "Tenant waives the right to an itemized statement" or "Tenant agrees the deposit need not be returned within fourteen days." Section 76-1415(1)(a) voids it, and section 76-1405(2) confirms that "[a]ny right or obligation declared by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is enforceable by action unless the provision declaring it specifies a different and limited effect" — section 76-1416 specifies no such limited effect.

3. "Tenant agrees to pay Landlord's attorney's fees in any dispute over the deposit." This one fails under its OWN subdivision as well: section 76-1415(1)(c) prohibits a term by which the tenant "[a]grees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees". Nebraska bars the fee-shift in both directions as a lease term, so you cannot buy back the section 76-1416(3) fee exposure by contract.

WHAT YOU CAN DO INSTEAD, AND IT IS THE WHOLE PRACTICAL POINT: SETTLE. Section 76-1406 is one sentence — "A claim or right arising under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or on a rental agreement may be settled by agreement." The line Nebraska draws is INSTRUMENT AND TIMING, not substance. Section 76-1415(1)(a) bars a waiver written into the RENTAL AGREEMENT, before any claim exists. Section 76-1406 permits a settlement of a claim that has ARISEN. So after move-out, a signed move-out settlement in which the tenant accepts a stated sum in full satisfaction of the deposit claim is lawful where the identical sentence buried in the lease would be void and penalised. Document it as a separate, dated, post-termination agreement with its own consideration — not as a lease addendum signed at the start of the tenancy.

Two limits on settling. Section 76-1412(2) expressly extends the unconscionability inquiry to a "settlement", so a settlement extracted at the door for a fraction of a plainly owed deposit is reviewable; and section 76-1412(1) lets the court refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision, enforce the rest without it, or limit its application. Also, section 76-1416(4) provides that "a tenant shall not be liable for damages directly related to the tenant's removal from the premises by order of any governmental entity as a result of the premises not being fit for habitation due to the negligence or neglect of the landlord" — that is a tenant protection inside the deposit section, so it travels with the non-waiver rule and cannot be charged against the deposit by agreement in the lease either.

WHAT IS NOT PROHIBITED, because section 76-1415(1) is a CLOSED FOUR-ITEM LIST. Nothing stops you stating your own deposit figure in the lease, so long as it is within one month's periodic rent, or stating a pet deposit within the one-fourth-of-a-month limit, or setting out in detail what the deposit may be applied to under section 76-1416(2). Those are your figures inside the statute's constraint, not waivers of it.

title: No Duty to Post or Pre-Disclose How You Set Deposits — and No Unit-Count Threshold Anywhere in Nebraska's Deposit Law
bodyText:
Nebraska has NO deposit-standards disclosure rule. You are not required to post the standards by which you calculate a security deposit, to give them to an applicant before signing, to keep them uniform across your units, or to explain in writing why one tenant's deposit is higher than another's. South Carolina imposes exactly that on a landlord of more than four adjoining units who uses differing standards; Nebraska has no counterpart, and — this is the part worth knowing — Nebraska's deposit law contains NO UNIT-COUNT THRESHOLD OF ANY KIND. There is no small-landlord exemption and no large-landlord trigger. Section 76-1416 applies the same way to the owner of one duplex and to the owner of four hundred apartments. The only carve-out in the whole section is at subsection (1), and it is not about size: the one-month cap "shall not be applicable to housing agencies organized or existing under the Nebraska Housing Agency Act."

WHY THE QUESTION LARGELY DISSOLVES HERE. Section 76-1416(1) caps security "however denominated" at "an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent", plus "a pet deposit not in excess of one-fourth of one month's periodic rent". That is a single formula tied to each unit's own rent, so deposits across a portfolio already vary with rent without any standard being applied, and the ceiling is the same everywhere. There is nothing for a posted standards sheet to add and no differing-standards problem for the statute to police.

WHERE A DIFFERING STANDARD CAN STILL GET YOU IN TROUBLE, because it is not the deposit statute. Charging different applicants different deposits is governed by FAIR HOUSING, not by section 76-1416. Section 20-318(2) makes it unlawful to "[d]iscriminate against any person in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling or in the provision of services or facilities in connection therewith because of race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, sex, or military or veteran status", subject only to the exemptions in section 20-322. A deposit is a term of the rental. So a deposit practice that varies between applicants needs a reason you could state out loud — credit history, rental history, income verification, pet, co-signer — and that reason needs to be applied the same way to everyone. The fact that no statute makes you publish your standards does not mean no statute cares what they are.

ONE ADJACENT RULE THAT DOES REQUIRE ADVANCE NOTICE, AND IS OFTEN CONFUSED WITH THIS ONE. If you reduce your deposit practice to house rules, section 76-1422 attaches: a landlord's rule or regulation "however described" is enforceable against a tenant only if, among the six conditions, "(3) It applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner" and "(6) The tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement." That is a rules provision, not a deposit provision — it will not make a posted deposit schedule binding or enforceable as such — but it is the reason a deposit practice written into a rules sheet handed over after move-in does no work.

PRACTICAL COURSE, and it is a RECOMMENDATION rather than a requirement. Write down your deposit criteria for your own use, apply them uniformly, and keep the decision record for each applicant. Nothing requires you to publish them, and publishing a schedule can create an expectation you then have to honour. But a consistent internal standard is the cheapest defence to a section 20-318(2) complaint, and it costs nothing. State the actual deposit figure in the lease — that is your own number inside the section 76-1416(1) constraint, and stating it is lawful and sensible. Do not attach a price list of future deduction charges; Nebraska deducts only damages actually suffered under section 76-1416(2), which the library's Nebraska row on deposit cost schedules covers.

title: No Deadbolt, Peephole or Rekey-at-Turnover Mandate — But Every Lock You Install Becomes a Maintenance Duty
bodyText:
Nebraska imposes NO security-device requirements on a residential rental. There is no keyed deadbolt mandate, no keyless bolting device, no sliding-door pin lock, no window latch specification, no door-viewer or peephole requirement (with or without a construction-date trigger), no window-guard rule, and — the one landlords most often assume — NO DUTY TO REKEY OR CHANGE LOCKS BETWEEN TENANTS. Texas's security-device chapter and California's lock requirements have no Nebraska counterpart. Nothing in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act specifies a lock at all.

THE LEGISLATURE PROVED THIS IS A CHOICE IN 2025. Section 76-1431.03, enacted by Laws 2025, LB80, § 49, is the only lock-change MANDATE in Nebraska law, and it is tightly conditioned: where an act of domestic violence is perpetrated against a tenant or household member by someone who is not a cotenant or occupant of the same unit, and the tenant supplies qualifying documentation plus "a written notice containing the request that the locks be changed immediately", then "[t]he landlord shall change the locks to the tenant's dwelling unit as provided in section 76-1431.04 within TWENTY-FOUR HOURS after receiving the tenant's written request." The legislature wrote a lock-change duty, gave it a twenty-four-hour clock, and still wrote no general turnover rekey duty. (The domestic-violence procedure and its cost allocation are their own subject and the library's Nebraska domestic-violence rows carry them.)

WHAT DOES ATTACH, AND IT IS THE WHOLE PRACTICAL POINT: THE MAINTENANCE DUTY IS SUPPLY-TRIGGERED, NOT SPECIFICATION-BASED. Section 76-1419(1)(d) makes the landlord "[m]aintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her." You were never required to fit a deadbolt; once you fit one, it is a facility you supplied, and a deadbolt that no longer throws is a section 76-1419(1)(d) problem. Sections 76-1419(1)(b) ("put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition") and (1)(c) ("[k]eep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition") point the same way for an exterior door that will not latch or a broken common-entry lock. So the exposure runs from the hardware you chose to install, not from a statutory list — which means that advertising a unit as secure, or installing a lock and then leaving it broken, is riskier in Nebraska than installing nothing at all.

CAN YOU PUT LOCK MAINTENANCE ON THE TENANT? Only inside section 76-1419's formalities, and they are textual. For a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE, section 76-1419(2) lets landlord and tenant agree that the tenant perform the (1)(e) and (1)(f) duties "and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, and remodeling, but only if the transaction is in writing, for good consideration, entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord." For ANY OTHER DWELLING UNIT, section 76-1419(3) reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling", and only if the agreement is in good faith, "set forth in a SEPARATE WRITING signed by the parties and supported by ADEQUATE consideration", and "does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises." Note the contrast the text draws: subsection (2) says GOOD consideration, subsection (3) says ADEQUATE, and subsection (3) enumerates no subdivisions at all. A lock repair is a "specified repair" and so can be delegated under either route; the duty to supply a habitable unit cannot. Section 76-1419(4) separately allows you to EMPLOY the tenant to perform your obligations, with no written-agreement conditions attached.

THREE RELATED RULES THAT CATCH LANDLORDS IN THE LOCK AREA, each flagged rather than restated here. (1) Keys: duplicating a master key without written permission from the person with legal control of it is a Class III misdemeanor under section 28-1316(1)(c), every master key and duplicate "shall be stamped with the words DO NOT DUPLICATE", and section 28-1315(4) sweeps submaster, grand master, great grand master, EMERGENCY and overriding keys into the definition — with no landlord or management exception in section 28-1316(2), whose carve-outs are all motor-vehicle ones. The library's Nebraska key-control row carries this. (2) Holding a key does not create a right to use it: section 76-1423(4) says "[t]he landlord has no other right of access except by court order, as permitted by subsection (2) of section 76-1432, or if the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises", and section 76-1423(3) requires twenty-four hours' written notice stating the purpose and the anticipated window except in an emergency or where it is impracticable. (3) A lease clause cannot push the cost of a statutory lock change onto the tenant where the statute places it on the landlord; section 76-1415(1)(a) voids a term by which the tenant agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under the Act.

RECOMMENDED COURSE, offered as a practice and not as law. Rekey or replace cylinders between tenancies even though nothing requires it: you have no record of who holds a copy of the old key, Nebraska gives the departing tenant no duty to account for duplicates, and the section 76-1419(1)(d) maintenance duty on locks you supplied is the frame a claim would be argued in. If you install a device, document the installation date and keep service records. If you do not want to supply a device, say nothing about security in the advertisement.

title: Nebraska's Ban Is Wider Than a Lockout Ban — "By Action or Otherwise", and the Forcible-Entry Statute Does Not Apply to Your Tenancy
bodyText:
Nebraska bans self-help eviction, and the statute is drafted more broadly than the usual "no lockouts" rule. Section 76-1436: "A landlord may not recover or take possession of the dwelling unit BY ACTION OR OTHERWISE, including willful diminution of services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water, or other essential service to the tenant, except in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act." Read the three parts. "By action OR OTHERWISE" reaches court proceedings as well as physical acts, so an action brought outside the Act's own route is barred too. Utility interruption is named as a prohibited MEANS of recovering possession, not merely as a separate wrong. And the exceptions are a closed set of three: abandonment, surrender, or what the Act itself permits.

THE POINT THAT CATCHES EVEN EXPERIENCED LANDLORDS: FORCIBLE ENTRY AND DETAINER IS NOT YOUR STATUTE. Nebraska's forcible entry and detainer article, sections 25-21,219 to 25-21,235, closes its jurisdiction section with this sentence: "This section shall not apply to actions for possession of any premises subject to the provisions of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act." Section 76-1440 supplies the substitute: "An action for possession of any premises subject to the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act shall be commenced in the manner described by sections 76-1440 to 76-1447." So for a residential tenancy there is exactly ONE lawful route to possession, and it is sections 76-1440 to 76-1447. A form or a filing built on the forcible-entry article is built on a statute that disclaims your case.

THE TWO OPENINGS, AND WHY NEITHER IS A DECISION YOU GET TO MAKE UNILATERALLY.

SURRENDER means the tenant gives the unit back; it is consensual and it is a question of fact. Get it in writing, dated, with keys returned, and keep it.

ABANDONMENT has a statutory definition and a statutory CONSEQUENCE that runs against you. Section 76-1432(3): "If the tenant abandons the dwelling unit, the landlord SHALL take immediate possession and SHALL make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental. If the landlord rents the dwelling unit for a term beginning prior to the expiration of the rental agreement, it is deemed to be terminated as of the date the new tenancy begins. Total absence from the premises without notice to landlord for one full rental period or thirty days, WHICHEVER IS LESS, shall constitute abandonment." Three things follow. The clock is the SHORTER of one rental period or thirty days, so on a month-to-month tenancy it is the rental period. On abandonment you do not merely MAY retake — you MUST retake and must mitigate. And re-letting early ends the old agreement, which caps the rent you can chase. The annotations printed with section 76-1432 add that abandonment is not displaced by the statute and that, short of explicit abandonment, a landlord's self-help recovery inside the first thirty days "may depend on unequivocal but circumstantial proof of the tenant's abandonment" (Mason v. Schumacher, 231 Neb. 929, 439 N.W.2d 61 (1989)); it points the same way as the text: if you are guessing, you are not within the exception.

THERE IS ONE MORE NON-COURT ENTRY AND IT IS NOT A POSSESSION RIGHT. Section 76-1432(2): "During any absence of the tenant in excess of seven days, the landlord may enter the dwelling unit at times reasonably necessary." That is an entry, and it is the exception section 76-1423(4) points to. Section 76-1423(4) otherwise closes the list hard: "The landlord has no other right of access except by court order, as permitted by subsection (2) of section 76-1432, or if the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises." Holding a key is not access and an unpaid-rent emergency is not an "emergency" under section 76-1423(2).

WHAT IT COSTS IS COVERED BY THE LIBRARY'S NEBRASKA OUSTER-REMEDIES ROW, and the short version is that section 76-1430 gives the tenant possession or termination PLUS "an amount equal to three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages, and a reasonable attorney's fee" — liquidated, so no proof of loss is needed — and requires return of all prepaid rent and security recoverable under section 76-1416 if the agreement is terminated. Read section 76-1430 alongside section 76-1436 rather than as an alternative to it: section 76-1436 tells you the act is unlawful, section 76-1430 tells you the price, and the utility shutoff appears in both.

THE TENANT'S BELONGINGS ARE A SEPARATE STATUTE, so a lawful recovery of possession is not a licence to dispose of what is left behind. The Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act, sections 69-2301 to 69-2314, carries the notice, storage, release, sale and liability rules, and section 76-1414(5) routes a deceased tenant's property into the same Act. Follow it; sections 69-2309 and 69-2312 are headed "liability of landlord" and "Landlord retaining personal property; civil action authorized".

ONE STATUTE THAT APPEARS TO AUTHORISE SELF-HELP AND SHOULD NOT BE ACTED ON. Section 28-826 says that a tenant's conviction for a violation of sections 28-807 to 28-829 (Nebraska's obscenity article, not its drug laws) "shall make the lease or other title which he holds void at the option of the owner, and without any act of the owner, cause the right of possession to revert and vest in such owner, who may WITHOUT FURTHER PROCESS OF LAW make immediate entry upon the premises and retake possession." Nebraska law does not say how that squares with section 76-1436 and section 76-1430. The cautious course, and the one this row recommends: use the conviction to TERMINATE if you wish, and take possession through the court under sections 76-1440 to 76-1447. The library's Nebraska nuisance and prohibited-use rows treat section 28-826 at length.

title: No Work Card for Staff in 55+ Housing — But Check Whether Your Services Make You a "Caregiver"
bodyText:
Nebraska has NO work-card regime. Nevada requires certain employees in age-restricted housing to hold a sheriff-issued work card; Nebraska requires nothing of the kind, for senior housing or for any other rental. There is no state registration, certification, identification card, licence, fingerprinting requirement or criminal-history check imposed on the staff of a 55-and-over apartment complex, a retirement community or an ordinary rental. The phrase "work card" does not appear anywhere in Nebraska's statutes.

Nor is there a general tenant-facing criminal-background requirement for landlord employees. The four Nebraska sections that use the phrase "background check" are sections 29-4013 (Sex Offender Registration Act rules and regulations), 69-2402 and 69-2409.01 (the firearm purchase-certificate database) and 69-2431 (fingerprinting in that same firearms context). None of them reaches a landlord's staff.

WHAT NEBRASKA DOES REGULATE AT THE AGE-RESTRICTED END OF THE MARKET IS THE COMPLEX, NOT THE EMPLOYEE — and there are two provisions a 55+ operator should know.

FIRST, QUALIFYING AS HOUSING FOR OLDER PERSONS IS ITSELF CONDITIONED. Section 20-322(4)(a) exempts housing for older persons from the Nebraska Fair Housing Act's familial-status rules, and section 20-322(4)(b) defines it three ways: housing under a state programme the commission determines is designed to assist elderly persons; housing "[i]ntended for and solely occupied by persons sixty-two years of age or older"; or housing "[i]ntended and operated for occupancy by at least one person fifty-five years of age or older per unit." For the 55+ route the commission must require at least three things, in the statute's own words: "(A) The existence of significant facilities and services specifically designed to meet the physical or social needs of older persons or, if the provision of such facilities and services is not practicable, that such housing is necessary to provide important housing opportunities for older persons; (B) That at least eighty percent of the units are occupied by at least one person fifty-five years of age or older per unit; and (C) The publication of and adherence to policies and procedures which demonstrate an intent by the owner or manager to provide housing for persons fifty-five years of age or older." Subsection (4)(c) grandfathers residents in place as of September 6, 1991 and does not count reserved vacant units against you. The statute tells the commission to adopt regulations on those factors. Its fair-housing rules (Title 140 of the Nebraska Administrative Code, effective 2008) cover complaint procedure and say nothing more on them.

SECOND, AND THIS IS THE ONE THAT ACTUALLY TOUCHES YOUR STAFF. Nebraska's Adult Protective Services Act makes certain people MANDATORY REPORTERS of abuse, neglect or exploitation of a vulnerable adult, and section 28-384 makes a willful failure to report a CLASS III MISDEMEANOR. The list in section 28-372(1) includes "caregiver or employee of a caregiver" and "owner, operator, or employee of any facility licensed by the department". An ordinary 55+ apartment complex is not licensed by the Department of Health and Human Services, so that limb does not catch it, and everyone outside the list falls into the Act's permissive sentence: "Any other person MAY report". But "caregiver" is defined broadly at section 28-353: "any person or entity which has assumed the responsibility for the care of a vulnerable adult voluntarily, BY EXPRESS OR IMPLIED CONTRACT, or by order of a court of competent jurisdiction." And "vulnerable adult" at section 28-371 is "any person eighteen years of age or older who has a substantial mental or functional impairment or for whom a guardian or conservator has been appointed under the Nebraska Probate Code" — note that it is impairment-based, not age-based; the Act's separate "senior adult" definition at section 28-366.01 ("any person sixty-five years of age or older") serves the penalty provisions, not the reporting list.

THE OPEN QUESTION, STATED RATHER THAN RESOLVED, because it cuts in a direction that costs the landlord. The 55+ fair-housing qualification in section 20-322(4)(b)(iii)(A) can require "significant facilities and services specifically designed to meet the physical or social needs of older persons." The caregiver definition in section 28-353 turns on having "assumed the responsibility for the CARE of a vulnerable adult... by express or implied contract." One reading is that a landlord who provides meals, personal-care assistance, medication prompting or similar hands-on services to an impaired resident has assumed that responsibility by implied contract, and so becomes a caregiver — making the owner, the operator and "employee[s] of a caregiver" mandatory reporters under section 28-372(1) and exposed to section 28-384. The other reading is that "significant facilities and services" of the social and recreational kind contemplated by the fair-housing provision are not the "care" of a particular vulnerable adult, so no caregiver relationship arises from running an amenity programme. Nebraska's text does not resolve which services cross the line, there is no Nebraska decision located on the point. Do not assume you are outside it because you call yourself a landlord.

PRACTICAL COURSE. There is no card to obtain and no staff registration to file. If your 55+ property provides anything beyond housing and social amenities, train staff on the section 28-372 reporting route (the Department maintains a statewide toll-free number under section 28-372(5), a report may be made by telephone, and a written report follows within forty-eight hours if the Department asks) and treat reporting as mandatory rather than permissive — the cost of over-reporting is nothing and section 28-375 provides immunity from liability in defined circumstances, while the cost of under-reporting is a criminal charge. Separately, if your complex has MORE THAN TEN UNITS and a minimum age limit, check the library's Nebraska row on the Retirement Subdivisions and Communities Act (sections 76-1301 to 76-1315): that Act's registration requirement can reach a plain age-restricted complex, and it is a live open question, not a settled exemption.

title: No Duty to Tell a Tenant About the Registry — and No Immunity If You Do
bodyText:
Nebraska imposes NO sex-offender disclosure duty on a landlord. There is no required registry notice in or with the lease, no duty to tell an applicant that a registered offender lives in the building or nearby, no prescribed statutory language, and no database-lookup instruction of the kind California and Wisconsin put into their leases. Nebraska's Sex Offender Registration Act, sections 29-4001 to 29-4014, is addressed entirely to the OFFENDER, the sentencing court, the sheriff and the Nebraska State Patrol. In the Nebraska statute chapters that govern a tenancy, no section connects the words "sex offender" or "sexual predator" to a landlord, lessor, lease or rental agreement in any obligating way; the only sections that put those words near "reside" or "premises" are the registration sections and the residency-restriction sections, and none of them names a landlord.

THE REGISTRY IS PUBLIC, SO YOU CAN LOOK, AND YOU CAN TELL PEOPLE WHAT IS PUBLIC. Section 29-4009(1) opens: "Information obtained under the Sex Offender Registration Act shall not be confidential", subject to a closed list of items "disclosed to law enforcement agencies... if appropriate" only. Those eight items are the offender's social security number; references to arrests that did not result in conviction; travel or immigration document information; remote communication device identifiers and addresses; e-mail, instant messaging, chat room and other internet identifiers; telephone numbers; driver's licence or state identification card number; and — worth noticing — "(h) The name of any employer of a sex offender." Section 29-4009(2) adds that "[t]he identity of any victim of a sex offense shall not be released." So if you learn any of those nine things, do not pass them on. Everything else on the public registry is not confidential and you commit no offence by telling a prospective tenant to check it.

THE TRAP IS THE OTHER DIRECTION: THERE IS NO IMMUNITY FOR YOU. Section 29-4012 is one sentence: "Law enforcement officials, their employees, and state officials shall be immune from liability for good faith conduct under the Sex Offender Registration Act." A landlord, a manager and a management company are none of those. So the Act gives you no good-faith shield if you repeat registry information and get it wrong, or if you characterise it in a way the subject says is defamatory. Point people to the official registry; do not become the source. And note the asymmetry in the Act's own access list — section 29-4013(4) gives access to the fuller "public notification information" to, among others, "any public housing agency in each area in which a registered sex offender resides or is an employee or a student", but a PRIVATE landlord is not on that list. Nebraska distinguished the two and gave the private landlord nothing.

YOUR DISCLOSURE DUTIES ARE A SHORT AND UNRELATED LIST. Section 76-1417(1) requires you to disclose in writing, "at or before the commencement of the tenancy", the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or a person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving notices and demands; section 76-1417(2) makes you keep that current and binds successors. That is Nebraska's statutory tenant disclosure, and the registry is not part of it. Federal lead-based paint disclosure applies to pre-1978 housing independently of state law.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD, AND WHAT NOT TO PUT IN THE LEASE. A neutral, factual sentence in your application materials — that a public sex offender registry is maintained by the Nebraska State Patrol and that applicants are encouraged to consult it — costs you nothing, does not adopt anyone's data as your own representation, and is the practice this row recommends. Do NOT draft a clause in which the tenant "acknowledges" that no offender resides nearby, or "waives any claim" arising from an offender's presence, or "represents" that no occupant is a registered offender and agrees the lease terminates if one is. The first two run into section 76-1415(1)(a), which voids any rental agreement term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act" and exposes a landlord who deliberately uses a known-prohibited term to the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees under section 76-1415(2). The third is the Alabama-style lease-statement safe harbour, and Nebraska has written no safe harbour for it to rest on, so it buys you nothing while inviting a fair-housing argument you do not need.

ONE MUNICIPAL EXCEPTION WORTH KNOWING if you run short stays. Section 18-1758(5)(a) lets a municipality adopt an ordinance that "limits or prohibits the use of a short-term rental" for the purpose of "[h]ousing sex offenders" — one of only five permitted purposes in an Act that otherwise bars municipalities from prohibiting short-term-rental use. A short-term rental there means a stay "not longer than thirty consecutive days" under section 18-1758(1)(b), so this does not reach an ordinary tenancy; and whether any particular city has adopted such an ordinance is a local-ordinance question.

title: Nebraska Caps Sex-Offender Residency Rules Instead of Imposing Them — 500 Feet, Predators Only, and Anything Wider Is Void
bodyText:
Nebraska law speaks to sex-offender occupancy, and it speaks in the LANDLORD'S FAVOUR: it is a ceiling on local restrictions, not a duty on you. There is no statewide residency restriction, no landlord proximity duty of the Ohio kind, no crime for knowingly leasing to two registered offenders of the Oklahoma kind, no city co-residence fine with a lease-statement safe harbour of the Birmingham kind, and no duty to screen, evict or report.

THE PREEMPTION, AND ITS THREE LIMITS. The Sexual Predator Residency Restriction Act, sections 29-4015 to 29-4017, provides at section 29-4017(1): "A political subdivision may enact an ordinance, resolution, or other legal restriction prescribing where sex offenders may reside ONLY IF the restrictions are limited to SEXUAL PREDATORS, extend NO MORE THAN FIVE HUNDRED FEET from a school or child care facility, and meet the requirements of subsection (2) of this section." And then the enforcement sentence that matters most to a landlord, section 29-4017(3): "Any ordinance, resolution, or other legal restriction prescribing where sex offenders may reside which does not meet the requirements of this section is VOID, regardless of whether such ordinance, resolution, or legal restriction was adopted prior to, on, or after July 14, 2006."

HOW NARROW "SEXUAL PREDATOR" IS, because this is where most of the protection sits. Section 29-4016(5) defines a sexual predator as an individual who (a) is required to register under the Sex Offender Registration Act, (b) "has committed an aggravated offense as defined in section 29-4001.01", AND (c) "has victimized a person eighteen years of age or younger" — three cumulative conditions. A registered offender who is not in that intersection cannot lawfully be subject to any municipal residency restriction at all. Section 29-4016 also narrows the two anchors: "[c]hild care facility means a facility licensed pursuant to the Child Care Licensing Act", and "[s]chool means a public, private, denominational, or parochial school which meets the requirements for accreditation or approval prescribed in Chapter 79." An unlicensed daycare or an unaccredited programme is not an anchor, and "[p]olitical subdivision" is broad — "a village, a city, a county, a school district, a public power district, or any other unit of local government."

THREE CARVE-OUTS THAT CAN TAKE YOUR TENANT OUT OF AN OTHERWISE VALID ORDINANCE. Section 29-4017(2) says a local restriction "shall not apply to a sexual predator who: (a) Resides within a prison or a correctional or treatment facility operated by the state or a political subdivision; (b) ESTABLISHED A RESIDENCE BEFORE JULY 1, 2006, AND HAS NOT MOVED FROM THAT RESIDENCE; or (c) Established a residence after July 1, 2006, and THE SCHOOL OR CHILD CARE FACILITY TRIGGERING THE RESTRICTION WAS ESTABLISHED AFTER the initial date of the sexual predator's residence at that location." Subdivision (c) is the practical one: if the school or licensed daycare arrived after your tenant did, the restriction does not reach that tenancy — which means the question is not merely how far your building is from a school, but WHICH CAME FIRST.

WHAT NEBRASKA DOES NOT GIVE YOU, stated plainly so you do not assume it. Nothing in the Act obliges or entitles a landlord to do anything. It creates no screening duty, no duty to notify other tenants, no termination right, and no safe harbour for a lease statement. If a municipal ordinance within the section 29-4017 limits makes a particular tenancy unlawful, the Act does not supply you a special eviction route; you would be back to the ordinary Nebraska possession route in sections 76-1440 to 76-1447, and to section 76-1431's grounds. The Act is also silent on whether an offender's presence breaches anything, so do not read a residency ordinance as self-executing against your lease.

SCREENING IS LAWFUL AT STATE LEVEL, WITH TWO CAUTIONS. Criminal history is not a protected class under the Nebraska Fair Housing Act — section 20-318's classes are race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, sex, and military or veteran status — so a Nebraska landlord may decline an applicant on registry grounds without infringing the state Act. First caution: apply the policy uniformly, because section 20-318(2) reaches discrimination "in the terms, conditions, or privileges of ... rental" and an inconsistently applied criminal-history screen is the classic route to a complaint on a protected ground. Second caution: federal fair-housing disparate-impact analysis of criminal-records screening is a real exposure; it is federal law and nothing in this row should be read as clearing it. Lincoln and Omaha also add protected classes the state list does not carry.

THE ONE PLACE A NEBRASKA STATUTE RESTRICTS YOUR USE, and it is narrow. Section 18-1758(2) bars a municipality from adopting or enforcing an ordinance that "expressly or effectively prohibits the use of a property as a short-term rental", but section 18-1758(5) permits a limiting or prohibiting ordinance for five named purposes, the first being "(a) Housing sex offenders". Section 18-1758(1)(b) confines a short-term rental to a stay "not longer than thirty consecutive days", so this does not touch an ordinary tenancy. Whether your city has such an ordinance is a local question.

DO NOT WRITE A CLAUSE PROMISING WHAT THE STATUTE DOES NOT. A term by which the tenant represents that no occupant is or will become a registered offender, and agrees the lease terminates automatically if one is, has no Nebraska safe harbour behind it, does not create a termination ground section 76-1431 does not already give you, and — if drafted as a waiver of the tenant's statutory cure or notice rights — is void under section 76-1415(1)(a) with a damages-and-fees penalty under section 76-1415(2).

title: No Font-Size or First-Page Rule for a Nebraska Lease, and No Single-Family-Residence Disclosure — With One Formatting Trap That Does Apply
bodyText:
Two absences here, and they need to be stated with their exact scope because Nebraska is not silent about contract formatting generally — it is silent about RESIDENTIAL LEASE formatting.

FIRST: NO POINT-SIZE OR PLACEMENT RULE FOR A RESIDENTIAL LEASE. Nebraska prescribes no minimum type size for any term of a residential rental agreement, no requirement that a disclosure be in type as large as or larger than the surrounding text, and no requirement that anything appear on the first page, in a box, above the signature line or in a separate initialled paragraph. Nevada's relative-font-size and first-page placement rule has no Nebraska counterpart. Nebraska DOES write point-size mandates — in seller-assisted marketing plan contracts, membership camping contracts, foreclosure consulting and equity purchase contracts, invention development contracts, structured settlement transfers, litigation funding contracts and rental-purchase disclosures — and not one of them is a residential lease. So the silence is a drafting choice, not a gap.

SECOND: NO SINGLE-FAMILY-RESIDENCE OCCUPANCY DISCLOSURE. Nothing in Nebraska law requires you to tell a tenant in the lease that the property is a single-family residence, that it is or is not subject to particular rules because it is one, or that occupancy is limited by that character. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act uses the phrase "single-family residence" for exactly one purpose, and it is a DELEGATION rule rather than a disclosure: section 76-1419(2) lets "[t]he landlord and tenant of a single-family residence" agree that the tenant perform the landlord's section 76-1419(1)(e) waste-removal and (1)(f) water-and-heat duties, and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling, "but only if the transaction is in writing, for good consideration, entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord." For any dwelling unit that is NOT a single-family residence, section 76-1419(3) reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" and requires a "separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration" that "does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants in the premises." Subsection (3) enumerates no subdivisions at all, so the waste and water-and-heat duties cannot be shifted in a duplex or an apartment by any writing. That distinction is worth getting right — but it is a WRITING requirement, not a formatting or disclosure requirement, and the statute specifies no type size, no placement and no language for it.

THE ONE FORMATTING RULE THAT DOES REACH AN ORDINARY LEASE, AND IT IS A REAL TRAP. Section 25-2602.02: "The following statement shall appear in CAPITALIZED, UNDERLINED TYPE ADJOINING THE SIGNATURE BLOCK of any standardized agreement in which binding arbitration is the sole remedy for dispute resolution: THIS CONTRACT CONTAINS AN ARBITRATION PROVISION WHICH MAY BE ENFORCED BY THE PARTIES." A standard-form residential lease is a standardized agreement. Note three things. There is NO POINT SIZE in the rule — the requirement is capitals, underlining and position next to the signature block. The trigger is binding arbitration as the SOLE remedy, so an arbitration clause that preserves other remedies may not engage it. And the consequence of getting it wrong falls on the clause, not on the lease: the annotation printed with the section reports that on a failure of strict compliance the arbitration clause is "voidable and unenforceable" (Kramer v. Eagle Eye Home Inspections, 14 Neb. App. 691, 716 N.W.2d 749 (2006)), while a contract governed by federal law is not made unenforceable by omitting the language (Aramark Uniform & Career Apparel v. Hunan, Inc., 276 Neb. 700, 757 N.W.2d 205 (2008)). If your Nebraska lease makes arbitration the sole remedy, set the statutory sentence in capitals and underline, next to the signatures, verbatim.

AND ONE COMPARATOR THAT SHOWS NEBRASKA KNOWS HOW. Section 76-1605(3), in the Self-Service Storage Act, provides that "[t]he rental agreement shall contain a statement, in bold type, advising the occupant" of the operator's lien. That is a bold-type mandate inside a document the statute itself calls a rental agreement. The legislature wrote one for storage units and none for homes.

PRACTICAL COURSE. Because no rule applies, nothing is gained by elaborate formatting and nothing is lost by it, with two exceptions worth acting on. Do the section 25-2602.02 statement if arbitration is your sole remedy. And set genuinely important terms — the rent, the term, the deposit, your access rights, late charges — in plainly legible type and have the tenant initial them, not because any statute requires it but because section 76-1412(1) lets a court "refuse to enforce" an unconscionable provision or "limit the application of any unconscionable provision", and section 76-1412(2) says the parties get "a reasonable opportunity to present evidence as to the setting, purpose, and effect of the rental agreement" — which is an argument about how the document was presented. Unreadable fine print is the fact pattern that invites it. The same point applies to house rules: section 76-1422(4) requires a rule to be "sufficiently explicit in its prohibition, direction, or limitation of the tenant's conduct to fairly inform him of what he must or must not do to comply", and (6) requires notice of it at the time the tenant enters the agreement.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure in Nebraska — the Word "Shoreline" Does Not Appear, and the Water Disclosure That Exists Is Sale-Side Only
bodyText:
Nebraska has NO shoreline access disclosure. There is no duty to tell a tenant about public rights of access along a lake, river or reservoir, no required statement of where a boundary lies relative to a water line, and no lease language prescribed for waterfront property. Rhode Island's shoreline-access disclosure, built on a constitutional public-access right and a mean-high-tide boundary, has no Nebraska analogue — unsurprisingly, since Nebraska is landlocked, but the absence is worth recording with its scope because Nebraska DOES have lakefront, riverfront and reservoir rentals and it DOES have a water-related real-property disclosure.

THE WATER DISCLOSURE NEBRASKA HAS IS SALE-SIDE, NOT LEASE-SIDE, and a landlord who owns rural property should know it for the day they sell. Section 76-2,124(1): "Any person transferring OWNERSHIP of real property not inside the corporate limits of a municipality shall complete and provide to the transferee, at or before the closing of the transfer, a water resources update notice acknowledging (a) whether any surface water rights issued pursuant to Chapter 46, article 2, and in the name of any party other than an irrigation district, public power and irrigation district, or mutual irrigation company are attached to the real property ... and (b) whether there are any water wells, except water wells used solely for domestic purposes and constructed prior to September 9, 1993, on the real property." If the notice discloses either, the TRANSFEREE completes it and files it with the Department of Water, Energy, and Environment "within sixty days after recording the deed or other instrument". The form is prescribed by the department under section 76-2,124(2), there is no filing fee under (3), and failure to file "does not affect the recording, legality, or sufficiency of a deed".

Read the trigger words. It is "transferring OWNERSHIP", not leasing; it reaches property "NOT INSIDE the corporate limits of a municipality", so urban property is outside it; and the content is surface water rights and water WELLS, not shoreline access. So it creates no landlord-to-tenant duty of any kind, and it is the sale-side contrast that shows Nebraska legislates about water on a transfer of title and not on a tenancy.

WHAT GOVERNS INSTEAD IF YOUR RENTAL FRONTS WATER. Three things, none of them a disclosure statute. (1) Your own lease. Section 76-1414(1) lets landlord and tenant "include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law", so if you want to define or exclude a tenant's use of a dock, a bank or a beach, the lease is where you do it and nothing requires any particular form of words. (2) House rules, if you prefer them to a lease term — but section 76-1422 makes a rule enforceable against the tenant only if it meets all six of its conditions, including that "(2) It is reasonably related to the purpose for which it is adopted", "(3) It applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner", "(4) It is sufficiently explicit ... to fairly inform him of what he must or must not do to comply" and "(6) The tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement." (3) Whatever public access actually exists under Nebraska's water and game statutes, which sit in chapters 37 and 46 — see the limits note below.

PRACTICAL COURSE, AND IT IS A RECOMMENDATION RATHER THAN A DUTY. If the public has a right of access across or along your water frontage, say so in the lease in a sentence, and say what the tenant may and may not do about it — not because Nebraska requires disclosure, but because a tenant who believes exclusive use of a bank or dock came with the unit will treat the discovery as a diminution of the bargain, and section 76-1412(2) makes "the setting, purpose, and effect of the rental agreement" evidence a court may hear. The same sentence is also what lets you decline responsibility for policing the public's use. Conversely, do NOT promise exclusive water access you cannot deliver; a Nebraska lease term is enforceable against you, and the Act provides no excuse for a promise you could not keep.

title: You Cannot Shorten the Entry Notice for Showings in the Lease — Nebraska Sets 24 Hours in Writing and Voids the Waiver
bodyText:
A Nebraska lease cannot give you a shorter entry notice for showings than for any other entry, and it cannot let the tenant agree to one. Two sections together close the door.

THE PERIOD IS FIXED AND IT IS IN WRITING. Section 76-1423(3): "The landlord shall not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant. Except in case of emergency or if it is impracticable to do so, the landlord shall: (a) Give the tenant at least TWENTY-FOUR HOURS' WRITTEN notice of the landlord's intent to enter. Such notice shall be provided to EACH INDIVIDUAL UNIT and include the INTENDED PURPOSE for entry and a REASONABLE PERIOD during which the landlord anticipates making entry; and (b) Enter only at reasonable times." Showings are expressly inside the access right rather than outside it — section 76-1423(1) lists "exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workmen, or contractors" among the purposes for which the tenant "shall not unreasonably withhold consent" — so a showing gets the same twenty-four hours, the same writing, the same purpose statement and the same anticipated window as a repair visit. There is no end-of-tenancy exception and no showing exception.

THE WAIVER IS VOID. Section 76-1415(1)(a): "No rental agreement may provide that the tenant: (a) Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act". The twenty-four-hour written notice is a right under the Act, so a clause by which the tenant accepts same-day, telephone or verbal notice for showings is unenforceable under section 76-1415(2) — and if you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know to be prohibited, "the tenant may recover actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees." There is no separate-signed-document cure of the Delaware kind: Nebraska has written no mechanism by which a tenant may consent in advance to a shorter period, so a stand-alone addendum fares no better than a lease paragraph. It is the same waiver in a different envelope.

AND DO NOT FIX A TEXT OR E-MAIL ROUTE IN THE LEASE. Section 76-1413(2)(c) gives three ways a tenant receives a notice — delivered in hand; mailed to the place the tenant holds out for communications or, absent a designation, to the tenant's last-known place of residence; or delivered by electronic means. Electronic delivery is available, but only on the tenant's affirmative, informed, withdrawable consent under section 76-1413(7), and section 76-1413(9) is categorical: "A landlord shall not, as part of a rental agreement or as a condition of entering into or renewing a rental agreement, require a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means." So a lease that designates text message as the showing-notice method is ineffective twice over. Note also that nothing in section 76-1413(2)(c) makes a notice POSTED ON THE DOOR effective receipt.

WHAT THE PRICE IS. Section 76-1438(2): "If the landlord makes an unlawful entry or a lawful entry in an unreasonable manner or makes repeated demands for entry otherwise lawful but which have the effect of unreasonably harassing the tenant, the tenant may obtain injunctive relief to prevent the recurrence of the conduct, or terminate the rental agreement. In either case, the tenant may recover ACTUAL DAMAGES NOT LESS THAN AN AMOUNT EQUAL TO ONE MONTH'S RENT and reasonable attorney's fees." That is a FLOOR, not a cap, and it does not require proof of loss up to the floor. An end-of-tenancy showing campaign run on short notice is precisely the "repeated demands" fact pattern. Section 76-1438(1) is the mirror and it protects you: if the tenant refuses lawful access you may compel it by injunction or terminate, with actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees.

WHAT YOU CAN LAWFULLY DO, AND IT IS ENOUGH IN PRACTICE.

GIVE A STANDING SCHEDULE WITH PROPER NOTICE. Nothing stops a single written notice from covering a defined series of showings, so long as it states the purpose and "a reasonable period during which the landlord anticipates making entry" and is delivered at least twenty-four hours ahead to each individual unit. One notice reading "to show the unit to prospective tenants, on weekdays between 5:00 p.m. and 7:00 p.m. and Saturdays between 10:00 a.m. and 2:00 p.m., from [date] to [date]" states a purpose and a window and is twenty-four hours ahead of the first entry. Keep the window genuinely reasonable; an "any time, any day" window states no period at all and invites the section 76-1438(2) argument.

ASK ON THE DAY. A tenant who, when asked, invites you in now is a different thing from a tenant who signed away the notice months ago: section 76-1415(1)(a) voids a term IN A RENTAL AGREEMENT, and a contemporaneous invitation is not a rental-agreement term. Confirm it in writing — a reply text is fine as EVIDENCE of consent even though it may not be designated as the lease's notice channel — and keep it. Be clear about the limit: nothing in section 76-1423(3) expressly says consent excuses the notice, so this works because an entry the tenant asked for on the day is not "an unlawful entry", a "lawful entry in an unreasonable manner" or a harassing "repeated demand" under section 76-1438(2). Treat it as a practical route, not as a waiver you can rely on in advance, and never as a reason to skip notice when the tenant has not answered.

USE A FIXED TERM, AND MIND THE HOLDOVER CONSEQUENCE INSTEAD. If your concern is turnover, the lever Nebraska gives you is not shorter notice but a definite term plus section 76-1437's notice periods — seven days for week-to-week, thirty days before the periodic rental date for month-to-month — and section 76-1437(3)'s holdover remedy. Market around the tenancy, not into it.

title: No Government-Shutdown Rent Protection in Nebraska — Seven Days Is Seven Days, and the Only Flex Is a Judge's Continuance
bodyText:
Nebraska has NO shutdown rent protection. There is no statutory grace period for a federal, state or local employee whose pay is delayed, no mandatory forbearance, no stay of an eviction, no late-fee moratorium, no required repayment plan, and no reinstatement right. Nevada, Wisconsin, Kentucky and Maryland each legislated some version of this; Nebraska did not. The words "shutdown", "furlough" and "lapse in appropriations" do not appear anywhere in Nebraska's landlord-tenant law; in the Nebraska statute chapters that govern a tenancy, the only two sections matching that family are sex-offender registration provisions using the word in an unrelated sense.

SO THE ORDINARY TIMETABLE APPLIES, UNCHANGED. Rent is due when the lease says: section 76-1414(3) provides that "[r]ent shall be payable without demand or notice at the time and place agreed upon by the parties", with periodic rent payable at the beginning of the term or in equal monthly instalments "[u]nless otherwise agreed". Nonpayment runs on section 76-1431(2): "If rent is unpaid when due and the tenant fails to pay rent within SEVEN CALENDAR DAYS after written notice by the landlord of nonpayment and his or her intention to terminate the rental agreement if the rent is not paid within that period of time, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." Seven calendar days, not business days, and the clock starts on written notice rather than on the due date. A delayed federal paycheque changes none of it.

NEBRASKA DOES NOT REGULATE YOUR LATE FEE EITHER, which cuts both ways in a shutdown. No Nebraska statute caps, delays or conditions a residential late fee: the only four chapter-76 sections that use the phrase "late fee" or "late charge" are sections 76-874 (condominium assessments), 76-1605 (self-service storage), 76-1708 and 76-1711 (time-share programmes), and NOT ONE of them is inside the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act at sections 76-1401 to 76-1449 or inside the Mobile Home Act at sections 76-1450 to 76-14,111. So your lease's late fee stands during a shutdown as at any other time — and nothing requires you to waive it. Where the legislature did write down its own view of a reasonable late charge it was in the Rental-Purchase Agreement Act, section 69-2110(1)(d), at five dollars or three dollars after a five or three business-day grace period, once per accrued payment, with an express bar on charging a fee against a timely payment. That is a drafting benchmark, not a residential rule.

THE ONE REAL FLEX IS THE COURT'S, AND IT IS DISCRETIONARY. Section 76-1443: "The court may grant a continuance FOR GOOD CAUSE SHOWN by either party, but no subsequent continuance shall be granted except by agreement or unless extraordinary cause be shown to the court. For any subsequent continuance extending the initial trial date into the next periodic rental period, the court may require a tenant to deposit with the clerk of the court such rental payments as accrue during the pendency of the suit." Compare what Massachusetts does for a delayed benefit payment: a mandatory continuance plus reinstatement. Nebraska's is neither mandatory nor tied to any cause, and there is no reinstatement — but note the second sentence, which is the landlord's protection: a continuance that pushes trial into the next rental period lets the court order accruing rent paid into the clerk. If a tenant asks for time because of a pay delay, that sentence is what you ask the court to apply.

WHAT YOU CAN DO VOLUNTARILY, AND HOW TO DO IT WITHOUT LOSING YOUR POSITION. You may agree to anything you like; nothing in Nebraska law forces it and nothing forbids it. Two cautions. First, put a forbearance in a SEPARATE DATED WRITING rather than amending the lease, state the new dates and the amount, and state expressly that it is a one-time accommodation that does not alter the lease or waive any other breach. Section 76-1406 is the authority that makes this clean: "A claim or right arising under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or on a rental agreement may be settled by agreement" — a claim that has ARISEN may be settled, which a late-rent claim has. Second, accepting part of the rent or accepting it late without a reservation can cost you the breach you were relying on; the library's Nebraska row on accepting a late payment carries that point and should be read before you take the money.

ONE THING NOT TO DO. Do not treat a shutdown as a reason to bypass the statutory route. Section 76-1436 bars recovering possession "by action or otherwise, including willful diminution of services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water, or other essential service", and section 76-1430 prices a breach of it at "an amount equal to three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages, and a reasonable attorney's fee." The tenant's financial distress does not change your route.

title: No Owner-Occupancy Condition on Renting a House in Nebraska — and the State Leans the Other Way
bodyText:
Nebraska has NO statute limiting the rental of a home in a single-family zone, and none conditioning it on the owner living on the lot. Kentucky did that for Jefferson County by statute (KRS 383.199, for new leases after June 27, 2025); Nebraska has no counterpart, no cap on the number of rental houses in a zone, no registration triggered by renting out a single-family house, and no owner-residency requirement of any kind. Across the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy, only two sections use the phrase "owner-occupied" or "occupied by the owner" — sections 18-2103 (Community Development Law definitions) and 18-3405 — and neither limits leasing.

WHERE THE STATE DOES MENTION OWNER OCCUPANCY, IT IS AN EXEMPTION FROM A DUTY, NOT A CONDITION ON LEASING — and it is a pair of traps worth knowing because both run against the landlord who assumes owner occupancy helps.

FIRST: the state fair-housing disability provisions. Section 20-131.02(1) defines "[h]ousing accommodations" for sections 20-131.01 to 20-131.04 and then excludes "any single-family residence IN WHICH THE OWNER LIVES and in which any room is rented, leased, or provided for compensation to persons other than the owner or primary tenant". That carve-out depends on the owner actually living there. Rent the whole house out and the exemption is gone. Separately, section 20-322(3) lets a person refuse to rent "a room or rooms IN HIS OR HER OWN HOME for any reason or for no reason" — "except that this exception shall not apply to any person who makes available for rental or occupancy MORE THAN FOUR SLEEPING ROOMS to a person or family within his or her own home."

SECOND: the lead-paint licensing exemption, which fails for precisely the reason your house is rented. The Residential Lead-Based Paint Professions Practice Act applies to everyone engaged in lead-based paint activities "except persons who perform lead-based paint activities within residential dwellings THAT THEY OWN, UNLESS the residential dwelling is occupied by a person or persons other than the owner or the owner's immediate family while these activities are being performed" (section 71-6318.01(2)). An occupied rental can never satisfy it. That Act confines "lead-based paint activities" to inspection, risk assessment and abatement (section 71-6319.27), so ordinary repainting is outside it — but the do-it-yourself exemption a landlord would reach for is the one provision an occupied rental cannot use.

THE STATE'S OWN DIRECTION OF TRAVEL IS TOWARD MORE RENTAL USE, NOT LESS, in the two places it has legislated.

Section 18-1758(2) forbids a municipality to "adopt or enforce an ordinance or other regulation that expressly or effectively prohibits the use of a property as a short-term rental". A municipality may regulate only on a demonstrated public-health-and-safety purpose (section 18-1758(3)), may tax (section 18-1758(4)), may limit or prohibit only for five named purposes (section 18-1758(5)), and must "apply an ordinance or other regulation regulating land use to a short-term rental in the SAME MANNER as another similar property" (section 18-1758(6)(a) to (c), covering residential use and zoning, noise and nuisance, and property maintenance). The limit is the day count: section 18-1758(1)(b) confines a short-term rental to a stay "not longer than thirty consecutive days", so a conventional lease is outside this protection.

And the Municipal Density and Missing Middle Housing Act, sections 19-5501 to 19-5507, points the same way: section 19-5505(4) requires a city that FAILS to adopt an affordable housing action plan to allow "[m]iddle housing in all areas in the city zoned for residential use that allow for the development of detached single-family dwellings" and "[a] duplex on each lot or parcel zoned for residential use" that allows a detached single-family dwelling, with section 19-5505(5) requiring conforming amendments. Two real limits: "[m]iddle housing" is a closed five-item list (duplexes, triplexes, quadplexes, cottage clusters, townhouses) under section 19-5503(6), so an accessory dwelling unit is not in it; and "[c]ity" means only a metropolitan, primary or first-class city with at least twenty thousand inhabitants under section 19-5503(3). It is also about what may be BUILT, not about who may rent.

WHERE THE LIMIT ACTUALLY LIVES, AND THIS IS THE ONE THING TO DO. Nebraska leaves single-family zoning to MUNICIPAL AND COUNTY ORDINANCE, and occupancy caps are expressly left alone: section 20-322(4)(a) says "[n]othing in the act shall limit the applicability of any reasonable local restrictions regarding the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling".
