So the questions that matter for your property — whether the zone permits a rental at all, whether it caps unrelated occupants, whether a rental licence or inspection is required, and whether short-term use is regulated — are answered by your city's or county's code and not by any statute in this row. Check the ordinance before you let a single-family house, and check it again before you let it to a group of unrelated adults.

title: No Smart-Lock Statute in Nebraska — But Revoking a Credential Remotely Is a Lockout, Priced at Three Months' Rent
bodyText:
Nebraska does NOT regulate smart access. There is no statute on smart locks or app-based entry in a residential rental: no tenant consent requirement, no right to refuse and keep a physical key, no limit on how long you may retain entry logs or credential data, no duty to disclose that a system is installed, no restriction on who may hold administrative rights, and no effective date to wait for. Washington's smart-access provisions (RCW 59.18.750 to 59.18.760, effective January 1, 2027) have no Nebraska counterpart.

THE ONE PLACE NEBRASKA MENTIONS KEYLESS ENTRY, AND IT PROVES THE SILENCE IS DELIBERATE. Section 76-1431.04, enacted by Laws 2025, LB80, § 50, tells a landlord how to comply with the domestic-violence lock-change duty: "(1) A landlord required to change locks under section 76-1431.02 or 76-1431.03 shall do so by either: (a) Replacing the entire locking mechanism with a locking mechanism of equal or better quality ...; or (b) If the lock is in good working condition: (i) Rekeying the lock; or (ii) IN THE CASE OF A KEYLESS ELECTRONIC LOCK, RESETTING THE ENTRY CODE." Three further points from the same section, all of them landlord-side and all specific to electronic systems: subsection (3) — "A landlord who installs a new lock pursuant to this section MAY RETAIN A COPY OF THE KEY OR ENTRY CODE that opens the new lock"; subsection (4) — the landlord "may require the tenant to pay for the actual and reasonable cost incurred ... in changing the locks"; and subsection (2)(b) — the tenant's self-help right where you fail to act "applies NOTWITHSTANDING ANY PROVISION IN THE RENTAL AGREEMENT TO THE CONTRARY", so that one cannot be drafted around. The legislature was writing about keyless electronic locks in 2025 and still created no general smart-access regime. Read that as a choice, not a gap.

THE EXPOSURE THAT MATTERS MOST, BECAUSE A SMART LOCK MAKES IT A SINGLE CLICK. Disabling a tenant's credential is a LOCKOUT, and Nebraska prices a lockout without caring how it was done. Section 76-1430: "If the landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises or willfully and wrongfully diminishes services ... the tenant may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, in either case, recover an amount equal to THREE MONTHS' PERIODIC RENT AS LIQUIDATED DAMAGES, and a reasonable attorney's fee", plus return of all prepaid rent and security recoverable under section 76-1416 if the agreement is terminated. Liquidated means no proof of loss is needed. Section 76-1436 reinforces it: a landlord "may not recover or take possession of the dwelling unit by action or otherwise ... except in case of abandonment, surrender, or as permitted in" the Act. Deactivating an app credential for unpaid rent is exactly the act those two sections forbid, and it is more likely to be provable than a changed cylinder because the system logs it.

RELIABILITY IS A MAINTENANCE DUTY, NOT A PRODUCT WARRANTY QUESTION. Section 76-1419(1)(d) makes you "[m]aintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her." Nothing required you to install a smart lock; once you did, it is a facility you supplied and an electrical one at that. A dead battery, a failed hub, an expired subscription or a network outage that leaves a tenant standing outside is a section 76-1419(1)(d) failure — and if you do not restore access promptly it starts to look like the section 76-1430 exclusion as well. Section 76-1419(1)(b)'s duty to "put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition" points the same way.

THE APP IS NOT A LAWFUL NOTICE CHANNEL JUST BECAUSE IT IS INSTALLED. Entry still requires section 76-1423(3)'s twenty-four hours' WRITTEN notice to each individual unit, stating the intended purpose and a reasonable anticipated window, except in an emergency or where it is impracticable; and section 76-1423(4) says "[t]he landlord has no other right of access" beyond the listed grounds. Holding administrative rights to the lock is not a right of access. If you want to serve notices electronically, section 76-1413(7) sets the consent conditions — affirmative consent, a clear and conspicuous statement of the right to withdraw it without condition or consequence, the types of notices covered, the right to a paper copy, the withdrawal procedure, and hardware and software requirements — and section 76-1413(9) is absolute: "A landlord shall not, as part of a rental agreement or as a condition of entering into or renewing a rental agreement, require a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means." A lease that makes the access app the notice channel is void on that point.

THE KEY-CONTROL CRIME, AND WHERE IT BITES ON A KEYLESS SYSTEM. Section 28-1316(1)(c) makes it an offence to duplicate "a master key for anyone unless written permission has been granted by the person who has legal control of the master key", requires that "[a]ll master keys shall be stamped with the words DO NOT DUPLICATE" along with all duplications, and section 28-1316(3) makes the offence a Class III misdemeanor — with subsection (2)'s only exceptions being motor-vehicle ones. Section 28-1315(4) defines a master key as "a key planned and CUT to operate all locks in a series or group of locks" and then adds that "[f]or the purpose of section 28-1316, submaster keys, grand master keys, great grand master keys, EMERGENCY KEYS, and overriding keys are to be considered as master keys." Two consequences. The better reading is that a digital credential, a code or a phone is not a key "planned and cut", so section 28-1316 does not reach the electronic side — but that reading rests on one word and no Nebraska decision construes it, so do not build a practice on it. What is NOT in doubt is the PHYSICAL OVERRIDE: almost every keyless lock has a mechanical emergency key or override cylinder, and section 28-1315(4) names emergency and overriding keys expressly. Stamp those DO NOT DUPLICATE, stamp any duplicate, and do not have one cut for a contractor without written permission from whoever has legal control of it. The library's Nebraska key-control row carries this in full.

AND THE DATA SIDE, FLAGGED NOT RESTATED. A smart-access system holds credentials and sometimes fingerprints. Section 87-802(5)(a)(iv) brings a "[u]nique electronic identification number or routing code, in combination with any required security code, access code, or password" within "personal information", and (a)(v) brings "[u]nique biometric data, such as a fingerprint, voice print, or retina or iris image"; section 87-802(5)(b) covers "[a] user name or email address, in combination with a password". Section 87-803 sets the breach investigation and notice duties and section 87-805 makes a waiver "void and unenforceable". The library's Nebraska tenant-data row carries the detail; the point here is that choosing fingerprint entry over a code moves you into that Act.

PRACTICAL COURSE, all of it recommendation rather than requirement. Give every tenant a NON-APP way in — a physical key or a keypad code — and say so in the lease; nothing requires it, and a tenant with no smartphone, no data or a dead phone is a section 76-1419(1)(d) problem waiting to happen. Never use credential revocation as leverage. Keep a documented manual override and tell tenants how to reach it out of hours. Prefer codes to biometrics unless you have a reason. And if you take over a building with a system already installed, find out who else holds administrative rights before you are the one explaining a log entry.

title: A Smoke-Drift Waiver Fails Twice in Nebraska — and a Mid-Tenancy No-Smoking Rule May Fail Too
bodyText:
Nebraska has no smoke-drift statute — no statutory standard for tobacco smoke migrating between units, no disclosure duty about smoking in a building, and no mandatory smoke-free policy. But the WAIVER question, which is what this subject is really about, Nebraska answers squarely, and the answer is no.

A SMOKE-DRIFT WAIVER FAILS ON TWO SEPARATE SUBDIVISIONS. Section 76-1415(1) provides that "[n]o rental agreement may provide that the tenant: (a) Agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act;... or (d) Agrees to the EXCULPATION OR LIMITATION OF ANY LIABILITY OF THE LANDLORD arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord or to INDEMNIFY the landlord for that liability arising due to active and actionable negligence or the costs connected therewith." A clause by which the tenant accepts that smoke may enter the unit and gives up any claim about it is a waiver of the section 76-1419 habitability remedies under (1)(a), and to the extent it reaches the landlord's own negligence — failing to seal a shared chase, ignoring a known ventilation defect — it is an exculpation or indemnity barred by (1)(d). Section 76-1415(2) makes such a provision unenforceable and gives the tenant "actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees" where the landlord "deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited." An acknowledgment of a KNOWN FACT is different from a waiver of a REMEDY: a sentence recording that the building permits smoking in designated areas, or that the unit is in a multi-unit structure with shared ventilation, states a fact and gives nothing up. A sentence saying the tenant "releases", "waives" or "holds harmless" crosses the line.

AND TORT LAW SURVIVES THE ACT. The closing sentence of section 76-1419(1) says "[t]he obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state." So a nuisance or negligence claim about smoke is not confined to the Act's remedies, and a clause drafted to cap the Act's remedies would not reach the tort claim anyway — another reason the waiver buys less than it appears to.

WHAT YOUR ACTUAL DUTIES ARE. Section 76-1419(1)(b) requires you to "[m]ake all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition", and (1)(c) to "[k]eep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition." Where a minimum housing code applies, the closing sentence of subsection (1) caps your maximum duty by (1)(a) — substantial compliance with that code, after notice. Nebraska has no statewide housing code; the applicable code, if any, is municipal.

THE OTHER TENANT IS THE ONE WITH THE DUTY YOU CAN ENFORCE. Section 76-1421(7) requires each tenant to "[c]onduct himself and require other persons on the premises with his consent to conduct themselves in a manner that will not disturb his NEIGHBORS' PEACEFUL ENJOYMENT of the premises." That is the hook for persistent smoke drift from a neighbouring unit, and it runs through section 76-1431(1): written notice specifying the acts and omissions, termination on a date not less than thirty days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in fourteen days, with no termination if the tenant adequately remedies it before the stated date — and if substantially the same act recurs within six months, termination on at least fourteen days' written notice with no cure right. Section 76-1421(6) adds that a tenant must not "deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises", which is where smoke damage to finishes is argued.

THE TRAP THAT CATCHES LANDLORDS GOING SMOKE-FREE MID-TENANCY. A no-smoking policy is a rule or regulation, and section 76-1422 makes a rule enforceable against a tenant only if all six of its conditions are met, including "(2) It is reasonably related to the purpose for which it is adopted", "(3) It applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner", "(4) It is sufficiently explicit in its prohibition, direction, or limitation of the tenant's conduct to fairly inform him of what he must or must not do to comply", and "(6) The tenant has notice of it AT THE TIME HE ENTERS INTO THE RENTAL AGREEMENT." Then the closing sentence: "A rule or regulation adopted after the tenant enters into the rental agreement is enforceable against the tenant if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the tenant and IT DOES NOT WORK A SUBSTANTIAL MODIFICATION OF HIS BARGAIN." Converting a building where a sitting tenant lawfully smoked in their own unit into a smoke-free building is the clearest candidate there is for a substantial modification of that tenant's bargain. Nebraska gives no answer on the point and no annotation construes the sentence. The cautious course: make the building smoke-free for NEW tenancies and at RENEWAL, in the lease itself rather than in a rules sheet; if you want existing tenants in, get a signed addendum with its own consideration rather than relying on a notice of adoption. Do not treat a mid-term rules notice as having converted the existing smoker's lease.

AND YES, THE CLEAN INDOOR AIR ACT REACHES YOUR COMMON AREAS, WITH A CRIMINAL PENALTY THAT ACCRUES DAILY.

THE CHAIN. (1) The prohibition is section 71-5729, "Smoking in place of employment or public place prohibited." (2) "Public place" is defined in section 71-5726 as "an indoor area to which the public is invited or in which the public is permitted, whether or not the public is always invited or permitted", and the carve-out is in that same definition rather than in the exemption list: "A private residence is not a public place." The words are "a private residence", NOT "a residential building" — so your tenant's dwelling unit is out, but your building's enclosed common areas (lobby, hallways, stairwells, laundry room, community room, leasing office) are indoor areas in which the public is permitted, "whether or not the public is always... permitted", and they fall inside the definition. (3) There is no residential exemption anywhere in the Act. Section 71-5730(1)'s list is closed and holds only designated smoking guestrooms and suites capped at twenty percent of an establishment's rooms, contiguous and non-infiltrating; indoor areas used for a research study on the health effects of smoking; tobacco retail outlets; and cigar shops as defined in section 53-103.08. Subsection (2) adds electronic smoking device retail outlets as to e-cigarettes only, and subsection (4)(b) describes the outlet and cigar-shop exceptions as "narrowly tailored in accordance with the intent of the act to protect public places and places of employment." Nothing residential appears. So the list is closed as of 2020, not as of 2008; check it again before relying on the absence of a residential entry, because a future session could add one. (4) YOU are the person the duty attaches to: section 71-5725 provides that "[p]roprietor means any employer, owner, operator, supervisor, manager, or other person who controls, governs, or directs the activities in a place of employment or public place" — "owner" is named expressly. (5) The duty, which is section 71-5731 in full: "A proprietor of a place of employment or public place where smoking is prohibited under the Nebraska Clean Indoor Air Act shall take necessary and appropriate steps to ensure compliance with the act at such place." That is affirmative and open-ended — not merely a duty to refrain from permitting smoking, but a duty to take the steps necessary to ensure compliance.

WHAT IT COSTS YOU IF YOU DO NOTHING. Section 71-5733(2): "A proprietor who fails, neglects, or refuses to perform a duty under the... Act is guilty of a Class V misdemeanor for the first offense and a Class IV misdemeanor for the second and any subsequent offenses." Subsection (3): "Each day that a violation continues to exist shall constitute a separate and distinct violation." Subsection (4): "Every act or omission constituting a violation... by an employee or agent of a proprietor is deemed to be the act or omission of such proprietor, and such proprietor shall be subject to the same penalty as if the act or omission had been committed by such proprietor." Read those three together: the exposure is CRIMINAL, it escalates on a second offence, it COMPOUNDS EVERY DAY the condition is left in place, and your on-site manager's omission is treated as yours. A tolerated common-area smoking problem does not sit still.

ENFORCEMENT, RETALIATION, AND THE WAIVER POINT THIS ROW IS ABOUT. Section 71-5732(1) lets the Department of Health and Human Services or a local public health department sue to enjoin a violation, and "[a]ny interested party may report possible violations". Section 71-5732(2) bars retaliating against an employee, applicant or "customer" who reports one. Section 71-5732(3) is the only waiver the Act allows: "The Department of Health and Human Services may waive provisions of the Nebraska Clean Indoor Air Act upon good cause shown." Its rule (178 NAC 7-006) requires an application, proof of good cause, and a temporary waiver. So a lease term cannot permit common-area smoking or waive a tenant's protection under the Act. Section 71-5729 makes it "unlawful for any person to smoke" there, and the only exits are section 71-5730's list and a Department waiver.

WHAT TO DO. Post the enclosed common areas, say so in the lease and in your rules, instruct on-site staff in writing, and treat a report of common-area smoking as something you must ABATE rather than mediate between neighbours. The daily accrual is the part that decides how fast you move.

THREE LIMITS, EACH OF WHICH MATTERS. First, do NOT read this as a prohibition on smoking inside the unit. Section 71-5726's private-residence sentence takes the dwelling out, nothing in the Act reaches it, and drift from one private residence to another is governed by what this row sets out above — section 76-1421(7)'s neighbours'-peaceful-enjoyment duty, section 76-1419(1)(b) and (1)(c), and your own rule under section 76-1422. The Act gives you a common-area answer, not a unit-to-unit one. Second, the common-area conclusion follows from the definition's text and the closed exemption list, but it is a reading and not a holding. Treat enclosed common areas as covered because that is the cautious course, not because a court has said so. Third, if you have staff, the common areas are covered a second way. Section 71-5724 defines a "place of employment" as "an indoor area under the control of a proprietor that an employee accesses as part of his or her employment without regard to whether the employee is present", and it names "hallway". Section 71-5721 makes anyone who "employs one or more employees" an employer. So a hallway your maintenance employee uses is covered even if it were not a public place. Neither the Act nor the Department's rule (178 NAC 7) sets a sign requirement for a residential building; the only sign rule, section 71-5735, is for tobacco retail outlets. Municipal smoking ordinances may go further than the Act.

title: A Late Benefit or Voucher Payment Is No Defense in Nebraska — and the Judgment You Win May Be Uncollectible Anyway
bodyText:
Nebraska has NO benefit-delay defense. If a tenant's Social Security payment, disability payment, general assistance or housing-voucher payment arrives late, nothing in Nebraska law pauses the rent, extends the cure period, requires the court to continue the case, or reinstates the tenancy on payment. Massachusetts gives a tenant exactly that — a continuance and reinstatement where a government benefit payment is delayed (ch. 186, §§ 11-12). Nebraska wrote nothing like it.

THE CLOCK IS THE ORDINARY ONE. Section 76-1431(2): "If rent is unpaid when due and the tenant fails to pay rent within SEVEN CALENDAR DAYS after written notice by the landlord of nonpayment and his or her intention to terminate the rental agreement if the rent is not paid within that period of time, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." Seven calendar days, running from written notice. The source of the money is irrelevant to the section.

AND THE ONLY STATUTORY DEFENSE TO A NONPAYMENT CASE IS YOUR OWN NONCOMPLIANCE, NOT THE TENANT'S CIRCUMSTANCES. Section 76-1428(1): "In an action for possession based upon nonpayment of the rent or in an action for rent where the tenant is in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for any amount which he or she may recover under the rental agreement or the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. In that event, the court from time to time may order the tenant to pay into court all or part of the rent accrued and thereafter accruing and shall determine the amount due to each party." If nothing remains due after that accounting, "judgment shall be entered for the tenant in the action for possession" — but the gateway is a claim the tenant could recover under the lease or the Act, which a delayed benefit payment is not. The subsection also protects you: "If the defense or counterclaim by the tenant is without merit and is not raised in good faith, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney's fees." Section 76-1428(2) lets a tenant no longer in possession counterclaim without paying rent into court.

THE ONE LEVER A TENANT CAN REACH IS A CONTINUANCE, AND IT IS THE JUDGE'S, NOT THE STATUTE'S. Section 76-1443: "The court may grant a continuance FOR GOOD CAUSE SHOWN by either party, but no subsequent continuance shall be granted except by agreement or unless EXTRAORDINARY CAUSE be shown to the court. For any subsequent continuance extending the initial trial date into the next periodic rental period, the court MAY REQUIRE A TENANT TO DEPOSIT WITH THE CLERK OF THE COURT such rental payments as accrue during the pendency of the suit." Discretionary, not mandatory; no reinstatement; and that second sentence is yours to invoke. If a tenant asks for time because a payment is coming, ask the court to condition it on accruing rent going to the clerk.

NOR IS THERE A SOURCE-OF-INCOME MANDATE AT STATE LEVEL. Section 20-318's protected classes are race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, sex, and military or veteran status — receipt of public assistance or a voucher is not among them, and the library's Nebraska row on voucher acceptance carries that. Two cautions. Lincoln and Omaha add classes the state list does not, and Lincoln added source of income by a 2025 voter-approved measure, so check the municipal code. And if you DO accept a voucher, your relationship with the housing authority is governed by the federal programme documents you signed, not by section 76-1431 — those can impose their own notice and termination requirements on top of the statute.

THE PART WORTH MORE THAN THE DEFENSE QUESTION: THINK ABOUT COLLECTION BEFORE YOU SPEND ON A MONEY JUDGMENT. A tenant living on benefits is frequently judgment-proof, and Nebraska's own collection machinery does not help you. Section 25-1556 lists the specific personal-property exemptions a debtor may select — immediate personal possessions, necessary wearing apparel, up to three thousand dollars in household goods, up to five thousand in tools of trade, up to five thousand in a motor vehicle, and professionally prescribed health aids — and benefits are not in the list, but that is not the obstacle. Section 25-1558 caps wage garnishment at the LESSER of twenty-five percent of disposable earnings for the week, the amount by which disposable earnings exceed thirty times the federal minimum hourly wage, or FIFTEEN PERCENT if the debtor is a head of a family, with only three exceptions (a support order, a Chapter XIII bankruptcy order, and a state or federal tax debt) — and it reaches "disposable EARNINGS", meaning wages, not benefit payments. Federal law separately shields Social Security benefits from legal process; that is 42 U.S.C. 407, and it is the reason a Nebraska money judgment against a benefits-only tenant commonly cannot be enforced. Decide whether you are suing for possession, for money, or both, before you file.

AND MIND THE SERVICE CHOICE, because it can take the money judgment away from you by itself. Where the plaintiff serves the summons by the posting-and-mailing route of section 76-1442.01, section 76-1446 provides that "a money judgment shall not be granted for the plaintiff." If the tenant is hard to find — which a tenant waiting on a delayed payment often is — the convenient service method costs you the money claim.

PRACTICAL COURSE. Nothing requires you to wait, and nothing stops you. If you choose to, do it as a one-time written forbearance with new dates rather than as a lease amendment, relying on section 76-1406 — "[a] claim or right arising under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or on a rental agreement may be settled by agreement" — and state expressly that it waives no other breach. Read the library's Nebraska row on accepting late payments before you take partial rent. Ask for proof of the payment date rather than taking it on trust, and keep your section 76-1431(2) notice properly dated in case the payment does not arrive.

title: Special Districts: You Keep the Vote, Your Tenant Never Gets One — and the Only Way to Lose It Is in Your Own Lease
bodyText:
NEBRASKA'S SPECIAL DISTRICTS ARE OWNER-FRANCHISE BODIES, NOT RESIDENT-FRANCHISE BODIES. If your rental sits inside a sanitary and improvement district (SID) or, as of 2026, a community improvement district (CID), the district's board of trustees levies a property tax and special assessments against the land you own — and the people who elect that board are PROPERTY OWNERS. Your tenant has no vote, no candidacy and no statutory voice, however long the tenancy runs.

The Community Improvement District Act, sections 18-3501 to 18-3559, was adopted by Laws 2026, LB1114 and is operative April 17, 2026. Section 18-3514(2)(b) and (d) split the five (or three) trustee seats between "the legal property owners resident within such community improvement district" and "all of the owners of real estate located in the community improvement district" — resident OWNERS, not residents. Section 18-3514(2)(c) adds that "[a]ny public, private, or municipal corporation owning any land or lot in the community improvement district may vote at an election the same as an individual" but that "[n]o corporation, estate, or irrevocable trust shall be deemed to be a resident owner". So if you hold the rental in an LLC or a corporation you vote as an owner in the at-large seats and are excluded from the resident-owner seats no matter who lives in the building. Section 18-3514(2)(c) also makes the franchise acreage-weighted and lot-weighted for the at-large seats: "one vote for each acre of unplatted land or fraction thereof and one vote for each platted lot". And section 18-3514(1)(c) requires a trustee to "be an owner of real estate located in the community improvement district" or a designated representative of an entity owner — your tenant cannot run.

THE ONE SENTENCE IN THE STATUTE THAT CAN COST YOU THE VOTE, AND IT IS YOUR LEASE THAT TRIGGERS IT. Section 18-3514(2)(c) continues: "For purposes of voting for trustees, each condominium apartment under a condominium property regime established under the Nebraska Condominium Act shall be deemed to be a platted lot and the lessee or the owner of the lessee's interest, under any lease for an initial term of not less than twenty years which requires the lessee to pay taxes and special assessments levied on the leased property, shall be deemed to be the owner of the property so leased and entitled to cast the vote of such property." Two conditions, both cumulative and both written by you: an initial term of at least TWENTY YEARS, and a lease that REQUIRES THE LESSEE TO PAY TAXES AND SPECIAL ASSESSMENTS on the leased property. Meet both and the statute hands your district vote to your tenant and takes it from you. An ordinary one-year or month-to-month residential lease meets neither condition, so nothing in a normal tenancy moves the vote. A long-term ground lease or a twenty-year net lease is where this bites. If you want the vote, do not require the lessee to pay the special assessments; if you are content for the lessee to vote, say so deliberately rather than by accident. Section 18-3514(1)(c) and (3) both key notice and ballots to "each person who is entitled to vote at the election ... whose property ownership OR LEASE GIVING A RIGHT TO VOTE is of record on the records of the register of deeds", so a vote-shifting lease only works if it is recorded — another reason to decide this on purpose.

THE SAME RULE, WORD FOR WORD, GOVERNS SIDS. Section 31-735, as printed whole by Laws 2026, LB1114, section 85, carries the identical sentence: the lessee under a lease of "not less than twenty years which requires the lessee to pay taxes and special assessments" is "deemed to be the owner of the property so leased and entitled to cast the vote". LB1114 also moved the SID resident-owner-majority milestone later, from the sixth-year election to the eighth-year election: resident owners elect two of the five trustees at the elections four and six years after the first election, and three of the five from the eighth-year election on. These SID election changes have been operative since July 18, 2026.

THE DISCLOSURE DUTY EXISTS AND IT IS PURCHASER-SIDE ONLY. Section 18-3513(1) makes the district clerk file an annual statement by December 31 naming the trustees, the district's professionals, its warrant and bond principal indebtedness as of the preceding June 30, and its current tax levy. Section 18-3513(2) then requires "[t]he real estate broker or salesperson or, if none, THE OWNER of the real estate" to "distribute the most recent statement ... to any prospective PURCHASER of any real estate located within a community improvement district", and (3) to obtain the purchaser's written acknowledgment that the property is in a district, which "may be obtained separately from the disclosure required under section 76-2,120". Section 18-3513(4) sets the timing (on or before the date the purchaser becomes obligated to buy) and the consequence: "[t]he exclusive remedy for failure to provide such statements and obtain such acknowledgments shall be an action for damages, and any such failure shall not affect title to the real estate or the validity of the conveyance." NOTHING IN SECTION 18-3513 REACHES A TENANT. There is no duty to tell a tenant the unit is in a district, no duty to disclose the district levy, and no tenant remedy for not being told. When you SELL the rental, the duty attaches and it attaches to you personally if no broker is involved.

PRACTICAL COURSE. (1) Nothing requires a special-district statement in your lease, so do not promise one. (2) Do not write a lease clause saying the tenant accepts or agrees to the district levy or assessments as rent unless you have priced it: section 18-3521 authorizes the district property tax and section 18-3522(5) makes a municipal sewer charge inside a CID "a lien upon the property served", which is your property and not your tenant's, so a tenant-pays clause allocates cost between you and the tenant and does nothing to the lien. (3) Keep the annual section 18-3513 statement in the property file: you will need the most recent one the day you list the property, and the late-filing penalty in (1)(b) falls on the district, not on you, so the only paper you control is the copy you kept. (4) If you are negotiating a ground lease or any lease of twenty years or more, decide the special-assessment clause with the district vote in mind, because that clause is the switch.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Requirement
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS NO SPRINKLER DISCLOSURE STATUTE. There is no Nebraska counterpart to New York's or Connecticut's rule requiring a residential lease to state whether the building has an automatic fire sprinkler system, no high-rise sprinkler notice or lobby sign of the Maryland kind, and no duty to tell a tenant that a sprinkler system was removed, never installed, or is out of service. The word "sprinkler" does not appear in the Nebraska statute chapters that govern a tenancy, nor in any of the 363 slip laws of the 2025 and 2026 sessions.

WHAT NEBRASKA DOES REQUIRE YOU TO DISCLOSE IN A RESIDENTIAL TENANCY IS A SHORT LIST, AND THIS IS NOT ON IT. Section 76-1417(1) requires the landlord or any person authorized to enter into a rental agreement to disclose to the tenant in writing, at or before the commencement of the tenancy, the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving notices and demands. That is the whole of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's disclosure duty. Nothing in sections 76-1401 to 76-1449 requires any statement about fire protection equipment of any kind.

THE SILENCE IS A CHOICE, NOT AN OVERSIGHT, AND THE PROOF IS IN THE NEIGHBOURING SECTIONS. Nebraska's legislature wrote a detailed, trigger-based alarm duty for rental housing and put it in the same chapter: section 76-606(1) makes the owner of a rental dwelling or unit ensure an operational carbon monoxide alarm is installed if the unit has a fuel-fired heater or appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage AND the owner makes any permit-requiring interior alteration, repair, fuel-fired appliance replacement or addition on or after January 1, 2017; section 76-606(2) attaches the same duty independently on any "change in tenant occupancy on or after January 1, 2017". Section 76-606(3) and (4) then split maintenance between you and the tenant — you replace an alarm stolen, removed, missing or non-operational before a new occupancy, supply the batteries at move-in, and fix or replace on the tenant's notice; otherwise the tenant keeps, tests and maintains it — and section 76-606(5) bars anyone from disabling one. Section 76-603 separately requires a carbon monoxide alarm in any dwelling constructed on or after January 1, 2017 with one of those three features. Even the only residential disclosure statement Nebraska law prescribes, section 76-2,120 (which runs to a PURCHASER, not a tenant), has a carbon-monoxide item written into its contents list at subsection (4)(k) — "[i]nformation relating to compliance with the requirements for a carbon monoxide alarm as provided in sections 76-604 and 76-605" — and no sprinkler item anywhere in subsections (3) or (4). A legislature that wrote a device-specific landlord duty, a device-specific construction mandate and a device-specific line in the seller's disclosure form, all for carbon monoxide alarms, and wrote nothing of the kind for sprinklers, has made a decision.

WHETHER YOUR BUILDING MUST HAVE SPRINKLERS IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION, AND IT IS NOT ANSWERED BY STATUTE EITHER. Section 81-503.01(1) directs the State Fire Marshal to adopt rules and regulations "constituting a State Fire Code" that must at a minimum cover, among other things, "[e]lectrical wiring and heating, protection equipment devices, materials, furnishings, and other safeguards within structures necessary to promote safety and reduce loss by fire" and "[t]he means and adequacy of exits, in case of fire, in ... residential ... occupancies". Fire protection equipment is therefore regulated BY RULE, not by the statute, and section 81-503.01(2) requires those rules only to "conform generally" to NFPA Pamphlet 1 (Fire Code, 2012 edition) and NFPA Pamphlet 101 (Life Safety Code, 2012 edition) "but not when doing so would impose an unduly severe or costly burden without substantially contributing to the safety of persons or property". So NFPA is not Nebraska law; the Fire Marshal's rules are. Any sprinkler requirement that applies to your building comes from those rules, from the building code your city adopted, or from a condition of a permit — never from a lease statute.

ONE THING THAT IS NOT THERE AND MATTERS: NO MANDATORY STATE INSPECTION OF RENTAL HOUSING. Section 81-502(1)(c)'s list of occupancies the State Fire Marshal must inspect is a closed list and rental housing is not on it. So nobody is coming to tell you whether your sprinkler system is compliant, and no inspection certificate exists for you to hand a tenant.

PRACTICAL COURSE, AND WHY VOLUNTEERING THE INFORMATION IS STILL THE RIGHT CALL. (1) Do not write a sprinkler disclosure into the lease believing a statute requires it, and do not copy a New York or Maryland sprinkler rider: the figures, the sign and the notice timing in those forms are their states' law and have no Nebraska basis. (2) If the building HAS a sprinkler system, say so in writing and say plainly that a tenant must not hang anything from a sprinkler head, paint one, or obstruct one — that is a legitimate use-and-care term supported by section 76-1421(1)'s tenant duty to "[u]se ... all ... facilities ... in a reasonable manner" and by section 76-1422's rule-making power, and it protects a system whose accidental discharge will flood your building. (3) If the building has NO sprinkler system, do not say or imply that it does, in the lease or in your advertising. That is where the real Nebraska exposure sits: section 87-302(a)(10) reaches advertising a price in a misleading manner and (a)(5) reaches representing that goods or services have characteristics or benefits they do not have, and section 87-303.07 makes a lease induced by a section 87-302 violation "unenforceable by the seller or lessor" with a right to rescind. Overstating fire protection is the one sprinkler statement that can cost you the lease. (4) Volunteer the fact in writing either way when a tenant asks. Nothing requires it, there is no immunity for silence, and a written answer removes the later argument about what you said.

title: A Lease Longer Than One Year Is VOID Without a Writing You Signed — Plus Three Traps: the One-Year Lease That Starts Later, the Manager's Written Authority, and the Acknowledge-and-Record Rule
bodyText:
THE RULE, IN ITS OWN WORDS. Section 36-105: "Every contract for the leasing for a longer period than one year, or for the sale of any lands, shall be void unless the contract or some note or memorandum thereof be in writing and signed by the party by whom the lease or sale is to be made." Not unenforceable — VOID. And note who has to sign: "the party by whom the lease ... is to be made", which is YOU, the lessor. The printed annotations are consistent on that point going back to 1885 ("Vendor only is required to sign contract or memorandum", Iske v. Iske, 95 Neb. 603 (1914)), so a lease over a year that the tenant signed and you did not is the one that fails.

BUT GET THE TENANT'S SIGNATURE TOO, BECAUSE A SECOND SECTION USES A DIFFERENT RULE ABOUT WHO SIGNS. Section 36-202 opens: "In the following cases every agreement shall be void, unless such agreement, or some note or memorandum thereof, be in writing, and SUBSCRIBED BY THE PARTY TO BE CHARGED THEREWITH: (1) Every agreement that, by its terms, is not to be performed within one year from the making thereof". A lease whose term runs past a year from signing is such an agreement. So the two sections point in opposite directions on signatures: section 36-105 voids the lease if YOU did not sign, and section 36-202(1) voids it against the TENANT if the tenant did not sign. A long lease signed by the landlord alone may be void as against the tenant you want to hold to it. There is no version of this where one signature is the right answer.

SECTION 36-103 IS THE SECOND HALF OF THE RULE AND IT IS THE HALF LANDLORDS MISS. "No estate or interest in land, other than leases for a term of one year from the making thereof, nor any trust or power over or concerning lands ... shall hereafter be created, granted, ASSIGNED, SURRENDERED, or declared, unless by operation of law, or by deed of conveyance in writing, subscribed by the party creating, granting, assigning, surrendering or declaring the same." So the writing requirement does not stop at making the lease. An ASSIGNMENT of a lease longer than a year, and a SURRENDER of one, each need a writing subscribed by whoever is doing the assigning or surrendering. If a tenant under a three-year lease hands you the keys and walks, an oral surrender does not discharge the lease; and if you let a tenant hand the unit to someone else on a handshake, you have no written assignment to sue on.

TRAP ONE, AND IT IS A REAL ONE: A ONE-YEAR ORAL LEASE IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY SAFE. Section 36-103's exception is "leases for a term of one year FROM THE MAKING THEREOF". The printed annotations read that literally: "An oral lease for only one year is void if entered into prior to the beginning of the term" (Prigge v. Olson, 154 Neb. 131 (1951); Kofoid v. Lincoln Implement & Transfer Co., 80 Neb. 634 (1908); Thostesen v. Doxsee, 77 Neb. 536 (1906)). So an oral deal struck in June for a twelve-month term starting in August runs past one year from the making and is outside the exception. These cases are not a holding you can rely on without checking them, but the statutory words "from the making thereof" are right there, and the practical answer is the same either way: put every lease in writing and have the landlord sign it.

TRAP TWO: YOUR PROPERTY MANAGER NEEDS WRITTEN AUTHORITY, NOT JUST AUTHORITY. Section 36-409: "Every instrument required by any of the provisions of sections 36-103 to 36-106, 36-202, and 36-402 to 36-409 to be subscribed by any party, may be subscribed by his agent thereunto authorized BY WRITING." A manager or leasing agent who signs a lease over one year on your behalf must hold written authority to do it. An oral appointment is not enough, and the annotations to section 36-105 make the same point from the other direction ("Agent must be authorized in writing", O'Shea v. Rice, 49 Neb. 893 (1896)). If you use a management company, the management agreement should say in terms that the manager may execute leases on your behalf, and it should be signed before the first long lease is signed.

TRAP THREE: WHAT THE WRITING HAS TO CONTAIN, AND AN UNRESOLVED TENSION ABOUT RENT. Section 36-408 says the consideration of a contract required to be in writing "need not be set forth in the contract or agreement or in the note or memorandum thereof, but may be proved by any other legal evidence." But the annotation printed with section 36-105 reports Gibbons Ranches v. Bailey, 289 Neb. 949 (2015): "The written evidence required by this section must contain the essential terms of the contract, and the amount of rent is an essential term when an express lease agreement contemplates the payment of rent in money." Those two can be read together (a general consideration rule in one section, a lease-specific essential-terms rule in the other) or as being in tension. THE CAUTIOUS COURSE IS NOT CLOSE: state the rent amount, the parties, the premises and the term in the signed writing. Nothing is gained by leaving the rent out and nothing protects you if a court takes Gibbons Ranches at its word.

A LEASE OVER ONE YEAR IS ALSO A DEED FOR RECORDING PURPOSES, AND THAT IS A SEPARATE REQUIREMENT. Section 76-211: "Deeds of real estate, or any interest therein, in this state, EXCEPT LEASES FOR ONE YEAR OR FOR A LESS TIME, if executed in this state, must be signed by the grantor or grantors, being of lawful age, and be ACKNOWLEDGED or proved and RECORDED as directed in sections 76-216 to 76-237." So the acknowledge-and-record formalities reach a lease longer than a year. The consequence of skipping them is in section 76-238(1): an unrecorded instrument takes effect "as to all creditors and subsequent purchasers in good faith without notice" only from delivery to the register of deeds, and is "void as to all creditors and subsequent purchasers without notice whose deeds, mortgages, or other instruments are recorded prior" — "However, such instruments are valid between the parties to the instrument." Read that last sentence carefully, because it is the whole of the comfort available: an unrecorded long lease still binds you and your tenant. What it does not do is survive a sale or a mortgage foreclosure against a buyer or lender who had no notice. If a long lease matters to the value of the deal — a below-market rent, a renewal option, a right of first refusal — record it or accept that a later purchaser may not be bound.

AND ONE MORE RECORDING RULE THAT CATCHES FAMILY ARRANGEMENTS. Section 76-238(2) provides that possession of agricultural or residential real estate by a person related to the owner of record within the third degree of consanguinity or affinity "shall not serve as notice to a creditor or subsequent purchaser" where that person claims under a lease (a) entered into on or after July 16, 2004, (b) "purporting to extend beyond a term of one year", and (c) which has not satisfied section 76-211 — unless the creditor or purchaser got a written copy of the lease before recording. Subsection (3)(d) defines residential real estate as "real estate containing not more than four units designed for use for residential purposes". So renting to a relative on a long unrecorded lease is the arrangement most likely to be wiped out, because the usual protection of visible occupancy is switched off by statute.

E-SIGNATURES: YES, AND THE ROUTE IS EXPLICIT. Section 86-634(3) and (4): "If a law requires a record to be in writing, an electronic record satisfies the law" and "If a law requires a signature, an electronic signature satisfies the law." Section 86-638 does the same for acknowledgment: where a law requires a signature or record "to be notarized, acknowledged, verified, or made under oath, the requirement is satisfied if the electronic signature of the person authorized to perform those acts, together with all other information required to be included by other applicable law, is attached to or logically associated with the signature or record." Section 86-630(2) excludes only wills and codicils and the Uniform Commercial Code outside articles 2 and 2A — real property leases are not excluded. TWO LIMITS YOU MUST RESPECT. Section 86-632(2): the act "applies only to transactions between parties EACH OF WHICH HAS AGREED to conduct transactions by electronic means", determined "from the context and surrounding circumstances, including the parties' conduct" — and section 86-632(3) makes the right to refuse electronic dealing for other transactions non-waivable. Separately, section 76-1413(9) prohibits requiring a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means. So an electronically signed lease is as good as an ink one in Nebraska, but you cannot make electronic signing a condition, and if a tenant wants paper you give them paper.

THE EQUITABLE ESCAPE HATCH, STATED SO YOU DO NOT RELY ON IT. Section 36-106: "Nothing contained in sections 36-103 to 36-106 shall be construed to abridge the powers of a court of equity to compel the specific performance of agreements in cases of part performance." The annotations show what that costs: part performance must "speak for themselves" and be "solely referable to the contract". And the annotations to section 36-105 also report that a parol lease for three years is good for one year and that a lessee who enters under a void long lease becomes a tenant for one year (Osgood v. Shea, 86 Neb. 729 (1910); Friedhoff & Co. v. Smith, 13 Neb. 5 (1882)) — meaning the fallback from a failed five-year lease is not nothing, but it is one year at a time, not five. That is a worse position than the one a signature would have bought you.

PRACTICAL COURSE. Sign every lease yourself or through an agent holding written authority; state rent, parties, premises and term in the signed document; take any assignment, any surrender and any modification of a lease over a year in a signed writing; and for any lease longer than a year that you actually care about, get it acknowledged and recorded, or at minimum give a written copy to any lender or buyer before they record.

title: Nebraska's Statutory Money Limits, Sorted by Shape — One Cap on What You May Demand, Two Ceilings, Two Fixed Sums, One Floor, and One Thing You Cannot Change by Contract
bodyText:
Nebraska does not have a general damages cap, and it does not have a schedule of lease fees. What it has is six specific money provisions scattered through the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and they come in FOUR DIFFERENT SHAPES. Getting the shape wrong is what costs money, because a ceiling, a fixed sum and a floor behave nothing alike in a courtroom.

SHAPE ONE — THE ONLY CAP ON WHAT YOU MAY DEMAND. Section 76-1416(1): "A landlord may not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent, except that a pet deposit not in excess of one-fourth of one month's periodic rent may be demanded or received when appropriate". Three things to carry. "HOWEVER DENOMINATED" means renaming money does not escape the cap — a cleaning fee, a redecorating fee, a key deposit or an administrative charge held against the tenant's performance counts toward the one month. The pet allowance is an EXTRA quarter-month, not part of the month, and it is available only "when appropriate". And the subsection does not apply "to housing agencies organized or existing under the Nebraska Housing Agency Act", so the cap is on private landlords. This is the ONLY statutory ceiling in the Act on an amount a Nebraska landlord may ASK FOR. There is no cap on rent, no rent control or rent stabilization statute of any kind, and no statutory cap on a late fee.

SHAPE TWO — TWO CEILINGS ON RECOVERY, AND THEY ARE HIGHER THAN THEY LOOK. Section 76-1426 (your failure to deliver possession, willful and not in good faith) and section 76-1437(3) (the tenant's holdover, willful and not in good faith) use identical wording: "an amount NOT MORE THAN three months' periodic rent OR THREEFOLD THE ACTUAL DAMAGES sustained by him, WHICHEVER IS GREATER, and reasonable attorney's fees." Read the whole phrase. "Not more than" sets a ceiling, but the ceiling's LEVEL is the greater of three months' rent and treble actual damages — so where the actual loss is large, the exposure is three times that loss and the three-month figure is irrelevant. A row or a clause that reports these as "capped at three months' rent" has the statute backwards in the direction that matters. Note also that section 76-1437(3) runs in YOUR favour against a holding-over tenant, and section 76-1426 runs against you; the formula is the same both ways, and so is the willful-and-not-in-good-faith gate.

SHAPE THREE — TWO FIXED SUMS, WHICH NEED NO PROOF OF LOSS AT ALL. Section 76-1430 (unlawful ouster, exclusion, or wrongful diminution of service): the tenant "may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, in either case, recover AN AMOUNT EQUAL TO THREE MONTHS' PERIODIC RENT AS LIQUIDATED DAMAGES, and a reasonable attorney's fee." Not "not more than" — "an amount equal to". The tenant proves the lockout and the number follows; no evidence of harm is required. AND NOTE THE GATE, BECAUSE IT IS ASYMMETRIC: the willfulness words in section 76-1430 attach only to the second limb — "willfully and wrongfully diminishes services" — while the first limb is simply "[i]f the landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises". A good-faith but unlawful lockout is still three months' rent. Section 76-1416(3) is the other fixed sum: where your failure to account for the deposit within fourteen days "is willful and not in good faith, the tenant may recover an amount equal to one month's periodic rent or two times the amount of the security deposit, WHICHEVER IS LESS, as liquidated damages" — again "an amount equal to", so a fixed sum, but here the lesser of two measures, and it sits on top of the deposit itself plus court costs and attorney's fees under the first sentence of (3).

SHAPE FOUR — A FLOOR, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE IN THE ACT. Section 76-1438(2): for an unlawful entry, a lawful entry made in an unreasonable manner, or "repeated demands for entry otherwise lawful but which have the effect of unreasonably harassing the tenant", the tenant "may recover ACTUAL DAMAGES NOT LESS THAN an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees." One month's rent is the MINIMUM, not the maximum: actual damages above it are recoverable in full. Compare section 76-1438(1), which gives you, for a tenant's refusal of lawful access, "actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees" — no floor, no multiplier, nothing but what you can prove. The access section is lopsided and the lopsidedness is in the statute's own words.

ONE MORE, EASY TO MISS: A CEILING INSIDE THE ESSENTIAL-SERVICES REMEDY. Section 76-1427(1)'s closing sentence: where your failure to supply running water, hot water, heat or essential services "is deliberate", the tenant may recover "the actual and reasonable cost or fair and reasonable value of the substitute housing NOT IN EXCESS OF AN AMOUNT EQUAL TO THE PERIODIC RENT, and in any case under this subsection reasonable attorney's fees." That is a one-month ceiling on the substitute-housing measure specifically, available only on a DELIBERATE failure, and it sits alongside the subdivision (a) procure-and-deduct right and the subdivision (b) diminution-in-fair-rental-value measure, which carry no ceiling.

NONE OF THESE CAN BE CHANGED BY YOUR LEASE, AND HERE IS HOW YOU KNOW. Eleven sections of chapter 76 open with the words "unless otherwise agreed" — sections 76-1414, 76-1420, 76-1424, 76-1433, 76-1475, 76-1476, 76-1477, 76-1495, 76-14,106, 76-2331 and 76-3303. NOT ONE of the money sections is among them. Sections 76-1416, 76-1426, 76-1427, 76-1430, 76-1437 and 76-1438 contain no contrary-agreement language at all, and section 76-1415(1)(a) separately voids any rental agreement term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act". Section 76-1415(1)(c) voids a term by which the tenant "[a]grees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees", so you cannot contract for fees either — the fee awards above come from the statute or not at all. And section 76-1415(2) prices deliberate use of a prohibited term at the tenant's actual damages plus reasonable attorney's fees. A liquidated-damages clause, a damages cap, a waiver of the one-month entry floor, or a clause letting you keep more than one month's rent as security is not merely ineffective; using one knowingly is itself actionable.

WHAT NEBRASKA HAS NO CAP ON, STATED PLAINLY SO YOU DO NOT GO LOOKING. No cap on rent or rent increases. No cap, grace period or formula for a residential late fee — the words "late fee" and "late charge" appear nowhere in sections 76-1401 to 76-1449 or in the Mobile Home Act. No cap on actual damages you may recover from a tenant for breach beyond what you can prove, which section 76-1435 confirms by giving you "a claim for rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement and reasonable attorney's fees". No statutory fee schedule for application fees, pet rent, parking or storage. And no cap on the deposit for a public housing agency, by section 76-1416(1)'s own exception.

PRACTICAL COURSE. (1) Count every up-front dollar you hold against performance toward the one-month section 76-1416(1) cap, whatever you call it, and keep the pet deposit separately stated at no more than a quarter of a month. (2) Never write a figure from these sections into the lease as your own number — restating a statutory remedy gains you nothing and misstating one is a section 76-1415 problem. (3) Treat the fourteen-day deposit accounting in section 76-1416(2) as the cheapest insurance in Nebraska landlording: it is the only one of these figures whose trigger is entirely within your control, and the fixed sum in (3) does not require the tenant to prove a loss. (4) Never lock a tenant out or shut off a utility to force a move, however clear the default: section 76-1430's first limb needs no willfulness and the number is three months' rent plus fees regardless of what the tenant actually lost.

title: The Six Statutory Grounds on Which a Nebraska Tenant Can End a Fixed-Term Lease Early — and the Grounds Nebraska Does Not Give
bodyText:
A fixed-term Nebraska lease does not run its term just because the tenant signed it. Six statutes let a tenant end it early, each with its own trigger and its own notice mechanics, and none of them can be bargained away. Know which six, because a tenant who follows one of these walks with no liability for the rest of the term and a landlord who treats the departure as an abandonment ends up suing for rent the statute already discharged.

GROUND ONE — YOUR MATERIAL NONCOMPLIANCE (section 76-1425(1)). Where there is "a material noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement or a noncompliance with section 76-1419 materially affecting health and safety", the tenant delivers a written notice "specifying the acts and omissions constituting the breach and that the rental agreement will terminate upon a date not less than THIRTY DAYS AFTER RECEIPT of the notice if the breach is not remedied in FOURTEEN DAYS". So the clock is two-layered: you get fourteen days to cure, and termination cannot bite sooner than thirty days after RECEIPT — receipt, not mailing. If you "adequately remedy the breach prior to the date specified in the notice", the lease does not terminate. BUT THE RECURRENCE RULE REMOVES YOUR SECOND CURE: "If substantially the same act or omission which constituted a prior noncompliance of which notice was given recurs within six months, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement upon at least FOURTEEN DAYS' written notice specifying the breach and the date of termination" — fourteen days and NO cure right at all. Fixing the same thing twice in six months is how a landlord loses a lease. Your one defence in the subsection: "[t]he tenant may not terminate for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of his or her family, or other person on the premises with his or her consent." And under section 76-1425(4), on termination you "shall return all prepaid rent and security recoverable by the tenant under section 76-1416."

GROUND TWO — YOU FAILED TO DELIVER POSSESSION (section 76-1426(1)). Rent abates until possession is delivered, and the tenant may, "[u]pon at least FIVE DAYS' written notice to the landlord[,] terminate the rental agreement and upon termination the landlord shall return all prepaid rent and security". Five days, not thirty, and no cure period is written into the subdivision.

GROUND THREE — FIRE OR CASUALTY (section 76-1429(1)(a)). Where the unit or premises are "damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty to an extent that enjoyment of the dwelling unit is substantially impaired", the tenant may "[i]mmediately vacate the premises and notify the landlord in writing within FOURTEEN DAYS THEREAFTER of his intention to terminate the rental agreement, in which case the rental agreement terminates AS OF THE DATE OF VACATING." Read the sequence: the tenant leaves first and tells you afterwards, and the termination date back-dates to the day they left. The alternative at (1)(b) is partial vacation with rent reduced "in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value". Section 76-1429(2) makes accounting run "as of the date of the casualty" and preserves the tenant's responsibility "for damage caused by his negligence" — and the annotation records SFI Ltd. Partnership 8 v. Carroll, 288 Neb. 698 (2014), that a lease provision holding a tenant liable for negligent fire damage is not void as against public policy. YOUR LEASE CANNOT CHANGE ANY OF THIS: section 76-1429 is not among the eleven chapter-76 sections that open "unless otherwise agreed".

GROUND FOUR — UNLAWFUL OUSTER OR CUT-OFF SERVICES (section 76-1430). If you "unlawfully remove[] or exclude[] the tenant from the premises or willfully and wrongfully diminish[] services ... by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water or other essential service", the tenant may "recover possession OR TERMINATE THE RENTAL AGREEMENT and, in either case, recover an amount equal to three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages, and a reasonable attorney's fee."

GROUND FIVE — BAD ENTRY PRACTICE (section 76-1438(2)). For "an unlawful entry or a lawful entry in an unreasonable manner or ... repeated demands for entry otherwise lawful but which have the effect of unreasonably harassing the tenant", the tenant may obtain injunctive relief "or TERMINATE THE RENTAL AGREEMENT", and in either case recover "actual damages not less than an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees." Termination here is an alternative to an injunction, not an add-on.

GROUND SIX — DOMESTIC VIOLENCE (section 76-1431.01). This one is a true no-fault release and it does not depend on anything you did. A tenant who is a victim of an act of domestic violence, or whose household member is, "may obtain a release from a rental agreement" on producing a protective order, restraining order or similar relief, or certification under section 76-1431(5)(a)(iii), plus a written notice naming an effective date "at least FOURTEEN DAYS after" and "no more than THIRTY DAYS after" the documentation is given, and naming any household members released with them. Four consequences in the statute's own words: the tenant "shall remain liable for rent for the month in which the tenant terminated" (subsection (3)); the released tenant and household members "[a]re not liable for rent or damages to the premises incurred after the release date" and "[a]re not subject to ANY FEE SOLELY BECAUSE OF TERMINATION of the rental agreement" (subsection (4)) — which kills any early-termination fee, re-letting charge or liquidated-damages clause as applied to this release; other co-tenants who are not household members of the released tenant stay fully bound (subsection (5)); and a perpetrator cannot use the section (subsection (6)). The documentation and lock-change machinery that goes with Nebraska's domestic-violence provisions, including sections 76-1431.02 to 76-1431.04, is a separate subject and is not restated here.

AND A SEVENTH THAT LIVES OUTSIDE THE ACT: SERVICEMEMBER TERMINATION. Nebraska has its own servicemember early-termination statute and it is narrower than the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. Its terms are not restated here; see the servicemember row. Do not assume the federal rule and the Nebraska rule are the same.

WHAT NEBRASKA DOES NOT GIVE A TENANT, AND THESE ABSENCES ARE WHERE THE MONEY IS. There is NO statutory termination for a landlord's fraudulent misrepresentation — North Dakota has one; Nebraska does not, and nothing in chapter 76 lets a tenant walk on a misrepresentation as such. (Your exposure for misdescribing the unit runs through the deceptive-practices act instead, where section 87-303.07 makes a lease induced by a section 87-302 violation "unenforceable by the seller or lessor" with a right to rescind — a worse outcome than a termination right, so this absence is not comfort.) There is NO statutory termination for a tenant's job loss, job relocation, illness, disability, loss of income, the purchase of a home, or a tenant's death — Nebraska has no tenant-death termination statute at all. There is NO Texas-style requirement to print a statement of early-termination rights in the lease, and so no Texas-style forfeiture for leaving one out: Nebraska prescribes no lease forms and no mandatory lease statements. And there is NO general right for a tenant to buy out of a fixed-term lease. If you want to offer a buy-out, that is a contract term you write; section 76-1414(1) authorises "terms and conditions not prohibited by" the Act, and the early-termination clause in this library is where it belongs.

THE THING THAT CUTS BOTH WAYS, AND LANDLORDS LOSE ON IT MORE THAN TENANTS. Section 76-1433: "Acceptance of rent with knowledge of a default by tenant or acceptance of performance by the tenant that varies from the terms of the rental agreement or rules or regulations subsequently adopted by the landlord constitutes a WAIVER OF HIS RIGHT TO TERMINATE the rental agreement for that breach, UNLESS OTHERWISE AGREED AFTER THE BREACH HAS OCCURRED." Note where the contrary-agreement words sit: "after the breach has occurred". A reservation-of-rights sentence written into the lease in advance does not work; the agreement has to be made after the default. That is the one termination rule in this set the parties CAN vary, and only in that direction.

PRACTICAL COURSE. (1) When a tenant hands you a notice, identify the section before you respond — the cure window is fourteen days under section 76-1425(1) and nonexistent under sections 76-1426, 76-1429 and 76-1431.01. (2) Diary every section 76-1425(1) notice for six months; a repeat of substantially the same problem inside that window ends the lease on fourteen days with nothing you can do. (3) Do not charge a termination fee, apply a liquidated-damages clause or withhold a deposit against lost rent on a section 76-1431.01 release — subsection (4)(b) forbids "any fee solely because of termination". (4) Return prepaid rent and security promptly on any of these terminations; sections 76-1425(4), 76-1426(1), 76-1429(2) and 76-1430 each say so expressly, and the fourteen-day accounting clock in section 76-1416(2) runs from the date of termination whatever the ground.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule and No Mandatory Rider — But One Burn-Prevention Statute Does Reach Your Building, and It Is Not About Radiators
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS NO RADIATOR COVER LAW. There is no counterpart to New Jersey's rule requiring a landlord to install a steam radiator cover on a tenant's request and to attach a prescribed notice or rider to the lease. The word "radiator" does not appear in the Nebraska statute chapters that govern a tenancy, in any form, singular or plural, and neither does "radiator cover", "steam heat" or "steam pipe". There is nothing to disclose, nothing to attach to your lease, and no request a tenant can make that a statute obliges you to honour.

SO DO NOT COPY THE NEW JERSEY RIDER. A mandatory-rider clause lifted from a state that has one is worse than useless in Nebraska. It tells a tenant you will install a cover on request, which is a promise the law did not make you give and which you will be held to as a contract term, and it attaches a notice whose statutory references do not exist here.

WHAT YOUR ACTUAL DUTY IS, AND WHERE A RADIATOR SITS INSIDE IT. Section 76-1419(1)(d) requires you to "[m]aintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her". A steam or hot-water radiator is part of the heating facilities you supply, so you must keep it in GOOD AND SAFE WORKING ORDER. That is a condition-and-operation duty, not a shielding duty: a radiator that works, does not leak and does not have a broken valve satisfies subdivision (1)(d), and nothing in the subdivision says anything about covering a hot surface. Section 76-1419(1)(f) separately requires you to "[s]upply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat", with the two exceptions written into it. And the unnumbered sentence closing subsection (1) matters here more than anywhere: "If there exists a minimum housing code applicable to the premises, the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a) of this section." So where your city has a minimum housing code, the code is the CEILING on your section 76-1419 duty, not an addition to it — and a municipal code is the only place in Nebraska law where a radiator-guarding requirement could live. Check the ordinance for the city your property is in.

ONE DELEGATION LIMIT YOU CANNOT WORK AROUND. Section 76-1419(2) lets the landlord and tenant of a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE agree that the tenant perform the (1)(e) waste-removal and (1)(f) water-and-heat duties plus specified repairs, only in writing, for good consideration, in good faith and not to evade. Section 76-1419(3) reaches a unit "other than a single-family residence" and enumerates NOTHING: it covers only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling", in a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration. So in a duplex or an apartment you cannot shift the heating duty to the tenant at all, and you cannot write a clause making the tenant responsible for the condition or safety of the radiators as a class. You can ask a tenant to do a named repair; you cannot hand over the heating system.

THE BURN-PREVENTION STATUTE THAT DOES EXIST, AND IT IS A LEAD YOU SHOULD FOLLOW. Section 18-1920, inside the municipal plumbing-board article, is a scald-prevention cross-reference that reads in its entirety "Nothing in sections 18-1901 to 18-1919 shall be construed to exempt persons from compliance with sections 71-1569 to 71-1571." Sections 71-1569 to 71-1571 are captioned as scald prevention device requirements, and neither section was amended in the 2025 or 2026 sessions. What section 18-1920 does establish is that whatever those sections require, a municipal plumbing ordinance does not excuse you from it: the exemption-stripping sentence is the whole point of section 18-1920. TREAT THIS AS AN OPEN QUESTION AND A REAL ONE. If sections 71-1569 to 71-1571 impose an owner-side duty to fit a temperature-limiting or anti-scald device, that duty attaches to your plumbing whatever your city's ordinance says, and it is a closer analogue to the New Jersey radiator-cover rule than anything else in Nebraska law. Do not assume either way; get those three sections read before you tell a tenant there is no burn-prevention requirement in Nebraska.

WHAT YOU CAN AND SHOULD DO ANYWAY, AND WHY IT IS CHEAP. (1) Nothing stops you from fitting radiator covers. It is not required, it is not a disclosure, and it costs very little against a scald claim from a household with a small child — and note that your section 76-1419 duty is a FLOOR of condition and safety, so a guard you install becomes something you then have to maintain in safe condition under (1)(d) like any other facility you supplied. (2) If you fit covers, say in writing that they were installed voluntarily and that they are not to be removed, painted or obstructed; a tenant's duty under section 76-1421(1) to "[u]se ... all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances ... in a reasonable manner" supports that, and section 76-1422 lets you adopt a rule to the same effect provided — per section 76-1422(6) — "the tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement". (3) Do not write a clause in which the tenant accepts the radiators as-is, waives claims about them, or agrees they are safe. Section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act" and section 76-1415(1)(d) voids any term agreeing "to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence" or indemnifying the landlord for it — and section 76-1415(2) makes deliberate use of such a term actionable for the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. A radiator-safety waiver is exactly the clause that subdivision targets. (4) Remember the closing words of section 76-1419(1): "The obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state." Your statutory maintenance duty and your negligence exposure for a hot surface in a rented unit are separate questions.

title: Nebraska Has No Stigmatized-Property Statute — No Duty to Tell, No Immunity for Not Telling, and One Thing You Absolutely May Not Do
bodyText:
NEBRASKA IS IN THE WORST OF BOTH WORLDS ON STIGMATIZED PROPERTY, AND THAT IS THE POINT OF THIS ROW. It has no statute requiring you to tell a prospective tenant that someone died in the unit, that a homicide or suicide happened there, that it was a meth lab, or that a registered sex offender lives next door — AND it has no statute giving you immunity for staying silent. Many states have one or the other. Arizona has a disclosure-immunity provision; California requires death disclosure for a period; Mississippi requires a landlord who knows registry information to answer if asked. Nebraska has written NONE of these. The terms of art and the everyday words alike are absent: "psychologically impacted", "stigmatized", "death on the premises", "haunted", "paranormal" and "not a material fact" all appear ZERO times in the Nebraska statute chapters that govern a tenancy.

WHAT THAT ABSENCE ACTUALLY MEANS FOR YOU. A statutory immunity clause is what lets a landlord in some states say "the law says this is not a material fact and I need not mention it." You cannot say that in Nebraska. Whether a past event on the property is material is left to ordinary law — misrepresentation, concealment, and the deceptive-practices act — all of which are reached by what you SAY rather than by what you omit. So the safe operating rule is simple and it is the opposite of the rule in an immunity state: say nothing you do not know to be true, and answer a direct question honestly or decline to answer it at all. Never deny something you know.

THE ONE PRESCRIBED DISCLOSURE STATEMENT NEBRASKA HAS IS A SALE DOCUMENT, AND ITS CONTENTS LIST IS THE PROOF OF THE ABSENCE. Section 76-2,120(2) requires "[e]ach seller of residential real property located in Nebraska" to give the purchaser "a written disclosure statement of the real property's condition". Its mandatory contents at subsection (4) are: the condition of included appliances, the electrical system, the heating and cooling systems, the water system, the sewer system, all improvements "and any defects that materially affect the value", "[a]ny hazardous conditions, including substances, materials, and products ... which may be an environmental hazard", title conditions including encroachments, easements and zoning restrictions, whether utility connections are public, private or community, any private transfer fee obligation under section 76-3107, and "[i]nformation relating to compliance with the requirements for a carbon monoxide alarm as provided in sections 76-604 and 76-605". NOT ONE ITEM IS A DEATH, A CRIME, A SUICIDE, A STIGMA OR A NEIGHBOUR. A legislature that itemised eleven disclosure subjects down to a carbon monoxide alarm and a private transfer fee, and included no stigma item, has decided.

AND HERE IS WHY A LANDLORD SHOULD READ SECTION 76-2,120 ANYWAY: IF YOU DO A LEASE-OPTION, IT APPLIES TO YOU. Subsection (1)(d) defines "Seller" as "an owner of real property who sells or attempts to sell, INCLUDING LEASE WITH OPTION TO PURCHASE, residential real property", and subsection (2) says "[t]he requirements of this section shall also apply ... to any lease with the option to purchase residential real property." So a rent-to-own or lease-option arrangement on a one-to-four-unit residential property triggers the full written disclosure statement, executed by you, delivered with a written acknowledgment of receipt "on or before the effective date of any contract which binds the purchaser" (subsection (7)) — and section 76-2,120(12) gives a non-complying purchaser "actual damages, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees", with the printed annotations reporting that the fee award is MANDATORY for a successful plaintiff (Pepitone v. Winn, 272 Neb. 443 (2006); Nelson v. Wardyn, 19 Neb. App. 864 (2012)). The action must be brought "within one year after the purchaser takes possession or the conveyance of the real property, whichever occurs first". Subsection (8) limits you to what was "within the personal knowledge of the seller", and the annotations report that violations "must be done knowingly" (Burgess v. Miller, 9 Neb. App. 854 (2001)) — but the duty to produce the statement at all is not knowledge-dependent. If you offer lease-options, this is a real obligation that has nothing to do with stigma and is easy to miss because it lives in a seller-disclosure statute.

THE SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY: PUBLIC INFORMATION, NO DUTY EITHER WAY, AND NO SPECIAL ACCESS FOR YOU. Section 29-4009(1) provides that "[i]nformation obtained under the Sex Offender Registration Act shall not be confidential", except that a listed set of items goes to law enforcement only — the offender's social security number, arrests not resulting in conviction, travel and immigration documents, remote communication device identifiers, email and messaging identifiers, telephone numbers, driver's licence or state ID number, and "[t]he name of any employer of a sex offender". Section 29-4009(2) bars release of a victim's identity. So the registry is open to you as it is to anyone. Section 29-4013(4) then lists who gets access to PUBLIC NOTIFICATION information, and the list includes "any public housing agency in each area in which a registered sex offender resides or is an employee or a student" — a PUBLIC housing agency. A private landlord is not on that list. Put together: there is no Nebraska statute requiring you to disclose registry information to a tenant, none requiring you to answer if asked, none barring you from looking the information up, and none giving you a privileged channel to it. Mississippi's ask-and-you-must-answer rule has no Nebraska counterpart.

THE ONE ABSOLUTE PROHIBITION, AND IT IS A DIFFERENT KIND OF STIGMA. Section 20-168(2): "A seller or LESSOR shall not refuse to sell or lease a dwelling as defined in section 20-310 to an individual on the basis that the individual, A MEMBER OF THE INDIVIDUAL'S FAMILY, OR A PERSON WHO WILL BE RESIDING WITH THE INDIVIDUAL is suffering or IS SUSPECTED OF SUFFERING FROM human immunodeficiency virus infection or acquired immunodeficiency syndrome." Read every part of that. It names a LESSOR expressly. It reaches a household member or anyone who will reside with the applicant, not just the applicant. It reaches SUSPICION, so you do not need to be right to be liable. "Dwelling" under section 20-310 is "any building, structure, or portion thereof which is occupied as or designed or intended for occupancy as a residence for one or more families". And section 20-168(5) gives the individual a civil action "in the district court of the county where the discrimination is alleged to have occurred", a remedy "in addition to any other remedy provided by law". CRITICALLY, THIS SECTION SITS OUTSIDE THE NEBRASKA FAIR HOUSING ACT.
