Section 20-322's exemptions — the religious-organization exemption, the private-club exemption, the rooms-in-your-own-home exemption, the housing-for-older-persons rule — every one of them is framed as "[n]othing in the Nebraska Fair Housing Act shall prohibit" or "[n]othing in the act shall ...". Section 20-168 is not in that act. So the owner-occupied and small-landlord exemptions landlords rely on for fair-housing purposes DO NOT REACH SECTION 20-168. A landlord renting rooms in their own home may refuse a tenant "for any reason or for no reason" under section 20-322(3) — but not for this reason.

SO THE PRACTICAL SHAPE OF THE TOPIC. There is nothing you must disclose about a property's history, and nothing protecting you if you lie about it. There is nothing you must disclose about a neighbour, and no bar on researching one. And there is one health condition about which you may not make a letting decision at all, under a statute that no landlord exemption touches.

PRACTICAL COURSE. (1) Do not write a stigmatized-property clause into the lease. There is no statute to reference, and a clause saying the tenant "accepts the premises without regard to its history" or "waives any claim based on prior events" is a waiver clause: section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act" and section 76-1415(2) makes deliberate use of a prohibited term actionable for the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. (2) Decide your policy on direct questions BEFORE you are asked, and apply it uniformly. "I don't discuss the history of the property" applied to everyone is defensible; applied selectively it becomes a fair-housing problem and a credibility problem at once. (3) Never state a fact about a property's history you have not verified, in the lease, in a listing or in conversation: section 87-302(a)(5) reaches representing that goods or services have "characteristics, ingredients, uses, benefits, or quantities that they do not have" and section 87-303.07 makes a lease induced by a section 87-302 violation "unenforceable by the seller or lessor" with a right to rescind — so a reassuring untruth converts a marketing question into a possession question. (4) Never ask about, record, or act on an applicant's or a household member's HIV status, and train anyone who shows units for you that section 20-168(2) reaches suspicion, household members and co-residents, and that no landlord exemption applies to it. (5) If you ever offer a lease-option, prepare the section 76-2,120 disclosure statement and get the signed acknowledgment; the attorney-fee award for failing is mandatory.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator — But Those Two Words Decide Whether Your Notice Period Is Seven Days or Thirty
bodyText:
NEBRASKA DOES NOT REQUIRE YOU TO SUPPLY A STOVE OR A REFRIGERATOR. California requires both in a residential rental and gives the tenant remedies if they are missing. Nebraska has no counterpart. In the Nebraska statute chapters that govern a tenancy, the word "refrigerator" appears in exactly ONE section, and "stove" in four, of which three are a biomass stove in a renewable-energy definition, a 1935 case name and an 1883 annotation about a stove bought by a wife. The one section that matters is a DEFINITION, and it does not require anything.

AND THIS IS THE CLASSIC TRAP, SO READ THE DEFINITION WITH THE JOB IT DOES. Section 76-1410(15): "Roomer means a person occupying a dwelling unit that lacks a major bathroom or kitchen facility, in a structure where one or more major facilities are used in common by occupants of the dwelling units. Major facility in the case of a bathroom means toilet, or either a bath or shower, and in the case of a kitchen means REFRIGERATOR, STOVE, OR SINK." Those three words are not a list of what you must install. They are the test for whether an occupant is a ROOMER. A unit missing any one of a refrigerator, a stove or a sink, in a structure where such a facility is shared, makes its occupant a roomer. Nothing in the subdivision says a landlord must provide any of the three, and nothing elsewhere in the Act says so either.

WHAT ROOMER STATUS ACTUALLY DOES, AND IT IS WORTH REAL MONEY TO KNOW. The word "roomer" appears in only two sections of chapter 76: the definition itself, and section 76-1414(4), which reads in full: "Unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy shall be WEEK TO WEEK in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent, and in all other cases MONTH TO MONTH." That is the whole consequence of roomer status in the Act. And it feeds straight into the termination notice: section 76-1437(1) lets either party end a week-to-week tenancy "by a written notice given to the other at least SEVEN DAYS prior to the termination date specified in the notice", while section 76-1437(2) requires "at least THIRTY DAYS prior to the periodic rental date" for a month-to-month tenancy. So in a rooming house or a shared-kitchen building, whether a unit has a stove or a refrigerator in it can be the difference between a seven-day notice and a thirty-day notice — provided the occupant pays WEEKLY and the rental agreement fixes NO DEFINITE TERM. Both conditions are in the subsection and both are necessary. If you fix a term in the lease, or take monthly rent, section 76-1414(4) does not deliver the week-to-week tenancy however the kitchen is equipped.

THE OTHER SIDE OF THAT COIN: INSTALLING APPLIANCES IN A SHARED-FACILITY BUILDING CAN COST YOU THE SHORT NOTICE. A landlord who adds a compact refrigerator and a hotplate to each room in a building with a common kitchen may be taking those occupants out of the roomer definition and into a month-to-month default. That is a decision to make deliberately, not a convenience to add thoughtlessly. (The reading is the subdivision's own: a roomer is someone occupying a unit "that LACKS a major bathroom or kitchen facility" in a structure where such facilities "are used in common". Both limbs have to hold.)

ONCE YOU DO SUPPLY ONE, YOU OWN ITS CONDITION. Section 76-1419(1)(d) requires you to "[m]aintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her". The four words "or required to be supplied" are the second route in: an appliance can be caught either because you actually supplied it or because something else requires you to. The two candidates are your own lease — remember that section 76-1410(14) defines "[r]ental agreement" as "ALL AGREEMENTS, WRITTEN OR ORAL", so a verbal promise at the showing to put a fridge in counts — and a municipal minimum housing code, which is where any local requirement to equip a kitchen would live. On the code point, note the unnumbered sentence closing section 76-1419(1): "If there exists a minimum housing code applicable to the premises, the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a) of this section." The code is the CEILING on your statutory duty, not an addition to it — but it can also be the thing that makes an appliance "required to be supplied" in the first place. Check the ordinance where your property sits.

THE DELEGATION LIMIT, BECAUSE THE OBVIOUS WORKAROUND DOES NOT WORK IN AN APARTMENT. Section 76-1419(2) lets the landlord and tenant of a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE agree in writing, for good consideration, in good faith and not to evade, that the tenant perform the (1)(e) and (1)(f) duties plus specified repairs. Section 76-1419(3) covers "a dwelling unit other than a single-family residence" and reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" in a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration. Neither lets you hand over the (1)(d) duty for appliances as a class. You can agree that the tenant will do a named repair to a named appliance. You cannot write "tenant is responsible for all appliances" in an apartment lease and have it bind.

SO WHERE DOES THAT LEAVE THE LEASE? Say what is included and say it precisely, in the appliances clause this library already provides, and do not say more than you mean. Three drafting rules follow from the sections above. (1) LIST WHAT IS SUPPLIED, BY NAME. Ambiguity is resolved against you by section 76-1419(1)(d)'s "required to be supplied" limb once anything was promised. (2) IF AN APPLIANCE IS THE TENANT'S OWN OR IS LEFT AS A CONVENIENCE, SAY SO AND SAY WHO MAINTAINS IT — but do not kid yourself that calling a working range you left in the unit a "convenience" removes it from (1)(d) if the tenant is relying on it as the kitchen's only cooking facility. (3) DO NOT WRITE A WAIVER. A clause in which the tenant accepts the appliances "as is", waives claims about them, or releases you from maintaining them runs into section 76-1415(1)(a), which voids any term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act", and section 76-1415(1)(d), which voids any term agreeing "to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence" or indemnifying the landlord for it. Section 76-1415(2) prices the deliberate use of such a term at the tenant's actual damages plus reasonable attorney's fees.

AND THE REMEDY A TENANT GETS IF A SUPPLIED APPLIANCE FAILS, SO YOU KNOW THE STAKES. A broken refrigerator or stove you supplied is a section 76-1419(1)(d) noncompliance, which routes to section 76-1425: a written notice, fourteen days to cure, termination no sooner than thirty days after RECEIPT, plus damages and injunctive relief under section 76-1425(2) and reasonable attorney's fees if the noncompliance is willful — and a repeat of substantially the same failure within six months lets the tenant terminate on fourteen days' notice with NO cure right. Note what the tenant does NOT get: there is no general repair-and-deduct in Nebraska. Section 76-1427(1)(a) lets a tenant procure and deduct only for "running water, hot water, or heat, or essential services", and a stove or refrigerator is not named there. So the tenant's route is notice, damages and termination, not self-help repair billed to you.

title: No Student-Housing Licence, Certification or Special Regime — Renting to Students Is Just Renting, With Two Exclusions That Are Not Yours
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS NO STUDENT-HOUSING STATUTE OF ANY KIND. There is no certification scheme of the Puerto Rico sort, no student-housing licence, no registration of properties let to students, no special deposit, lease-form or disclosure rule for a student tenancy, and no cap on what a student may be charged or required to sign. In the Nebraska statute chapters that govern a tenancy, "student housing", "dormitory", "fraternity", "sorority" and "rooming house" each appear ZERO times, and "boarding house" appears once — in an 1891 annotation to a debtor's-exemptions section about what counts as the necessaries of life.

SO THE OPERATIVE RULE IS THE PLAIN ONE, AND IT IS THE ONE LANDLORDS LETTING TO STUDENTS MOST OFTEN GET WRONG: YOUR STUDENT TENANCY IS AN ORDINARY RESIDENTIAL TENANCY AND THE UNIFORM RESIDENTIAL LANDLORD AND TENANT ACT APPLIES TO IT IN FULL. A nine-month lease to four undergraduates in a house off campus is governed by the same Act, the same one-month deposit cap in section 76-1416(1), the same fourteen-day deposit accounting in section 76-1416(2), the same habitability duties in section 76-1419, the same entry rules in section 76-1423 and the same prohibited-terms list in section 76-1415 as a lease to anybody else. Nothing about a tenant being a student changes any of it.

THERE ARE TWO EXCLUSIONS IN THE ACT THAT TOUCH STUDENT LIVING, AND NEITHER OF THEM IS AVAILABLE TO A PRIVATE LANDLORD. Section 76-1408 lists eight arrangements "not governed by the act". Two are relevant here. Subdivision (1): "Residence at an institution, public or private, if incidental to detention or the provision of medical, geriatric, EDUCATIONAL, counseling, religious, or similar service." That is the university residence hall — residence AT AN INSTITUTION, incidental to the provision of educational service. Subdivision (3): "Occupancy by a member of a FRATERNAL OR SOCIAL ORGANIZATION in the portion of a structure operated for the benefit of the organization." That is the chapter house. Neither reaches a commercial landlord renting a house or an apartment to students, however close to campus and however student-only the building is: you are not an institution providing educational service, and your tenants are not occupying a structure operated for the benefit of a fraternal organization.

AND READ THE WORDS THAT OPEN SECTION 76-1408, BECAUSE THEY ARE THE ANTI-AVOIDANCE RULE: "UNLESS CREATED TO AVOID THE APPLICATION of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the following arrangements are not governed by the act". So an arrangement dressed up to fit one of the eight — a "licence to occupy", an "educational housing agreement", a nominal affiliation with a club or society — fails if its purpose was to escape the Act. Do not build a structure around subdivision (1) or (3) and expect it to hold.

ONE OTHER EXCLUSION WORTH KNOWING ABOUT IN A STUDENT CONTEXT, BECAUSE IT CUTS THE OTHER WAY. Section 76-1408(8) excludes "[a] lease of improved or unimproved residential land for a term of FIVE YEARS OR MORE". A long ground lease is outside the Act. That is a separate subject and this library carries it elsewhere.

WHAT ACTUALLY REGULATES STUDENT RENTALS IN NEBRASKA IS MUNICIPAL, AND THE STATUTE SAYS SO IN ONE SENTENCE. Section 20-322(4)(a) provides that "[n]othing in the act shall limit the applicability of ANY REASONABLE LOCAL RESTRICTIONS REGARDING THE MAXIMUM NUMBER OF OCCUPANTS PERMITTED TO OCCUPY A DWELLING, and nothing in the act regarding familial status shall apply with respect to housing for older persons." That first clause is the whole student-housing law of Nebraska in practice. Occupancy caps — the unrelated-persons limits that decide whether you may let a three-bedroom house to four or five students — are a CITY ordinance question, and the Nebraska Fair Housing Act expressly declines to disturb a reasonable one. Before you sign a group lease, check the occupancy ordinance and the zoning for the address. No state statute answers it.

THERE IS EXACTLY ONE NEBRASKA PROVISION THAT USES THE WORDS "STUDENT HOUSING", AND IT IS A TAX EXEMPTION YOU ALMOST CERTAINLY CANNOT USE. Section 77-202(1)(d)(iv) exempts from property taxes "a building that (A) is owned by a CHARITABLE ORGANIZATION, (B) is made available to students in attendance at an educational institution, and (C) is recognized by such educational institution as approved student housing, EXCEPT THAT THE EXEMPTION SHALL ONLY APPLY TO THE COMMONS AREA of such building, including any common rooms and cooking and eating facilities". Three conditions, all cumulative, and the first is the gate: the owner must be a charitable organization. A for-profit landlord gets nothing from this subdivision however close to campus the building is and however formally the university "approves" it. And even for a qualifying charitable owner the exemption is confined to the COMMONS AREA — the bedrooms stay taxable. If you are a nonprofit or a church letting approved student housing, this is worth an application; if you are an ordinary landlord, it is worth knowing only so that you do not expect a student-housing tax break that does not exist. (A separate 2026 provision defines "[h]otel" for the human-trafficking poster scheme so as to EXCLUDE "dormitories or facilities operated by an educational institution and regularly used to house students", which is another carve-out for institutions rather than anything for a landlord.)

THE TRAP IN A STUDENT LEASE IS ALMOST ALWAYS THE SAME ONE: JOINT AND SEVERAL LIABILITY AND CO-SIGNERS, NOT A STUDENT-SPECIFIC RULE. A few points follow from the sections above rather than from anything about students. (1) A GROUP LEASE WORKS, AND SECTION 76-1414(1) IS THE AUTHORITY: "The landlord and tenant may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law including rent, term of the agreement, and other provisions governing the rights and obligations of the parties." Joint and several liability among co-tenants is such a term and this library provides the clause. (2) BUT THE PARTS OF THE ACT THAT RUN TO THE TENANT RUN TO EVERY TENANT. Each co-tenant is a "tenant" within section 76-1410(17) — "a person entitled under a rental agreement to occupy a dwelling unit to the exclusion of others" — so each has the full remedy set, and one co-tenant's section 76-1425(1) notice can start the clock on the whole lease. (3) AN AGE-BASED REASSURANCE AND AN AGE-BASED CAUTION: Nebraska's age of majority is NINETEEN, not eighteen, but that does not make an eighteen-year-old's lease voidable — a person eighteen or older who is not a ward of the state may "[e]nter into a binding contract or lease of whatever kind or nature and shall be legally responsible for such contract or lease, including legal responsibility to third parties." Whether a person UNDER eighteen can be bound is a different question; the cautious course for a seventeen-year-old freshman is a co-signing adult. (4) DO NOT WRITE A WAIVER INTO A STUDENT LEASE THINKING STUDENTS WILL NOT ENFORCE IT. Section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies" under the Act; section 76-1415(1)(c) voids a term agreeing "to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees"; section 76-1415(1)(d) voids exculpation and indemnity for the landlord's active and actionable negligence; and section 76-1415(2) makes DELIBERATE use of a prohibited term actionable for the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. Student-let leases are exactly the population where university legal clinics and tenant advocates read the lease afterwards.

AND THE ONE THING YOU MAY NOT DO WITH A STUDENT POPULATION: discriminate on a protected basis. The protected classes under Nebraska law and the municipal exceptions are a separate subject carried by this library's fair-housing row and are not restated here. Two specific cautions, though, because they arise constantly in student letting and both have a Nebraska statute behind them. FAMILIAL STATUS is protected under the Nebraska Fair Housing Act, so a "no children" or "students only" policy expressed as an exclusion of families is a fair-housing problem even though an occupancy cap is not (section 20-322(4)(a) protects the CAP, not a family exclusion). And section 20-168(2) bars a "seller or lessor" from refusing to lease a dwelling because an applicant, a family member or a co-resident "is suffering or is suspected of suffering from" HIV or AIDS — and that section sits OUTSIDE the Fair Housing Act, so none of section 20-322's exemptions reach it, including the rooms-in-your-own-home exemption at section 20-322(3) that a landlord letting rooms to students might otherwise rely on. Note the limit on that exemption anyway: it "shall not apply to any person who makes available for rental or occupancy MORE THAN FOUR SLEEPING ROOMS to a person or family within his or her own home."

title: No Nebraska Statute on Subsidy-Program Inspections — Your Obligation Is Contractual, and the Access You Need Comes From One Limb of Section 76-1423(1)
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS NO STATUTE ABOUT SUBSIDY-PROGRAM INSPECTIONS AT ALL. There is no Illinois-style provision about a landlord refusing an inspection of an assisted unit, no statutory consequence for a failed inspection, no statutory right of entry for a housing authority inspector, and no statutory duty on you to permit one. The decisive words are simply not in the statutes: in the Nebraska statute chapters that govern a tenancy, "housing assistance payment", "housing choice voucher" and "rental assistance" each appear ZERO times, and the only two sections containing the phrase "housing agency" are a sex-offender-registry access list and the security-deposit section.

SO WHAT GOVERNS YOU IS CONTRACT AND PROGRAM RULE, NOT NEBRASKA LAW. If you take a voucher or any other assisted tenancy, your obligation to admit the inspector comes from the housing assistance payments contract you signed with the housing authority and from the federal program rules behind it. The consequence of refusing an inspection — abatement of the assistance payment, termination of the contract, removal from the programme — is a contract and programme consequence. The point of the row is the opposite: do not go looking for a Nebraska statute, because there is none, and do not assume state law gives you cover for a refusal or gives the inspector a right of entry.

THE PRACTICAL PROBLEM IS REAL THOUGH, AND IT IS AN ACCESS PROBLEM. The inspector is not a party to your lease. You cannot simply hand over a key, and you cannot let a stranger into an occupied unit because a third party asked you to. What you can do rests on section 76-1423(1): "The tenant shall not unreasonably withhold consent to the landlord TO ENTER into the dwelling unit IN ORDER TO INSPECT THE PREMISES, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, WORKMEN, OR CONTRACTORS." An inspection required to keep the tenancy's funding in place is an inspection of the premises, and a programme inspector accompanying you fits the workmen-or-contractors limb comfortably. But note the architecture: the right is YOURS to enter and the tenant's duty is not to withhold consent unreasonably — it is not a right of the inspector, and it is not an entitlement to enter over an objection.

AND THE NOTICE REQUIREMENT IS NOT OPTIONAL, WHICH IS WHERE SUBSIDY INSPECTIONS GO WRONG. Section 76-1423(3): "Except in case of emergency or if it is impracticable to do so, the landlord shall: (a) Give the tenant at least TWENTY-FOUR HOURS' WRITTEN NOTICE of the landlord's intent to enter. SUCH NOTICE SHALL BE PROVIDED TO EACH INDIVIDUAL UNIT AND INCLUDE THE INTENDED PURPOSE FOR ENTRY AND A REASONABLE PERIOD DURING WHICH THE LANDLORD ANTICIPATES MAKING ENTRY; and (b) Enter only at reasonable times." Four separate requirements: twenty-four hours, IN WRITING, to EACH INDIVIDUAL UNIT, stating the PURPOSE and a reasonable ANTICIPATED WINDOW. A housing authority's inspection appointment letter addressed to the tenant is not your notice. And the clock is yours to manage: if the authority gives you three days' warning for a building-wide inspection, your written notices to every affected unit must still go out at least twenty-four hours ahead with the purpose and the window stated.

WHAT IT COSTS TO GET THIS WRONG, AND IT IS A FLOOR NOT A CEILING. Section 76-1423(4): "The landlord has NO OTHER RIGHT OF ACCESS except by court order, as permitted by subsection (2) of section 76-1432, or if the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises." That list is exhaustive — a subsidy contract is not on it. And section 76-1438(2) prices an unlawful entry, a lawful entry made in an unreasonable manner, or "repeated demands for entry otherwise lawful but which have the effect of unreasonably harassing the tenant" at "actual damages NOT LESS THAN an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees", with termination or an injunction as the tenant's alternative. One month's rent is the minimum. Letting an inspector in without notice, or pressing a tenant repeatedly because the authority is pressing you, is the fact pattern that subsection was written for.

THE OTHER DIRECTION: IF THE TENANT REFUSES. Section 76-1438(1) gives you, where "the tenant refuses to allow lawful access", injunctive relief to compel access or the right to terminate the rental agreement, plus actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. Note how thin that is compared with the tenant's remedy: no multiplier, no floor, only what you can prove. And your access has to have been LAWFUL — which means you gave the section 76-1423(3) notice in the form that subsection requires. A refusal of an inspection you never properly noticed is not a refusal of lawful access.

DO NOT TRY TO FIX THIS WITH A LEASE CLAUSE THAT GOES FURTHER THAN THE STATUTE. A clause in which the tenant "consents in advance to all inspections by any government or housing agency", or "waives notice for subsidy inspections", or "agrees that refusal of an inspection is a material breach", runs straight into section 76-1415(1)(a), which voids any rental agreement term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act" — and the twenty-four-hour written notice with its two mandatory contents is such a right. Section 76-1415(2) then makes DELIBERATE use of a prohibited term actionable for the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. Also note that section 76-1423 is NOT among the eleven chapter-76 sections that open "unless otherwise agreed", so there is no contrary-agreement route into it.

WHAT THE LEGISLATURE DID WRITE ABOUT INSPECTING ASSISTED HOUSING, AND WHO IT BINDS. The 2026 session legislated inspections of subsidized housing — but only where the landlord IS the public housing agency, and only in Omaha. Section 14-102(40), as amended by Laws 2026, LB1114, empowers a city of the metropolitan class to regulate a housing agency with respect to "[p]roviding for code enforcement for all properties owned and controlled by such housing agency", "[p]roviding for complaint-based inspections of all properties managed by such housing agency", "[r]equiring all properties managed by such housing agency to be registered pursuant to any rental registration ordinance adopted by such city", "[s]etting penalties for code violations and failure to properly manage properties", and monthly reports to the city council including "complaint information on pest control issues and any mitigation efforts". The same act rewrote the metropolitan-class housing agency's resident complaint process at section 71-15,169 — an online, telephone or in-person complaint form, a five-business-day acknowledgment, a unique case number, "a thorough investigation ... including ... inspecting property", resolution within fourteen days, and written notice of the outcome within five business days — and added an annual report to the Legislature's Urban Affairs Committee covering pest control activities, eviction filings, complaints and occupancy. THAT IS THE SIBLING-ACT CONTRAST AND IT IS A STRONG ONE: in 2026 Nebraska wrote a code-enforcement, complaint-inspection, registration, penalty and reporting regime for subsidized housing, and every word of it is addressed to a public housing agency and to the city that oversees it. Nothing in it reaches a private landlord with a subsidized tenant. The silence as to you is a demonstrated choice made in the most recent session.

PRACTICAL COURSE. (1) Treat every programme inspection as your own entry and paper it as such: a written notice to each affected unit, at least twenty-four hours out, naming the purpose ("annual housing quality inspection by [authority]") and the window. Keep the copies; the section 76-1438(2) floor makes this the cheapest file in your office. (2) Never let an inspector in on the authority's notice alone. (3) If a tenant refuses, do not force it — reschedule once with fresh written notice, tell the authority in writing that access was refused after proper notice, and only then consider section 76-1438(1) relief. (4) Do not put an advance-consent or notice-waiver clause in the lease. Put a plain sentence saying you will give the notice section 76-1423(3) requires and that inspections may be required under any assistance contract; that is accurate, it is not a waiver, and it sets the expectation.

title: No Rule for Splitting a Rent Abatement Between the Tenant's Share and the Subsidy — and One Definition That Leaves the Question Genuinely Open
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS NO SUBSIDY-PRORATION RULE. Colorado tells a landlord how a habitability reduction is apportioned where part of the rent is paid by a housing programme. Nebraska says nothing. There is no statute allocating an abatement between the tenant's portion and the assistance payment, no statute saying the tenant's reduction is limited to the tenant's share, and no statute saying it is not. The vocabulary is absent from the statutes entirely: "housing assistance payment", "housing choice voucher" and "rental assistance" each appear ZERO times in the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy, and the only two sections in those chapters containing "housing agency" are a sex-offender-registry access list and the security-deposit section.

WHAT NEBRASKA DOES HAVE IS THREE RENT-REDUCTION MECHANISMS, NONE OF WHICH MENTIONS A SUBSIDY. (1) Section 76-1426: where you fail to deliver possession, "rent ABATES until possession is delivered". (2) Section 76-1427(1)(b): where you "deliberately or negligently" fail to supply running water, hot water, heat or essential services, the tenant may "[r]ecover damages based upon THE DIMINUTION IN THE FAIR RENTAL VALUE of the dwelling unit" — and under (1)(c) may instead procure substitute housing, "in which case the tenant is excused from paying rent for the period of the landlord's noncompliance." (3) Section 76-1429(1)(b): after fire or casualty, a tenant who vacates the unusable part has "liability for rent ... REDUCED IN PROPORTION TO THE DIMINUTION IN THE FAIR RENTAL VALUE of the dwelling unit." Each of the three is written in terms of the whole unit's rent or its whole fair rental value. Not one of them distinguishes a tenant's contribution from a third party's.

AND HERE IS THE OPEN QUESTION, STATED RATHER THAN RESOLVED, BECAUSE THE TEXT CANNOT SETTLE IT. Section 76-1410(13) defines rent as "all payments to be made to the landlord UNDER THE RENTAL AGREEMENT", and section 76-1410(14) defines "[r]ental agreement" as "all agreements, written or oral, BETWEEN A LANDLORD AND TENANT". TWO READINGS FOLLOW AND BOTH ARE AVAILABLE ON THE WORDS. READING ONE — THE WHOLE CONTRACT RENT IS "RENT". The lease you sign with an assisted tenant states the total rent for the unit; those are payments to be made to the landlord under that agreement, whoever actually writes the cheque, so a reduction "in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value" bites on the whole figure and the tenant's claim is measured against the whole. READING TWO — ONLY THE TENANT'S PORTION IS "RENT" AS BETWEEN YOU AND THE TENANT. The assistance payment is made to you under the housing assistance payments contract with the authority, which is not an agreement "between a landlord and tenant", so it falls outside section 76-1410(14) and therefore outside section 76-1410(13); on that reading the tenant's abatement is confined to what the tenant pays and the authority's remedy, if any, lives in the authority's own contract. NOTHING IN THE NEBRASKA STATUTES CHOOSES BETWEEN THESE, and no annotation printed with any of the three sections addresses it. This row does not pick a side, and you should be suspicious of anyone who does without a citation.

WHY THE DIFFERENCE IS LARGE AND NOT ACADEMIC. On a unit with a 900-dollar contract rent where the tenant pays 150, a one-month total abatement is worth 900 under reading one and 150 under reading two. The gap is the subsidy, every month, for as long as the condition lasts.

THE CAUTIOUS COURSE, WHICH DOES NOT DEPEND ON WHICH READING IS RIGHT. (1) FIX THE CONDITION. Every one of these mechanisms is triggered by your noncompliance and every one of them stops when the noncompliance stops. Section 76-1427's remedies run only "during the period of the landlord's noncompliance". (2) DO NOT SELF-HELP THE SUBSIDY. Do not reduce, refuse or return the assistance payment on your own view of the proration, and do not reduce the tenant's portion as a gesture that you have settled the question. Tell the housing authority in writing what the condition is and what you are doing about it, and let the authority apply its own contract. For a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, the federal rule is 24 C.F.R. § 982.404 (for HAP contracts signed or renewed after June 6, 2024). Once the authority notifies you in writing of a deficiency, it may withhold the payment. If you do not repair within 24 hours (life-threatening) or 30 days (other), it "must abate the HAP". If you repair within 60 days of the abatement notice, payments restart, but "[t]he PHA does not make any payments to the owner for the period of time that the payments were abated." You "may not terminate the tenancy of any family due to the withholding or abatement". And under § 982.310(b)(1), "[t]he family is not responsible for payment of the portion of the rent to owner covered by the housing assistance payment." So you cannot bill the tenant for an abated subsidy. Those rules govern the subsidy. They do not say how a Nebraska court measures the tenant's own claim, which is the open question above. (3) ASSUME THE LARGER NUMBER WHEN YOU PRICE THE RISK. Reading one is the more natural reading of "all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement" where your lease states a single contract rent, and planning on the smaller number is the way to be surprised. (4) DO NOT WRITE A PRORATION CLAUSE. A clause providing that "any rent abatement shall be limited to the Tenant's portion" or that "Tenant waives any claim to abatement of the housing assistance payment" is a term by which the tenant agrees to forego a remedy under the Act, which section 76-1415(1)(a) makes unenforceable, and section 76-1415(2) makes DELIBERATE use of a prohibited term actionable for the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. Note also that none of sections 76-1426, 76-1427 or 76-1429 is among the eleven chapter-76 sections that open "unless otherwise agreed", so there is no contrary-agreement route into any of them. (5) AND REMEMBER WHAT NEBRASKA DOES NOT GIVE THE TENANT: there is no general repair-and-deduct right here. Section 76-1427(1)(a) is the only procure-and-deduct-from-rent right in chapter 76 and it is confined to "hot water, running water, heat and essential services". A tenant in an assisted unit cannot lawfully fix a non-essential defect and dock the rent, whichever portion of it they pay.

THE ONE PLACE NEBRASKA LAW NOTICES ASSISTED HOUSING AT ALL, FOR COMPLETENESS. Section 76-1416(1) caps security at one month's periodic rent "but this subsection shall not be applicable to housing agencies organized or existing under the Nebraska Housing Agency Act" — a carve-out for the agency AS LANDLORD, not for a private landlord with an assisted tenant. That single clause is the whole of the Act's acknowledgment that subsidised housing exists, which is itself the measure of how little the legislature has said about it.

title: No Rule About Late Fees When the Subsidy Pays Late — Nebraska Caps No Residential Late Fee at All, So the Only Limits Are the Ones in Your Own Lease
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS NO SUBSIDY LATE-FEE RULE, AND IT HAS NO RESIDENTIAL LATE-FEE RULE EITHER. Colorado, Massachusetts and Connecticut each have something to say about late charges where a housing programme pays part of the rent — whether a fee may be charged at all, whether the tenant may be charged for the agency's delay, how long the grace period runs. Nebraska says nothing about any of it. The subsidy vocabulary is absent from the statutes entirely: "housing assistance payment", "housing choice voucher" and "rental assistance" each appear ZERO times in the Nebraska statute chapters that govern a tenancy. And separately, the words "late fee" and "late charge" appear in only four chapter-76 sections — the condominium assessment lien, the Self-Service Storage Act and the two time-share sections — and NOT ONE of them is in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (sections 76-1401 to 76-1449) or in the Mobile Home Act (sections 76-1450 to 76-14,111). There is no cap, no maximum percentage, no mandatory grace period and no prohibition.

SO THE WHOLE QUESTION IS ANSWERED BY YOUR OWN LEASE, WHICH MAKES THE DRAFTING DECISIVE. Section 76-1414(1) is the authority: "The landlord and tenant may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law including rent, term of the agreement, and other provisions governing the rights and obligations of the parties." A late fee is such a term. Whether a tenant owes one when the housing authority pays late therefore depends entirely on what your lease says the tenant has to pay and when.

AND THAT IS WHERE ALMOST EVERY ASSISTED-TENANCY LATE-FEE DISPUTE ACTUALLY TURNS. Ask one question of your own lease: does it obligate the tenant to pay THE WHOLE CONTRACT RENT, or only THE TENANT'S PORTION? If the lease says the tenant pays a stated tenant portion by the first, then a late assistance payment is not the tenant's default at all and a late fee charged to the tenant for it has no contractual basis — you are charging the tenant for somebody else's lateness. If the lease makes the tenant liable for the full contract rent with the subsidy merely credited against it, you have drafted a lease under which a late subsidy IS the tenant's default. Decide which you meant. A fee charged with no contractual basis is not merely uncollectible: it is money demanded under the rental agreement that is not owed under it, and the deliberate use of a term or a practice you know to be unsupported is the fact pattern section 76-1415(2) and the deceptive-practices sections below are aimed at.

THE LEGISLATURE'S OWN VIEW OF A FAIR LATE FEE EXISTS IN NEBRASKA LAW — JUST NOT FOR LEASES — AND IT IS THE BEST DRAFTING BENCHMARK YOU HAVE. Section 69-2110(1)(d), in the Rental-Purchase Agreement Act, allows a lessor to contract for and receive "[l]ate fees as follows: (i) For consumer rental purchase agreements with monthly renewal dates, a late fee of NOT MORE THAN FIVE DOLLARS may be assessed on any payment NOT MADE WITHIN FIVE BUSINESS DAYS after the payment is due; (ii) For ... more frequent than monthly renewal dates, a late fee of NOT MORE THAN THREE DOLLARS ... not made within THREE BUSINESS DAYS after payment is due; and (iii) A late fee ... MAY BE COLLECTED ONLY ONCE ON ANY ACCRUED PAYMENT no matter how long such payment remains unpaid, may be collected at the time it accrues or at any time thereafter, and SHALL NOT BE ASSESSED AGAINST A PAYMENT THAT IS TIMELY MADE EVEN THOUGH AN EARLIER LATE FEE HAS NOT BEEN PAID IN FULL." That Act governs rent-to-own of goods and not a dwelling, so none of those figures binds you. But subdivision (iii) states a principle that transfers exactly to an assisted tenancy and that landlords breach constantly: A LATE FEE MAY NOT BE ASSESSED AGAINST A PAYMENT THAT WAS TIMELY MADE JUST BECAUSE AN EARLIER FEE IS STILL OUTSTANDING. In a voucher tenancy where the tenant pays 150 on the first every month and the authority is occasionally late, applying each month's tenant payment to an old late-fee balance and then calling the tenant's rent late is exactly what subdivision (iii) forbids in the Act where the legislature had to choose. Nothing requires you to follow it; everything about how it reads suggests a court asked what is reasonable would not be impressed by the opposite practice.

THE ORDER YOU APPLY PAYMENTS IN IS THEREFORE THE REAL CONTROL, AND IT HAS TO BE IN THE LEASE. Nebraska has no statutory application-of-payments rule for residential rent. If your lease is silent, you have no stated authority to apply the tenant's rent to fees first, and doing so manufactures a rent default out of a fee dispute. This library has an application-of-payments clause; use it, and in an assisted tenancy consider stating plainly that the tenant's portion is applied to the tenant's portion of rent first.

THE TRAP THAT CATCHES LANDLORDS WITH LATE SUBSIDIES MORE THAN ANY OTHER: ACCEPTING THE MONEY. Section 76-1433: "Acceptance of rent with knowledge of a default by tenant or acceptance of performance by the tenant that varies from the terms of the rental agreement or rules or regulations subsequently adopted by the landlord constitutes a WAIVER OF HIS RIGHT TO TERMINATE the rental agreement for that breach, UNLESS OTHERWISE AGREED AFTER THE BREACH HAS OCCURRED." Read where those saving words sit — "after the breach has occurred". A reservation-of-rights sentence printed in the lease in advance does not do the job; the agreement has to be made after the default. And a further point that runs hard against the landlord in assisted tenancies: SECTION 76-1433 SAYS NOTHING ABOUT WHO TENDERED THE RENT. It turns on your acceptance with knowledge of the default. A payment from the housing authority, from a charity, from a rent-assistance fund or from a relative waives the termination as readily as a payment from the tenant. If you are terminating for nonpayment and a cheque arrives from anywhere, you have a decision to make before you bank it.

AND THE SEPARATE EXPOSURE FOR HOW YOU DESCRIBE FEES, WHICH IS LARGER THAN THE FEE. Section 87-302(a)(10) reaches advertising a price "in any manner calculated or tending to mislead" and (a)(12) reaches "false or misleading statements of fact concerning the reasons for, existence of, or amounts of price reductions"; section 87-303.07 provides that where a lessee "is induced by a violation of section 87-302 ... to enter into a sale or lease, the agreement is unenforceable by the seller or lessor" with a right to rescind. So misdescribing what the tenant will actually owe each month — quoting a tenant portion and then charging fees that make the real monthly figure higher — converts a fee problem into a possession problem.

PRACTICAL COURSE. (1) Read your own assisted-tenancy lease and make it say which rent the tenant owes. (2) Do not charge the tenant a late fee for the authority's lateness; pursue the authority under the assistance contract instead. (3) State a grace period and a flat fee you can defend, state that the fee is charged once per late payment, and state that a timely payment is never treated as late because a fee is outstanding — the three limits the legislature itself wrote in section 69-2110(1)(d). (4) Put the application-of-payments order in writing. (5) Before you bank any payment on a tenancy you are terminating, remember section 76-1433 and that it does not care who wrote the cheque. (6) Do not write a clause in which the tenant waives notice, waives a defence to a fee, or agrees that any fee is "liquidated damages" or "additional rent" conclusively: section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act", section 76-1415(1)(c) voids a term agreeing "to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees", and section 76-1415(2) makes deliberate use of a prohibited term actionable for the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Nobody Takes Your Building Over in Nebraska — No Housing Receivership Statute, But the City Can Post It, Record It, Repair It and Lien It
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS NO SUBSTANDARD-PROPERTY RECEIVERSHIP STATUTE. Missouri, Oregon, Kentucky, West Virginia, Massachusetts and Connecticut all let a court put a rental building into receivership for housing-code violations, collect the rents and spend them on repairs. Nebraska does not. The place such a power would have to come from is section 25-1081, which lists the nine grounds on which "[a] receiver may be appointed by the district court", and NOT ONE OF THEM IS A HOUSING-CODE OR HABITABILITY GROUND. The nine are: a vendor's action to vacate a fraudulent purchase, a creditor subjecting property to a claim, or disputes between partners, limited liability company members or co-owners where the property "is in danger of being lost, removed, or materially injured"; mortgage foreclosure or trust-deed foreclosure where the property is in such danger or "is probably insufficient to discharge the ... debt"; the exercise of a power of sale after a notice of default under the Nebraska Trust Deeds Act on the same conditions; an action under section 52-1705 to enforce a written assignment of rents where the agreement provides for a receiver; "any other case in which a mortgagor or trustor has agreed IN WRITING to the appointment of a receiver"; after judgment, to carry it into execution or preserve property pending appeal; an action under the Foreign-owned Real Estate National Security Act; "in all cases provided for by SPECIAL STATUTES"; and "in all other cases when receivers have heretofore been appointed by the usages of courts of equity." Subdivision (8) is the door a housing receivership would come through, and no special statute exists to open it.

SO THE RECEIVERSHIP RISK IS A CREDITOR RISK, NOT A CODE RISK — AND NOTE WHERE THAT LEAVES YOU. The realistic route to a receiver over your rental is your LENDER's, under section 25-1081(2), (3), (4) or (5). Subdivisions (4) and (5) are the ones you sign up for: a receiver may be appointed to enforce a written assignment of rents "and the agreement provides for the appointment of a receiver", or in any case where the mortgagor "has agreed in writing to the appointment of a receiver." Those clauses are in most commercial mortgages and many investor loans. Read your own loan documents; the receivership exposure you actually have is contractual and self-inflicted, and it has nothing to do with the condition of the building.

WHAT THE CITY CAN DO INSTEAD, AND IT IS SUBSTANTIAL. FIRST, A HOUSING CODE MAY NOT EVEN EXIST WHERE YOUR PROPERTY IS. Section 18-2146: "Each city and village SHALL adopt a minimum standards housing ordinance IF such city or village has completed an approved workable program or is in the process of the preparation of such a program." The duty is conditional, so whether there is a minimum standards housing ordinance at your address is a municipal fact, not a given.

SECOND, AND THIS IS THE ONE LANDLORDS DO NOT SEE COMING: A RECORDED DETERMINATION AGAINST YOUR TITLE. Section 18-1722.01: "Whenever the governing body of a municipality has decided by resolution or other determination that a property is unsafe or unfit for human occupancy because of one or more violations of its minimum standard housing ordinance or has decided by resolution or other determination that a building is unsafe because of one or more violations of its local building or construction code, IT SHALL BE THE DUTY OF SUCH MUNICIPALITY TO POST THE PROPERTY ACCORDINGLY AND TO FILE A COPY OF SUCH RESOLUTION OR OTHER DETERMINATION IN THE OFFICE OF THE REGISTER OF DEEDS OF THE COUNTY TO BE RECORDED. No fee shall be charged for such recording or for the release of such recording." Three things follow. The municipality's duty is MANDATORY, not discretionary — "it shall be the duty". The determination goes on the land records, where every title searcher, lender and buyer will find it. And the statute contemplates a RELEASE of the recording, free of charge, which means the paper comes off when the violations are cured — so curing and obtaining the release is a step you have to take affirmatively, because nothing in the section makes the release automatic.

THIRD, THE CITY CAN DO THE WORK AND PUT THE BILL ON THE PROPERTY. Section 18-1722: "If any owner of any building or structure fails, neglects, or refuses to comply with notice by or on behalf of any city or village to repair, rehabilitate, or demolish and remove a building or structure which is an unsafe building or structure and a public nuisance, the city or village may proceed with the work specified in the notice to the property owner." The governing body may then either "[l]evy the cost as a special assessment against the lot or real estate upon which the building or structure is located" — and "[s]uch special assessment SHALL BE A LIEN on the real estate and shall be collected in the manner provided for special assessments" — or "[c]ollect the cost from the owner ... and enforce the collection by civil action". Note the trigger: it is non-compliance with a NOTICE, and the standard is a building that is both "unsafe" AND "a public nuisance". Note also what the city does NOT get: it does not get the rents, it does not get management of the building, and it does not get possession. It gets a repair bill secured by a lien.

FOURTH, THE MUNICIPAL NUISANCE POWER, WHICH REACHES BEYOND THE CITY LIMITS. Section 18-1720(1): "All cities and villages in this state may by ordinance define, regulate, suppress, and prevent nuisances, declare what constitutes a nuisance, and abate and remove such nuisances", exercisable "within its corporate limits AND EXTRATERRITORIAL ZONING JURISDICTION"; subsection (2) lets a city and county act jointly in that extraterritorial area by interlocal agreement. So a rental just outside the city line is not outside the nuisance power.

FIFTH, MAINTAINING A NUISANCE IS A CRIME AND CONVICTION CARRIES A MANDATORY ABATEMENT ORDER. Section 28-1321(1): "A person commits the offense of maintaining a nuisance if he erects, keeps up or continues and maintains any nuisance to the injury of any part of the citizens of this state." Subsection (4): "Maintenance of nuisances is a CLASS III MISDEMEANOR." Subsection (5): "The court, in case of conviction of such offense, SHALL ORDER every such nuisance to be abated or removed." There is a separate and much heavier nuisance-abatement sequence in the obscenity article at section 28-825, which can close a building for a year and which runs a presumption of knowledge of the place's general reputation against the owner; that is a different subject and is not restated here.

THE PART THAT HITS YOUR RENT ROLL, AND IT IS IN THE DEPOSIT SECTION WHERE NOBODY LOOKS. Section 76-1416(4), second sentence: "However, a tenant shall NOT be liable for damages directly related to the tenant's REMOVAL FROM THE PREMISES BY ORDER OF ANY GOVERNMENTAL ENTITY as a result of the premises not being fit for habitation DUE TO THE NEGLIGENCE OR NEGLECT OF THE LANDLORD." So if the city posts the property and the tenant has to leave, you cannot charge that tenant for the damages flowing from the removal — not lost rent for the remainder of the term, not a re-letting charge, not an early-termination fee — where the unfitness was down to your negligence or neglect. And the tenant's own exit routes stay open: section 76-1425(1) on fourteen days' cure and thirty days after receipt, and the six-month recurrence rule that removes your cure right entirely.

AND WHAT YOU CANNOT FIX BY CONTRACT. Section 76-1419(1)(a) requires you to "[s]ubstantially comply, after written or actual notice, with the requirements of the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety", and the unnumbered sentence closing subsection (1) makes the code the CEILING on your statutory duty where one exists: "If there exists a minimum housing code applicable to the premises, the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a) of this section." That cuts both ways and a landlord should not misread it: it caps the statutory duty, it does not excuse code non-compliance, and section 76-1419(3) cannot shift it — subsection (3) reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" in a dwelling other than a single-family residence. A clause making the tenant responsible for code compliance, or for correcting a cited violation, is a term by which the tenant agrees to forego a remedy under the Act: section 76-1415(1)(a) makes it unenforceable and section 76-1415(2) makes deliberate use of it actionable for the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees.

PRACTICAL COURSE. (1) Treat a municipal unsafe-or-unfit resolution as a title event, not a maintenance ticket: it is recorded against the property by mandatory duty under section 18-1722.01, and you have to cure and obtain the free release. (2) Answer a repair-or-demolish notice within its time, because section 18-1722 only reaches an owner who "fails, neglects, or refuses to comply", and once the city does the work the cost becomes a lien you cannot negotiate. (3) Do not bill a displaced tenant for anything if the displacement followed your own neglect — section 76-1416(4) forbids it. (4) Read your mortgage for an assignment-of-rents-and-receiver clause; that, not the housing code, is how a Nebraska landlord actually loses control of a building. (5) Find out whether your municipality has a minimum standards housing ordinance at all, and get a copy. Section 76-1419(1)(a) measures your duty against it.

title: No Cable, Satellite or Broadband Access Right in a Nebraska Rental — No Mandatory Access, No Rent-Differential Ban, and the Federal OTARD Rule Is What Actually Governs the Dish
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS NO TELECOM-ACCESS STATUTE FOR RENTAL PROPERTY. New York, Indiana, Virginia and Wisconsin each have something: a cable operator's right of access to a multiple dwelling, a bar on charging a subscriber more rent than a non-subscriber, a compensation procedure for the owner, a prohibition on exclusive-provider agreements. Nebraska has none of it. Not one Nebraska section connects a communications service to a rental relationship.

SO AS A MATTER OF NEBRASKA LAW, THESE ARE ALL ANSWERED THE SAME WAY — BY YOUR LEASE. Can you refuse to let a cable company wire the building? Nebraska law does not require you to let them in. Can you sign an exclusive deal with one provider? No Nebraska statute forbids it. Can you charge a subscriber a different rent, or a wiring fee, or a fee for roof access? No Nebraska statute caps or forbids it. Must you provide an internet connection, or maintain one? Nothing requires it. Section 76-1414(1) is the authority running through all of it: "The landlord and tenant may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law including rent, term of the agreement, and other provisions governing the rights and obligations of the parties."

BUT THE ANSWER IS NOT "YOU CAN DO WHAT YOU LIKE", AND THE TWO REASONS ARE BOTH OUTSIDE NEBRASKA LAW. FIRST, THE FEDERAL OTARD RULE. The FCC's over-the-air reception device rule (47 C.F.R. 1.4000) limits a landlord's power to prohibit a tenant's small satellite dish or television antenna in an area within the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a balcony or a patio. THAT RULE is federal. What this row says is that Nebraska adds nothing to it and takes nothing from it, so a Nebraska landlord's satellite policy is a federal-compliance question, not a state one, and a flat no-dishes-anywhere clause is the single most likely place for a Nebraska lease to be unenforceable for a reason that has nothing to do with Nebraska. GET THE OTARD RULE READ BEFORE YOU WRITE A SATELLITE CLAUSE. SECOND, THE SERVICE AGREEMENTS THEMSELVES. A cable or fibre provider's building access agreement, any right-of-entry you have signed, and any bulk-billing or marketing agreement are contracts which may already commit you.

WHAT SECTION 76-1419 DOES AND DOES NOT MAKE YOU MAINTAIN. Section 76-1419(1)(d) requires you to "[m]aintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her." Communications service is not on the enumerated list, but "other facilities and appliances ... supplied or required to be supplied" is open-ended, and the four words "or required to be supplied" are the route in. So: if you ADVERTISE included internet, promise a working cable outlet, or include a service in the rent, you have made it a facility you supplied — and remember that section 76-1410(14) defines a rental agreement as "ALL AGREEMENTS, WRITTEN OR ORAL", so a promise at the showing counts. A service you never promised and never supplied is not your maintenance obligation. A service you did promise becomes one, with the section 76-1425 remedy route behind it: written notice, fourteen days to cure, termination no sooner than thirty days after receipt, damages and injunctive relief under section 76-1425(2), reasonable attorney's fees if your noncompliance is willful, and — on a repeat of substantially the same failure within six months — termination on fourteen days' notice with NO cure right. Note also that there is no repair-and-deduct for it: section 76-1427(1)(a) confines the only procure-and-deduct-from-rent right to "hot water, running water, heat and essential services", and a cable outlet is not that.

IF YOU DO WANT TO INCLUDE A SERVICE, PRICE IT HONESTLY, BECAUSE THAT IS WHERE NEBRASKA LAW BITES. Section 87-302(a)(10) reaches advertising a price "in any manner calculated or tending to mislead" and (a)(12) reaches "false or misleading statements of fact concerning the reasons for, existence of, or amounts of price reductions"; section 87-303.07 provides that where a lessee "is induced by a violation of section 87-302 ... to enter into a sale or lease, the agreement is unenforceable by the seller or lessor", with a right to rescind. So advertising "internet included" and then billing a separate mandatory service fee is not a billing problem — it is a possession problem. (Section 87-302 is quoted in the version operative January 1, 2027.) And if you pass through a provider's charge, remember section 76-1410(13): "Rent means ALL PAYMENTS to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement", so a mandatory monthly service charge collected under the lease is rent for every purpose of the Act, including the nonpayment route in section 76-1431(2).

THE WIRING AND THE WALLS. Your no-alterations clause does the real work here. A tenant drilling through an exterior wall for a dish mount or running coax through a window frame is making an alteration, and section 76-1421 requires the tenant to keep the unit clean and safe, dispose of waste, "[u]se ... all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances ... in a reasonable manner", and not deliberately or negligently destroy or damage any part of the premises. A clause requiring written consent before any penetration of the building envelope, specifying professional installation and restoration at move-out, is a legitimate property-protection term — but write it as an alteration and installation rule, not as a ban on the service, so that it does not collide with the federal rule described above.

TWO ADJACENT NEBRASKA PROVISIONS THAT ARE NOT ABOUT TENANT ACCESS BUT ARE WORTH KNOWING. Sections 86-5,105 to 86-5,107 let an electric utility and a commercial broadband supplier agree to use an EXISTING ELECTRIC UTILITY EASEMENT across your land for broadband, with a ninety-day window for the property owner to claim compensation; that is a hard deadline running against you as owner. Separately, section 28-515.01 makes theft of telecommunications service an offence — a provider's remedy against a service thief, not a landlord duty and not a tool you can use.

PRACTICAL COURSE. (1) Say in the lease exactly which services are included in the rent and which are not, and do not advertise more than you provide. (2) Write the satellite and antenna provision as a consent-and-installation requirement for areas OUTSIDE the tenant's exclusive use, and get the federal OTARD rule read before you finalise it. (3) Do not write a clause charging a subscriber a different rent or conditioning tenancy on using your preferred provider without pricing the deceptive-practices risk above, and do not describe either as required by law, because no Nebraska law requires or forbids it. (4) Do not write a waiver clause about service interruptions: section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act" and section 76-1415(1)(d) voids exculpation or indemnity for the landlord's active and actionable negligence, with section 76-1415(2) making deliberate use actionable for the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Nebraska Has No Tenancy at Will in a Residential Rental — The Statute Converts It to a Periodic Tenancy, and the At-Will Categories Survive Only Outside the Act
bodyText:
THE PHRASE "TENANCY AT WILL" DOES NOT APPEAR ANYWHERE IN NEBRASKA'S STATUTES. South Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Kentucky, West Virginia, Maryland and Massachusetts all have tenancy-at-will statutes with their own notice periods. Nebraska took a different route: it made the at-will tenancy impossible in a residential rental by supplying a default.

SECTION 76-1414(4) IS THE WHOLE ANSWER, AND IT IS ONE SENTENCE. "Unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy shall be WEEK TO WEEK in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent, and IN ALL OTHER CASES MONTH TO MONTH." So there is no gap for an at-will tenancy to occupy. If you never wrote a lease, if the lease expired and the tenant stayed with your consent, if the term is unstated or unclear — the tenancy is month-to-month by statute (or week-to-week for a weekly-paying roomer, on which see the stove-and-refrigerator row, since "roomer" under section 76-1410(15) turns on whether the unit lacks a refrigerator, stove or sink where such facilities are shared). A periodic tenancy, unlike a tenancy at will, cannot be ended at a moment's notice by either side.

WHICH MEANS YOU ALWAYS OWE A NOTICE PERIOD, AND THAT IS THE PRACTICAL POINT. Section 76-1437(1): either party may end a week-to-week tenancy "by a written notice given to the other at least SEVEN DAYS prior to the termination date specified in the notice." Section 76-1437(2): either party may end a month-to-month tenancy "by a written notice given to the other at least THIRTY DAYS prior to the PERIODIC RENTAL DATE specified in the notice." Note the drafting difference between them, which this library's periodic-termination row also flags: the seven-day clock runs to a termination date, the thirty-day clock runs to a PERIODIC RENTAL DATE — a rent-due date, not an arbitrary calendar day. A landlord who thinks of an unwritten tenancy as "at will" and gives a few days' notice has given no effective notice at all.

AND IF YOU CONSENT TO THE TENANT STAYING ON AFTER A FIXED TERM, SECTION 76-1414(4) IS WHERE YOU LAND. Section 76-1437(3)'s closing sentence says so expressly: "If the landlord consents to the tenant's continued occupancy, subsection (4) of section 76-1414 applies." So a consented holdover is not an at-will arrangement and is not a continuation of the old term — it is a fresh month-to-month tenancy needing thirty days' notice keyed to a rental date. A holdover WITHOUT your consent is a different matter and is governed by section 76-1437(3), which this library carries separately.

THE AT-WILL AND AT-SUFFERANCE CATEGORIES DO STILL EXIST IN NEBRASKA — OUTSIDE THE ACT. Sections 25-21,219 to 25-21,235 are the older forcible entry and detainer statutes, and section 25-21,220 lists whom they reach: "(1) In all cases against TENANTS HOLDING OVER THEIR TERMS, and a tenant shall be deemed to be holding over his or her term whenever the tenant has FAILED, NEGLECTED, OR REFUSED TO PAY THE RENT or any part thereof when the rent became due; (2) In all cases when a tenant has threatened the health or safety of other tenants, the landlord, or the landlord's employees or agents, WITHOUT THE RIGHT OF THE TENANT TO CURE the default; (3) In all cases of sales of real estate or executions, orders, or other judicial process when the judgment debtor was in possession ...; (4) In all cases of sale by executors or administrators or guardians and on partition ...; and (5) In all cases when the defendant is a SETTLER OR OCCUPIER of lands or tenements, WITHOUT COLOR OF TITLE, and to which the complainant has the right of possession." Subdivision (5) is the at-sufferance and unauthorized-occupant case, and subdivision (1) carries a deeming provision worth knowing: non-payment of rent, or of any part of it, MAKES a tenant a holdover.

BUT READ THE LAST SENTENCE OF SECTION 25-21,219 BEFORE YOU REACH FOR THAT ROUTE, BECAUSE IT TAKES IT AWAY FOR A RESIDENTIAL TENANCY: "This section shall not apply to actions for possession of any premises subject to the provisions of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act." Section 25-21,219 is the JURISDICTION section of the article — it is what gives the district and county courts jurisdiction over forcible entry and detainer complaints and directs restitution — so if it does not apply to your premises, the article has no jurisdictional foundation to rest on for them. The forcible entry and detainer route is therefore for premises OUTSIDE the two Acts: commercial and industrial tenancies, farm tenancies, the five-year-or-longer land leases that section 76-1408(8) excludes, occupancy after a foreclosure or judicial sale, and the no-colour-of-title occupier. (One textual caution, stated rather than resolved: the exclusion is worded "This section", not "sections 25-21,219 to 25-21,235", so on a narrow reading only the jurisdiction section is switched off while the rest of the article is untouched. The practical answer is the same either way — the article's proceedings are brought "under sections 25-21,219 to 25-21,235" by section 25-21,220's own words, and without the jurisdiction section there is nothing to bring them under — but a landlord should not rely on that article for residential premises and should use the Act's own possession action.)

TWO FEATURES OF THE OUTSIDE-THE-ACT ROUTE THAT HAVE NO COUNTERPART IN THE ACT, AND BOTH MATTER. FIRST, A THREE-DAY NOTICE TO LEAVE, WITH A POSTING ROUTE. Section 25-21,221: "It shall be the duty of the party, desiring to commence an action under sections 25-21,219 to 25-21,235, to notify the adverse party TO LEAVE THE PREMISES ... This notice shall be served AT LEAST THREE DAYS before commencing the action by leaving a written copy with such adverse party, or at his usual place of abode, if he cannot be found. Where the defendant or his usual place of abode CANNOT BE FOUND IN THE COUNTY where the premises are located, such notice MAY BE SERVED BY LEAVING SUCH NOTICE AT OR POSTING IT ON THE DETAINED PREMISES." Three days, and a posting route that exists nowhere in the residential Act. SECOND, AND THIS IS THE TRAP: A ONE-YEAR LIMITATION. Section 25-203: "An action for the forcible entry and detainer, or forcible detainer only, of real property, can only be brought WITHIN ONE YEAR after the cause of such action shall have accrued." Compare the Act's holdover action, where the annotation printed with section 76-1437 reports Blankenau v. Landess, 261 Neb. 906 (2001), holding that an action to recover possession from a tenant holding over without consent "is an action for the possession of real property and is therefore subject to the TEN-YEAR statute of limitations ... as provided in section 25-202", accruing when the lease expires or is terminated and the tenant remains without consent. SO THE SAME DELAY THAT IS HARMLESS UNDER THE ACT CAN BE FATAL OUTSIDE IT: one year against ten. Case law is a lead and not a holding you can rely on without checking it, but the one-year figure in section 25-203 is statutory text.

AND THE ONE PLACE THE ACT REACHES INTO THE OLD ARTICLE. Section 76-1431(4) opens "Notwithstanding subsections (1) and (2) of this section OR SECTION 25-21,221", and then allows a landlord, "after five days' written notice of termination of the rental agreement and WITHOUT THE RIGHT OF THE TENANT TO CURE the default", to sue for possession where violent criminal activity, the illegal sale of a controlled substance, or other activity threatening health or safety occurs on the premises. So the Act displaces section 25-21,221's three-day notice for that route and substitutes five days. Note what this also shows: the legislature knew section 25-21,221 was there and legislated around it, which is further reason not to treat the old article as freely available for residential premises.

PRACTICAL COURSE. (1) STOP CALLING ANY RESIDENTIAL ARRANGEMENT "AT WILL". If there is no definite term, section 76-1414(4) has already made it periodic, and the notice period is seven or thirty days depending on which periodic tenancy it is. (2) Put the term in writing. The default only applies "[u]nless the rental agreement fixes a definite term", and that is the one sentence you control. (3) For a residential tenancy, use the Act's possession action and not the forcible entry and detainer article. (4) If you do hold property outside the Act — commercial, farm, a land lease of five years or more, or an occupier with no colour of title — diary the ONE-YEAR limit in section 25-203 from the date the cause of action accrued, and serve the three-day notice to leave under section 25-21,221, using the at-or-on-the-premises posting route only where the defendant and the usual place of abode cannot be found in the county. (5) Do not try to contract out of any of this: section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any rental agreement term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act", section 76-1437 is not among the eleven chapter-76 sections that open "unless otherwise agreed", and section 76-1415(2) makes deliberate use of a prohibited term actionable for the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. A clause declaring the tenancy terminable at will, or shortening the thirty days, is exactly that kind of term.

title: No Nebraska Tenant-Bankruptcy Rule — The Act Imports Bankruptcy Law Instead of Legislating It, and One Utility Section Survives the Discharge
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS NO TENANT-BANKRUPTCY STATUTE. Nothing in Nebraska law says what happens to a lease when the tenant files, whether you may terminate, whether you may keep the security deposit, how you prove a claim for unpaid rent, or what notice you owe. In the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy, the word "bankrupt" appears in forty-four sections and not one of them is a landlord-tenant provision.

AND THE ACT SAYS WHY, IN TERMS. Section 76-1403: "Unless displaced by the provisions of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the principles of law and equity, including the law relating to capacity to contract, mutuality of obligations, principal and agent, real property, public health, safety and fire prevention, estoppel, fraud, misrepresentation, duress, coercion, mistake, BANKRUPTCY, or other validating or invalidating cause, supplement the act's provisions." That is the ONLY reference to bankruptcy anywhere in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and it is not a rule — it is an importation. The legislature named bankruptcy as a body of law that fills the Act's gaps rather than writing a provision of its own. (The Mobile Home Act does the identical thing at section 76-1452.) So the absence here is a deliberate structural choice, not an oversight, and it means the answer to every question in this topic is FEDERAL.

WHICH THIS ROW WILL NOT STATE. The federal Bankruptcy Code is Title 11 of the United States Code. Nothing below states what it requires. What this row can tell you is where the Nebraska-law answer stops, which is immediately, and what that means for how you behave.

THE FOUR THINGS A LANDLORD DOES WRONG, AND WHY EACH IS A NEBRASKA-LAW PROBLEM AS WELL AS A FEDERAL ONE. (1) AN IPSO FACTO CLAUSE. A lease term providing that the tenancy terminates automatically, or becomes terminable at your option, on the tenant's filing or insolvency is a standard commercial-lease import and it is the first thing to strike from a residential lease. Nebraska does not prohibit it in terms — section 76-1415(1)'s four prohibited categories do not name it — but section 76-1403 imports bankruptcy law to supplement the Act, so a Nebraska court applying the Act applies that law to the clause. GET THE FEDERAL TREATMENT OF SUCH CLAUSES CHECKED BEFORE YOU RELY ON ONE. The cautious course is not to include it: an unenforceable termination clause buys you nothing and, if you act on it, you have terminated a tenancy you had no right to terminate — which exposes you to section 76-1430's fixed three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages plus a reasonable attorney's fee if you also lock the tenant out, and that sum requires no proof of loss. (2) SELF-HELP OF ANY KIND. Section 76-1430's first limb — "[i]f the landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises" — carries NO willfulness requirement at all; only the second limb ("willfully and wrongfully diminishes services") does. A good-faith lockout based on a mistaken view of a bankruptcy filing is still three months' rent. (3) APPLYING THE DEPOSIT. Your section 76-1416(2) duty is to apply prepaid rent and security to rent and damages on termination and to deliver the balance with a written itemization within FOURTEEN DAYS of termination, and section 76-1416(3) prices a willful and not-in-good-faith failure at the deposit plus court costs and fees PLUS a fixed sum of one month's periodic rent or twice the deposit, whichever is less. Whether you may apply the deposit at all once a tenant has filed is a federal question — so the Nebraska point is simply this: your fourteen-day clock and your itemization duty are statutory and do not pause themselves. Get advice rather than guessing in either direction. (4) CONTINUING TO DEMAND RENT. Nebraska gives you no rent-collection privilege here and section 76-1403 imports whatever the federal stay does.

TWO NEBRASKA SECTIONS THAT DO MENTION BANKRUPTCY AND ACTUALLY MATTER TO A LANDLORD. FIRST, A UTILITY SECTION NO NEBRASKA ROW CITES. Section 70-1601: "No applicant for the services of a public or private utility company furnishing water, natural gas, or electricity at retail in this state shall be denied service because of unpaid bills for similar service WHICH ARE NOT COLLECTIBLE AT LAW because of statutes of limitations or DISCHARGE IN BANKRUPTCY PROCEEDINGS." So a tenant or applicant whose old utility debt was discharged cannot be refused new service on that ground — which is worth knowing both because it removes an obstacle to getting a unit's utilities turned on in a new tenant's name, and because it means a discharged utility debt is not a reason to treat an applicant as unable to take service. SECOND, SECTION 76-2,120(6)(b) exempts a transfer "[b]y a trustee in bankruptcy" from the residential seller-disclosure statement — relevant if you are buying a rental out of a bankruptcy, because you will not receive the disclosure statement you would otherwise get.

AND ONE THAT SHAPES WHAT COLLECTION IS WORTH EVEN WITHOUT A FILING. Nebraska's personal-property and wage exemptions sit in sections 25-1552 to 25-1563.01, and they are the reason a judgment against a residential tenant is frequently uncollectable whether or not the tenant ever files. Price your decision to sue accordingly, and note the one Nebraska figure that is on point and is a real remedy: section 76-1437(3) gives you "an amount not more than three months' periodic rent or threefold the actual damages sustained by him, whichever is greater, and reasonable attorney's fees" where a holdover is willful and not in good faith — a claim worth proving up, against a tenant who has assets.

PRACTICAL COURSE. (1) Take any ipso facto or insolvency-termination clause out of the lease. (2) The moment you learn of a filing, stop: no notice, no termination, no lockout, no utility shutoff, no application of the deposit, no further demand — and get the federal position checked. The Nebraska exposure for getting this wrong is section 76-1430's fixed three months' rent plus fees, and the first limb needs no willfulness. (3) Keep doing the things that are purely record-keeping: document the condition of the unit, keep the itemization you would have to deliver under section 76-1416(2), and keep your accounting current, so that whatever the federal answer turns out to be you can act on it immediately. (4) Do not write a waiver clause about any of it. Section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act", section 76-1415(1)(b) voids a term authorising "any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement" — which is exactly what a bankruptcy-related stipulation can look like — and section 76-1415(2) makes deliberate use of a prohibited term actionable for the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees.

title: No Nebraska Bar on Disclosing Tenant Information — But Two Data Statutes Bind You, One of Them Reaches a Sole Proprietor, and the Vendor-Contract Duty Catches You on Renewal
bodyText:
FIRST, THE ABSENCE, BECAUSE IT IS WHAT THIS TOPIC IS USUALLY ABOUT. Nebraska has NO statute barring a landlord from disclosing tenant information. Oregon enacted one in 2026. Maryland restricts disclosure of criminal records and applicant data; Connecticut has a sensitive-data rule; Rhode Island, Maine and West Virginia have their own. Nebraska has nothing of the kind: no consent requirement before telling a prospective landlord about a former tenant, no restriction on sharing a rental history, no rule about who may see an application, no tenant right to see or correct what you hold, and no statutory confidentiality in the tenancy relationship at all. If a current or former tenant asks you to keep something confidential, that is a matter of your own practice, not of Nebraska law.

BUT THE SECURITY SIDE IS A DIFFERENT STORY. Nebraska's data-security act binds you whatever the size of your business: reasonable security for computerized tenant data, including on disposal; a security clause in every vendor contract; and breach notice to the tenant and the Attorney General (§§87-803, 87-808). Any waiver of that act is void (§87-805). This library's data-security guidance for tenant records sets out those duties in full.

THE SECOND STATUTE, AND THE SMALL-BUSINESS CARVE-OUT THAT IS NOT COMPLETE. The Data Privacy Act, sections 87-1101 to 87-1130, was enacted by Laws 2024, LB1074. Section 87-1103(1) says it "applies only to a person that: (a) Conducts business in this state or produces a product or service consumed by residents of this state; (b) Processes or engages in the sale of personal data; and (c) IS NOT A SMALL BUSINESS as determined under the federal Small Business Act, as such act existed on January 1, 2024, EXCEPT TO THE EXTENT THAT SECTION 87-1118 APPLIES to a person described by this subdivision." All three conditions must hold, so most landlords are outside the Act's consumer-rights, privacy-notice, data-protection-assessment and processor-contract machinery. BUT NOT ENTIRELY, AND THE EXCEPTION IS IN THE SAME SENTENCE.
