Section 87-1118(1): "A person described by subdivision (1)(c) of section 87-1103 shall not engage in the SALE of personal data that is SENSITIVE DATA without receiving PRIOR CONSENT from the consumer", and (2) makes a violation subject to the penalty in section 87-1124. So the sensitive-data sale prohibition reaches a small business that the rest of the Act does not. If you ever sell, license or trade tenant or applicant data — to a marketing list, a data broker, an affiliate, or as part of a portfolio sale — stop and get advice on whether the federal Small Business Act definition covers you, and what "sensitive data" and "sale" mean in sections 87-1102. Two further features of the Act worth knowing: section 87-1125 provides that it "shall not be construed as providing a basis for, or being subject to, A PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION for a violation of the Data Privacy Act or any other law"; and section 87-1130 "supersedes and preempts any ordinance, resolution, rule, or other regulation adopted by a political subdivision regarding the processing of personal data" — so Omaha and Lincoln cannot add to this, which is unusual and good news.

PRACTICAL COURSE. First, follow the data-security guidance: collect less, redact, encrypt, put security terms in vendor contracts and keep a written disposal practice. Then two points for this subject. (1) DO NOT PUT A WAIVER OR CONSENT CLAUSE IN THE LEASE AND THINK IT HELPS. Section 87-805 voids any waiver of the breach act outright. And a broad "Tenant consents to Landlord's disclosure of any information" clause gains you nothing under Nebraska law — there is no disclosure prohibition for it to waive — while section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act" and section 76-1415(2) makes deliberate use of a prohibited term actionable for the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. (2) If you screen applicants, remember that the credit-reporting side is FEDERAL.

title: No Flag, Political-Sign or Religious-Display Right in a Nebraska Rental — Which Means Your Rule Governs, and Section 76-1422's Six Conditions Are the Whole Test
bodyText:
NEBRASKA GIVES A TENANT NO DISPLAY RIGHTS AT ALL. There is no flag-display statute of the Nevada, Ohio or Utah kind, no political-sign protection, no common-interest-community sign provision, and no religious-display or doorpost protection. None of these terms appears in the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy: "political sign", "campaign sign", "yard sign", "mezuzah", "crucifix", "doorpost" and "religious display" (and "religious object", "religious symbol" and "religious item") each appear ZERO times, and no section anywhere in the property chapter pairs a flag with a display, an owner, a tenant, a lessee or an occupant. Nothing in the Nebraska Condominium Act protects a unit owner's or occupant's flag or sign either.

THE ONLY FLAG STATUTE NEBRASKA HAS RUNS THE OTHER WAY AND YOU MUST NOT USE IT. Section 28-928(1): "A person commits the offense of mutilating a flag if such person intentionally casts contempt or ridicule upon a flag by mutilating, defacing, defiling, burning, or trampling upon such flag", with "flag" defined at (2) to include "any flag, ensign, banner, standard, colors, or replica or representation thereof which is an official or commonly recognized symbol of the United States or the State of Nebraska", and mutilation made a Class III misdemeanor at (3). That is a criminal prohibition on destroying a flag, not a right to fly one, and it gives a landlord nothing. It is also squarely in the territory of federal constitutional law about expressive conduct. DO NOT REFERENCE IT IN A LEASE AND DO NOT THREATEN A TENANT WITH IT.

SO THE QUESTION IS ENTIRELY YOURS TO ANSWER BY RULE — AND SECTION 76-1422 IS THE WHOLE TEST. "A landlord, from time to time, may adopt rules or regulations, however described, concerning the tenant's use and occupancy of the premises. It is enforceable as provided in section 76-1431 against the tenant ONLY IF: (1) Its purpose is to promote the APPEARANCE, convenience, safety, or welfare of the tenants in the premises, preserve the landlord's property from abusive use, or make a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for the tenants generally; (2) It is REASONABLY RELATED to the purpose for which it is adopted; (3) It APPLIES TO ALL TENANTS in the premises IN A FAIR MANNER; (4) It is SUFFICIENTLY EXPLICIT in its prohibition, direction, or limitation of the tenant's conduct to fairly inform him of what he must or must not do to comply; (5) It is NOT FOR THE PURPOSE OF EVADING THE OBLIGATIONS OF THE LANDLORD; and (6) THE TENANT HAS NOTICE OF IT AT THE TIME HE ENTERS INTO THE RENTAL AGREEMENT." All six are cumulative and every one of them matters here.

WHAT THE SIX CONDITIONS MEAN FOR A SIGN-AND-DISPLAY RULE, TAKEN ONE AT A TIME. CONDITION (1) IS THE GOOD NEWS AND IT IS BETTER THAN LANDLORDS EXPECT: "appearance" is named FIRST in the list of legitimate purposes, so an aesthetic rule about what may be hung, posted or displayed on the exterior, in windows, or on balconies is within the statute's own purposes. You do not have to dress it up as a safety rule. CONDITION (2) means the rule must fit that purpose — a blanket ban on anything visible from outside is harder to justify as an appearance measure than a rule about size, location, attachment method and duration. CONDITION (3), "applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner", is the condition that destroys most display rules in practice, and it is about ENFORCEMENT as much as drafting: a rule you enforce against one tenant's sign and not against another's is unenforceable against the first. Decide the policy and apply it to everybody, including the tenant whose sign you agree with. CONDITION (4) requires explicitness — "no signs" is not explicit about a window decal, a wreath, a flag bracket or a political poster facing inward; name the categories, the sizes and the places. CONDITION (6) IS THE ONE THAT CANNOT BE FIXED LATER: the tenant must have NOTICE OF THE RULE AT THE TIME THE TENANT ENTERS INTO THE RENTAL AGREEMENT. A rule adopted mid-tenancy and posted on the laundry-room wall is not enforceable against an existing tenant under section 76-1422, because that tenant did not have notice of it when the agreement was made. Attach your rules to the lease, list them in it, or have them signed for at signing — and note that section 76-1410(14) makes "valid rules and regulations adopted under section 76-1422" part of the "rental agreement" itself, which is precisely why the delivery-and-receipt step is the whole of their enforceability.

AND THERE IS A SECOND LIMIT ON MID-TENANCY RULE CHANGES WORTH KNOWING. Section 76-1424 — the tenant's use-and-occupancy section — is one of only eleven chapter-76 sections that open "unless otherwise agreed", so use and occupancy is a subject the parties can address by agreement. Section 76-1422, by contrast, is NOT on that list: its six conditions are not variable by the lease, so a clause purporting to let you adopt binding new rules at will does not work. You can agree with a tenant to a new rule; you cannot reserve a power to impose one.

THE THREE PLACES A DISPLAY RULE CAN STILL GO WRONG, NONE OF THEM IN THE LANDLORD-TENANT ACT. FIRST, FAIR HOUSING, AND SPECIFICALLY RELIGION. A facially neutral appearance rule applied uniformly is one thing; a rule written or enforced so that it reaches a religious item and not a decorative one is a different thing, because religion is a protected basis under Nebraska's fair-housing law. The protected-class list is set out in the fair-housing row; the practical rule is: never apply a display rule differently to a religious item, and never write an exception for some holidays and not others. Note too that section 20-322's exemptions are confined by their own words to the Nebraska Fair Housing Act (each opens "[n]othing in the Nebraska Fair Housing Act shall prohibit" or "[n]othing in the act shall..."), so a landlord relying on the religious-organization or own-home exemption should check that it reaches the provision they are worried about. SECOND, THE CONSTITUTIONAL QUESTION. Article I, section 5 of the Nebraska Constitution provides that "[e]very person may freely speak, write and publish on all subjects, being responsible for the abuse of that liberty". Whether that provision or the First Amendment reaches a private landlord's rule is CONSTITUTIONAL LAW AND CASE LAW, so nothing in this row should be taken as saying either that it does or that it does not. If your property is publicly owned, publicly financed, or operated by or with a public housing agency, treat the question as live and get advice. THIRD, YOUR OWN HOA OR CONDOMINIUM DECLARATION. If the rental is in a common-interest community, the declaration and its rules may either restrict displays further or protect them, and a tenant's display can put you in breach of the association's rules. Nebraska gives no statutory display protection in a common-interest community, so the declaration is the only text that matters; this library's association-compliance clause is where that belongs.

ENFORCEMENT, AND THE PRICE OF GETTING IT WRONG. A valid section 76-1422 rule is enforceable "as provided in section 76-1431" — which means a written notice specifying the breach, fourteen days to cure, and termination no sooner than thirty days after receipt, with the six-month recurrence rule allowing fourteen days and no cure for a repeat of substantially the same breach. It does NOT mean self-help. Do not remove a tenant's flag, sign or display yourself, do not enter the unit to do it, and do not condition anything on removal: section 76-1423(4) makes the landlord's access list exhaustive ("no other right of access except by court order, as permitted by subsection (2) of section 76-1432, or if the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises"), and section 76-1438(2) prices an unlawful entry at "actual damages NOT LESS THAN an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees". And do not write the rule as a waiver: section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act", with section 76-1415(2) making deliberate use of a prohibited term actionable for the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees.

PRACTICAL COURSE. (1) Write the rule as an APPEARANCE rule, because section 76-1422(1) names appearance as a legitimate purpose, and write it by category, size, location, attachment method and duration rather than as a blanket ban. (2) Deliver it at signing and get a receipt; section 76-1422(6) makes that the difference between an enforceable rule and a decorative one. (3) Permit a mounting method that does not penetrate the building envelope and say what it is, so the rule is about your building rather than about the message. (4) Enforce uniformly and keep a record of every instance, because condition (3) is judged on your conduct. (5) Never treat a religious item differently from a secular one. (6) Enforce through section 76-1431's notice and cure, never by self-help.

title: No Nebraska Rule on Claiming Against the Tenant's Insurance - and No Anti-Subrogation Waiver Either
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute on tenant insurance claims. Nothing in Nebraska law stops you from requiring the tenant to carry renter's insurance, from asking the tenant to put a loss through their own policy, or from pursuing the tenant's insurer - and nothing requires the tenant's written permission before you do. Colorado's rule (C.R.S. 38-12-503(13)) and Maryland's anti-subrogation rule have no Nebraska counterpart. Three Nebraska rules do set the boundaries, and one of them cuts the other way. (1) You cannot use the tenant's policy as a substitute for your own repair duty. Section 76-1419 is your habitability duty, and the only ways to move any part of it are the two narrow written-agreement routes in section 76-1419(2) and (3) - (2) is confined to a single-family residence and (3) reaches only specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling. A lease term making the tenant's insurance the funding source for repairs you owe is an attempt to have the tenant 'waive or to forego' a remedy under the Act and is unenforceable under section 76-1415(1)(a); if you deliberately use a provision you know is prohibited, section 76-1415(2) gives the tenant actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. (2) You cannot use insurance language to exculpate yourself. Section 76-1415(1)(d) voids a term by which the tenant agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord 'arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord', or to indemnify you for it. Nebraska's ban is negligence-specific, not a general ban - which is why the library's Nebraska renter's-insurance clause keeps the active-and-actionable-negligence carve-out. (3) And the direction that favours you: Nebraska gives the residential tenant NO anti-subrogation protection. The Nebraska Condominium Act requires the association's policies to provide that 'the insurer waives its right to subrogation under the policy against any unit owner or member of his or her household' (section 76-871(d)(2)); the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no comparable sentence anywhere, so your own insurer may subrogate against a tenant who caused a loss. Practical course: require renter's insurance with an evidence-of-coverage condition, keep the negligence carve-out intact, and treat a claim against the tenant's policy as an ordinary tort or lease-breach claim that will in practice need the tenant's cooperation or a judgment - not as something the lease can compel.

title: Tenant Portals - You May Run One, But You May Not Put the Consent in the Lease
bodyText:
Nebraska legislated on this in 2025 and the answer splits in two.

PAYMENT: you may require rent through a portal. Section 76-1414(3) says rent is payable 'without demand or notice at the time and place agreed upon by the parties', and only 'unless otherwise agreed' is rent payable at the dwelling unit - so the lease can name the portal as the place of payment, and no Nebraska statute caps or forbids a convenience or processing fee on it.

NOTICES AND DOCUMENTS: here the portal is recognised and then fenced. Section 76-1413(4)(b) expressly treats 'posting on an electronic network or site accessible via the Internet, mobile application, computer, mobile device, tablet, or any other electronic device' as delivery by electronic means - but only 'together with separate notice of the posting', which must go to a consented email address or another consented method. Posting alone is not delivery.

Then section 76-1413(9): 'A landlord shall not, as part of a rental agreement or as a condition of entering into or renewing a rental agreement, require a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means.' A lease paragraph by which the tenant consents to electronic notices is the thing that subsection prohibits. Take the consent on a separate, genuinely optional form instead, and build it to the section 76-1413(7) checklist: affirmative consent not withdrawn; a clear and conspicuous statement of the right to withdraw at any time 'without the imposition of any conditions or consequences', of which notices the consent covers, of the right to paper by mail and how to get a paper copy, and of how to withdraw or update the email address; a statement of hardware and software requirements; and an electronic consent or confirmation that demonstrates the tenant can actually open that form.

Four more traps.
- (i) Where a law requires verification or acknowledgment of receipt, electronic delivery works only if the method provides it (section 76-1413(11)(a)); if it is not obtained the notice must be mailed (section 76-1413(11)(b)(i)).
- (ii) If two or more electronic communications come back undeliverable in a thirty-day period, all future communications must go by first-class or other mail until the tenant re-confirms electronically.
- (iii) You must fall back to another method if you have a reasonable basis to believe the notice was not received or you learn the email address is no longer valid (section 76-1413(15)).
- (iv) Electronic delivery changes nothing about content or timing (section 76-1413(10)).

The Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, routed in by section 76-1413(5), adds two rules that cannot be contracted around: section 86-632(3) - 'A party that agrees to conduct a transaction by electronic means may refuse to conduct other transactions by electronic means. The right granted by this subsection may not be waived by agreement' - so a portal-for-everything clause is unenforceable to that extent; and section 86-635(3) - if the sender inhibits the recipient's ability to store or print an electronic record, 'the electronic record is not enforceable against the recipient', with section 86-635(4) saying those requirements 'may not be varied by agreement'. A portal that shows a notice on screen but does not let the tenant download or print it can therefore defeat your own notice.

title: Tenant Records - Nebraska Requires One Accounting and No Rent Ledger
bodyText: Nebraska has no rent-ledger duty. There is no statute requiring you to give a tenant a rent ledger or payment history on request, none requiring one to accompany a nonpayment notice, and no tenant records-request regime with a copying charge of the kind Virginia has. Section 76-1431(2) sets out everything the nonpayment notice must contain, and it is only two things: written notice by the landlord of nonpayment, and notice of your intention to terminate if the rent is not paid within seven calendar days. An amount, a running balance and a ledger are good practice and good evidence, but they are not statutory contents, and adding them does not create a requirement you then have to meet. You are also not required by statute to give a rent receipt. TWO RECORDS DUTIES DO EXIST, AND BOTH ARE REAL. First, the deposit accounting: under section 76-1416(2), on termination of the tenancy the balance of any security and prepaid rent 'and a written itemization' must be delivered or mailed to the tenant within fourteen days after the date of termination; if the tenant gave no mailing address or instructions, you must mail both by first-class mail to the tenant's last-known mailing address, and if that comes back undeliverable or the balance stays outstanding for a year it becomes abandoned property reportable to the State Treasurer under the Uniform Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act. Section 76-1416(3) prices a failure: the tenant recovers the property and money due, court costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and if your failure is willful and not in good faith, liquidated damages of one month's periodic rent or two times the deposit, whichever is less. Second, the identity record: the owner-and-manager disclosure, in writing at or before the start of the tenancy and kept current (§76-1417(1), (2)); this library's required-disclosures guidance sets it out. Keep the lease, the application, the deposit itemization, the move-in and move-out condition record and your notice-delivery proof regardless - section 76-1416(2) damages and section 76-1431's notice requirements are both proved out of your own file.

title: What a Nebraska Tenant Can Actually Do If You Don't Repair - and the Two Things They Cannot
bodyText: Nebraska gives the tenant three routes and withholds two that landlords in other states worry about. ROUTE 1 - TERMINATE, section 76-1425(1). For a material noncompliance with the rental agreement, or a noncompliance with section 76-1419 materially affecting health and safety, the tenant delivers a written notice specifying the acts and omissions and stating that the agreement terminates on a date not less than THIRTY days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in FOURTEEN days. Read the two clocks together: you get fourteen days to cure, and the termination cannot bite before thirty days after the tenant's notice was received, so a cure on day twelve stops it. If substantially the same act or omission recurs within six months, the tenant may terminate on at least fourteen days' written notice with NO cure right at all - the recurrence rule is the real exposure, and it is why a patched-over problem is worse than a fixed one. The tenant cannot terminate for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act of the tenant, a family member, or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent. On termination you must return all prepaid rent and security recoverable under section 76-1416 (section 76-1425(4)). ROUTE 2 - DAMAGES AND AN INJUNCTION, section 76-1425(2), and this one needs no termination notice. The tenant 'may recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for any noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement or section 76-1419'; reasonable attorney's fees follow if the noncompliance is WILLFUL; and if the noncompliance is caused by conditions beyond your control the tenant cannot recover consequential damages but keeps the section 76-1427 remedies. Section 76-1425(3) says this remedy is additional to the termination route. ROUTE 3 - ESSENTIAL SERVICES, section 76-1427, and this is the only place Nebraska lets rent be touched. Where you deliberately or negligently fail to supply running water, hot water, heat or essential services, after written notice the tenant may (a) procure reasonable amounts and 'deduct their actual and reasonable cost from the rent', (b) recover damages based on the diminution in fair rental value, or (c) procure reasonable substitute housing and be excused from rent for the period; if the failure was deliberate, add the cost or fair value of substitute housing up to one periodic rent, and reasonable attorney's fees in any case under the subsection. The tenant cannot combine this with section 76-1425 for the same breach (section 76-1427(2)), and the rights do not arise until written notice is given (section 76-1427(3)). THE TWO THINGS NEBRASKA DOES NOT HAVE. There is no general repair-and-deduct: section 76-1427(1)(a) is the only procure-and-deduct-from-rent right in the Act, and it is confined to water, hot water, heat and essential services. And there is no rent escrow and no certified-unfit withholding scheme - no Nebraska statute lets a tenant pay rent to a court, an agency or an escrow agent as a self-help remedy. The nearest thing is procedural and runs the other way: section 76-1428(1) lets the court, in an action for possession for nonpayment or an action for rent where the tenant is in possession, 'from time to time' order the tenant to pay rent into court - 'may order', not must, and it is the court's power, not the tenant's right; and if the tenant's defence or counterclaim is without merit and not raised in good faith, you recover reasonable attorney's fees. FINALLY, THE CEILING THAT CUTS FOR YOU: section 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence - 'If there exists a minimum housing code applicable to the premises, the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a) of this section' - so a local code caps the duty rather than adding to it, and the same sentence preserves existing tort law unchanged.

title: Tenant Organizing in Nebraska - One Sentence of Protection, and No Access Right
bodyText: Nebraska protects tenant organizing in exactly one sentence and gives organizers nothing else. Section 76-1439(1) says a landlord 'may not retaliate by increasing rent or decreasing services or by bringing or threatening to bring an action for possession' after either (a) the tenant has complained to a government agency charged with enforcement of a minimum building or housing code of a violation applicable to the premises materially affecting health and safety, or (b) 'the tenant has organized or become a member of a tenants' union or similar organization.' That is the whole of it, and four things follow. (1) THE PROTECTED CONDUCT IS A CLOSED TWO-ITEM LIST. A complaint made to you rather than to a code agency is not on it; neither is exercising a remedy under the Act generally. (2) THE PROHIBITED ACTS ARE ALSO A CLOSED LIST - rent increase, decrease in services, and bringing or threatening a possession action. NON-RENEWAL IS NOT LISTED. The contrast is deliberate and inside the same chapter: the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act's twin, section 76-14,106(1), prohibits retaliation by 'increasing rent, decreasing services, bringing or threatening to bring an action for possession, or FAILING TO RENEW A RENTAL AGREEMENT', and its protected-conduct list runs to four items including a complaint to the landlord and the exercise of 'any of the rights or remedies provided by the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act or otherwise available at law'. The legislature wrote the broader rule for mobile home parks and left the narrower one in place for ordinary rentals. (3) THE PRICE IS FIXED, NOT A CEILING. Section 76-1439(2) sends the tenant to section 76-1430, which gives 'an amount equal to three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages, and a reasonable attorney's fee' - a fixed sum needing no proof of loss - plus possession or termination at the tenant's election, and return of prepaid rent and security. The same subsection preserves your position too: 'Nothing in this section shall be construed as prohibiting reasonable rent increases or changes in services notwithstanding the occurrence of acts specified in subsection (1).' And section 76-1439(3) lets you bring a possession action anyway if (a) the code violation was caused primarily by lack of reasonable care by the tenant or someone in the household or on the premises with the tenant's consent, (b) the tenant is in default in rent, or (c) compliance requires alteration, remodeling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of use of the unit - though maintaining that action does not release you from liability under section 76-1425(2). (4) WHAT NEBRASKA DOES NOT GIVE. There is no statutory right for a tenants' organization to meet in common areas, no right of access for non-resident organizers, no duty to recognise or meet with an organization, no notice-posting right, and no bar on a lease rule restricting solicitation or canvassing. Section 76-1423(4) in fact runs the other way on access: 'The landlord has no other right of access except by court order', which allocates entry and says nothing about third-party organizers, whose position on the premises is governed by ordinary trespass law and by the tenant's own power to license a person onto the unit. There is also no retaliation presumption and no burden-shifting: a sweep of 'presum' across chapter 76 returns 25 sections and not one of them is in sections 76-1401 to 76-1449. PRACTICAL COURSE: treat an organizing tenant like any other tenant, document the non-retaliatory reason for any rent increase or service change contemporaneously (section 76-1439(2) expressly permits reasonable ones), rely on non-renewal rather than a possession action if you simply want the tenancy to end, and keep house rules about solicitation content-neutral and delivered as section 76-1422(6) requires.

title: No Nebraska Statement of Tenant Rights to Attach, Deliver or Have Signed
bodyText: Nebraska has nothing like Virginia's or Illinois's statement of tenant rights. No state agency publishes a tenant-rights summary you must hand over; nothing has to be attached as the first page of the lease or of a renewal; there is no signed-acknowledgment requirement, no page-by-page signing requirement, and no statute that bars you from suing or from bringing a possession action until a summary has been provided. There is also no Nebraska analogue to Delaware's Attorney General summary or to Michigan's and New Jersey's truth-in-renting statements. WHAT NEBRASKA REQUIRES YOU TO HAND OVER IS SHORT AND SPECIFIC. Section 76-1417(1): the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises, and of an owner or a person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands - 'in writing at or before the commencement of the tenancy', kept current under section 76-1417(2). That is a contact disclosure, not a rights summary, and it need not sit in the lease. The Carbon Monoxide Safety Act's duty at section 76-606 is an equipment duty, not a document. THE ONE PAMPHLET IN NEBRASKA LAW THAT MENTIONS A TENANT IS NOT YOURS TO DELIVER. Section 76-2421(1)(a) requires a licensee offering brokerage services, at the earliest practicable opportunity during or following first substantial contact with 'a seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant' who has no written brokerage agreement, to provide 'a written copy of the current brokerage disclosure pamphlet which has been prepared and approved by the commission'. Three things about that: it is a duty on a real estate licensee, not on a landlord as landlord; it is about brokerage relationships, not tenant rights; and it reaches you only if you are yourself licensed or if your leasing agent is - in which case the agent owes it and you should confirm it was delivered. SO: nothing to attach, nothing to have signed, and no suit precondition. A voluntary one-page plain-English summary of the deposit timeline, the entry-notice rule and the repair-notice routes is still worth giving - it costs nothing, it reduces the arguments that produce section 76-1416(3) and section 76-1425 claims, and because no statute prescribes its contents there is no defective-summary exposure. Do not make it an acknowledgment of waiver of anything: a term by which the tenant agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Act is unenforceable under section 76-1415(1)(a), and deliberate use of a provision you know is prohibited costs actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees under section 76-1415(2).

title: The Eight Duties Nebraska Imposes on Your Tenant Without a Lease Clause
Changing a Term Mid-Tenancy - Nebraska Gives You One Clean Route and No Modification Notice
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute on modifying a tenancy. There is no modification-notice provision, no rent-increase notice, and no rule that raising a fee the lease already provides needs a longer notice than raising rent. What Nebraska gives you is a termination notice, and that is the mechanism. SECTION 76-1437: 'The landlord or the tenant may terminate a week-to-week tenancy by a written notice given to the other at least seven days prior to the termination date specified in the notice' (subsection (1)); 'The landlord or the tenant may terminate a month-to-month tenancy by a written notice given to the other at least thirty days prior to the periodic rental date specified in the notice' (subsection (2)). Note the two differences between them: the week-to-week clock runs to 'the termination date specified in the notice', while the month-to-month clock runs to 'the periodic rental date' - so a 30-day month-to-month notice has to land on a rent date, not on any day you pick, and a notice given on the 5th cannot terminate on the 5th of the following month. THE SAFE ROUTE TO A NEW TERM is therefore: give the section 76-1437(2) notice and offer the new terms at the same time, in one document that says plainly that the current tenancy ends on the stated periodic rental date and that you offer a new month-to-month tenancy from that date on the stated terms. The tenant accepts by staying and paying, or leaves. Nothing in the Act requires you to offer anything, and section 76-1439(2) separately preserves 'reasonable rent increases or changes in services' against a retaliation claim. FOR A FIXED-TERM LEASE there is no notice route at all: a term you both agreed to runs to its end and can be changed only by a new agreement, because the parties' power to set terms under section 76-1414(1) is a power to agree, not a power to impose. HOUSE RULES ARE THE ONE THING YOU CAN CHANGE UNILATERALLY, AND THE LIMIT IS SUBSTANTIVE, NOT PROCEDURAL. Section 76-1422's closing sentence: 'A rule or regulation adopted after the tenant enters into the rental agreement is enforceable against the tenant if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the tenant and it does not work a substantial modification of his bargain.' Reasonable notice is not a stated number of days, and the second condition is a ceiling - a new rule that shifts rent, charges a new fee, or takes away an amenity the tenant bargained for works a substantial modification and is unenforceable however much notice you give. WHY WE DO NOT OFFER A UNILATERAL-MODIFICATION CLAUSE. A clause letting the landlord change any term on 30 days' notice with continued occupancy deemed acceptance is tempting and is not offered here, for two reasons that pull together. It would do by contract what section 76-1422's closing sentence refuses to allow by rule, and the Act's own anti-waiver provision, section 76-1415(1)(a), voids a term by which the tenant 'agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Act' - with actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees under section 76-1415(2) if a landlord deliberately uses a provision known to be prohibited. No Nebraska decision located in this canvass settles whether such a clause survives, so the cautious and completely effective course is the section 76-1437(2) terminate-and-offer notice, which needs no clause at all. THE CONTRAST THAT PROVES THE SILENCE IS DELIBERATE: in a mobile home park, section 76-1490 requires that 'each tenant shall be notified in writing of any rent increase by actual notice or by United States mail at least sixty days prior to the effective date of the increase.' The same chapter, the same legislature, a 60-day rent-increase notice for one kind of tenancy and none at all for ordinary residential rentals.

title: No Rent Cap, No Just Cause, No Tenant-Protection Notice in Nebraska
bodyText: Nebraska has no tenant-protection act of the California type and therefore no notice to give under one. There is no statewide rent cap or rent stabilization, no allowable-annual-increase formula, no tenure-based just-cause eviction requirement, and no statute requiring you to tell a tenant that a rent cap or just-cause regime applies. There is also no statewide tenant opportunity to purchase - nothing requiring you to offer a rented house or apartment building to the sitting tenant or to a tenant association before you sell it, and no right of first refusal on a sale. A month-to-month tenancy ends on the section 76-1437(2) thirty-day notice regardless of how long the tenant has lived there, subject only to the section 76-1439 retaliation bar and to fair housing law. TWO QUALIFICATIONS, BOTH REAL. First, the one place Nebraska does give sitting tenants a conversion notice and a purchase-related protection is the Nebraska Condominium Act, section 76-886, where a declarant converting a building owes sixty days' notice with the public-offering statement, cannot require a tenant to vacate on less than sixty days' notice except for nonpayment, waste or disturbing conduct, cannot alter the terms of the tenancy during that period, and - if the declarant chooses to offer the unit to the tenant - cannot offer it to anyone else on better price or terms for the following thirty days. That is a separate subject with its own guidance in this library; see the conversion-building row. Note what it is not: section 76-886(b) says the converter 'may offer' the unit to the tenant, so it is a price protection conditional on an offer being made, not a mandatory opportunity to purchase. Second, this row is about STATE law. Nebraska's general municipal-powers chapter contains no rent-control prohibition and no rent-control authorization, so whether a particular city may do anything in this area is a question about that city's own charter powers and ordinances, which are outside this library. Check your city before assuming the state silence settles it. WHAT THIS MEANS PRACTICALLY: you need no coverage notice, no exemption notice and no pre-sale offer, and the notices Nebraska does require of you are the section 76-1417(1) owner-and-manager disclosure at or before commencement, the section 76-1437 periodic-tenancy notice when you end the tenancy, and the federal lead-based-paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing.

title: No Exemption Notice - There Is Nothing in Nebraska to Be Exempt From
bodyText: California landlords whose property falls outside the state's rent-cap and just-cause law must serve a specific statutory notice saying so, and the exemption is lost if the notice is not given. Nebraska has no equivalent, and it cannot have one: there is no statewide rent cap and no just-cause eviction requirement here, so there is no coverage to be exempt from and no exemption notice to serve. Do not put a California-style exemption notice or an 'this property is exempt from rent control' recital in a Nebraska lease. It states a legal conclusion about a regime that does not exist, it has no statutory effect, and if it ever misleads a tenant about their rights it is the kind of representation section 87-302 of the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act reaches. NEBRASKA'S EXEMPTIONS WORK THE OTHER WAY ROUND - THEY ARE SELF-EXECUTING AND NEED NO NOTICE. Section 76-1408 lists eight arrangements that 'are not governed by' the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act - residence at an institution incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counseling or religious service; occupancy under a contract of sale; occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in a portion of a structure operated for its benefit; transient occupancy in a hotel or motel; occupancy by an employee of a landlord whose right to occupancy is conditional upon employment in and about the premises; occupancy by a condominium owner or a cooperative proprietary lessee; occupancy primarily for agricultural purposes; and a lease of improved or unimproved residential land for a term of five years or more. Not one of them requires a notice, a recital or an acknowledgment, and none of them can be created by saying so: the section's opening words are 'Unless created to avoid the application of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act', so an exclusion depends on the real arrangement and a lease recital claiming one is at best inert and at worst evidence that the arrangement was created to avoid the Act. The same goes for the security-deposit cap: section 76-1416(1)'s one-month limit has a single carve-out, for 'housing agencies organized or existing under the Nebraska Housing Agency Act', and it applies by status, not by notice. PRACTICAL COURSE: if you believe a tenancy falls outside the Act, build the facts - the employment condition, the agricultural use, the five-year term - and say nothing in the lease about the Act not applying.

title: Nebraska's Landlord-Tenant Act Has No Repeal Clock - and the Legislature Just Expanded It
bodyText: No Nebraska tenant-protection statute is on a dated repeal clock. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, sections 76-1401 to 76-1449, contains no sunset clause, no expiry date and no termination provision - its applicability section, section 76-1448, runs in one direction only: 'The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies to rental agreements entered into or extended or renewed after July 1, 1975'; neither does the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act, sections 76-1450 to 76-14,111, nor the Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act in chapter 69, nor the Nebraska Fair Housing Act in chapter 20. So you do not need to track an expiry date, you cannot plan around one, and a lease term that tries to - a clause keyed to the Act 'while in effect', or one that reverts to common-law terms on repeal - is drafting for an event that is not scheduled. The recent legislative direction is the opposite of a sunset. Laws 2025, LB80, section 47 amended section 76-1401 to read 'Sections 76-1401 to 76-1449 and sections 48 to 50 of this act shall be known and may be cited as' the Act - that is, the legislature ADDED three sections to the Act in 2025, which became sections 76-1431.02, 76-1431.03 and 76-1431.04. As codified, section 76-1401 reads 'Sections 76-1401 to 76-1449', a range that now takes them in. Laws 2025, LB185 rewrote section 76-1413's notice and electronic-delivery scheme in the same session. An act being added to twice in one session is not an act on its way out. WHAT YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY TRACK, since a sunset is the wrong thing to watch for. Nebraska landlord law changes by amendment, and three of the changes already on the books have their own dates: section 76-1413(13) says the LB185 electronic-delivery changes do not apply to a notice delivered electronically before September 3, 2025 to a party who consented before that date; section 76-606 of the Carbon Monoxide Safety Act attaches on a change of tenant occupancy on or after January 1, 2017 or on a permitted interior alteration, repair or fuel-fired-appliance replacement; and section 87-302 of the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act carries an operative date of January 1, 2027, which matters because section 87-303.07's trigger is section 87-302. Those are commencement and transition dates, not sunsets - they turn obligations ON, which is the opposite of the risk this topic is about in a state like California.

title: Lease Translation - No General Duty, But One Statute Names a Lease and It Can Catch You
bodyText: For an ordinary Nebraska residential tenancy there is no translation duty. No statute prescribes lease text verbatim, none sets a minimum type size for a residential lease, and none requires a translation because you advertised, negotiated or did business in another language. You may lease in English to a tenant whose first language is not English, and the lease is not void or voidable for that. ONE STATUTE IS DIFFERENT, AND IT NAMES A LEASE EXPRESSLY. Section 76-2727, in the Nebraska Foreclosure Protection Act: 'Any equity purchase contract, RENTAL AGREEMENT, LEASE, or option or right to repurchase and any notice, conveyance, lien, encumbrance, consent, or other document or instrument signed by a homeowner shall be written in English and shall be accompanied by a written translation from English into any other language principally spoken by the homeowner, certified by the person making the translation as a true and correct translation of the English version. The translated version shall be presumed to have equal status and credibility as the English version.' Read the three conditions, because together they are narrow. (1) The document must be signed by a 'homeowner', which section 76-2711 defines as 'the owner of a residence in foreclosure, including a vendee under a contract for deed'. (2) Section 76-2712 defines a residence in foreclosure as one 'occupied as the HOMEOWNER'S principal place of residence' against which a foreclosure action has commenced - so the Act does not reach a rented investment property, and it creates no duty between an ordinary landlord and an ordinary tenant. (3) The duty therefore lands on you in one real situation: a SALE-LEASEBACK, where you buy a home out of foreclosure from its occupying owner and lease it back to them. In that transaction you are the equity purchaser, the lease is a document 'signed by a homeowner', and it must be in English with a certified translation into any other language principally spoken by that person. The translation is not a courtesy copy - it is 'presumed to have equal status and credibility as the English version', so an inaccurate translation is a version of your lease that can be enforced against you. Use a translator willing to certify. Section 76-2718 does the same for a foreclosure consulting contract, and section 76-2728 provides the penalty for violations of the Act. THE CONTRAST THAT SHOWS THE GENERAL SILENCE IS DELIBERATE. Nebraska does have a translate-because-you-did-business-in-the-language rule, and it is not in the landlord-tenant act. Section 69-1604(3): a seller 'who in the ordinary course of business regularly uses a language other than English in any advertising or other solicitation of customers or in any printed forms for use by buyers or in any face-to-face negotiations with buyers, shall give the notice described in this section to a buyer whose principal language is such other language, both in English and in the other language.' But section 69-1601(1) confines a 'home solicitation sale' to 'a sale, lease, or rental of consumer GOODS OR SERVICES' - a dwelling is neither, so the rule does not reach a lease of a home. The legislature wrote the California-style trigger once, for consumer goods, and did not write it for housing. FINALLY, A FORMATTING POINT OFTEN MISSTATED: Nebraska imposes no minimum POINT SIZE on a residential lease, but it is not true that formatting never matters. Section 25-2602.02 requires a statement in capitalized, underlined type adjoining the signature block of any standardized agreement in which binding arbitration is the sole remedy, and a strict-compliance failure can make the arbitration clause voidable and unenforceable.

title: Barring Someone From the Property - How Nebraska's Trespass Statute Works, and Why Your Tenant Can Undo It
bodyText:
You can bar a non-tenant from your property, and Nebraska's criminal trespass statute is the tool.

THE TWO DEGREES. Section 28-520(1)(a): first degree criminal trespass is entering or secretly remaining 'in any building or occupied structure, or any separately secured or occupied portion thereof, knowing that he or she is not licensed or privileged to do so' - a CLASS I MISDEMEANOR. An apartment building's interior common areas - lobbies, hallways, laundry rooms, stairwells - are inside a building, so this is the provision that fits an indoor ban, and the standard is actual, subjective knowledge (State v. Stanko, 304 Neb. 675 (2019)).

Section 28-521(1): second degree criminal trespass is entering or remaining 'in any place' knowing one is not licensed or privileged to do so, where notice against trespass is given by '(a) Actual communication to the actor; or (b) Posting in a manner prescribed by law or reasonably likely to come to the attention of intruders; or (c) Fencing or other enclosure manifestly designed to exclude intruders'. That is a CLASS III MISDEMEANOR, and it steps up to a CLASS II MISDEMEANOR under section 28-521(5) 'if the offender defies an order to leave personally communicated to him or her by the owner of the premises or other authorized person.'

So the practical hierarchy is clear: a posted sign or a written ban letter builds the second-degree case; an order to leave delivered to the person's face, by you or by your authorized manager, raises it. Deliver the ban in writing, keep proof of delivery, say exactly what property it covers and for how long, and record the date and the person who gave any in-person order to leave.

Section 28-521(2) separately covers drones: intentionally causing an unmanned aircraft to enter into, upon or above the property of another - 'including such property owned by such person and leased or rented to another' - with intent to observe someone without consent in a place of solitude or seclusion. Note those words: as a landlord you can commit that offence on your own rented property.

FOUR AFFIRMATIVE DEFENCES, AND TWO OF THEM MATTER TO YOU. Section 28-522 gives an affirmative defence that (1) the building was abandoned; (2) 'the premises were at the time open to members of the public and the actor complied with all lawful conditions imposed on access to or remaining in the premises'; (3) 'the actor reasonably believed that the owner of the premises or other person empowered to license access thereto would have licensed him to enter or remain'; or (4) the actor was portaging a nonpowered vessel.

Defence (2) is why a leasing office, a public-facing lobby or a commercial space on the ground floor is weak ground for a ban - impose and document the lawful conditions of access if you want the ban to hold there.

DEFENCE (3) IS THE ONE THAT DEFEATS MOST APARTMENT BANS. A tenant is a person empowered to license access to the leased unit, and the printed annotation to section 28-522 is explicit: 'A valid license from ANY owner or other person empowered to license access to a property is sufficient to show that a defendant reasonably believed that he or she was licensed to be on the premises. A defendant need not show that EVERY owner licensed his or her presence' (State v. McCave, 282 Neb. 500 (2011)). So if your tenant keeps inviting the person you barred, a trespass charge as to the unit, and probably as to the route to it, is likely to fail.

SO AIM AT THE TENANT INSTEAD. Section 76-1431(4) lets you terminate on five days' written notice with no right to cure where a 'guest, or other person who is under the tenant's control or who is present upon the premises with the tenant's consent' engages in violent criminal activity, the illegal sale of a controlled substance, or other activity threatening the health or safety of other tenants, you or your employees or agents - subject to the section 76-1431(5) protections for a tenant or household member who sought a protective order, reported the activity to law enforcement, or obtained qualified-third-party certification of domestic violence.

For conduct below that threshold, section 76-1421(7) makes the tenant responsible for requiring 'other persons on the premises with his consent' to behave, enforceable through section 76-1431(1). Do not draft a clause saying you may bar a person from the tenant's unit - the tenant's licensing power is real and the clause would promise what you cannot deliver. Draft the tenant's own covenant instead.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Act in Nebraska - and What Does the Same Work
bodyText: Nebraska has no truth-in-renting statute. There is no act of that name, no state-published tenant-rights statement you must attach or deliver, no Attorney General lease summary, no state-approved or model lease form, and no provision making a lease unenforceable because it failed to carry a prescribed notice about the lease's own terms. New Jersey's and Michigan's regimes, and Delaware's Attorney General summary, have no Nebraska counterpart. THREE NEBRASKA PROVISIONS DO THE SUBSTANTIVE HALF OF THE SAME WORK, AND THEY ARE WHAT YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY BE CHECKING YOUR LEASE AGAINST. (1) Section 76-1415(1) voids four categories of term: the tenant agreeing to 'waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act'; authorizing anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement; agreeing to pay the landlord's or the tenant's attorney's fees; and agreeing to 'the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord' or to indemnify the landlord for that liability or its costs. Section 76-1415(2) makes such a provision unenforceable and - this is the Michigan-style sanction, and Nebraska does have it - 'If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees.' So in Nebraska the penalty attaches to KNOWINGLY using a prohibited term, not to omitting a prescribed notice. (2) Section 76-1412 lets a court that finds a rental agreement or any provision 'unconscionable when made' refuse to enforce the agreement, enforce the rest without the provision, or limit the provision's application, and subsection (2) requires the parties to be given a reasonable opportunity to present evidence 'as to the setting, purpose, and effect of the rental agreement'. (3) Section 76-1413(9) bars requiring a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means as part of or as a condition of entering into or renewing the lease. ONE IMPORTANT LIMIT ON HOW FAR THE SECTION 76-1415(2) PENALTY REACHES. It opens 'A provision prohibited by subsection (1) of this section', so the damages-and-fees remedy is confined to those four categories. It does not reach a section 76-1413(9) violation, and section 76-1413 gives itself no damages remedy either - its subsection (12) attaches only to a subsection (7)(d) failure. Enforcement there runs through section 76-1405(2): 'Any right or obligation declared by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is enforceable by action unless the provision declaring it specifies a different and limited effect.' A row or clause that lumps all of Nebraska's ineffective-term provisions together and attributes the section 76-1415(2) penalty to all of them overstates the exposure for some and understates the remedy route for others. AND NOTE A CONTRAST INSIDE THE SAME CHAPTER, because it shows the URLTA list is narrower than it looks: the Mobile Home Act's section 76-1477(1) prohibits the tenant OR LANDLORD from waiving rights, from agreeing to pay 'the other party's attorney's fees', from exculpating or indemnifying 'the other party' for liability 'arising under law' - not merely for active and actionable negligence - and from agreeing to a designated agent for the sale of the tenant's mobile home, with a two-way damages remedy at section 76-1477(2) for either party. Nebraska's residential exculpation ban is negligence-specific; the park version is not.

title: Removing Someone Who Was Never Your Tenant - Nebraska Has No Squatter Statute, and the Route Depends on One Unsettled Phrase
bodyText: Nebraska has none of the fast squatter remedies other states have passed. There is no sheriff or constable removal on an owner's sworn complaint, no police removal of a transient occupant on an affidavit, no ex parte court removal with a hearing in 24 hours, no lock change after arrest, no squatting crime with a document-production citation, and no treble-fair-market-rent penalty for wrongful use of such a procedure. The word 'squatter' does not appear in Nebraska's statutes at all. You have four real routes, and they are graded. ROUTE 1 - CRIMINAL TRESPASS, for a person with no colour of claim. Section 28-520(1)(a) makes entering or secretly remaining in a building or occupied structure, or any separately secured or occupied portion of one, knowing one is not licensed or privileged to do so, a Class I misdemeanor; section 28-521 covers notice-based trespass elsewhere on the property and steps up to a Class II misdemeanor under section 28-521(5) where the person 'defies an order to leave personally communicated to him or her by the owner of the premises or other authorized person'. Call law enforcement. This is not a possession remedy - it does not give you a writ - but it is the only same-day option. ROUTE 2 - THE URLTA FIVE-DAY NO-CURE ROUTE, which expressly reaches a non-tenant. Section 76-1431(4) opens 'Notwithstanding subsections (1) and (2) of this section or section 25-21,221' and lets you, after five days' written notice of termination and WITHOUT any right to cure, 'file suit and have judgment against any tenant OR OCCUPANT for recovery of possession of the premises' where the tenant, occupant, household member, guest or other person under the tenant's control or present with the tenant's consent engages in violent criminal activity on the premises, the illegal sale of a controlled substance on the premises, or any other activity threatening the health or safety of other tenants, you, or your employees or agents. The word 'occupant' is doing real work there. But it is conduct-gated - it is not a route against a quiet unauthorized occupant - and section 76-1431(5) bars it where the activity was by someone other than the tenant or a household member and the tenant or household member sought a protective order, reported the activity to law enforcement, or obtained qualified-third-party domestic-violence certification. Section 76-1441(2) requires the complaint to set out the incident or incidents. ROUTE 3 - FORCIBLE ENTRY AND DETAINER, chapter 25, which is the one written for this situation. Section 25-21,220(5) allows proceedings 'in all cases when the defendant is a settler or occupier of lands or tenements, without color of title, and to which the complainant has the right of possession' - that is a squatter, described in 1929 language. Section 25-21,221 requires you first 'to notify the adverse party to leave the premises', served at least three days before commencing the action by leaving a written copy with the person or at the usual place of abode, and - the provision that makes this workable against someone whose name you may not know - 'Where the defendant or his usual place of abode cannot be found in the county where the premises are located, such notice may be served by leaving such notice at or posting it on the detained premises.' ROUTE 4 - EJECTMENT under sections 25-2124 and 25-2125, the slow title-based action, where the occupant does assert a claim to the property. THE UNSETTLED PIECE, AND IT DECIDES WHICH OF ROUTES 2 AND 3 YOU USE. Section 25-21,219's final sentence says the forcible entry and detainer statute 'shall not apply to actions for possession of any premises subject to the provisions of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act', and section 76-1440 uses the same phrase from the other side: 'An action for possession of any premises subject to the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act shall be commenced in the manner described by sections 76-1440 to 76-1447.' Nobody has told us what 'premises subject to the Act' means when the occupant has no rental agreement. On one reading it describes the property - a residential rental dwelling is subject to the Act, so even a squatter in it must be removed through sections 76-1440 to 76-1447, which is awkward because section 76-1441(1)(d) requires the complaint to plead 'the requisite compliance with the notice provisions' of an Act that prescribes no notice to a person who never had a rental agreement. On the other reading it describes the occupancy - the Act governs rental agreements (section 76-1448 applies it to 'rental agreements entered into or extended or renewed after July 1, 1975'), so a person occupying without one is outside it and section 25-21,220(5) applies as written. THE CAUTIOUS COURSE, which works on either reading: give BOTH notices - a section 25-21,221 three-day notice to leave, posted on the premises if the person cannot be found in the county, and, where the conduct supports it, a section 76-1431(4) five-day termination notice - plead your statutory authority in the alternative as section 76-1441(1)(a) requires the complaint to state, and let the court pick. WHAT YOU MUST NOT DO is handle it yourself if there is any chance the person is a tenant. Section 76-1430 gives a tenant unlawfully removed or excluded, or whose electric, gas, water or other essential service is willfully and wrongfully interrupted, possession or termination at their election PLUS 'an amount equal to three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages, and a reasonable attorney's fee'. That is a fixed sum requiring no proof of loss, and the whole risk of a lockout is that you were wrong about the person's status.

title: No Unbundled-Parking Rule in Nebraska - But Unbundling Has Two Side Effects Worth Knowing
bodyText: Nebraska has no unbundled-parking statute. Nothing requires you to price parking separately from rent, nothing gives a tenant a right to decline a parking space and pay less, nothing caps what you may charge for a space, and nothing requires a disclosure of the parking charge. California's rule has no Nebraska counterpart. Whether parking is included in rent or charged separately is entirely yours to set under section 76-1414(1), which lets the landlord and tenant 'include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law including rent, term of the agreement, and other provisions governing the rights and obligations of the parties.' TWO SIDE EFFECTS OF UNBUNDLING THAT THE STATUTES DO IMPOSE. First, any deposit you take for a parking space counts against the security-deposit cap. Section 76-1416(1): 'A landlord may not demand or receive security, HOWEVER DENOMINATED, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent, except that a pet deposit not in excess of one-fourth of one month's periodic rent may be demanded or received when appropriate.' The only exception in the subsection is the pet deposit; there is no parking carve-out, so a parking deposit, a gate-fob deposit or a permit deposit is security 'however denominated' and goes inside the one-month figure. Second, unbundling does NOT shrink the deposit base, and the definitions are what settle it. Section 76-1410(13): 'Rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement.' Section 76-1410(14): 'Rental agreement means all agreements, written or oral, between a landlord and tenant, and valid rules and regulations adopted under section 76-1422 embodying the terms and conditions concerning the use and occupancy of a dwelling unit and premises.' And section 76-1410(12): 'Premises means a dwelling unit and the structure of which it is a part and facilities and appurtenances therein and grounds, areas, and facilities held out for the use of tenants generally or whose use is promised to the tenant' - which is a parking lot at the building. So a monthly parking charge payable to you under the lease, or under a side parking agreement with the same tenant for a facility held out to tenants, is rent for Act purposes and does count in 'one month's periodic rent'. The practical upshot: separately pricing parking does not cost you deposit headroom, but a separately labelled parking deposit still has to fit inside the single one-month figure. THE ONE PLACE NEBRASKA DOES REGULATE A PRIVATE LOT IS ACCESSIBILITY AND TOWING, NOT PRICE. Sections 18-1736 and 18-1737 govern the designation of spaces for persons with disabilities in a privately owned offstreet parking facility and the conditions on removing an unauthorized vehicle from one - including a second sign designating a tow-in zone and notifying the police or sheriff's department before the tow. That is a different subject with its own guidance in this library; do not read the absence of a pricing rule as an absence of parking regulation. FINALLY, A SCOPE LIMIT ON THIS ROW. Parking minimums, parking maximums and any requirement to decouple parking from a dwelling unit are, in Nebraska, a matter of municipal zoning, and municipal ordinances are outside this library. If you are developing or converting, check the city.

title: Interest on What the Tenant Owes You - Two Statutes Supply It, and the Lease Clause Most Landlords Use Is Half Void Here
bodyText: Neither Nebraska landlord-tenant act says anything about interest. Sections 76-1401 to 76-1449 and sections 76-1450 to 76-14,111 contain no interest provision at all - no rate, no accrual date, and no requirement that a rate be stated in the lease before it can be charged. So nothing in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act stops you putting an interest term in the lease, and nothing requires you to. THE SMALL-CLAIM STATUTE THAT SUPPLIES INTEREST WITHOUT ANY LEASE TERM, and it fits most landlord claims. Section 25-1801 applies to 'any lawsuit of four thousand dollars or less, regardless of whether the claims are liquidated or assigned' - which covers the great majority of unpaid-rent and damage claims after a tenancy. If you secure a judgment you recover the full judgment and all costs, plus, under section 25-1801(1)(b), 'Interest at the rate of six percent per annum. Such interest shall apply to the amount of the total claim beginning THIRTY DAYS after the date each claim accrued, regardless of assignment, until paid in full', plus, under section 25-1801(3), a statutory attorney's fee 'in no event ... less than ten dollars when the judgment is fifty dollars or less, and when the judgment is over fifty dollars up to four thousand dollars, the attorney's fee shall be ten dollars plus ten percent of the judgment in excess of fifty dollars'. THREE CONDITIONS, AND THEY ARE EASY TO TRIP OVER. (i) A CONDITION PRECEDENT: section 25-1801(1) requires that 'at the expiration of ninety days after each claim accrued, the claim or claims have not been paid or satisfied' before you may file. Sue on day sixty and you may lose the whole section. (ii) You must SECURE A JUDGMENT for the interest and fee - if the defendant pays in full after filing but before judgment, section 25-1801(1) gives you the costs of the lawsuit and nothing more. (iii) The accrual date is defined, and the lease can move it: section 25-1801(4) says 'the date that each claim accrued means the date the services, goods, materials, labor, or money were provided, or the date the charges were incurred by the debtor, UNLESS SOME DIFFERENT TIME PERIOD IS EXPRESSLY SET FORTH IN A WRITTEN AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE PARTIES.' That is a drafting opportunity, and it is the only part of section 25-1801 the lease touches. THE CLAUSE MOST LANDLORDS COPY IS PARTLY VOID IN NEBRASKA. The standard sentence - 'unpaid amounts bear interest at X% and Tenant shall pay Landlord's costs and attorney's fees of collection' - fails on its second half. Section 76-1415(1)(c) prohibits a rental agreement providing that the tenant 'Agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees', and section 76-1415(2) makes such a provision unenforceable and gives the tenant actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees if you deliberately use a provision you know is prohibited. Note that it cuts both ways - a clause promising to pay the TENANT'S fees is equally prohibited. Nebraska gives you fees by statute instead, where they are available: section 76-1431(3) where the tenant's noncompliance is willful; section 76-1437(3) where a holdover is willful and not in good faith, together with the greater of not more than three months' periodic rent or threefold actual damages; and section 25-1801(3) on a small claim. So write the interest term and leave the fee-shift out. THE GENERAL STATUTE, FOR ANY SIZE OF CLAIM. Section 45-104 says: 'Unless otherwise agreed, interest shall be allowed at the rate of twelve percent per annum on money due on any instrument in writing, ... and on money loaned or due and withheld by unreasonable delay of payment.' A written lease is an instrument in writing, so rent due under it can carry twelve percent even when the lease is silent. A rate you put in the lease replaces that twelve percent, so a lower lease rate gives up the difference. On a claim of four thousand dollars or less, whether you get section 25-1801's six percent or section 45-104's twelve is for the court; do not count on more than six percent there unless the lease states a rate. After judgment, section 45-103 sets interest at two percentage points above the 26-week Treasury bill yield, unless the contract agreed a different rate. DRAFTING THE INTEREST RATE. Section 45-101.03(1) validates an agreed rate 'not exceeding sixteen percent per annum' on 'any loan or forbearance of money, goods, or things in action'. Under section 45-105, proof of a higher rate costs you all the interest: you 'recover only the principal, without interest'. Whether unpaid rent is a 'forbearance' is a question only a court could settle. Take the cautious course: keep any lease rate at or below sixteen percent a year. State it as the lesser of your figure and the maximum rate Nebraska law permits. Section 45-101.04(2)'s exception for loans to a corporation, partnership, limited liability company or trust does not help with an individual tenant.

title: Nebraska Has No Usufruct - But It Has the Same Problem Under a Different Name, and Your Lease Can Die With Your Landlord
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS NO USUFRUCT. The word does not appear anywhere in Nebraska's statutes or its constitution. Usufruct is a civil-law institution, and the library's rows on it are Louisiana, Puerto Rico and Guam rows for that reason: in those jurisdictions a usufructuary can lease out property he or she does not own, and the lease ends when the usufruct ends. Nebraska is a common-law state and has no such estate, so none of those rows states Nebraska's law.

BUT DO NOT READ THE ABSENCE AS MEANING THE PROBLEM GOES AWAY. The usufruct rows exist to answer one practical question: what happens to a tenant's lease when the person who signed it as landlord held only a limited, temporary interest in the property? Nebraska answers that question with the life estate and the estate for years instead of the usufruct, and the answer is structurally the same. Section 25-2132 provides that "[t]he owner of an estate in remainder or reversion, may maintain an action for trespass or waste for injuries done to the inheritance, notwithstanding any intervening estate for life or years" - so the remainderman's rights exist and are enforceable DURING the life tenancy, not just after it. The printed annotation to that section reports the direct application: a "[l]essee remaining in possession after death of life tenant becomes liable to the reversioner for reasonable value of the use and occupation of premises" (Guthmann v. Vallery, 51 Neb. 824, 71 N.W. 734 (1897)). Treat that case as a pointer rather than settled law - but it is the one that costs money.

WHAT THIS MEANS WHEN YOU ARE THE LANDLORD. If you hold a life estate, a term-of-years interest, or any other estate that will end on a date or an event outside the lease, you cannot grant a tenant more than you have. Your lease is good against you and good against the tenant; it is not good against the remainderman after your estate ends. Three practical consequences. FIRST, do not grant a term that outruns your own interest; if you do, the tenant's possession after your estate ends is a holdover against the reversioner, who has a claim for the reasonable value of use and occupation. SECOND, section 76-120 limits a waste claim against you to "compensatory damages" and bars "multiple damages" and forfeiture "except in accordance with covenants, agreements or conditions binding such defendants" - the closing words matter, because a covenant in the instrument that created your estate can restore the forfeiture the statute otherwise takes away. Read the instrument, not just the statute. THIRD, the tenant's own protections under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act run against you as "landlord" regardless of how thin your title is - section 76-1410(7) makes the 'owner, lessor, or sublessor' the landlord, whatever the quality of the estate.

WHAT TO DO. If you are letting property you do not own outright, say so in the lease: identify the interest you hold, state the event that would end it, and either match the lease term to it or give the tenant a termination mechanism that fires when your interest does. Nebraska gives you no statutory template for that, which is exactly why it has to be drafted.

A life estate created by will is administered under the Nebraska Probate Code (chapter 30), and an instrument-specific covenant governs over the statutory default under section 76-120's own closing words.

title: Nebraska Does Not Make a Non-Metered Utility Apportionment Unenforceable - and the One Attack That Is Left Is Unconscionability
bodyText:
THE QUESTION OTHER STATES ANSWER, AND NEBRASKA'S ANSWER. Several states make a lease term unenforceable if it requires the tenant to pay for a utility that is not separately metered to the tenant's own unit - Connecticut's version takes effect for leases entered into or renewed on or after October 1, 2026. NEBRASKA HAS NO SUCH PROVISION. There is no statute that voids, limits, or conditions a term apportioning a master-metered or non-separately-metered utility among tenants, no prescribed formula, no required basis (square footage, occupancy, fixture count), no accuracy standard, and no agency with declared authority over a landlord's allocation method in a residential tenancy.

WHY THAT IS A DELIBERATE SILENCE. The Nebraska Legislature wrote an apportionment rule twice, in two neighbouring acts, and did not write one in the residential act. Section 76-873(c)(3), in the Condominium Act, provides that "the costs of utilities not separately metered must be assessed in proportion to usage" - but read the whole subsection, because it is conditional twice over: subsection (c)'s chapeau is "To the extent required by the declaration", and (c)(3) adds "if reasonably determined". And section 76-1482, in the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act, requires the landlord to "provide a written explanation of utility rates, charges, and services to the prospective tenant before the rental agreement is signed unless the utility charges are to be paid by the tenant directly to the utility company." Two acts, two different mechanisms, and the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has neither.

WHAT ACTUALLY CONSTRAINS YOU. Section 76-1414(1) is the enabling provision: the parties "may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law". Section 76-1415(1) is the list of what IS prohibited, and it is a closed list of four - waiver of the tenant's rights or remedies, confession of judgment, an agreement to pay either side's attorney's fees, and exculpation or indemnity for the landlord's active and actionable negligence. An apportionment formula is not on it. So the attack on your allocation method is not voidness; it is SECTION 76-1412 UNCONSCIONABILITY, and that section is unusual in two ways you should know about. First, unconscionability is decided "as a matter of law" and is measured "when made", so it is judged on the bargain at signing, not on how the numbers came out later. Second, subsection (2) lets the court raise it "upon its own motion" - a tenant does not have to plead it - and then "the parties shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present evidence as to the setting, purpose, and effect of the rental agreement". That is an evidentiary hearing about your allocation method that you did not ask for. Section 76-1411 adds an obligation of good faith to "every duty" under the Act and to "every act which must be performed as a condition precedent to the exercise of a right or remedy".

THE THREE THINGS TO DO. (1) STATE THE METHOD IN THE LEASE. Because no statute supplies a default, there is nothing to fall back on if the lease is silent - you will be arguing fair rental value under section 76-1414(2) instead of a formula. State the basis, the billing period, when payment is due, and that you will provide the provider's bill. (2) KEEP THE SUPPLY DUTY OUT OF IT. Section 76-1419(1)(f) makes supplying running water, hot water and reasonable heat your duty; section 76-1419(2) lets you shift that duty only for a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE, in writing and for good consideration, and section 76-1419(3) - the provision for everything else - enumerates no subdivision at all and reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling". So in a duplex or an apartment building, an apportionment clause allocates the COST and cannot touch the DUTY. (3) REMEMBER WHAT YOU ARE COLLECTING. Section 76-1410(13) defines rent as "all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement", so an apportioned utility charge is rent: it is reachable by the section 76-1431(2) nonpayment notice, and it counts in every figure measured in rent, including the section 76-1416(1) one-month security cap.

Check whether a landlord who resells or allocates utility service becomes a regulated utility under chapter 75 (Public Service Commission) or chapter 70 (electric and public power districts).

title: A "Utility Deposit" You Collect Is a Security Deposit in Nebraska - It Counts Against Your One-Month Cap and It Comes Back in Fourteen Days
bodyText:
THE THREE WORDS THAT DECIDE THIS. Section 76-1416(1) says a landlord "may not demand or receive security, HOWEVER DENOMINATED, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent". Calling money a utility deposit, a utility guarantee, a service deposit or an account-transfer deposit does not take it out of section 76-1416. If you collect it, it is security. "However denominated" appears in only four sections of the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy, and this is one of them - the Legislature used the phrase deliberately.

THREE CONSEQUENCES, IN THE ORDER THEY BITE. (1) IT COUNTS AGAINST THE ONE-MONTH CAP. A one-month security deposit plus a separate $150 utility deposit is security in excess of one month's periodic rent. Section 76-1416(1) contains exactly ONE itemised add-on - "a pet deposit not in excess of one-fourth of one month's periodic rent" - and there is no utility-deposit counterpart. The Legislature itemised the one extra deposit it was willing to allow; a utility deposit is not it. (2) IT RETURNS ON THE SAME CLOCK. Under section 76-1416(2), on termination the money "may be applied to the payment of rent and the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or section 76-1421", and "[t]he balance, if any, AND A WRITTEN ITEMIZATION shall be delivered or mailed to the tenant within fourteen days after the date of termination of the tenancy." An unpaid utility bill the tenant owed you is a damage you may apply it to - so you do not need a separate deposit to be protected; you need the itemisation. If the tenant leaves no forwarding address, the statute tells you what to do: mail the balance and the itemisation first class to the last-known address. (3) THE PENALTY IS REAL. Section 76-1416(3): the tenant "may recover the property and money due him or her, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees", and if your failure "is willful and not in good faith", liquidated damages of "one month's periodic rent or two times the amount of the security deposit, whichever is less".

WHAT IF NOBODY CLAIMS IT. Section 76-1416(2) finishes the job for you: "[i]f the mailing is returned as undeliverable, or if the returned balance of the security deposit remains outstanding for one year, it shall be considered abandoned property to be reported and paid to the State Treasurer in accordance with the Uniform Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act" (sections 69-1301 to 69-1329). Do not keep it.

THE OTHER KIND OF UTILITY DEPOSIT - THE ONE THE TENANT PAID THE UTILITY - IS NOT YOURS AND IS NOT ON YOUR CLOCK. Where the tenant holds the account and paid the provider a deposit, that money is governed by section 69-1304(a), which presumes abandoned "[a]ny deposit made by a subscriber with a utility to secure payment for, or any sum paid in advance for, utility services to be furnished in this state, less any lawful deductions, that has remained unclaimed by the person appearing on the records of the utility entitled thereto for more than THREE YEARS after the termination of the services for which the deposit or advance payment was made." Three years, not fourteen days, and the duty is the utility's.
