You have no claim on it, you cannot direct its application to the tenant's rent arrears, and you should not promise a tenant you will chase it.

SELLING THE BUILDING. Section 76-1420(1) relieves you of section 76-1416 liability on a good-faith sale only if you ASSIGN the deposit to the buyer AND give the tenant written notice - and section 76-1416(5) makes "[t]he holder of the landlord's interest in the premises at the time of the termination of the tenancy" bound by the section. Assigning without notice, or giving notice without assigning, leaves you exposed.

Utility tariffs and the Nebraska Administrative Code set what a provider may require as a deposit.

title: No Nebraska Statute Puts a Utility Disclosure In or On Your Lease - and the One Utility Disclosure Nebraska Does Require Is a Separate Sheet Handed Over Before Signing
bodyText:
THE VEHICLE QUESTION, AND NEBRASKA'S ANSWER. Some states not only require a utility disclosure but dictate how it is delivered - attached to the lease as an exhibit, printed on the first page, in type of a stated size, or signed on a separate page. Nebraska requires NONE of that for a residential tenancy. There is no utility disclosure requirement at all in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and therefore nothing about attachment, position, type size or a separate signature.

In the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy, the only section saying a rental agreement "shall contain", "state", "include" or "set forth" something is not a lease: section 76-1605(3), in the Self-Service Storage Act, which requires a storage rental agreement to carry a statement "in bold type". There is no second instance. Neither "attached to the lease" nor "attached to the rental agreement" appears in those chapters.

THE ONLY DISCLOSURE THE URLTA DOES REQUIRE IS NOT A LEASE TERM EITHER - AND THAT CUTS BOTH WAYS. Section 76-1417(1) requires the landlord to "disclose to the tenant IN WRITING AT OR BEFORE THE COMMENCEMENT OF THE TENANCY the name and address of (a) The person authorized to manage the premises; and (b) An owner of the premises or a person authorized to act for and on behalf of the owner for the purpose of service of process and for the purpose of receiving and receipting for notices and demands." Note what it does not say: it does not say "in the rental agreement". A separate sheet complies. But the timing is a trap in the other direction - a lease signed AFTER the tenancy commenced does not satisfy "at or before the commencement", so a landlord relying on the lease as the disclosure vehicle can be late without noticing.

NEBRASKA DID LEGISLATE A UTILITY DISCLOSURE - IN THE OTHER ACT, AND IT CHOSE A SEPARATE PRE-SIGNING SHEET. Section 76-1482, in the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act, provides: "The landlord or any person authorized to enter into a rental agreement on the landlord's behalf shall provide a written explanation of utility rates, charges, and services to the prospective tenant BEFORE THE RENTAL AGREEMENT IS SIGNED unless the utility charges are to be paid by the tenant directly to the utility company." Three things are worth taking from it even though it does not govern an apartment. The duty is discharged by a document given to a PROSPECTIVE tenant before signing, not by a lease clause. It has a built-in off switch - it does not apply where the tenant pays the provider direct. And its existence is what makes the residential silence a legislative choice rather than an oversight: the Legislature wrote this duty in 1984 for one act and has never written it for the other.

NO TYPE-SIZE RULE EITHER, BUT DO NOT OVERSTATE THAT. Mandatory point-size rules exist in Nebraska - twenty sections across the twelve chapters - and not one of them reaches a residential lease. What DOES reach an ordinary standard-form lease is section 25-2602.02, which requires an arbitration statement in "capitalized, underlined type adjoining the signature block of any standardized agreement in which binding arbitration is the sole remedy". That is a formatting rule with no point size, and it has nothing to do with utilities - but it means the sentence "Nebraska imposes no formatting requirement on a lease" is only true if you say "no POINT-SIZE requirement".

WHAT TO DO ANYWAY (A LAWFUL OPTION WORTH TAKING EVEN THOUGH IT IS NOT REQUIRED). Because no statute requires a utility disclosure, no statute supplies a default: if your lease does not say who pays which utility and how a shared cost is allocated, there is no statutory formula to fall back on and you are arguing fair rental value under section 76-1414(2). Put the utility allocation in the lease itself or in an addendum the tenant signs, hand it over before signing, and keep the signed copy. Nebraska will not void your lease for the vehicle you choose - and will not fill the gap if you leave one.

A provider's own disclosure obligations live in the Nebraska Administrative Code and the Public Service Commission's rules. The federal lead-based-paint disclosure rule is the one genuine attachment requirement reaching a Nebraska lease, and it is federal, not state, law.

title: Nebraska Gives You No Lawful Way to Cut Off a Submetered Tenant - and the Price Is a Fixed Three Months' Rent
bodyText:
TEXAS HAS A PROCEDURE. NEBRASKA HAS A PROHIBITION. Where a landlord submeters electricity and resells it, Texas regulates the interruption - notice, timing, restoration, the lot. Nebraska has no such regime at all: the words "submeter", "submetering", "master meter", "shared meter" and "single meter" appear NOWHERE in the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy. What Nebraska has instead is section 76-1430, and it does not care whether the meter is yours.

THE OPERATIVE SENTENCE, IN FULL. "If the landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises or willfully and wrongfully diminishes services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water or other essential service to the tenant, the tenant may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement and, in either case, recover an amount equal to three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages, and a reasonable attorney's fee. If the rental agreement is terminated the landlord shall return all prepaid rent and security recoverable under section 76-1416."

FIVE THINGS IN THAT SENTENCE THAT COST MONEY. (1) "CAUSING THE INTERRUPTION" reaches indirect routes - not paying the provider on an account in your name, directing a city to discontinue service, pulling a breaker, removing a fuse, closing a valve. It is not limited to you walking out to the meter. (2) THREE MONTHS' PERIODIC RENT IS A FIXED SUM, NOT A CEILING. The tenant does not prove what the lost service was worth; the number is the number. Nebraska's other figures are shaped differently - section 76-1426 and section 76-1437(3) are ceilings, section 76-1438(2) is a floor - and section 76-1430 is the fixed one. (3) THE FEE AWARD IS NOT DISCRETIONARY LANGUAGE. "[A]nd a reasonable attorney's fee" sits in the same breath as the damages. (4) THE TENANT CHOOSES. Possession or termination, at the tenant's election, and on termination you return all prepaid rent AND the security recoverable under section 76-1416. (5) THERE IS NO NONPAYMENT EXCEPTION. Nothing in section 76-1430 makes the tenant's failure to pay a submeter bill a defence, and nothing in the Act makes self-help interruption a remedy for nonpayment. Your remedy for an unpaid utility charge is the same as for unpaid rent - section 76-1410(13) makes it rent ("all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement"), so the section 76-1431(2) nonpayment notice and the sections 76-1440 to 76-1447 possession action reach it.

AND THE SUPPLY DUTY RUNS UNDERNEATH ALL OF IT. Section 76-1419(1)(f) requires you to "[s]upply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat", and section 76-1419(1)(d) to maintain "in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances ... SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her". Two consequences. The "or required to be supplied" half means a submeter or a utility connection you installed voluntarily becomes a thing you must keep in good and safe working order for as long as it is there. And the duty cannot be delegated away in an apartment: section 76-1419(2) permits shifting subdivisions (1)(e) and (1)(f) only for a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE, in writing and for good consideration, while section 76-1419(3) - the provision for every other unit - enumerates no subdivision at all and reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling".

IF THE INTERRUPTION WAS NOT WILFUL, THE TENANT STILL HAS A REMEDY. Section 76-1427(1) applies where the landlord "deliberately or NEGLIGENTLY fails to supply running water, hot water, or heat, or essential services": after written notice the tenant may "[p]rocure reasonable amounts of hot water, running water, heat and essential services during the period of the landlord's noncompliance and DEDUCT THEIR ACTUAL AND REASONABLE COST FROM THE RENT", recover diminution-in-value damages, or procure substitute housing and stop paying rent for the period. If the failure is deliberate the tenant adds the value of the substitute housing up to one periodic rent, and "in any case under this subsection reasonable attorney's fees". That procure-and-deduct right is the ONLY one in chapter 76 - Nebraska has no general repair-and-deduct - and it is the reason an essential-services failure is in a different class from an ordinary repair complaint. Section 76-1427(3) gives you the three defences that exist: no right arises until the tenant gives WRITTEN notice; none arises where the condition was caused by the tenant, a family member, or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent; and "[t]his section is not intended to cover circumstances beyond the landlord's control."

THE CONTRAST THAT SHOWS THE LEGISLATURE MEANT IT. Nebraska's Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act has its own version at section 76-14,100, and it differs in both directions: the liquidated-damages figure is "not to exceed ONE AND ONE-HALF months' periodic rent" - a CEILING and half the size - but the park tenant may also "require the RESTORATION of essential services", a remedy the residential Act does not give. So the Legislature wrote this provision twice, chose a bigger and fixed number for ordinary residential tenancies, and withheld the restoration remedy there. Neither point is an accident.

AND THE DISCONNECTION ARTICLE CONFIRMS IT RATHER THAN RESCUING YOU. Sections 70-1601 to 70-1615 are Nebraska's utility disconnection article, reachable from the landlord-tenant chapters only through section 28-515.02(1)(c)'s cross-reference. Section 70-1615 sets out when the article steps aside: sections 70-1602 to 70-1614 "shall not apply to any disconnections or interruptions of services made necessary BY THE UTILITY for reasons of REPAIR OR MAINTENANCE or to protect the HEALTH OR SAFETY of the domestic subscriber or of the general public." Those are the utility's own grounds. The article does not carve out a landlord-requested interruption and nothing in it authorises one - so there is no statutory procedure anywhere in Nebraska by which a landlord may lawfully interrupt a submetered tenant's service, and the only provision on point remains the prohibition in section 76-1430. Two further points from the same article: section 70-1602 excludes "businesses of any nature" from "domestic subscriber", so the seven-day notice and the reasonable-cost fee cap in section 70-1605 do not protect an account in your company's name; and section 70-1607 requires every covered utility to establish a third-party notice procedure, which is the lawful way to learn of a pending shutoff.

§§ 70-1603 and 70-1604 are the VILLAGE-owned municipal utility track expressly carved out of § 70-1605.

title: Keeping the Utility Account in Your Name Costs You the Seven-Day Notice and the Fee Cap - and You Keep the Duty Either Way
bodyText:
THE TRADE-OFF NOBODY TELLS YOU ABOUT, AND IT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THIS ROW. Nebraska's utility disconnection article, sections 70-1601 to 70-1615, gives a residential account holder real protection: under section 70-1605 a utility furnishing water, natural gas or electricity at retail may not discontinue service to a DOMESTIC SUBSCRIBER for nonpayment without notice, "[s]ervice shall not be discontinued for at least SEVEN DAYS after notice is sent or given" with "HOLIDAYS AND WEEKENDS... EXCLUDED from the seven days", a mailed or electronic notice must be "conspicuously marked as to its importance", electronic notice may be used only where "the subscriber has specifically elected" it, and the utility "shall not charge a fee for the discontinuance or reconnection of utility service that EXCEEDS THE REASONABLE COSTS of providing such service".

NONE OF THAT PROTECTS AN ACCOUNT IN YOUR NAME. Section 70-1602 defines "domestic subscriber" purely as an EXCLUSION: it "shall not include municipalities, cities, villages, political subdivisions, companies, corporations, partnerships, limited liability companies, or BUSINESSES OF ANY NATURE." So every protection in sections 70-1602 to 70-1614 - the seven days, the conspicuous marking, the dispute conference, the appeal, the reasonable-cost fee cap - turns on WHO HOLDS THE ACCOUNT. Hold it through your LLC, corporation or partnership and it is not a domestic subscriber's account. A landlord who keeps utilities in the landlord's name to avoid transfer gaps gains control and simultaneously gives up every notice and appeal right the tenant would have had on that service.

AND YOU KEEP THE DUTY. Section 76-1419(1)(f) requires you to "[s]upply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat", with two exceptions written into the subdivision itself: where the building "is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose", and where "the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation WITHIN THE EXCLUSIVE CONTROL OF THE TENANT AND supplied by a direct public utility connection" - and that second exception needs BOTH limbs, so a unit with its own water heater that you pay for on a master account does not satisfy it. You cannot write it away in a multi-unit building either: section 76-1419(2) allows a tenant to take on subdivisions (1)(e) and (1)(f) only for a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE, in writing, for good consideration, in good faith and not to evade the landlord's obligations, while section 76-1419(3) - the provision that governs every other unit - enumerates no subdivision at all and reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling". So the landlord-held account is the arrangement in which you have the least warning and the most liability.

ONE EDGE IS GENUINELY UNSETTLED: whether a NATURAL-PERSON landlord - an individual letting a house in their own name, with no entity - is a "business of any nature" within section 70-1602. The phrase is broad and sits in a list of business entities, which points one way; section 70-1602's chapeau is "unless the context otherwise requires" and a single owner letting one house is not obviously a business, which points the other. No annotation addresses it and the text cannot settle it. Plan on the exclusion applying to any rental operation, because the cost of being wrong is the loss of the seven-day notice on a service you are obliged to supply.

THE BETTER ARRANGEMENT, AND IT IS IN THE SAME ARTICLE. Section 70-1607: "Each utility subject to section 70-1603 or 70-1605 SHALL ESTABLISH A THIRD-PARTY NOTICE PROCEDURE for the notification of a DESIGNATED THIRD PARTY of any proposed discontinuance of service and shall advise its subscribers, including new subscribers, of the availability of such procedures." The utility's duty to establish it is mandatory; using it is the subscriber's choice. So put the account in the TENANT'S name and have the tenant designate YOU as the third party. You get notice before the service to your building is cut - which is the frozen-pipes problem a landlord-held account is usually chosen to solve - and the tenant keeps the section 70-1602 protections. Ask for it as the tenant's election, because the statute gives the designation to the subscriber.

IF YOU DO KEEP THE ACCOUNT, THIS IS THE REMEDY THE TENANT HAS AND IT COMES OUT OF YOUR RENT. Section 76-1427(1) applies where "contrary to the rental agreement or section 76-1419 the landlord deliberately or negligently fails to supply running water, hot water, or heat, or essential services". On written notice specifying the breach, the tenant may "(a) Procure reasonable amounts of hot water, running water, heat and essential services during the period of the landlord's noncompliance and DEDUCT THEIR ACTUAL AND REASONABLE COST FROM THE RENT; (b) Recover damages based upon the diminution in the fair rental value of the dwelling unit; or (c) Procure reasonable substitute housing during the period of the landlord's noncompliance, in which case the tenant is excused from paying rent for the period". If the failure is DELIBERATE the tenant adds, on top of (a) or (c), "the actual and reasonable cost or fair and reasonable value of the substitute housing not in excess of an amount equal to the periodic rent, and IN ANY CASE UNDER THIS SUBSECTION REASONABLE ATTORNEY'S FEES" - the fee award attaching to the whole subsection, not only to the deliberate cases. THAT IS THE ONLY PROCURE-AND-DEDUCT RIGHT IN NEBRASKA: there is no general repair-and-deduct in chapter 76, which is why keeping this one bill current matters more than any other.

YOUR THREE DEFENCES, ALL IN SECTION 76-1427(3). No right arises until the tenant has given WRITTEN notice. None arises where the condition was caused by "the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of his family, or other person on the premises with his consent" - which is the answer where the tenant held the account and let it lapse. And "[t]his section is not intended to cover circumstances beyond the landlord's control." Section 76-1427(2) adds a point in your favour: a tenant who proceeds under section 76-1427 "may not proceed under section 76-1425 as to that breach".

IF IT WAS WILFUL, THE NUMBER CHANGES SHAPE. Section 76-1430 catches a landlord who "willfully and wrongfully diminishes services to the tenant by interrupting or CAUSING THE INTERRUPTION OF electric, gas, water or other essential service". Letting a utility shut off an account in your name because you did not pay it is "causing the interruption". The tenant may recover possession or terminate and, either way, recover "an amount equal to three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages, and a reasonable attorney's fee" - a FIXED sum needing no proof of loss - and on termination you return all prepaid rent and the security recoverable under section 76-1416. And note that section 70-1615 carves the disconnection article aside only for interruptions "made necessary by the utility for reasons of repair or maintenance or to protect the health or safety" - NOT for a landlord-requested one, and nothing in the article authorises one.

FOUR THINGS NEBRASKA DOES NOT GIVE EITHER SIDE. (1) NO RECEIVERSHIP. There is no tenant petition for a rent receiver when a landlord does not pay the heat bill - the Missouri model. Measured over chapter 76, "receiver" appears in seven sections and NOT ONE is inside the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act. (2) NO RENT ESCROW. Section 76-1428(1) says the court "from time to time MAY order" a deposit in a possession action - permissive and judicial, not a tenant's self-help route. (3) NO DUTY TO IDENTIFY YOUR TENANTS TO THE UTILITY, and no liquidated damages for failing to; that is a Wisconsin-style provision Nebraska has not enacted. (4) NO MASTER-METER NOTIFICATION DUTY: "master meter", "shared meter" and "single meter" appear nowhere in the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy.

TWO THINGS THAT SURVIVE WHOEVER HOLDS THE ACCOUNT. SEWER FOLLOWS THE PROPERTY. Section 18-509(1): in any city or village, sewer charges "shall be charged to each property served by the sewerage system, SHALL BE A LIEN UPON THE PROPERTY SERVED, and may be collected either from the owner or the person, firm, or corporation requesting the service". Whose name is on the account does not matter to the city. AND THE TENANT CAN GET SERVICE IN THEIR OWN NAME EVEN AFTER AN OLD WRITE-OFF. Section 70-1601: "No applicant for the services of a public or private utility company furnishing water, natural gas, or electricity at retail in this state shall be denied service because of unpaid bills for similar service which are not collectible at law because of statutes of limitations or discharge in bankruptcy proceedings." Given section 70-1602, the tenant's own name is where you want the account - and section 70-1601 is what makes that possible for a tenant with stale arrears.

WHAT TO DO. Decide deliberately, not by inertia. Default to the tenant's name plus a section 70-1607 designation. Where you must hold the account - a master-metered building, a short gap at turnover - treat the bill as a non-negotiable monthly payment ranking with the mortgage, because you will get no seven-day letter; allocate the cost in the lease (section 76-1414(1) permits any term "not prohibited by" the Act, and section 76-1410(13) makes what you collect rent, reachable by the section 76-1431(2) seven-day nonpayment notice); and never let an arrears dispute become a shutoff.

WHAT ELSE A DOMESTIC SUBSCRIBER GETS, AND A BUSINESS ACCOUNT GIVES UP. Section 70-1606(1) requires the notice to state the reason, the disconnection date, the right to a conference, and the right to an installment plan. Under section 70-1606(1)(g), a physician's, physician assistant's or advanced practice registered nurse's certificate of a household member's serious illness or handicap, filed within five days, postpones disconnection "for a period of at least thirty days". Sections 70-1608 to 70-1611 give a conference within fourteen days of a request. Under section 70-1609, a written dispute statement means "a conference shall be held before the utility may discontinue service". Section 70-1611 allows termination "only as a measure of last resort". Sections 70-1612 and 70-1613 add an appeal hearing with counsel and access to the utility's file. A VILLAGE-owned utility follows its own track: section 70-1603 requires written notice by mail "at least seven days prior to termination" (with no weekend exclusion), and section 70-1604 gives a conference with the village board instead of sections 70-1608 to 70-1614. Sections 16-682 (first-class cities) and 17-538 (second-class cities and villages) make delinquent water charges a lien on the premises. The first-class city sixty-day notice sequence in § 16-682 is described in its own education row.

title: Nebraska's Utility Disconnection Article: Seven Days' Notice, a Capped Reconnection Fee - and None of It Protects an Account in Your Name
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS A UTILITY DISCONNECTION STATUTE. It is sections 70-1601 to 70-1615, and nothing in the landlord-tenant act points to it - the only route in from the chapters that govern a tenancy is a criminal statute's cross-reference, section 28-515.02(1)(c), which makes it unlawful to reconnect service "if the service has been disconnected pursuant to sections 70-1601 to 70-1615".

THE GENERAL RULE, SECTION 70-1605. No public or private utility company, "other than a municipal utility owned and operated by a VILLAGE", furnishing "water, natural gas, or electricity" at retail may discontinue service to a DOMESTIC SUBSCRIBER for nonpayment of a past-due account without first giving notice. The notice must be given "in person, by first-class mail, or by electronic delivery, except that electronic delivery shall only be used if the subscriber has SPECIFICALLY ELECTED to receive such notices by electronic delivery", and a mailed or electronic notice "shall be CONSPICUOUSLY MARKED as to its importance". Then: "Service shall not be discontinued for at least SEVEN DAYS after notice is sent or given. HOLIDAYS AND WEEKENDS SHALL BE EXCLUDED from the seven days." And the fee is capped - a utility "shall not charge a fee for the discontinuance or reconnection of utility service that EXCEEDS THE REASONABLE COSTS of providing such service."

AND HERE IS THE PART THAT RUNS AGAINST YOU. Section 70-1602 defines "domestic subscriber" purely as an EXCLUSION: it "shall not include municipalities, cities, villages, political subdivisions, companies, corporations, partnerships, limited liability companies, or BUSINESSES OF ANY NATURE." Every protection in the article - the seven days, the conspicuous marking, the conference, the appeal, the reasonable-cost fee cap - therefore turns on WHO HOLDS THE ACCOUNT. An account in the name of your LLC, corporation or partnership is not a domestic subscriber's account, and the article's protections do not attach to it. A tenant with service in their own name gets seven working days and a capped reconnection fee; the same service on your company's account may get neither.

THAT INVERTS THE USUAL REASON FOR KEEPING UTILITIES IN YOUR OWN NAME. Landlords hold the account to avoid transfer gaps and to control the service. The price, which nothing in the landlord-tenant act tells you, is that you give up every notice and appeal right the tenant would have had on that service - and you keep the duty. Section 76-1419(1)(f) still makes supplying running water, hot water and reasonable heat YOUR obligation; section 76-1427 still gives the tenant procure-and-deduct, diminution damages, substitute housing and "reasonable attorney's fees" if you fail; and section 76-1430 still gives a fixed three months' periodic rent plus a fee where the diminution is wilful and wrongful. A shutoff you did not see coming is still your breach.

ONE EDGE IS GENUINELY UNSETTLED: whether a NATURAL-PERSON landlord renting out property is a "business of any nature" for section 70-1602. The phrase is broad, section 70-1602's chapeau is "unless the context otherwise requires", and no annotation addresses it. Assume the exclusion reaches any rental operation, and plan as if it does.

THE PROVISION YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY USE: SECTION 70-1607. "Each utility subject to section 70-1603 or 70-1605 SHALL ESTABLISH A THIRD-PARTY NOTICE PROCEDURE for the notification of a DESIGNATED THIRD PARTY of any proposed discontinuance of service and shall advise its subscribers, including new subscribers, of the availability of such procedures." The utility's duty to establish the procedure is mandatory; using it is the subscriber's choice. So the right answer to the frozen-pipes problem is NOT to put the account in your name - it is to have the TENANT designate you as the third party on the tenant's own account. You get notice before the service to your building is cut, and the tenant keeps the section 70-1602 protections they would have lost. Ask for it as the tenant's election, because the statute gives the designation to the subscriber and not to you.

WHEN THE ARTICLE STEPS ASIDE: SECTION 70-1615. Sections 70-1602 to 70-1614 "shall not apply to any disconnections or interruptions of services made necessary by the utility for reasons of REPAIR OR MAINTENANCE or to protect the HEALTH OR SAFETY of the domestic subscriber or of the general public." So the article governs nonpayment disconnections and carves out the utility's own repair, maintenance and safety work. It does NOT carve out a landlord-requested interruption, and nothing in the article authorises one.

THE REST OF THE ARTICLE, FOR A DOMESTIC SUBSCRIBER. Section 70-1606(1) says what the notice must contain: the reason, the disconnection date, the right to a conference, the right to an installment plan, and the cost of restoration. There is a MEDICAL DEFERRAL. Under section 70-1606(1)(g), a physician's, physician assistant's or advanced practice registered nurse's certificate that a household member has an illness or handicap that disconnection would make "an immediate and serious health hazard", filed within five days of the notice, prevents disconnection "for a period of at least thirty days". Only one postponement is required for each incidence of nonpayment. Sections 70-1608 to 70-1611 give a conference within fourteen days of a request. A written dispute statement means "a conference shall be held before the utility may discontinue service" (section 70-1609), and termination is allowed "only as a measure of last resort" (section 70-1611). Sections 70-1612 and 70-1613 add an appeal hearing with counsel and access to the utility's file. NO STATUTORY WINTER RULE, BUT A NATURAL GAS ONE BY REGULATION. The article has no winter moratorium. The Public Service Commission's rule for the natural gas utilities it regulates (291 NAC 9-013) adds one. It covers investor-owned gas companies, not a city-owned utility or the Metropolitan Utilities District. It bars disconnecting a residential customer "on a weekend, legal holiday, or at any time when the Utility's business offices are not open" (013.04). From November 1 to March 31 it adds "an additional thirty (30) days" before disconnection (013.05). It bars any winter disconnection of a customer certified for low-income energy assistance (013.05(B)). And it lets the Commission order a temporary ban in extremely severe weather (013.05(A)). Electricity and water carry no state winter rule; Nebraska's electricity is public power, so check the district's own policy.

TWO MORE THINGS YOU ALREADY HAVE TO WORK WITH. In a VILLAGE, section 70-1605 does not apply. Section 70-1603 requires the village utility to give "written notice by mail... at least seven days prior to termination", with no weekend exclusion and no in-person or electronic option. Section 70-1604 gives a conference with the village board of trustees in place of sections 70-1608 to 70-1614. And the printed annotation to section 18-503 reports that an "[o]rdinance authorizing water supply to be shut off for nonpayment of delinquent sewer charges is not in conflict with this section" (Michelson v. City of Grand Island, 154 Neb. 654, 48 N.W.2d 769 (1951)); in a city with such an ordinance an unpaid SEWER bill can end the WATER service, and under section 18-509(1) the sewer charge is "a lien upon the property served" collectible "either from the owner or the person, firm, or corporation requesting the service".

SECTION 70-1601, THE ONE THAT HELPS AT TURNOVER. "No applicant for the services of a public or private utility company furnishing water, natural gas, or electricity at retail in this state shall be denied service because of unpaid bills for similar service which are not collectible at law because of statutes of limitations or discharge in bankruptcy proceedings." So a tenant whose old arrears are time-barred or discharged can still put service in their own name - which, given section 70-1602, is where you want it.

AND WHATEVER CAUSED THE SHUTOFF, DO NOT RECONNECT IT YOURSELF. Section 28-515.02(1)(c) makes reconnection without the supplier's knowledge and consent a Class III misdemeanor where the service was disconnected under this article, and section 28-515.02(2) makes proof of the reconnection "prima facie evidence of the guilt of the person in possession of the premises". Call the supplier.

In a public-power state, individual utility tariffs and public power district rate schedules may carry their own disconnection procedure.

title: No Submetering Disclosure Regime in Nebraska - No Unit Threshold, No Billing Limits, No Late-Fee Cap, and the Unpaid Charge Is Evictable Rent
bodyText:
WHAT OTHER STATES HAVE HERE, AND WHAT NEBRASKA HAS. In Colorado, Texas, Arizona, California, Minnesota and Maryland a landlord who submeters or ratio-bills a utility walks into a disclosure regime: prescribed text in the lease, a building-size threshold, a cap on what may be billed, a cap on the late fee, sometimes a bar on disconnection or eviction for the unpaid charge, sometimes a type-size rule and a separate signed page. NEBRASKA HAS NONE OF IT. The words "submeter", "submetering", "sub-meter", "master meter", "shared meter" and "single meter" appear in NO section of the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy, and "utility allowance" and "ratio utility" appear in none either. There is no prescribed disclosure, no threshold at five units or more than five or any other number, no accuracy or calibration standard, no billing-interval rule, no cap on the charge, no late-fee cap, and no type-size rule.

NEBRASKA WROTE THE DISCLOSURE ONCE, FOR THE OTHER ACT. Section 76-1482, in the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act: "The landlord or any person authorized to enter into a rental agreement on the landlord's behalf shall provide a written explanation of utility rates, charges, and services to the prospective tenant before the rental agreement is signed unless the utility charges are to be paid by the tenant directly to the utility company." That is the only utility-billing disclosure duty in Nebraska law, it dates from 1984, it applies to mobile home parks and not to apartments, and its existence is what makes the residential silence a legislative choice rather than an oversight. The condominium analogue, section 76-873(c)(3), allocates "the costs of utilities not separately metered ... in proportion to usage" - but only "[t]o the extent required by the declaration" and only "if reasonably determined", so it is doubly conditional and is not a disclosure rule at all.

THE FOUR PLACES WHERE THE NEBRASKA ANSWER IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE REGULATED STATES', AND ALL FOUR FAVOUR YOU. (1) THE UNPAID SUBMETER CHARGE IS RENT. Section 76-1410(13): "Rent means ALL PAYMENTS to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement." (2) SO IT IS EVICTABLE. Section 76-1431(2): "If rent is unpaid when due and the tenant fails to pay rent within SEVEN CALENDAR DAYS after written notice by the landlord of nonpayment and his or her intention to terminate the rental agreement if the rent is not paid within that period of time, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." The states that bar eviction for an unpaid utility charge have said so expressly; Nebraska has not. (3) THERE IS NO LATE-FEE CAP. No Nebraska statute constrains a residential late fee - in chapter 76, "late fee" and "late charge" appear in four sections (sections 76-874, 76-1605, 76-1708 and 76-1711) and NOT ONE is inside the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act. If you want a benchmark, the Legislature wrote its own view of a reasonable late fee in the Rental-Purchase Agreement Act, section 69-2110(1)(d): five dollars or three, with a five or three business-day grace period, once per accrued payment, and no fee against a timely payment. That is a drafting guide, not a limit. (4) THERE IS NO TYPE-SIZE RULE. Mandatory point-size requirements exist in twenty sections across the twelve chapters and not one reaches a residential lease.

BUT CHECK ONE FORMATTING RULE BEFORE YOU CONCLUDE YOUR LEASE HAS NO FORMATTING RULES. Section 25-2602.02 requires an arbitration statement in "capitalized, underlined type adjoining the signature block of any standardized agreement in which binding arbitration is the sole remedy", with no point size at all. It has nothing to do with utilities, but it is why the sentence "Nebraska imposes no formatting requirement on a lease" has to be narrowed to "no POINT-SIZE requirement". If your lease sends disputes to arbitration as the sole remedy, that rule reaches it.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD OF COMPLYING WITH A RULE THAT DOES NOT EXIST. Because nothing requires a disclosure, nothing supplies a default - and the gap runs against you, not against the tenant. Section 76-1414(1) lets you include any term "not prohibited by" the Act; section 76-1414(2) is what happens if you do not ("[i]n absence of agreement, the tenant shall pay as rent the fair rental value"), which is an argument, not a formula. So write it down: which utilities are submetered, what the meter measures, the unit rate or the method of deriving it from the provider's bill, the billing period, the due date, that you will provide the provider's bill, and that the charge is rent. Then hand it over before signing and keep the signed copy - that is what section 76-1482 requires in a park, and it is the sensible practice in an apartment even though no statute compels it. Two Nebraska limits on how far a clause can go: section 76-1415(1) is a closed list of four prohibited provisions, and section 76-1412 lets a court find a provision unconscionable "as a matter of law" and measured "when made", on its own motion under section 76-1412(2), with an evidentiary hearing "as to the setting, purpose, and effect of the rental agreement".

ONE QUESTION COULD CHANGE THE ANSWER: whether a landlord who submeters and resells utility service becomes a regulated utility under chapter 75 (Public Service Commission) or chapter 70 (electric and public power districts) - and so picks up a tariff-level disclosure or billing duty from a source other than the landlord-tenant act. Check it before you rely on the answer above. Nebraska's utility disconnection article, §§ 70-1601 to 70-1615, answers a different question: it regulates the utility's notice to its own customer, not a landlord's billing of a tenant. Do NOT reason from section 25-21,275(6)'s wide definition of "Utility" to a regulatory classification: that definition serves the private diversion remedy in sections 25-21,275 to 25-21,278 and nothing else.

title: Nebraska Caps Your Delivered Water at 115 Degrees - in Any Building With More Than One Unit, on Every Tub or Shower Installed Since 1987, and a City Plumbing Permit Does Not Excuse It
bodyText:
THERE IS A HARD NUMBER AND IT IS NOT IN THE LANDLORD-TENANT ACT. Section 71-1569(1): "all bathtubs and showers installed in buildings which contain MORE THAN ONE DWELLING UNIT after August 30, 1987, shall be equipped with either a PRESSURE BALANCING OR THERMOSTATIC-MIXING scald prevention device which is designed and installed to prevent (a) sudden unanticipated changes in the temperature of the water delivered and (b) the temperature of the water delivered from exceeding ONE HUNDRED FIFTEEN DEGREES FAHRENHEIT." Section 71-1569(2) excludes only showers and bathtubs installed in modular housing units as defined in section 71-1557, manufactured homes as defined in section 71-4603, and recreational vehicles as defined in section 71-4603.

FOUR THINGS TO GET RIGHT, BECAUSE EACH IS EASY TO GET WRONG IN THE EXPENSIVE DIRECTION.

(1) IT IS A MULTI-UNIT DUTY, AND BEING A LANDLORD IS WHAT BRINGS YOU IN. "[B]uildings which contain more than one dwelling unit" reaches an apartment building and a duplex, and does not reach a single-family rental. Note the polarity: Nebraska's other safety and licensing provisions repeatedly carve out the owner-occupier and so cannot be used by a landlord. This one is the reverse - it attaches BECAUSE the building is multi-unit.

(2) THE TRIGGER IS THE FIXTURE'S INSTALLATION DATE, NOT THE BUILDING'S AGE. The words are "bathtubs and showers INSTALLED ... after August 30, 1987". So a 1960s fourplex whose shower you replace this year acquires the duty for that fixture. "My building predates 1987" is not an answer, and a row or a contractor telling you otherwise costs you the retrofit later.

(3) IT IS A DEVICE, NOT A THERMOSTAT SETTING. The statute names two types - pressure balancing or thermostatic-mixing - and two separate design objects: preventing sudden unanticipated temperature change AND capping delivered temperature. Turning the tank down does neither reliably, and it runs you into the opposite duty in paragraph (5) below.

(4) A CITY PLUMBING PERMIT DOES NOT EXCUSE IT. Section 18-1920, captioned "Scald prevention device requirements; compliance required", exists for exactly this purpose and says in its entirety: "Nothing in sections 18-1901 to 18-1919 shall be construed to exempt persons from compliance with sections 71-1569 to 71-1571." Sections 18-1901 to 18-1919 are the municipal plumbing-board article. And section 18-1906 gives a metropolitan-class plumbing board power to "grant a variance from the ordinances, rules, and regulations in the kind and size of materials to be used or in the manner in which the work is to be performed", applying "only to a single building", with no occupant notice required - a variance that section 18-1920 puts out of reach of the scald requirement. Satisfying your city inspector under a local code is not satisfying this.

WHO CHECKS, AND WHO CAN BE PROSECUTED - AND THE TWO DO NOT MATCH. Section 71-1570: "Persons employed by political subdivisions to inspect plumbing fixtures shall inspect showers and bathtubs for compliance with section 71-1569." Section 71-1571: "Anyone who installs FOUR OR MORE showers or bathtubs, in a single building, in violation of section 71-1569 shall be guilty of a CLASS V MISDEMEANOR." READ THOSE TWO TOGETHER AND DO NOT COLLAPSE THEM. The DUTY in section 71-1569 is unconditional for a multi-unit building and has no threshold. The CRIMINAL PENALTY reaches only someone who installs four or more fixtures in a single building, and it is addressed to whoever INSTALLS them - your plumber, or you if you do the work in house. So a landlord who replaces one or two showers without a compliant device has breached section 71-1569 and committed no offence; a landlord refitting a whole building has done both.

THAT DOES NOT MAKE A SMALL NON-COMPLIANT INSTALLATION SAFE. Two routes run past the four-fixture threshold. The duty is a plumbing requirement that municipal inspectors are directed to check (section 71-1570). And independently it feeds your habitability duty: section 76-1419(1)(a) requires you to "[s]ubstantially comply, after written or actual notice, with the requirements of the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety", and section 76-1419(1)(d) to "[m]aintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and other facilities and appliances ... SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her" - and "required to be supplied" is the half that catches a device section 71-1569 obliges you to have. A fixture that does not meet section 71-1569 is a candidate section 76-1419 breach with the section 76-1425 and section 76-1427 remedies behind it, and that route has no threshold at all.

(5) AND THE TWO DUTIES PULL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, WHICH IS WHY THE DEVICE IS THE ONLY ANSWER. Section 76-1419(1)(f) requires you to "[s]upply running water and REASONABLE AMOUNTS OF HOT WATER AT ALL TIMES and reasonable heat", subject to two exceptions in the subdivision itself - where the building "is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose", and where "the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation WITHIN THE EXCLUSIVE CONTROL OF THE TENANT AND supplied by a direct public utility connection", which needs BOTH limbs, so a unit with its own heater on your master account does not qualify. Turn the tank down to 115 and you risk failing that; leave it up and you fail section 71-1569 at the tub. A thermostatic mixing or pressure-balancing valve at the fixture serves both at once, which is precisely what section 71-1569 requires.

AND YOU CANNOT DELEGATE EITHER ONE. Section 76-1419(2) lets a tenant take on the (1)(e) and (1)(f) duties only for a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE, in writing, for good consideration, in good faith and not to evade - and a single-family residence is outside section 71-1569 anyway. Section 76-1419(3), the provision for every other unit, enumerates NO subdivision and reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling". So in the multi-unit buildings section 71-1569 actually covers, you cannot make the tenant responsible for the water heater as a class or for its temperature.

WHAT TO DO. (1) Fit a compliant pressure-balancing or thermostatic-mixing device on every tub and shower you install or replace, and on every one installed since 30 August 1987 that lacks one. (2) Record the device type, the fixture and the date for each - section 71-1570 makes this an inspectable item, and the record cannot be reconstructed later. (3) Tell your plumber the statute by number: section 71-1571's misdemeanour falls on the installer, so the person doing the work has their own exposure at four or more fixtures. (4) You MAY tell tenants not to alter or remove the device - section 76-1421(5) already requires the tenant to "[u]se in a reasonable manner all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances", and section 76-1422 lets you adopt a rule to that effect provided, per section 76-1422(6), "the tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement". (5) Do NOT write a clause in which the tenant accepts the water temperature as-is, agrees it is safe, or waives claims about it: section 76-1415(1)(a) voids a term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under" the Act, section 76-1415(1)(d) voids exculpation or indemnity for the landlord's "active and actionable negligence", and section 76-1415(2) gives the tenant actual damages AND reasonable attorney's fees where the landlord deliberately used a provision known to be prohibited. (6) Remember the closing sentence of section 76-1419(1): "The obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state" - your statutory duty and your negligence exposure are separate questions and this row answers only the first.

title: No Waterbed Statute in Nebraska - So You May Simply Ban Them, But You May Not Charge an Extra Deposit for One
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS NO WATERBED LAW IN EITHER DIRECTION. California gives a tenant a qualified right to keep a waterbed and lets the landlord charge an extra deposit for it; Florida has a flotation-bedding provision. Nebraska has neither. The words "waterbed", "water bed", "flotation" and "liquid-filled furniture" appear in NO section of the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy. There is no tenant right to keep one, no notice you must give, no insurance you may compel by statute, and no statutory extra deposit.

WHICH MEANS THE BAN IS THE EASY PART. Section 76-1414(1) lets the parties "include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law", and nothing in section 76-1415(1)'s closed list of four prohibited provisions comes near a waterbed. So a flat lease prohibition is lawful. If you would rather do it by house rule than by lease term, section 76-1422 sets six conditions and two of them are where house rules usually fail: the rule is enforceable "only if ... (3) It applies to all tenants in the premises IN A FAIR MANNER" and "(6) The tenant has notice of it AT THE TIME HE ENTERS INTO THE RENTAL AGREEMENT." A rule adopted later is enforceable only "if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the tenant AND IT DOES NOT WORK A SUBSTANTIAL MODIFICATION OF HIS BARGAIN" - so banning waterbeds mid-tenancy, for a tenant who already has one, is the case that sentence was written for. Put it in the lease, not in a rule adopted afterwards.

AND THE EXTRA DEPOSIT IS THE TRAP. Section 76-1416(1): a landlord "may not demand or receive security, HOWEVER DENOMINATED, in an amount or value in excess of one month's periodic rent, except that a PET DEPOSIT not in excess of one-fourth of one month's periodic rent may be demanded or received when appropriate". That subsection contains EXACTLY ONE itemised add-on and it is the pet deposit. A waterbed deposit is not on the list, so a California-style extra deposit on top of a full month's security is security in excess of the cap, whatever you call it. The consequence is not merely that the charge is bad: under section 76-1416(3) the tenant may recover "the property and money due him or her, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees", and for a willful and not-in-good-faith failure, liquidated damages of "one month's periodic rent or two times the amount of the security deposit, whichever is less".

WHAT PROTECTS YOU INSTEAD, AND IT IS ENOUGH. (1) THE DEPOSIT YOU ALREADY HOLD COVERS IT. Section 76-1416(2) lets the deposit be applied on termination to "the payment of rent and the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or section 76-1421". Water damage from a waterbed the lease prohibited is noncompliance with the rental agreement; water damage from one you permitted is still reachable through section 76-1421(6), by which the tenant must "[n]ot deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or knowingly permit any person to do so". (2) THE DAMAGE CLAIM IS NOT CAPPED BY THE DEPOSIT. Section 76-1416(4) preserves "other damages to which he or she may be entitled", and section 76-1431(3) lets the landlord "recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for any noncompliance by the tenant with the rental agreement or section 76-1421" - with reasonable attorney's fees "[i]f the tenant's noncompliance is willful". (3) THE EVICTION ROUTE EXISTS IF THE BED ITSELF IS THE BREACH. Section 76-1431(1): written notice specifying the acts and omissions, termination on a date not less than thirty days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in fourteen days; and if substantially the same act or omission recurs within six months, termination on at least fourteen days' written notice with NO cure.

IF YOU WANT TO PERMIT WATERBEDS AND INSURE AGAINST THEM, THERE IS A FORM OF WORDS THE LEGISLATURE ITSELF WROTE. You may require a tenant to carry liability insurance, but section 76-1415(1)(d) voids any term by which the tenant "[a]grees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord or to indemnify the landlord for that liability" - so an insurance requirement has to be confined to the TENANT'S negligence, not the landlord's. The Legislature's own definition does exactly that, in the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act at section 76-1475(2): "liability insurance shall mean insurance that protects the landlord from NEGLIGENCE ON THE PART OF THE TENANT AND ANY INVITEES OR GUESTS OF THE TENANT." That provision does not govern an apartment, but the phrase is the narrowing section 76-1415(1)(d) requires, written by the same Legislature - use it.

A floor-loading limit would sit in municipal housing, building and property-maintenance codes; the State Fire Marshal's rules, rather than any NFPA standard, are the operative state fire law; and an insurance policy's own terms are the real source of a waterbed exclusion.

title: No Window Guard Rule and No Bold Lease Notice in Nebraska - and the Proof Is That the Legislature Wrote Exactly This Kind of Mandate for Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText:
NEBRASKA HAS NO WINDOW GUARD REQUIREMENT AND NO WINDOW GUARD NOTICE. New Jersey requires a window-guard notice in the lease in bold type with model text set by regulation; New York City's rule is the best-known version. Nebraska has nothing of the kind. The words "window guard" and "window screen" appear in NO section of the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy, "railing" and "guardrail" in none, and no section is captioned for a window, a balcony, a railing or fall protection. There is no duty to install, no duty on a tenant's request, no notice, no bold type, no model text and no registry of requests.

WHY THAT IS A LEGISLATIVE CHOICE, AND THE PROOF IS IN THE SAME CHAPTER. Nebraska knows exactly how to write a trigger-based safety-device mandate for rental property, because it did so ten years ago. The Carbon Monoxide Safety Act, sections 76-601 to 76-607 (Laws 2015, LB34), puts the duty on "[t]he owner of... a dwelling unit in a multifamily dwelling that is used for rental purposes" and fires it on two triggers: under section 76-606(1), where the unit has a fuel-fired heater or appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage AND the owner on or after January 1, 2017 makes "[a]ny interior alteration, repair, fuel-fired appliance replacement, or addition" for which a permit is required; and under section 76-606(2), on "a change in tenant occupancy on or after January 1, 2017". It then does everything a window-guard statute would do: a pre-occupancy replacement duty for any alarm "stolen, removed, found missing, or found not operational after the previous occupancy" (section 76-606(3)(a)(i)), a duty to supply the batteries "at the time the tenant takes residence" (3)(a)(ii), a duty to replace or fix on the tenant's notice (3)(a)(iii) and (iv), an express allocation of ongoing maintenance to the TENANT (section 76-606(3)(b) and (4)), and a tamper prohibition binding "[n]o person" (section 76-606(5)). The Legislature had the template, used it for carbon monoxide, and has never used it for window guards. That is the strongest form of proof an absence can have.

AND THERE IS NO STATE INSPECTION THAT WOULD FIND A MISSING GUARD EITHER. Section 81-502(1)(c)'s list of premises subject to mandatory State Fire Marshal inspection is a closed list - liquor establishments, foster care, certain health and human services programmes, health care facilities and mobile home parks - and ORDINARY RENTAL HOUSING IS NOT ON IT. So there is no state inspection of a Nebraska apartment building or rental house, and no inspector who would raise this.

WHERE A WINDOW GUARD RULE COULD STILL REACH YOU: YOUR CITY. Municipal housing, building and property-maintenance codes can still reach you. They matter doubly here because of the unnumbered sentence closing section 76-1419(1): "If there exists a minimum housing code applicable to the premises, the landlord's maximum duty under this section SHALL BE DETERMINED BY subdivision (1)(a) of this section." That makes a local code the CEILING on your section 76-1419 duty rather than an addition to it - but it is a real ceiling, which means a local window-guard requirement would be enforceable through section 76-1419(1)(a)'s duty to "[s]ubstantially comply, after written or actual notice, with the requirements of the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety". Check the ordinance.

WHAT YOUR SECTION 76-1419 DUTY DOES COVER, STATED CAREFULLY. Section 76-1419(1)(b) requires you to "[m]ake all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition" - and the printed annotation records that this duty is "not limited under the plain language to conditions arising after commencement of the lease term" (Vasquez v. CHI Properties, 302 Neb. 742, 925 N.W.2d 304 (2019)). Section 76-1419(1)(c) requires you to "[k]eep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition". A window that will not stay shut, a sash with a broken catch or a rotted frame is a repair-and-habitability matter under (1)(b); the absence of a GUARD on a sound window is not, because no code or statute requires one unless your city says so.

IF YOU INSTALL GUARDS ANYWAY (A LAWFUL OPTION, WITH TWO CONSEQUENCES WORTH KNOWING). (1) ONCE IT IS THERE, IT IS YOURS TO MAINTAIN. Section 76-1419(1)(d) reaches facilities and appliances "SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her" - the first half of that phrase, not the second, is what catches a device you fitted voluntarily, and it must be kept "in good and safe working order and condition" for as long as it is there. (2) DO NOT BLOCK AN EGRESS WINDOW. A guard that prevents a bedroom window being used as an emergency exit is a fire-safety question governed by the State Fire Marshal's administrative rules and your city's code, and it is the Fire Marshal's rules rather than any NFPA standard that are the operative state law. Use a releasable or hinged guard and say so in writing.

AND DO NOT PAPER OVER IT WITH A CLAUSE. A term in which the tenant accepts the windows as-is, agrees they are safe for children, waives claims about falls, or indemnifies you is void: section 76-1415(1)(a) voids any term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under" the Act, and section 76-1415(1)(d) voids any term agreeing "to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord or to indemnify the landlord for that liability arising due to active and actionable negligence or the costs connected therewith" - with section 76-1415(2) giving the tenant actual damages AND reasonable attorney's fees where the landlord deliberately used a provision known to be prohibited. What you MAY do is adopt a rule that guards and screens are not to be removed, obstructed or painted, which section 76-1421(5) and section 76-1422 support provided - per section 76-1422(6) - "the tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement"; and note that the closing sentence of section 76-1419(1) keeps your tort exposure separate from your statutory duty ("[t]he obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state").

Municipal housing, building and property-maintenance codes are the only place a Nebraska window-guard duty could live. The State Fire Marshal's administrative rules under § 81-503.01 need only 'conform generally' to NFPA 1 and NFPA 101 (2012 editions), and not where that 'would impose an unduly severe or costly burden without substantially contributing to the safety of persons or property' - so NFPA is not Nebraska law and the rules themselves are.

title: Which Nebraska Notices Must Be in Writing - and What "Written" Has Meant Since September 3, 2025
bodyText:
NEBRASKA'S LANDLORD-TENANT ACT REQUIRES WRITING IN A LOT OF PLACES, AND IN ONE IMPORTANT PLACE IT DOES NOT. Measured across chapter 76, "written notice" appears in thirty-six sections and "in writing" in fifty-nine. Inside the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act the ones you will actually meet are these.

THE LANDLORD'S WRITTEN NOTICES. Section 76-1417(1) - the owner and manager disclosure, "in writing at or before the commencement of the tenancy". Section 76-1416(2) - on termination, the balance of the deposit "and a written itemization" within fourteen days. Section 76-1420(1) and (2) - written notice to the tenant of a conveyance, and of the termination of a manager's management, which is what shifts liability. Section 76-1423(3)(a) - at least twenty-four hours' WRITTEN notice before entry, with the intended purpose and the anticipated window, and note the two prefatory exceptions, "[e]xcept in case of emergency or if it is impracticable to do so". Section 76-1431(1) - written notice specifying the acts and omissions for a material noncompliance, terminating on a date not less than thirty days after receipt if not remedied in fourteen days, with a fourteen-day no-cure route for a recurrence within six months. Section 76-1431(2) - written notice of nonpayment AND of your intention to terminate, with seven calendar days to pay. Section 76-1431(4) - five days' written notice of termination, without a right to cure, for violent criminal activity and the other listed conduct. Section 76-1437(1) and (2) - seven days' written notice to end a week-to-week tenancy, thirty days' to end a month-to-month.

THE TENANT'S WRITTEN NOTICES, WHICH ARE YOUR DEFENCE. Section 76-1425(1) and section 76-1427(1) both require the tenant to give written notice specifying the breach before any remedy arises, and section 76-1427(3) says so expressly: "[t]he rights under this section do not arise until the tenant has given written notice to the landlord". A tenant who complains by phone and withholds rent has not started the clock.

AND THE EXCEPTION THAT MATTERS MOST TO YOU. Section 76-1419(1)(a) and (1)(b) - your two central habitability duties - are triggered "after WRITTEN OR ACTUAL NOTICE". Not written notice. Actual notice. So the one place a landlord would most like a writing requirement is the one place the Act does not give one: if your on-site manager sees the leak, you are on notice.

WHAT "WRITTEN" MEANS NOW, AND THIS CHANGED IN 2025. Section 76-1410(18), added by Laws 2025, LB185, section 1: "Writing or written, when used in reference to a notice or document to be provided by or to a landlord or tenant, INCLUDES A NOTICE OR DOCUMENT PROVIDED BY ELECTRONIC MEANS IN ACCORDANCE WITH SECTION 76-1413." So every statutory "written notice" above can now be satisfied electronically - but only on section 76-1413's terms, and they are not light. Section 76-1413(7) requires the tenant's affirmative, un-withdrawn consent, preceded by a clear and conspicuous statement of the right to withdraw "at any time without the imposition of any conditions or consequences", of which notices the consent covers, of the right to a paper copy by mail, of how to withdraw or update an address, and of the hardware and software needed - with the consent itself given or confirmed electronically "in a manner that reasonably demonstrates that the tenant can access information in the electronic form that will be used". Section 76-1413(6) makes compliant electronic delivery equivalent to first-class, registered or certified mail, "except that [i]n any instance in which proof of receipt is required for a mailing, the electronic delivery method used shall provide for verification or acknowledgment of receipt". Section 76-1413(11)(b)(i) adds the fallback: if verification is not obtained the notice must go by mail, and "[i]f two or more electronic communications to the tenant are returned as undeliverable during a thirty-day period, all future communications shall be sent to the tenant by first-class or other mail". Section 76-1413(15) requires another method where you "ha[ve] a reasonable basis for believing that the notice or document has not been received" or learn the address is no longer valid. Section 76-1413(12) makes a withdrawal effective "within a reasonable period of time after receipt" and lets the tenant treat your failure to re-paper a hardware or software change as a withdrawal.

THREE THINGS SECTION 76-1413 DOES NOT DO. (1) IT DOES NOT LET YOU MAKE ELECTRONIC DELIVERY A CONDITION OF THE LEASE. Subsection (9): "A landlord shall not, as part of a rental agreement or as a condition of entering into or renewing a rental agreement, require a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means." A clause that designates e-mail or text as THE method of notice is prohibited outright - this is not a waiver question, it is a flat bar. (2) IT DOES NOT CHANGE WHAT A NOTICE MUST SAY OR WHEN. Subsection (10): "This section does not affect any requirement related to the content or timing of any notice or document required under applicable law." (3) IT DOES NOT SUPERSEDE FEDERAL LAW - subsection (16) preserves the federal E-SIGN Act, 15 U.S.C. 7001 et seq., "as such act existed on January 1, 2025".

TWO TRANSITIONAL RULES, BOTH EASY TO MISS. Section 76-1413(13): the LB185 changes "do not apply to a notice or document delivered by electronic means BEFORE SEPTEMBER 3, 2025, to a tenant or landlord who, before such date, consented". Section 76-1413(14): where a consent predating September 3, 2025 is on file and you now want to send ADDITIONAL types of document electronically, you must first give the tenant a statement describing the new document types and the right to withdraw consent.

WHERE YOU RECEIVE NOTICE, WHICH IS A LEASE DRAFTING POINT RATHER THAN A DUTY. Section 76-1413(2)(b) says you receive a notice when it "comes to [your] attention" or is "[d]elivered at the place of business of the landlord through which the rental agreement was made or at any place held out by the landlord as the place for receipt of the communication", or delivered by electronic means. So designate a single address in the lease and keep it current - and remember that section 76-1417(2) requires the disclosure information to be "kept current" and makes section 76-1417 enforceable "against any successor landlord, owner, or manager", with section 76-1417(3) turning a non-complier into an agent of each landlord for service of process and for performing the landlord's obligations.

TWO VOCABULARY WARNINGS. The URLTA does NOT use the phrases "notice to quit" or "notice to vacate" - each appears once in the twelve statute chapters that govern a Nebraska tenancy and neither in the Act - so a lease or form built on either phrase is built on words Nebraska's statute does not use. And a lease term by which the tenant "[a]grees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under" the Act is unenforceable (section 76-1415(1)(a) and (2)), so a term waiving the written notices the Act requires you to give the tenant will not hold; if you deliberately use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees (section 76-1415(2)). Section 76-1415 does not address a term waiving the tenant's own written-notice duties under sections 76-1425 and 76-1427.

Section 76-1413(5) routes electronic notices through the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (§§ 86-612 and following). Court rules and forms for the possession action under §§ 76-1440 to 76-1447 prescribe their own documents.

title: No Nebraska Carpet-Cleaning Rule - and No Carpet Age Table Either
bodyText:
Nebraska has no carpet statute at all. Nothing in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and nothing anywhere else in the landlord-tenant law, mentions carpet, carpeting or floor coverings; there is no rule permitting a mandatory professional-cleaning clause and no rule forbidding one, no precondition like Alaska's (where the charge is allowed only if the carpets were professionally cleaned before the tenancy began), and no depreciation table like Colorado's ten-year carpet rule limiting what you may deduct by the carpet's age and condition. That cuts both ways, and the second half is the half landlords forget.

WHAT YOU HAVE INSTEAD IS A CLEANLINESS STANDARD, NOT A CARPET RULE. Section 76-1421(2) requires the tenant to 'keep that part of the premises that he occupies and uses as clean and safe as the condition of the premises permit, and upon termination of the tenancy place the dwelling unit in as clean condition, excepting ordinary wear and tear, as when the tenancy commenced.' That is a comparison between two states of the same unit, so your move-in record is the whole case: dated photographs, a cleaning invoice if you had the carpets done, a signed condition sheet. Nebraska imposes no move-in inventory requirement, so nobody will make you create that record - and nobody will excuse you for not having it either.

Section 76-1416(2) then lets you apply the deposit to 'the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or section 76-1421', with the balance and a written itemization delivered or mailed within fourteen days of termination; miss that and section 76-1416(3) gives the tenant the money plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and a willful bad-faith failure adds one month's periodic rent or twice the deposit, whichever is less.

THE TRAP: 'ORDINARY WEAR AND TEAR' IS UNDEFINED. Section 76-1421(2) carves it out and the Act never says what it is. Normal traffic patterns, fading and flattened pile over a few years' use are the obvious candidates; pet urine, burns, stains, grease and unremoved filth are not. Because the line is undefined, the only safe position is documentary: charge the cost you actually paid, keep the invoice, and tie it to a specific condition rather than to a policy.

A flat nonrefundable cleaning fee is a bad idea in Nebraska for a separate reason - section 76-1416(1) limits security 'however denominated' to one month's periodic rent, with a pet deposit of up to one-fourth more, so a fee collected up front and not refunded is at risk of being counted against that ceiling.

WHAT YOU MAY PUT IN THE LEASE. Section 76-1414(1) lets the parties 'include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by' the Act, so a professional-cleaning clause is lawful here. The library offers one: Professional Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out, now tagged for Nebraska. Use it only if the carpets really were professionally cleaned immediately before the tenancy, because that recital is what makes the charge a restoration of the move-in condition rather than a charge for ordinary wear - which is the one thing section 76-1421(2) will not let you recover.

SIBLING-ACT CHECK, because it shows this silence is a choice: Nebraska's Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act has its own deposit section, section 76-1485, which lets the landlord withhold only amounts reasonable 'to restore the mobile home space to its condition at the commencement of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted' and then, in subsection (2), expressly puts the burden of proving the reason for withholding on the landlord by a preponderance of the evidence. The Legislature wrote that burden clause for mobile homes and did not write it into section 76-1416 - but if your deduction reaches court you will be the one proving it either way.

title: In a Nebraska City With an Air-Conditioning Board, Doing Your Own HVAC Work on a Rental Is a Misdemeanor
bodyText: This one catches hands-on landlords and no Nebraska row in the library mentions it. Secs. 18-2301 to 18-2315 let any Nebraska city or village set up an "air conditioning air distribution board" that issues certificates of competency. Where a city or village has one, Sec. 18-2312 makes it "unlawful for any person to engage in business as an air conditioning air distribution contractor or to engage in the business of installing, altering, repairing, cleaning, adding to, or changing in any manner any air conditioning air distribution system or any furnace, any restaurant appliance hood or its duct system, or any other exhaust or intake ventilating system" in that city or village — or, for a metropolitan-class city, within its extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction — "unless such person holds a certificate or is employed by a person, firm, or corporation holding such a certificate." Sec. 18-2315 makes a violation a misdemeanor: a fine of up to five hundred dollars, up to six months' imprisonment, or both, and the person's license may be revoked. THE EXEMPTION DOES NOT COVER A LANDLORD. Sec. 18-2308's only carve-out is for "a homeowner from personally performing air conditioning air distribution work on the property in which the homeowner resides" — and even then the work "must conform to the rules and regulations set forth by the city council or village board of trustees." A rental you own but do not live in is not property in which you reside, so the homeowner exemption is unavailable for it. Two more teeth. Sec. 18-2306 requires that "All plans and specifications for any such system to be placed in a building shall be first submitted to the board or other body designated by the city council" before installation. And Sec. 18-2314 lets the city employ inspectors to inspect any such system under construction, alteration or repair, and a system found not to comply must be REMOVED if not corrected after notice to "the owner or contractor or certificate holder doing the work" — the owner is named, so the removal notice comes to you. What to do: before you or a handyman touch a furnace, duct, exhaust hood or ventilating system at a rental, find out whether the city or village (or, in Omaha's extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction, the metropolitan-class city) has an air-conditioning air-distribution board, and use a certificate holder or an employee of one. Note the breadth of the definition: Sec. 18-2301(1) defines "air conditioning air distribution" as "the control of any one or more of the following factors affecting both physical and chemical conditions of the atmosphere within a structure: Temperature, humidity, movement and purity," and Sec. 18-2301(4) defines a "ventilating system" as "each process of removing air by natural gravity exhauster or mechanical exhaust fan from any space" — which on its face reaches a bathroom exhaust fan. Sec. 18-2312's operative words, though, are "any air conditioning air distribution SYSTEM," so swapping a plug-in window unit is very likely outside it while replacing a furnace plainly is not. Where the work is near that line, use a certificate holder.

title: A Pet Left Behind After the Writ Makes You Its Custodian — and That Is a Criminal Statute, Not a Lease Problem
bodyText: Nebraska's landlord-tenant act says nothing about an animal left in a unit, and the Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act is no help either: its definition of "personal property" is "movable property not affixed to land," illustrated by "goods, wares, merchandise, motor vehicles, mobile homes, watercraft, household items, and furnishings" (Sec. 69-2302(6)) — a notice-and-public-sale machine that cannot sensibly be run on a living dog. The duty comes from the criminal code instead, and it attaches to you by definition the moment you have the premises. Sec. 28-1008(9): "Owner or custodian means any person owning, keeping, possessing, harboring, or knowingly permitting an animal to remain on or about any premises owned or occupied by such person." A landlord who has had possession restored and knows an animal is in the unit is knowingly permitting it to remain on premises the landlord owns. That makes you a custodian, and a custodian owes the Sec. 28-1008(5) duty: "cruelly neglect" means "to fail to provide any animal in one's care, whether as owner or custodian, with food, water, or other care as is reasonably necessary for the animal's health." Sec. 28-1008(1) defines "abandon" as "to leave any animal in one's care, whether as owner or custodian, for any length of time without making effective provision for its food, water, or other care as is reasonably necessary for the animal's health" — note "for any length of time." The penalty is not small. Sec. 28-1009(1): a person who intentionally, knowingly or recklessly abandons or cruelly neglects an animal commits a Class I misdemeanor, "unless the abandonment or cruel neglect results in serious injury or illness or death of the animal, in which case it is a Class IV felony," and Sec. 28-1009(4) exposes a person convicted of the misdemeanor to Sec. 28-1019's order not to own, possess or reside with any animal. There is no landlord exception, no safe-harbour period and no notice-and-wait provision anywhere in Secs. 28-1008 to 28-1020. WHAT TO DO, in order. Treat the animal as the first item on the set-out, not the last. Call your city or county animal control, or the sheriff: Sec. 28-1012(1) and (2) give a law enforcement officer or animal control officer who has reason to believe an animal has been abandoned or is being cruelly neglected the power to seek a warrant to enter, inspect, care for or impound it, and make prompt investigation a duty; Sec. 28-1012(3) makes an animal involved in a Sec. 28-1009 violation subject to seizure with distribution or disposition under Sec. 28-1012.01 as the court directs. Getting the animal into official custody is both the humane course and the thing that ends your custodianship. Until someone takes it, provide food and water. Document the time you discovered the animal, who you called and when. Do NOT put the animal out, and do not simply lock the unit and leave. Two notes on the lease. You can require in your pet addendum that the tenant remove the animal on vacating and that you may remove a pet in the circumstances the Pet Policy clause already describes; what you cannot do is contract out of Sec. 28-1008 and Sec. 28-1009, because they bind "any person" and a lease cannot licence a crime. And Sec. 28-1017's mandatory-reporting duty does not reach you — it applies to employees of governmental agencies dealing with child or adult protective services, animal control, or animal abuse — so reporting is your protection, not your obligation.

title: Your Repair Duty Starts on Notice - and "Actual" Notice Counts, Whatever the Lease Says
bodyText:
Nebraska wrote a notice precondition into its habitability duty that the uniform act does not have, and it cuts both ways. § 76-1419(1) requires you to "(a) Substantially comply, AFTER WRITTEN OR ACTUAL NOTICE, with the requirements of the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety" and to "(b) Make all repairs and do whatever is necessary, AFTER WRITTEN OR ACTUAL NOTICE, to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition".

IN YOUR FAVOUR: for those two duties the clock does not start until you have notice, so a condition nobody told you about and that you did not know about is not yet a breach of (1)(a) or (1)(b).

AGAINST YOU, and this is the part lease language cannot fix: the statute says "written OR ACTUAL" notice, so your own knowledge counts. A manager who sees the problem, a maintenance visit that reveals it, a phone call, a neighbour's complaint, a photograph in a group text - any of those can be actual notice, and a lease clause requiring repair requests in writing does not make writing the only route. A term purporting to make it the only route is an agreement by the tenant to "waive or to forego rights or remedies" under the Act and is unenforceable, with actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees against you if you deliberately use a rental agreement containing a provision you know is prohibited (§ 76-1415(1)(a), (2)).

FOUR LIMITS ON THE PRECONDITION, so you do not over-read it.
- (1) It is attached only to (1)(a) and (1)(b). Subdivisions (1)(c) to (1)(f) - common areas clean and safe, maintaining the systems and appliances you supply or are required to supply, waste receptacles and removal, running water and reasonable hot water and heat - carry no notice qualifier at all, so those duties are continuous.
- (2) It does not postpone the duty to conditions arising after the term begins; the duties "to 'put and keep' the premises in a fit and habitable condition are not limited under the plain language to conditions arising after commencement of the lease term" (annotation to § 76-1419, Vasquez v. CHI Properties, 302 Neb. 742, 925 N.W.2d 304 (2019)).
- (3) The tenant's remedies have their own, separate notice requirements, which are stricter: § 76-1425(1) needs a written notice specifying the acts and omissions and the termination date, and § 76-1427(3) says the essential-services rights "do not arise until the tenant has given WRITTEN notice to the landlord". So an oral complaint can start your duty without yet unlocking the tenant's self-help.
- (4) § 76-1419(1)'s closing sentence caps the whole section where a local minimum housing code applies, and its last line reserves tort law: "[t]he obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state" - so a notice analysis under the Act does not answer a negligence claim.
