PRACTICAL UPSHOT: date every report you receive by any route, including the ones that arrive by phone or in person, and log what your own staff saw. The record you want is not "the tenant never put it in writing" - that argument does not work in Nebraska - it is "here is when we learned of it and here is what we did".

title: Broadband in an Existing Electric Easement on Your Land: Ninety Days to Claim Compensation, Then Two Years, Then Nothing
bodyText:
THIS IS NOT A TENANT TOPIC. It is an owner topic with a hard deadline, and it is in this delta because it was found while canvassing telecom law and because no Nebraska row in the library cites any of its sections. If an electric utility easement crosses your rental property — and on a great many Nebraska lots one does — a broadband company can be put inside that easement without your agreement, and your right to be paid for it expires on a clock the utility starts.

THE MECHANISM. Section 86-5,105(1) lets "[a]n electric utility and a commercial broadband supplier ... enter into a broadband facility agreement for the use of an electric utility easement or electric utility infrastructure, or both", to install, maintain or own an attached facility for broadband service, and to lease out excess capacity. Section 86-5,105(2)(a) then requires the agreement to contain one of three statements about the easement: that the utility "has the legal right to authorize the use"; that the broadband supplier "has compensated property owners"; or — the one that should concern you — "that the electric utility HAS GIVEN NOTICE to property owners pursuant to subdivision (2)(b) of this section AND THE TIME FOR MAKING A CLAIM HAS EXPIRED."

THE NOTICE, AND WHERE IT WILL ARRIVE. Section 86-5,105(2)(b) requires the notice to be "sent by CERTIFIED MAIL from or on behalf of the electric utility to the property owner" at BOTH "[t]he last-known address for the property owner based on the electric utility's records" AND "[t]he address listed for the property owner in the records of the office of the county assessor". It must name a point of contact for the utility and for any designated broadband supplier, give "[t]he recording number, if any, of the electric utility easement or recorded memorandum", reference the Broadband Internet Service Infrastructure Act, state "that the electric utility intends to enter into a broadband facility agreement, WITHIN NINETY DAYS after the notice is delivered", give "an estimated time for the start of installation or construction", and "[i]nclude a statement regarding the statute of limitations for the property owner to file a claim". IF YOU HOLD RENTALS THROUGH AN ENTITY, OR YOUR ASSESSOR ADDRESS IS A MANAGEMENT OFFICE OR AN OLD ONE, THIS IS THE LETTER THAT GETS FILED AND FORGOTTEN. Fix the assessor address.

THE NINETY-DAY WINDOW. Section 86-5,105(5): "If, WITHIN NINETY DAYS after a notice pursuant to this section is sent by an electric utility or a designated commercial broadband supplier acting on the electric utility's behalf, a property owner submits a WRITTEN CLAIM FOR COMPENSATION relating to the use of an electric utility easement in connection with a broadband facility agreement, then the commercial broadband supplier, through communications handled by the electric utility, SHALL BE RESPONSIBLE FOR THE PAYMENT of compensation to the property owner for such claim, and the electric utility shall cooperate with the commercial broadband supplier in connection with the resolution of the claim." So a timely written claim puts the payment obligation squarely on the broadband supplier. Note the trigger word: ninety days after the notice is SENT, not after you read it.

AND THE TWO-YEAR BACKSTOP. Section 86-5,106(1)(a): "No cause of action against an electric utility or a commercial broadband supplier concerning the use of an electric utility easement for commercial broadband facilities pursuant to a broadband facility agreement may be brought by or on behalf of a property owner MORE THAN TWO YEARS after the later of: (i) November 14, 2020; or (ii) The date of mailing of notice ... pursuant to subsection (5) of section 86-5,105." THREE CARVE-OUTS SURVIVE THAT CUT-OFF, and they are the claims worth preserving: subdivision (1)(b) says it "does not apply to a cause of action based on: (i) PHYSICAL DAMAGE TO PROPERTY; (ii) INJURY TO NATURAL PERSONS; or (iii) BREACH OF THE TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF A WRITTEN ELECTRIC EASEMENT as the terms and conditions apply in accordance with subsection (3) of section 86-5,105." And subdivision (1)(c) adds that nothing in the section "extends the statute of limitations applicable to a claim or revives an expired claim" — so the two years is a ceiling, not a floor.

WHY YOUR OWN EASEMENT DOCUMENT IS THE MOST VALUABLE PAPER YOU HAVE HERE. Section 86-5,105(3): "The terms and conditions of a WRITTEN electric utility easement APPLY to the use of the electric utility easement for commercial broadband facilities pursuant to a broadband facility agreement. A PROHIBITION ON ABOVEGROUND electric utility infrastructure contained within a written electric utility easement CONSTITUTES A PROHIBITION ON ABOVEGROUND ATTACHED FACILITIES. An electric utility or its designated commercial broadband supplier shall comply with any NOTICE REQUIREMENTS CONTAINED IN A WRITTEN electric utility easement ... relating to entering the real property ... or commencing any construction or installation." So if your recorded easement says underground only, aboveground broadband is barred; and if it requires notice before entry, that requirement binds the broadband supplier too — and breach of those written terms is one of the three claims that outlive the two-year cut-off. Pull the recorded easement before you respond to any notice.

BUT READ SUBSECTION (4), WHICH IS THE PART THAT RUNS AGAINST YOU. Section 86-5,105(4): "Nothing in this section requires an electric utility to comply with subdivision (2)(b) of this section in order to take any action or exercise any rights under an electric utility easement that is ALREADY PERMITTED WITHIN THE SCOPE of the electric utility easement. AN ELECTRIC UTILITY EASEMENT SHALL BE LIBERALLY CONSTRUED IN FAVOR OF ITS USE FOR COMMERCIAL BROADBAND FACILITIES pursuant to a broadband facility agreement." Two consequences. If the utility takes the view that broadband is already within the easement's scope, you may get NO notice at all and no ninety-day window. And the interpretive thumb is on the scale against you by statute.

ONE EXCLUSION. Section 86-5,105(7): the section "shall not apply to railroad right-of-way or electric utility easements in or to railroad right-of-way property", crossings of which are governed by section 86-164.

PRACTICAL COURSE. (1) Make sure the owner address in the COUNTY ASSESSOR's records is an address you actually read, for every property you hold. The statute requires notice to that address, and a notice sent there is effective whether or not it reaches you. (2) Treat any certified letter mentioning the Broadband Internet Service Infrastructure Act as a ninety-day clock. Calendar it the day it arrives. (3) Pull the recorded easement or memorandum — section 86-5,105(2)(b)(iii) requires the notice to give you its recording number — and check it for an underground-only restriction and for any entry-notice requirement, because those written terms bind the broadband supplier under subsection (3) and a breach of them survives the two-year cut-off under section 86-5,106(1)(b)(iii). (4) Submit any compensation claim IN WRITING inside the ninety days, however provisional; section 86-5,105(5) makes a timely written claim the broadband supplier's payment obligation. (5) Preserve physical-damage and personal-injury claims separately; they are not caught by the cut-off. (6) None of this is a lease matter and none of it should go in a lease. It belongs in your property file alongside the title work.

title: Applicant and Tenant Data - Nebraska's Data-Security Act Reaches You, Including Your Vendor Contracts
bodyText: Nebraska's Financial Data Protection and Consumer Notification of Data Security Breach Act of 2006 (sections 87-801 to 87-808) applies to 'an individual or a commercial entity that conducts business in Nebraska' - the word 'individual' means a sole-owner landlord is inside it, and there is no small-landlord exemption. Rental applications are exactly what the Act is about: section 87-802(5)(a) defines personal information as a Nebraska resident's name or first initial and last name together with any of a social security number, a driver's licence or state ID number, an account or credit or debit card number with its security code or password, a unique electronic identification number or routing code with its password, or unique biometric data; section 87-802(5)(b) adds a user name or email address with a password or security question and answer that permits access to an online account. Three duties follow. (1) SECURITY. Section 87-808(1): if you own, license or maintain computerized data that includes personal information about a Nebraska resident you 'shall implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices that are appropriate to the nature and sensitivity of the personal information' and to the nature, size and resources of your business, 'including safeguards that protect the personal information when the individual or commercial entity disposes of the personal information' - so destroying old applications matters as much as storing them. (2) VENDOR CONTRACTS, the duty most often missed. Section 87-808(2)(a): if you disclose that data to a nonaffiliated third-party service provider - a screening company, a payment processor, a portal vendor, an off-site manager, a collection agency - you 'shall require by contract' that the provider implement and maintain reasonable security procedures appropriate to the information and reasonably designed to protect it. Section 87-808(2)(b) grandfathers contracts entered into before July 19, 2018 but requires any such contract renewed on or after that date to comply, so the duty arrives on renewal. (3) BREACH NOTICE. Section 87-803(1): on becoming aware of a breach of the security of the system you must conduct in good faith a reasonable and prompt investigation, and if unauthorized use has occurred or is reasonably likely, give notice to the affected Nebraska resident as soon as possible and without unreasonable delay; section 87-803(2) requires notice to the Attorney General no later than the time the resident is notified; section 87-803(3) adds a notify-and-cooperate duty where you merely maintain data you do not own. CONSEQUENCES AND ONE LIMIT. Section 87-805: any waiver of the Act 'is contrary to public policy and is void and unenforceable' - so no lease term and no application form can contract out of it. Section 87-806(1) lets the Attorney General subpoena and recover direct economic damages for each affected Nebraska resident injured by a section 87-803 violation. Section 87-806(2) makes a section 87-808 violation a violation of section 59-1602 under the Consumer Protection Act - and expressly provides that it 'does not give rise to a private cause of action', so the security and vendor-contract duties are enforced by the Attorney General, not by tenants. Safe harbour: section 87-808(3) treats compliance with a state or federal law giving greater protection, or with the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act Title V regulations or HIPAA as they existed on January 1, 2018, as compliance with subsections (1) and (2).

title: In a First-Class City the Council Must Tell You When Your Tenant's Water Bill Is 60 Days Late - and What You Do Next Is the Hard Part
bodyText:
THERE IS ONE PLACE IN NEBRASKA LAW WHERE A LANDLORD IS AUTOMATICALLY TOLD ABOUT A TENANT'S UTILITY DELINQUENCY, AND IT IS NOT IN THE LANDLORD-TENANT ACT. Section 16-682, which applies to cities of the FIRST CLASS, does four things in sequence. (1) "With respect to water rates, taxes, or rents only", those charges, "when delinquent", are a lien upon the premises - so gas, power, light and heat are expressly OUTSIDE the lien, and the lien bites only on delinquency. (2) Delinquent water rentals unpaid three months may by resolution be assessed against the real estate as a special assessment, certified by the city clerk to the county clerk and put on the tax rolls, "subject to the same penalties and to be collected in like manner as other city taxes." (3) "The city council SHALL NOTIFY IN WRITING NONOCCUPYING OWNERS of premises or their agents whenever their tenants or lessees are SIXTY DAYS DELINQUENT in the payment of water rent." That is a duty on the city, owed to you. (4) Thereafter, if the owner or the owner's agent in the city "shall notify the city council in writing to discontinue water service", the water department officer must promptly do so, "and rentals for any water furnished to the occupants of such real estate IN VIOLATION OF SUCH NOTICE SHALL NOT BE A LIEN THEREON."

SO THE SIXTY-DAY LETTER IS A DEADLINE YOU CAN ACTUALLY ACT ON. Act on it and the lien is capped at what has already accrued. Ignore it and it keeps growing against your title. Nobody will send you a second one.

BUT STEP (4) IS NOT SAFE TO USE WHILE SOMEONE IS LIVING THERE. Section 76-1419(1)(f) makes it the landlord's own duty to "[s]upply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times", and section 76-1419(3) cannot shift that duty at all for any unit that is not a single-family residence. Section 76-1430 then provides that a landlord who "willfully and wrongfully diminishes services to the tenant by interrupting or CAUSING THE INTERRUPTION OF electric, gas, water or other essential service" is liable: the tenant may recover possession or terminate, and in either case recover "an amount equal to three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages, and a reasonable attorney's fee". That figure is a FIXED sum, not a ceiling and not a cap on proven loss - the tenant does not have to prove what the lost water was worth. Section 16-682(4)'s words are "notify the city council in writing to discontinue water service", which is as literal a case of "causing the interruption" as the Act describes. TWO READINGS ARE OPEN AND THE TEXT CANNOT SETTLE THEM. On one reading, an owner exercising an express statutory right conferred by section 16-682 is not acting "wrongfully" within section 76-1430, and section 76-1403 (other law supplements the Act "[u]nless displaced by the provisions of" the Act) leaves room for the municipal statute to operate. On the other, section 76-1419(1)(f) is a duty the Act imposes on the landlord personally and section 76-1430's "causing the interruption" was drafted precisely to catch indirect routes, so the statutory permission to ask the city to stop supplying does not license a breach of the landlord's own supply duty. A THIRD STATUTE NOW LEANS ON THE SECOND READING, and it is worth knowing which way the weight falls even though it does not settle the question. Nebraska's utility disconnection article contains its own list of when the article's protections step aside, and section 70-1615 confines it to "any disconnections or interruptions of services made necessary BY THE UTILITY for reasons of repair or maintenance or to protect the health or safety of the domestic subscriber or of the general public." Those are the utility's own grounds. The Legislature wrote out the permitted interruptions in that article and a landlord-requested one is not among them - so nothing outside section 16-682 itself treats an owner-requested shutoff as a recognised category. Whether a court would harmonise section 16-682 with sections 76-1419 and 76-1430 is for the courts, so the question stays open and the cautious course below stands.

THE CAUTIOUS COURSE, WHICH DOES NOT REQUIRE RESOLVING THAT. Treat the sixty-day letter as an early-warning system, not as a shutoff trigger. On receiving it: (a) pay the delinquency yourself if the exposure is worse than the arrears, and recover it from the tenant - under section 76-1410(13) "[r]ent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement", so if your lease makes municipal utility accounts the tenant's obligation, what you advance is recoverable as rent and reachable by the section 76-1431(2) seven-day nonpayment notice; (a-bis) get the warning the lawful way - section 70-1607 requires each covered utility to "establish a third-party notice procedure for the notification of a designated third party of any proposed discontinuance of service", so ask the tenant to designate you on the tenant's own account instead of relying on a city letter you may only get at sixty days; (b) terminate for nonpayment and recover possession through the court under sections 76-1440 to 76-1447 rather than through the water department; and (c) use step (4) only once the unit is genuinely vacant, where there is no tenant whose services could be diminished.

WHERE THIS DOES AND DOES NOT APPLY. Section 16-682 is a cities-of-the-first-class provision. Second-class cities and villages have a water lien under section 17-538 with no sixty-day notice and no discontinuance route. Sewer is different everywhere and worse: under section 18-509(1), in "any city or village", sewer charges "shall be charged to each property served by the sewerage system, shall be a lien upon the property served, and may be collected either from the owner or the person, firm, or corporation requesting the service" - no delinquency precondition, no owner notice, no escape. And the printed annotation to section 18-503 reports that an "[o]rdinance authorizing water supply to be shut off for nonpayment of delinquent sewer charges is not in conflict with this section" (Michelson v. City of Grand Island, 154 Neb. 654, 48 N.W.2d 769 (1951)) - so in a city with such an ordinance your tenant's unpaid SEWER bill can end your WATER service, which puts you in breach of section 76-1419(1)(f) through no act of your own. Check the ordinance.

Section 17-925.01 adds that in second-class cities and villages "[a]ll sewer charges shall be a lien upon the premises or real estate for which the same is used or supplied". Omaha's water is supplied by the Metropolitan Utilities District under chapter 14, article 21. Municipal ordinances are where the shutoff power actually sits.

title: Turning the Service Back On, or Letting a Tenant's Bypass Sit There, Is a Crime in Nebraska - and the Presumption Runs Against Whoever Possesses the Premises
bodyText:
THERE IS A CRIMINAL STATUTE HERE, NOT ONLY A CIVIL ONE, AND IT HAS NONE OF THE CIVIL STATUTE'S GATES. Nebraska's civil diversion provisions (sections 25-21,275 to 25-21,278) give a utility a damages action, but only "when such act results in damages to the utility" and, for the actual-damages and $750 measures, only "upon proof of willful or intentional" conduct. Section 28-515.02 is the criminal counterpart and it carries neither gate. It makes four things unlawful for "any person":

(a) connecting any instrument, device or contrivance to a wire supplying electricity, or any pipe or conduit supplying gas or water, "WITHOUT THE KNOWLEDGE AND CONSENT OF THE SUPPLIER", in such a manner that any portion may be supplied "without passing through the meter made or provided for measuring or registering" it;

(b) "To KNOWINGLY USE OR KNOWINGLY PERMIT THE USE of electricity, electric current, gas, or water obtained unlawfully pursuant to this section";

(c) "To RECONNECT electrical, gas, or water service without the knowledge and consent of the supplier of such service if the service has been disconnected pursuant to sections 70-1601 to 70-1615"; and

(d) willfully injuring, altering, or "by any instrument, device, or contrivance in any manner interfer[ing] with or obstruct[ing] the action or operation of any meter", again without the supplier's knowledge and consent.

A violation is a CLASS III MISDEMEANOR (subsection (3)).

THE EVIDENTIARY SENTENCE IS THE ONE TO WORRY ABOUT. Subsection (2): "Proof of the existence of any wire, pipe, or conduit connection or reconnection or of any injury, alteration, interference, or obstruction of a meter is PRIMA FACIE EVIDENCE OF THE GUILT OF THE PERSON IN POSSESSION OF THE PREMISES where such connection, reconnection, injury, alteration, interference, or obstruction is proved to exist." Read that against who possesses what. A tenant is "entitled under a rental agreement to occupy a dwelling unit TO THE EXCLUSION OF OTHERS" (section 76-1410(17)), so inside the unit the presumption points at the tenant. But a master meter, a meter bank, a service entrance and a mechanical room are not in any tenant's dwelling unit - they are in the common areas and plant that YOU possess and that section 76-1419(1)(c) makes you keep "in a clean and safe condition". So in a master-metered or submetered building, the presumption for anything found at the meters points at the landlord.

THREE SITUATIONS WHERE THIS LANDS ON A LANDLORD. (1) RESTORING SERVICE AFTER A SHUTOFF. Subdivision (1)(c) is the whole provision in one line: if the supplier disconnected under sections 70-1601 to 70-1615 and you turn it back on - to show the unit, to finish a repair, to stop pipes freezing, or because a tenant is without water - you have committed a Class III misdemeanor unless the supplier knows and consents. There is no emergency exception, no landlord exception and no "it was my own building" exception in the section. Call the supplier and get the consent; reconnection is theirs to do. (2) A TENANT'S BYPASS YOU KNOW ABOUT. Subdivision (1)(b) catches whoever "knowingly PERMIT[S] the use" of unlawfully obtained service. If you learn a tenant has jumped a meter, doing nothing is the offence - the same shape as section 28-417(1)(e)'s "knows or should know" exposure for a dwelling resorted to for controlled substances, and like that section it has no landlord safe harbour. Act on it: section 76-1431(1) is the route for a material noncompliance, and section 76-1421(6) already forbids the tenant to "deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises". (3) INSTALLING YOUR OWN SUBMETER. A submeter sitting DOWNSTREAM of the supplier's revenue meter does not put anything past that meter, so subdivision (1)(a) is not engaged on its face. But subdivision (1)(d) is wider than bypassing - it reaches interfering with or obstructing "the action or operation of any meter" - and the civil side defines "unauthorized metering" to include "removing, moving, installing, connecting, reconnecting, or disconnecting any meter or metering device for utility service by a person other than an authorized employee or agent of such utility" (section 25-21,275(5)). The cautious course, which costs one letter: get the supplier's WRITTEN knowledge and consent before any work at or upstream of the revenue meter, have the work done by the utility or a licensed electrician, and leave the revenue meter untouched.

THE ARTICLE (1)(c) DEPENDS ON does not help you. Section 70-1605 sets the seven-day notice a utility must give a domestic subscriber before discontinuing water, natural gas or electricity for nonpayment, with holidays and weekends excluded and any discontinuance or reconnection fee capped at "the reasonable costs of providing such service". Section 70-1602 excludes "businesses of any nature" from "domestic subscriber", so none of that attaches to an account in your company's name. Section 70-1615 steps the article aside only for interruptions "made necessary by the utility for reasons of repair or maintenance or to protect the health or safety" - so a landlord-requested interruption is nowhere authorised. And section 70-1607 requires every covered utility to establish a third-party notice procedure, which is how to learn of a pending shutoff instead of discovering it and reaching for the valve. Section 28-909 (falsifying records of a public utility, Class I misdemeanor) does not reach a landlord - it is addressed to records "of a public utility operating in the State of Nebraska" affecting its investment, rate of return, receipts or expenditures, and to certifications made to a regulatory body.

title: Property You Believe Was Lost Goes to the Police First
bodyText: Nebraska treats property you reasonably believe was lost differently from property a tenant left behind. Lost property is to be handled 'as otherwise provided by law', so offer it first to the police or another government agency. If that agency refuses custody, you may use the abandoned-property procedure under the Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act. If you follow that Act, you aren't liable to the owner (§69-2313). Keep a record of the agency you contacted and its refusal. Don't simply keep it: a person who controls property he or she knows was lost, and fails to take reasonable measures to return it with intent to deprive the owner, commits theft (§28-514(1)).

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Nebraska follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Neb. U.C.C. § 3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Neb. U.C.C. § 1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Nebraska's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the act, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1411). That binds you and the tenant alike. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
